this is the Prajnapathshala Mandal Granthamala Mimamsa Kosa.
The sixth part (bha-va): the compiler.
Brahmabhūta Kevalānanda Sarasvatī;
Kārtika, Kṛṣṇa-pakṣa, 6th day, Saturday; Śaka year 1884. Table of Contents.

Publisher’s Note … … … … Brief Account of the Work, etc., and its Explanation … … … 1–7 Errata … … … … … 9–11 Mīmāṃsākoṣaḥ … … … … 2997–3631 Publisher’s Note: The publication of the fifth volume of the Mīmāṃsākoṣa was completed on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa in the Śaka year 1882, at the forenoon hour, by His Excellency the former President of the Republic of India, Śrī Rājendra Prasād.

We consider it a matter of great fortune for us that even this sixth volume is being brought to the light of publication with great enthusiasm by His Excellency Śrī Rādhākṛṣṇa, the second President of the Republic of India—a man of world-renowned fame, mature wisdom, and a great philosopher deeply versed in both Eastern and Western systems of thought.

The editing of this sixth part, composed by the venerable Guru, was accomplished by Dattātreya Śāstrī, known as Tāmravedi—a disciple of the Guru’s feet, an adherent of the Mīmāṃsā-bhūṣaṇa, devoted to austerity and Vedic study, and a maintainer of the sacred fires (Āhitāgni).
The proofreading and other editorial tasks for this sixth part were performed with meticulous care, as previously done, by Śrī Raṅganātha Śāstrī, the executive editor of the Dharmakośa.
The venerable Guru himself placed his trust in Śrī Raṅganātha Śāstrī regarding his capacity to carry out such work.
To avoid the faults of deficiency or excess, the Gurus have also engaged in repeated deliberations with him.

It is our long-standing experience that Śrī Raṅganātha Śāstrin’s mind finds complete satisfaction only upon the perfection of a work’s literary merits; placing our trust in him, we are also conducting the work on the *Dharmakośa*.

The number of topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth for this sixth part: there are 81 *bhāṣya* topical sections, 41 *saṃkarṣa* topical sections, 100 topical sections from the *Kevalānandī* commentary, 19 *tautātita* topical sections, 184 logical principles (*nyāya*), and 4,634 minor conclusions (*laghusiddhānta*).

[Sāhasī, 175. By the word *bhāmā*, Satyabhāmā is denoted. [Su., p. 699:
"Just as whatever burden is to be carried by someone must first be understood..."

In the same way, it is impossible to determine the agent by asking, "Who shall carry that burden? For the burden that is to be carried by someone must first be understood as an object [prior to the action].
At that time... [the agent is determined].
This is the reading in the *Vārttika* (on Pāṇini 1.3.12, p. 651).

Although in common usage one may speak of determining the weight for a carrier by saying, "This man is a carrier; what is his load?", nevertheless, even in common usage, such a determination of the load for a carrier must be understood as occurring only after having ascertained his capacity to carry—such as, "This man has previously carried this much, and he is now capable of carrying this much. Thus, the determination of the load for a carrier is predicated upon the prior ascertainment of the state of being a carrier.
The certainty that "he is capable of carrying this much" depends upon the uncertainty regarding the extent of what is to be carried.

Thus, in common worldly usage, when one analyzes the determination—"This is the carrier; this is his burden"—and investigates the meaning of "he is capable of carrying this much," which is understood as a general substance, it results merely in a specific determination of that substance as "this is its burden. Therefore, even in the world, there is no defining of a burden apart from the carrier.
Soma. 6|1|1, p. 444. Bhāratavarṣa.
The region for the accomplishment of dharma and artha; Bhāratavarṣa of Jambūdvīpa. Su. (Sudhākara).

Having derived the word *bhāva*, he provides the example "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) and "he gives" (*dadāti*). It has been stated [in the Vārttika] that *bhāva* is not merely the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Vā. 3.1.67 (4.2), p. 903: "The verbal root-meaning alone, in its pure form, is designated as *bhāva*."

Su. Pṛ. 547: Regarding the existence [of a substance], when there is a transgression of a deity, the injunction is for the sake of the rite (*ṛtvartha*); in the case of the destruction of the quality of being a prescribed substance, there is an injunction for clarified butter (*ājya*): "Whichever deity one has omitted, one should sacrifice to that deity with clarified butter as a substitute.

Bāla. Pṛ. 20: Regarding the existence [of an action], the injunction is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*): "Having resolved to undertake the *sattra*, one should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*. Pṛ. 20: According to the principle stated in the *Ślokavārttika* (Nirālambana, v. 118), "Non-existence is not something other than another existence," non-existence independent of existence cannot be spoken of.
Su. Pṛ. 510: Existence and non-existence cannot be combined in a single place. Śā. 1.1.5, p. 78:
Words denoting action have existence as their meaning; from them, action is understood, for it is this [action] that is enjoined as the sense [of the injunction].

Regarding the section on the meaning of entities (*bhāvārtha*) from [verse] 3006: "If the meaning of an entity does not exist in its primary form, then at the time of application (*prayoga*), the meaning does not exist"—this is the point of contention. This is the *Kutūhala*.

Regarding this, we shall explain the meaning by proposing the reading: "yeṣāṃ tatpattau sve prayoge na vidyate. In the context of *utpatti*—that is, in originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*) such as "one should sacrifice with Soma"—the phrase "of those words for which there is no perception of form" (*rūpopalabdhiḥ*) is understood to carry over from the preceding sūtra; "form" (*rūpa*) here refers to the denotative capacity (*vācyatva*), and "perception" (*upalabdhi*) means cognition. Thus, the meaning is: "those [words] which perish as soon as they have arisen, and for which there is no cognition of their denotative capacity at the time of their own usage—that is, at the time of their utterance—those words expressing that meaning would be *ākhyātas*, i.e., what is designated by the term *ākhyāta*."
This and so forth is the same for all [words].
Therefore, from those verbal forms (ākhyāta-śabda) such as "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) and the like, the action—the task, namely the *apūrva*—would be cognized; that is, it would be understood.
Those words are the indicators of the *apūrva*.

"Because the application [of the word] is dependent [on it]"—this is another argument stated for the purpose of making known the *apūrva* (the unprecedented). Since the application consists in being employed, and because the meaning [of the root] depends on a single word together with the *bhāvanā*, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) alone is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the *bhāvanā* by virtue of its status as a single-word hearing (*ekapadaśruti*). Therefore, from that very [root-meaning], the action is the *apūrva*.
Without an object,
the agent of the sense of "becoming" (bhū) becomes the object of the verb "to do" (kṛ).
Since the root *kṛ* is invariably transitive (*sakarmaka*), as long as that which is being produced is not obtained, the meaning of the action does not reach its completion.
When all causal factors are designated as agents with respect to their intermediate actions, they arise as objects and so forth in the division of the primary action.
Due to the difference in capacity for each specific action, there occurs a variety of intermediate actions.

In this regard, it is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the agent of the action "to be" (*bhū*) becomes the object (*karman*) of the action "to do" (*kṛ*).
For instance: "That which does not have origination, or that for which origination has become eternal, cannot possess the state of being produced, like a sky-flower or space.
Indeed, only that which is the locus of manifestation (*prapañca*)—or that for which manifestation is possible—is impelled by another; it alone is understood as being produced, and nothing else.
And thus, no one attempts to produce their own flower or the sky.

Even in cases such as "make a foot" (*pādī kuru*), where the use of the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle) appears to denote the object (*karman*), there is no deviation [from the rule], because the word "foot" (*pāda*) is employed with the intention of referring to something whose formation or refinement has not yet been completed.

Furthermore, although the root *kṛ* has many meanings, in all instances—whether in "hinting" (*gandhana*), "scattering" (*avakṣepaṇa*), or the like—it is understood that this [root] shares a commonality with the sense of "production."

Alternatively, since it is observed that at the very moment this [agent] possesses the capacity for production, it simultaneously possesses a common substratum with a specific [action], it follows logically that what is being produced is itself the object (*karman*). By this, the action of "becoming" (*bhūti*) is first established. And thus: "The agent of the sense of 'doing' (*karoti*) is the instigator (*prayojaka*) of the action of 'becoming'."
It will become that which you shall observe; it attains the state of being the "instigated" (*prayojya*).

Because of the difference in power between the roots *bhū* ("to become") and *kṛ* ("to do"), just as in the case of *viklidi* ("to soften") and *pac* ("to cook"), they invariably express the activity of the instigator and the instigated.

In that context, sometimes the activity of the instigated is implied by the power of the expressed object—as in "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), where the activity called "becoming" belonging to the jar (the instigated) is implied by the power of the object denoted by the accusative case. This is the meaning of the verbal root [in such cases].
In response to the doubt as to how there can be an implication (*ākṣepa*) when only the root [the verbal base] is employed, he says: "by itself" (*svayam eva*). The meaning is:

in cases such as *ghaṭo bhavati* ("the pot comes into being"), the agenthood expressed by the nominative case implies the operation of the prompted (*prayojya*), within which [operation] the root resides. Thus, since the other [operation] is understood through implication alone in verbal roots that denote either the operation of the prompted or the prompter (*prayojaka*), there is no occasion to postulate a linguistic function (*śabda-vyāpāra*) for that [operation]; this is the intended sense. Alternatively, when the operation of the prompted is implied by itself, only the operation of the prompter is intended to be expressed, as in *kaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a mat") or *odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice").

Sometimes the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is not expressed, and there is the expression of the operation of the prompted agent (*prayojya*) alone, as in "the pot comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*) or "the rice grains soften" (*viklidyanti taṇḍulāḥ*).
Sometimes both operations are used together in combination, as in "Devadatta makes a mat, and it comes into being" (*karoti kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ sa ca bhavati*).

Sometimes the operation of the prompted agent occurs with the operation of the instigator as a subordinate element, as in the expressions "it is made by Devadatta" (*kriyate devadattena*) or "by itself" (*svayameva*).

Sometimes, when the causal operation (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) is intended to be expressed as having its subordinate action (*pasarganabhūta-prayojya-kriyā*) conveyed by a single word or a part of a word that is not repeated, then—because the roots *kṛ* and *pac* do not occur in their identity with [the subordinate action], and because *bhū* and *vklid* terminate solely in the subordinate action and thus lack the capacity to directly instigate [the agent]—another suffix *ṇic* is employed, either as a denoter (*vācaka*) or as an indicator (*dyotaka*), as in *bhāvayati* and *vikledayati*.
And so it has been said: "They convey the exclusive operation of the instigated agent (*prayojya-kartṛka-ekānta-vyāpāra*)."

Only those [roots] ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*) are employed in the actions of those who instigate others to perform such acts. Nor is it the case that these [causatives] lack capacity; therefore, it cannot be argued that they are incapable.
Or, if others possess the capacity, then these [causatives] must likewise be understood to possess it.
It has been established: "The powers of all entities are by their very nature beyond questioning;
therefore, bases, suffixes, and the like express various meanings."

Thus, by way of the meaning of "doing" (*karoti*), [the *bhāvanā*] is established in all verbal roots (*dhātu*) through the objects to be brought about (*bhāvya*). Therefore, those who know *bhāvanā* call it the "instigating action" (*prayojaka-kriyā*) of a thing that has assumed agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to its results (*bhūti*).

As for what was said—that the *liṅ* and other suffixes do not denote an object other than an injunction—that is incorrect. Why? Because: "The *liṅ* and other suffixes express something else entirely, namely the *abhidhā-bhāvanā* (the efficient force of expression)."
However, another kind of *bhāvanā*, consisting of the object (*artha*), is understood in all verbal forms (*sarvākhyāteṣu*).

For when the *bhāvanā*—which is expressed by the root *kṛ*, which conforms to all verbal suffixes, and which consists in human effort—is apprehended, then its specific features—such as injunction (*vidhi*), prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), the past, the future, and the present—are perceived through specific words distinct from the general verbal suffix.

And thus, everywhere, the general meaning of "doing" (karoti) is understood: "What does he do? He cooks"; "What did he do? He cooked"; "What will he do? He will cook"; "What should he do? He should cook"; "What would he not do? He would not cook. In that regard, within the *bhāvanā* consisting of the object, that instigating activity (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) directed toward the person is the second [type of *bhāvanā*], which is a property of speech (*śabda-dharma*), consisting of expression (*abhidhātmikā*). This is called the injunction (*vidhi*). And this has been described in detail in the section concerning the object (*arthādhikaraṇa*).
As for that which is obtained through the persistence of grammatical derivation (*paryāya*) and is not obstructed by other conditions,
it is said therein: "Because the root alone is not employed [independently], because it encompasses the agent, number, and so forth,
and because the non-destruction of the verbal form is established, the suffix (*pratyaya*) is also employed."
For if the roots *kṛ* or *bhū* were ever used in isolation as fit for linguistic application,
then, just as the word *pika* is not employed when the word *kokila* is used, the suffix would not be employed; however, there is no usage of the verbal base alone,
because that would result in the fault of being a corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*).

Therefore, when any suffix whatsoever is to be employed, that very one which is expressed by its own meanings is used as a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of favoring the verbal root (*prakṛti*), and no other is used, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of introducing an additional meaning.

Now, it might be argued: "Since the suffixes *kvi* and *tip* are prescribed for the indication of a verbal root (*dhātunirdeśe*), then *karoti* and *bhāvayati* should be employed when those [suffixes] are expressed.
This is not so.
That being the case, the meaning would be expressed by those two [the verbal root and the suffix] through the very conceptualization of the word and its referent.

As for the fact that the verbal root *yaj* is sometimes used with the suffix *-ti*, as in *yajati*, it should be understood that the cognition of the meaning occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on what has already been denoted by the word.
Furthermore, there is no purpose here in hearing any such indication that would require the use of a non-denotative form.
In that case as well, an undesirable consequence would follow, namely, that both the root and the suffix would be denoted by the *tiṅ* ending.
Therefore, because they are intended to convey meaning, they are employed together with the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*) in order to achieve their purpose.

If, moreover, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) were the sole meaning of the suffix, then either *karoti* or *bhāvayati* would be capable of conveying the entire meaning of the suffix; consequently, they could even be heard used in isolation. Since neither of these two occurs [in such a way], the efficient force is expressed by *karoti* and *bhāvayati*, whereas the suffix is uttered again to express the meaning of the suffix itself, such as the number of the agent.

However, that portion which consists of the expression of *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is mentioned because it has not [otherwise] been established; for otherwise, there would be the misconception that *bhāvanā* alone is the meaning of the suffix, or that both *karoti* and *bhāvayati* denote the agent, number, and so forth.
Furthermore, *bhāvanā*, as a process consisting of prior and subsequent stages, is always expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

In that case, if a word ending in a different suffix were employed, then—by analogy with the way substances are subsumed under the verbs *karoti* and *bhāvayati*—it would not be described as being similar to a verbal suffix.

Therefore, that too must necessarily be employed. Furthermore: "When *bhāvanā* is being understood in the proximity of both a verbal root and a suffix, it is never clearly perceived as to which one's denotation it is."

For if its status as a suffix were determined by the final [element] alone, then there would be a redundancy of suffixes with respect to the roots *karoti* and *bhāvayati*; however, that is not the case, because [the meaning] is understood when both are present.
Since there is no occurrence of the root and suffix in isolation, their distinction cannot be discerned.
Indeed, it can be said that the meaning is expressed by the suffix together with the root, or by the root assisted by the suffix, or by both.

Nor is there any distinction in the postulation of a capacity, since in every respect the presumption (*arthāpatti*) is identical. Furthermore, there is no purpose served by the knowledge of such a distinction.
It might be argued that because the suffixes *kṛt* and so forth are not perceived [in this context], the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is indeed variable.
As it has been said:
"Because [the suffix *lyap*] is not seen even in the presence of suffixes such as *asti*, *vidyati*, and *bhavati*;
nor is it the case that there is absolutely no productive activity (*bhāvanā*) in words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, since some form of it is perceived when its nature is slightly drawn out."

First, regarding actions (*kṛtya*), that which is to be eaten (*bhoktavyam*) is slightly less [denotative] than a verb (*ākhyāta*), because it expresses the object (*karman*) among the factors of action. Even there, in cases such as "A Brahmin is not to be killed" (*brāhmaṇo na hantavyaḥ*), it is even less [denotative] than verbal nouns (*bhāva-vācya*),

because in the former case there is no predominance of the agent's activity (*prayojyavyāpāra*), whereas in the latter case there is predominance of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) on one hand, and on the other, a focus on the agent qualified by his own activity.
By this, the status of [terms such as] *bhāva*, *karman*, *upalakṣaṇa*, and *kāritā* is also explained.
For even in those cases, there is a distinct cognition of the subordinate nature (*guṇatva*) of the operation of the prompted agent (*prayojya*).
Therefore, verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) do not possess an equal status [with nominal suffixes].

Likewise, although there is no difference in the traditional rule (smaraṇa) stating that "kṛt-affixes denoting the indeclinable (avyaya) occur in the sense of the abstract action (bhāva)," the cognition of an intentionality (bhāvanā) that is slightly deficient [in its object] is self-evident. In all cases—such as "he offers oblations toward the village," "he offers oblations by striking with a blade of Darbha grass," "having pressed and offered, they shall eat," and "before the utterance of speech"—an intentionality that requires another intentionality is understood through the Vedic text itself. Even in the case of "cooked" or "cooked ones," the perception of a substance subordinate to an intentionality whose nature is already accomplished is directly evident.
The same should be understood regarding the terms *pācaka* (cook) and others as well.
Thus, in all cases, dependence upon a *kāraka* (grammatical factor) is observed;
otherwise, this [dependence] would not exist, just as it does not in compounds such as *ruditadravita* ("wept and flowed").
Furthermore, designations do not apply to that which is devoid of an object;
nor does such an activity exist wherein any part whatsoever is produced.
Consequently, the meaning of the roots *karoti* (to do) and *bhāvayati* (to bring into being) is established.
Moreover, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) can be demonstrated in all these cases even without a sequence of prior and posterior [actions].

For example: "What is to be done? It is to be cooked" (*paktavyam*); "In what manner does he offer? Toward the village" (*abhigrāmam*); "Having done what does he offer? Having pressed [the Soma]" (*abhiputya*); "What has he done? He has cooked" (*pakvān*); "What was done? Cooking" (*pakkam*); "What is Devadatta doing? He is cooking" (*paktā*); "What is the action? Cooking" (*pākaḥ*).
Furthermore, there is no evidence for *bhāvanā* (productive activity) even in verbal forms other than those that are coreferential with the root *√kṛ* ("to do").
Therefore, for this reason as well, they do not abandon the notion of *bhāvanā*.
And so they have said: "The root *kṛ* (to do) pervades all verbal roots.

As for its predominance, let that be expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) or by the optative (*liṅ*), according to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); however, it is not [the predominance of] its own essential form (*svarūpa*).

But even so, once the meaning of the verbal root has been extracted as "by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is already attained by that very [root-meaning]; therefore, the further employment of the term "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*) would not be required.
This is not a fault.
For it is thus: from the verbal root *bhū*, the specific form "by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena*) is extracted in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
On the other hand, that which consists of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)— namely, the general form— is expressed by the phrase "one should bring about [the result] by means of another word.
Alternatively, some [hold this to be] the section concerning the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*).

In the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*), it is held that the instrument, the objective, the agent, the number, and so forth, are denoted by the base and the suffix respectively through their distinction.
However, it can also be argued that since there is no deviation between the whole and its parts regarding *bhāvanā*, it is the meaning of both together.

And likewise, the author of the Sūtras and the commentator have relied upon grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "words denoting action [are those] whose meaning is bhāva," rather than stating that suffixes are denoters of bhāva. Yet, throughout the treatise, there is the conventional usage of "bhāvanā" for suffixes.
In this regard, the intention is as follows: "The base and the suffix always express their meanings together."
Because of its predominance, the meaning of the suffix is determined to be *bhāvanā*.

Even though there is no other cause for distinguishing [the meanings], nevertheless, observing that predominance is a property of the suffix's meaning, it is understood with certainty that this [meaning] belongs to the suffix.
Likewise, from that, the sequence between the portions of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is established.
At the time of hearing the suffix (*pratyaya*), that which consists of the *bhāvanā* is understood.

It is not only these two—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—which are obtained through mutual exclusion; rather, the distinction (*viveka*) is determined by the principle: "For when that [suffix] is introduced, that [bhāvanā] is expressed.
As for the claim that even the suffix following a root such as *as* (to be) abandons the *bhāvanā*, this applies equally to the root and the verbal complex (*samudāya*).
In every case, wherever a meaning is understood, there the status of being the referent of the suffix is determined; however, in other instances, this inquiry does not even arise.
Furthermore, a response to the objection regarding deviation has already been stated in the *tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* (PMS 1.1.7).
Alternatively, there is no deviation here either. Why? Because even at the beginning of this [process], the creative urge (*bhāvanā*) indeed exists within the aspect of the agent;
however, because it does not exist in other respects, it does not manifest in that way.

Although, because it resembles an agent and lacks a separate bringer-into-being (*bhāvayitṛ*), the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is not particularly evident in the case of [verbs] such as *as* (to be) and others, nevertheless, by the force of the suffix, it is understood that "one brings into being" (*bhāvayati*).

When the expectation "what? arises regarding the agent—which is as yet unaccomplished—since nothing else can be conceived, it is connected with "himself" (*ātmānam*) alone; and when the expectations "by what? and "how?
arise, they are satisfied by "bringing into being" itself, through the manner of generating parts and so forth, since no other operation is possible.
In this regard, some say that certain operations are *bhāvanās* (productive activities), while others are instigators (*prayojakas*) whose becoming is already established.
And because the universal (*sāmānya*) exists in contact with both the established and the unestablished becoming, it is called *bhāvanā*.
By this, the terms "is born," "is accomplished," and "is established" are explained.
Furthermore, when one intends for the sake of another birth, one brings about a subsequent state of existence;
thus, by means of its actual being (*sattā*), it attains the verbal suffix of the root *bhū* (to become), as in "it becomes" (*bhavati*).

Even in that case, due to the nature of the prior generality (*sāmānya*) characterized by a temporal distinction, the relationship between the prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*) remains exactly as before.
The postulation of an activity must be followed.
However, in cases such as these involving *saṃyāma* (restraint), since the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) has as its object an agent already established, injunctions and prohibitions are impossible.
This might be argued:

A rule is also seen [in the scriptures]: "Therefore, one must become a priest (ṛtvij) for that which is to be cultivated," "The Rathantara [sāman] occurs," "In this case too, there should be an Adhvaryu," and "In this instance, there should be offerings.
It is true that such is seen; however, it is not the case here that the person is first brought into being [as a priest].

For the person is already established, and it is said that he should bring about his status as a priest—which is the cause for the designation of the ritual action—by means of other activities prescribed by the sentences.

Likewise, although in the case of the *rathaṃtara* and other [sāmans] there is a connection with the root *bhū* (to become) through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), it is the inferred productive activity (*bhāvanā*) itself that is enjoined as possible therein.

However, where the usage is "let such-and-such be here" (*ihāmuko bhavet*), since the root *bhū* has the sense of "standing" or "remaining," it is understood that a distinct productive agent (*bhāvayitṛ*) is indeed possible, such as:
"one should offer something else by means of this."

Therefore, by the mere mention of past, future, and present [tenses], the status of *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) belongs only to the verbal activity (*vyāpāra*) that is not ultimate in nature, and not to [the meanings of] injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth.

Even when there is a description of the past and so on, if one takes the entire activity as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), then—because of the clear contradiction arising from the distinctions based on its parts such as time—the meaning of the root alone and the number of the agent are determined as the referents of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*), and not the *bhāvanā*.
Nor is there a fault due to the deviation of the *bhāvanā*, as has already been stated.
As for the claim that even in the case of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, verbal roots (*dhātu*) do not deviate from *bhāvanā*:

it is true that they do not deviate from the meaning of the root; however, because [the *bhāvanā*] is understood by those very [suffixes], it can also be said that it is their expressed meaning (*abhidheya*).
For instance: "The *bhāvanā* is understood as subordinate precisely through the factors of action (*kāraka*) belonging to the meaning of the root."

Therefore, [the agent] is denoted by those [kṛt suffixes] which end in *bhāvanā*. Just as in the case of a verb (*ākhyāta*), because the *bhāvanā* is predominant, the cognition of the factors of action (*kāraka*) as subordinate is established through its very accompaniment, and thus there is no denotation of the agent or the object; likewise, since the *bhāvanā* is established even without the denotation of the agent due to the impossibility [of its realization otherwise], there is no denotation [of the agent]. Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Devadatta" in the case of the word "cooks" occurs precisely in relation to that which is understood [as the agent]. And the dependence on a factor of action (*kāraka*) is not possible for that which is not of such a nature [i.e., not understood as the agent].

Alternatively, because the factors of action (*kāraka*) are subordinate to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) within the context of productive activity (*bhāvanā*), their connection is established with the meaning of the verbal root alone. For it is the verbal root that requires them for its own accomplishment, and productive activity likewise takes up those very factors as they exist [in relation to the root]; thus, the connection is firmly established. However, in the case of injunctions (*praiṣa*) and the like, even though productive activity is expressed, there is no completion of their own purpose until productive activity is obtained as complete with its three constituent parts (*aṃśatraya*).
Why? Because "A person is enjoined as an agent with respect to his own activity;
and the nature of that [enjoining] is the *praiṣa* (directive), as established in the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*."
The section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*) holds that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) consists essentially in the locus of activity.
For a person cannot perform anything other than his own activity; thus, the injunctions (*praiṣa*) cause one to perform [the action].

If those [words] do not somehow adopt that operation [of the injunction], they are unable to restrict it; thus, even in this way, the accomplishment of the *bhāvanā* (productive urge) follows by implication.

Furthermore, whatever command (*praiṣa*) originates from a Brāhmaṇa, all of it occurs through the very nature of the rule (*vidhi*) due to the absence of any other means of attainment; therefore, the injunctive character of *kṛtya* suffixes must be stated even without a traditional rule (*smaraṇa*).
And this indeed is the distinction between an injunction (*vidhi*) and a command (*praiṣa*).

"The recollection that prompts action, when [the object] is already attained, is called an *praiṣa* (command); everything that is not yet attained is undertaken according to the injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, it is established that the meaning of the suffix is *bhāvanā* (productive activity)."

Now, if it is maintained that *bhāvanā* resides in the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*), then in the case of the root *pac* (to cook), acts such as placing [the pot] on the fire would be *bhāvanā*, and in the case of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth would be *bhāvanā*. Consequently, since these alone would be the meanings of the verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), *bhāvanā* would be denoted by the verbal root itself. Alternatively, would the word "placing on the fire" denote merely a conjunction, or specifically the conjunction between the pot and the hearth? In the first alternative, all verbal roots would become synonyms.
In the second, there would be the undesirable consequence of the pot and the hearth themselves being denoted [by the root].

There is the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, if [the root *pac*] were to denote conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then even when the act of placing [the pot] on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) has ceased, because the conjunction still exists, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "the placing on the fire is occurring.
Alternatively, if it were to denote the conjunction being produced, then [the action] would have to be expressed by the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*).

Since the process (*prakriyā*) is not perceived prior [to the verbal root], it cannot function as a qualifier; consequently, it would follow that the verbal root itself must denote the conjunction qualified by the action. Thus, the status of being denoted by the causal root (*prayojaka-dhātu*) becomes unavoidable.
By this very logic, the view that roots such as *gam* (to go) denote conjunction and disjunction (*saṃyoga-vibhāga*) should be rejected.

Furthermore, there would be excessive complexity (atigaurava) due to the necessity of providing distinct designations for both the conjoined and the disjoined entities, as well as for the specific acquisition of conjunction and disjunction.

Moreover, since [the root *vi-yuj*] would have to denote both conjunction and disjunction, it would also have to express the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consisting of conjunction and disjunction.

Even if one were to accept that the meaning of the root consists of the disjunction between owner and owned, the objection remains unresolved to this day, because conjunction and disjunction cannot be established in any way in cases such as "he knows" (*jānāti*).

"Because there is a difference in capacity between the root *bhū* and the suffix *kṛt*, just as in the case of *vikalidapaca*, they necessarily denote the operations of the prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*).

From this Vārttika (p. 377), it is determined that only the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), since only the root is mentioned [in the rule]; it cannot be explained away by claiming that [the operation] is the object of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, because the suffix lacks the *ṇic* affix, it is not tenable to claim that only those forms ending in *ṇic* express a single operation performed by a prompted agent.

Furthermore, since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consists of conjunction and disjunction, it lacks the nature of an activity (*vyāpāra*); therefore, it is not logical for [substances] such as the *godohana* vessel to be grasped as its substratum (*āśraya*). If one were to accept that the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) alone, as delimited by the meaning of the verbal root, possesses the status of a substratum, then—in the injunction of a relationship between a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and a fruit (*phala*)—there would be no possibility of a distinction in the productive urge (*bhāvanābheda*), because there would be a requirement for a substratum already under discussion (*prakṛta*) out of fear of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Consequently, the investigation into whether the rule regarding qualities and desires (*guṇakāma*) shares the same or a different rule (*sāmāna-asāmānavidhya*) with respect to the substratum—which was to be conducted in the *saṃsthādhikaraṇa* (PMS 2.3.1–6)—would be rendered untenable.

Even though it has the nature of an activity (*vyāpāra*), there is no contradiction in its being a *kāraka* (a factor of action) with respect to *bhāvanā*, which itself has the nature of an action, because it consists of purposeful causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). [Objection:
"Let there be a difference between the meaning of the verbal root as an activity and [the *bhāvanā*];
however, the description of the meaning of the verbal root as a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is made for the sake of establishing their distinction."
Is that [activity] distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which consists of an operation (*vyāpāra*), since it is of the nature of motion?
Is it of the nature of effort (*prayatna*), or is it of two forms? In no way is this tenable. If *bhāvanā* were identical to effort, then [in the case of] "the chariot goes," [it would be illogical].
There would have to be an application [of the injunction], for effort is possible only in conscious beings.
But if the act of trembling (*spanda*) were the object of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) would not apply to a conscious being.
Furthermore, if it were of a dual common nature, it would be impossible for the word to express it.
For sound is not characterized by vibration, because it is devoid of mass and is conscious;
and this being the case, the general meaning of the verbal root would fall into the category of *bhāvanā*.
Now, if there were something else that served as the cause for these two, that would be perceived there.

Furthermore, the production of what was non-existent is seen as distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). When [the action] is conducive to the production of something else, and that [action] is a single *bhāvanā*,
then there would be no distinction in the *bhāvanā* based on a distinction in the meaning of the verbal root.
Nor is this [action] understood as having the sense of counteracting;
for the distinction of the result is established merely by the distinction of the root-meaning.
Now, by whatever property the root-meaning becomes the means of accomplishing the result...

That dharma is held to be distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) for the sake of the root's meaning; however, if it were the very nature of the root's meaning, its being a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*) would be contradicted. For effort (*prayatna*) would be the property of the person, and that has already been refuted.
Furthermore, that [efficient force] is *bhāvanā* because it extends to the completion of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
For how could that which is to be accomplished by the meaning of the verbal root be resorted to as a means for attaining a result?
Now, even if it is produced by the meaning of the verbal root, it exists as a potency (*śakti*) residing in the person (*puruṣa*).
This other [element] for the sake of each respective constituent (dhātu) does not exceed what is not already present;
because it is of the nature of non-activity (avyāpāra), its status as *bhāvanā* is not accepted.
Even if it were an activity, it would not be *bhāvanā* because it is not the activity of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The meaning is as follows: that [activity] is indeed the pervasion (vyāpti) of its agent, and it is the meaning of the suffix; however, this is not the case for you.
Therefore, since a *bhāvanā* distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is untenable, it is not logical for it to be the meaning of the suffix. (Sudhā, pp. 574–575)

(He refutes this: This is not a fault. Even if this [action] is not found apart from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it is nevertheless understood through its nature as a universal common to all.

And this has been explained by Caitanyadaṇḍa [in the *Bhāvanāviveka*, p. 80]: "How can there be a twofold connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) due to a difference in form, without a difference in form resulting from the suffix *kathaṃmāna*? [Otherwise] the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*) would be undermined."

The reading in the *Bhāvanāviveka* is: "Because of the transition to another realm" (*dhātvantarād gateḥ*). [And: "How could *bhāvanā*, whose nature is the mutual conformity [of the means], become corrupted?
(Śābarabhāṣya 2.1.1, p. 109).

In this context, the meaning of the verbal root *soma-* is denoted by the root itself in its specific form as a sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth; however, it is understood through the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*) in its general form consisting of the mutual conformity [of the agent and the action]. Thus, because of the distinction between the general and the specific characterized by the verbal root and the suffix respectively, the connection of the meaning of the root with the sentence-meaning occurs in two ways. And so, why should the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), which consists of mutual conformity, be corrupted? The meaning is that it is not corrupted by anything at all.

For in all cases, such as placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth, it is understood from the general operation that "one acts. By words such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), actions like placing on the fire are understood as residing in the object (*karma-stha*).
In that context, that which is defined as a form of movement consisting merely in the departure from indifference is *bhāvanā*.

Apathy (*audāsīnyam*) is the state of being non-productive (*akurvadrūpatva*); from that, "instigation" (*prayukti*) brings about productivity (*kurvadrūpatva*). This means that there is a mutual conformity (*anyonyānukūlyatva*), and that which is defined by such a form is *bhāvanā*.

The word "only" (*mātra*) is used to demonstrate the distinction between this and verbal roots (*dhātu*) such as "motion" (*spanda*), which are causes of conjunction, disjunction, and so forth. It is not restricted [to only transitive roots], because it is observed even in the case of intransitive roots, where the meaning of the root is understood as residing in the object, such as wealth; furthermore, in the case of transitive roots, conjunction and disjunction arise immediately after actions such as "going."

The intention is as follows: because there is no desire for a teacher (*upādhyāya*), and because the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*)—which is devoid of mutual conflict in its successive stages (*paryāya*) characterized by being an object-to-be-accomplished (*bhāvya*) through the desire for the fruit—is essentially a state of indifference (*audāsīnya*) defined by not performing an action; and because, immediately thereafter, due to the attainment of the fruit, it is conducive to the production of moments that are mutually favorable toward the final stage culminating in the object-to-be-accomplished, there is a distinction of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

Consequently, this indicates the resolution of the following objection: "Just as the operation of rice and the like—though it is the operation of the prompted (prayojya) and has cooking (*viklitti*) etc. as its result—is not *bhāvanā* because, despite being an operation, it lacks the status of being the operation of the prompter (*prayojaka*), so too, although the act of placing [the pot on the fire] (*adhiśrayaṇa*) etc. is the operation of the prompter, it is not *bhāvanā* because it does not reside in that which is to be brought into being (*bhāvya*)."

One might object: "Since acts such as placing [the pot on the fire] consist of physical motion (*parispanda*), there exists a causal operation (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) directed toward the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) that is distinct from the operation of the agent; why then is it not perceived apart from those [motions]? Anticipating this doubt, it is stated that [the *bhāvanā*] is "of the nature of motion. The point is this: since the *bhāvanā* is defined—either by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as its objective domain (*viṣaya*), or by the meaning of the verbal root as its effect (*kārya*) functioning as its instrument (*karaṇa*)—it is logically impossible to perceive it without the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, it is conceptually constructed (*kalpitā*).

The word *parispanda* (movement) is employed in the sense of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) for the purpose of indicating the measure [of effort] by means of the factors that effect the cutting off of the mental disposition (*bhāvanā*). It is used sometimes in reference to the mental disposition itself, and sometimes, through proximity, in reference to both; it is not used as a designation of its own essential nature.
Why? "Just as the mental disposition is enjoined, so too is the meaning of the verbal root."
It is never expressed by other words in that very same form.

For the word *bhāvanā* denotes a realized entity (*niṣpannātmaka*) which possesses the nature of a substance (*sattva*) and is connected with gender and number; however, this [action] is not denoted in such a way by the verb, because it is understood as being devoid of gender and number.
The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) should also be understood in the same way.

Likewise, even from the two verbal roots *karoti* (he does) and *bhāvayati* (he causes to be), the meaning that is understood through direct scriptural expression (*śruti*) is simply the act of depositing a hump-backed limb; it is not of the nature [of the *bhāvanā*] which exists in [the injunctions] such as *yajeta* (one should sacrifice). Therefore, they are not synonyms. In this regard, one must establish a correspondence of meaning between the two internal cognitions by preserving the twofold nature of the *bhāvanā*.
Thus, their usage is based merely on a lack of great distance [from the primary sense], and not on identity of meaning; such is established the fact that the *bhāvanā* is denoted by other words.

But that [efficient force], as soon as it is recognized—primarily because it is dependent on other expectancies—first requires the element of the goal (sādhya), thinking, "What should one bring about?

In this regard, as long as the efficient force (bhāvanā) is not fully manifested, its previously recognized status as an injunction (vidhitva) is maintained; however, this status is relinquished as soon as the efficient force becomes complete in its purpose and fit for performance.
Furthermore, due to the sequence of the injunctive process, it is understood from the very beginning that this injunction must be fulfilled by such constituent parts as would make it complete.
Furthermore, a person acting with conscious intent would not, even by means of a hundred words, undertake an activity devoid of human purpose.

Nor is human purpose sought by anyone with an excellence that transcends the relationship with what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because there exists no other goal more beneficial than that. In this regard, if in this cultivation (*bhāvanā*) the goal were something other than human purpose, then a person would not engage in it, and the cognition would fail to function as an instigator of action.

Therefore, although it might be argued that the meaning "of the suffix denoting the ablative within the same word" is appropriate for completing the required sense of the proposition, it is nevertheless set aside due to its lack of logical fitness (*ayogyatva*). For proximity (*pratyāsatti*) alone is not the sole cause of grammatical connection; rather, logical fitness (*yogyatva*) is also required.
And so he will state later: "Whichever [element] has a semantic connection with whichever [other], that [connection] belongs to it, even if it is at a great distance.
("Whichever [element] has a semantic connection with whichever [other], that [connection] belongs to it, even if it is in a difficult position.")

"By implication, there is no immediate sequence (*anantarya*) between the name of the *dharma* and the name of the object," and so forth, as the former teachers will state in the *Viśvajit* section (4.1.7).
Furthermore: "The mere relationship between the meaning of the verbal root and the existence [of the result] is expressed by the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)."
However, its operation does not extend to the placement of [the word] in only one part [of the sentence].
Once the Vedic revelation (śruti) has ceased its operation after merely establishing the relationship, the placement in either one of the two parts must be resorted to on the basis of suitability.
Therefore, if it is the thing to be accomplished (sādhya)—
The understanding [of the object] as a mental cultivation (bhāvanā) follows;
for indeed, "by whichever states are most desired, the 'what' (kimaṃśa) portion is occupied.
Thus, by that [occupation], there would be no verbal root-meaning whatsoever that is intransitive."
"Or else, it would follow that all verbal roots (*dhātu*) are transitive; or alternatively, there would be no realization (*bhāvanā*) from intransitive roots.
This is not a fault.
Why? Because in a transitive root, the object to be reached is indeed distinct from the meaning of the root itself."
Furthermore, the basis for the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya) is entirely different everywhere.

In the cases "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) and "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), there is one object (*karman*) to be attained at the completion of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), and another, which is the object of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

In that regard, sometimes the very object of the root-meaning also assumes the status of being the object of the productive urge, as in: "he brings about rice by means of cooking" (*pākenaudanaṃ bhāvayati*).

Sometimes, however, a *bhāvanā* (efficient force) that is connected with the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) qualified by its own object is connected with another object, as in "he brings about his own purpose by going to the village" or "by cooking rice.

And this [object], being understood as something merely to be attained subsequent to the meaning of the verbal root, is determined everywhere as the object of the *bhāvanā*, even when it is obscured by another meaning of the verbal root.
Furthermore, that [object] generally enters into a connection with words expressing desire (*kāma*), such as "one desiring happiness should sit," or "one desiring health should fast."

Even though the roots *ās* (to sit) and *śī* (to lie down) are intransitive, those such as sleeping (*svāpa*) are determined to be their objects by virtue of the fact that the meaning of "doing" (*karoti*) is expressed by the suffix, and [sleeping] is understood as the object of that [action].

Therefore, since the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is always transitive, and because we observe the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even with intransitive verbs—as in "What is he doing? He is sitting" (*kiṃ karoti? āste*) and "What is he doing? He is lying down" (*kiṃ karoti? śete*)—the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) remains transitive even in such cases.
Furthermore, regarding the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), its object is indeed that which is worthy of worship (*pūjyatva*). Thus, these [examples] are established.
The status of being an object (*karmatva*) belonging to the son and so forth in the case of [the root] *hve* (to call) is dependent upon the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

Therefore, is there a distinction between transitive and intransitive roots? It is said: "A verbal root is transitive when its own meaning directly and invariably possesses an object; it is intransitive when [the possession of an object occurs] through a mediated succession."

For actions such as sitting (*āsana*) or lying down (*śayana*) are not defined as "this" or "that" with necessity or continuity; therefore, they are called intransitive (*akarmaka*). However, verbs such as *pac* (to cook) and *gam* (to go) possess transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) because there is no deviation from their direct connection with that which is being moistened or joined. Yet, there is no fault whatsoever in [the agent] having the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) as its qualifier.

This very efficient force, being complete in its two parts [the end and the means], requires the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—namely, "How should one bring it about?"—since it is impossible for all the instruments (*karaṇa*) grasped through their adoption to function as instruments unless this requirement is met.

And that [efficient force], being understood from the existence of the perception of the auxiliaries of the verbal root and so forth, is—either according to proximity when that [proximity] is possible, or otherwise as it may present itself in accordance with the scripture, through the instruction of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), or through extension (*atideśa*) based on the commonality of the injunction (*codanā-sāmānya*)—postulated by the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) as the means for ultimate assistance.
Consequently, because it is complete, it is enjoined as being fit for performance.

And since its injunction implies the injunction of the sacrifice and so forth by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the *Sūtra* on the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha-sūtra*) is thus established.

There are certain words for action (*karmaśabda*); examples such as "sacrifice" (*yāga*), "performing sacrifice" (*yajana*), and "the act of sacrificing" (*ijyā*) should be cited to establish their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). An example from outside this category is easily understood because of its dependence on being a word for action that occurs at a time subsequent to the injunction (*codanā*), just like the instrument of sacrifice and so forth. This is because it is impossible for independent [words] to ever possess the status of words denoting the sense of "becoming" (*bhāvārtha*).

For words such as "sacrifice" are not words for action even when they exist independently, since they do not occasionally denote [the process of becoming]; thus, "one should cause to become" (*bhāvayet*) and so forth are cited as examples.

However, as for *bhūyādi* [verbs] such as *bhāvayati*, because they denote the operation of the prompted agent (*prayojya-vyāpāra*), they do not have the meaning of "being" (*bhāva*) as previously described; thus, they are not examples.
In that regard, although one instance of the word *bhāva* is cited by deriving it from a causative (*ṇijanta*) form in some way or another, the other is not.
Nevertheless, even those two are cited as having the meaning of "being" (*bhāva*) in some sense through the operation of the prompted agent.

Alternatively, by explaining the meaning of the second sūtra, it is shown that there is no purpose for the cultivation [of the meaning] if the word denotes only a part [of the action]; thus, even without the explicit mention of "bhāva," those words whose meaning is the action (bhāvārtha) are established as such.

But how is it that these are not "karma-śabda" (action-words), given that the root alone has been called a "karma-śabda"? Since a general term without qualification cannot be performed, it lacks the status of being a "karma-śabda.
Therefore, because the status of being a "karma-śabda" is attributed only to those roots that denote a specific [action], this [status] is something to be manifested by another factor.

For if the words *śyena*, *citrayā*, and *darśapūrṇamāsa* were connected with results, then—since there would be no status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) for the sacrifice—the designation as a name (*nāmadheya*) based on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be untenable; consequently, they would simply be injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*) by virtue of their well-known meanings and so forth. Therefore, he says, "This being established in this section. Why, then, was this not brought into that very [section]? Because it has no connection with the definition of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And why is the status of being a name not brought here? Because it has no connection with the definition of difference (*bheda*).
Therefore, in this case, there is indeed a fixed order of placement (nyāsa), because the priority and posteriority [of the elements] are established.
The phrase "not by the seeker of these" refers to the word denoting the result (phala). [The rule] "because of the case-endings" [is stated].

Alternatively, *vibhaktitva* (the state of being a case-ending) consists in the connection with a specific case-ending that expresses an accomplished entity (*niṣpanna-abhidhāyin*), arising from the division of case-endings based on the meaning of the relation's cause.

Therefore, there is a connection with the fruit for words denoting substance (*dravya*) and so forth. And it has been said: "The relationship between the goal to be accomplished and the means is always the locus of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)."
Therefore, its accomplishment would arise from the cognition of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

If it is argued that "the meaning of all words is existence" (*bhāva*), the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states: "If you view it thus, then because they are words denoting non-existence, words for substances and qualities would also be enjoiners of the *apūrva*; therefore, the meaning of all words is existence."

The injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" will express the relationship between these two [sacrifices] and the result; likewise, "one practicing sorcery should sacrifice with a substance," and "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā.
Therefore, these too, because they possess expectancy, are expressions of the bhāvanā (the efficient force).

In all cases where words denote an entity (*bhāva*), there is no reason for a definitive distinction that "words beginning with *katham*" (interrogative adverbs) are the enjoiners of the *apūrva*, while words denoting substances (*dravya*) or qualities (*guṇa*) are not. [Response:
First of all, it is not accepted that the suffix (*pratyaya*) conveys the *apūrva*.
Nor can it belong independently to the verbal root (*dhātu*); nor is it equal [in status] whether it follows a noun (*nāman*) or a verb.

For if it were intended that only the meaning called *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) is expressed by the verbal root, independent of the suffix, then the position of the noun (*nāman*) would be weak. But here, just as the verbal root—when assisted by its connection with a suffix—possesses the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) due to the coloring (*añjana*) of the *bhāvanā*, so too does the nominal word; thus there is no distinction. Those words whose form is perceived when they are produced in their own usage are nouns (*nāmāni*); therefore, because they are already established in their own usage, they have no further expectancy for another.

Commentary: Those words whose form is perceived when they are employed in their own meaning through the act of utterance—meaning that which, having once arisen, persists for a period of time, and does not perish immediately upon arising like an action—those are "names" (*nāman*). They are the words denoting substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*).
Such is the meaning of the terms "substance" (dravya) and "quality" (guṇa).

While it would have been appropriate to say "those are the terms for substance and quality," the author has formulated the sūtra as "those are the names" (tāni nāmāni). Furthermore, the word "names" (nāmāni) is a synonym for these two.
How is this understood? Because their case-endings are called nominal endings (*nāmika*).
Which are they? *vṛkṣaḥ*, *vṛkṣau*, *vṛkṣāḥ*; *śuklaḥ*, *śuklau*, *śuklāḥ*, and so forth.
Therefore, it has been correctly formulated in the sūtra.

Since these [words] do not have a momentary object, there is no further expectation (*parākāṅkṣā*)—that is, no primary expectation—from them; thus, their production need not be performed, because they are already existent (*bhūtatvāt*), meaning they exist at the time of their own employment (*svaprayogakāla*) within their own usage.

Or rather—as it was said: "When there is a preceding [word], this shall become the subsequent meaning"—that being so, he now demonstrates a distinction by means of the property of the thing (*vastudharma*).
How? "For a property is not desired at every step, as it would lead to the undesirable consequence of excessive proliferation."
There is no resolution for the connection between a name and its fruit; nor is there one for that [other view].

If, when one unseen principle (*adṛṣṭa*) is postulated, the other is understood to serve that same purpose by virtue of having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), then parsimony (*lāghava*) is achieved.

However, for the sake of establishing that [name] serves that purpose, one must indeed postulate another visible [result] even beyond that; therefore, it is better that all [elements] are connected directly with the fruit.

Nor is there any need to resort to the laborious assumption of a disparity in the nature of the connection; for if the name were connected to the fruit, the meaning of the verbal root would necessarily have to be admitted as subserving it.
And since that [verbal meaning] is something to be accomplished, it cannot provide a visible benefit to the name-meaning, which is already established in its form.

The object does not depend on the name, because it is understood as already accomplished at the very moment of the word’s employment; nor is there a logical connection with something that must be depended upon, since such a thing would already be established. Alternatively, "employment" (prayoga) refers to the signified object itself, in the sense of "that in which [the word] is employed. For it is precisely that substratum, characterized by its accomplished form, that is indicated when the state of being unproduced is to be expressed. Furthermore, the demonstration of perishability—even for that which is accomplished—is appropriate because of its momentariness, given that it requires repeated production again and again.

From them, there is no further expectation (*parākāṅkṣā*), nor any expectation for something else, or rather, no primary expectation (*pradhānākāṅkṣā*) as something yet to be accomplished—this is the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).
"Beyond these" means that there is no further distance or expectation.
Why? Precisely because they have already come into being (*bhūtatvāt*).
It was accepted [by the opponent] that the statement of the word's own form (*svarūpa*) is due to its being already established;
furthermore, the author of the Sūtras stated that very same point as the reason:
"But for those [words] whose usage is not found in their own produced meaning, they are verbal roots (*ākhyāta*); therefore, the meaning is understood from them, because usage depends upon them."

The Commentary (Bhāṣya): "But those words for which there is no usage in their own sense arising from their utterance"—the meaning is that at the time of usage, their meaning is not perceived. These are the verbal roots (ākhyātāni); thus he teaches these bhāva-words by means of synonymous terms.
How are the synonymous words for nouns [distinguished]?
Because their inflections are said to be verbal (ākhyātika).
Which are they? "He cooks" (pacati), "they two cook" (pacantau), "they cook" (pacanti), and so forth.

Therefore, from them, the apūrva should be understood. Those words denoting things to be accomplished (bhavyārtha) are connected with words denoting accomplished entities (bhūtārtha). When an accomplished entity serves the purpose of a thing to be accomplished, it has a visible purpose; thus, the production of that which is to be accomplished, being purposeful, is meaningful.

And that [action] is performed by means of what is already existent; thus, its purpose is perceived. However, if a thing yet to be produced (bhavya) were to have an existent entity as its purpose, nothing would be perceived, and something unperceived would have to be postulated.
Therefore, the sacrifice has the substance as its purpose.
Furthermore, because the application [of the means] is dependent;
the application of these [means] is resorted to by a person, and it is said that the cultivation (bhāvanā) is connected to the person. For one tells the person: "One should cultivate."
Therefore, in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the person is understood, as is the sacrifice, and also the relationship [between them].
In the expression "One desiring heaven [should act] with a substance," the substance and the person are understood, but not the relationship.

Now, it might be argued that this is what is being said: the word "yajeta" (he should sacrifice) will express the relationship between the seeker and the substance, namely, "one should effect [the result] by means of a substance"; thus, the production (*bhāvanā*) of the object by means of the substance is understood, as is the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

It is true that [the object] is understood; however, "one should effect [the result] by means of a substance" is understood through the syntactical connection (*vākya*), whereas "one should effect [the result] by means of a sacrifice" is understood through direct statement (*śruti*).

When, however, the connection with the sacrifice is enjoined—namely, "one should effect [the result] by means of a sacrifice"—then at that time, the connection with the substance—namely, "one should effect [the result] by means of a substance"—is not [enjoined].

Furthermore, when a connection with a substance is being enjoined, it cannot be done by the word "one should sacrifice" (yajeta); rather, such a connection is possible when that word is being used as a restatement (anuvāda). Moreover, injunction (vidhi) and restatement (anuvāda) cannot occur simultaneously.
Therefore, there is a contradiction between the direct Vedic statement (śruti) and the syntactical connection (vākya).
And in the case of a contradiction, the direct statement is more authoritative.
Consequently, the person desiring the result has no connection with the substance.

In that case, it is untenable to argue that "the substance exists, and through its connection with heaven, it will serve the purpose of heaven. This is the reason for the definitive conclusion: that words denoting actions (*bhāva-śabda*) are the indicators of the *apūrva*, whereas words denoting substances (*dravya-śabda*) and qualities (*guṇa-śabda*) are not.

When it is said, "one should perform by means of sacrifice," then the expression "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa" is indeed a designation for the sacrifice, since the sacrifice is enjoined in both the Darśa and the Pūrṇamāsa.
Or, as it is said: "The meaning of the verbal root, which is of the nature of something to be accomplished, is understood from the verb;
when that [accomplishment] is desired as possessing the fruit, the name [of the rite] is held to have a visible purpose."

First, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is distinguished by its very nature as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). That [meaning], however, is expressed by the verbal root through its being a verb-form (*ākhyātatva*).

If that [meaning] is further expressed as a means to a result (*phala-sādhanatva*), then, since it exists in an unestablished form and thus possesses a requirement for a means (*sādhana-ākāṅkṣā*), the nominal word (*nāmapada*)—whether as an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or as a name (*nāmadheya*)—attains its subservience to that [root-meaning] in both cases through a visible purpose alone.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of a name (*nāmadheya*), even the word for the name will have the object of accomplishment as its meaning, and thus it would be equivalent to a verbal root (*dhātu*).
[Reply: No, because when that [name] exists as a result, it functions as an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) and therefore has an already established meaning.
Moreover: "Even when the meaning of the verbal root, though consisting of something to be accomplished, is denoted by a name..."
At that time, this [action] is perceived as having its self-nature accomplished through the substance and the verbal root.
Although the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by way of its own essential nature,
nevertheless, when expressed by a nominal word (*nāmapada*), it is denoted as being of an accomplished form (*siddharūpa*), because it is associated with gender and number.
Furthermore, the arising of expectancy is produced by verbal expression (*abhidhāna*), not by the thing itself (*vastu*).

Therefore, it is logical that expectancy belongs to the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone, and not to the nominal stem (*nāman*). Moreover, since the connection (*yoga*) is dependent [on the agent], even though the meaning of the root consists in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) which is of the nature of human effort, it is not the nominal word that is grasped; for the root-meaning is what is resorted to by the person, and because it is the cause for transcending [the mere state of being].
Therefore, there is a distinction.
Śabara [says]: When there is a single [apūrva], then the doubt arises whether it originates from words denoting action (bhāva-śabda) or from words denoting substance and quality (dravya-guṇa-śabda).
And for that purpose, the question is whether those whose meaning is action are connected with the fruit, or rather the words denoting substance and quality.
In this regard, some (the Prābhākaras) state the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there is indeed no ascertainment (*anadhyavasāya*).
As it has been said:
"For [otherwise] there would be non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*) itself, and that is untenable."
If that were the case, this investigation would pertain only to the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and not here, because validity (*prāmāṇya*) is already established.
[Objection: But surely, since the performance of the ritual is determined to be of a single form in both positions, there is no lack of validity.
[Response: This is the prattle of a fool.
If there were no difference in the performance [of the rite] between the two positions, what would be the purpose of this section?

Furthermore, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since *dayana* and the others are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), one must sacrifice with the substance *dayana*; however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since they are names (*nāmadheya*), one must sacrifice with *soma*. Thus, there is a distinction. As the author of the Bhāṣya says: "Once this section is settled, the inquiry is whether [the term] is an injunction of an accessory quality or a name" (Bhā. p. 386).

However, where even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) there is no [independent] name—as in the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma"—the presence or absence of a substitute (*pratinidhi*) is the purpose [of the discussion].

Regarding this, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) says (Bhā. p. 405): "If words denoting substances and qualities convey the *apūrva*, then in the event of the loss of a substance or a quality, no substitute would be required, as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*); but according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the performance must be carried out by employing a substitute substance or quality" (Bhā. 2.1.16, p. 405).
Therefore, it does not follow that there is a lack of authority; such is not the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Rather, the *apūrva* arises from substances and so forth, and these alone are the means for accomplishing the fruit.
Why? Because "the fruit, being something yet to be accomplished, seeks an already established means."
The same applies to substances and so forth; the sacrifice itself is that which is to be accomplished, not the means of accomplishment.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"Indeed, it is *bhāvanā* alone that is capable of being connected with the fruit to be brought about."

The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in that [efficient force], because of its proximity and its lightness. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: those words which denote an action (*bhāvārtha*) through the suffixes are the conveyors of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*);
from those words which express the object (*karman*) by means of the verbal base (*prakṛti*), the *apūrva* is understood.

When those verbal roots which are action-words (*karma-śabda*)—meaning words whose meaning consists of an action and which impel the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)—are understood to convey the *apūrva*, then this is the purpose:

if the position were that substance-words and quality-words convey the *apūrva*, then because substances and the like would have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and because there is no substitute for that which has an unseen purpose, there would be no substitute.
However, when [the *apūrva* is understood] from words denoting action...
Mīmāṃsākośa 308: The Section on the Meaning of Verbal Roots (Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa).
By the principle of the Section on the Meaning of Verbal Roots (Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa) [at Mīmāṃsāsūtra 2.1.1], 3020. By the logic of the Section on the Meaning of Verbal Roots.

It will be explained in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* (Soma. 1.1.4) that the verbal root-meaning alone possesses the status of being the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), and not the meaning of a nominal stem.

Furthermore, the connection between a quality (*guṇa*) and a fruit (*phala*) occurs only in those cases where the verbal root-meaning is already established through another scriptural injunction (*guṇaśāstra*), as determined by the section on the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*; it does not occur where the quality itself is also [already] established.

Therefore, even in other cases such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, when both the time and the sacrifice are already established by the sentences concerning the Āgneya and other offerings, it is impossible for a relationship between a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and a fruit (*phala*) to exist. (Kau. 1.4.8.24) Furthermore, the two previously mentioned definitions—the visible utility (*dṛṣṭopakāritva*) being the definition of a subordinate act (*guṇakarman*), and the absence of visible utility (*iṣṭopakārābhāva*) being the definition of a primary act (*pradhāna*)—do not concern the distinction between the subordinate and the primary, but rather concern the presence or absence of the *apūrva* (transcendental result).
That alone is established as the subject matter of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* section, because it is the reality of the comprehension [of the meaning].
(Śābarabhāṣya 2.1.4, p. 108).

Furthermore, in the *Nyāyasudhā*, the author of that commentary, at the beginning of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* section, accepts that even *tātparya* (implicatory power) is a mode of signification (*vṛtti*), stating: "In the case of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, although the *bhāvanā* is not directly expressed (*avācyatva*), it possesses the status of being verbally conveyed (*śābdatva*) by way of *tātparya*. etc. (See the relevant passage).
What is that which has the state as its primary meaning? The verbal suffix (bhāvanā);
the verb has the state as its primary meaning.

In a verb, neither the agent nor the action is primary (Bhāṣya 1.1.4.24). According to the traditional rule of the *Nirukta*, "A verb has the state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning" (1.1.9), it is understood that the activity denoted by the word *bhāva* is primary. According to the traditional rule "A verb has the state as its primary meaning" (Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa 2.1.15), a restriction is established that among verbs which express multiple meanings, the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is invariably primary.
*Maṇi*, p. 112: According to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "the verb is predominant in its meaning" (*bhāvapradhānamākhyātam*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) holds primacy within the verb.

*Sūtra*, p. 701: An expression is "predominant in its meaning" (*bhāvapradhāna*). Even in the absence of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), an expression whose primary focus is on the entity capable of receiving the suffix is called an expression "predominant in its meaning."
In that context, it is explained: "The quality exists as primary from the very beginning.

To the question, "How can an expression be primary with respect to the state [of being] (*bhāva*) without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*)?", it is answered: "It occurs when the quality itself exists as primary from the very beginning."
For it is said: "In some cases, a quality (guṇa) is enjoined independently from the very beginning;
in others, as a subordinate part of a substance (dravya); and in yet others, by being extracted [from that].

Where a quality is intended to be primary from the outset, there coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is possible even without an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya), simply through the relation of subsistence—as in the case of 'the white of the cloth' (paṭasya śuklaḥ)."

However, where the extraction [of the quality] is not intended because it is subordinate to the substance, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in "the white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*).

On the other hand, where the extraction is intended after first intending the quality to be subordinate, then the abstract suffixes *tva* and *tal* arise according to the rule: "When the application of a word to a substance occurs due to the existence of a certain quality, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote that [quality]. Thus, there is the production of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

But when there is an intention to express its own predominance, the quality (*guṇa*)—because it lacks the status of a subordinate member (*anaṅgatva*)—is no longer a quality at all; consequently, there is no application of the word to the substance by means of that quality. Therefore, in that case, the word for that substance is not applied to it. Furthermore, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) cannot grasp the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) without the specific meanings of the verbal roots.
