Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.6.16.43, p. 1069: "But *bhāvanā* is determined to be distinct because it does not appear [in the other verbal form].

At the time of examining whether there is a difference or non-difference in *bhāvanā*, even though it possesses the nature of being the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), *bhāvanā*—because it lacks any other means of cognition—is not brought forward by another verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) and thus cannot be recognized in any way; therefore, it is established that there is a difference in purpose (i.e., a different action). 2.2.12.4, p. 616: *Bhāvanā*.

"Therefore, those who know *bhāvanā* call *bhāvanā* the instigating action (*prayojaka-kriyā*) of that entity which has assumed the status of an agent with respect to the results (*bhūtiṣu*, i.e., the states of being). (The meaning is:
*bhāvanā* is a specific operation of the bringer-about (*bhāvayitṛ*) which is conducive to the coming-to-be (*bhavana*) of that which is to come-to-be (*bhavitṛ*).)"
2|2|12, p. 378. *Bhāvanā* has three components. By the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the necessity of performing the triad—the result, the instrument, and the procedure—is expressed.
At the very moment that heaven attains the status of being the object to be produced (*bhāvya*), at that same instant, the instrument and the procedure also become operative.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 5.1.5.8: The efficient force (*bhāvanā*) has three factors. In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is enjoined by the text, "He draws the *ṣoḍaśin*.
Therein, the efficient force of that which is being enjoined possesses three factors: what [is to be produced], by what [means], and how.
In this regard, the assistance provided by the instrument renders the "what" (kimaṃśa) portion free of expectancy;
the *ṣoḍaśī* [cup] renders the "by what" (kena) portion free of expectancy;
and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) prescribed for the *ṣoḍaśī* renders the "how" (katham) portion free of expectancy.
In that regard, the sentence is complete.

[JS 1.1.25] 9.167. Bhāvanā, when qualified by substance and deity, cannot have a sacrifice as its substrate merely through the act of sacrifice itself; it therefore either postulates a sacrifice or adopts one already present in the context. This is bhāvanā.

When the meaning of the verbal root in the expression "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is explained as "one should bring about [the result] by means of a sacrifice" (*yāgena bhāvayet*), the specific form of the instrument (*karaṇa*), namely "by means of a sacrifice," is extracted by itself. The other part, the general form of the meaning of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), is expressed by another word, namely *bhāvayet* ("one should bring about").
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 2.1.2.12, page 380: "Bhāvanā is twofold: śabdabhāvanā (verbal productive energy) and arthabhāvanā (objective productive energy).
Among these, the investigation of arthabhāvanā is to be found in the *Mīmāṃsākośa*, page 629, under the entry 'arthabhāvanā' in the *Bindu*."
The investigation of *śabdabhāvanā* (verbal productive energy) is to be found in the *Cintāmaṇi*.
*Bhāvanā* is a form of activity (*kṛti*) distinct from the meaning of the verbal root; it is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).
Its substratum (*āśraya*), however, is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*).
Maṇi, p. 119: Bhāvanā.

Although this [cognition] depends on the generality [of the word], because it appears as a specific instance of bhāvanā due to its distinction from the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), it is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) since there is no sublation (bādhā).
Bhāvanā is the operation of an instigator that is conducive to the becoming of that which is to become.
Therefore, the very operation conducive to the arising of heaven is called svargabhāvanā (the productive operation of heaven). Soma. 3.1.4, p. 227. Bhāvanā.
When the husband says, "She cooks," all people understand this meaning.

In that context, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as expressed by the words *pākaḥ*, *paktiḥ*, or *pacanam* is established in nature (*siddhasvabhāva*), being fit for gender, case-role (*kāraka*), and number. However, the meaning as expressed by the word *karoti* is to-be-accomplished in nature (*sādhyasvabhāva*), being devoid of gender and the like.

In that regard, just as suffixes such as *ghañ* are prescribed to indicate a perfected (*siddha*) nature, so too is there a rule for verbal suffixes (*ākhyātapratyaya*) to indicate a nature yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

And that meaning of the verbal suffix is conducive to the production of the rice (*odana*). Therefore, because it is the instigating activity (*prayojakavyāpāra*) of the rice which is the agent of becoming (*bhavituḥ*), it is expressed by the word *bhāvanā* when derived with the causative suffix (*ṇijanta*).
Others have stated that [effort] depends upon cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
If it is argued that effort is cultivation, no; for then it would follow that such [effort] is absent in the case of "the chariot goes.
If it is argued that it is vibration (*spanda*), no; for that would not apply to sacrifice, which consists of mental activity.

If it is argued that "bhāvanā" is a commonality consisting in the exclusion of indifference shared by both [the verbal and the objective], we say no; for this would apply even to the verbal *bhāvanā* (*śabdabhāvanā*).
Indeed, there is neither vibration nor effort in the case of the Word, which is all-pervading and insentient.
Verbal *bhāvanā* resides solely in the suffixes *liṅ*, *leṭ*, and *loṭ*.

The cultivation of meaning (*arthabhāvanā*) resides in all verbal suffixes. As it has been said: "Those who know declare that the *liṅ* and other [suffixes] have one cultivation as their denotation (*abhidhābhāvanā*), whereas the cultivation of the object itself (*arthātmabhāvanā*) is understood from all verbal suffixes."
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, even for those who maintain the doctrine of *spanda* (vibration) and so forth, [the self] is not [consciousness] by its own nature (*svarūpa*), because vibration and the like are mental constructs (*bhāvanā*); rather, it is a nature conducive to the production of something else.
Therefore, the mental construct is exactly as we have described it.

Just as in the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*), [the action] is conducive to the production of the result, namely rice, so too in the case of "he sacrifices" (*yajati*), it is conducive to the production of results such as heaven.

And in that efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the suffix, because it is expressed by the same word and thus has the suffix as its locus, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is [the verbal root-meaning], and not the substance and so forth, since those are remote due to being expressed by another word.

Even though the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛti*) is of the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is capable of bringing about the result once it has been produced by its own means.
However, in the case of substances (*dravya*) and so forth, the assistance is indeed perceived through their inclusion as the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*).

When the fruit such as heaven arises by means of an instrument such as a sacrifice—which is denoted by the verbal root and brought about by substances and the like—there are certain favorable operations, namely effort (*kṛti*), verbal command (*abhipreṣa*), and the production of the fruit; this [operation] is not denoted by any one of the verbal roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice), because it is common to the meanings of all verbal roots.
Therefore, it cannot be suspected that the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is the meaning of the verbal root.
If it is argued that the bhāvanā is simply the general meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), we say no; for they possess distinct natures in their respective oppositions.
For the favorableness of cooking toward the rice is one thing, while that of motion toward conjunction and disjunction is another, since otherwise the prior disjunction could not be accounted for.

Granted that the universal property of *bhāvanā*-ness (*bhāvanātva-sāmānya*) may persist through the various individual instances of *bhāvanā* that differ from one another; yet, for this reason alone, that [universal] does not become identical with the primary root-meaning (*prakṛti*).
Therefore, the *bhāvanā* denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*) is indeed distinct from the specific and general forms expressed by verbal roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice).
This being the case, in the expression "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the meaning of the verbal suffix is "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*).

In this regard, when there arises the expectation—"What should one bring about? By what means should one bring it about? How should one bring it about?"—this expectation is fulfilled by the presentation of the objective (*bhāvya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) as follows: "One should bring about heaven; one should bring it about by means of sacrifice; one should bring it about by accomplishing the assistance [required] through such acts as the laying of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) and the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*). Thus, the entire collection of words within the context constitutes an elaboration of the verbal root that expresses *bhāvanā*. This three-part *ārthī bhāvanā* (objective productive activity) is what is referred to here.

All of that is the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) by the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*); the injunctive suffixes (*liṅgādi*) and so forth are the instrument (*karaṇa*); and the praise accomplished by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
This very verbal productive energy is understood through the injunctive suffixes and so forth alone.
It has been stated that the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) is understood by all verbal suffixes (*ākhyātapratyaya*).

And in that efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*), the fact that heaven is the object to be brought about is understood from its connection with the root *kam* (to desire). The status of the meaning of the verbal root as the instrument is based on the third case ending.

Thus it is heard in scripture: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*) and "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā [sacrifice]" (*citrayā yajeta paśukāmaḥ*).
And it will be explained that this status as an instrument is not possible without the postulation of an *apūrva* (p.
211, section 2).
*Bhāvanā* is a synonym for human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*).
Su. pṛ. 744:
Since *bhāvanā* (the productive operation) is the primary factor, being independent of any other entity, it first requires an object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), asking "What?
Furthermore, a person acting with deliberation will not undertake an activity devoid of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), even if told so a hundred times.

In this regard, if in this [grammatical] operation (*bhāvanā*) the object to be accomplished were something that does not serve human ends (*apuruṣārtha*), then, since persons would not engage in it, the causal power (*prayojakaśakti*) of the suffix would be sublated.

Therefore, even though the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is perceived as subordinate to the object to be accomplished when there exists a suffix that introduces a word with the same base, nevertheless, due to its lack of fitness (*ayogyatā*), it is set aside for a long time.
For effort and proximity are not the causes of syntactic connection; rather, it is fitness (*yogyatva*) as well.
Furthermore, the goal to be accomplished—such as heaven, sons, or a village—is already understood by all persons even prior to the scripture.
Consequently, when the mere expectation arises, "What should one bring about?", this much is understood even without the scripture: that there is some human purpose (puruṣārtha).
In that case, only the specific [result] is set aside because it is already understood;
yet even that is not as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), but rather as the object of this cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Consequently, there is a connection with heaven and the like, which, though distant, have already found their locus [in the mind].

Thereupon, the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)—which has for its objective portion the *avabhṛtha* rite—requires an instrument, as in the question "by what should one bring [the result] about? In this context, since its operation depends upon the Vedic text, when its proximity and so forth are taken into account, and because the suitability or unsuitability of things is known from other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no reason to bypass the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which is presented with extreme effort in order to avoid contradicting the injunction. Furthermore, since all productive urges toward results are untenable without some specific verbal root-meaning, it is understood that [the instrument is] "by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena*).

This meditation, being complete in its two constituent parts, requires a specification of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—namely, "how one should meditate"—because it is impossible for any instrument (*karaṇa*) to function as such unless it is assisted by an auxiliary means (*upāya*). And since that procedure cannot be known through perception or other ordinary means of knowledge, as it is entirely beyond their scope, it is established in whatever way possible according to proximity; that is, it is postulated through the authority of scripture, through direct instruction, through general injunctions, or through extended application (*atideśa*), by means of an entirely unseen assistance (*adṛṣṭopakāra*), as otherwise it would be inexplicable.

Therefore, because the means [of knowledge] are complete, it is enjoined that [the person] is qualified; and from the injunction of that [qualification], by implication (*arthāpatti*), the injunction of sacrifice and so forth follows.
Or: (Laṇḍaśaḥ), p. 383–386.
Regarding *bhāvanā*:

since effort (*prayatna*) is a property of consciousness (*cetanā*), it cannot occur without consciousness; thus, consciousness possesses independence with respect to effort because its status as an agent (*kartṛtva*) is absolute. Since there is no action whatsoever—whether expressed by the term *bhāvanā* consisting of effort—that is devoid of an agent, it is impossible for the agent and *bhāvanā* not to be concomitant. As stated in the *Sphuṭārthā* (p. 1398): "The *bhāvanā*, which is called the suffixal meaning, is not established without an agent."
Page 1399, *bhāvanā*:

Since the distinction from the *bhāvanā* called "effort" (*prayatna*)—due to its having a different nature—is self-evident, the unity of the universal must be asserted through the appearance of that distinction; and that is indeed desired.
Page 706, *bhāvanā*.

And when, because it depends solely on the pure cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and does not require any other verbal root meaning (*dhātvartha*), there is no expectancy for a divisible [element], and because a difference in cultivation necessarily entails a difference in the *apūrva* to be produced, it is not logical for that which is to be accomplished to be delimited by a single cultivation. (Page 709) As long as the cultivation is not fulfilled by the "what," "by what means," and "how" factors, the injunction (*vidhi*) does not operate.
Or rather: [Sūtra 3.4.67] Bhāvanā, whether as an operation (*vyāpāra*) or as effort (*yatna*), is expressed by the suffix;
and that [effort] is always...
Bhāvanā (3026): [The term] bhāvanā is transitive;
and its connection occurs precisely as the primary qualificand (mukhyaviśeṣya) of that bhāvanā.

Maṇi, p. 110: Bhāvanā is obtained as qualified by all the kārakas [through the nominal suffixes], whereas it is obtained as qualified by all the kārakas through the verbal root (kriyāpada). Bāla., p. 74: Bhāvanā, qualified by all its qualifiers, is enjoined. Ṭup., 1.1.13: Bhāvanā.

Since an accomplished existence (*siddhabhāvanā*) lacks the capacity to produce an unaccomplished state of being due to its fixed terminus, and since productivity is impossible without an operation (*vyāpāra*), and since a productive activity cannot be directed toward another without being established elsewhere, and because it must necessarily involve the operation of constituent parts that cause the accomplished existence, and because it resides in those constituent parts which are themselves caused by that accomplished existence, one must admit a general operation whose nature consists in being colored by the meanings of all verbal roots residing therein.

And that [activity] is called *bhāvanā* because it possesses both the state of having a goal to be accomplished (*sādhyabhāvakatva*) and the nature of being an operation directed toward that which is to be brought into being (*bhāvya-niṣṭha-bhava-vyāpāratva*).

(Su. p. 569). Since even verbal roots denoting intransitive actions are observed to be coreferential with the root *kṛ* (to do)—as in "What is he doing? He sits" (*kiṃ karoti? āste*) and "What is he doing? He lies down" (*kiṃ karoti? śete*)—it is established that *bhāvanā* is transitive (*sakarmaka*) even in such cases.
Therefore, there is no distinction between transitive and intransitive [roots] in this regard.
It is to be set aside.
Furthermore, we shall establish later how, this being the case, the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) functions as the primary qualifier (*mukhya-viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to that [object].

Moreover, in your view, the causal relation would have to terminate as follows: for a verbal cognition produced by a verb-form, delimited by the property of being a verbal cognition, which is characterized by a qualificative relation (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*) determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) residing in an object distinct from the three times; there must be a cause consisting in the presentation of an object that is not a qualifier of anything else, produced by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta-pada*), and related to it by the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*). Such a causal relation would be untenable.
And that [alternative] is not possible;

for in cases such as ‘Caitra does not cook’, ‘Caitra indeed cooks’, and ‘Caitra also cooks’, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix, being construed with Caitra alone. Consequently, it would be impossible to construe the meaning of the particle *nañ* (negation) with the absence [of cooking], or the meaning of the particle *eva* (indeed) with the exclusion [of others], or the meaning of the word *api* (also)—which consists in conjunction—with a partial difference [in the action]. Furthermore, because number would be construed with Caitra in those instances, the rule that “number is construed with the qualificand of the *bhāvanā*” would also be subject to violation.

For this very reason, "not being co-uttered with a particle" (*nipātāsamabhivyāhṛtatvam*) is not a qualifier of the verb (*ākhyāta*), because otherwise number (*saṃkhyā*) would fail to apply to Caitra. Nor can it be argued that, even with that qualifier, one might accept a separate causal relationship between number and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) in instances where they are not co-uttered with a particle, thereby accounting for their respective applications to their own substrata;
for this would entail the postulation of multiple causal relationships.

However, if [the particle] is not so designated, then since all [elements] would be the primary qualificand (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) through their connection with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)—by virtue of a single cause-and-effect relationship in the manner to be described—that [undesired] consequence would not arise.
Furthermore, there is no uniformity even by way of being common to all particles (*nipāta*);

for in cases such as "Caitra alone cooks" (*caitra eva pacati*) or "A jar alone is seen" (*ghaṭa eva dṛśyate*), even when a particle is used in close conjunction, both number and the productive urge are perceived as connected to Caitra.

Nor is there any rule that such a disparity between number and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) occurs only in cases where they are expressed by the same verb and not elsewhere; for in examples such as "Caitra does not cook" (*pacati na caitraḥ*) or "Caitra is not cooking" (*caitro na pacati*), the disparity exists in both ways.

Therefore, according to your view, because of the relation of cause and effect and because of the resulting inconsistency, the productive urge cannot have the word ending in the nominative case as its qualificand.

Moreover, in the sentence "He cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), since there is no word ending in the nominative case, the cognition of the *bhāvanā* as a qualifier (of the subject) is impossible precisely due to the absence of that cause. Therefore, when the *bhāvanā* is the primary qualificand by virtue of other causal factors, there is no obstacle [to its being so]. Nor should it be argued that, in accordance with experience, one should postulate a causal relation for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) only toward that which is delimited by being a qualifier of the *bhāvanā*, and thus assume the ellipsis of a nominative word to account for such a cognition; for it would be overly complex (*gaurava*) to postulate such a causal relation based on a determination that relies on mere testimony of experience.

Furthermore, even in cases such as "Caitra is struck" (*paṇihataścaitraḥ*), where there is no finite verb (*ākhyātapada*), there is no possibility of the nominative-ending term being the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*); for the suffix (*suv*) is a cause only with respect to a cognition whose content is delimited by having the meaning of the nominal suffix (*suvartha*) as its qualifier, and because, according to the method to be explained, the nominative case also possesses a meaning other than number.

Even if [the verb] is redundant, there is no fault, because one can postulate that the word generated by a nominative case-ending (*prathamāntapada*) is the cause for a cognition delimited by having as its qualifier (*prakāra*) that which is established by a nominative case-ending; thus, the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of a verbal form (*ākhyātapada*) is justified in such instances.

Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vini-gamanāviraha*), because this is not a defect since it is sanctioned by the traditional rule (*smṛti*): "The verb *as* (in the present tense, *bhavantīpara*) in the first person is understood even when it is not explicitly used" (*bhavantīpara* means *laṭpara*, i.e., referring to the present tense). For in the absence of such an injunction, the aforementioned cognition would simply not arise.

Furthermore, if the knowledge of a verbal suffix (*ākhyātapada*) is held to be the cause for a cognition delimited by the nature of a cognition whose mode is a type of *bhāvanā* (productive activity), then in cases of *bhāva*-suffixes such as "it is slept by Caitra" (*caitreṇa supyate*) or "it is stayed in the sky" (*gagane sthīyate*), there would be the undesirable consequence of having to supply a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntapada*).

If, on the other hand, one accepts that in those instances there is indeed a cognition of a specific meaning of the suffix and posits "being born from a *bhāva*" (*bhāvamijatva*) as the delimiting factor of the causality, then even that involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

In our view, however, since in all cases the meaning of the verb is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣyaka*), and because in instances of impersonal (*bhāva*) verbal forms the agent is not expressed, there is no possibility for a nominative case ending on a word ending in the first case suffix.

Furthermore, if the connection between the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) and number were to occur with that which is in the nominative case and not qualified by anything else, then in cases such as "Caitra alone cooks" (*caitra eva pacati*) or "Only a jar is seen" (*ghaṭa eva dṛśyate*), where would the connection of the productive operation and number take place, or how would the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arise? It cannot be in Caitra and the like, because he (Caitra) functions as a qualifier through the relation of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) in relation to the difference—which is a part of the indeclinable *eva*—that is fit for connection with the meaning of *eva*.

Nor can there be a connection of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) with the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), which constitutes the meaning of the particle *eva*, through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitātva*); nor can there be a connection of number with another entity, which also constitutes the meaning of *eva*, through the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatā*), because neither of these two possesses the status of being the referent of a word ending in the nominative case. Furthermore, the application of the nominative case after an indeclinable (*avyaya*)—as in the case of "curd remains" (*dadhi tiṣṭhati*)—is not possible here. Even if that status were granted, the connection of the *pākabhāvanā* (the efficient force of cooking) with Caitra would still be untenable.
Just as in the case of Caitra, even when there are many [agents], the use of the singular number—as in “Caitra alone cooks”—is observed.

For this very reason, the view that the word *pacati* (‘cooks’) possesses a variety of etymological derivations (*vyutpatti*) such that one accepts the connection of both [the agent and the absence of action]—resulting in a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) where the object of the injunction is specified as “one distinct from Maitra who possesses an effort conducive to cooking, and the absence of an effort conducive to cooking”—is refuted. This is because the singular number cannot logically apply there [to both], and furthermore, since Caitra functions as a qualifier for another [the absence], it is likewise illogical for him to be connected to both.

Furthermore, the word "Caitra" does not convey its meaning twice—once as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and once as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Consequently, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) would result in: "Caitra possesses an effort conducive to cooking" and "Caitra lacks an effort conducive to cooking. Moreover, being a qualifier for another [term] must be defined as the absence of being a qualificand;
or rather, it should be stated as the absence of that specific kind of qualifierhood which constitutes being a qualificand.

Nevertheless, just as in the cases of "Caitra and Maitra go" (*caitro maitraśca gacchataḥ*) and "Caitra, Maitra, and others go" (*caitro maitrādyaśca gacchanti*), there would result only dual and plural endings;

nor would it be the case that, as in "Caitra goes, but Maitra does not," where there is a difference of sentences due to a difference in the primary subjects, here too there would result a difference of sentences due to a difference in the primary qualificands. Rather, the understanding is that there is a single productive activity (*bhāvanā*) residing in Caitra and residing in one other than Caitra, having a single agent.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction because the property of having Caitra as the counter-correlative is only optional, or because the word *eva* itself has a secondary figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) in that context.

In reality, however, if one asks, "What are Caitra and Maitra like? when it is known that "Caitra cooks and Maitra does not cook," the answer "Caitra alone cooks" would result [as the only possible response].
For this very reason, if one asks, "What is Caitra like?", the answer "He cooks" would [otherwise] result.
It has been stated that there is no cognition whose primary qualificand (viśeṣya) ends in the nominative case.
Furthermore, it has been stated that the answer to the question "Of what nature is the effort? does not involve metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).
Therefore, the fact that the productive urge (bhāvanā) is the primary qualificand is established by direct experience itself.
*Rahasya*, pp. 25–30. Furthermore, as was stated previously, even in the case of a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), agency and so forth are merely indicated (*lakṣaṇa*);
moreover, that agency and so forth is not the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), but rather the productive urge itself is the qualificand of that [agency].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*apatti*) of the usage "He says he cooks" (*pacati brūte*).
This is because [the agent] is fit for that [action], just as in the expression "the cooker says" (*paktā brūte*).
Furthermore, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of not accounting for the usage cited in the Bhāṣya: "he cooks and exists" (*pacati bhavati*).

As for the usage cited as "he has cooked and exists" (*apākṣīt bhavati*) and "he cooks and exists" (*pacati bhavati*), that is not improper, because we accept a verbal cognition based on the fact that the action of cooking—whether past or future—is connected with the present through the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being connected with the root *bhū* (to exist). Thus, it is connected with the present by virtue of its connection with existence.
And in this way, the usage *loke bhavati* occurs in the sense of "it is appropriate";

likewise, even the usage *pacati bhavati* is not tenable if [the verb] functions as a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇatva*). For if that were the case, the usage *pacanti bhavanti* would result.

This is because the traditional authority of the *Nirukta*, which states that "the verb denotes the efficient force (*bhāva-pradhānam ākhyātam*)," declares that the efficient force denoted by the verbal root is the primary element with respect to the entire meaning of the verb, excluding the efficient force itself; for here, it is not understood that the efficient force is primary with respect to the meaning of the verbal root alone. This is established by the traditional rule itself—"The root and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, but of these two, the suffix is primary"—which demonstrates that the primacy of the suffix-meaning relative to the root-meaning applies universally, including to the meanings of nominal suffixes.

Nor should it be argued that the view of the Grammarians alone is correct, on the grounds that—following the grammatical tradition (*vaiyākaraṇasmṛti*) which states, "The mere, pure meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is designated as *bhāva* (action/state)"—the word *bhāva* is determined to refer to the meaning of the root; and that by this very tradition (*bhāvapradhānamākhyātam*), the primacy of that [root-meaning] over the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is established, while the tradition regarding the primacy of the suffix-meaning must be explained as referring generally to the meaning of nominal suffixes (*suvartha*). [Reason: This is because the rule "the verb has the action as its primary meaning" (*bhāvapradhānamākhyātam*) is a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) that establishes the primacy of the root-meaning (*bhāva*) in relation to the meaning of the verbal suffix. However, the tradition concerning the primacy of the suffix-meaning is of a general scope and should be interpreted with reference to the meaning of nominal suffixes. Therefore, the position of the Grammarians alone is logical. [Response: This is not so. Why? Because... [text continues].
Since this [rule] is of the nature of a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), it does not apply elsewhere, just as in the case of *nadī-dvandva* and similar rules.

For this very reason, its application occurs only within the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) in instances such as "the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state" (*bhāve ghañ*, Pāṇini 3.3.18).
Even that [application] does not occur everywhere, as it does not apply in cases such as "the suffix *kvun* is used in the sense of an abstract state" (*bhāve kvun*).

Therefore, by the word *bhāva* as explained etymologically, derived from the root *bhū* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *a*, and because it shares the same suffixal ending, what is expressed is precisely the *bhāvanā* consisting of the activity of the agent, not the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). For this very reason, the argument that— since the traditional rule (smṛti) stating "every verb is a noun" implies that the word *ākhyāta* refers to the verbal root, and since even by this rule the predominance of the *bhāva* belongs to the root alone— the status of the meaning of the root as the primary qualificand is established— is also refuted.

In the case of *kṛdanta* forms such as *pācaka*, since there is no employment of a finite verb (*ākhyāta*), it has been demonstrated in the *Kaustubha* that the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself possesses the character of the finite verb in those instances. Consequently, when the question arises as to which among the meanings of the finite verb is primary and which is secondary, the traditional rule (*smṛti*)—“The finite verb has the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) as its primary meaning” (*Nirukta* 1.1)—establishes that, with respect to any meaning of the finite verb other than the efficient force, the efficient force alone is primary.
For this very reason, the causal relationship [between the finite verb and its meaning] is one that applies equally to time and other factors, which is a matter of parsimony (*lāghava*).
*Rahasya*, pp. 38–39: On *bhāvanā*: its status as the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*).

Since everything denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) other than *bhāvanā* functions solely as a qualifier (*prakāratā*) with respect to *bhāvanā*, it is established that *bhāvanā* possesses the status of the primary qualificand.
p. 46: On *bhāvanā*: its status as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthatva*).

Su. P. 683: Regarding *bhāvanā*, [the opponent in] the *pūrvapakṣa* maintains that since the requirement for the *itikartavyatā* (the "how" of performance) is satisfied merely by its connection with the *saṃnipatyopakārin* (directly contributing) *itikartavyatā*, the nature of the requirement for the *itikartavyatā* consists in [the need for] the *ārādupakārin* (remotely contributing) *itikartavyatā*. P.
1193: Regarding *bhāvanā*, there is a requirement for the form consisting of the end (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the *itikartavyatā*.

p. 449: Even when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is being analyzed, the injunction (*vidhi*) is understood to apply to the *bhāvanā*, which constitutes the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), even though that *bhāvanā* is intended as a qualifier [of the root-meaning]. p. 1132: A pure *bhāvanā* cannot be the object of an injunction.

p. 154. Regarding the inquiry as to whether or not there is a desired fruit (*iṣṭaphala*) in *bhāvanā*, one should consult the section titled "The Topic of One Desiring Heaven" (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*) in the *Bhāṭṭa* treatise.

In *bhāvanā*, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) possesses a mode-of-presentation (*prakāratā*) through its relation as either the object (*karman*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). Rahasya, p. 57: In *bhāvanā*, [cognitions] such as excellence (*prāśastya*) have the object of worship (*ārādhya*) as their mode-of-presentation.

Just as in the case of a meal, where rice is the primary instrument (*karaṇa*), vegetables, soup, and so forth are the "conjointly assisting" factors (*saṃnipatyopakārin*), and the seat, lamp, and so forth are the "remotely assisting" factors (*ārādupakārin*); it is the same here. (Vivaraṇa 8.13, Section 2). In the Brāhmaṇa, by means of sentences concerning the Agnihotra and other rites, persons are enjoined toward the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) consisting of the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*).

In reality, since a suffix expresses its own meaning precisely as that which excludes the meanings of the verbal roots [it precedes], therefore, even in the sentence expressing the result (*phalavākya*), it is not possible for multiple exclusions of root-meanings to occur within a single efficient force (*bhāvanā*) by means of those [meanings] residing in a pure efficient force.

(Sphuṭārthā, p. 707). If it is argued that this is because [in cases like] *āsittikṣaya* ("the cessation of pouring") there is no requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*), and in [cases like] "moving" or "falling," there is merely the bringing about of a specific designation, [we reply: no, because that [suffix] is not accepted as having the meaning of a suffix.

If the suffix were a single entity, it would be impossible for there to be a plurality of denotata due to the difference in the denoters; for [otherwise] there would be no connection between the distinct denoters and a single denotatum.
It is therefore correct that verbal roots (*dhātu*) are manifold in nature, as they denote various meanings by virtue of being in grammatical apposition with the verb *karoti* (‘to do’).
Furthermore: because the usage of the suffix is observed in two ways, both when an action exists and when it does not.
The universal residing within the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) arrives at the meaning of "doing" (*karoti*).
In the expression "What is he doing? The bell rings," there is nothing other than the sound that is produced.
Or, even if such [an action] exists, it is not intended to be expressed, because there is a desire to know only the meaning of the verbal root.
And thus, there is no manifestation of what was previously non-existent.
Therefore, even though that [manifestation] is absent in reality, when the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is employed in the sense of "accomplishment" (*sādhana*), as in "I have done," it is so;

likewise, because here there is an inquiry into the mere meaning of the verbal root—as in "What is the action? Cooking"—there is grammatical coreferentiality (*aikādhikaraṇya*) based on the nature of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) itself, which serves as the cause for the specific qualification of that activity.
If it is argued that [the object] is dependent on the "being traversed" (*gamyamāna*), we say no, because this would apply even to verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) ending in *pratyaya*.

If it is argued that [the object] is denoted by suffixes ending in *śit* due to their predominance, we say no, because here too the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is understood as a qualifier of that very [object].

The meaning of the verse is as follows: from the expression “he cooks with wood” (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*), there arises the cognition of [wood] as an instrument (*karaṇatva*); however, since substances are grasped by their mode of being (*kathaṃbhāvanā*), there would be no syntactic connection (*samabhivyāhāra*) such as “he cooks with wood.

First of all, the wood cannot have a relation to the meaning of the verbal root, because factors of action (*kāraka*)—which depend upon an action—cannot be connected with another factor of action that does not share their nature.

Nor can there be a connection through the act of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because that [cultivation] does not depend upon another factor (*kāraka*). Nor can there be a connection by way of being a different constituent part, because the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is established by verbal testimony (*śabda*). Thus, since the state of being an instrument is restricted to an action, and since there is no instrumentality in the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which is non-actional in nature, there is a relationship [of instrumentality] in the expression "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*).

If it is argued that the connection [of the word] is through the meditation on the noble eye (*aryākṣitabhāvanā*), we say no; for the connection is destroyed by the intervention of intermediate parts.
Indeed, the understanding of the connection is not the same in "a pot with clay" (*mṛdā ghaṭam*) as in "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*);
because in the former case there is a desire for those [intermediate parts], whereas in the latter case one perceives something else.

Umbeka: If one accepts a relationship mediated by the mental impression (bhāvanā) implied by the meaning, then one would be accepting a mediated relationship, because that necessarily presupposes the supply of an unexpressed action that is required, as in the case of "a jar with clay" (*mṛdā ghaṭam*).

But here it is not so, because there is no requirement for an unexpressed action. For instance, when "a jar" (*ghaṭam*) is said, the verbal root "to make" (*karoti*) is indeed supplied, but it is not in this manner [of implication].
No distinction is conceived between "they cause to cut" (*vicchidyanti*) and "they cut" (*pacanti*).
If agency resides in the operation of the verbal root (*dhātu*), what then is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)? Umbeka comments:
Since the suffix expresses the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) in both cases, it serves as the indicator (*liṅgi*) for the verbal root. Thus says Āditya.

Furthermore, in both cases—*vicchidyante* and *pacanti*—the causal operation (*prayojakavyāpāra*) is expressed by the suffix, while the action of softening (*viklitti*) is expressed by the two verbal roots; thus, there would be no difference in meaning. [Objection:
But surely there is a difference in the agent and a difference in the operation; since these are expressed, there is no fault.
For instance, in *vicchidyante*, the agents are the rice grains (*taṇḍula*), whereas in *pacanti*, the agents are Devadatta and others.

Furthermore, you have spoken as if considering the agent (*kartṛ*) to be defined by [the action], such as the application of the means (*sādhana-niyoga*) and so forth; however, if that were so, how could rice grains possess agency? This would lead to the undesirable consequence (*avaśeṣa-prasaṅga*) that only Devadatta and others are agents. Alternatively, if [agency] is defined by the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) as being devoid of qualities (*aguṇatayā*), then the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya-artha*) would be [that very operation]; for the operation of the agent, which is *bhāvanā*, is already denoted by the verbal root itself. Thus, the operation that constitutes *bhāvanā*—which consists of both the fruit and the meaning of the verbal root—is what is expressed by the verbal root.
But [it is argued that] the meaning of the result (phalārtha) is expressed by the suffix and has the meaning of the verbal root as its instrument (dhātvarthakaraṇaka).
This is not sound.
For the meaning of the verbal root as an instrument does not possess the power to bring about a distinction in the result.
[Umbeka: There is an alternative reading: "The operation is seen between the meaning of the verbal root and the difference in the result.

Even that which is observed in cases where the result is remote is not the meaning of the suffix; rather, it consists of something internal to the meaning of the verbal root such as *han* (to kill) and the like.
This is because the production of a further effort cannot be brought about by the influence of the preceding verbal root.

[Umbeka:—Therefore, just as in the case of *pāka* (cooking) and so forth, the meaning of verbal roots such as *pacati* (he cooks), which arises from a distinct effort (*prayatna*), is not the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), so it is here as well; this is the sense. ...
There is a variant reading: *sa prāyo dhātugocaraprabhāvanīyaḥ*.

Even there, this is the meaning: although in cases like the *śyena* sacrifice, where the result is remote, there exists another operation denoted by the suffix, nevertheless that activity of the agent is indeed to be brought forth (*prabhāvanīya*) within the scope of verbal roots such as *pacati*.]
Indeed, there is no second action of the fruit (*phala-karma*) by which it could be expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*).
Therefore, only that which constitutes its constituent part is to be stated as the meaning of the suffix.
The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that whose manifestation (*prabhāvanīya*) is within the scope of the verbal root (*dhātu*)."

That is to say, it has as its object the meaning of verbal roots such as *pāka* (cooking) and so forth. Furthermore, since the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do) is pervaded by the object, there is an absence of that [object] even when the suffixes serve to establish the meaning of the affix (*pratyaya*). Thus, the case-endings (*vibhakti*) are not connected to it.
Umbeka says: "In this way, there is no other action expressed by the suffix"—this is what he means by the words "by the object" (*karmaṇā*).
Since actions reside in that which is being acted upon, in the absence of that [object], there is an absence of action.
As it has been said: "The verb 'to do' (*karoti*) never exists without an object in relation to that which is being done."
Furthermore, in such injunctions as "one who desires heaven should sacrifice," heaven and the like are indeed objects (*karman*).

As for the notion of "objectness" that arises in that context, it occurs because of the absence of the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*). That absence, however, is due to the fact that case-endings (*kāraka-vibhakti*) have as their domain the *kārakas* that are the meanings of the verbal root.

And thus, in the example “Devadatta cooks wood for the sake of both [eating and offering]” (*ubhayāmodanaṃ kāṣṭhair devadattaḥ pacati*), case-endings are observed for the factors (*kāraka*) of the verbal root’s meaning, but not for the factors of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), such as heaven and so forth. To this doubt, he says: “In the meaning of the suffix. This is its meaning: a case-ending must be applied even to the factor of the productive activity, which is the meaning of the suffix; for no specific rule for case-endings is prescribed by such injunctions as “the second case for the object” (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) or “the third case for the agent and the instrument” (*kartṛ-karaṇayos tṛtīyā*).

Furthermore, we do not perceive a second [agent] in heaven; therefore, it is understood that action does not exist there. Since the verb *karoti* (to do) is always transitive, we perceive the absence of the meaning of "doing" in the absence of an object, just as we perceive the absence of smoke in the absence of fire.
For instance, such a connection as "one should sacrifice for heaven," "one should lie down for health," or "one should sit for pleasure" has never been observed.

[Umbeka says: Because an action possesses an object, in the absence of something being acted upon, that action cannot exist—just as in the absence of its pervader, there is an absence of smoke; this is what he means by the word *karoti*.
If one should think that this is so simply because of the absence of a distinct case-ending capable of expressing the connection, [then the following applies].

For instance, the case-endings (*suvibhakti*) grasp the *bhāvanā* whose meaning is the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because they are seen to function with respect to the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), which is the meaning of the suffix, such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).

[Umbeka states: This is the meaning: with respect to heaven and the like, which are the objects of the *bhāvanā* denoted by the suffix; and with respect to the sacrifice and the like, which are the objects of the injunction (*niyoga*)—a synonym for "prescription" (*vidhi*)—which serve as its instrument; the second and third case-endings, signifying the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), are not observed.
The status of the sacrifice and so forth as the object of the injunction is due to their being the objective domain (*viṣaya*).

In the phrase "svargakāmādi" (one desiring heaven, etc.), the locative case is used with a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) in reference to the object of the injunction that constitutes the meaning of the suffix.

The meaning is that the case-ending denoting a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is observed in the word "svargakāmādi" when it functions as the object of the injunction which is the meaning of the suffix.
Alternatively, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Because the proponent of the final doctrine (siddhāntavādin) accepts that words such as "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma) refer to the fruit [of the action],
the meaning [of the objection] therefore becomes this:

because no case-ending indicative of an instrumental factor (kāraka-vibhakti) is observed for the ritual act (karman), which is the specific object of the productive urge (bhāvanā) directed toward heaven and so forth.
And that is trivial;
for if it were so, the genitive case, which is the cause of the relationship in the state of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*), would have its application unimpeded.
[Umbeka: "That is trivial" means this has not been understood and is not authoritative.]

If, because there is no second [word] for heaven (*svarga*), the status of heaven as the object (*karman*) is not intended to be expressed, then—by the maxim that "the non-intention of case-factors (*kāraka*) constitutes the remainder (*śeṣa*)"—there would be a genitive case based on the definition of the remainder, such as *svargasya yajeta* (one should sacrifice for the sake of heaven), which would express a relationship between heaven and the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). Yet we do not perceive such a [genitive]. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no distinct connection with the object.

Furthermore, this cannot be determined from names such as *viśvajit* and others, which denote the object of the suffix (pratyaya) and function as instruments (*karaṇa*) within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), because they are capable of being construed with the instrumental case-ending.

If it is argued that there is indeed a connection with the object (*karman*) in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), [Umbeka replies: But surely, in the word "one desiring heaven," heaven itself is what is heard.

But that [object] is fit to be accomplished as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) requires something to be produced; therefore, there is indeed a connection with the action even without another accusative case-ending—this is what he objects with the words "there certainly is.
No, because it is directly connected as a qualification of the person.
If it is argued that it is directly connected in the sense of "one should sacrifice for the sake of heaven" (*svargārthaṃ yajeta*).

No, because it does not have the nature of an action (*karma*), and there is an absence of connection with the nature of an action due to the absence of the expression of *bhāvanā*. Furthermore, its status as a non-action is established by the use of the dative case. [Umbeka: But surely, since the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is understood through the force of the context to be one who desires the fruit, the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) does not intend to convey anything other than the mere attainment of heaven; consequently, there is no connection with any other person.
And thus the meaning is this: "One should sacrifice for the sake of heaven. This is what he objects to with the words "for heaven" (*svargeya*).

And because there is a connection even with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), as in "the sacrifice is for the sake of heaven," Umbeka says: "The status of being an object (*karmatva*) is not understood for that which is indicated by the dative case."

In expressions such as "he cooks after having eaten" (*bhukte pacati*) or "he eats for the sake of satisfaction" (*tṛptaye bhuṅkte*), even though satisfaction and the like are indicated by the dative case, the action is understood as having rice and the like as its object (*karmika*), not satisfaction and the like as its object; this is the meaning. Furthermore, the dative case is not established [by rule] in reference to the object (*karman*). If the connection with an object were admitted solely on the basis of the dative indication, then, since there is no distinction [in that regard], it would follow that heaven (*svarga*) and so forth would also have the status of being an object (*karmatva*) in relation to the act of eating; thus he says: "for the sake of heaven" (*svargāya*).
Therefore, it is established that due to the absence of action (*karman*), there is an absence of further activity (*kriyā*).

It follows [absurdly] that the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*) would be identical [to the root meaning]. For who is the referent of the suffix (*pratyaya*) when the agent (*kartṛ*) is indeed the operation of the verbal root (*dhātu*)?

It would follow that one could say "the potter produces the jar" (*bhāvayati ghaṭam*) as well as "the jar comes into being" (*bhavati ghaṭam*), because the meaning is identical. For in the former case, there is an inquiry into the activity of the agent, the potter, while in the latter case, it is expressed by the verbal suffix; thus, the meaning does not differ.

The meaning of the verbal root (*nijartha*) [is expressed] through the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*), while the operation of the agent (*kartṛvyāpāra*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*); thus, even for one who maintains that there is a plurality of meanings [in a single word], he must explain here the distinction between the agent and the instigator.

If the agent is the one who sets the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) into motion and withdraws them, and if that agent is one and the same—namely, the potter (*kumbhakāra*) himself—then because his own operation is being denoted, the meanings are identical.

If it is argued that the jar is the agent (*kartṛ*) and the potter is the instigator (*prayojaka*), how can there be such agency for one who has arisen through an impulse directed toward an unsharpened instrument, bypassing the potter? Or, if [agency] consists in the state of having an activity denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) regardless of its qualities, then what now remains as the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)? Since the activity would already have been denoted by the root, there would be no perception of a distinction in activity by which a division between the root and the suffix could be established.

Furthermore, since the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) of the root-meaning—whether derived from the verbal suffix itself or from something else—is equally distinguished in both cases, it is unavoidable that they have the same meaning.
Therefore, it is well said that the suffix does not denote the efficient force (bhāvanā). By what aspect, then, is the meaning of the causative form of the root *bhū* expressed?

Furthermore: If *bhāvanā* were observed as the activity of the agent in the case of roots such as *pac* (to cook), then that [activity], which consists of placing the pot on the fire and so forth, would have to be a different entity from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). And if *bhāvanā* is the activity of the agent, and that [activity] exists in the case of [roots like] *path* (to go) and others—
When it is required that "it acts slowly," meaning that the specific qualities such as rapidity and so forth are being considered, [the agent] perceives that very [quality];
otherwise, it would be established [differently]. He says: "by rapidity."
There would be no distinction between *viklidyati* (it softens) and *āviśati* (he enters).

Umbeka explains: This is the meaning— if, like *sidhyati* (it is accomplished) and *viklidyati*, the root *pac* were also to denote the operation of the instigator (*prayojya*), then, just as in the case of "Devadatta accomplishes it," one would not obtain grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the agent through a difference in agents, as in "Devadatta cooks.

Even if one does not accept that, since [the action of] placing on the fire and so forth is the meaning of other verbal roots (*dhātu*), there can be no sublation of the primary meaning of the root otherwise.

Now, if it is thought that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—which is not manifest as a self-sufficient entity and which is the object of a cognition appearing as "he does" (*karoti*)—is distinct from these [other meanings] and is the category of *bhāvanā*, that is incorrect.
For in that case, being included within the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it would be merely the general form of the meaning of the verbal root;
the category of *bhāvanā* would not be a distinct category of meaning.
Now, it may be thought: it is true that the universal [of action] is not established as having a specific form like "cowness" (gotva) and so forth;

rather, because it is connected with its own particular universals—such as "it performs quickly for each person" or "it performs slowly"—there exists only the universal of the instrument (karaṇa-sāmānya) within the meaning of the verbal root.
And it has been said: "The general form of the root-meaning, characterized by its instrumental function, is indeed one thing;
and that which is called *bhāvanā*, established as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is another."
This is untenable;
for indeed, there is no single cognition that persists through the performance of various actions,
since we perceive two universals associated with what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

For the cognition "the instrument is an instrument" does not arise regarding objects such as a path (pathin) and so forth in the absence of action and its factors; otherwise, one would have to postulate a general meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consisting of the instrument itself, distinct from the form of action.

Furthermore, [terms like] "swift" and so forth are merely internal distinctions within the general meaning of the verbal root—as explained by the word *karoti*—just as "red-eared" and so forth are internal distinctions of a horse.
And it has been said: "Indeed, the operation [of the agent] does not consist in the performance of the root-meaning due to the influence of a difference in the result;
rather, an operation is observed in the interval between the root-meaning and the difference in the result."
Umbeka: If you do not accept another *bhāvanā*—distinct from the form of the action (*kriyā*) and expressible by the suffix (*pratyaya*)—then what is it that is said to "perform quickly"?

Furthermore, in that case, there would be a distinction in definition between the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and the *bhāvanā*. Moreover, if *bhāva* is defined as "motion" (*parispanda*), it would be impossible in the case of sacrifices (*yajña*) and the like.

[Umbeka: "If there were a difference between the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), then a difference in form (*rūpabheda*) would have to be demonstrated, just as in the case of a jar and a cloth. Since that cannot be demonstrated, he says 'vācya' (denoted) with this intention. Now, one might object: 'A difference in form can indeed be demonstrated, for the *bhāva* consists of motion (*spanda*), whereas the meaning of the verbal root consists of non-motion (*aspanda*). Anticipating this doubt, he says 'bhāva'."
Furthermore, one who maintains that there is a difference between *bhāvanā* and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) must clearly demonstrate a formal distinction between the two.

If it is argued that the meaning of the root consists of non-motion while *bhāvanā* consists of motion, then in cases such as "he sacrifices" (*yajate*) or "he knows" (*jānāti*), where the agent is essentially non-moving and the meanings of the roots are unreal [in terms of physical motion], it would follow that *bhāvanā* is absent.
Conversely, in cases such as "he goes" (*gacchati*), it would follow that the meaning of the root itself is *bhāvanā*.
But the operation of volition was already addressed previously.

And what is this "motion" (*parispanda*)? Indeed, it is not perceived as distinct from its intended substratum. [Umbeka: This statement regarding "motion" intends to refer to disjunction; the meaning is that no motion characterized as something other than the conjunctions and disjunctions of Devadatta and so forth is perceived.]
How is it not understood? When, even though the substratum is perceptible, the cognition "it moves" occasionally arises, it must take an object distinct from that [substratum].
This is not sound.
The cognition "it moves" has as its object the effect characterized by disjunction and conjunction.
Therefore, no distinction is perceived between that which is grasped and that which remains ungrasped.
Umbeka: Furthermore, because the cognition "it moves" has as its objective basis the conjunctions and disjunctions that are the effects of Devadatta.
The meaning is that a distinct activity characterized by conjunction and disjunction, namely *spanda* (motion), is perceived as belonging to Devadatta.

By the word "effect" (*kārya*), he demonstrates the occasional nature of the cognition based on the occasional nature of the objective basis located therein; this is indicated by the phrase "therefore" (*tataḥ*).

The meaning is that when Devadatta moves from a stationary state, the distinction consists solely of conjunctions and disjunctions; there is no "motion" (spanda) as conceived by you that exists apart from those.
Indeed, that vibration is within the range of the senses and is accepted as having the result of conjunctions and disjunctions with preceding and succeeding locations.
And thus, those two alone constitute the cognition of being an object.
Indeed, one who does not perceive the abandoning of a preceding location and the taking up of a succeeding location is not understood to be "moving."
And ordinary people do not perceive [the movement] even when it is present before them with skill;
rather, it is only in space that the operation of the sense faculty, which has no contact with any location, is perceived as moving.
We perceive that space is the locus of objects;

therefore, conjunctions and disjunctions with that space [are what constitute motion]. Indeed, even one who has stopped after having moved possesses conjunctions and disjunctions, and thus [the definition] would over-apply to him as well.
To this we reply: since [motion] is established as having that [conjunction and disjunction with a limited portion of space] as its basis, there is no such over-extension.
It is understood.
[Umbeka says: By saying "having moved, it stands," he demonstrates that it possesses both conjunction and disjunction, which are its effects.
In this context, "stands" indicates possession of conjunction, while "having moved" indicates possession of disjunction.

Furthermore, since conjunction and disjunction produced by the action of either one [of two objects] possess a dual nature, there would follow the undesirable consequence that they would be perceived as resulting from the actions of both.

If it is argued that their status as such is due solely to the disjunction between the post and the hawk when they are joined together, then the same consequence would apply to those produced by the action of either one;
for at the moment the post is conjoined with one hawk, it is simultaneously disjoined from another.

[Umbeka: The meaning is that when a conjunction produced by one action occurs at the same time as a disjunction produced by another action, then—because of the simultaneous presence of both conjunction and disjunction—the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) follows that even a stationary post (sthāṇu) would be perceived as "moving.

Nor can those two [conjunction and disjunction] possessing a specific sequence be the objective basis [of the cognition], because such a cognition does not arise even when there is a subsequent conjunction with another hawk following a disjunction from a hawk previously in front.]
[Umbeka: This assumption of a whole (avayavin) is useless; for even if conjunction is preceded by disjunction from what is conjoined, there is no cognition that "it moves.
It is said in reply: The abandonment and acquisition of specific locations occur in an uninterrupted succession;
therefore, space is accepted as the location of those objects which move therein.

Umbeka: By the phrase "there is no production of non-existence," the objection regarding the contingency of the cognition [of motion] while [the object] remains stationary has been refuted; and by the mention of a specific location, [the objection regarding] the post-stump has been addressed.
This is what is meant:
the basis for the cognition "it moves" is the conjunction and disjunction with various contiguous locations.
Furthermore, when earth and other substances are present, a state of non-interruption cannot arise from conjunction and the like;
nor can there be dependence on a specific location in the case of a post, because the hawk does not occupy that location.
For it is held that space alone is the locus for all entities.

Indeed, the cognition "it moves" does not arise merely from conjunction and disjunction; rather, it arises when there is a continuous series of conjunctions and disjunctions produced without interruption. Furthermore, in the case of a stationary object, such a series is absent.
Moreover, conjunction and disjunction do not have a specific location as their object in the case of a post, because a location belongs only to that which possesses conjunction (the conjoined).
For it is not the case that the hawk is the location of the post.

Now, since space is not perceptible, and because conjunctions and disjunctions—such as those occurring between air and trees—are not resident in what is perceptible and are thus non-sensory, it is not logical for them to be the objects of a cognition produced by the senses.
[Umbeka notes: In some places the reading is "vāyuvanaspatiyogavibhāgānām," and in others "vāyuvanaspatiyogavad"; the latter is indeed correct.
The only fault lies in the failure to provide a philosophical justification.]
In the present case, however, this [objection] is to be set aside, because another resolution is possible; it should be understood as referring to the conjunction of a bird with a stone.
This is because the conjunction with a region of space and the conjunction of a bird with a stone occur respectively through direct and indirect operation—this is the meaning.
[Objection: But surely [the objection] is valid.
Otherwise, how could it be understood that the age [of the sound] has a fixed location other than its own?
For there would be conjunctions with locations through the production of disjunctions from two points, as manifested by the moving axle.
Umbeka: When a bird flies in the sky, there arises a visual cognition that "it is here" or "it is not here.
How could this be possible if the conjunction with space were imperceptible? For such a cognition occurs only when the conjunction is perceptible.
Likewise, space (*vyoman*) is also perceptible.
There exists a cognition of the nature of blue color, consisting of the earth and so forth, when the body is expanded; space is the objective support (*ālambana*) of that [cognition].
Otherwise, it would be entirely without an objective support.

Furthermore, the non-existence of earth and so forth cannot be the object [of cognition], because the cognition of the form of an existent thing is sensory in nature, and a cognition of non-existence is not sensory.
If it were claimed that non-existence is its object even though it does not appear [to consciousness], then the cognition of a cow would [likewise] have a horse as its object.
In this case, it would also follow that [space] is the primary objective support (*ālambana*).
But is it not the case that space is thus [defined]? Even though it is formless (*amūrta*), because it is omnipresent (*sarvagata*), it is independent (*svatantra*).

For if it were imperceptible (*apratyakṣa*), how could there be the momentary basis for the different locations of a bird in flight, resulting from its conjunction with and separation from the divisions of space?

If it is argued that "action [is known] through the inference of the effect from the cause," [Umbeka replies: "But even though the region of space is not perceptible, the cognition 'it has arrived here' arises precisely when there is a falling leaf occupying different points of space. How can this inference—which has as its object the effects of conjunction and disjunction—be produced by a cause that is action grasped through perception? Thus, he raises the objection with the words 'kriyā' (action), asserting that there is no fault."
Regarding the isolation through cultivation (*bhāvanāviveka*):
although inference (*anumāna*) [is a means], even when all other means are present,
one might object that a qualification of the person (*puruṣaviśeṣaṇa*) is simply not possible.
"Because there is no non-connection, the cognition 'he cooks' may occasionally arise;
for it is possible to exclude any one of these: connection, absolute non-connection, or something other than both."
[Answer]: Furthermore, it does not apprehend anything distinct from the factors of action (*kāraka*), because such a thing does not exist by way of its own nature (*jāti*).
Some have even proposed an inference regarding the aforementioned factors of action—wood, fire, rice, Devadatta, and so forth—[as follows]:
[Ummeka: But surely heaven does not function as a qualifier with respect to the person.
When there is a depositing of the village [as the object], at times the cognition "he cooks" occurs; at other times—
This is correct;
for a qualifier is indeed of three kinds: some [qualify] by connection—
It becomes established.
If it were caused solely by a producer,
then it would be [understood] through exclusion, as in the case of "Devadatta is fat."
But here, another condition would always be required, and such is not the case;
therefore, it must have another cause.
The exclusion of [the agent] through yoga is possible, because others such as Yaśadatta are also fat;
thus it is determined.
Therefore, from the cognition "he cooks," which is an effect, [one infers] the cause.
To this it is replied: "The charge of having multiple meanings or being otherwise [than what is intended] does not apply, because they share a single substratum;
by means of the verb 'to do' (karoti), the non-difference of the action (bhāva) is inferred in all finite verbal forms."

In the expression “he makes a jar” (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the verb *karoti* denotes a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) that falls within the scope of verbal roots such as *jan* (to beget) or *ut-pad* (to produce). Even when this [activity] stands in grammatical apposition with the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, it cannot apply to anything else; for if it were to have multiple meanings, there would be a lack of definiteness (*anaikāntikatva*), which would render it impossible to determine the specific denotation and lead to a failure in linguistic usage (*avyavahārāṅgatva*).

Since the application [of the verb] is established according to the capacity already understood, it is illogical to postulate another capacity; furthermore, because it is already perceived, one does not postulate what is unperceived. Moreover, even in a different usage, there is cognition of exactly that which was determined in another usage. And since the question "What does he do? is understood as having the sense of production (*utpādana*), it follows that verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta-pada*) denote specific instances of that [action], by virtue of their being in grammatical apposition with the word *karoti*, which expresses the general productive activity (*bhāvanā*). [Umbeka—He explains the meaning of the verse: "He makes a pot."]

For if the word *karoti* were multivalent, then upon its utterance, doubt would arise regarding its meaning even when it is not based on linguistic convention (*aśābda*), because of its lack of exclusivity (*anekāntikatva*). And in this way, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would not be possible;
yet such usage is observed to be grounded in a determined meaning, independent of considerations such as context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, the root *kṛ* (to do) has as its very meaning the act of bringing something into being (*bhāvanā*).

Although the suffix (*pratyaya*) conveys a specific distinction due to its own variation, the word (*pada*), however, primarily conveys a meaning of the suffix that corresponds to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), because of the difference in the base. Furthermore, the suffix is not independent like a word (*pada*) because it is constrained by its position relative to what precedes and follows; it does not convey a mere generality. Rather, in relation to the meaning of the base, it presents a specific meaning of its own that is distinct from it. In every respect, the word refers to a particular instance.

Therefore, since they are non-different from that [root-meaning], the inference of a specific denotation therein—which would clarify the distinction in the prescription of the root-meaning—is contradicted.
[Objection: But surely the general sense is the denotable object of the suffix; how then can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*aikādhikaraṇya*) between two [words] that denote a general sense?

[Umbeka replies: The suffix does not denote the general sense of *bhāvanā*, and *karoti* also does not denote the general sense of *bhāvanā*; nor is there coreferentiality between two [words] that denote a general sense.
It is said: Even when a general term is used as qualified by a particular, there is no separate mention; for example, when one asks "Which king is going?", the answer given is "The King of Pañcāla."

Umbeka: This is what is meant. Just as in the case of "King of Pañcāla," when the referent of the word "king" is understood as qualified by a specific Pañcāla—whether through proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) or through denotation (*abhidhāna*)—the word "who is the king? (which expresses the unqualified universal) stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the subsequent word "king," which denotes the universal as it is thus qualified; so too here. Therefore, there is no objection regarding the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), nor is there a lack of coreferentiality.

For the formulation of questions consists of scriptural statements whose general subject matter is delimited by a general term, and which employ a coreferential construction with the term "appropriation" (*parigraha*), as in: "Which king is going? The King of Pañcāla.
Moreover, the indication of the general in the answer is entirely appropriate; otherwise, that [general] would have to be sought within the question itself.
Furthermore, because meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not perceived as having distinct parts, its specific character is manifested through the influence of another [factor].
Therefore, there is neither the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), nor the proving of the opposite (*viparyayasādhana*), nor is it without an example (*adṛṣṭānta*).

[Umbeka: Therefore, when a specific entity is understood through the utterance of words such as "cooking" (*pāka*) due to the proximity of the suffix (*pratyaya*) and other factors, there is no proving of that which has already been established by the word "does" (*karoti*); for if that were so, the co-occurrence [of the two words] would be untenable due to redundancy.
Nor is there the proving of the opposite.]
Because we observe grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*).
For example: "Which king is going? The King of Pañcāla.
As for the phrase "not because there is no example," this is its meaning: it is not the case that there is no existing example to support this [position], since such an example does indeed exist.

Therefore, since there is an observed instance, the reason is not contradictory. Alternatively, even though the expression "the tree is the student" (*vṛkṣaḥ śiṣyaḥ*) lacks actual existence, it does not lack the status of being an instance.

Just as in the case of "student" (*chātra*), there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) restricted by both general and particular properties, so too is it in the case of the two verbal suffixes in "What does he do? He cooks" (*kiṃ karoti? pacati*).
The application [of the suffix] in the sense of existence or non-existence is not observed in either of the two ways;
ultimately, even that is seen to have its scope within the meaning of the verbal root itself.

Umbeka: It is never observed that the verb *karoti* (to do/make) is used without a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) when it is in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with either a verb or a noun, by which one could conclude that it does not denote the general sense of the verbal root-meaning.
For instance, in the expression "the bell rings" (*ghaṇṭā dhvanati*), the meaning of the action is expressed even in the absence of a productive activity;
yet this is incorrect, because every verbal root-meaning, by its very nature, consists in the production of something else and is therefore necessarily connected with a productive activity.

And here too, there exists pleasure or pain produced by soft or intense sound. If, however, because the verbal root [√dhvan] is intransitive, pleasure or pain is not accepted as the object of realization (bhāvya) based on the understanding of the word "sound" (*dhvani*) itself, then we must ultimately state that the object of realization is simply the meaning of the verbal root: "he performs sounding" (*dhvananaṃ karoti*). And this "sounding" consists of conjunction and disjunction, or the sound produced by them, as well as vibration (*parispanda*).
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of *karoti*":

even as for what was cited, such as "What is action? Cooking," there too the grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) is based on the non-distinction of the state (*bhāva*), not on the specific word "cooking" (*apaka*) as heard [in the sentence], by which the root *kṛ* would denote the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
This is what he says: "It is indicated in that way."

The statement "the bell rings" expresses the absence of productive activity (*bhāvanā*) due to the absence of fortune (or a causal agent). Since the meaning of every verbal root (*dhātvartha*) produces something that was previously non-existent—whether it be sound, pleasure, or pain—it is the verbal root-meaning itself, being infinite, that is to be brought about (*bhāvya*). [Umveka: In this regard, he demonstrates that just as there is no usage of the verb *karoti* (to do) when it is coreferential with a finite verb (*ākhyāta*) in the absence of productive activity, by saying "the bell": "The bell...
