Furthermore, if they were in grammatical apposition (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), it would follow that the word is an injunction of a subordinate accessory (*guṇavidhi*), which would result in the loss of the observed fact [of the word being a name].

Therefore, since the instrumental ending in *udbhidā* is certain to express the instrument (*karaṇa*), its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *yajate* (he sacrifices) confirms that the meaning is "by means of the sacrifice" (*yāgena*).

Having thus established that [the suffix] has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Bhāṣya—in the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*)—established that the meaning of the root comes first; they explained the meaning of "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) as "one should effect by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena kuryāt*).
Consequently, because it is understood to be in grammatical apposition with another word whose meaning is instrumental, there is the certainty that the meaning of the instrument has been explained.
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is indeed *bhāvanā* (productive activity) endowed with three factors.
It is established that [the accusative] does not denote the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

In the same way, even in a prescriptive sentence such as "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice" (*agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāmaḥ*), the accusative case must be explained as having the sense of the instrumental (*tṛtīyārtha*).
If it is asked, "How so with respect to the object (*karman*)? [the answer follows].
Because the sentence requires completion, words expressing desire (*kāma*) are indeed directed toward that [end].
That the qualifier is primary in cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) has already been demonstrated.
[Umbeka: But in the phrase "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), heaven is heard as the qualifier of the person, while the person is the qualificand.]

Therefore, it is logical that the word "desiring" (kāmin) refers to the qualified person (*viśeṣya-puruṣa*), and not that the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) refers to heaven which is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); having stated this and so forth, [the opponent asks] "How so?
[The author] provides the answer: "It is required."

Just as, because the selection of priests (*ṛtvij-pravaraṇa*) occurring within the Jyotiṣṭoma—including the primary injunctions and so forth—is already established by that [general] context, the statements “the priests proceed wearing red turbans” (*lohitoṣṇīṣā ṛtvijaḥ pracaranti*) and “the one with a staff recites the *praiṣas*” (*daṇḍī praiṣānanvāha*) are understood to be for the purpose of enjoining the qualifying attributes of the red turbans and the staff; likewise, since the person (*puruṣa*) is already established from another source, the meaning of the word *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven) is that its qualifying attribute, heaven (*svarga*), is what is being enjoined.

Although heaven and the like are heard in scripture as qualifiers of the person, nevertheless, the scriptural injunctions regarding desire (*kāma*) have those [results] as their purpose. This is seen from such examples as, "The one with the staff recites the *praiṣa* formulas," and "The priests wearing red turbans proceed with the ritual.

Why? Because the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) requires an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), and because heaven and the like are understood to be the objects to be brought about by virtue of being desired.
Because, just as in the case of using a word ending in the accusative case, the desired object (*iṣṭa*) is likewise understood [as the goal] to be brought about.
[Umbeka: "Tathā" means that even because of its being something desired (*kāmyatva*), the desired thing is understood as the *bhāvya* (that which is to be produced).]

Therefore, the cognition of the person [as the agent] in the word *svargakāma* (desiring heaven) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Only "heaven" (*svarga*) is what is enjoined, because the focus is on the specific object to be brought about (*bhāvya*). This is because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), by virtue of direct statement (*śruti*) and other means, is in contradiction with being the object of the injunction; and even if it were the instrument (*karaṇa*), it would contradict the favoring of the direct statement. Furthermore, since it is the purpose of the scripture, even if it were the instrument, there would be no lack of knowledge regarding the two [factors]. For all productive operations aimed at results (*phalabhāvanā*) have the meaning of the verbal root as their specific means of accomplishment. It might be argued that even if the focus is on the qualification of heaven, there would still be a lack of a subordinate element (*guṇa*) for heaven and so forth.
No, because that which is to be cultivated must first be required. [Umveka: No. First of all, one asks "What should one cultivate? based on its capacity.]
If it is argued that performing [the rite] otherwise is improper, we say no; for that is not required.
Since heaven, being of the nature of pleasure, is a human goal (puruṣārtha), there is a requirement for it; this is because we accept that [heaven] arises from the mandate (niyoga) alone.
If it is argued that there must be syntactic unity (ekavākyatva), the meaning is that what is capable of fulfilling [the mandate] is connected as the end to be achieved (bhāvya).

What is the contradiction? [The contradiction lies in] saying that one desires one thing but performs another; for when it is said "one who desires heaven," the term "desire" is applied figuratively to the means of accomplishment.
Thus, there is a contradiction in the statement "one should perform a sacrifice.
Therefore, [Umveka says: "not in the means of accomplishment."

The scriptural injunctions such as "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma) must indeed be understood as referring to a specific type of person (puruṣaviśeṣa) by their own inherent force; let them, however, be taken as referring to the fruit.
For that which is desired is not the means, such as the instrument (karaṇa), because it is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha).
But surely, even the means is desired by virtue of being known? Indeed, it is so.

Speech is desired [by the person]. When the goal is to be accomplished— [in the case] of a person who is dependent on the injunction (niyoga) and whose desire is for something else— that desire is metaphorically attributed to the means of accomplishment.

Furthermore, heaven cannot be metaphorically attributed to something else, nor can an action performed by one person be contrary [to what is required]; thus, the injunction (*niyoga*) is not the primary element.
We see this; therefore, heaven alone is the desired object by its own inherent force (*svarasāt*).
This is the section concerning the accentuation of the words expressing the desired result.

The section concerning the accents of speech. Another commentator [Durga] says: By virtue of its inherent capacity, that which a mantra is able to express is not enjoined there, precisely because it is already established.
However, the *bhāṣika* accent is not obtained for that [mantra]; it is prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa.
Or rather, even when being prescribed, the mantra is prescribed as qualified by its specific accent.
Or else, there is the instruction of the mantra itself, and not the *bhāṣika* accent; the mention of the *bhāṣika* accent occurs because of its general application.
Commentary: This instruction pertains to the mantra, not to the accent.
How is this known? Because this word takes the form of an instruction regarding the mantra.
What is its similarity to that [instruction]? He says: "He takes up the horse's halter."
And this [cord] is taken up with a mantra, not with ordinary speech-sounds (*bhāṣika*).
The employment of a mantra serves for purification (*prāyatya*), not for anything else.
Why is that taught? Because the hearing of ordinary speech-sounds would lead to a loss of purity (*prāyāpatti*).
The *bhāṣika* accentuation is employed in the Brāhmaṇa.

If it were recited according to the *pravacana* (the Vedic) accentuation in the midst of that [Brāhmaṇa], the continuity of the *bhāṣika* accent would be interrupted; to avoid this, the instruction is given using the *bhāṣika* accent.
It is just as singers [preserve] a song.

In another commentary (bhāṣyakārāntara): regarding the statement "because the application is distinct" (bhinna-pravṛtti-pakṛtatvāt), that which will be stated by the venerable Bhāṣyakāra [is intended].

It is stated in the Vārttika and other works (at 3.4.11–13, p. 31) that other commentators have established that the Vāruṇī sacrifice is to be performed by the recipient alone.
Parākrama, 911.
Alms.
That which was begged for the sake of the sacrifice is intended as a fee for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and for accomplishing other matters for the sake of the sacrifice. Bhāṣya 10.2.8127.
This is the maxim of the mendicant’s stepping forward with his feet (*bhikṣupādaprasaraṇanyāya*).

Just as one who has entered among officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in order to obtain garments and other gifts according to his desire, considering it difficult to receive all six types of benefits at once, accepts a small portion of alms with the thought, "May there first be a gift for my feet here; later, having established a relationship, I shall gradually accomplish [the rest]," so too the Śruti, like a mother exceedingly desirous of welfare, is understood to wish for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) to enter. Considering it impossible to achieve everything at once, she teaches him how to be liberated from *saṃsāra* through the previously mentioned sequence. This is how it should be understood. (Sāhasī. 43)
The logic regarding the pot not being placed on the fire by mendicants is as follows: "It is not because there are no beggars that pots are not placed on the fire" (*Bhāmatī* 1.2.11, Basu p. 74).
This is the summary.
The analogy of the pot not being placed on the fire by the monks:

just as no one would place a pot on the fire out of fear of beggars, so too, because independent inquiry is impossible without the knowledge of reality, and because teachers are subject to the suspicion of being deceivers, it is not correct to say that the investigation into Brahman by the teacher and others occurs only under their authority, due to the impossibility of suspecting anyone else.

However, the sense is that because one can determine correctness or incorrectness through a thorough examination according to the methods prescribed in the scriptures, and because the possibility exists of resorting to an improper sacrifice or an improper refuge, the inquiry into Brahman must not be abandoned for fear of being deceived by such [unworthy] means.
This follows the maxim: "A beggar seeks another beggar. (Sāhasī 347).

For the sentence would indeed be split if there were an injunction in both cases; for then there would be two distinct sentences [as in the case of "One desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the Vājapeya"].

Bhāṭṭadīpikā 4.1.14: Regarding the passage, "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the locative case in "putre" is used solely for the sake of indicating the occasion (*nimitta*), just as in the expression "when [the moon] is divided" (*bhinne*).

That which remains capable of fulfilling its purpose even when a fragment has fallen off is considered "broken" in one part (*ekadeśabhinna*).

The oblation prescribed for breaking and so forth—such as "he offers when [the vessel] is broken" and "he offers when [the ghee] has spilled"—must be repeated whenever the occasion arises; it is not to be performed only once.
This oblation occurs in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites upon the breaking of vessels and the like, or upon the spilling of clarified butter and the like. (Vi.

6.1.9) Regarding these various occasional rites such as the oblation for breaking and so forth, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) because they are all included within the injunction for the performance (*prayogavacana*), and not an option (*vikalpa*), since they are prescribed in dependence upon specific occasions such as breaking and the like.
There is a difference in the agents of the injunction and its purpose.
Even for the King and the Family Priest, who have distinct ritual procedures (*kalpa*), there is eligibility (*adhikāra*) in the *Kulāya* sacrifice.
[This applies to] the qualities of those with distinct functions.

VI.1.5: Regarding the passage "Now this [is] *bhūḥ*," the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the one-syllable [Sāman] is a cow (*dhenu*). In that context, because of the general term "cow" in the phrase "A cow, a horse, a mule, and so forth," there is a sublation of the specific [mention of] horses and the like; therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that exactly twelve hundred cows must be given as *dhenu*s, while horses and the like are not to be given at all.
Only a single cow should be given;
and by that cow, there is the warding off of all defects—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). This is the principle of the *bhādī* [or *bhādinī*] maxim.

Just as the verbal root *bhū*, meaning "to exist" (*sattāyām*), and others, assume various forms through the differentiation of their inherent prefixes, suffixes, and upapadas; for example, in the case of *bhavati*: "The root *bhū* [is used] in the sense of existence (*sattā*), auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), intellect (*buddhi*), dwelling (*nivāsa*), pervasion (*vyāpti*), attainment (*sampad*), desire (*abhidhyā*), power (*śakti*), manifestation (*prādurbhāva*), and motion (*gati*)."

Thus, through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), a difference in meaning is perceived in cases such as *prabhāva*, *anubhāva*, and *paribhava* at the beginning; through the distinction of prefixes (*upasarga*), as in *bhavana*, *bhūyate*, and *bhavita*; and through the distinction of suffixes (*pratyaya*). In exactly the same way, this very Brahman appears as manifold due to the distinction of limiting adjuncts. [Sāhasī. 708] *Bhū-vādi* is a verbal root (*dhātu*);
*abhidhātrī* is the expressive scripture (*śruti*).
Bāla, p. 41. *bhū-vikṣipta*: being restricted solely to the action of the instigator (*prayojaka*). Vārttika 2.1.1, p. 378. The maxim of the heat of the earth (*bhū-staiauṣṇya-nyāya*).
This is the principle: it operates when the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of one thing is the object of superimposition (*āropa*) upon another.

*Sāhasī*, 303. In the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) called *bhū*, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the twelve-hundred-fold sacrificial fee (*dvādaśaśatadakṣiṇā*) prescribed by extended application (*ātideśika*) by the sacrificial fee of a cow (*dhenu*) directly taught (*aupadeśika*).

In such cases as "bhūtam bhavyam bhaviṣyat dṛṣṭvā svāhā namaḥ," there is no difference in the mantra.

In passages such as "To the past, to the present, to the future—*vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, obeisance! To the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*—*vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, obeisance! it might be argued that the utterances of *vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, and obeisance (*namaḥ*) serve the purpose of offering (*pradāna*), because they can be construed with the triad of "past" and so forth in their respective order, thus forming three distinct mantras. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: Since there is no evidence establishing a general connection [between these utterances and the acts of offering], it is impossible to assume that they constitute separate homas based on mere indicative power (*liṅga*) alone. Furthermore, it is logical to interpret these utterances as praise (*stuti*) directed toward the "past" and so forth, serving as a single unified element. Therefore, like the *svāhākāra* occurring within the *sudhikaraṇa-mantra*, these too do not serve the purpose of offering.
*Saṃkarṣa* 2.4.29: "That which has already come into being (*bhūtam*) is taught for the sake of that which is yet to be (*bhavyāya*).

This is a maxim heard in the *Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa*. To explain: in the section concerning the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, 2.1.1–4), it was doubted whether substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*) possess the status of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*) for the production of the fruit (*phalabhāvanā*), or rather the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Having raised the objection that substances and qualities alone possess the status of being the instrument for the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) on the basis of the maxim "that which has already come into being is taught for the sake of that which is yet to be," it was stated therein that the meaning of the verbal root alone possesses the status of being the instrument for the productive operation.

[The opponent argues: It is rash [to say that the substance is for the sake of the action]. An existing substance brings about an action that is yet to be; thus, the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) follows from the action.

Alternatively, even though the sacrifice benefits the deity by refining it, nevertheless, in order to attain the status of a means (*sādhana*), it must serve as a substratum (*āśraya*); otherwise, it could not do so.
Therefore, an existing thing is taught for the sake of that which is yet to be accomplished.

*Duṣa* 4.1.7.18: Since [the fruit such as] heaven is established as being denotable by a noun (*nāmapada*), it is related to the verbal meaning—the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) expressed by the verb—as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) by way of being a means (*sādhana*), according to the maxim: "That which is already accomplished (*bhūta*) is taught for the sake of that which is to be accomplished (*bhavya*). Thus, in the *Bhāmatī* on *Brahmasūtra* 3.2.8.39: "That which is accomplished (*bhūta*) is fit for the sake of that which is to be accomplished (*bhavya*). *Sāhasī* 777: It is well understood that the purpose of ritual actions (*karman*) is precisely this: that the accomplished (*bhūta*) is for the sake of that which is to be accomplished (*bhavya*).

Bhāṣya 10.1.6.10: The *bhūta* mantras are those such as "Svāhā to the Earth," etc., used in the Rājasūya sacrifice, as well as those in the Abhicāra section, such as "Thou art the Earth by birth," etc. Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that both sets of mantras should be employed—either collectively or alternatively—during the placing of the *bhūteṣṭakā* bricks.

Not all [words] are to be accepted; rather, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that only those which possess expectancy (*sākāṅkṣā*)—that is, those situated within a specific context—are to be accepted.

This is because, according to the principle of the simultaneous utterance of the past and the future, [the former] would be purposeless;
however, it is not the case that the future has the past as its meaning.
Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 6.1.1.9, p. 1348: "The existence of that which has come into being for the sake of that which is yet to be shall come to pass.
For this is well-known as the function of ritual acts (*karma*): namely, providing indirect assistance (*ārādupakriyā*).

Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 10.4.2.38: It will be stated that there is a connection of the existent (*bhūta*)—the substance denoted by the word *svarga*—as a subordinate factor (*guṇatvena*) with respect to the act to be accomplished (*bhavya*).

It must be performed with the *mantras* themselves, specifically with those *mantras* containing the exclamation *svāhā*.

(Saṃkarṣa. 2.4.24; Mīko., p. 45). This should be seen in the context of the statement: "The piling of the fire-altar (*agni-cayana*) and the placing of the *bhūteṣṭakā*s [bricks] belonging to the *rājasūya* should be done with the *mantras* of the *rājasūya* itself.

Regarding the placing of the *bhūteṣṭakā*s, if there were an application (*viniyoga*) of the *rājasūya* *mantras* such as "To Earth, *svāhā*" (*pṛthivyai svāhā*), then the performance would include the utterance of *svāhā*; this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
The established conclusion is that the application [of the mantras] is according to their names.

Vedic action that is of the nature of an active engagement for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), which serves as an auxiliary by way of presentation (*saṃnivedya*) for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*)—namely, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the enjoyment of an existing entity (*bhūtopayoga*)—is, for example, the burning of the offered oblation (*hutahavirdāha*). This is established by the injunction regarding the ritual propriety of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācārakalpatva*). Bāla. pṛ. 83. pṛ. 82. "Existing-ness" (*bhūtatva*) is the state of being the counter-positive of a present non-existence (*vartamānadhvaṃsapratiyogitva*).

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the section concerning one who desires heaven (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*— 6.1.1), [the word "heaven"] is a denotation of something already existing (*bhūta*), according to the principle of the co-utterance of the existent and the to-be-accomplished (*bhūtabhavyasamuccāraṇanyāya*). This concludes the section on abundance (*bhūmādhikaraṇa*).

They say that this section (adhikaraṇa) is intended to refute the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in the injunctions (*codanā*), characterized by their dependence on external causes, on the grounds that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are connected as reasons for the purpose of the injunction according to the principle of the "mention of the past and the future" (*bhūtabhavyasamuccāraṇanyāya*).
According to the principle of the "mention of the past and the future," in the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* sacrifice, Soma is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) due to the inherent capacity of the substance.
Furthermore, by the principle of the "mention of the past and the future," it is determined in all cases that the substance serves to bring about the meaning of the verbal root.
Page 622: For it is held that a substance to be consecrated (saṃskārya) is that which is to be employed for the sake of what has been or what is to be;
however, roasted barley flour (saktavaḥ) is neither to be employed nor has it ever been employed for any such purpose.
Such is the nature of the *saktunyāya* (the maxim of the barley-meal).

Vārttika 2.4.412, p. 411. A Vedic ritual action (*vaidikaṃ karma*) that is of perceptible utility (*dṛṣṭārtha*), which is an auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) contributing to the purpose of both the past and the future, and which serves to consecrate the deities—such as the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśāyāga*)—is of the nature of an active engagement (*pravṛttirūpa*).
This will be discussed further under the sub-divisions of those [actions] that have a substratum (*āśrayika*).

Bāla, p. 82: However, there is no such thing as an action that sanctifies a substance for the sake of both past and future utility; this is the topic of the *bhūmādhikaraṇa* (the section on abundance), according to the principle of favoring the greater number (*bhūyo'nugrahanyāya*).

Although the act of placing [the bricks] would necessarily follow from the fact that the bricks must otherwise fail to serve as components of the piling (cayana), it is nevertheless enjoined by an explicit injunction even prior to that. Its purpose is the accomplishment of each individual primary rite and the establishment of the common agency with the piling;
otherwise, the placing might sometimes result in being performed collectively.
Furthermore, because it is required by the sense (*ārthikatva*), there is also a difference in the agent for the leading forward (*nayana*).

However, when this [injunction] exists—which, through the consecration of the bricks (*iṣṭakā-saṃskāra*), teaches that [the leading forward] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the piling (*cayana*)—then, by the principle of "following each primary" (*pratipradhānānuvṛtti-nyāya*), the result of a single agent for both the primary [piling] and the subordinate [leading forward] is established.

As for the word *sṛṣṭi*, the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that it is a figurative restatement (*gauṇānuvāda*) of the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras obtained through indicative mark (*liṅga*) and context (*prakaraṇa*).
The author of the Vārttika, however, maintains that this is not merely an injunction for placing [the bricks].
For if that were the case, there would result the redundancy of numerous other injunctions for placing, such as "he places the living beings" (*prāṇabhṛta upadadhāti*).
Therefore, either the mere mantra is enjoined by reference to the act of placing, or the placing qualified by the mantra is enjoined for the purpose of consecrating the bricks.
The result of the rule concerning the placing (upadhāna), however, is as before.
As for the result of the rule concerning the mantras, it is that they are restricted to the act of placing;
for since the mantras reveal the bricks, they might otherwise apply even to the picking up of them and so forth, but by this rule, they are restricted specifically to the act of placing.

Therefore, there is a threefold rule: either the fruit is to be protected from the time of the taking up [of the bricks] onwards, or it is connected with the middle layer (*madhyamaciti*). This is because of the scriptural injunction: "Whatever brick one brings that is accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa passage, one should place it in the middle layer. By this statement, the connection of those bricks which possess explicit Brāhmaṇa texts with the middle layer is ordained. Otherwise, since the mantras would have been drawn away by the specific context (*prakaraṇa*) of their respective individual layers, they would—by virtue of the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) of the piling (*cayana*)—either apply to all layers or, alternatively, result in being placed only in the final layer.

Therefore, the injunction of the mantra is for the purpose of connecting it with the middle layer (*madhyamaciti*). Furthermore, the fact that the bricks possess a direct Brāhmaṇa text (*pratyakṣabrāhmaṇavattva*) consists in their being enjoined by words read in a direct Brāhmaṇa text that denotes bricks. For the word "sṛṣṭi" refers to those bricks which are intended for the employment of mantras that manifest the act of creation (*sṛṣṭi*).

And in that case, because the mantra—which constitutes the qualifying portion—is itself what is to be enjoined, it follows that those respective bricks possess the status of being directly prescribed by a Brāhmaṇa text.

Furthermore, since there is the possibility that a mantra serving as a quality (guṇa) of a brick already employed would also be connected with the middle layer (madhyamaciti), the word "brick" is used as a qualifier for the term [mantra].
Consequently, only the act of laying down (upadhāna) qualified by the mantra is enjoined.

The term "sṛṣṭi" (creation) refers here to the seventeen creation-mantras (*sṛṣṭimantra*) by way of secondary figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), in accordance with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "because he lays down seventeen bricks.

In that context, there are fourteen mantras that are "creations" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.1–14), while three are "non-creations" (1.5.15–17); thus, the abundance of "creations" constitutes the quality (*guṇa*) serving as the basis for the figurative designation.
As Maṇḍana states: "By virtue of their abundance, they are considered to be 'creations'."

16. Śaṅkara: "The secondary nature [of the term] regarding creation and so forth due to its abundance (bhūman), its possession of a directly perceived Brāhmaṇa passage, and its being that upon which mantras containing the word *iṣṭakā* (brick) are to be deposited—this has already been stated in the *Bhūmādhikaraṇa* (Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya, p. 137). Due to the connection with the quality of abundance, the word 'creation' (*sṛṣṭi*) is applied even to non-creation and mixed creation, as in the phrase 'He deposits the creation' (*sṛṣṭir upadadhāti*)."

VI. 1.4.14. A secondary [figurative] usage based on abundance (*bhūmamūlakagauṇī*) sublates another secondary usage. Bāl. p. 143: A secondary usage based on the sevenfold indicative marks (*liṅgasaptavāyamūlikā gauṇī*) is sublated by one based on abundance, because in the former case there is the principle of the meaning of many sentences, whereas in the latter that is absent.
p. 143: Land should not be given away.
What, then, is the "earth" (bhūmi) intended here? It is that distinct substance composed of clay known as the terrestrial globe; it is not merely the field or the soil.
Bhāṣya 6.1.2: "In the Viśvajit sacrifice, earth should not be given.
6.1.2: "Earth is like a cow."
The stage for the purpose of practice consists in grasping and retaining [the teachings], just like one who desires land.
For example, one who desires land draws a chariot on the ground and practices; thus, he will have an advantage in battle.
(Bhāṣya)

The smaller is generally sublated by the larger; or rather, the former is sublated by the latter. (Bāla.pṛ. 132, vā. 3|1|7 pṛ. 860). This is the maxim: "That which consists of more [elements] should possess the same character [as them]."
(This is a portion of the sūtra: *vipratiṣiddhadharmāṇāṃ samavāye* [Jaimini Sūtra 12.1.22].

Regarding the statement, "The *soma*-purchase animal is a three-year-old bull with testicles," where the means of purchase are obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*), both bovinity (*gotva*) and goat-nature (*ajatva*) are obtained as optional alternatives. However, because bovinity serves as the means for two distinct acts of purchase prescribed by the two sentences—"He purchases with a pair of bulls" and "He purchases with a one-year-old female"—it follows by the maxim *bhūyasāṃ syāt sadharmatvam* ("the majority should possess the common property") that goat-nature and the like are sublated by the one-year-old female and other such elements.

However, by this very principle (*jāti*), the extension [of the rule] to other instances of purchase (*krayāntara*) is established! (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 3.1.6.2, p. 169). Furthermore, there are many *praiṣas* (directions) and so forth, yet they constitute a single *nigada*. Based on the principle that "that which is more numerous should possess the same character," since the Adhvaryu is [otherwise] occupied with the purpose of the *praiṣa*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the Hotṛ [should recite the *nigada*] by way of elimination. (Vārttika 3.8). This is the principle of favoring the majority (*bhūyo'nugrahanyāya*).

Since the description of the vast manifold within the small ether (*daharākāśa*) necessarily serves the purpose of realizing the reality contained therein and for the purpose of meditation, the principle of favoring the majority (*bhūyovānugrahanyāya*) applies; by favoring those many [descriptions] which would otherwise be rendered inconsistent, the passage beginning with "In that, there is a small lotus-palace" is intended to show that the small ether is not something else. This is the principle of favoring the majority.
It is so understood; it is not [determined] merely by following the application of the fruit of its presence.
*Parākrama*, 592. The principle of favoring the majority (*bhūyo'nugrahanyāya*) pertains to the subject matter of substances and properties.
*Sudhā*, p. 813. The principle of favoring the majority (*bhūyo'nugrahanyāya*): the principle of favoring the many (*bahvanugrahanyāya*).

When primary elements are performed together, in case of a conflict between their respective properties (*dharma*), the performance should follow those properties that are more numerous. When there is a conjunction of conflicting properties, the character of the majority shall prevail.
Commentary: In the *pañcadaśarātra* sacrifice, the *agniṣṭut* one-day rite (*ekāha*) constitutes the first day.
Then follows a three-day period consisting of the Jyotis, Go, and Āyus sacrifices.
The remaining eleven days have the twelve-day sacrifice as their archetype.
In that regard, when there is a conflict of ritual rules, the intended meaning of these eleven days is now considered.

Should the ritual procedure (*dharma*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) be performed in these [one-day sacrifices], or that of the *agniṣṭut*? Now, this has already been established: in the examination of the relative strength of the extended injunction (*codaka*) and the name, it was stated that the procedure of the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) must be performed, according to the principle: "Or rather, because the time is designated, the names of the one-day sacrifices do not apply" (7.4.316). Thus, what is established by one line of reasoning is here challenged by another. Alternatively, this is a mutual inquiry regarding the names themselves.

In this case of a conjunction of these two sets of days—those characterized by contradictory properties, namely the Agniṣṭut and the eleven days—within this fifteen-night rite (*pañcadaśarātra*), the commonality of the eleven days shall prevail.
Their specific property must be performed.
What is the reason? It is simply their numerical majority.
When there are many endowed with virtuous qualities, the fruit is great; when there is only one, the fruit is small.
For this is the observed analogy in the world.
In the world, when this house is well-supplied with oil, there is great light from eleven lamps; in the opposite case, it is small.
What, then, is the illustration here?
In the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, the Subrahmaṇyā formula is addressed to Agni, while on the other days it is addressed to Indra.
In that case, the *aindrī* [verse] should be employed.
Duh— (Here, the author of the Bhāṣya has cited the fifteen-night sacrifice (*pañcadaśarātra*).
In it, the first day is the *agniṣṭut*; then follows the three-day period consisting of *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus*; the remaining eleven days consist of the twelve-night rite.)

In that regard, in the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, the Subrahmaṇyā formula belonging to Agni is obtained by direct designation (*nāmadheya*); however, in the twelve-day sacrifices (*dvādaśāha*), an Indra-formula is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*). Thus, the relative strength (*balābala*) of these two is considered.
Alternatively, in the three-day sacrifice (*tryaha*) named Jyotir-gaur-āyuḥ, an Indra-formula is obtained by name, while in the Agniṣṭut, an Agni-formula is obtained by name alone;
thus, the relative strength of names themselves is considered.

This example stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* is not rejected: in this sūtra, the *pañcadaśarātra* sacrifice is not an illustration. (How so? First, as for the *subrahmaṇyā* mantra pertaining to the *vatsavatī* [rite], which occurs after the formal acceptance [of the calves], it is performed every day; for it is appropriate [to say] that it belongs to that time, according to [the rule] "But that which belongs to that time [is used]" (*tatkālā tvāvarte*, 1.1.12.124).
And it must be performed according to the respective deity: the *abhiṣṭuti* is addressed to Agni, while in the others it is addressed to Indra.
In that case, there is no doubt at all [regarding the performance] because it is performed separately (*bhedena karaṇāt*) and there is no contradiction.

However, as for that [recitation] which is performed at the end of the *ātithyā* and during the *upasads*, a contradiction might be suspected if it were performed by way of a single ritual framework (*tantra*).
Even there, since the *nigada* serves to consecrate the deities, its differentiation must follow the respective deity; there is no simultaneous recitation (*tantravāraṇa*).
Just as the *nirvāpa-mantra* differs for each offering because it is a consecratory act (*saṃskāraka*), so too is this case.
Therefore, both *subrahmaṇyā*s should be recited (this is not the correct example).

What, then, is the correct example here? It is where five sacrifices are enjoined together toward a single result, and among them, three follow the procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsika*) and two follow that of the New Moon sacrifice (*dārśika*). In that situation, there is a conflict between the *abhimarśana* (touching) and the *ājyabhāga-mantra*.

(An example of this: For instance— "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni the Giver; a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Bestower; and a cake on five potsherds [to Indra the Giver]; curd, honey, ghee, water, and parched grains for Prajāpati"—these are the seven sacrifices.
Among them, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the offering to Agni applies to both the cake for Agni and the parched grains.

Therefore, there is no conflict with the *ājyabhāga* offerings of the *Paurṇamāsī* sacrifice belonging to Agni. However, the other five sacrifices are dependent [on these two]. Among them, in the case of the *puroḍāśa* for Indra and the curd (*dadhi*), the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) is that of the New Moon sacrifice (*darśika*). As for the honey and the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), because they are modifications of the *upāṃśuyāja*, the procedure is that of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsika*). In that context, there is a conflict between the touching (*abhimarśana*) and the *ājyabhāga* mantras; specifically, there is a conflict between the two sets of *caturhotṛ* formulas and the two touching mantras, and between the two *vārtraghnī* verses and the two *ghṛtānuli* verses of the *ājyabhāga* mantras—this is the meaning.
[He states the established conclusion: In that case, the adoption of the properties [of one sacrifice] in another is for the sake of favoring the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*).

Soma—Is the extension (*prasaṅga*) of the properties of only the primary [sacrifice] to the other, or rather of the majority of properties? [The connection is established] through this investigation into the specific nature of the extension.
Vi—That *Subrahmaṇyā* of the fifteen-night rite which occurs at the initial time...

It should be the Āgneyī or the Kimandī, according to what is consistent with the first [verse]. Since there is no arising of contradiction, the Āgneyī is primary; however, because it is for the sake of the *kula*, the Aindrī is not favored. This is based on the maxim: "One should sacrifice one for the sake of the *kula*. This is the meaning.
This has been stated according to the opinion of the Bhāṣya.
According to the opinion of the Vārttika, he says: "For one who possesses truth, renunciation, and courage, [the sacrifice] is enveloped by clarified butter and the *nīvāra* grain;
by the *vārtraghna* [mantras], the *ājyabhāga* offerings, and so forth; from the first [offering] come curd and for Indra."
The Āgneya [offering] is obtained through the instruction of the Darśa-dharma, because it is the last. For ghee, honey, and water, a large quantity is appropriate for the bali-offering.
The principle of greater favor applies; by virtue of their abundance, both are heard in the scripture. (Verse 3068)

Bhaṭṭa: In the section on optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), it is revealed in scripture: "One desiring cattle should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni the Giver; a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the Bestower; curd, honey, ghee, water, and parched grains—that combined [offering] belongs to Prajāpati.

In that context, there are several sacrifices with curd and other substances as their materials, each having two deities. Among these, the first and the others [subsequent ones] are modifications of the *āgneya* sacrifice; because they share both times [of performance], they are not contradictory.
The cake on eleven potsherds for Indra is a modification of the offering to Indra;
the curd-offering belongs specifically to the curd-offering itself. The ritual characteristics of the new moon sacrifice apply to both of these.
Since honey, ghee, and water are modifications of the *upāṃśuyāja*, they follow the ritual rules (*dharma*) of the Full Moon sacrifice.

Thus, when these seven sacrifices are performed together here, the rules of the New Moon sacrifice apply to the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*), or to the other oblation-mantras (*haviryajñiya-mantra*), and to the touching of the oblation (*havirabhimarśana*) with the *caturhotṛ* and *pañcahotṛ* formulas; for in case of conflict, the rules of the primary [sacrifice] prevail due to the principle that the original nature prevails over the modified.

This being the prima facie view, since the favoring of the primary element (*mukhya*) is first understood, one must accept the sublation of that primary element’s specific rule (*upasaṃkhyā*) in accordance with the greater number of favors (*bhūyo'nugraha*), because the favoring of the many depends upon the benefit (*upakāra*). Therefore, among the many modifications (*vikāra*) of the *Paurṇamāsī*, there is a common procedure (*tantritva*), while for the few [modifications] regarding conflicting properties, there should be a case of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). However, in the case of non-conflicting properties, they proceed by way of the common procedure (*tantra-dharma*). This is illustrated by the example of the *Upāṃśuyāja* not being present on the *Amāvāsyā* day, which results from the sublation of its presence.
If that [quality] exists in both cases, however, another example must be sought.

As for what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "The Agniṣṭut is the first day of the fifteen-day sacrifice; because it is modified from the Agniṣṭut by its name, its [ritual] details are those of the Agniṣṭut.
The three-day period consists of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus; their ritual details are likewise those of the Jyotis and others as recited in the section on names."
Therefore, the *aindrī* verse should be recited.
In the other eleven [cases], the *aindrī* is applied by extension (*atideśa*) on account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the injunction.
Thus, in this instance, since the recitation of the *satyākālīna-sūtra* is performed through the breaking of that [connection], there is no point for deliberation.

Since it has been established that the *tantritva* (the status of being the primary agent) belongs to the *sūktavāka* occurring at the time of the *ātithyā* and *upasad* offerings—which is easily available in its entirety—when a conflict arises, it was stated that "the *aindrī* [mantra] should be employed" for the sake of favoring the more numerous [elements]. However, because the *sūktavāka* is intended to reveal the deity, and since there is an absence of the oblation (*havis*) and other elements in the form of revealing Agni when Indra is revealed, it is understood that both must be performed separately; this is what is required.
For this very reason, the eleventh section (*adhikaraṇa*) concerns the *sūktavāka* whose deities are common to both.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that even the touching (*abhimarśana*) would have to be performed separately for each distinct substance—thereby precluding the principle of *prasaṅga* (extension of application)—because the performance of touching is established through *prasaṅga*. This is because the injunctions "with the *Caturhotṛ* [mantras]" and "with these two" merely prescribe the mantras by way of restating the touching already enjoined in another scriptural passage, namely, "He touches the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) which are close at hand. Since it is possible to touch all the various offerings simultaneously, there is no evidence for their repetition beyond the mere application of the mantras; thus, the establishment of *prasaṅga* is logically justified.

For this very reason, there is no over-extension [of the rule] to the case where, in the absence of [a specific rule], the application [of a mantra] depends on direct perception; in such a case, that [perceived mantra] alone is the mantra.
Maṇḍana states: "In case of conflict, the quality of being numerous prevails. Śaṅkara states: "The majority should be those possessing the same characteristics."

If it is argued that the scriptural mention of *ākāśa* is also repeated five times, and thus the principle of "favoring the majority" (*bhūyo'nugraha-nyāya*) applies equally to both cases, we say no. [This is because] according to the principle of "favoring the majority," even by way of intermediate purport (*avāntaratātparya*), it is precisely the connection of *ākāśa* with being the goal for all the worlds that is to be established. In the *Anuvākyādhikaraṇa*, when the principle of favoring the majority would lead to the acceptance of the *anuvākyā*, there is a sublation of the principle of favoring the primary [element] (*mukhyānugraha-nyāya*) by the principle of favoring the majority, provided that no distinction is perceived among all the constituent parts (*tantri*). This is the principle of favoring the majority.

However, where a distinction is recognized such that one [rite] is the primary application (*tantra*) while the others are incidental (*prasaṅga*), there the ritual details (*dharma*) belong to the primary one alone; for the incidental ones, being dependent upon that reality, do not necessitate their own ritual details.
On days designated by specific names, those [details] that are not contradictory should be performed in both cases.

But those [rites] which are not obtained by name—even if they are contradictory—are all the duties (dharmas) to be performed in the ritual system (tantra) of all the Great Ones (Agnis). These must be performed according to the principle of "favoring the majority" (bhūyo'nugraha-nyāya), as they are enjoined by direct injunction (codanā), and not merely because they are obtained by name.

Since the earth-world (bhūloka) is well-known as the place of rest (pratiṣṭhātva) according to the alternative view that it is understood through the hearing of the word "here" (atra) and its connection with the intermediate space, [the rites] find their conclusion in the world of earth alone, due to the principle of favoring the majority.
Parākrama 6511:

Regarding the greater frequency of both [Vedic branches], the scriptural statement is identical in both the Yajurveda and the Sāmaveda: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Thus, the injunction is exactly the same.

In this regard, since it is not certain whether what is taught in the Sāmaveda is for the sake of ritual action (*kriyārtha*) and what is in the Yajurveda is for the sake of qualities (*guṇārtha*), or vice versa,
[this doubt] having arisen, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): there is scriptural authority for both.
The determination [of the ritual] is based on its predominance.
Where there are many common qualities, there the injunction for its performance should apply.
And where there is an injunction for performance, there the requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is expected.
The injunction regarding what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*) is inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*).
Thus, because the Jyotiṣṭoma belongs to the Yajurveda, its performance is in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). (Ke.)
§ Because both [Vedas] hear it predominantly.

In the Yajurveda, they prescribe the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice thus: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Likewise, it is also prescribed in the Sāmaveda: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."
Once the cognition of the ritual action has been established, there occurs a second hearing for the sake of a subordinate element (guṇa).
In this regard, a doubt arises: is the Yajurvedic version for the sake of the subordinate element, or is it the opposite?

Having established previously that the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) and the ritual application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) are obtained through the force of the injunction of application, there now arises a doubt regarding a case where the primary [injunction] itself is heard as being twofold: in such a case, when it is uncertain which Veda is connected with the performance of properties such as loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*), since the governing statement (*adhikāra-vākya*) makes no distinction between the two, it is settled that the performance must take place precisely where the originative injunction occurs. Now, it is investigated where that very originative injunction lies.
Here, this is the intention of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
First of all, the hearing [of the mantra] in one place cannot be for the purpose of restricting it to another, because there is no difference in its being heard in both places.

Nor is it for the purpose of assigning it to a specific result, because there is likewise no difference in the result being heard in both cases. Therefore, the only appropriate explanation is that there is an option based on the distinction between different reciters.
Since, when it is possible for a single person to study the Vedas, his own branch (*svaśākhā*) must first be studied;
therefore, that very Veda which was first studied by him is superior even to yours, and thus the combination of different branches or Vedas is restricted to being merely an option (*vikalpa*).
This being the position reached, it is replied as follows.
This would indeed be so if there were no removal of distinctions merely through non-hearing.
For in the Yajurveda, a greater extent of the *itikartavyatā* (procedural details) for the Jyotiṣṭoma, such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, is heard than in the other Vedas.
Since the *itikartavyatā* belongs to the context (*prakaraṇa*), and the primary context is that very [Yajurvedic] one, [the procedure remains there].

And since the performance of an action is understood only where there is a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), whereas in other cases the mention [of a detail] is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*),
it has been said: "Where there is an abundance of subordinate qualities, that constitutes the nature of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)."
In that case, its status as something to be performed is accepted by means of that very same indicative mark.
Thus (Vākyapadīya, p. 816).
The purpose [of this discussion] has been stated regarding the position.
As for the Sūtra, however, it means that whatever action is mentioned in both [the Śruti texts], its determination is by way of being common to both.
The venerable authors of the Vārttika do not accept this as the reason for their established doctrine (siddhānta) according to the Bhāṣya.

For if this were the indicative mark (liṅga) for understanding that [the number] is part of the injunction of performance (*itikartavyatā*), then what would be the difference between its being few or its being many? Indeed, even smoke that has been determined as such by its nature as smoke does not fail to lead to an inference when it is perceived.
As it has been said: "If something is determined as the indicator of another thing by its own nature..."
Whether that [result] be small or great, there is no distinction in its being cognized by him.
Thus, because smoke is determined to be an indicator of fire, that smoke— whether it is of such a kind or abundant— certainly makes fire known.
Thus (Vākyapadīya, p. 816).
Therefore, the reason for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) should be described exactly according to the Vārttika:
the arising [of cognition] is the specific form of consciousness corresponding to each respective object.
Furthermore, the specific determination of a ritual action occurs by means of its substance and deity;
and the entire substance and deity of the Jyotiṣṭoma are recited in the Yajurveda alone.
Therefore, it is precisely there that the origin of the ritual action takes place.

In the other Veda, having merely set forth the specific forms of ritual actions, there is only the injunction of the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns; therefore, the scriptural mention [of qualities] is solely for the purpose of indicating attributes (*guṇa*).
Now, although many attributes are indeed enjoined in each Veda, they are not heard as injunctions in every sentence by way of restating the ritual action (*karma-anuvāda*).
Nor can it be understood that there is an injunction of all [qualities] by way of referring back to a single action;
therefore, an injunction of multiple qualities does not occur through syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Nor does it occur through context (*prakaraṇa*), because there is no such context for the performance.
Context (*prakaraṇa*) is the requirement for the manner of performance (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) of that which is to be performed.

Since a restatement (*anuvāda*) cannot involve that which is to be performed, there is no connection by way of context; therefore, the hearing of this sentence is for the purpose of [enjoining] a quality (*guṇa*).
It is said: indeed, performance in its own form does not obstruct the requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*).
What then? It is the status of being inferred as the object of prescription (*vidhātum uddeśyatvena anumeyatvam*).

But here, the purpose of that hearing of the Śūdra mentioned in another context—which is brought about by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*)—is such as it is understood from the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) regarding the ritual action.
However, it is determined that [the mention in another Veda] is solely for the purpose of understanding the connection with the procedure (itikartavyatā) as traditionally handed down in proximity.
Therefore, it is established that the Jyotiṣṭoma belongs to the Yajurveda alone,
and its mention in another Veda is intended solely for the purpose of connecting it with certain subsidiary elements (guṇa).
The purpose [of this discussion] is as stated regarding the *pakṣa* (the prima facie view).

As for the *sūtra*, however, it is established that because of the abundance of the collection of substances, deities, and so forth, the origin (*utpatti*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma occurs in the Yajurveda alone, even though its [explicit] mention is not heard there. This is the conclusion of the Tautātita school.

According to the principle "where both are mentioned, [the injunction applies] by virtue of the greater number," the injunction for the sacrifice occurs only where there is a deity or other element that characterizes the sacrifice (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 2.4.4.9).

Now, regarding the two [passages], by the principle "where both are mentioned, [the injunction applies] by virtue of the greater number," since they are injunctions of subordinate qualities within the section on the *aupānuvākya* formulas, they are also injunctions of the primary act.
*Saṃkalpa* 4|3|14:

When a certain ritual action has many auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) prescribed in one recensional branch (*śākhā*), then by the principle that "the primary [action] is also prescribed there because of the greater number [of auxiliaries]," the principal rite itself is prescribed in that very branch;
whereas in another branch, only a few auxiliaries are prescribed. In that case, regarding the ritual action...
There is the apprehension that the entitlement [to perform the rite] should belong only to those who study that specific Vedic branch (*tacchākhādhyāyin*).

[Somaśarman replies: Because the purpose is accomplished through incidental application (*prasaṅga*), there is no need for an injunction even regarding a subsidiary element such as the *iṣṭi* or the animal sacrifice. However, if the mantra is prescribed in both [Vedas],...

It will be stated [later] that there is the attainment of the *nyāhārya* sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). At that point (Kau. 2.1.5.2), because both [options] exist as abundant, the rule "when both are heard, [the one with the greater number]" and so forth does not apply. On pages 83–84, an option (*vikalpa*) is accepted there due to necessity.
Or [it is] so.
3|1|17| Oṃ. And because it is already possessed, there is a purchase. Oṃ. "Because it is already abundant" is the principle (nyāya).

Regarding the statement "wherein these things"— the meaning is that although various items are used for the purchase (*parikraya*) of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), popular convention refers to that specific item which is present in the greatest abundance.
That purchase, known as the *anyāhārya*, even though obtained through the force of the general rule (*codaka*), applies here to the Soma sacrifice and the Iṣṭi-related rites.
This is clear.
[Sāhasrī 759:
It should not be performed.

Because they have been hired—by means of a purchase consisting of cows and so forth for the sake of the Soma sacrifice—the priests are "hired" (bhṛta) in a single ritual action involving numerous mantras. This concludes the section concerning the numerous mantras.
The priests are those who have been remunerated.
The purchase [of the officiants] at the Soma sacrifice is performed by means of the primary and subsidiary elements and so forth;
since the mantra is present, its recitation is optional.
Therefore, the conclusion is that the *anvāhārya* (the supplementary fee) need not be performed.

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, during the division of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) into portions, there are many [formulas] such as "Oṃ, according to your respective shares," "The fee (bhṛti) is for the purpose of hiring the performer of the rite," and "May you two separate," "May Bhaga divide you two. These are intended for the purpose of securing the services of the ritual officiant.
Bhāṣya 10.2.8.27: Maintenance is provided in three ways; the mantras are recited accordingly.
All of these are combined in the distribution [of the offering]:
by way of function, by way of result, and by way of verbal expression.
First, the labor is for the ignorant; in the absence of a specific criterion for determining one [of many], it belongs to a single person.
There is no wage of twelve hundred [paṇas] for bean seeds.
For when there is an application of a specific action, the expectancy for another [action] remains unappeased; thus,
even among many laborers, one may receive a single day's wage.

The correspondence of the result [to the action] is not [established] for the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices alone; rather, it is understood that this principle applies equally even to the combination of other [sacrifices] in a single fire. However, when there is a specific ritual fee (*bhṛti*), the statement refers to a particular measure [of that fee].
Because of the possibility of performing [the rite] again for the sake of manifesting what has already been accomplished;
for where even a single foot of a verse cannot be obtained, that [gift] is not a *dakṣiṇā*, since the requirement for a mantra is satisfied even by its optional application (*vikalpena viniyoga*).
Thus it is said: "In that case, it does not occur."
For she is not capable of performing that ritual action.
Furthermore, because of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the passage beginning with "He takes [the ladle] with four," there is an optional application (vikalpena viniyoga).
Whether by way of affection or by some other means, the entire ritual action of the day is to be carried out. (Saṃkarṣa 1.2.13)
One should perform [the rite];
one is not incited by a thousand and two hundred *vrīhi* grains.
As it is said in the section on mantras concerning the *āśita* (1.2.13): "according to their respective portions."
The substance that exists within the womb is the fee (*bhṛti*).
(In the *Saṃkarṣa*, an option regarding the mantras beginning with "Of that, one hundred and twelve [cows], you two should turn away" has been stated.)
In this context, "dakṣiṇā" refers to that which is sufficient for filling the belly, namely, the result of being well-fed (āśitaga-bhava). 1.2.16.
10|3|1|145: The maxim of the *bhūr-liṅga-śakuni* (the bird on the ground). In a region bordering the Himalayas, wages are paid to one who performs much work;
tell this to him.

10|3|1|154. A bird known as the *liṅgākhyā* repeatedly cries out, "Do not act rashly! (oṃ). It is well known that even for one who possesses wealth, the solicitation of wages (*bhṛti-yācana*) in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice is like one desiring to seize meat caught between the fangs of a lion, despite speaking loudly;
this is constant.

6|8|7|26–27. Mīko., p. 1823. Likewise, one who is merely skilled in instructing others while himself habitually acting according to his own whims is the subject matter here, as in the passage "the hiring of laborers in the Jyotiṣṭoma. The sense is that such a person, being a giver of wages [only for appearance], is indeed to be abandoned.
And it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"The soliciting of alms for the sake of a sacrifice, the acquisition of materials for the patron,
and the initiation— these do not censure the singer, even though he may sing much."
Nature [is so called] because of the statement, "Having been saluted" (Vi. 6.5.8).
Living beings proceed [toward their destination] just as birds go toward the earth-marks.
Thus ends the *Sāhasrī*.
Oṃ. Like the hiring of laborers (*bhṛtivanana*).
Just as the hiring of laborers is obligatory. 340.
In that case, the property acquired by one who has not previously won it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*ṛtvarthatva*), just as the acceptance [of gifts] and so forth do for the *mṛgus*;
thus, because it serves the purpose of the sacrifice, the property acquired thereby also serves the purpose of the sacrifice. (Vārttika 1.3.170).
Bhāṭṭa 4.1.2: Oṃ. There is no entitlement for the Bhṛgu, Aṅgirasa, and Vasiṣṭha lineages in the Sattra sacrifice.
Section 3.24–26:
Oṃ. The master must bargain with the servant for the purpose of hiring.

692. Regarding the existence and atomicity of the mind: now, the existence of the mind and its limited atomic dimension are being established.

Cognition and its like are, first of all, effects; since they must inhere in the self, their non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) must be sought in nothing other than conjunction with another substance. For instance, in the case of cognition and other effects, the conjunction with another substance that serves as their inherent cause must have the status of a non-inherent cause, because they are eternal specific qualities residing in an eternal substance, just like the color and other qualities residing in the atoms of earth. That substance is designated by the term "manas" (the internal organ), and it must be accepted as eternal;
otherwise, one would be forced to postulate a further cause for it as well.
Furthermore, a permanent substance must be either atomic or all-pervasive (*vibhu*).

Its being all-pervasive is untenable, because it would entail the absence of conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for conjunction—whether direct or indirect—has action alone as its cause, since this is observed in established cases of conjunction.
Nor is mere contiguity (*nairantarya*) conjunction, for that would entail the consequence of conjunction even between a quality and its possessor.

Furthermore, there is no difference in substance between a part and its whole, because of the fallacy of deviation. Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the meeting of two substances that were previously unmet; however, such a thing is not possible for two all-pervading (*vibhu*) entities. [Objection: But surely conjunction is possible even for two all-pervading entities.
For instance, two all-pervading substances must be conjoined with one another, because they possess substantiality and are without interval, like a rope and a jar.

Likewise, there is conjunction between space and the self, because [space] is conjoined with another substance that is itself conjoined with the self, like a cloth conjoined with a substance already conjoined with the self, and so forth.
This is not so, because the subject matter is sublated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is logical to establish the conjunction of two all-pervading entities (*vibhu*) by observing it elsewhere; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), as in the statement, "This man possesses a rabbit's horn.

Furthermore, conjunction elsewhere is observed to be produced by action; however, when conjunction is to be proved in the case of all-pervading substances, the subject is sublated because the absence of the effect follows from the absence of its cause.
Therefore, there is no conjunction of two all-pervading entities.

As for the inference establishing its all-pervasiveness (vibhutva)—such as: "The mind is all-pervasive, because it is the substratum of the conjunction that is the inherent cause of cognition, like the self; because, while being a substance, it is devoid of touch, like space; because, while being partless, it is a substance that initiates other substances, like space; because, while being a substance, it is an element (bhūta), like space; because, while being devoid of touch, it is a sense organ, like the ear"—all of this is set aside precisely by the contradiction with the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (dharmin) itself, namely the conceptualization of the self as having conjunction [with the mind].
Therefore, by the method of elimination (pariśeṣa), its atomicity (aṇutva) alone is determined.

If it is argued that [the mind] should therefore reside in the atoms of earth alone and not be a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*), we say no; for while there is a rule that atoms of earth are initiators of substances (*dravyārambhaka*), the mind is not an initiator of substances because it is devoid of touch (*sparśaśūnyatva*), as has been explained at length in the *Vyomīyakā*.

Furthermore, the conjunction with substances such as earth under dispute is not the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of cognition, because it is a conjunction with a substance such as earth, like the conjunction with another substance of earth or like the conjunction with a different substance altogether.

In the view that [the soul] possesses omnipresence (*vibhutva*), whether it be conjunction with space or conjunction with time, the objection—"what is the use of another substance, namely the mind?"—is equally applicable.
Therefore, the existence and atomicity (*aṇutva*) of the mind are established.

The *manuvata* ritual procedure for the *manotā* [verse] is for those whose Brāhmaṇa [text] is different from that of the Jyāyeya.

"The one who chooses others [as priests] is indeed cut off from the plants and trees"—thus, after censuring the description of choosing a priest from another lineage (*jyāyeyavarṇa*), the Śruti states, "One should say, 'As Manu did.
And this procedure of acting like Manu refers to the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas;
for they are descended from Brāhmaṇas, [and thus their authority] is derived from the Brāhmaṇa.

This being the position reached, [the conclusion is as follows]: because Manu’s rule regarding the *āryeya* and the *amanvata* is preceded by a prohibition against the *āryeya* for those of non-Aryan color (*varṇa*), and because that [prohibition] presupposes a prior possibility [of its application], and because of another scriptural statement—"One should cause the *āryeya* to be known for the Purohita as among the Brāhmaṇas"—which establishes it for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya as well, there is thus an equal option between the *āryeya* and the *amanvata* for all three social classes (*traivarṇika*).

In reality, however, since the statement regarding the *nindāryavādya* (the deprecatory explanatory passage) is incapable of implying a prohibition because it functions as a supplement to an injunction, and since assuming such a prohibition would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), and because Manu’s alternative arrangement finds scope among Brāhmaṇas other than those eligible for the *jyāyeyī* sacrifice, the word "option" (*vikalpa*) used in the Sūtra refers to a restricted option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*).
The phrase "of the domestic priest," etc., is merely a supplementary rule (*guṇasūtra*) for this very point;

its purpose is to establish the restriction that the four-fold portioning (*caturavatta*) applies specifically to those other than Brāhmaṇas, while the five-fold portioning (*pañcāvatta*) applies to others, thereby refuting the alternative arrangement proposed by Manu.

It should be explained that for the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, there is a distinct rule regarding the remaining [pravaras], such that the practice of the *manuvat* option applies invariably to them. (Saṃkarṣa. 3.4.15). However, according to the *manuvat* view, whether one has only one *pravara* or even five, there is only a single recitation, namely "according to Manu" (*manuvat*). (Dūṣaṇa).
