Regarding the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*), which is a constituent part of the ritual of cutting the sacrificial grass (*dharmalavanāṅga*): it is not a common procedure (*tantra*) for both the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

*Bhāṣya* 1.4.14.44–45. Regarding the mantra "Thee, by the impulse of the god... (*devasya tvā*), which pertains to the act of pouring out the grain (*nirvapaṇa*): it is not a common procedure (*tantra*) for both the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
1.4.14.44–45: A mantra that reveals a deity, such as "May I attain the victory of Agni," and so forth, is employed for the sake of the *apūrva* (the unseen transcendental result).
9.1.3.14–15: Mantras are of two kinds: those that reveal an action and those that reveal a result; like the former, they are not merely instruments of the ritual act.

In this context, mantras of this kind serve as examples: "O Agni, you are the giver of life; give me life. O Agni, you are the bestower of luster; give me luster. O Agni, you are the giver of sight; give me sight. Regarding these, there is a doubt: are they to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest or by the sacrificer?
Here too, the previously stated principle—which excludes the expectation of additional subsidiary parts—is extended by means of that same terminology.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: [the status of] being low (*nīcaistva*) and so forth, which are enjoined for the sake of a result, belongs to the sacrificer because the result is included within the performance of the archetype (*prakṛta*). Since it is the sacrificer who desires the result, the result also belongs to the sacrificer. As for mantras such as "giver of life" (*āyurdā*), since they are not injunctive, they merely restate results as they have already been established.

And just as there is a fruit for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) in the form of heaven and so forth in the ritual action under discussion, so too there is indeed a fruit for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the form of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
The primary status of the mantra portions is due to their being explanatory restatements (*anuvādaka*) of the sacrificer's fruit;
for the fruit of heaven is denoted by words such as "longevity" (*āyus*) and the like.

And just as [the indicative power] functions as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), so too it is indeed possible for it to function as a restatement of the fruit belonging to the officiant (*ṛtvij*).

Therefore, in accordance with the agency of the Adhvaryu priest understood from the name (*samākhyā*), the fruit consisting of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is itself invoked in the form of longevity and so forth for the purpose of encouraging the Adhvaryu alone.
Consequently, mantras of this kind must be employed by the Adhvaryu alone.
This being the case, it is replied:
this would indeed be so if the fruit were something that could be obtained from another;
for then one would deserve to have it bestowed by another.
Therefore, we pray for this fruit from Agni;
and the fruit of the sacrificer is also connected [to him] by way of the ritual action (*karma*).
However, the fruit of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is to be prayed for by name alone.
Because it is obtained from the sacrificer himself, there is no [independent] connection [between the result and the ritual].

Furthermore, this benediction is intended to generate enthusiasm; and the fruit of the sacrifice is that which is to be accomplished through the performance exactly as prescribed. That which is to be desired, by generating enthusiasm and becoming the cause for the successful completion of the application exactly as prescribed, is thereby accomplished; thus, that alone is what should be desired.
However, since the fruit belonging to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is already established by virtue of his performing the actions of the sacrificer, it is not [the object of] the prayer.

Therefore, because the designation (*samākhyā*) is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the indicative mark of being fit for prayer, which belongs specifically to the form of the sacrificer—the conclusion is established that the benedictory mantras (*āśīr-mantra*) must be recited by the sacrificer alone.
The purpose [of this discussion] is as stated in the respective positions.
But the Sūtra says: "Those mantras by which no ritual action is performed are also for the sacrificer (yājamāna), just like a desire for a quality. [This is] the Tautā [tīkā].
And the Veda consists of both mantra and Brāhmaṇa.
Bhāṣya 2.1.8.33:
"And the mantras [are to be repeated] because they are occasional (saṃnipātin).

In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, when there is a separation of the ritual stations (vihāra-pṛthaktva), those mantras which are occasional—such as those used in the taking of the clarified butter (ājyagrahaṇa), the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), and the touching (abhimarśana)—must be performed separately."

Because they are combined (*saṃnipātin*). These mantras are auxiliaries by way of combination; they denote the ritual action as it has presented itself. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they must be employed separately by the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ.
Which mantras?

At the division of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices, there is the combination (*samuccaya*) of all [the mantras], such as "May you two separate according to your respective portions" (*yathābhāgaṃ vyāvartethām*) and "May Bhaga divide you two" (*bhago vāṃ vibhajatu*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is an option (*vikalpa*) in their application. For, since what has already been manifested cannot be manifested again, and because the requirement for a mantra is satisfied even by an optional application, and furthermore because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text, "He takes it up with four," there is an optional application.
In the Saṃkarṣa: Mantras are of two kinds;
these are those that describe an action as it is being performed (kriyamāṇānuvādinaḥ).
The *karaṇas* produce the cognition "I am doing"; those that merely describe what is being done (*kriyamāṇānuvādinas*) produce the cognition "it should be done in this way.
For the Adhvaryu priest, however, there is no need for the cognition "I am doing."
And those [mantras] which describe what is being performed (kriyamāṇānuvādinaḥ) restate the matter being carried out by the Adhvaryu priest;
that restatement is intended to cause the recollection of the two objects to be obtained.
Mantras that describe what is being performed serve the purpose of bringing [the action] to mind.
By virtue of the power inherent in the mantra, recollection must be produced by means of the mantra;
and because the mantra has the purpose of causing recollection, that which is recollected through its power serves one's purpose.
Furthermore, in the case of extensive rituals, there is a need for a continuous stream of recollection.
The mantras are a means of valid cognition regarding dharma. (Bhāṣya 12.3.16.370;
Maṇi, p. 13).
The mantras belonging to the Adhvaryu in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are of various forms;
the mantras belonging to the sacrificer (Yajamāna) are for the purpose of encouragement, such as:
"O Agni, you are the giver of life."
And so forth. Bhāṣya 3.8.6.15–16:
Mantras should be employed in ritual action exactly as they are recited in the collection of mantras (mantrasāmnāya), and not with the accentuation used for Brāhmaṇa texts.
The section concerning speech-forms: Those mantras which are intended for addressing others are *nigadas*, and they possess the very nature of *yajus*.

Those mantras which are taught in the Brāhmaṇa itself and are not recited in the collection of mantras (the Saṃhitā) must be employed with the very accent of the Brāhmaṇa. Those mantras which are not established by their inherent indicative power (*liṅga*) but are enjoined by a direct statement (*vacana*), because they are otherwise unestablished, fulfill their purpose solely through that injunction of the mantra; such a sentence does not further enjoin the accent, for fear of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*). [Durmādhava on PMS 12.3.8.21] Those mantras which are applied by their inherent indicative power...
Mantras must be employed exactly as they are known to be.
In this regard, there is no active role for the Brāhmaṇa at all.

Mantras—possessing the powers of the word *yat*, vocatives, the first person plural, and injunctions—are undertaken as means for accomplishing Dharma; even though they are heard repeatedly through verbal forms such as "with which [mantras] the sacrificer worships and gives to the gods," they do not lead to the postulation of a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).
Or [the word "mantra" refers to] the mantras, which are a portion of the Veda. (Vārttika 3.1.1.1, p. 649)
Dharma is the authority. (Vi.
1.4.1) First of all, with respect to the subject matter to be expressed, the mantras provide the basis for their application by means of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).

In that case, if the secondary (gauṇī) scriptural mention (*śruti*) were one that abandons its own primary meaning, then a scriptural mention would have to be postulated equally for both [the primary and the secondary meanings]. However, if even when expressing a secondary meaning, the previously established primary meaning must first be denoted, then—since there is no reason to bypass that [primary meaning]—once a scriptural mention for its application has been postulated, the mantra, the context (*prakaraṇa*), and the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*) become devoid of further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*). Consequently, there is no basis for postulating another scriptural mention; thus, there is no application [of the mantra to the secondary meaning]. Or rather: [text fragment]

"The *kuśa* grass, the *darbha* grass, and so forth, as well as the mantras and the Brāhmaṇas that have been extensively studied—these do not become useless simply because they are employed again and again."
Furthermore,
the capacity to denote is not the cause for being a mantra;
rather, it is the actual employment of that which denotes.
Those which are not designated as mantras by those who are learned [in the matter] are not mantras.
Bhāṣya 2.1.9.34:
"Among those being recited in Vedic study, those in which the word 'mantra' is traditionally recorded..."
Those [sounds] are indeed the designations; for this is remembered as the defining characteristic of mantras.
Or rather,
the mantras assist [the ritual] when they are uttered, not otherwise.
Bhāṣya 3.1.6.17.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agniṣoma at the Kauṇḍapāyana Agniṣṭoma, the Hotṛ should recite the mantra used for wrapping the sacrificial post, namely, "parivarīsaḥ" (Vi.
3.8.11). In the Vājapeya sacrifice, one should cause the sacrificer himself to recite the mantras designated as *klṛpti*.

The mantras beginning with “May life be perfected through sacrifice” (*āyuryajñena kalpatām*) are *klṛptis*. In the Jyotiṣṭoma Soma-sacrifice, there is the solicitation by means of the mantra “Do thou invite” (*upahvayasva*), and the response by means of the mantra “I am invited” (*upahūtaḥ*). (Bhāṣya 3.1.6.42) When an action has been performed by one mantra, the employment of a second is purposeless.
The mention of a deity by means of a mantra has a visible purpose, because it depends upon recollection.
Since the mantra serves the function of an instrument, its repeated use occurs, such as "do, do, may I do."
There is a rule that a mantra being drawn forth must have the same agent as the ritual action.
Vārttika 3.8.126.

Since a mantra cannot function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) unless it reveals a meaning connected with the ritual action (*karma-samaveta-artha*), the fact that it is heard to be an instrument necessitates—by the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*)—the assumption that its meaning is so connected; it is not otherwise.

(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 728). The capacity of a mantra to reveal a meaning connected with the ritual action and the capacity to achieve syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) constitute its "verbal power" (*śabda-sāmarthya*).
Bāla, p. 9:

The procedure (tantra) belongs to the mantra, not to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—[namely] for every handful at the pouring out [of grain], for every cutting at the reaping, for every layer at the strewing of the altar, and for every taking at the taking up of the clarified butter.
Since a mantra is not prescriptive, it would be weaker than an indicative mark (*liṅga*) or a direct statement (*śruti*) [in the case of prescribing a deity].
Vārttika 2.1.23, p. 533. However, there is no contradiction whatsoever in a mantra speaking even while being dependent [on other factors].

There is a sublation of the mantra and of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) ritual element by the chariot and so forth, which are prescribed as the means for the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) of the Mahendra cup in the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 10.4.1, Section 1–2, Part 3: Regarding the mantra "patnīṃ saṃnaha," there is no substitution [of the word *patnīm*] even in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti-yāga*) involving two wives;
there is no substitute for this mantra.
see Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2930, under the entry "devatāgniṣaddhikriyāṇām.

A mantra lacks the capacity to convey a meaning already established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); because it is not intended for that purpose, it is non-authoritative (*anārthatva*), and because it is not injunctive (*avidhāyakatva*).
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 10.8.10.20: The mantra, as another means of valid cognition, is to be employed once;
[this applies] to the state of being consecrated (*dīkṣitatva*) in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

The mantra functions in accordance with the Brāhmaṇa; for when there is a conflict between the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa, it is said: "But the mantra is subordinate because it illuminates the meaning declared by the Brāhmaṇa. (The remainder is: "For when [the mantra] encounters a primary sense that is contradictory, it is indeed joined to a secondary sense as its cause.
This is the supplement.
Thus it is stated in the *Aindrī-ādhikaraṇa-vārtika* (Su. p.
1248): "Whichever mantra is enjoined in whichever Veda, that [Veda] alone is designated by that [mantra]. (vā. pṛ. 752)
If, however, it were prescribed in both cases, then an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the fire-altars would be accepted.
(Vārttika 3.1.17). In the inquiry as to whether there is a definition of a mantra or not, the conclusion is that there is one.
The definition of a mantra is its being well-known as such through established usage (abhiyukta-prasiddhi).
Bhāṣya 2.1.7.32. The purpose of a mantra’s utterance is the presentation of the ritual object at the time of performance.
It is made known that the object presented by the mantra is to be performed;
there is no subsumption under an injunction for the mantra;
this is the *parākrama*.
The mantra is uttered once.
Because there is no temporal sequence in the abandonment of specific [defilements] through a non-conjunctive action, it is uttered once.
As stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya: "The gods are the Brahmins" (Bhā.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, at the time of spreading the sacrificial grass for the Āgnīṣomīya animal, a separate repetition must be performed for the *ātithyā* grass—the grass that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the mantra used for spreading—on the day of the fast (*aupavasathya*).

Because the purpose of the mantra is for the sake of recollection, that which has been performed is brought to mind for the sake of the present action, just as that which has been dispatched is brought to mind. But is it not the case that recollection occurs solely by the force of the injunction?
It is true that [the performance] occurs from the injunctive word by virtue of its inherent capacity;
it also occurs from the mantra.
Because the mantra possesses the capacity for instruction, the action must be performed with the mantra.

Bhāṣya 1.2.15.37: For this is the purpose of a mantra, namely that it causes one to remember either the action or the means [of its accomplishment]. Without such remembrance, the action does not proceed.
Thus, the mantra prescribed for the *hiraṇyagarbha* verse in the *vāyavya* sacrifice is to be inserted at the subsequent pouring (*uttarādhāra*).

Since even words whose meanings are not inherently connected [to the ritual action] can serve the purpose of recollection by virtue of being words whose meanings are connected [to the action], the status of the entire mantra as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is established.
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 110). Regarding the mantra "uttiṣṭhannanvāha" (Rising, he recites), there is an injunction of time (*kāla-vidhi*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
There is an option regarding the mantra for touching in the modifications of the Āgneya sacrifice.
In the *avījeṣṭi* sacrifice within the *rājasūya*, there is no repetition of the mantra for threshing (*avaghāta*).
However, in the *cayana* (brick-piling) ritual, when the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick is repeated, the mantra for it is also repeated.
Furthermore, there is no relationship of priority and posteriority between an injunction and a mantra;
therefore, a mantra lacks the quality of being a supplement to an injunction. This is the argument of Parākrama.

The mantra for the consecration of the sacrificial cakes (*pūpānumantraṇa-mantra*) is displaced from the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). (Bhāṭṭa 3.2.1) Without an action that serves as the cause for manifestation, there is no logical connection for a mantra that functions as a manifestor.
The plural number [in the mantra] finds its application in the archetype (prakṛti) itself;
the Manotā mantra, however, is applied to a figurative sense (gauṇārtha).
Bhāṭṭa 3.2.1: The application of the mantra for cutting [the grass] is to the primary *barhis* (sacrificial grass).
By means of the application of the injunction's power, the mantra is not established [independently]; rather,
this [injunction] will, by its very nature, prescribe the mantras and cause them to be recalled through the force of that application.
(This refers to the prima facie view.
Vārttika 2.1.6.30:
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the injunction regarding the time for the mantra used in performing the vow is expressed by the phrase "he releases his speech."
A modification of the *śrīhimantra* does not occur even when a substitute is employed.
The mantra "haviṣkṛdehi" (O preparer of the oblation, come! is to be used for the purpose of summoning.
The priority of application belongs to those two mantras that reveal the fruit and the deity;
this is the "Section on the Fruit and the Deity" (*Phaladevatādhikaraṇa*).
In a modified ritual (*vikṛti*) involving two sacrificial animals, there is a substitution of the dual number for the singular and plural endings of both the *pāśa* (noose) and the mantra.
This is the "Pāśa-nyāya" (the principle of the noose).
Furthermore, regarding mantras, their function is the illumination of the matter prescribed [in the ritual].
Therefore, the gift of a cow (*godāna*) and the sacrifice of a cow (*goyāga*) have not become distinct from mere repetition [of words].
[This establishes] that the purpose of mantras is the comprehension of meaning.
The section concerning mantras:
when the number of mantras is insufficient, the required number is completed by repetition;
[this applies to] the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
The application (*viniyoga*) of mantras such as "drunk by Indra" (*indrasya pītasya*) in their entirety within the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is established through direct injunction (*anuṣṭha*).

The recitation of these mantras by the Pratiprasthātṛ in place of the Adhvaryu occurs during the Varuṇapraghāsa rites of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices in the southern sacrificial enclosure (*dakṣiṇavihāra*).

Since mantras were composed by ṛṣis and because their usage exists eternally in the form of an unbroken tradition (*pravāha*), they do not entail the contingency of the Vedas being non-eternal (*anityatva*).
Su. Pṛ. 111:

Even with a single-minded focus, there is no production [of the result] from the mantras because they have not been performed [as a collective]. Since mantras serve as the means for hymns (*stotra*) and so forth by way of denoting their own respective meanings, and since there is a difference in the sentence-meaning for each individual mantra, each one possesses its own intermediate function called "denotation of its own meaning. When these mantras thus function as means for the hymns and so forth through their respective intermediate functions, a statement accompanied by a number [such as "twelve"] implies a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the means. Consequently, because there is an absence of a collective means, the status of being a means does not reside distributively (*vyāsaṅgi*).
Page 817: Mantras have a connection with their primary meaning as understood through their innate authority (*autpattika-prāmāṇya*).
Page 1084:

Since mantras serve the purpose of performance (*karaṇārthatva*), there should be a conjunction of the ritual action and so forth at the end of the mantra, because the entire [mantra] has the purpose of expression (*vacanārthatva*).

With the words "For food, thee" (*iṣe tvā*), he cuts [the grass]. Because the mantras mentioned in the passages beginning with "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ" (*devasya tvā savituḥ prasave*) serve as instruments (*karaṇa*) and possess the nature of instruments, the conjunction of the action with the mantra must occur at the end of the mantra—that is, at the beginning of the action. The "beginning of the action" refers to the first part of the action;
their "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*) means they must be performed together.
Thus, at the time of uttering the final word "thee" (*tvā*) in the mantra "For food, thee," or even the final syllable "ā," the blow of the sacrificial knife upon the hall must be performed.
Thus it is in all cases.
Therefore, in the case of ritual (karaṇa) mantras, the commencement of the rite occurs at the end of the mantra;
this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).
The commencement of the ritual action occurs at the end of the mantras that function as instruments.
There is an optionality (*vikalpa*) among those mantras functioning as instruments that serve a single purpose.

Since it is logical that mantras are recited within a specific context for the purpose of denoting the auxiliaries of the ritual action, it is not appropriate to assume an unseen transcendental result (*adṛṣṭa*).
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 102).
Mantras serve the purpose of illuminating the ritual action.
Or [it may be that]: "Because the mantras are connected with ritual acts, their application should be according to their own specific property (*svadharma*), since that property is caused by them.

Because the mantras are connected with ritual acts—that is, because they are to be employed in rituals—their specific property at the time of learning, such as "one should not study on a festival day" (*parvaṇi nādhyeyam*) and so forth, should qualify their application at the time of the ritual performance according to that very property.
Because that [non-study] is the cause for the Dharma; that is, because the application of the mantra has that as its cause.
Therefore, during times when study is prohibited, mantras should not be uttered in ritual acts.
This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Alternatively, because they are prescribed with respect to knowledge (*vidyā*), there should be the application [of mantras] at all times, since the application is subordinate to the ritual action (*karman*). Since rules such as "one should not study on a festival day" are prescribed with respect to knowledge—that is, they apply to the time of receiving and studying [the Veda]—and since the application is subordinate to the ritual action, and because the application of mantras is for the purpose of performing the ritual, the mantras should be applied at all times, both during formal study (*svādhyāya*) and during periods when study is prohibited (*anadhyāya*).
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Furthermore, for mantras, the expression of their meaning must be performed, not their mere form;
for if one were to rely on the form alone, an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) would have to be postulated.
A visible benefit is observed through the expression of meaning;
Bhāṣya 9.1.1.1.
And the efficacy of mantras lies in their own form, not in a form produced by the apūrva.

*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 9.1.1.4: There is a combination (*samuccaya*) of mantras—whether they consist of recitation (*japa*), praise (*stuti*), benediction (*āśis*), or direct denotation (*abhidhāna*)—and not an option (*vikalpa*).

Although there is no repetition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-abhyāsa*) in the case of mantras—since they concern matters already known through other means such as the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) which possess the essence of the deity and so forth—they nonetheless possess validity because they are non-contradictory (*avisaṃvāditva*); thus say the ancients (*jīrṇāḥ*).

Someśvara maintains that for mantras, both [the status of being an auxiliary and the status of being a means to a desired end] are established through the sequential production of relations—such as being a qualifier of specific acts like the pouring of oblations (*nirvāpa*)—which are manifested by the mode of being a means to the desired goal, via the alternative applications of the injunction regarding their status as auxiliaries (*aṅgatva*). (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 388).

The Miśras maintain that the authority of mantras—as instances of ritual acts—lies in their function as *padārtha-vidhi* (injunctions regarding constituent elements) within the *prayoga-vidhi* (injunction of performance), which prescribes that "one should bring about [the result] by means of the specific [mantra], such as the *prayāja* mantra.

In reality, however, the authority of mantras consists in their capacity to generate the cognition of the meaning of the mantra-sentence itself. This is because they are established through the process of determination (*nirṇaya*) and so forth; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*apatti*) of the loss of the status of being an "unapprehended object" (*anadhigata-arthatva*), since the specific nature of what is to be accomplished by the means of action (*sādhana*) is already known here. Furthermore, the authority of the mantras as *dharma* is thus appropriately established.

If, moreover, "novelty of object" (*anadhigatārthatva*) is understood as having as its object something that was not the object of a cognition occurring in a moment immediately preceding the one in which it itself occurs, and which is co-referential with it, then the validity of [the mantra] is all the more established even in its capacity as a reminder.

*Maṇi*, pp. 10–11. According to the *Śāstradīpikā*, the validity of mantras lies in their being the words (*padārtha*), because validity is admitted based on the fact that the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is derived from the meanings of the words.
However, the venerable Guru (Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa) maintains that their validity consists precisely in their correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*), just like recollection (*smṛti*).

Bhaṭṭa Someśvara, however, states that it also consists in "having an object not already known. (Bālakrīḍā, p. 70). But since validity regarding the investigation of the meaning of mantras is possible, that [latter view] alone is correct. (p. 72).
Among the mantras and the directly perceived Brāhmaṇas, the middle layer is the *citri* (the interspersed portion).
However, for those [mantras] that depend on the *Aupānuvākya* section, there is no connection at all through syntactical unity (*vākya*).
Vārttika 14.12.23, p. 364. For mantras known as *brāhmaṇas*, the accent of the *brāhmaṇa* portion should be employed.
Mīmāṃsākośa 12.3.9.23–24, p. 1497; see under the entry "of mantras known as *brāhmaṇas*."
There is an option regarding mantras prescribed by the Brāhmaṇas.
For example, there is an option between the two mantras for the offering of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices.

And because all [mantras] prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa are indicated as being for the sake of number. The Commentary states: Furthermore, regarding those mantras that are enjoined in the Brāhmaṇa—such as "He spreads the sacrificial cake with the mantra, 'Spread wide! and "He spreads the sacrificial cake with the mantra, 'O you who are wide-spreading, may the lord of the sacrifice spread wide!'"—there should be a combination (samuccaya) of them, because all of them are indicated [as required].
The instruction for one who does not apply [the ritual] is contradicted;
furthermore, the injunction regarding the performance will favor the inclusion of all constituent parts,
and the fact that they are prescribed by number will result in their meaningfulness through repeated mention.
Therefore, there is a combination.
And the observation of the combination of the *yājyā* and the *vaṣaṭ*-call is likewise.
Commentary: In the case of combination, there is thus an observation of the combination of the *yājyā* and the *vaṣaṭ*-call, namely: "He utters the *vaṣaṭ*-call over the *yājyā*."
For sequence occurs in the case of a conjunction;
therefore, there is also conjunction.
Or rather, there is an option, because conjunction is not explicitly stated.
Commentary: There is indeed an option (*vikalpa*) regarding these mantras, not a combination (*samuccaya*).
Why? Because the principle has been stated:
"Since mantras are directly effective (*saṃnipāti*) and have a single purpose, there should be an option" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 12.1.12.9).
[Objection: But surely even those [factors] that share a single referent, when prescribed by number, are conjoined through repeated mention.
[Reply: This is not correct.
Why? Because conjunction is not explicitly stated in the text.

Just as in that case, because a number was heard, a repetition—though its purpose had already been fulfilled—was resorted to; such is not the case here, for there is no hearing of a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Therefore, since the *yājyā* verses have a single purpose, there is a single option (*ekavikalpa*), because the instruction is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
Commentary: As for the argument that "the instruction will be meaningful for all," that is not a valid reason,
because the instruction is intended for the sake of the [specific] qualities.
This is not an instruction regarding the meaning of the mantra;
rather, it is for the purpose of a quality (guṇa).
That is to say, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) will enjoin a quality.
As it has been said: "The repetition is for the sake of a quality," "It is an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)," or "It is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*)" (Jaimini Sūtra 12.1.43–46).
If, then, this is not an instruction regarding the mantras at all, why is it said that "all [mantras] have been instructed"?
In that case, let it be considered as a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvācintya*).
This is considered under the heading of "instruction regarding mantras.
Alternatively, another example should be observed:
there is no combination [of mantras] in the case of the *vaṣaṭ*-call, because it serves no purpose [for the mantra].

Commentary: The *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is for the purpose of offering, while the *yājyā* verse is for the purpose of indicating the deity. Since they do not serve the same purpose, there is no combination [of both], because it is not taught that they apply to all [cases].
Śāstradīpikā: The author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) has presented the prima facie view by accepting the application [of the *yājyā*] through direct scriptural statement (*vacana*).

The author of the Vārttika, however, maintains that since the application of mantras is already established through application by indicative power (*liṅga*) alone, their combination (*samuccaya*) serves merely as the purpose of the scriptural statement (*vacana*).
[This is] the connection with the example of Soma.
When there is an injunction of combination by means of a scriptural statement, the operation of indicative power, which functions independently, becomes blunted.

In the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, however, even in the case of an injunction for simultaneous performance (*samuccaya*), the operation of the statement that enjoins the mantras remains unimpeded because there is no other statement [to the contrary]; thus, there is a difference [between this case and others].

Ratna—[the author of the *Ratna-mālā*] considers that since the mantras are already obtained through their indicative power (*liṅga*), the statements are intended solely for the purpose of simultaneous performance.

But the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: those [mantras] are indeed obtained by the indicative power of the mantras; once they have achieved their purpose through the application of the mantras, the syntactical statement (*vākya*) [does not apply].
Regarding mantras:
it serves as the authoritative standard for the collection of mantras.

It was stated in the section on mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*) that even when a mantra is obtained through an indicative mark (*liṅga*), its repetition is for the sake of a specific quality (*guṇārtha*). Viśvarūpa says:

"The two initial mantras are to be combined or are to be treated as alternatives, like the number four. [Objection: The first [position] would be sublated; [Reply: Not so, because they are uttered in combination."

Bhaṭṭa: As for those cases where multiple mantras are enjoined individually by the Brāhmaṇa even without a specific number, or where, although they are already enjoined by their indicative power (*liṅga*), there is a repeated mention in the Brāhmaṇa itself for the sake of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and so forth—in those instances, regarding those mantras that are indeed enjoined by a direct statement (*vacana*), there must be a combination (*samuccaya*) precisely because of their purpose, just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings; otherwise, the injunction of them would be rendered futile.

Even in the case of those mantras assigned by indicative power (*liṅga*), such as "He spreads the sacrificial cake with the words *uru pratha uru prathasva*" and "He spreads the sacrificial cake with the words *uru te yajñapatiḥ*," the purpose of the repeated scriptural mention (*punaḥśruti*) is for the sake of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Similarly, even in the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*), there is a subsequent [interpretation] based on the authority of the mantra; for even if the application by direct statement (*vacana-viniyoga*) has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), as in the case of "He cuts the branch with the words *iṣe tvā*," it is appropriate that each instance serves a distinct purpose. Since a visible purpose is possible, one should not assume an invisible one. Therefore, because they are independent means of accomplishment, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*).

Thus, even when mantras are assigned by indicative power (*liṅga*), because the repeated mention of the mantra serves merely as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), it does not lead to the assumption of a combination (*samuccaya*) according to the logic of the "mantra and medicine" analogy.
For this very reason, it is stated therein that since the Adhvaryu is the performer from the very beginning, [the action] is enjoined in those respective scriptures.
Maṇḍana says: "When multiple mantras are mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa, they are to be treated as options (*vikalpya*)."

Śaṅkara: "In the case of [rites] prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, there is an option (*vikalpa*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule [stated in] 1.2.1–2, *mantrāṇāṃ mukhye'nyaṃ viniyogaḥ*, which is the principle of the *aindrī* mantra."
Alternatively, even when mantras are heard within a sacrifice, they serve as auxiliary elements to the ritual action by illuminating the meaning inherent in that action (Su. p.
477). The determination of the conclusion of mantras in the form of *yajus* occurs through the determination of their status as single syntactical units (*ekavākyatva*).
VI.2.1.14. The "indicative power" (*liṅga*) of mantras is their capacity to convey a meaning.

And this [capacity] is considered to apply in some manner to both the primary and the secondary sense [of a word] (for if the secondary sense were not denoted by the word itself, it could not be connected with other words whose meanings are denoted by those words).

(There is) the verbal operation even in a secondary sense—thus [says] Su. (Vārttika). The authority of mantras is through their application (*viniyoga*), not directly. Vi. 1.4.1. Since mantras, whose status as auxiliaries of the sacrifice is established by means of *śruti*, *liṅga*, and other authorities, cannot function as auxiliaries of the sacrifice in their mere form without an operation, there arises an expectancy for an operation. Among the options, utterance is rejected because its purpose would be merely transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*); rather, the denotation of the meaning, which consists of verbal cognition, is accepted as the operation because it has a perceptible purpose in the form of the recollection of the object to be performed, which serves the performance itself.
This is easily established in the case of instrumental mantras such as "I offer the *juhū* ladle at the front" (*agre juhvaṃ nirvapāmi*).

However, even in cases where there is no natural comprehension of an action to be performed, yet the mantra is nonetheless applied—as in "He cuts the branch with [the mantra] 'For food thee, for strength thee' (*iṣe tvorje tvā*)"—there too, one must assume the expression of an action to be performed by supplying the word "I cut" (*chinadmi*).

In the case of *kriyamāṇānuvādins* (mantras that describe what is currently being performed), such as "The youth, well-dressed... (*yuvā suvāsāḥ*), actions like the wrapping of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-pariṣyāṇa*) occupy a long duration of time. Consequently, there arises the possibility of an interruption in the chanting of the mantra—such as the mantra for wrapping, "You are being wrapped" (*pariṣyāse*)—due to the need for breath. To ensure the firmness of the recollection of that action, the expression of meaning is purposeful, as it serves as a cause for strengthening the memory of what is to be performed by relying on a reminder. Even though the ritual act itself does not depend on a reminder, there is no fault, because the requirement for the mantra is fulfilled precisely by the act's own need for one.

The combination (*samuccaya*) of mantras prescribed by statements containing specific numbers is as follows: for example, four [mantras] at the taking up of the fire-wood (*abhyādāna*) in the *Agnicayana*, two at the obtaining [of the fire-wood], and six in the illustrative examples (*udāharaṇa*). See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 51, under the entry "In the *Agnicayana*, of those prescribed by number."
There should be an option (*vikalpa*) among mantras that are co-present (*saṃnipātin*) and have a single purpose (*ekārtha*).

For mantras that have a single purpose—that is, those that perform a single function—such as "May Pūṣan divide," "May Bhaga divide," or "May Aryaman divide," there should be an option. This is because they are co-present, being collectively associated (*samaveta*) as instruments (*karaṇa*).
The conjunction of the ritual action and so forth with the instrumental mantras has been stated. And it is not possible to effect this conjunction for all of them without an option.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that there is an option (vikalpa) among the instrumental mantras that serve a single purpose.

"Because the mantras are brought together [in the ritual], there should be an option (*vikalpa*) among those that serve a single purpose" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.1.12.9). There is indeed an option between these mantras (such as "uru prathasva," etc.), not a combination (*samuccaya*).
Why? Because the principle has already been stated regarding "the mantras" (Bhāṣya 1.2.1.15). 13. Even though mantras serve as reminders, they possess authority.

Maṇi, p. 12. Since the *hautra* mantras describe actions as they are being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvāditva*), they are to be used in combination; there is no optionality (*vikalpa*) when they have the same purpose.

A thing cannot be assisted by anything else; thus, even without an explicit statement, there is the inclusion of fire in the act of cutting grass, and the term "Viśvedevas" in the mantra for sowing seeds.
"In the *ṣoḍaśistotra*, one should fill heaven and earth with clarified butter by means of the *audumbarī* [pillar]"—
thus it is enjoined.
From this we understand that they assist [the ritual] merely through their utterance.
Why? Because of the scriptural injunction for that purpose.

When a mantra is capable of denoting a certain meaning, the scripture enjoins it specifically for that purpose, as in: "He spreads the sacrificial cake with the words, 'O wide one, spread yourself wide!
This statement would be meaningless if mantras did not assist by means of denoting their respective meanings.
Moreover, since the application (viniyoga) has already been stated merely by the act of utterance, it need not be stated again;
therefore, it is not [established] by the expression of meaning.
Just as it is understood that a person does not see directly with his eyes when they are covered by another.
If it is argued that this must be for the purpose of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), we say no; for it has been stated that an explanatory passage is a supplement to that which is enjoined.

Therefore, the statement is not for the purpose of an explanatory passage.
