Although they are already applicable for the act of taking up by virtue of their indicative power (*liṅga*), they are enjoined by a direct statement (*vacana*) in the passage: "He takes it up with four [mantras].
If it is argued that this is for the purpose of the number four, we say no, because there is no word expressing a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Likewise, there is the example: "Imāmagṛbhṇan raśanāmṛtasya" (They have grasped this rein of immortality), "He takes up the horse's halter," and so forth.
Since the taking up of the halter is already established [by other means], the scripture serves as the restrictive injunction (*viniyojaka*) specifically for that taking up of the halter.
That [scriptural statement] would not be consistent if its meaning were not intended to be significant.
But surely it will enjoin the exclusion of the donkey’s bridle?
It is not able to enjoin an exclusion;
for in enjoining an exclusion, it would abandon its own primary meaning, it would assume a secondary sense, and it would subvert what is already established.
Therefore, mantras do not have the intention to convey a meaning.

Consequently, the application of the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*)—which has that specific form—to the act of grasping the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is not authoritative.
Or rather: since some [opponents] hear of its lack of purpose here, they raise this doubt: "Are mantras meaningful or meaningless?"
That is correctly stated:
"When the meaning is clearly understood from the word, it cannot be said to be meaningless;
for when fire burns, whether one says *dahati* or *dahe*, what need is there for deliberation regarding its power to burn?"
For, since an effect is observed everywhere, the capacities of words are inferred;
and that communication of meaning is perceived only from mantras that have ritual purposes.

Nor do the prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣa) become as they are described merely on the basis of a bare proposition such as "the sentence-meaning [is established] when [the words] are undistinguished."
Thinking that this presentation is inappropriate because of such [precedents], he asks: "Are mantras intended to convey meaning, or are they not intended to convey meaning?
Now, one might object: "But surely this too should not be investigated by means of another reason.
This is not a fault.

Since even meaningful sentences are observed to be of two kinds—namely, utterance and the communication of meaning, which are invariably concomitant—it follows that when either one is intended and employed, the other necessarily occurs as well. For instance, if the communication of meaning is intended, then utterance follows by implication; or, if utterance is intended, then the communication of meaning follows as a matter of course.

Just as there is an occasion for reflection on whether there is thought of sense objects during recitations (*japa*), how then does this relate to the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? This has already been stated previously (at the beginning of the section on *arthavāda*):

namely, that "because the Veda has action as its purpose" (1.2.1.2) is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) here, and by the very refutation of that, its lack of further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) has been restated.

For he thinks as follows: if a connection can somehow be established even for such passages as "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*), then what doubt could there be regarding the mantras? Therefore, it is only the specific utility that must be considered.

Regarding that, the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself will refute the view that the literal meaning is intended (at *api vā prayoga...* [JS 2.1.6.31]), because their nature is indistinguishable [from other speech] and because praise prescribed in another context is impossible.
By process of elimination, since they are employed according to their own form, it is now deliberated whether either the verbal expression itself or the external meaning is intended.
However, since the Sāmans lack denotative power (*vācakatva*), there arises a doubt as to whether they are intended merely for the manifestation of the self-recitation (*ātmaprayoga*).

But how, then, can the opponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) establish the employment of certain mantras that are not connected by direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*)? Some say: he strives to show that they are not to be employed at all, on the grounds that their meaning is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitārthatva*).

No one employs mantras whose meanings are not based on anything [real]. Therefore, as for the statement regarding the established efficacy [of mantras]—namely, "Do they assist merely by being uttered?"—this is certainly not [the case] for this very [mantra].
For in that context, the intention is directed toward what is defective.

If he intends to state that there is benefit merely from the utterance of the name, then he will explain that this refers to the non-application [of the mantra] by virtue of its inherent power (*śakti*).

Furthermore, as for what will be explained regarding the purpose of the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*)—namely, its application to the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)—that should be understood as being established precisely through the cognition of its application in this manner.
Alternatively, this investigation is conducted without considering the establishment of application based on the undisputed observation of ritual practitioners (*yājñika*).
But for what purpose is the consensus of the ritualists (*yājñika*) being examined, since that very consensus is not itself being analyzed as to whether it is logical or illogical?
The intention here is this:
in any case, their status as a practice established by tradition (*smṛti*) is firmly settled, and it is impossible to subvert that within the system (*tantra*).
Now, the root of this very matter is being examined.

If it should be the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), then, due to the absence of any other means of knowledge, we shall postulate a root by inferring an applicatory scriptural statement (*viniyojaka-śruti*).
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the determination is that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*) alone constitute the root.
Alternatively, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
"The mantras are directed toward the human goal by the very injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*). To explain:
By means of the sequence (*krama*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), everything touched upon by the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices is accepted as being contributory;
this includes both the sentences concerning the fore-offerings (*prajāya*) and the mantras.

In that regard, sentences such as those beginning with *prajāpati* have fulfilled their purpose by conveying the meaning; thus, even though they touch upon their own verbal form, they do not attain the status of being employed [in the ritual].

Mantras, on the other hand, because they express what is not useful for the action, are not required in that respect. However, since praise (*stuti*), injunction (*vidhi*), and recollection (*smṛti*) are established through other means, it is only the form of these [mantras] that is taken up by the performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*).

Even the injunction regarding the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*) fulfills its purpose by imparting the very form of the mantra that is most proximate; it does not extend so far as to convey a remote meaning. In the case of sentences such as those concerning the *praiṣas* (directions), it was indeed possible for them to be understood through the apprehension of their form, and thus it was appropriate for them to take up their intended meaning; but here, nothing is like that. Furthermore, since an operation (*kārya*) is impossible with respect to the word itself, the operation is understood to apply to the meaning.
In the case of mantras, however, it is sound alone that comes into being.

For even on the view that meaning is not primary, a person must necessarily be enjoined to [utter] the sound; for its expression occurs either through the non-separation from that [sound] or because of its posteriority in time.
Therefore, it is indeed sound alone that is the object of the injunction.
And thus, the *arthavāda* passages such as "for that purpose" (*tadarthaśāstra*) and so forth are mentioned.
In accordance with the sequence of the sūtras providing the refutations, even though they were cited in reverse order, [the mantras] beginning with "āśrayādāna" (taking hold) must be supplied.

However, the author of the Bhāṣya, considering that the purpose is accomplished even by citing them in whatever way they may be, has presented them in this manner, starting with "uru prathas uru prathas."
Regarding the phrase "as one with eyes":

although it is said by others that the sense organ of one afflicted by jaundice (nīlīroga) and so forth is like a healthy eye, yet when being led by another, it is known that he does not see; likewise, let the nature of a mantra be considered: even though there exists the cognition of its power to illuminate meaning, nevertheless, seeing its application by another, it is understood that it lacks the power to apply itself independently.
Therefore, it is dependent on another.
Otherwise, it would be applied by itself.
The phrase "for the sake of an explanatory passage (arthavāda)" intends to praise the injunction regarding the mantra, which is established by its indicative mark (liṅga) and context (prakaraṇa).
The word "na" (not) is indeed a particle used for division [of the sentence].

Arthavādas are postulated as being for the purpose of praise because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction. However, since an injunction—whether directly perceived or inferred—that exists in another location, by removing its own deficiency through the manifestation of the power of persuasion inherent in its proximity, has its requirement satisfied, it stands in need of the function of praise provided by something distant. Likewise, because the taking up [of the fire-wood] is already established by the very nature of the act, the statement "He takes it up with four" would be meaningless regarding the number four; rather, it should be understood as establishing the fact that the mantras used are those addressed to Tvaṣṭṛ.
For a quality belonging to one thing does not go over to another.
Furthermore, because [the fire] is devoid of action, it cannot be designated as an object (*karman*).

Therefore, the sentence would have to be: "One should perform the act of taking up with these four"; yet, since they are already four even prior to this statement, [the mention of them as] "four" is redundant.

Furthermore, since doubt regarding [the combination] is not a constituent part of the ritual action (*kriyānaṅga*) and there is no word expressing a conjunction (*samuccaya*), the option (*vikalpa*) resulting from the individual capacity [of each element] cannot be prevented. Moreover, because that which is non-existent is understood through repetition, and because that which is invisible is not heard [in the text], it is logical that their combination is established on the basis of the evidence for prior existence. Thus, both [elements] are enjoined for the purpose of bringing about what is not otherwise stated by the words, since they are obtained through implication (*arthāpatti*).
If the mantra is also obtained from the form [of the action], then the statement is purposeless;
for it would serve as an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) because it is intended for recitation by others, and thus the cognition is said to be produced by you.
That [cognition] too would apply either to the taking up of the donkey’s bridle or to the mantra.
In both cases, there would be a threefold defect;
furthermore, by taking it as being intent upon the injunction (*vidhipara*), one would abandon its own primary meaning and fail to refute the "donkey's reins" in the other sentence.
Furthermore, it would obstruct either the form already obtained or the taking up of the mantra.
Since its purpose is transcendental (adṛṣṭa), according to the established principle, it must function exactly where it is led.
If there were a connection with the phrase "the horse's halter" (aśvābhidhānīm), then it would constitute an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā); however, that is not the case.
Because there is no mutual relationship among the factors of action (*kāraka*) apart from their connection with an action,
even a sentence must be connected through action alone; and that action is one.
Since the connection with the preceding context is indistinct, he states the purpose of the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*):
"Therefore, the *barhis* [grass] is not a means of knowledge," and so forth.
For in that case, by virtue of the statement regarding the great sacrifice (*mahāproga*), all mantras would pertain exclusively to the primary rite.
Therefore, it comes about that those who possess the knowledge of its application are not to be gathered together by the ignorant.
Even then, due to the requirement of following the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), there is no performance out of sequence.
Without bringing the ritual acts together, one performs them after having recited either a single *anuvāka* or the entire [text] all at once.
Because of the fixed order of the sentences.
The Commentary states: Mantras indeed possess a fixed sequence, such as "Agni is the head of heaven," and not in reverse order.
If they were for the purpose of conveying meaning, then since the meaning would be understood even in reverse order, the fixed rule would be purposeless.

Now, because of the distinction in pronunciation, when there is a reversal, another pronunciation is adopted; thus, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is resorted to, by which that side upon which the restriction is meaningful is surely the correct side.
But is it not the case that even where there is meaningfulness, a restriction is observed, as for example in *indrāgnī*?
That is appropriate in that case.
Because the meaning is communicated even when the order is reversed.

Or rather—just as the meaning understood from the phrase "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*) is the same as that understood from the phrase "the head, etc., [is Agni]" (*mūrdhādirityanena*), there is a restriction [of word-order] based on another source.

However, for that whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), since there would be no authority for the unseen merit arising from its utterance if the order were changed, a change in order is not appropriate; thus, the restriction is purposeful.

Now, if it were assumed that an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) arises from the restriction [of word usage], then that [unseen result] would be established as dependent upon the utterance [itself]; for comprehension occurs by virtue of that utterance.

As for the restriction observed in the case of roots, suffixes, and compounds whose purposes are seen—such as *indrāgnī*, *nīlotpalam*, *rājapuruṣaḥ*, *citrāgaḥ*, and *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*—that is appropriate, because there, despite the difference in subject matter, the consequence of [the words] being ungrammatical (*apaśabda*), meaningless, or redundant would otherwise arise.

For in that context, a fixed initial placement (pūrvanipāta) is prescribed based on specific causes such as being a word beginning with a vowel other than *a* (*ajādya*) or ending in *a* (*adanta*), or being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Consequently, *agnīndrī* is incorrect; *puruṣarājaḥ* is a different [unauthorized] form; and *kauśāmbibhiḥ* is meaningless.
As for the usage *agnīndrī* found in some places, it must be understood as either Vedic (*cchāndasa*) or intended to express the state of being a noble person (*āryahantatva*).
The status of the term *indrāgnī* is established as being of equal rank [with other dual compounds].

But surely, here too, because of the difference in sequence, it would lack the status of a mantra? In that case, since its purpose is to convey the meaning, we perceive no reason whatsoever for its destruction [or alteration] to occur.

Therefore, regarding the establishment of the mantra, the sūtra "because of the restriction of the sentence" (*vākyaniyamāt*) is also [applicable]—the word "sūtra" is used for a portion of a sūtra (as seen in the usage "he has come to the village" when referring to a part of a village).
Alternatively, let it be "because of the restriction of sentences studied outside of the context.
For in the communication of meaning, there is no distinction between that which belongs to another and that which belongs to oneself.
Alternatively, since the capacity to denote a meaning is equal for both a mantra and an ordinary human statement, a restriction to the use of the mantra-statement is observed.
Or rather, because there is a restriction of the statement when there is the possibility of various means of recollection such as meditation;
for in the case of a perceptible object, there is no distinction whatsoever between a mantra and meditation or other such means—this is what must be illustrated.
From the *Yuddhaśāstra*.
The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): Furthermore, regarding what has already been understood, through recitation, a mantra becomes capable of conveying that meaning, such as "O Agni and Indra, move apart.

Would it then cause that which is already understood to be understood? Or rather, if its purpose is for a specific mode of utterance, then even in the case of what is already understood, a specific mode of utterance is appropriate.
But surely, through repetition, there will be a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
In this way, you have merely resorted to our own position.
"Repetition" means the utterance of speech.
For that [protection] can indeed be provided, but not the attainment of the object itself; once that [object] has passed, it is impossible,
just as it is impossible to place a second sandal on a foot that already has a sandal.

Or rather—as in the statement, "For one who is ignorant is not entitled [to perform rites]" (3.8.8)—the meanings of the words studied in the Veda must necessarily be understood primarily through the context of ritual action (*karma*).

In that regard, an injunction (*praiṣa*) is incapable of providing knowledge according to the maxim of "grinding what is already ground" (*piṣṭapeṣaṇanyāya*), and thus it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Now, if it is argued that the mantra is a reminder (*smāraka*):
That too is not the case;
for that [result] is accomplished solely through the impressions (*saṃskāra*) caused by the cultivation of Brahminical knowledge.
Alternatively, the cause for the manifestation of those impressions will be either the completion of the preceding ritual action or the attainment [of the goal]; there is no need for mantras.

In this regard, as for what is said—that there will be a specific modification of the impression (*saṃskāra*)—this cannot possibly be something other than the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); therefore, it is the position of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

For if even a perceived [cause] does not accomplish the effect when another [unseen cause] is absent, then having gone even a short distance, one must necessarily postulate that very thing; thus, [the result] arises from the utterance itself.
This is because of the mention of what is non-existent.

The Commentary states: Just as a means (*sādhana*) is to be manifested, there is no such object as that which they express, such as in the verse, "Four are its horns" (*catvāri śṛṅgā*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.10.17).
For there exists no sacrificial implement whatsoever that has four horns, three feet, two heads, and a thousand [limbs].
If its purpose were to denote that [action], what would it denote?
However, it is postulated as being for the purpose of utterance.
Likewise, in the case of "Do not harm me," even though no actual harming is taking place, what would it denote?
Or rather—there exists no ritual act such as the four-horned [sacrifice] or anything related to it, whether in the archetype (prakṛti) or the ectype (vikṛti).

Even if there were something by way of a subordinate element (guṇa), nevertheless, because those subordinate elements are not brought forth, the purpose must be accomplished through their recollection;
and it is not known in which specific context it should be employed.
In that case, since the recitation must follow the sequence of the mantra, this position is established.

Passages such as "Do not harm me" and "May I not be terrified," because they concern those who know the Veda or the like, serve as examples under the rule "because of the connection with meaning in non-sentient things.
However, in the present instance, since injury is not even a possibility, the prohibition would be purposeless.
"Because they are bound to insentient objects.
Commentary: Indeed, they bind [mantras] to insentient objects, such as "O herb, protect him!
They assist by means of naming; mantras of this kind would thus cause the plants to provide for the cattle.
Furthermore, it is not possible to convey that which is insentient;
however, this fault does not apply when the purpose is utterance.
Therefore, they exist for the purpose of utterance.
"Listen, O pressing-stones," is an example.
Furthermore, [the examples] "O herb, protect! and "Listen, O pressing-stones! are for the purpose of making the object of address inclined toward the performance of the task;
yet such inclination is not possible for that which is insentient.

Furthermore, activity [toward a ritual act] cannot be justified by a directive (praiṣa) in the case of "protection of cattle" or "listening to the morning litany" (prātaranuvāka); thus, there would be pointlessness if there were an intention to convey a meaning.
This is because of a contradiction in meaning.
The Commentary states: "There is also a contradiction in meaning, as in: 'Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the mid-region'."
And who would ever maintain that "this very [fire] is the intermediate space"?
And if it cannot be so maintained, what purpose would a name serve?
However, this contradiction does not arise when [the mantra] is used merely for recitation.
Therefore, mantras are intended for recitation.
"There is one Rudra; he did not stand as a second," and "The thousands of Rudras who are upon the earth"—these are the examples.
Or rather—the nature of being the sky (*dyutva*) and the nature of being the intermediate space (*antarikṣatva*), as well as both unity and multiplicity, are contradictory attributes of Rudra.
Nor is this contradictory matter applicable to ritual action (*karmopāyika*).
Or how could the deity Aditi be the intermediate space or the sky?
Nor can the two reasons be set aside even by treating them as praise;
for in the Brāhmaṇa, praises are meaningful as supplements to injunctions,
whereas the praise in a mantra, being purposeless, is not to be taken seriously.
Because there is no mention of speech as in the case of Vedic study.
The Commentary states: At the time of Vedic study, Pūrṇikā (this is a general term for a woman) performs the threshing;
the young student recites the mantra for threshing.

He does not practice the recitation of that name by means of that mantra; rather, he exerts himself solely in the mastery of the sequence of syllables. And that which serves a purpose must indeed be practiced.
Therefore, we understand from the practice of pronunciation that the purpose lies in the act of pronunciation itself.

Or rather—since the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*) has ritual action as its purpose, whatever constitutes a ritual action must be practiced; likewise, even though the meaning is present, learned elders direct their students toward the mere grasping of the syllables and not toward the practice of that meaning.
Therefore, it is necessarily intended that for them, the mere utterance [of the words] is the primary goal.
Because [the meaning] is unintelligible (*avijñeyāt*).
Commentary: Furthermore, the meaning of certain mantras is simply impossible to understand.
For example: "Ambyak sā ta indra ṛṣirasme," "Suṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū," and "Indraḥ somasya kāṇukā.
What could these possibly signify?
However, there is no fault if they are for the purpose of recitation;
therefore, mantras are for the purpose of recitation.
Or—some objects are not to be understood through [ordinary] cognition.

For some, the very meaning of the sentence is not understood; nor does the meaning of a mantra assist by its mere existence when it is not remembered at the time of the ritual action. Therefore, that which can be performed with certainty—namely, its recitation—is determined to be the very thing to be done. (Mīmāṃsākośa 389)
"Because of connection with impermanent things, mantras would be purposeless.

Commentary: Furthermore, there would indeed be a connection with impermanent things in those mantras that denote [specific individuals], such as: "What do your cows produce in the Kīkaṭas? They yield no milk-mixture, nor do they provide warmth for the ritual.
Bring us the wealth of Pramaganda; O Maghavan, subject Naicāśākha to us! (RV 3.53.14).
The Kīkaṭas are the name of certain regions, Naicāśākha the name of a city, and Pramaganda the name of a king.
If [the word *pramaganda*] were intended as a proper name, it would be understood that this mantra had never been experienced before the time of Pramaganda.

Thus, for these reasons—such as the existence of various Vedic branches (śākhās) and so forth—the mantras do not have their literal meaning intended (*avivakṣitavacanatā*). Or rather: if one adopts the position that they reveal meaning, then whatever meaning belongs to a mantra, that alone is revealed by it;
and some mantras are observed to have meanings that pertain to non-eternal ritual acts and objects, such as: "What do your cows do among the Kīkaṭas? (*kiṃ te kṛṇvanti kīkaṭeṣu gāvaḥ*).
For this [meaning] is reached by those who study it through a firm recollection, as it is near to Viśvāmitra.
It is said that Indra was addressed by one seeking wealth for the sake of performing rituals:
"O Lord of the Three Worlds, what do those cows do there in the Kīkaṭa regions?"
For those nihilists, saying "What is the use of ritual? do not perform any sacred rite.

Therefore, they do not milk the *āśīr* (milk mixed with Soma) for the purpose of preparing the Soma; nor do they heat the *dharma* (the residue remaining when milk is poured into hot clarified butter); nor do they become the means for the heating of the *dharma* by the gift of milk.
Therefore, bring to our city of Naicāśākha that wealth which belongs to Pramaganda, the lord of Kīkaṭa.
The letter *bh* [is inserted] according to Pāṇini 3.1.84, vārttika: *hyamormṛcchasi*.
Alternatively, it means: "O Maghavan, grant us this—that you may bestow, maintain, and nourish that [wealth] toward us"; let this be accomplished for us.
The lengthening of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
If this is what is intended, then because the Veda would be denoting something that has a beginning, it would follow that it is artificial and thus lacks authority.
Nor can any other meaning of the mantra be asserted, as no such meaning is perceived.
Therefore, since the recitation of meaningless syllables is fruitless, one must resort to the recitation of meaningful syllables.
"But the meaning of the sentence is not distinct.
The Commentary states: "But the meaning of words as they are used in common worldly speech and in the Veda is not distinct. Just as it is intended in the world, so too must it be in the Veda."
It is not so; in the world, there is conventional linguistic usage (*saṃvyavahāra*) of those objects by means of cognition. Here, in a conversation with conscious beings such as Devadatta, no one—
The section concerning mantras.
The section concerning mantras is that which provides assistance.
If an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) were to be postulated, it would suffice to assume that very [force] from the mere utterance [of the word].

For whatever is to be performed must have a purpose; however, utterance itself is not something that ought to be performed, unless it serves toward an unseen force (*apūrva*) in accordance with its actual meaning.
If the meaning were not conveyed, nothing would be purposeful;
if it were not employed [in the ritual], the recitation would be meaningless. Therefore, from the utterance [itself], there arises the *apūrva*.
And thus, the *tadarthaśāstra* and other such [arguments] have been stated. This is said:
the recitation of mantras in a sacrifice is solely for the purpose of conveying meaning.

As for what was stated—that there is no purpose in conversation with deities or sacrificial priests—the purpose at a sacrifice is simply the manifestation of the constituent parts of the sacrifice. How so? For manifestation itself cannot be the purpose unless [those parts] have already been established.
Therefore, it follows that this [result] must be produced by that;
we say: no.
It is said: "How will there be praise?
[The answer is: How can the word "one who exerts effort" (*prayatnī*) apply when there is no exertion?
[The answer is: Because it is designated by a mantra.

When it is heard in the scripture, "The Adhvaryu [prepares] the sacrificial cake with the mantra," he who says "thus he prepares" (*prasthati*) is like one who says "he performs" (*kārayati*) when another says "he acts" (*kurute*).

Or rather— although the injunction of the mantra is not praised because it resides in another location, nevertheless, because of the injunction of spreading (*prathana*) and the praise thereof, the entire sentence is meaningful.
For this is indeed its originative injunction (*utpattivākya*).

Now, one might object that spreading (*prathana*) need not be enjoined, as it is already established by the impossibility of otherwise preparing the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). This is not so, because it does not follow from that [inability].
For flour that is ground too quickly would indeed fail to spread even if it were not [otherwise] spread out.
However, when the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) exists, one must act in such a way that the spreading occurs;
and in this manner, the role of the Adhvaryu priest is also fulfilled.

For when the [text] being recited— known as the *adhvaryu* or *vasatkartr*— is obtained, it seeks a specific agent; however, since that agent is already established by the sense of the matter, the section concerning mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*) would serve here as the restrictive rule.
The section concerning mantras, as well as the fear and the repetition of syllables, have been raised;
it is now explained.
The practice of knowledge consists in ease, whereas the practice of syllables involves difficulty due to their subtlety.
Or rather—although this intention was not even suggested in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is nevertheless appropriate because it is possible;
for if the word "or" (*atha*) were useful at the time of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), then it would indeed be relied upon.
But this is not the case, because there is no connection with [the results of] actions.
However, the lack of practice regarding that [meditation] is due to its ease, like the act of sprinkling water and so forth.
Thereafter follows the supreme knowledge of what exists.
Commentary: Even though a meaning exists, it may not be perceived due to negligence, laziness, and so forth.
The meaning must be inferred from the verbal root by means of grammatical derivation and etymological analysis.
For example: "suṇyeva jabharī turpharītū" ("suṇyeva jabharī turpharītū naitaśaiva turpharī pharpharīkā").
Like two victorious ones born from water, you have drunk; that has become for me an aging, mortal body.
In such passages as *Ṛgveda* 10.106.6, names of the Aśvins ending in the dual number are observed. By this, the construction [of the compound] in "aśvinor kāmam aprāḥ" and so forth is established.
In this context, the recitation of mantras is meaningful because it must be performed;
their recollection serves the purpose of application, and from that application arises the emergence of the fruit.
Thus, since the visible result is obtained, there is no need for the postulation of an invisible (adṛṣṭa) result.

Therefore, the utility of mantras is established solely through their illumination [of ritual acts]. However, the postulation of unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) arises precisely from the restriction of the means [to those acts].

[Regarding the term] *soma-saṃgati*: following the inquiry into the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) associated with injunctions (*vidhi*), the inquiry into the mantras not so associated follows by way of "contextual connection" (*avasara-saṃgati*).
Are the mantras, such as "uru prathasva," causes for the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)?

[If so,] they would merely serve to illuminate the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and other such acts during sacrifices. However, since their meaning is also explained by the Brāhmaṇa, mantras are solely causes of merit.
Because that [result] is seen, the seen is better than the unseen;

according to the opinion of the Guru: "When there is a conflict between the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa regarding application, the purpose is established by the indicative mark (liṅga) of the Mantra, not by the other when it is not so stated."

Bhaṭṭa: In the inquiry as to whether mantras possess authority (*prāmāṇya*) regarding *dharma* and *adharma*, they do not first have authority by way of being injunctions (*vidhi*), since that [topic] is to be refuted in the second [chapter].

Nor do they have it by way of being indicators (*jñāpaka*), like explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). For in the case of those [arthavādas], because they form a single syntactical unit with a proximate injunction (*padaikavākyatva*), it is appropriate that they generate a verbal cognition whose object is an efficient force (*bhāvanā*) conjoined with the excellence (*prāśastya*) provided by themselves.
But for mantras, because they are situated at a distance, a single-syntactical-unit relation is untenable; therefore, their connection to authority does not occur in that manner.

Nor can excellence (*prāśastya*) constitute the sentence-meaning independently, because it is presented as a word-meaning (*padārtha*). Nor can there be validity (*prāmāṇya*) by virtue of having a meaningful object, since that is impossible due to the absence of the capacity to convey an unapprehended object. Furthermore, for *sāman* mantras, even the quality of being "true to the fact" (*yāthārthya*) is untenable insofar as they lack a referential meaning.

Nor is it the case that, even in the absence of authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*), there is a lack of purpose because they serve as reminders; for if remembrance could be accomplished through other means such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth, the injunctions would be useless. Furthermore, there would be a redundancy of the Smṛti texts regarding those things that remind one of matters inherent in the performance (*prayoga*).

Therefore, since the nature of *bhāvanā* has been understood through the section known as "Qualification" (*adhikāra*) and so forth, the mere utterance of mantras within that *bhāvanā* is enjoined for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

There is no fault in this, as the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) likewise enjoins study by having as its result the absence of application [of the text] other than for the purpose of utterance.
This being the position reached, it is replied: [The following is the response:]... (The remainder of the argument follows).

Since the postulation of an unseen effect (*adṛṣṭa*) is untenable when a visible purpose is possible, the purpose of mantras that have a possible application must simply be the recollection of the object associated with that performance. For those [mantras] whose application is impossible, let there be an unseen purpose at will;
however, even in that case, it can be asserted that the mantras serve to reveal the meaning, and that this revelation itself has an unseen purpose as its ultimate aim.

In the case of the *saṃhitā*, however, the purpose observed through the mere manifestation of the syllables of the *ṛc* remains unimpeded even in the absence of a semantic meaning; this has been explained in detail regarding the fact that the *ṛks* and *sāmans* have only an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.
Yet, by this much alone, it does not follow that they have an unseen purpose in every respect.
Nor is the recitation of mantras necessarily useless; for by their power, one may assume a restrictive rule (*niyamakalpanā*) that the rite is to be performed by the mantras alone.
And there is no fault even if that restriction results in an invisible fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*).

Nor should it be argued that, since the application of mantras in various instances is already established through such inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), it would be redundant to state their application again elsewhere.

This is because [the statement] has purpose by way of specifying the number of qualities (*guṇaparisaṃkhyārthakatvena*). To explain: although the taking up (*abhyādāna*) is already established by the sense of the context, and the mantras are obtained through their indicative power (*liṅga*), yet—prior even to the means of proof that would establish them—the injunction "He takes it up with four" prescribes a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of taking up characterized by a specific number of mantras. Even though the mantras and the taking up could have been obtained even in the absence of this statement, when there arises an inquiry into the purpose of the operation of this specific statement, it is determined that the number, as a quality (*guṇa*), serves the result of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Likewise, when the mantra—which has already attained applicability through its indicative power (*liṅga*) as a subordinate factor for the act of naming the horse’s bridle—is enjoined by the previously operative injunction, "Having [recited] 'this one for Agni,' he takes up the bridle," as the means for taking up the bridle qualified by that mantra, there arises a desire to know its result. In this case, the result is the exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the donkey’s bridle by means of the remainder (*pariśeṣa*). Nor does the threefold defect—consisting of the abandonment of one's own meaning, the assumption of another's meaning, and the sublation of what was already established—apply here, because the exclusion is based on the result.

Because one's own purpose (svārtha) is that which is to be enjoined as something to be heard through the mention of the horse-rein (*aśvābhidhānī*), and because the exclusion of others (*anyaniṣṭitti*)—being for the sake of another—is not to be postulated since it is established by the very fact of the purpose; and because there is no sublation of what has already been obtained (*prāptabādha*) due to the non-operation of a source of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that would establish it.

These same [conditions] apply where the operation of a source of knowledge that establishes [an alternative] is precisely the operation of a restrictive rule (*parisaṃkhyāśāstra*), as in "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten" and so forth; in such cases, once the eating of five-nailed animals is already obtained, the restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*) is made to exclude those other than the five, and it applies only there.
Furthermore, even in cases where there is an explicit scriptural exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), such as "one should not speak untruth," that [objection] does not apply here either.
Thus, although mantras serve to remind one of the meaning, there is no lack of purpose for their application (*viniyoga*).
Nor is there an impossibility of their being authoritative even in this way, because the defining characteristic of authority—namely, correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*)—remains unimpaired.

However, by way of being the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), [the mantra] is common to all mantras beginning with the *sāman*. For just as the word-meaning is a cause for the cognition of a verbal meaning because it is also a cause for the knowledge that serves as the cause for that cognition, so too can it be said [of the mantra].
Therefore, since mantras possess the status of word-meanings within the injunctions regarding their application (*viniyoga*), their authority (*prāmāṇya*) is appropriate.
Or, let it be that they lack authority.
There is no fault on the grounds that [the mantra] appears to have a purpose, since its status as a rule for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) is established;
the purpose is clearly evident from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) themselves.
Maṇḍana states: "The meaning of the mantra is intended to be expressed."
Śaṅkara: "And the authority of mantras.
[This is] the section on mantras (mantrādhikaraṇa).
The specific purpose of mantras will be explained in the section on mantras."
[In the section concerning the Arthavādas,] it is established merely that the mantras also possess authority because they serve a purpose (Śābarabhāṣya 1.2.1).

In the section concerning the mantras, within the cognition of dharma— known as the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of the verbal root's meaning, which is delimited by the names of substances, deities, and so forth, brought forward by the mantras and impelled by the Arthavādas— the authority and purposefulness of the mantras is established through their role as motivators.

In the passage "soma" (1.2.4.42), it has been elaborated that, by virtue of being intended for continuous practice, this constitutes an injunction for the eternal *brahmayajña* (Vedic study sacrifice). Regarding the verse "amyak sā te" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.169.13), in the subsequent verse "tvaṃ na indra taṃ rathiṃ dāḥ," that very [meaning] is to be understood through the context (*anuvākya*).

(Vākyapadīya, p. 167; Vāl., p. 60). For even in the case of mantras, that which is to be known is their capacity to bring about prosperity through the very injunctions regarding their application, not the mantras themselves.
Therefore, it was stated in the section on Mantras (Mantrādhikaraṇa) that the authority of mantras lies solely in their [contribution to] the performance of ritual acts (padārtha).

And just as the statement, "Even though the animal is dedicated to another deity, the *manotā* must be performed as if for Agni," does not imply that it is subject to modification (*ūha*) in the case of animals dedicated to Vāyu and others— because such a rule was never applicable in the archetype (*prakṛti*) since it was restricted to another [deity]— but rather serves only to exclude what has been stated, so too this has been explained in detail in the section on Mantras (Jaimini Sūtra 10.4.23–28), page 369.

We have already explained in the *Mantrādhikaraṇa* (Ku. 2.1.32–42) that if the act of praising (*śaṃsati*) were primarily intended to produce a verbal cognition residing in the agent, then for an agent whose mind is occupied with comprehending the meaning of each preceding verse, the continuity (*sāṃtatyam*) of the succeeding verses would be impossible. Furthermore, even if [the mantra] merely restates a possible meaning, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is established by its capacity to convey a collective sense or other aspects not previously understood; this was also stated in the *Mantrādhikaraṇa*.

Even in the rules concerning the closing [of the eyes] and so forth, there is no intention to refer to the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] and the like; rather, according to the principle of the section on the mantras for the various *pṛṣṭha* [stotras], there is the comprehension of the meaning of those mantras.

"Knowledge of the meaning, context, well-spoken verses (*sūkta*), deity, seer (*ārṣa*), Vedic citation (*nigama*), etymology (*nirukta*), and grammar are the means for comprehension. (Vārttika 1.2.1.41).

Regarding this, the *Sudhā* commentary states: "Meaning (*artha*) is capacity (*sāmarthya*), such as the fitness [of words] to have a common substratum with the meanings of other words, and so forth."
The *prakaraṇa* (context) is the introductory sequence.

*Bhūta* (the elemental) refers to the knowledge of the deities; because it is characterized by unmanifest signs (*avyaktaliṅga*), it serves as a means for knowing the meaning by being a cause for the knowledge of the deities.

Regarding *ārṣajñāna* (knowledge derived from the seers), its status as a means for knowing the meaning is due to its being a cause for our own realization, as seen in such [Vedic] passages as "I became Manu and Sūrya."
