An investigation into whether the meaning of a mantra is intended for the one who employs the mantra or for the one who hears the mantra.
It has been established in the section on Mantras (1.2.31–45) that the entire portion of a mantra possesses an intended meaning.
In this regard, the following appears:
in this section, by means of fifteen sūtras beginning with "tadarthaśāstrāt," it has been understood merely that mantras convey meaning;
however, whether the comprehension of the mantra's meaning belongs to the one who employs the mantra or to the one who hears it has not been clearly determined from the words of the sūtras.

In this regard, the authors of the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vārttika*, and other works, who maintain that the purpose of ritual (*karaṇa*) mantras is to convey the meaning of the mantra for the sake of performance, consider the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by the mantra to belong solely to the reciter of the mantra.
However, we do not seek that [cognition] for the reciter, but rather for the listener alone; for the utterance of words is equally productive of verbal cognition for another.
Indeed, the employment of a sentence is not meaningful if it results in verbal cognition for the speaker himself alone.
This is because the speaker's understanding of that meaning must necessarily exist prior to the verbal usage;
for the composition of a sentence regarding an incorrect meaning is not appropriate.
The author of the Sūtras as well [states] in "But the meaning of the sentence is not distinct" (1.2.132) that [the meaning] of the worldly and the Vedic...

By asserting that the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is indistinguishable [from ordinary cognition], one accepts that the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by a mantra belongs to the listener alone.
Otherwise, there would arise the inconsistency of verbal cognition occurring for the listener in common worldly usage, but for the reciter in the case of mantras.
Furthermore, the fact that verbal cognition from a mantra belongs solely to the listener is clearly obtained from the very words contained within the mantra itself.
For generally, all mantras have the vocative as their domain.
To illustrate: this mantra, "iṣe tvorje tvā" (for food thee, for strength thee), is enjoined for the cutting of the branch.

Since the word "tvā" (thee) directly refers exclusively to the vocative case, by the force of its application (viniyoga), the phrase "I cut [the branch] in the sacred scripture" must be supplied as an ellipsis.
In the word *śāstre*, the first case ending (*prathamā*) is prescribed by the grammatical rule "the first case is used for address and also for non-address.
Address (*saṃbodhana*) means making known.
In the scriptural passage, "I cut thee for food, thee for strength," the meaning to be made known is the scripture itself.
One who employs each mantra makes it known;
the Teacher permits it with a blaze [of light].
For by the word "Teacher," the deity presiding over that [mantra] is figuratively designated without distinction.
Consequently, there is no contradiction therein regarding the cutting [of the branch] and the indication of that [branch];

for this is clear from Bādarāyaṇa’s Sūtra (2.1.13), "But the designation of the one who possesses the conceit [is based on] the accompaniment of the qualification," and from its commentary and other works.
In cases such as "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation," however, this is easily established.
[Objection: But will not the corporeal form, consciousness, and so forth of the deities be refuted in the ninth [book]? [Reply:
True, they will be refuted by the author of the Bhāṣya outside of the Sūtras; however, they are not refuted by the author of the Sūtras.

On the contrary, it will be elaborated upon in the section concerning the *ṣaṣṭhātithi* that the corporeal form of the deities and so forth is indeed intended by the author of the Sūtras and is also accepted by the Vārttikakāra.
Furthermore, the *ṛc* verses known as *stotra* are intended for the praise of deities;
they convey the qualities of those deities who are the objects of praise,
because it is established in common worldly experience that sentences of praise function only to inform the object being praised.

For in the world, a panegyrist praises the one worthy of praise with prose, verse, and so forth; and the one worthy of praise, recognizing the aesthetic wonder produced by that [praise], becomes pleased. The same must be understood to apply in the case of the Veda as well.

Furthermore, the *sāmans* are unable to bring about the cognition of the qualities intended for the one who sings them (*gātṛ*), nor can the *ṛks*—whether those belonging to the *stotra* or the *śastra*—bring about such cognition for the one who recites the *śastras* (*śaṃsituḥ*).
This is because [in the case of the *ṛks*], there is no occurrence of the vocative case, as seen in "O Agni, come for the feast" (*agna āyāhi vītaye*) and so forth.
Moreover, continuity (*sāṃtatyam*) is prescribed for the *ṛks* belonging to the *śastra*, according to the injunction: "He recites continuously" (*saṃtatamanvāha*).

The definition of *sāṃtatyam* (continuity) is as follows: having uttered the latter half-verse of each preceding *ṛc* ending with the *praṇava*, one pauses only after uttering the former half-verse of each subsequent *ṛc* without interruption.

Indeed, it is not possible for the chanter to have a comprehension of the meaning of each verse in this manner; for at the conclusion of each word, the mind is occupied with the comprehension of that specific meaning, and thus the continuous manifestation of the subsequent verses is impossible.
However, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the understanding of the meaning [of the mantra] as pertaining specifically to the deity being praised in each instance.
Furthermore, in the third section of the twelfth book, in the section beginning with "Because mantras serve the purpose of performance, the action is joined with the end of the mantra;

for that much is the purpose of the statement" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.3.10–12), it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that in the case of *karaṇa*-mantras, the commencement of the ritual act is to be synchronized with the end of the mantra.

If the recollection of the meaning of the mantra residing in the performer were the cause of the performance, the sequence would have to be as follows: first the utterance of the mantra, then the recollection of the object to be performed, and then the performance itself.
Consequently, because it would be intervened by the recollection of the object to be performed, how could the commencement of the ritual action coincide with the end of the mantra?
However, if one accepts that the verbal cognition of the deity intended by the mantra arises directly from the mantra itself, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of ritual action mantras (*karaṇamantra*) having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding the deity produced by the mantra lacks the status of being a cause for performance (*anuṣṭhānahetutva*).

For it is possible for them to have a seen purpose precisely by producing a verbal cognition regarding the deity; indeed, this is accepted as the case even in the instance of mantras used for recitation (*japa*) and the like, which do not denote anything connected with a ritual act.
Nor should it be argued: "How can the verbal cognition occurring in the listener-deity be considered 'observed,' given that deities are not perceptible?
For, in that case, even in the world, the observed fact of a sentence producing cognition in another would be untenable, since the mind of another is not perceptible.

If it is argued that in the world the verbal cognition in another is "observed" through inference and other means, then the same applies to the Veda; for its [the cognition's] occurrence is established there by signs such as the addressing of deities.
"Thou art that which has been winnowed for the gods," he says; for whatever exists here, that is what has been winnowed for the gods.
Just as one would announce to a calf, "I shall do this," even so the Adhvaryu, having announced it to the gods,
brings out the sacrificial grass for his own non-injury, saying: "O Agni and Viṣṇu, may I not step upon you two."

"Agni is in front; Viṣṇu is behind. Having announced it to those two, he steps across [with the words]: 'I invoke Agni and Viṣṇu, the two Hotṛ-priests. Having thus announced it to the gods, he performs the sacrifice with the sacrifice. Thus he says.
"O Brahman, I shall bind the horse sacrifice for the gods and Prajāpati; may I prosper thereby.
For the Brahman is indeed the Brahman. Having thus informed the Brahman for the sake of the gods and Prajāpati, he binds the horse sacrifice.
The supplementary passages, such as "He is not seized by the deities; he becomes more prosperous," are also favorable here. However, there is this distinction:

Since the composition of sentences in the world depends upon an authorial person, and since such composition is impossible when [the meaning] is unknown, the employment [of words] is invariably concomitant with the knowledge of the meaning; however,
that [knowledge] does not become the cognition of another simply because one is the employer [of those words].
This is because one employs a sentence only with the desire to communicate to another.

However, since mantras are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) and are thus eternally established, it is not necessary to know the intention of their user. Consequently, even an unlearned person’s employment of a mantra is not contradictory.
Furthermore, even the speaker’s knowledge of the meaning is not a necessary condition for the hearer’s comprehension of the sentence-meaning;
for we observe that those who are proficient in language derive verbal cognition from prose and verse composed by Kālidāsa and others when uttered by unlearned persons such as parrots and mainas.
In the case of "Devadatta, bring the jar," the nominative case is used in the sense of address (*saṃbodhana*).
Addressing (*saṃbodhana*) means making [the listener] attentive by causing them to know.
Knowledge resides in the hearer, while causing to know resides in the speaker.

Consequently, the meaning of the sentence is the activity residing in the speaker that is conducive to the knowledge of the bringing of the jar, which resides in Devadatta who has been made attentive.
And although such an understanding may be possible for the person being enlightened, as well as for the other listeners and the speaker, it does not produce the effect for everyone.
The knowledge regarding the bringing of the jar residing in the one who has been enlightened is the *mantrōha*.
The principle of modification (ūha) is threefold: modification of the mantra, modification of the sāman, and modification of the ritual refinement (saṃskāra). Bhāṣya 9.1.1.9.

The Principle of Mantra-Modification (Mantra-ūha): In a modified sacrifice (vikṛti) such as the Saurya, there is a modification (ūha) of the word denoting the modified substance and so forth within the mantra that has been extended by analogy (atideśa).

For, just as in the archetype (prakṛti) the words for the substances are used according to their actual occurrence, so too in the subsequent performance (uttarāyāṃ tatau), because it has that [archetype] as its model, the word must be used for the actual purpose and not for what was done in the archetype. (Jaimini Sūtra 9.1.1.9)
Commentary: The modified rites (*vaikṛta*) serve as the examples.

"One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya"; "One desiring progeny should offer an eleven-potherd cake (*ekādaśakapāla*) to Indra and Agni"; "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *Citrā*" [oblation]; "One desiring a village should offer the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* oblation to the Viśvedevas.
However, in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), there exists a mantra for the pouring out [of the grain]: "I pour out what is pleasing to Agni."
Likewise, [there is the injunction]: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
However, in the archetype (prakṛti), there is a mantra containing the characteristic mark of rice (*vrīhi*): "I prepare a pleasant seat for you; I fashion it well-favored with a stream of ghee.
Sit upon it, O immortal one, established in the essence of rice, being well-disposed."
Thus it is said.

And that very same [mantra], having been extended by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) into the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), becomes a matter of doubt: should it be employed without modification, or with *ūha* (modification)? What is the prima facie view? That it should be used without modification.
Likewise, it is supported by the *ārṣa* [tradition]:
"Whatever is to be performed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), that is to be performed in the ectype (*vikṛti*). And in the archetype, the two words *abhīṣṭi* and *iṣṭi* are employed.
Therefore, those two [mantras] themselves should be employed in the modification (vikṛti).
This being the position reached, we reply:

True; just as in the archetype (prakṛti) the expression of the objects was performed in the mantra according to their origin, so too in the subsequent performance—the modification—it must be expressed by that very same mantra, because it has that as its archetype.
This being the case, it is said in reply:
"It is not so;
because the object is not something to be produced."
To this extent, the two words *iṣṭi* and *viśvajit* would denote both the sun and the *nīvāra* grain;
here, the word *ca* has the sense of *tu*.
Furthermore, the function of mantras is to convey meaning, not to express their own literal form.
For in the case of the essential form (svarūpa), something unseen must be postulated;
whereas by means of the statement of the purpose (arthavacana), a visible benefit is established.
Therefore, it is "ūha" because of modification.
*Dup*—(The modification (*ūha*) concerning the refinement of the *Sāman* has been considered); now the modification concerning the *mantra* is being considered.
And that is of six kinds. [First:
If the *mantras* possess meaning (i.e., they serve the purpose of manifesting the meaning, and do not merely produce a visible result through their mere utterance).
Likewise—) they denote their primary meanings (and not figurative ones);
likewise—) the ritual properties (*dharmas*) are prompted by the *apūrva* (and not prompted by forms such as fire, etc.);
likewise—) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), they denote meanings that are inherent (*samaveta*) (and not, like words such as *savitṛ*, denoting meanings that are non-inherent).
Likewise— the principle of the *mantrohinī* [plant] being non-synonymous.
The principle of the *mantrohinī*.

[The mantra] is made free of expectancy (by the principle of the section on the end of injunctions, 7.4.2). Furthermore, because of the commonality of being a sentence—just as there is an extension (*atideśa*) here for injunctive sentences such as those concerning the *prayāja* offerings in order to enjoin their own meaning—so too is there an extension of the mantra-sentences for the purpose of recollection; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is based on the requirement of a beneficial result (*upakāra*).
On account of its being the meaning (i.e., the purpose) of the water (as the cause), that (extension of the rule regarding the benefit) is stronger.

(Why? For it is for the sake of expressing the meaning that the word-conveyor proceeds to operate; there is no separate extension (of the rule) regarding the nature of the word itself by the treatise, due to the fear of postulating an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, there is no extension of these syllables in their own form.
And there is the extension of the purpose (which is necessary because it serves to accomplish the primary effect directly).
And because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
The Commentary states: "The indicative mark occurs only in that [context] where it says, 'Neither the mother increases, nor the father, nor the brother, nor the friend.'"
We perceive that the brother and the friend are actually increasing;
therefore, this is not a prohibition regarding the increase of the object.
Rather, it is a prohibition regarding the increase of the word: "the word *bhrātṛ* does not increase, nor does the word *sakhi*."
And what is their increase? It is the production of another phoneme. That [occurs] in the case of one [syllable] as "āteti," and in the case of two as "bhātrāviti.
This is what is meant.
The word "brother" (bhrātṛ) is not modified, nor is the word "friend" (sakhi).
From this it is understood that others are modified.
Just as when it is said, "You do not go to the assembly, you are not spectators," it is understood that surely others do go.

Similarly here as well, when it is stated, "Neither the brother is inferred nor the friend," the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is that other [relations] are indeed inferred. Bhāṣya: That which was established remains indeed unfinished; meanwhile, another intermediate consideration must be undertaken. (In this context, the section concerning the intermediate [topic] has been composed within the sūtra *jātinaimittikaṃ*.)
(See *Tattvamīmāṃsā*, p. 1226, under the rule: "The word *rakta* [is used] for *ūha*").

From that very point, another two sūtras (*sūtradvaya*) are explained regarding the *antarāgarbhaṇīyā*: "And because of the observation of indicative marks; the generic [form] is occasional, according to its place.
And because of the observation of indicative marks.
Commentary: For this reason as well, we understand that modification (*ūha*) must be performed in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*).
Why? Because an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is observed.
What is the indicative mark? It is stated thus: "Recite for the omenta and the fat of the Viśvedevas."
The modification according to genus (*jāti*) occurs according to the specific place [in the ritual].
The Commentary states: There is a substitution of genus-words that have been modified; this is possible only on the view that mantras express their literal meaning.

If modification were not performed, and [the mantra] were intended merely as a non-sensical utterance, then words such as "fire" (*agni*) and "goat" (*chāga*) would be employed exactly as they are, without change.

In that case, the mention of these [words], whose purpose is not action, would be meaningful only as a restatement of what is already established. Furthermore, these words are not being enjoined here, because they lack injunctive force.
[Objection: But surely they will be enjoined by the *prayogavacana* (the statement of performance). [Reply: If that were so, then the aforementioned fault remains.
Therefore, there is modification (*ūha*).
Because there would be no purpose in the absence of modification.
The Commentary: However, some teachers maintain that there is no modification.
Regarding this matter, he will state the indicative mark (liṅga). This is its application: if one were to say [this], the word "ārṣa" would be contradicted.
"Therefore, it is ūha.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
The Bhāṣya states: "An indicative mark is seen in this matter."

In the modified animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni, it is recited in the scripture: "Recite the invitatory prayer for the fat of the goat's omentum for Agni. If the principle of modification (*ūha*) were not accepted, this would not need to be enjoined;
yet, it is indeed enjoined.
Therefore, it is *ūha*.

Furthermore, this other indicative mark (*liṅga*) is heard in the context of the *paśu* sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma: "If he should touch a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*), he should say, 'This is for you, Vāyu';
if two, 'These two are for you, Vāyu'."
If there are many [deities], then [the formula] is "These are your winds.
If there were a modification (ūha), even this would not need to be prescribed, as it would already be established by implication;
however, it is indeed prescribed.
"Therefore, it is ūha.
Or rather, it is a modification; that is the reason stated.
Commentary: By the word "or" (vā), the previous position is set aside.
As for what was stated—that there is no modification—that is not so;
there should be modification.
The reason previously stated for this point is: "And because it is not something to be produced in the case of the meaning."
For when there is a correspondence with the meaning of the mantra, it is the prompter [of the action] that is intended, not the syllables of the mantra;
for those syllables have the meaning as their primary concern, not their own formal nature.
Therefore, modification (*ūha*) should take place by the very same reason stated previously.
Only the avoidance of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) needs to be stated;
the indicative mark serves the purpose of indicating the mantra.

The commentary says: as for the indicative mark that was mentioned—namely, "Recite the invitatory verse for the omentum and fat of the goat for Agni"—that is prescribed by way of the desire for the mantra.
Otherwise, because it would have been modified, it would not be a mantra;
therefore, there is a restatement.
Or rather, it is a restrictive rule (niyama), because both parts are involved.
Commentary: That indicative mark which was stated in the mantra "O Vāyu, this for you," is now refuted.
If it were said here [that the number of objects] is also expressed—as in "if he should touch two" or "if he should touch many"—then all these mantras would be of a single form.
The rule is established so that neither of these two cases may occur:
if he should touch two, he should say, "These are your winds";
if many, he should say, "These are your winds."

Therefore, this too has been stated [as follows]: Now, the modification (*ūha*) of mantras is being considered (the meaning is: that modification of mantras which remains from the *prakṛti* sacrifice is now being considered). Regarding the two mantras, "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" and "O essence of rice, being well-disposed," there arises a doubt: should these be modified for the *saurya* and other sacrifices, as well as for *nīvāra* and other grains, or not? In this doubt, [it is argued]: "In the *prakṛti*, the mantra is of such a nature; indeed, it is of that very same nature [in the *vikṛti*]."
It is obtained in the case of a modification; therefore, modification (ūha) is appropriate there.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"Whatever form of the mantras is indeed intended in the archetype (prakṛti), that very same form is to be extended to the ectype (vikṛti), not that which is unintended."

Therefore, [this is] *ūha* (modification). Soma: Having concluded the discussion on *sāmoha* (modification of chants) along with its introduction (*sapodghāta*)—by way of the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṃgati*) consisting in the contingency of the modification of mantras in the first quarter (*pāda*)—and having likewise concluded the discussion on the modification of *saṃskāra* (preparatory rites) connected therewith, that very *mantroha* (modification of mantras) is now introduced; thus there is immediate sequence (*anantarya*).
In the first quarter, for the most part, the modification of the *prakṛti* (archetype) was discussed.
In this third quarter (*pāda*), however, changes (*ūha*) generally rely on the wording (*vacana*), whereas changes to the original form (*prakṛti*) are rare.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the mantras were produced in connection with specific words so as to denote their respective objects, and because the subsequent performance is a modification (*vikāra*) of that, it follows that even in the modified rite (*vikṛti*), the denotation must be performed using those very same words containing the term "abhi. The word *ca* refutes this prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*). It is not thus.

Now, because it is not something to be performed, there is a possibility that the mantra might illuminate a modified (vaikṛta) meaning just as it is recited. Regarding this, [the author] says: "The *agnīṣoma* and so forth are either not to be modified (*anūhya*) or they are to be modified (*ūhya*). It is not because of the injunction (*codanā*); rather, because there is an intention (*vivakṣā*) regarding the deity and the oblation, one modifies [the mantra] from that."
(Regarding the passage "To the great Indra, a *naivāra* cake on eleven potsherds," etc., the modification (*ūha*) concerning *nīvāra* grain is to be observed.

According to the Bhāṭṭa school: In mantras such as "By the sacrifice to Agni, may I [attain]" and "The essence of rice-grains," because the meaning is inherently present (*samavetārthatva*), the modification (*ūha*)—consisting in the absence of a connection to another means (*dvārāntara-sambandha-nimitta*) for words like *Agni* and *Soma* in rites such as the *Saurya*—is already established, just like the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
The figurative modification (*bhākta ūha*) consists in the substitution of another word in place of that [original] term.
Even that which is established in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) is raised as an objection and then resolved:

For in the primary injunction (*prakṛti*), Agni, Soma, and the others are indeed presented by their respective words only through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the form of being means to the *apūrva*; therefore, it is logical that even the sun, wild rice (*nīvāra*), and so forth, are revealed by that very same form. Consequently, the introduction of other words [into the original formula] is not appropriate.

For this very reason, in the case of the mantra ending in the plural "pāśān" (the bonds), even though the modified ritual (*vikṛti*) involves only a single portion to be consumed—just as in the original ritual (*prakṛti*)—there is no modification (*ūha*), because it indicates singularity only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

For words such as *agnīṣoma* do not denote, by their primary power (*śakti*), the substance or deity that serves as a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), but rather [denote them] only through secondary indication, according to the maxim: "Secondary indication occurs when an object is known through a form other than its own primary power. Furthermore, since the word itself constitutes the deity, and since that [word] is perceived through secondary indication by the term *agni*, the perception of Sūrya alone is established; thus, the absence of modification is proven.

This being the position reached: even though the status of being a means to the *apūrva* (unseen potency) serves as the delimitor of the objecthood (*uddeśyatā*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the meaning understood through the word "Agnīṣoma" and so forth—by way of the cognition generated by its own expressive power (*śakti*)—is that "the substance and deity which have become means to the *apūrva* [are to be consecrated].
For this very reason, even the cognition produced by the expressive power has "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so forth as its qualifiers, and not the status of being a means to the *apūrva* as its qualifier.

This is because, although that which is delimited by such [qualifiers] is the object of the injunction when established by a scriptural statement inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is no evidence for [the application of] the word "rice" and so forth within the mantra itself through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

For this very reason, even by such a cognition, a refinement (*saṃskāra*) is produced only in the substantive—such as the substance or the deity—just as in the case of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) or the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, and not in the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), namely, the status of being a means to the *apūrva*.

Consequently, since the door [of the ritual] is established through the influence of the beneficial effect (*upakāra*), when that door is extended (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is entirely appropriate to insert another word in place of words such as "Āgneya" which are obtained there by the force of that [extension], for the sake of providing a door for the *Saurya* and other such sacrifices.

For this very reason, although words such as *agnīṣoma* are prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) in that same form as being productive of a specific effect—just like the *aghāra* libation—and thus, even when that effect is absent or when it is impossible to produce that effect by means of them, their omission in the modification (*vikṛti*) is indeed proper.
However, there is this distinction:
in the case of the absence of the effect, there is simply an omission; but in the case of impossibility, one must perform another means for producing that effect.

As for the claim that in the archetype (*prakṛti*), threshing is not enjoined as such, but rather as a means characterized by the non-distinction of being a *sādhana* (instrument) for the *apūrva* (unseen potency)—otherwise, it would result in having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*)—and therefore, since the specific nature of the word "fire" (*agni*) and so forth is not intended to be expressed, the introduction of another word is indeed appropriate; that is not so. For if that were the case, there would be no defect in the performance of actions such as splitting (*vidalana*) even when using synonyms for *vrīhi* in the archetype itself. Furthermore, it is logical that in whatever form something is a generator of the primary effect, in that very same form it should also be a generator of the restrictive unseen potency (*niyamādṛṣṭa*).

As for the claim that the word "Agni" functions as an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the purpose of manifesting the deity in the form of sound, we reply here that this is the principle of the *mantra-hāni* (the abandonment of the mantra). 3121. [We respond] based on the mantra itself.

Even if there were metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the introduction of another word is appropriate because of a difference in the means (*dvārabheda*): the metaphorical indication of the word in the archetype occurs through a relationship consisting in being the denoter of what is possible [to be expressed], whereas in the modification (*vikṛti*) it does not occur through that same relationship.

However, in reality, even though the word itself is the deity, since the object also serves as a means to the *apūrva*, it is logically established that it too must be manifested through the relationship of being denoted by the word in its form as a deity pertaining to the *apūrva*; thus, there is no metaphorical indication of the "word" in the word *ādi-* occurring within the mantra, and the introduction of another word is therefore appropriate, just as in the case of the word *vrīhi*.

For this very reason, even the prohibition against altering (*ūha*) the syllables of the *ṛc*—namely, "This imperishable syllable indeed putrefies when one alters it; therefore, one should not alter it"—is consistent with the view that everyone must perform the sacrifice using those [original] texts.

Consequently, for the purpose of manifesting that ritual action, one should employ only the alteration of a mantra capable of manifesting it, due to the commonality of its being Vedic; in the absence of such a mantra, however, an alteration of a secular sentence may be used.

Likewise, although there is an alteration of the words "mother" and so forth in the passage "May his mother think of him," etc., when the fire is being carried forward, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the rule "The mother does not increase, nor the father," etc., remains intact.

Although it was stated in the *Mantrādhikaraṇa-kaustubha* that this is not an injunction of prohibition because it is established by logical necessity (*nyāya*), nevertheless, this is indeed a perpetual restatement (*nityānuvāda*) which serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the modification (*ūha*).

Nor is the recitation of mantra-texts such as "Recite the invitatory prayer for the omentum and fat of the bulls" (*viśeṣaṃ devānāmullāṇāṃ vapānāṃ medaso'nubrūhi*) or "Recite the invitatory prayer for the omentum and fat of the goat" (*chāgasya vapāyā medaso'nubrūhi*) redundant when modification is established by logical necessity; for their purpose is to establish the status of those mantras as being subject to expiation (*prāyaścitta*) if they are used without modification.
Maṇḍana: "In the mantra for the offering (nirvāpa), there must certainly be the word *dhruva*.
Śaṅkara: "There should be a modification (*ūha*) of the mantra regarding the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and so forth.

The prohibition to be inferred from the mantra is of two kinds: first, by inferring a prohibition from the negative particle (*nañ*) attached to the present tense form within the mantra itself; and second, by inferring a separate sentence containing the prohibition.

Bāla, p. 30: The injunction (*vidhi*) to be inferred from a mantra is of two kinds: [first] by inferring the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood inherent in the mantra, and [second] by inferring another sentence containing the injunction.

p. 12: In the sections on Mantras and Injunctions, the *upāṃśugraha* is the first; the *antaryāmagraha* is the second; the *aindravāyava* is the third; and the *maitrāvaruṇa* is the literal meaning of the scriptural statement (*śruti*).
However, among the *dhārāgrahas*, the *aindravāyava* is the first.

VI. Performance is carried out solely according to the sequence of the mantra; in its absence, however, the injunction itself serves as a reminder, and thus the authority for that sequence resides therein.
Consequently, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the properties of the Āgneya [offering] come first, followed by those of the Agnīṣomīya.

Bhāṣya 5.1.9.16: The sequence of the Brāhmaṇa is stated according to the sequence of the Mantras, as it has been said in the Mīmāṃsākośa (p. 391): "But in case of conflict, [the order] shall be according to the Mantra" (5.1.9.16).
Because [the object] has not been previously attained (*aprāptatvāt*).

[This is stated in] Bāla., p. 143. A verb (*ākhyāta*) occurring in a mantra is not injunctive (*vidhāyaka*). This point should be examined in the section titled "The Section on Injunctions and Mantras" (*vidhimantrādhikaraṇa*).

The *liṅga* (indicative power) residing in a mantra indicates that which has already been obtained [by another means], whereas the *liṅga* residing in an injunction (*codanā*) is that which brings about its attainment.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the verbal forms expressing an action—such as "he sacrifices" (*yajate*) or "he gives" (*dadāti*)—residing in a mantra are injunctive or not, they are not injunctive, but rather expressive of the denotation [of the action].
(Section on Injunctions and Mantras) | Even those [words] occurring in mantras are seen in some cases to be injunctive, such as "He sacrifices the kapiñjala birds to Vasanta," and so forth.
Vārttika 2.1.6.30.

Since a prohibition is postulated only for that present-tense verbal form occurring within a mantra which is joined with a negative particle (*nañ*), the prohibition is to be inferred from the mantra itself (Bālakrīḍā, p.
30). Among the verbal forms found both in mantras and in Brāhmaṇas, those whose injunctive power is obstructed possess the function of mere denotation (*abhidhāyaka*).

Or [it may be argued]: because the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood is likewise assumed for the *ārāti* found in the mantra, the injunction is to be inferred from the mantra, as in "He sacrifices the *kapiñjala* birds to Vasanta.
(*Bālakrīḍā*, p. 12). The recollection of the meaning produced by the mantra is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the ritual act.
The recitation of mantras (*mantrajapa*) is omitted when [the deceased] resides in the bones, according to the view that the authority for the rite belongs to the dead;
[this is stated as a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvācintā*)].
VI. 10|2|18. Regarding the collection of mantras:

since the entire collection of mantras—consisting of the *stotra*s and so forth, which are *ārādupakārin* (remotely assisting) and distinct from the *mantra*s that provide immediate assistance (*saṃnipatyopakārin*) such as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*—is fruitless [in itself], one cannot determine its status as belonging to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices through knowledge alone. Therefore, just like the *savanīya* offerings and others, even the *stotra*s and so forth possess only the status of being a substratum (*ādhāra*) for the *savana*s; they do not possess the status of being the primary act (*pradhāna*). Thus, it can be stated that they are equal to the *savanīya* offerings and the like.

*Sūtra-pṛṣṭha* 1|80: Regarding the grasping of a specific agent residing in the mantra, in the case of the *savanīya-paśu*, the function of the Maitrāvaruṇa is [performed] by the mantra: "The Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu should lead forth the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma" (*agnim atha hotāram ṛṇītām sutāsutiḥ yajamānaḥ*). Since this is not extended from the *āgneya* (or *āgnīṣomīya*) sacrifice due to its being a *sūktavāka*, and because that [mantra] is established by *prasaṅga* (extension) for the *savanīya-havis* offerings which are devoid of the Maitrāvaruṇa—[this is stated] in the *Bālamanoramā*, p. 148. In the section [of the *Tantravārttika*] beginning with: "But on account of the mantra, there would be [a difference] in case of conflict, because of the capacity for performance; therefore, that is the place of origin" (*mantratas tu virodhe syāt prayogopasāmarthyāt tasmād upapattideśaḥ saḥ*, 5|1|9|16), it is established that the time of the action [is determined] by the mantra.
From the perspective of mantra: at the time of the application of mantra.

Since the mantra is employed through its very expression of form, it possesses the capacity for performance during the application of the ritual; furthermore, because it serves as a reminder and since performance follows the sequence of the reminder, it is logical that the order [of performance] follows the order of the mantra-text. Thus, when it is stated that in the case of a conflict between the order of the mantra-text and the Brāhmaṇa-text, the Āgneya sacrifice—which, though prescribed later, is performed first—in accordance with the order of the mantra-text, one might object: "But the purpose of the Brāhmaṇa-text is also the same visible [purpose], namely, the recollection of what is to be performed. Anticipating this doubt, the portion of the Sūtra stating "that is the place of origin" (utpattideśaḥ saḥ) will declare that the Brāhmaṇa-text serves solely for the purpose of the originative injunction (*utpatti*) of the rite.

"That which the author of the Sūtras will state as 'it is the place of origin' applies when there is a contradiction, but not even when there is no contradiction" (Su. p. 667). *In the case of a contradiction regarding the essence of the mantra, it would be [the place of origin] due to the capacity of its form in usage; therefore, that is the place of origin.* Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice is recorded first, and the Āgneya sacrifice is recorded later.

In the *hautrakāṇḍa*, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the sacrifice to Agni are recited first, while those for the sacrifice to Agni-Soma are recited later; the same order is found in the *ācāryakāṇḍa* and the *yājamānakāṇḍa*.

This being the case, when considering whether the sequence of the Brāhmaṇa text or the sequence of the Mantra text is more authoritative, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that there is no fixed rule—is set aside by the word "but" (*tu*), and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated:
in the event of a conflict between the sequence of the Brāhmaṇa and the sequence of the Mantra, the performance should follow the sequence of the Mantra.

The recitation of the mantra is more powerful because of the efficacy of its form in the performance; that is, due to the efficacy and inherent connection of the form of the mantra within the ritual performance.
For the mantra is indeed inherently present in the performance.
Once the Brāhmaṇa has been employed and its purpose fulfilled, it no longer participates in the actual performance (*prayoga*).
Therefore, that Brāhmaṇa text is the "place of origin" (*utpattideśa*); it is the location from which the performance originates, serving as its source (*pradeśa*).
In practice, the mantra is proximate, whereas the Brāhmaṇa is remote.
Therefore, the recitation of the mantra is more authoritative than the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa.

Accordingly, following the mantra, the conclusion is that the offering to Agni comes first and the offering to Agni-Soma comes later. Ke. ✱ "Even though it is injunctive, it will cause the meaning to be remembered."
"In the case of a contradiction with the reality of mantras, this [following] would be intended. Thus it is stated here.

Vārttika 2.1.6.31, p. 432: In the inquiry as to whether the status of being a mantra (mantratva) exists or does not exist for *ūha*, *pravacana*, and names (*nāmadheya*), the conclusion is that it does not exist.
Vārttika 2.1.9.134: The status of being a mantra does not exist for [terms] such as *udbhid* and the like, because there is an absence of recollection by the students.
Vārttika 1.4.1.12: The status of being a mantra belongs to a specific type of sentence consisting of a collection of words arranged in a particular sequence.
Su. Pṛ. 99. ✱ There is no rule that only those specific [texts] designated as *mantras* possess injunctive power (*vidhiśakti*).
Vā. 2.1.6.30, p. 431. ✱ The purposefulness of the restriction regarding *mantras*:

For one who holds that [the *mantra*] has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), a change in the order [of its recitation] is not appropriate because there would be no authoritative basis for the invisible merit produced by its utterance; thus, the restriction is purposeful.
Or [it may be otherwise]. 1.2.4.
✱ For this is the purpose of the words of the mantra: that they manifest the meaning as it is present [in the ritual action].
Bhāṣya 1.2.1.136. ✱ The recitation of the mantra is more authoritative than the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa, as in the case of the sequence between the Āgneya and the Agnīṣomīya offerings.
5|1|9|16. ✱ The recitation of the Brāhmaṇa, when supported by the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the Mantra, is stronger than the mere recitation of the Mantra.
(Saṃkarṣa 4|2|16). ✱ The performance of the ritual act follows precisely the sequence of the Mantra's recitation.
✱ Since both a Mantra and a human-authored sentence possess equal capacity to convey meaning, the restriction to using the Mantra sentence serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Alternatively, since there is a restriction on the wording regarding the contingency of employing various means such as the recollection of multiple meditations (*dhyāna*),
[the mantra] serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*).
(This constitutes the prima facie view.)

✱ The Authority of Mantras.

The masters Pārthasārathi Miśra state in the *Śāstradīpikā* that mantras possess authority as word-meanings (*padārtha*), because it is accepted that word-meanings possess authority with respect to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

The meaning of this was stated by the Teacher in the *Tarkapāda* under the sūtra "Or, in the case of origination, they would be non-verbal" (1.1.24): "It is said that even if there were no other basis for us, the meanings of words (*padārtha*) are accepted as the basis because they are understood therein.
Thus, it is stated that the meanings of words function as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the cognition of the sentence-meaning.

In the injunctions for the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, the mantras—applicable by means of direct statement, indicative mark, and so forth—are included as constituent elements (padārtha) through syntactic unity with the sentence. Thus, since the injunction for the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites—which is a "great sentence" (mahāvākya) enjoining the ritual realization (bhāvanā) qualified by the mantras—bestows authoritative status upon the mantras as constituent elements within its own great-sentence-meaning, the mantras thereby attain the nature of a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).

Gurucaraṇa, however, having refuted this by stating that if it were so, their authority would arise solely as a means of knowing the ritual substance (*padārtha*), like rice and other materials, and not as a means of knowing the word itself, says that the authority of these [Mantras] consists precisely in their correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*) as produced by memory.
Bhaṭṭasomeśvara, moreover, asserts that they also possess the quality of conveying an object not previously known (*anadhigatārthagantṛtva*).
He states: "The fact that Mantras serve as indicators (*liṅga*) for the *Prapā* and other [rituals], which will be explained here..."

**Siddhānta:** Vārttika 3.4.2, Paṭasūcī—6. Regarding the Mahāpitṛyajña, where the selection [of priests] is obtained through the *codaka* (extended application), it is stated: "He does not choose an Āgnīdhra, nor a Hotṛ.
On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the selection, based on both the *codaka* and the direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*).

The final conclusion (siddhānta) is that, because the injunction of the *codaka* (archetypal rule) and the direct statement (*vacana*) form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), the purpose of the latter is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), meaning that everything other than the selection (*varaṇa*) is to be performed as known from the archetype.
Vi. 10.8.1. Oṃ. In the Mahāpitṛyajña, of the three verses, only two are the *puronuvākyās*, while the third is the *yājyā*.

In the Mahāpitṛyajña, three verses are prescribed as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*. Among these, two verses are combined to function as the *yājyā*, because it is stated in the context of "the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* of the gods are indeed two," followed by the Śruti text, "For the ancestors are superior to the gods," which declares their superiority over the gods. Furthermore, this superiority pertains specifically to the mantra for the offering, as explained in the Śruti: "Therefore, with the third [verse], he indeed offers."

When two [verses] are obtained through their sequence as *anuvākyās*, and there remains a third [verse], it is logical that this remaining one be employed together with the *yājyā* itself, because of its proximity and the aforementioned indicative mark (*liṅga*).
This being the prima facie view, [the correct conclusion is: two [verses] are to be employed as *puronuvākyās*, since the indicative mark applies equally to both.
"By the first and by the second he causes [him] to go."
And because of the explicit application [of the mantra] in the Kauṣītaki [Brāhmaṇa], which states: "He bestows the neck [ornament] with the third [verse]" (Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa 4.4.5).

The Commentary states: There is a Great Sacrifice to the Ancestors (*mahāpitṛyajña*): "A cake on six potsherds for Soma accompanied by the ancestors; parched grains (*dhānā*) for the ancestors who sit on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣmat*); and a stirred drink (*mantha*) in the milk of a cow that has recently calved for the ancestors consumed by fire (*agniṣvātta*).
Regarding the term *dhānā*, a doubt arises: should the act of threshing (*hanti*) be performed upon the parched grains, or not?
What is established? That it should not be performed.
Why? Because of the destruction [of the substance]. For if it were performed, the nature of being grains (*dhānātva*) would be destroyed; indeed, they would become flour-balls (*saktu*).
Therefore, it should not be performed.
This being the position reached, we reply:
it should be performed for the sake of an additional quality that destroys the highest obstacle, just like the application of collyrium.
He said:
"Collyrium does not destroy [the eye], but killing indeed destroys the state of being alive.
To this it is replied:
It will be done in such a way that it does not cause obstruction;
it is inverted, yet in this way it is not destroyed.
In the inversion, only the sequence is changed, but the referent itself does not cease to exist.
As it has been said: "When a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) is omitted, the primary action (*mukhya-kriyā*) still takes place" (Pāṇini 1.4.82).
Therefore, having first performed the act of *hanti*, the cooking (*pāka*) must be carried out;
for in that case, *hanti* will have the sense of cooking, and its nature as a verbal root (*dhātutva*) is not destroyed.
"Ḍupadhānāḥ" is the example. It is untenable in two ways.
How is it untenable? Even by means of the *codaka* (the rule of extension), only a reversal [of the order] is obtained.
Previously, threshing was performed; then, cooking.
Now, although threshing would logically follow after cooking, it must nevertheless be performed in that same original order.
Regarding this, it has been stated: "And when there is a reversal due to the purpose."
Even though both [threshing and cooking] would thus result from the act of striking, nevertheless, a reversal of the purpose is not logical (because the performance must follow that very sequence).

Now, if it is argued that "the injunction [of the archetype] applies once the sacrifice has been enjoined," then since the injunction here applies once the *dhānās* (parched grains) have been prepared, the injunctive force (*codaka*) consequently brings about both threshing and cooking.
Similarly, regarding the statement that "when threshing is reached, there is a reversal by virtue of the purpose" (because that which is reached later is performed first), that too is untenable.

If a substance already in its completed form were taken—like the *khalevālī* (the wooden hitching-post used as a sacrificial post)—then there would be no performance of threshing and so forth, just as there is none for cutting and other such acts; even then, what is called a "reversal of order" would not exist (since the very nature of the act of striking would have been lost).

On the other hand, if there is no taking of substances already completed, then in that case too the performance must follow exactly as it was originally reached, and there can be no reversal (therefore, parched grains are not a valid example for this).

What, then, is the illustrative example? In that very context (the Mahāpitṛyajña), regarding the instruction "one should prepare a stirred drink (*mantha*) in the milk of a cow that has lost its calf (*amivānyā*)," the grinding of the ingredients follows after the cooking of the *mantha* by virtue of the purpose.

Regarding that grinding, there arises a doubt: do the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the original (*prakṛta*) grinding apply, or do they not? (And for that purpose, one must determine whether this [grinding] is the original one, or something else, namely, a worldly one.)
In that regard, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), this grinding (*peṣaṇa*) is something subsequent [to the original].
For this reason, this grinding is indeed devoid of its own specific purpose (*adharmaka*).
However, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), that very same grinding [is intended], because it serves the same function as the original.
The difference is merely one of sequence (but not a difference in being an effect).
Therefore, even when there is a reversal of purpose (since the act of grinding has that as its aim because it is its effect), its very nature remains the same and not otherwise;
thus, the ritual properties (dharmas) indeed persist.
(He states another example: Regarding the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces, there arises the doubt: "Do the cooking-rites (*pākadharmāḥ*) apply, or do they not?
If the cooking—even though it is for a transcendental purpose (*apūrva*)—is performed [as in the injunction] "he cooks them in clarified butter," then the cooking-rites do not apply.
But if this is a reinstatement (*pratiprasava*) of the original (*prākṛta*) procedure, then they do apply.

(Regarding this, the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] is that in this rule of re-introduction, because it would result in a syntactical split [vākyabheda], it is an injunction for another kind of cooking.
The established conclusion [siddhānta] states: In this case, there is this re-introduction.
How so? The ritual properties of cooking, though obtained through the extended application [codaka], have ceased to apply due to the loss of their purpose.
Because of the injunction regarding cooking, they are restored [to their original state]. Now, in this restoration, only the cooking itself should be enjoined, not the ghee;
for if ghee were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (since both a restoration of what was already obtained and an accessory quality would be enjoined).

If, however, it is an injunction of what has not been previously established, then there is no fault in this being an injunction of a qualified entity, because [the object] was not already established. It is said in reply:

Because it is already established, ghee is not enjoined in this sentence ("he cooks in ghee"), but rather only the act of cooking itself is enjoined! Why is the ghee already established? Because in the originative injunction, ghee alone is heard as the substratum—as in "a pap for Prajāpati in ghee"—due to the connection with the locative case-ending and the force of the word *caru*.
Just as milk is the substratum for the *āditya* [pap], so too here, by virtue of the locative case, the vow is the substratum in the injunction of the observance (*avratti-vākya*).

And that [cooking] occurs precisely at the stage of boiling—after the purposeful boiling has begun—due to the force of the word *caru*. Therefore, in the sentence concerning the accessory (*guṇavākya*), ghee is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Thus, this is not a new injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) for a different kind of cooking; rather, it is merely a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) prescribed for the sake of parsimony.

Śābarabhāṣya: In the Mahāpitṛyajña, it is heard: "He offers a six-potherd cake (*puroḍāśa*) to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs; parched grains (*dhānāḥ*) to the Pitṛs associated with the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); and parched grains unmixed with salt to those Pitṛs who are unmixed, in the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time."

(He states the method of supporting the Bhāṣya as propounded by the Prābhākara: "As for those who say: 'There is no such quality as sequence (*krama*) distinct from the objects themselves, whose separate existence could be established;
for it is only the objects themselves that are perceived in their extended form.

Therefore, since it is impossible for sequence alone to be sublated, if that [sequence] were absent, the object itself would be sublated; thus, the act of threshing (*avaghāta*) need not be performed'—this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to refute such a view."

As for the statement that "there is no reversal," on this point they say: having performed the cooking of the grains (*dhānā*), one performs the threshing; whereas in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the order is reversed. Thus, there is indeed a reversal.
If there is a reversal, how then can the performance of the threshing take place? For the priority [of the threshing] cannot possibly exist separately.
True; however, there is no subversion of the sequence here from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the threshing was performed on the rice grains (*vrīhi*) as they were directly enjoined; here too, the threshing is performed on the roasted grains (*dhānā*) as they are directly enjoined—thus, there is no inversion of sequence. The argument for inversion is based solely on the fact that in the archetype the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) follows the threshing, whereas here the order is reversed.

[Objection: "Surely, if the act of threshing (*hanti*) were performed upon the grains (*dhānāsu*), it would cause damage to them; yet no such damage occurs. Therefore, we shall act in such a way that the threshing is performed only once, and thus there will be no damage.
[This refutes the Prābhākara explanation. That is incorrect, for the sublation of a separate sequence is indeed possible.
For those very ritual acts (*padārtha*) can be performed by one sequence or another; therefore, even in the absence of the original sequence (*prakṛtakrama*), the ritual acts do not cease to exist.

As for the statement, "Having performed the cooking (*śrapaṇa*), [then] the threshing (*avaghāta*)," that is not in contradiction with the Bhāṣya, which says, "First, having done the threshing, afterwards the cooking.
Furthermore, even though the threshing occurs after the cooking, there is no reversal [of the essential nature of the acts], since the substance has been heard [in the scripture].
As for the argument "because of the performance of threshing," that too is without substance.
For in the archetype (prakṛti), there are two mentions of substances: the mention of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and the mention of rice (vrīhi).
Among these, the parched grains (dhānā), by virtue of their connection with the deity, function in the place of the sacrificial cake, not in the place of the rice.

Furthermore, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the threshing has rice (*vrīhi*) as its object, not the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Therefore, even when the threshing is extended by the rule of transfer (*codaka*) to the parched grains (*dhānā*), it has rice as its object and not the parched grains themselves. If it were performed upon those [grains], there would necessarily be a reversal of the sequence. Moreover, if threshing were applied to the parched grains, their status as parched grains (*dhānātva*) would be destroyed.

If it were the rule that the threshing must be performed on the substance all at once, then in this case the threshing would be performed for an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), as its visible function would not have been accomplished.

Furthermore, if it were performed like the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*) upon the grain-stalks (*oṣadha*) while still possessing their husks (*tuṣa*), the status of being roasted grains (*dhānātva*) would be destroyed.
Therefore, this interpretation of the section (*adhikaraṇa*) is not tenable.
The connection [of this section] is established by demonstrating the inconsistency regarding the scattering (*paryūhaṇa*) and other rites in the case of *soma*.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: according to the position of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), since the act of striking (*han*) implies the sense of "shaking" (*dhunana*) by implication, its true nature (*tattva*) would remain as that of "grains" (*dhānā*) itself, thus being uncontradicted.

However, according to the position of the Vārttikakāra, the true nature of the grinding (*peṣaṇa*) would indeed be archetypal (*prākṛta*), because it is a modification of the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥ*).
Whether there is threshing or no threshing of the grains, there is no destruction [of the purpose].
There is no loss when the sequence is sublated; therefore, threshing is not sublated here.
Consequently, threshing must be performed even by sublation of the sequence.
Thus is the position according to the Bhāṣya.
According to the Vārtika, however: "I consider the grinding to be either new or archetypal (prākṛta), depending on the alternative sequence.
It is new, because there is parsimony in the case of the sublation of merely the archetypal property."

The author of the Bhāṣya has deliberated on whether or not threshing should be performed after roasting in a sacrifice where parched grains (*dhānā*) are the sacrificial material, as prescribed by the injunction: "Parched grains for the *barhiṣmat* ancestors; a preparation of the milk of a cow suckling another's calf for the *abhivānyā* ancestors," and so forth. His intention is this: since threshing is enjoined such that it should properly occur prior to cooking by means of the *codaka* (extended application), it would follow [by extension] after roasting; however, if one were to perform threshing after that, the state of being parched grains (*dhānātva*) would be destroyed by the act of threshing. Therefore, threshing should not be done after roasting.

This being the position reached, [the author replies]: In the world, when certain roasted barley grains (*dhānā*) have been previously parched and are subsequently subjected to threshing again, their status as *dhānā* is established only after that threshing has been performed. Even if this overrides the original sequence (*prakṛtakrama*) for the sake of the purpose, the original threshing—possessing its own specific characteristics (*sadharmaka*)—must indeed be performed even after the parching, according to the maxim "when a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is omitted, the primary element (*mukhya*) remains" (Jaimini Sūtra 10.2.27).
Nor does this result in the destruction of their status as *dhānā*, because that status is not lost provided one refrains from striking with an excessively heavy pestle.
For in the archetype, the threshing is for the purpose of preparing the sacrificial offering; it must be performed in such a way that the offering is prepared.
Therefore, regarding the Mahāpitṛyajña, the author of the Mahābhāṣya [states]: [3131]

Thus, in accordance with that [requirement], threshing must indeed be performed even before roasting for the sake of achieving some degree of dehusking; otherwise, the well-known worldly state of being *dhānā* (parched grains) would not be accomplished.
For this very reason, repetition [of the act] in accordance with that requirement is not defective.
In that case, the former threshing is for the purpose of cooking, while the latter is for the purpose of establishing the state of being *dhānā*.
Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
For Pārthasārathi, who understands the intention of the Bhāṣya in this manner, the effort made to embellish [his position] should simply be disregarded.

As for the Vārttikakāra, however, it is not the case that only those grains which have been threshed twice possess the status of *dhānā*s; for when barley-grains that have already been properly dehusked are subsequently roasted, their status as *dhānā*s remains unimpaired.

Therefore, since threshing is logically to be performed according to its very nature even before roasting, *dhānā* (fried grains) cannot serve as an example here; rather, it is *mantha* (a stirred drink).
And that consists of barley meal mixed with milk.
In the present context, the milk intended is that of a cow whose calf has died, specifically one that has been suckled by another cow.

In this context, since parched barley and rice grains are well-known as *saktu* (flour) only when ground after being parched, grinding must indeed follow the parching—even though this deviates from the original sequence—because grinding is performed after parching for the sake of producing the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), in accordance with the principle of the "omission of subordinate elements" (*guṇalopādhikaraṇanyāya*). Nor does a change in sequence imply the non-performance of the constituent acts (*padārtha*), for even in the case of inversion, such recognition of the act persists from the time of threshing (*avaghāta*).
Furthermore, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), grinding is not for the purpose of cooking, such that one might suspect its omission here due to the absence of cooking after parching.
Even though it is true that [grinding] nourishes the baking of the *puroḍāśa*, both baking and grinding serve the purpose of preparing the substance, as indicated by the accusative case ending.

Therefore, just as in one instance grinding is performed prior to baking solely for the sake of preparing the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), so too here there is no contradiction in performing it after baking for the sake of preparing the groats (*saktu*).

Regarding this, Mādhava maintains that the *tāpya* is a woolen blanket (*kambala*) smeared with ghee. However, if it were prescribed for the purpose of wearing (*paridhāna*), then it would follow that it must be worn by the wife and others as well; if it were prescribed for the purpose of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), then it would follow that it must be used even on the bed and so forth. Therefore, what is prescribed here for the sake of the sacrificer and others is specifically the act of wearing (*paridhāna*) characterized by the *tāpya* and other qualities. And that [act] is indeed the original (*prākṛta*) one, since it is obtained through general application (*atideśataḥ*). Whether it is prescribed prior to its attainment or whether it constitutes an entirely different ritual action (*karmāntara*) is another matter.

And because that [cloth] is prescribed solely for the purpose of the original function (*prākṛta-kārya*), there is the displacement (*nivṛtti*) of the original unhemmed cloth (*ahata*). It should not be argued that there is no displacement of the unhemmed cloth because the unhemmed cloth of the archetype is enjoined for the covering of the private parts (denoted by the word *kaupīna*), whereas the *tāpya* and other cloths are unsuitable for that; for suitability is established only for the act of wearing (*upaparidhāna*), since it is understood that the injunction of the *tāpya* and others extends to that very act of wearing as a substitute for the original. Furthermore, since the private parts can also be covered by the *tāpya* and other cloths, [the displacement stands].

In reality, however—since the term *paridadhāti* is used even when covering something other than the private parts, as in the injunctions "Spread [the grass] around" (*paristṛṇīta*) and "Cover the altar" (*paridhatta vedim*)—it is true that the rule does not apply solely to the covering of the private parts. Nevertheless, because in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the injunction "He puts on new (unwashed) cloth" (*ahataṃ vāsaḥ paridhatte*) applies both to the covering of the private parts—as well as to the covering of the upper body as established by custom—the wearing of unwashed cloth is excluded in both instances by the injunction of dyed cloth (*tāpyādi*).

This being the position reached: since for a householder covering the private parts (*kaupīnācchādana*) is possible through the use of a waist-cloth (*kaccha*) and so forth, and since the injunctions regarding *tāpya* (woolen cloth) and other materials are understood to apply specifically to what is worn over [the body], there is no exclusion of the *ahata* (unbeaten, new) cloth in the case of covering the private parts.

For this very reason, when by logic the exclusion of the ordinary *ahata* cloth would follow in the case of the upper garment (*uparidhāraṇa*) as established by custom, the specific disposal-injunction (*pratipatti-viśeṣa-vākya*), "He shall cast off his garments" (*vāsāṃsi vibhraṃśyati*),—because of the plurality of the word "garments" (*vāsaḥ*) and the resulting perception of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) through that sentence—therefore, even in that case, there is no exclusion of the *ahata* cloth.

And thus, although the cloth used for covering the loincloth (*kaupīna*) might somehow be suitable as that which is to be heated, nevertheless, because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the plurality of garments, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of that with the new (*ahata*) cloth.

As for the cloth made of dharma, however, even though its suitability as something to be heated is questionable, since an injunction is perceived specifically regarding wearing it, there is likewise a conjunction with it by virtue of the restatement of the plurality of garments.

For this very reason, where there is no restatement of the plurality of garments—as in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, where the scripture states, "He puts on the wet garment [used] for the *avabhṛtha* bath"—there, because of the suitability of the unwashed (*ahata*) garment for covering the private parts, even though the application of the unwashed garment (which would otherwise be obtained by extension) is set aside, its exclusion does not apply to wearing it over the upper body.

For a connection with another meaning is indeed heard [in scripture], such as "They praise in front of the *sadas*," and so forth.
Furthermore, a word that is connected with a certain other word as a qualifier cannot possibly be connected with yet another word; it would be too restricted.
For example, in the expression "The king's wife, the man of Devadatta," the word "king's" (*rājñaḥ*), being uttered as a qualifier for "wife," is not further connected with the word "man."

If the location were being prescribed for the praise, and it were said "and with a *śloka*," then it would be appropriate for there to be a single sentence. The *Śākyānām Ayana* (also read as *Śākyānāmayana*) is a sacrificial session (*sattra*) lasting thirty-six years. Regarding this, the Vedic scripture states: "On each day that concludes [the rite], the master of the house goes out hunting; the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) for the *savanīya* offerings are made from the flesh (*tarasa*) of the animals he kills there.

In considering whether this quality of being "made of flesh" (*tarasamayatva*)—meaning consisting of meat—applies to all the sacrificial cakes or only to the *savanīya* cakes, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains, contrary to the established rule, that it applies to all of them. The author of the Siddhānta replies:
The word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
By the word "taras," that which is called meat belongs specifically to the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes.
Why? Because of the specific injunction (*codanā-viśeṣāt*).
In the statement, "The *tarasa* cakes are the *savanīya*s," the connection between the *tarasa* and the *savanīya*s is what is being enjoined.
The term "cakes" (*puroḍāśāḥ*), however, is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that meat is to be taken in place of all five substances—namely, the parched grains (*dhānā*), the flour-mash (*karambha*), the fried grains (*parivāpa*), the curd-mixture (*payasyā*), and the cake (*puroḍāśa*)—which are designated by the term "sacrificial cakes at the Soma-pressing" (*savanīyapuroḍāśa*), because of the specific mention of the word "sacrificial" (*savanīya*).
If it is argued that [the rule] applies to other [sacrifices] by way of proximity (*bhakti*), [the Siddhāntin replies]:

In the *Ayana* sacrifice of the Śākyas, known as the *Nāma-sattra*, it is stated, "The *puroḍāśa* cakes are made of meat (*tarasa*)," where the word *tarasa* denotes meat. That [meat] belongs only to those *savanīya* *puroḍāśas* whose constituent substances are *dhānās* (fried grains) and so forth, and not to all *puroḍāśas*. This being stated in the previous sūtra as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says:

The proponent (siddhāntin) accepts that the term *puroḍāśa* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) with respect to the parched grains (*dhānā*), the flour-mash (*karambha*), the fried grains (*parivāpa*), and the curd-mixture (*payasyā*). However, it would be better to accept the term *savanīya* itself—though not explicitly heard in this context—as denoting the entire collection of *savanīya* offerings. Thus he says: "In the absence of proximity" (*asannidhau*). "Proximity" (*saṃnidhi*) means non-difference; "absence of proximity" (*asannidhi*) means absolute difference. When there is an absolute difference between the parched grains and so forth from the *puroḍāśa*, it is improper for the word *puroḍāśa* to apply to the parched grains and so forth through metaphorical usage (*bhakti*), figurative sense (*gauṇatā*), or indication (*lakṣaṇikatā*).
And therefore, the word *puroḍāśa* should not be accepted as having a secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) when its primary meaning is possible.
Here the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) says: "If the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) should say this," [the answer is:
"It would be so, because it possesses the characteristic mark of the archetype (*prakṛti*), like the *vairāja*."
If the term *puroḍāśa* were to include the parched grains (*dhānā*) and other such items as well, there would be a figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *puroḍāśa*;
and that is improper when the primary meaning is possible.
This was the objection raised by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) in the preceding sūtra.
In this regard, the following is the sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhānta) for the sake of the subsequent argument:

It would be logical for the word *puroḍāśa* to have a figurative meaning (*lākṣaṇikatva*) when applied to parched grains (*dhānā*) and so forth; however, it is not logical for the word *savanīya* to have a figurative meaning when applied to the entire collection of *savanīya* offerings.
"Because it is a characteristic mark of the archetype (prakṛti).

Since, in the archetype—the Agniṣṭoma—the word *puroḍāśa* serves as a characteristic mark for the pentad of oblations beginning with the *dhānās* and ending with the *savanīya*, this figurative usage (*bhakti*) may also apply by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Even though the word *puroḍāśa* is primary (*mukhya*), its secondary application (*gauṇatva*) is appropriate."

The *Sudhā* commentary states: "Because the word *puroḍāśa-savanīya* is equivalent to a derivative descriptive reference (*avayutpannānuvāda*) to the collection of fried grains (*dhānā*) and so forth; and because, according to the *Māṃsādhikaraṇa*, there is no connection between the *savana-brāhmaṇa* and the definition of the *asavanīya-puroḍāśa* through the properties of the fried grains and the like, it is not possible for that [word] to function as a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, the intention is that even for the primary word *puroḍāśa*, the occurrence of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*) is appropriate."

"In the *prakṛti* [archetype], the *jyotiṣṭoma*, cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are offered at each pressing," and so forth; that word "cake" (*puroḍāśa*) possesses a secondary indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the capacity for the offering of parched grains (*dhānā*) and other such items—which is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).
Therefore, according to the *Kutūhala*, even in the *vikṛti* [ectype], figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate.
The phrase "like the *vairāja*" is an example from the Sūtra.

Just as in the archetype *jyotiṣṭoma*, in the passage “If the *soma* sacrifice should have the *rathantara-sāman*,” the word *sāman* is seen to be used figuratively (*lakṣaṇika*) for the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*; likewise, in the modified form (*vikṛti*), in the passage “The *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] is twenty-one-fold and has the *vairāja-sāman*,” the word *sāman* is used figuratively for the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*.
Here, the term *vairāja* serves as an illustration for the term *vairāja-sāman*.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that according to the Śākyas, meat is prescribed only for the five oblations denoted by the term *savanīya-puroḍāśa*.

[The view of] some [is that] the meat, however, possesses the status of being for the *savanīya* offering, because of the specific injunction. This is the section concerning the meat (*māṃsādhikaraṇa*).

Even though the *savanīya* term is taught in a branch of the Yajurveda, because it falls under the definition of a "thing to be accomplished" (*kāryalakṣaṇa*), the primary *savanīya* word itself possesses the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatā*) for the *savanīya* sacrifice.
The fact that the nominative case carries the sense of the accusative is established in both ways [by grammatical convention].
Therefore, the five items beginning with parched grains (*dhānā*) are enjoined for the purpose of that [sacrifice] by means of the *savanīya* sacrifice itself as the object of reference.
The word *puroḍāśa*, however, is singular and secondary; it is a figurative reference (*lakṣaṇika*) to the *savanīya* sacrifices by virtue of its connection with the *puroḍāśa*.

Indeed, in expressions such as "adorn the *puroḍāśas*," the word *puroḍāśa* is observed to refer to the sacrificial oblation related to the *savanīya*; thus, its function as an indicator (*lakṣaka*) of the *savanīya* sacrifice is easily established.
In this manner, the status of being known through the means of valid cognition, beginning with direct audition (*śruti*), has been described.
Hereafter, the status of being that which is to be employed (*prayojyatva*) will be examined.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The meat is to be prescribed for the function of the *savanīya*. Śaṅkara [states]: "The *tarasa* is the *savanīya* sacrifice."
