*Vārttika* 1.3.17, page [number].

In the case of practices contrary to the Smṛtis—such as the marriage of a maternal uncle’s daughter—it is clearly observed that other causes, such as desire and the like, are at work; therefore, a basis in the Śruti cannot be conceived in any way whatsoever.

For it is impossible that both the production of demerit (*pratyavāya*) from marrying a maternal uncle’s daughter and its non-production could occur simultaneously; thus, one must necessarily accept the lack of authority for one or the other.
In this regard, since the practice based on the authority of the household is unauthoritative, it is established that such customs are indeed "bad conduct" (*durācāra*).
Marriage with the Daughter of a Maternal Uncle:
In certain regions of the South, marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle occurs; however, there is no such relationship [among us], for we are not inhabitants of Mathurā.

If it is argued that "it is done in such a way, therefore it is authoritative," we say no; for the names such as "Dākṣiṇātya" (Southerner) and so forth are not fixed for the Āhīnaibukas, as they are sublated by traditional memory (smṛti).
"One has married the daughter of a maternal uncle, as well as one belonging to the mother's *gotra* or having the same *pravara*.
(Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.3.12.2).

Regarding this, there is a *vārtika*: "But having abandoned [a girl] from Mathurā, one who belongs to the same *gotra*, or one who has the same *pravara*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance."

Regarding the statement by the author of the Bhāṣya, "Thus [the suffix] *māthura* is applied when one has set out," that refers to the case where "one remembers [the destination] as he goes there" (*tad-racchati smṛtiḥ*). Furthermore, Smṛti is more authoritative than established custom (*sadācāra*).

Alternatively, under the rule *pathituyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.85), one should construct a variant (*varṇaka*) concerning a messenger; or else, it should be disregarded because it is stated that the person is not being dispatched. This is because, even when someone has set out, there is no application of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix in all such cases.

Regarding the marriage to the daughter of a maternal uncle: "One who has married the daughter of a maternal uncle, or likewise one from the mother's *gotra*, or even one with the same *pravara*, shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance after abandoning her."
This is prohibited by the Smṛtis.

In this context, the prohibition against marrying the daughter of one's maternal uncle (*mātulasutā*) is intended for cases where there is no cessation of the mother’s lineage (*mātṛgotra*), such as when she has been made an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) or in marriages such as the *gāndharva* form.
This has been explained in detail in the *Smṛticandrikā*.

The measuring of the Soma is performed at the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*); therefore, because it is observed [in that context], there is a bringing down (*upāvaharaṇa*) [of the cloth].
At the multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), for the purpose of measuring the Soma—that is, to perform the measurement—one should produce a cloth at the time of measuring.

Since the bringing down of that measuring-cloth is observed in the model sacrifice, the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, one need not produce a separate cloth at the multi-day sacrifice for the purpose of bringing it down.
Or rather, even though it arises [as a separate rite], it should be performed at the very time of the measuring;
this is the prima facie (pūrva) position.
Or, because of its connection with the scriptural injunction regarding the removal, it [belongs] to the archetype by implication. 80.

The word "yā" (which) serves to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). In a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), the cloth for the purpose of bringing down the Soma (*soma-upāvahaṇa*) should not be produced at the time of measurement; rather, it should be produced at the time of carrying (*haraṇa*), that is, at the time of bringing down.

This is because of the connection with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), meaning there is no connection [with the time of measurement] according to the direct statement, as it is prescribed by the direct statement.
For it is not heard [in the scripture] that one should produce [the garment] at the time of measuring.
If it is argued that—since in the archetype (prakṛti) the removal of the measuring-garment is observed, the removal-garment must be produced precisely at the time of measuring—the author replies:
"Because of the connection with what is heard," that is, because it is stated by direct scriptural injunction (śruti).
For it is not heard [in the scripture] that the bringing down (*upāvaharaṇa*) of the *mānavāsa* (the cloth for the measuring) must be performed;
rather, because there is oneness of the act in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it follows by implication (*arthāt*).
For the *mānavāsa* is not occupied elsewhere at the time of the bringing down; therefore, it is performed by that very same [cloth].

In the case of a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*), however, the *mānava* garment is used on each subsequent day because it is pervaded by the Soma through its connection with the Soma; since it is therefore possible to bring it down separately every day, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that a separate garment must be produced at the time of bringing it down each day.
[The word] *māna* refers to a characteristic of the Soma.

The principle is that "the establishment of the object of knowledge depends upon the means of knowledge" (or "the establishment of the *prameya* depends upon the *pramāṇa*). [Sāhasrī 466] By the principle that "the establishment of the object of knowledge depends upon the means of knowledge," the determination of the means of knowledge serves as the cause for the determination of the true nature of *dharma*.
Nor is there an absence of determination when two factors of relative strength (balābala) meet in this way;

for, since the relative strength or weakness of the means of knowledge—consisting of being based on direct Vedic statement (śrautatva) versus being based on continuity (sāṃtatyatva)—is dependent upon the means of knowledge itself, the object of knowledge (prameya) is understood to be stronger due to its dependence on the means of knowledge, according to the maxim "dependent on the means" (mānādhīna), because it arises before any contradiction has occurred and because it precedes the final determination.
The acts of removing the *māna* vessel and so forth belong exclusively to the ritual of the Soma sacrifice.
The bringing together (*samānayana*) of the eleven *mānavī* verses from the *Daśatayī* collection for the purpose of the *sāmidhenī* verses occurs in the *Somāraudra* offerings.
See 10.16.9.73–76, specifically regarding the rule: "In the *Somāraudra* offerings, [the verses are used] for the purpose of the *sāmidhenīs*."
Among human [sacrifices], the greatness of the mind [is intended];
among human [sacrifices], only fifteen [verses] have the status of *sāmidhenī* verses. (Vi. 10.16.9)
The *mānasa* is a day.
"This *mānasa* is indeed the release (*visarga*) of the tenth day.
[In the] *Dvādaśāha*: "On the tenth day, they proceed for the *mānasa*."

Bhāṣya 10.16.13.39–40: The mental [rite] should be a distinct day, because it is designated as separate. Regarding the Dvādaśāha, it is heard in scripture: "With another vessel, I take for Prajāpati that which is pleasing to him, the mental draught (mano-graha) belonging to Prajāpati. This mental rite, the mental draught, should be a distinct day, separate from the Dvādaśāha.
Because of the distinct designation of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) and the mental rite (*mānasa*) in the passage, “Speech indeed is the twelve-day rite; the mind is the mental rite.
Furthermore, by the statement “Speech indeed is the twelve-day rite,” the twelve-day rite is praised through speech; and by “the mind is the mental rite,” the mental rite is praised through the mind.
Since the distinction between speech and mind is well known, the distinction between the twelve-day rite and the mental rite is likewise understood.
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that the Mānasa day is distinct from the Dvādaśāha,
because it is praised as such;
for it is understood that the Mānasa is a separate day from the Dvādaśāha on account of the praise bestowed upon it by means of that [Dvādaśāha].
"Indeed, the meters of the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) that have been exhausted are replenished by means of the mental [day].

By stating that "those meters of the twelve-day sacrifice which have been exhausted are replenished by means of the mental [day]," he shows that the mental [day] is distinct from the twelve-day sacrifice;
for it is not praised as being identical to it.
Because the distinction between the object of praise and the praiser has not been established;

therefore, in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), another reason is stated: "The mental [sacrifice] is an additional day, like the twelve-day sacrifice," and because it follows after the [actual] day, there is an injunction.

The mental cup-offering (mānasa-graha) belongs to Prajāpati; he also speaks of a twelve-day period as being distinct from the twelve-day rite. Why? Because it is a different day (ahantaram). The Patnīsaṃyāja offerings constitute the end of the day.

"Having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, the wise ones go out and proceed toward the *mānasa* [offering]"; thus, there is an injunction for the *mānasa* to follow immediately after the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Therefore, the *mānasa* is an intermediate day (*ahantara*) within the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
If it were merely an accessory (*guṇa*) of the twelve-day sacrifice, however, it would have to occur prior to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

It is prescribed later; therefore, "because it is not separated from that" is stated as another reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). In that position, the number is like [the case of] a thousand.

The *mānasa* cup belongs to Prajāpati; although it lasts for twelve days, it is distinct from the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice. This objection was raised as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), and the following is stated as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
[Objection: "In that case, they say there are thirteen days, so the designation 'twelve-day sacrifice' (*dvādaśāha*) would not be appropriate. To this it is replied:

In the alternative view, even though the state of being a thirteen-day sacrifice (*trayodaśāha*) exists, the term *dvādaśāha*— composed of a word expressing a specific number— is appropriate because it is the name of a ritual action,

just like the word *sahasra*. For example, in the passage "One should sacrifice with the *atirātra* consisting of a thousand [verses]," the word *sahasra* is seen to be used even when there are more than a thousand.
It is like that.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the mental [sacrifice] is a distinct day from the twelve-day rite;
for there is no injunction to the contrary regarding the two days.

Regarding the mental cup (*mānasa-graha*), when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached that it may occur even on the twelfth day—that is, at an interval of twelve days from the [preceding] day—the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view.
The mental cup should belong to the second day—that is, the tenth day—[of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice], and not to any other day.
"Because of the absence of an injunction," that is, because of the absence of an injunction that would establish another [deity].
"But with the vessel of the ocean, I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati"—this is the *manograha* for Prajāpati, belonging to the set of ten *grahas*.
It is like the case of the *aṅguri*, just as when two horse-givers (*aśvadāmī*) are enjoined in a particular ritual act.
In that case as well, it is understood that "the pressing and the consuming" refer to these very acts and not to other rites;
likewise, therefore, this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) specifically on the tenth day.
This is also because of the statement regarding the conclusion on the tenth day.
In the Siddhānta, he states another reason:

"This indeed is the conclusion (*visarga*) of the tenth day, namely the mental [rite] (*mānasa*). By stating that "this is the conclusion" and "namely the mental," he shows that this is the conclusion of the tenth day and not an independent rite; thus, he demonstrates the scriptural statement regarding the conclusion of the tenth day.
And [the conclusion] that it occurs on the tenth day is based on the scriptural teaching of its specific quality (*tadguṇaśāstra*).

Because of the scriptural teachings regarding the quality of that tenth day—such as "On the tenth day they proceed for the *mānasa* [cup]" and "On the tenth day they praise with the verses of the *Sārparājñī*"—it is established as the final position (*siddhānta*) that the *mānasa* cup is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the tenth day and not a separate day.
This is the *Mānasa-saṅkarṣaṇa*.
Because of the consistency of the number [of days] in the Mānasa-saṅkarṣaṇa.
The Commentary states: "And because of the consistency of the number twelve in the expression 'twelve-day rite' (dvādaśāha), the Mānasa cup is an auxiliary of the tenth day."
If, however, the *mānasa* were a different day, the statement regarding the number—"thirteen days for the twelve-day rite"—would be inconsistent.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is an additional *prahara*.
Furthermore, this is because there is the presence of only one [additional element] when there is an excess of animals.

Commentary: Regarding the animals of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) and the eleven-day sacrifice (*ekādaśinī*), when there is an excess—that is, an addition—of one day, it is understood that because of the existence of one additional day and the absence of two [additional] days, the mental rite (*mānasa*) is not a separate day. For if it were a separate day, there would be an excess of two; for in that case, there would be thirteen days, whereas the animals are eleven.

"Whichever animal remains in excess, that one should be made for Indra and Agni"—having thus prescribed the *ekādaśinī* (the set of eleven animals) for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), this statement shows that there is an excess of one among them.
There are eleven animals and twelve days;
by stating the excess of one, it makes it understood that these [days] are twelve.

Therefore, the established conclusion is that the mental [sacrifice] is the tenth limb and not a separate ritual action. Regarding the objection raised by the proponent of the prima facie view—that it is a distinct entity because of its designation as different from others (10.6.13.4), and because of its praise as being "with that mental [sacrifice] of the twelve-day rite" (10.6.13.5)—the proponent of the conclusion states the following reply: [it would be] contradictory, like a religious vow, if it were to subvert the scriptural injunction.
We consider the designation of the whole by means of a part for the sake of praise to be unobjectionable;
as in the case of a vow, for example, when the year [is praised] by means of the property of the Mahāvrata.
"Those who undertake the year-long rite indeed go away from the pair."

"A couple unites within the altar; by that very union they proceed"—here, desiring to favor the constituent part, namely the Mahāvrata, with the property of the whole, [the text] shows the praise of the whole by means of a property belonging to its parts.
Even in common worldly usage, a whole is praised by means of a property of its parts, as in: "Devadatta has long, beautiful hair.
Therefore, there is no fault.
The state of not ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings follows from a direct scriptural statement.

Regarding what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*)—namely, "And because there is an injunction for that which follows after the end of the day" (10.6.13.6)—the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*) says:

Because of the statement, "Having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, the wise ones, having risen, proceed toward the *mānasa* [offering]," the tenth day does not end with that [i.e., the *patnīsaṃyāja*], and thus there is an absence of the quality of ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
In general, the rites of the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) end with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings; however, specifically regarding the tenth day, it is stated that they end with the Mānasa offering.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Consequently, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the Mānasa is an auxiliary part (aṅga) of the tenth day, not a separate day within the twelve-day sacrifice itself.
The *mānasa* cup is [a part] of the tenth day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
In that context, there is a praise of the twelve-day sacrifice by means of the *mānasa*, stating: "The other meters of the twelve-day sacrifice—these they satisfy with the *mānasa*."
"Speech indeed is the twelve-day rite, and the mind is the Mānasa [rite]"—this is a distinction in designation.
"This indeed is the release of the tenth day, namely the Mānasa"—this is a statement regarding its release.
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 10.6.13)
In the case of mental cognition (*mānasa-jñāna*), the causal complex for visual perception and the like acts as an obstacle (Maṇi, p.
63). In a ten-day sacrifice (*daśarātra*), the rites conclude with the mental offerings; in a twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), they do not conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Those ending with the *mānasa* and the *saha* are stated by the verbal injunction as belonging to the tenth day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
Bhāṣya 9.12.19.
Some maintain that largeness (*mahattva*) is the cause of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), while others say it is not. (Maṇi, p. 21).
The *graha* known as *mānasa* is a constituent part of the tenth day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
The section concerning the mental [sacrifice].
The mental [sacrifice] is a contraction;
it should be a distinct interval from the mental [sacrifice], because of the designation as "Veda."

The Commentary: In the context of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it is heard in scripture: "With this vessel, I take for Prajāpati what is pleasing to him; thus he takes the mental cup (*mānasa*) dedicated to Prajāpati. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the mental cup a separate day within the twelve-day sacrifice, or does it consist of two days?
In this regard, several grounds for distinction appear.

Desiring to refute those [arguments], the Teacher presents [the following]: "There would be an interval of a *mānasa* day. Why? Because of the designation by way of distinction; it is designated as distinct from the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).

How so? Because it designates the mental [sacrifice] as being within the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), stating, "Speech indeed is the twelve-day sacrifice; the mind is the mental [sacrifice]. This is because of the praise of speech in the phrase "Speech indeed is the twelve-day sacrifice," and the praise of the mind in the phrase "The mind is the mental [sacrifice]. Just as this difference in expression is understood from the actual wording, so too is it the case here regarding the twelve-day sacrifice and the mental [sacrifice].
Therefore, since they are distinct, there is a designation by way of their difference, and not otherwise.
Therefore, it is distinguished by the designation "this day";
[it is] the Mānasa-saṃkarṣaṇa.
The Mānasa-saṃkarṣaṇa.
And because of the similarity with that.
The Commentary says: "For this reason also, it is another day. Why? Because the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) is praised by means of that mental day (*mānasa-ahar*).
How so? [The text says]: "The meters of the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) have indeed been drained of their essence; they are replenished by means of the mental [sacrifice].
By stating that the meters of the twelve-day sacrifice which have lost their essence are replenished by the mental [sacrifice], it shows the twelve-day sacrifice to be distinct.
How? Because of the praise [of its excellence].
For there can be no praise of something by means of its own self.
Why? Because praise occurs between two things that are distinct;
indeed, Devadatta is not praised by Devadatta himself.

Just as [the sacrifice] is praised by means of its severed heads, hands, and so forth, so too here the Dvādaśāha is praised by means of the Mānasa; thus, from this praise, a distinction [between the two] is understood. Furthermore, there is an injunction subsequent to the end of the day.
Commentary: For this reason as well, it is understood that it is indeed another day.
Why? Because after the final day of the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha), it is enjoined: "Having performed the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings, the wise ones go out and proceed toward the Mānasa [offering].
If this were an injunction of a subsidiary detail (guṇavidhi) pertaining to the day of the twelve-day rite, then the twelve-day rite would end with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.
Now, if there is another day, then this rule belongs to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) and not to any other; thus there will be no fault.
For this reason as well, it is understood that the establishment of another day follows from the difference in characteristics.
In one case, the number is like that of a thousand.
Commentary: This is the refutation of an objection.
What is this objection? [The objection is: "In that case, the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) would not be applicable to the thirteen-day rite. To this it is replied:

When it is understood through another means of knowledge that the word is employed in this much of a meaning, then, due to its proximity to the number, its application as a quality (*guṇatva*) in respect to thirteen will be established.

Just as in the cases "The *Atirātra* has a thousand [cows]" and "One should sacrifice with the *Atirātra* which accomplishes a thousand," the word "thousand" is seen to be used even when there is an excess over a thousand; so too will it be here in the case of an excess.
Alternatively, this term *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day rite) is a name for a collection of ritual acts.
Because it is stated that "as many actions as there are," it is determined that [the word] is expressive because it is employed according to that reality.
Since it is employed by taking all [actions] into account through the context and so forth, it will be expressive of all of them; thus, there is no fault.
Alternatively, it is not unknown [to whom], because there is an absence of any restriction.
Commentary: This would be an injunction regarding a quality of the tenth day, not an injunction for another day.
Why? Because there is no statement that could establish another day.
How so? It is heard as follows: "With this vessel, I take [the draught] acceptable to Prajāpati from the ocean; I take the mind-offering acceptable to Prajāpati. Thus it is.
It takes the tenth day as its subject because of the injunction for the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) stating "it takes [the day].
Furthermore, a difference in the ritual action (*karman*) does not necessarily follow from a difference in the preparatory rite;
for it has been stated: "And preparatory rites are not injunctive [of new actions]" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.2.6.18).
"Where the substance is scattered, there the quality [is primary]" (2.1.318); thus, the action is not the principal factor.
For example, when two portions are being enjoined, the action is not distinct.
It is understood that those two further cup-drawings (*grahābhyāsa*) occur within that same action, and not in a different action.

And if this is merely an accessory (*aṅga*) and not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), then there will be the conceptualization of eight inferences in this very manner: it is connected with the archetype (*prakṛta*), and what is not part of the archetype is not a separate performance.
Therefore, it is not a different day.
"The injunction regarding the accessory pertains to the tenth day itself," because of the statement concerning the "emission on the tenth.
The Bhāṣya says: For this reason as well, there is no other day; the injunction regarding the accessory applies to that very [day].
Why? Because of the statement regarding the "emission" (*visarga*) of the tenth day.
For there is indeed a statement concerning the emission of the tenth day: "This, namely the mental [sacrifice], is the emission of the tenth day.
By stating that this emission of the tenth day—the end—is the mental [sacrifice], it shows that this is the conclusion of the tenth day which has an end, and not that it is independent.
Therefore, it is understood that this is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the tenth day, and not something independent.
This is because of the scriptural injunction regarding its quality, namely, "on the tenth day.
The Commentary states: For this reason also, it is a subsidiary part.

How so? In this way, the scripture concerning the quality will be consistent with such passages as, "On the tenth day they proceed for the sake of the mental [offering]," and, "On the tenth day they praise with the Sārparājñī verses using the limbs.

Because the tenth day is designated as the primary element and the cup (graha) as the subordinate element to be placed upon it, it is understood that this is a quality of the tenth day and not a separate matter;
this is because the numerical consistency is thus maintained.
Commentary: And if this is a quality (guṇa), then the number will be consistent as "the twelve-day sacrifice" (dvādaśāha).
Otherwise, the numerical designation "twelve-day sacrifice" applied to thirteen days would be inconsistent, because that number is not applicable.
As for what was stated—that it is by way of figurative application (guṇavṛtti), like the word "thousand"—that is reasonable.

Why? Because in that case, since the number itself is understood through another means of knowledge, it is determined that the word "thousand" is used figuratively with respect to something in excess. However, here there is no evidence for anything beyond the number, by virtue of which a figurative application would have to be resorted to.

If this statement, "With this vessel for you," is intended as such, it is understood that because it prescribes the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the cup (*graha*), it enjoins a repetition of the sacrifice on the day of the cup-offering, and not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*). If this is so, this direct statement does not establish a different [action], nor is there any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it, by which one would necessarily conclude that there is an application of a distinct substance when the number [of cups] is exceeded.
Therefore, in this case, the application is by way of a figurative sense (*gauṇī vṛtti*).

As for the argument that— because it is the name of a group of rituals— it will function either by virtue of its being a name or by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*) which necessitates the inclusion of that many [subsidiaries]—
that too is not tenable.
This is truly the name for a collection of rites, not by way of an unreal association.
These twelve rites, limited by days and brought together in one place in this form, constitute the name of that collection of rites; it is not [the name] according to the sequence of syllables.

For indeed, in all cases, a word used as a name functions through its connection with the meaning of the rites, not by setting aside the worldly meaning as a mere technical convention (*paribhāṣā*), like the qualities of the intellect.
Just as [the names] Agnihotra, Śyena, and Jyotiṣṭoma [are applied],
so too is "Dvādaśāha" a name by means of something else, not due to an absence of meaning. Therefore, this is not a valid objection.
And because there is an excess of one [victim] over the animals.
The Commentary states: For this reason also, it is understood that he is ignorant.
Why? Because it shows an excess of one [victim] beyond the animals, not an excess of two.

How so? By prescribing the rule "that which is the animal sacrifice is to be made for Indra and Agni" within the context of the eleven-day rite (*ekādaśinī*) while it is being performed as part of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), [the text] demonstrates an excess.
In that case, there is indeed an excess; it does not remain as one.
How? There are eleven animals, but twelve days.
By stating that there is an excess of one [day], he implies that these twelve days are passed;
if there were thirteen days, there would be an absence of two, not of one.
Therefore, for this reason as well, it is an auxiliary part of the day (*ahar-aṅga*) and not a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*).
"By the ignorant, the designation of praise is not contradicted, just like a vow.
Commentary: In this sūtra, the refutation of two previous sūtras is stated.
As it was said: "The mind is greater, because of its designation as distinct [from speech]."
And because of familiarity with that mental [self], there is a distinction;
for indeed, the self is not familiarized by the self alone.
To this, it is replied:
This is not contradictory;
for it is observed that praise of a whole may be expressed through its part,
as in the case of the *mahāvrata* rite being praised as the *dharma* of the *saṃvatsara-sattra*.

"Those who enter upon the year-long rite depart from the union; by performing the union within the sacrificial altar, they do not depart from that very union. Having thus stated this comparison regarding the whole, [the author], desiring to grasp the group of ritual characteristics belonging to the Mahāvrata—which is a constituent part of that whole—praises it by means of the characteristic of a part of the whole, just as one might say, "Devadatta has long, beautiful hair."

Therefore, here too, there is no fault in the view that the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) will be the final form (saṃsthā); its lack of a dental [suffix] is due to a specific scriptural injunction. The Commentary states: As for what was said—that if this were a different day-sacrifice, then the existence of the Mānasa cup would appropriately constitute a distinction from the characteristics of the twelve-day sacrifice, but not if it were a subordinate part (aṅga) of it.
"The conclusion should be at the Patnīsaṃyājas. To this we reply:
"The conclusion shall occur at that point because of the scriptural injunction."

In general, for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), the conclusion at the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is common; however, specifically regarding the tenth day, the conclusion at the *mānasa* [offering] is stated: "Having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, the wise ones go out and proceed to the *mānasa*.
There is no overburdening of the scriptural injunction.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Consequently, the *mānasa* cup on the tenth day is not independent.

Regarding the consumption of *soma* and *madhu*: although both the *sattra* and the *dvādaśāha* involve this, the *mānasa* cup does not possess the character of the *dvādaśāha*; thus, its distinctness is established.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: regarding the *mānasa* (mental cup) in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *daśarātra*, there is its non-application according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, it is applied because it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*). Vi— "Is the *mānasa* a part of the dharma on the tenth day?"
Indeed, by the statement beginning with "bhinnaṃ khalu," it follows that a constituent part (*aṅga*) would be [defined] by its qualifiers (*viśeṣya*) and so forth.

The Bhaṭṭas [state]: In the context of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), on the tenth day, it is heard in scripture: "He takes the mental cup (*mānasa-graha*) dedicated to Prajāpati. For in that case, there is an injunction for a different sacrificial procedure (*sutyā*).

In considering whether this is an injunction for a separate extraction (*graha*) by virtue of being a tenth *suyāja*, they hold that it is an injunction for another day (*aharantara*), because of the mention of a distinction in the text, "Speech is the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*); the mind is the *mānasa*," and because of the inference of a distinction from the statement regarding the nourishment of the twelve-day sacrifice by the *mānasa*: "The meters of the twelve-day sacrifice are indeed separated and devoid of essence; they nourish them with the *mānasa*. As for the word "twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāha*), it is either unetymological or conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) in the sense of a specific delimitation. This being the prima facie view, [the siddhāntin replies: the mention of a distinction is also possible through the distinction between parts and the whole.

Since there is no evidence for this [text] prescribing a different sacrifice as the one that prescribes the drawing [of the cup], and since there is no evidence for assuming that the term *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day rite) has a conventional meaning [apart from the sacrifice itself], there is a prescription for a different drawing of the cup in that very context.

For this very reason, the indicative marks found on the tenth day—such as "They proceed to the *mānasa* [cup]" and "The *mānasa* is indeed the release (*visarga*) of the tenth day"—are appropriately explained. *Visarga* means the end.

Furthermore, having prescribed the set of eleven animals (*paśvekādaśinī*), the text shows the surplus of only one animal by stating: "Now, whichever animal is left over, that should be made for Indra and Agni," and not the surplus of two.
As for the statement that all [days] end with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, [it refers to] the day known as the *mānasa*... [3145] ...the garland.

Regarding the statement, "Having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, they proceed with the *mānasa* [cup]," the notion that the *mānasa* cup is excluded from that [sequence] is refuted; for since the rule ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* is a general injunction, it is logically established that its scope extends to all offerings except the *dadhnāhoma*.

Therefore, when the ten-day rite (*daśarātra*) is being performed in its modified forms (*vikṛti*), the *mānasa-graha* also applies by virtue of being part of the tenth day; however, if it were considered a separate day, it would be set aside. This constitutes the connection to the chapter. Maṇḍana says: "The *mānasa* is not distinct from the day."
Śaṅkara: "There is nothing else that could be mental.
[The rule for the deity is based on the verbal form] in the final fore-offering (*prayāja*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
*Mīmāṃsā-darśana* 10.1.7.14. The rule for the deity in the fore-offerings is based on the verbal form.
The words *samit* and so forth, however, are names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*).
Bhāṣya 9.2.1.59–60. There is a scriptural injunction regarding the restriction of substances (*dravyaniyamavidhi*) [in the case of] the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*āgneyī-paśu*).
6.8.1.13. There is a scriptural injunction regarding the deity (*devatā*) in the *āghāra* libation: "With the mantra 'Indra, stand upright, O sacrifice,' he performs the *āghāra* libation."

The postulation of a deity based on the words of the mantra occurs in the case of the *ādhāra* (supporting oblations) and others because they consist of action, and because of the application of the mantra by virtue of a direct scriptural injunction (*vacana-viniyoga*) when there is a requirement for a mantra.
According to the principle of the "mother of all" (*sarvajananyāya*), this constitutes an injunction regarding the deity.
Vārttika 4.4.6, p. 341. Rather than postulating a deity from the words of the mantra, it is better that [the mantra] serves as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).

The principle of the monthly Agnihotra (māsāgnihotranyāya):

It has been stated as "the principle of the monthly Agnihotra"; if that [term] were perceived [as referring to the same rite], then upon hearing the word "Agnihotra" in another context, there would be an extension (pradeśa) of the properties being enjoined.
Vi— "One offers the Agnihotra for a month"—this name [is applied] to the Agnihotra.
It is not an extended application (*atideśa*) of the ritual rules (*dharma*) from the obligatory (*nitya*) Agnihotra to this [monthly] one;
nor is it an extended application, because the two names are identical.

Since the *agnihotra* mentioned in the phrase "first, the *agnihotra*" has already been established as being obligatory (*nitya*), its primary sense applies there; however, for the sake of establishing its figurative application elsewhere,
the ritual characteristics (*dharma*) of the obligatory *agnihotra* are extended here by means of that name.
Bhaṭṭa: Now, the extension of names (*nāmātideśa*) is introduced.

In cases such as "He performs the *māsa-agnihotra*," the name—which denotes the occasional *agnihotra*—does not, first of all, denote a different ritual action, because that would entail the postulation of multiple denotative powers (*anekaśaktikalpanā*). Furthermore, since there is no indicative mark (*liṅga*) from the injunction (*codanā*) such as the nature of a *dadhi-homa*, there is no extension of the name; and in the absence of such extension, there is no evidence for identity, which would render the application of that [occasional] rule inappropriate.

Nor can there be a connection [of the word *agni*] with another substratum on the grounds that it is already established by the rule "one offers in the Āhavanīya," for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakti*). Furthermore, to assume a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) or the like would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*),
and it would also be inconsistent with the fact that the word is heard in the locative case with an udātta accent on its final syllable.
Furthermore, this is untenable because the *saptamī-tatpuruṣa* compound is not included in the *śauṇḍādi* group [of words that allow such a formation].

If, however, one were to accept the genitive sense as denoting the locus—based on the etymological derivation *agni-hotram* meaning "the offering (*hotra*) into the fire (*agni*)"—as in the case of the obligatory *agnihotra*, and thereby apply this etymological connection (*yoga*) even to the monthly *māsāgnihotra*, even then, since the term *agnihotra* is used for the obligatory rite through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) due to its frequent usage, and since that [indication] functions as a primary power (*śakti*), it is necessary to admit a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) when it is applied to the monthly *agnihotra*, as that [primary power] cannot possibly apply there.
In this very manner, the justification for the figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) in passages such as "I sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" should be understood.
Otherwise, since the time of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) would already be established by the injunction "He who, having sacrificed...
and so forth, there would be no difference between the two cases regarding their being based on secondary indication (*lākṣaṇikatva*).

Even if the time for *dadhī* (curd) has arrived, since there is a rule that [a term] must be primary in one instance and secondary in the other, a well-established conventional (*nirūḍha*) indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is indeed necessary in cases such as the *darśa* sacrifice.

For, while the acquisition of the ritual form is possible through the extension (*atideśa*) based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the Soma-related injunction (*saumika-codanā*), its absence would render it ineffective here.

By this, the view that—even in the absence of secondary usage—the acquisition of the *agnihotra* properties occurs solely through the extension based on the indicative mark of the injunction due to the association with a single name, is refuted.

Since there is no evidence for a conventional (nirūḍha) secondary sense (lakṣaṇā) in both cases, the assumption of a single name is not established. Furthermore, even so, since it is possible [to explain the term] as enjoining a quality such as the deity or the time, there is no evidence for a figurative (gauṇa) sense; this has been stated in the *Kaustubha* on that specific section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Because a compound is impossible according to the rule [of grammar], the injunction regarding the deity is untenable; and since time is already established, an injunction [regarding it] is likewise untenable.
Therefore, words such as "agnihotra" and others are used figuratively for different rituals.

In this regard, it might initially appear that the secondary (gauṇī) application [of the term] refers to a different ritual action, preceded by the characteristics of the nature of the object denoted by the word.

However, according to the Kaustubha as stated in the *Tatsiddhi-sūtra*, because the function of the secondary sense is to denote the result, it is possible to say that there is indeed a comprehension of a different ritual action qualified by the properties of the Agnihotra through the word itself.

In that case, although secondary application is impossible due to non-difference from what is established by other means of knowledge—as in the case of "Devadatta is a lion"—the status of being secondary is nonetheless justified here by the similarity between the goal [to be accomplished] and the prescription of a different ritual action qualified by its specific properties within this very sentence.

Thus, the extension by name (nāmātideśa) is established. Furthermore, even in the case of the extension of the ritual element (padārthātideśa), since only that whose form has been determined is extended, the establishment of modification (ūha) and annulment (bādha) follows. Maṇḍana [states]: "In the extension of properties, the word *agnihotra* [is used]."
Śaṅkara: "And from this [it follows] the extension of the name.
This is the principle of the Māsāgnihotra.
(The two sections at 2.3.1.24 and 7.3.1.1–4 are both well known by way of the principle of the Māsāgnihotra.)"

In this regard, an analysis of the distinction between rituals is to be made under [PMS] 2.3.1–24, and an analysis of extended application (*atideśa*) under 7.3.1–4; thus, the discernment should be carried out according to the context. Regarding the statement, "Having sacrificed with the *Vājapeya*, one should sacrifice with the *Bṛhaspatisava*," if the *Bṛhaspatisava* were a subordinate part (*aṅga*), then because it would lack the established status of being a *Bṛhaspatisava* as a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*), the use of that specific term [*Bṛhaspatisavena*] would be untenable.
If this is argued, it is not so; for [the passage] serves to extend those characteristics by means of the principle of the "Monthly Agnihotra" (māsāgnihotranyāya).

Nor can there be a distinct ritual action here on the basis of the previously mentioned principle regarding the monthly *agnihotra* (2.3.1.24), as in the case of the injunction: "One desiring splendor should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni" (*āgneyamaṣṭākapālaṃ nirvapet rukmakāmaḥ*). Here, however, since the text is not studied after beginning [another], there is no change of context at all; how then could there be a change of context?

In the case of the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice, although the scriptural injunction regarding the occasion (nimitta) would imply that the Sātyayajña should take place, it is set aside by the requirements of food, movement, and other such factors. Consequently, according to the principle of the Jāteṣṭi and the Māsāgnihotra, even if the Paurṇamāsī and other rites are favored, there arises the undesirable consequence of having to perform the Sātyayajña again and again, as it cannot be entirely superseded. (Kau. 2.3.1.9).

By employing the word *avabhṛtha*—which denotes a ritual act belonging to the Soma sacrifice—within the context of the *varaṇaprayā* [the preliminary offerings], the scripture states: "They go to the *avabhṛtha* with the scrapings of the *vāruṇī* and the husks. Following the principle of the *māsāgnihotra*, this prescribes a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) associated with the properties of that [Soma] sacrifice, thereby enjoining the extension (*atideśa*) of Soma-ritual characteristics.
(Vi. 7.3.4). This refers to the *māsāgnihotra*.
The monthly Agnihotra; the monthly Agnihotra; the investigation into the difference or non-difference of the monthly Darśapūrṇamāsa rites.

Now, regarding the statement "He performs the Agnihotra for a month," it is considered whether this constitutes a distinct ritual act or whether it is a modification of the regular (naiyamika) Agnihotra.

In this regard, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is as follows: "The principle established in such cases as 'He offers three oblations' is that where two mutually contradictory qualities are mentioned in the originative injunction of a rite—such as the distinctions of *medas* and so forth—and the rite is otherwise untenable without assuming one or the other, then only a difference in the rite (*bheda*) is assumed, not a repetition (*āvṛtti*).

And in the sentence concerning the monthly *Agnihotra*, by means of the transfer of name (*nāmātideśa*), there exist two mutually contradictory times, evening and morning, which are contained within the originative injunction of the rite.

By this, a split of the ritual action (*karmabheda*) alone is implied, just as in the case of "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*yad āgneyo’ṣṭākapālaḥ*), where [the action is repeated] due to the two times, namely the full moon and the new moon.
To this it is replied:

because the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅgatva*) is established through the extension of the name (*nāmātideśa*), there is no contradiction; thus, repetition is indeed obtained even for the two times.

Furthermore, because repetition is already established by the very act of undertaking [the ritual], there is no implication of a difference in the action (*karmabheda*) due to the occurrence of two different times.

However, in such cases as "He offers three oblations," repetition is not established by any word; rather, it is only there that the number three is applicable. Therefore, for that number to be applicable, a difference in the action itself must be implied. This is likewise the case with the *Āgneya* injunction; thus, there is a disparity between these two examples.

Now, this is considered: regarding the injunction "One should sacrifice for a month with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]," there is no dispute that, just as in the case of "He sacrifices the two Ājyabhāgas," two distinct acts are enjoined by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) due to the number two.

Likewise, it is also undisputed that by each of the two terms—*darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*—the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) associated with the three original constituent rites, such as the Āgneya, is extended (*atidiśyate*) to each respective act.

Now, it must be considered whether the triad of *itikartavyatā* (procedural details) consisting of substances, deities, and so forth—which are mutually contradictory—is implied by the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) as a distinction for each individual rite, or not.

Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: even if there is no such thing here as the assumption of repetition—as in the case of "He performs the Agnihotra for a month"—nevertheless, because the non-aggregation of *itikartavyatā* and other elements was refuted in the section on the extension of ritual procedure (*vidhyanta-adhikaraṇa*, 7.4.2), just as in the case of the *saurya* sacrifice, where despite the difference from the original *āgneya* rite, there is an extended application (*atideśa*) of the respective *itikartavyatā*s of the *paurṇamāsa* and *amāvāsyā* sacrifices by way of option (*vikalpa*).

In the same way here as well, since there is no factor of exclusion (*vinigamaka*), three sets of procedures (*itikartavyatā*)—those connected with the triad beginning with the *Āgneya* sacrifice—are extended by means of the words "Darśa" and "Pūrṇamāsa" respectively. These are placed optionally within a single ritual action; thus, there is not a sixfold division of the ritual, but rather a twofold one.
To this, we reply:

Thus, even the doubt regarding the alternative performance of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is dispelled; nevertheless, in the case of the injunction "for a month, [one should sacrifice] with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*māsaṃ darśapūrṇamāsābhyām*), because each single term—namely *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*—functions as an indicator (*lakṣaṇā*), and because of the employment of these singular terms, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*). Consequently, due to being sealed by the seal of the *Āgneya* injunction, there are six constituent acts (*ṣaṭkarmāṇi*). In the case of the *Saurya* sacrifice, however, there is no direct employment of a single term for the two archetypal (*prākṛta*) procedures of the *Āgneya*, whereby a conjunction could occur and, by that definition, a difference in ritual acts (*karmabheda*) would arise. Rather, in that case, a verbal construction is inferred on account of the requirement for a single procedure; and since that requirement is satisfied by a single procedure alone, such an indicative word is inferred, as in: "like the *Paurṇamāsa-Āgneya*," or "like the *Daśamiya*."

Thus, because the word of extension (*atideśaka*) is construed as being joined with the particle *vā*, there is no combination (*samuccaya*) of the two archetypal (*prākṛta*) procedures (*itikartavyatā*), nor does it result in a distinction of rites (*karmabheda*) characterized by that [combination]; this is the point of difference.

Now, one might object: "In this case, just as the three sets of procedures related to the three rites are extended by implication (*lakṣaṇayā*) through the words *pūrṇamāsa* or *darśa*, and since the procedures belonging to each respective triad are grasped through the employment of each single term, a combination is understood and thus there are six rites."

Thus, along with the *sānnāyya* sacrifice, even the optional *aindrāgna* sacrifice—including its material, deity, and procedure—is included by the term "Darśa" through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its archetypal nature and because it is mentioned by the same word. Therefore, the seventh rite is also enjoined by the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves; thus, the claim of ritualists that only six rites are to be performed is indeed to be reconsidered.
For although the *aindrāgna* is optional in the archetype, here its procedure is also enjoined as a collective whole through its inclusion by the same word.

In this regard, however, there is this distinction: in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the offering to Indra and Agni (*aindrāgna*) occurs prior to the Soma; here, however, even though it is [performed] before that, because the Soma is the primary element of the sacrificial session (*satra*), it takes precedence according to the principle of "conflict between a subordinate and its quality" (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*, 12.2.1.25). But if they were of equal status (*samaprādhānya*), it would be due to the Soma being prior, according to the principle that "the majority shall have the common character" (*bhūyasāṃ syāt sadharmatvam*, 12.2.1.22). It is true that the seventh ritual action is established as a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *aindrāgna*; yet, if it were performed as a permanent rule (*nityavat*), the term *darśa* would be extended by analogy, and it would remain in the state of the archetype.

And likewise, in the eleventh [book] (1.1.2; 15.16–65), regarding the statement "They perform the *avabhṛtha* with the dregs of the *vāruṇī* and the husks," it is stated that there is no extension (*atideśa*) from the context because it would result in the contradiction of the *avabhṛtha*—which is an auxiliary act (*guṇakarma*)—becoming a primary act (*arthakarma*).
Therefore, the performance of the six rites by the ritualists (*yājñika*) is indeed proper.

Now, one might object: let there be a sublation of the extended application (*atideśa*) by the word "according to the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*), which indicates their combination (*samuccaya*); but this is not so.
For by means of two original natures (*prakṛti*), the principal constituent (*pradhānāṅga*) is indeed heard; however, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)— such as the *māsāgnihotra*—
is mutually purposeless.

Regarding the *yāma* [offering]: there, by the principle of the conflict between the primary and the subordinate (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*), even the combination (*samuccaya*) prescribed by direct injunction (*aupadeśika*) is set aside by the optional alternative (*vikalpa*) derived through extension (*ātideśika*). Thus, it is established that the performance is exactly as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

In this context, it will be stated that because the sequence of the *ājyabhāga* offerings is not known, the *vārtraghnī*, *dhruva*, and *ājya* mantras are subordinate to them. Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 722: "And because there is no mutual connection of purpose."

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "The *vārtraghnī* verses are recited at the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), and the *vṛdhanvatī* verses at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). In considering whether this set of four *anuvākyā* verses belongs to the primary sacrifice or to the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The meaning is that they belong to both together, mutually combined.

There is no connection with a purpose—that is, with the objective—regarding the two *vārtraghna* invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) of the full-moon ritual and the two *vṛdhanvatī* verses of the new-moon ritual. There is no utility whatsoever for them in the primary sacrifice. "Connection with a purpose" (*arthasaṃbandha*) means a relation to an objective; "non-connection with a purpose" (*anarthasaṃbandha*) means the absence of such a relation to an objective.
Therefore:
"Agni, strike down the Vṛtras"—this is a *vārtraghni* verse addressed to Agni; "Thou, O Soma, art the lord of beings"—this is a *vārtraghni* verse addressed to Soma.
"Agni by his ancient birth"—this is a *vṛdhanvatī* verse addressed to Agni; "Having impelled Soma, we"—this is a *vṛdhanvatī* verse addressed to Soma.
Because there is no *soma* at all on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), and because there is absolutely no *soma* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*),
there is no purpose for the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) prescribed for the principal offerings.
As for the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*), their utility is minimal.
Thus, there would be an application of the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) to the two *ājyabhāga* offerings; this would result in mutual inconsistency.
This would result in mutual inconsistency.

The established conclusion (siddhānta) is as follows: There is no mutual relationship of purpose—meaning a relationship between the primary act and the invitatory verses (anuvākyās)—because such a relationship would result in the application of [the verses] based on indicative power (liṅga) and other such factors; this is the superior meaning of the sūtra as stated in the Kaustubha:
"And because there is no mutual relationship of purpose."

In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "The two *vārtraghnī* verses are recited at the Full Moon sacrifice; the two *vṛdhanvatī* verses at the New Moon sacrifice.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the pair of *anuvākyā* verses to be applied to the principal sacrifice (*pradhāna*), or to the two *ājyabhāga* offerings?

Having concluded the discussion on the application [of mantras] based on the principle of "uselessness otherwise" (*ānarthakya*) and their inclusion in subsidiaries (*tadaṅga-prasaṅga*), we shall now, by way of a further incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), establish the proper arrangement according to the principle of "uselessness otherwise" and its distinction from that [subsidiary inclusion] (*ānarthakya-tadanvaya-vaidharmya*).
In this regard, the intention of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is as follows:

although the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* are primarily denotative of time, nevertheless, because it is impossible for the pair of invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*), which reveal the deity, to have time as their purpose, they must—by their very nature and due to their connection with sacrifice—refer to the sacrifice itself through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In that case, do these two mantras refer to the *ājyabhāga* offerings in accordance with the sequence (*krama*), or do they refer to the primary sacrifices in accordance with the context (*prakaraṇa*)?

In that case, because the context (*prakaraṇa*) is more powerful, the connection of the two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) with the recitation (*vācana*) according to their sequence is established by the sentence (*vākya*) contained within that context. As it has been said: "In that instance, there is a connection between the *anuvākyās* and the singing (*gāna*) itself; not with the two times."
"Therefore, sequence [establishes] the status of being a subordinate part of the primary," so it is said (Vārttika, p.

739). Furthermore, just as the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are for the sake of the primary through the context (*prakaraṇa*), so too is the pair of invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) [for the sake of the primary].
For this reason also, because these two serve the purpose of the primary [rite], there is no mutual connection between them.
As it has been said: "And by this reason also—that qualities exist for the sake of another—the four *anuvākyā* verses are not connected with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings."

Thus (Vārttika, p. 739). Therefore, setting aside the sequence of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, it follows by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*) that the *anuvākyās* serve the purpose of the principal sacrifice (*pradhāna*) alone.
This being the position reached, it is replied as follows.
This would indeed be so if the two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) were directly connected in meaning to the principal ritual act.
For instance, one invitatory verse is dedicated to Agni (*āgneyī*), while the other is dedicated to Soma (*saumī*).
Even in the procedure for the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī-karman*), in the offering to Agni-Soma (*agnīṣomīya*), Soma accompanied by Agni constitutes the deity.

The manifestation of Soma alone is not possible by means of the *mahendrādhikaraṇa* principle. Nor should it be argued that the manifestation of Agni and Soma occurs through the two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) themselves; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting the singularity intended for the invitatory verses in a single ritual action, as expressed in the injunction "he recites the invitatory verses."
Nor is duality also enjoined by this very sentence,
because that would result in a syntactical split (vākyabheda) due to enjoining both duality and a specific mantra with respect to a rite already established.
However, in the case of "he recites the *puro'nuvākyā*," since many *puro'nuvākyās* are obtained through their sequential order, it is logical that only singularity is being enjoined.

But here, even if one intends to specify a particular mantra, there would indeed be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); since it is possible to explain [the mention of the mantras] as referring to a specific time, why resort to a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*) by assuming they refer to something else? Nor should it be argued that because it is impossible for the mantra to have time as its purpose, the words "Full Moon" (*paurṇamāsī*) and "New Moon" (*amāvāsyā*) indicate the ritual acts themselves; for the statement of the sentence is justified as being for the sake of establishing a restriction (*vyavasthā*). Even so, two pairs of invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) are prescribed for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, just like the statements regarding optional desires (*kāma*).
Regarding the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, Agni is the deity of the first and Soma of the second.
Thus, by means of both sequence (*krama*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is understood that there are two pairs of invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) intended for the *ājyabhāgas*.

And since the two *ājyabhāgas* are subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) to the primary sacrifices, they must be performed repeatedly according to the principle of repetition for each primary act, within the two composite groups of the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices as determined by their respective sequences.
In that context, the rule regarding the clarified butter (*ājya*) is stated for the purpose of establishing the application of the mantras:

"The two *ājyabhāga* offerings at the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) are to be performed with the *vṛdhanvat* mantras; the two *ājyabhāga* offerings at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) are to be performed with the *vṛdhanvat* mantras. This has been explained in detail precisely in the section concerning the full moon (*paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*).

Therefore, since the sentence is logically consistent by taking the primary time as its purpose, it is not appropriate to assume that the two principal acts (pradhānakarma) are intended through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) by overriding the indicative mark (liṅga) and the order (krama).
Consequently, it is established that the pair of invitatory formulas (anuvākyā) is to be inserted into the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) alone.
The practical application (prayojana) is as stated in the respective positions.

The Sūtra, however, states that there is "mutual lack of connection with the purpose" (*mithaścānarthasaṃbandhaḥ*) because the subordinate elements (*anuvākya*s) and the primary sacrifice, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), do not have a relationship of mutual dependence; that is to say, there is no connection of purpose between them.
(Tautātita). Now, if someone were to say, "Agni will be the deity," he should be told: "There is a mutual lack of connection with the purpose.

The justification for that has been set forth by Śubhramata as follows:

the author of the *Sūtras* composed the aphorisms—“For the primary [agent] is [denoted] in the primary sense, because of its absence,” “If it is argued that it occurs even when [the agent is] engaged,” and “No, because of meaninglessness”—in order to refute the preceding prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) and to demonstrate three types of established conclusions (*siddhānta*). Consequently, these have been explained separately by the commentators (*bhāṣyakāras*) as demonstrating distinct topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*).

In that regard, the first sūtra demonstrates the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that when one has begun to employ a substitute because the primary material was unavailable, if the primary material becomes available in the interim, then the primary material itself must be employed.

However, the second sūtra establishes the conclusion that when some preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) have already been performed after employing a substitute, even if the primary material subsequently becomes available, the primary material itself must be used; the prepared substitute is not to be employed.

In the third sutra, however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that once the consecratory acts (*saṃskāra*) have been performed upon a substitute, even if the primary substance is subsequently obtained, the primary substance is not to be adopted; rather, the substitute alone is to be used.
Furthermore, in all such cases, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is to be understood as being outside the sutra itself.
Alternatively, the sutra "If it be argued that [the rite] has already commenced" (*pravṛtte 'pīti cet*) is itself the sutra stating the prima facie argument.

Then, since the purpose has already been accomplished, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the Vedic text itself must be brought forward; this is answered by the sūtra, "Not so, because it would be meaningless" (nānarthakatvāt). In that context, that which is separated by a single moment is sublated by the statement of simultaneity (*sahavacana*), which was required [for the other]. Bhaṭṭa [states]: "The sequence of the primary (mukhyakrama) is also an authority for determining the sequence of subsidiaries. And 'primacy' (mukhyatva) means being principal (pradhānatva)."

For where there is a requirement for several principal acts along with their subsidiaries to be performed together, although the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*) establishes the concomitance (*sāhitya*) of the subsidiary and the principal, one may still accept as many intervening intervals as are permitted in order to comply with the concomitance required by other principal acts; yet, since there is no authority for exceeding that limit, the sequence is determined by the primary order (*mukhyakrama*) in order to maintain proximity (*pratyāsatti*) to the principal act.

Therefore, the distinction between these two is as follows: in the case of *pravṛtti* (the order of performance), the basis for determining proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is that which is defined by the subsidiary (*aṅga*), whereas in the case of *mukhyakrama* (the order of the principal), the basis for determining proximity is that which is defined by the principal (*pradhāna*). It will be stated later that their relative strength or weakness is determined by the reverse of this [preceding rule].

An example of *mukhyakrama* is the sequence of the three oblations in the *Citrā* sacrifice, which follows the order of the principals as prescribed by the sentence: "The two [deities] belong to Sarasvatī; for Sarasvatī and Sarasvant constitute a divine pair."

For here, although there is no co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two substances, since it is possible for the word denoting the general class (*saṃgraha-sāmānya*), namely "divine" (*daivya*), to refer to a deity based on the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), two sacrifices with deities [Sarasvatī and Sarasvant] are enjoined by the dual ending.
Therefore, it is not the case that Sarasvant alone is the deity in both sacrifices;
rather, because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) functions to indicate a *virūpaikaśeṣa* (a single remainder of dissimilar forms), it is understood that the deities are Sarasvatī and Sarasvant.

Nor should it be argued that, even on this view, each [offering] might individually have Sarasvatī as its deity based on the etymology "Sarasvatī and Sarasvant are both Sarasvatī" (i.e., those two whose deities are Sarasvatī); for when the *anuvākyā* verses are recited for each individual deity, it is understood that each has only one deity.

Therefore, since there is no established deity for the *prājāpatya* offerings, and since the order of the principal acts follows the order of the mantras' recitation, the sequence of their preparation (*nirvāpa*) is determined precisely by the order of the principal deities.

In reality, however—by the same principle, it has been stated that the performance of the subsequent constituent element (padārtha) also determines the sequence for the preceding constituent element; and since in the present case, the performance of the subsequent elements such as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses is compatible with the sequence of the *nirvāpa* (offering), this is not a primary example of the order of principal acts (*mukhyakrama*). Nevertheless, the ritual details (*dharma*) such as bringing the sacrificial shed are prescribed before the curd, whereas those such as the *nirvāpa* of the *āgneya* offering are prescribed afterwards; conversely, the recitation of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses occurs in the opposite order.
