The Analogy of Extracting a Soft Reed from its Sheath:

Just as a soft reed situated within the sheath of grass or other stalks is extracted by separating it from the primary qualities of the external covering, so too the Self—when distinguished from the threefold body through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—becomes the Supreme Brahman itself, because the characteristic of being of the nature of consciousness and bliss (*cid-ānanda-rūpatva*) is common to both.

And it is said in the *Pañcadaśī*: "Just as a cotton-seed is extracted from its husk and so forth, so too the Self, when separated from the three bodies and the like through reasoning, becomes the Supreme Brahman itself."
[This is] the Sāhasrī [section]. 22.
Beans (*māṣa*), chickpeas (*caṇaka*), and *kodrava* grains are not substitutes for *sūda* (rice/food).
This is because of the scriptural statement: "Beans, chickpeas, and *kodrava* grains are indeed unfit for sacrifice."

Murārimiśra states that after the cognition of a jar, there arises a subsequent reflective awareness (*anusavāya*) such as "I know the jar"; by this, he asserts that there is the apprehension of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) having "jar-ness" as its qualifier, while that which possesses "jar-ness" is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
(Maṇi, p. 18)
Having testicles is a quality of males.
By this, he shows the suffering of males [in the state of being plants]: "They have testicles because they possess sense organs," Bhāṣya 4.1.1.
In the case of the *muṣṭikapāla* and other rites, there is performance by groups (*anusamaya*) through the aggregate of actions such as the pouring out of four handfuls;
this is the principle of performance by groups (*samudāyānusamayanyāya*). (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 316)

Regarding the *muṣṭikapāla* (the handful of sacrificial vessels), because of the omission of the handful: "Oṃ; [the ritual is performed] with a single [mantra] for the placing of the *muṣṭikapāla*, the under-pads, the taking up, the anointing, the sprinkling, and the purification."
This is the sūtra of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position.

Regarding the Full Moon sacrifice (pūrṇamāseṣṭi), the pouring out (nirvāpa) of rice for the sake of the *āgneya* and *āmīṣomīya* sacrificial cakes is prescribed by the rule: "He pours out four handfuls. In that context, having poured out one handful for the sake of the *āgneya*, one handful must be poured out for the sake of the *āmīṣomīya*.
Therefore, the accusative case is used for both purposes, and so forth.
Thus, regarding the four handfuls, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the sequential performance (*anusamaya*) should be carried out one handful at a time.

Similarly, in the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāseṣṭi*), eight potsherds (*kapāla*) are placed for the purpose of baking the cake (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni, whereas eleven potsherds are used for that dedicated to Agni and Soma.
In that case as well, having placed one potsherd for the sake of the offering to Agni, one should place one potsherd for the sake of the offering to Agni and Soma;
thereafter, the second and subsequent ones are for the sake of both.
However, the ninth and following potsherds for the sake of the offering to Agni and Soma should be placed with an intervening space [between them]; such is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
Likewise, having taken one portion (avadāna) from the cake (puroḍāśa) dedicated to Agni, one portion from that dedicated to Agni and Soma should be taken;
then, a second portion from both—this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
Similarly, regarding the consecration (dīkṣā) in the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is stated that the anointing of the sacrificer's eyes occurs "three times" (trir āṅkte).
In that regard, having applied collyrium to the right eye once, one should apply collyrium to the left eye once;
thereafter, both eyes should be treated a second time, and likewise both eyes a third time with collyrium.

Similarly, when there are many sacrificers at the beginning of a sacrificial session (*sattra*), after performing the anointing of all limbs with fresh butter for one sacrificer, then for the second sacrificer, then for the third, and so forth—the procedure follows a sequential order (*anusamaya*) by treating each one individually.
Likewise, regarding the shaving of the sacrificer at the beginning of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice, it is stated: "He shaves three times in each direction.

In that context, the shaving of the head is performed once in the eastern part, then once in the southern part, and so on; in this manner, the number three must be accomplished for all four directions.

Likewise, at the beginning of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [the priest] purifies [the sacrificer] with seven stalks of *piñjūla* grass: first, with the mantra "May Citpati purify you," from above the throat; then, with "May Vākpati purify you," starting from the throat down to the navel; and finally, with "May the god Savitṛ purify you," starting from the navel down to the feet.

Regarding this *pāvana* [purification] at the beginning of the *sattra* sacrifice, when there are multiple sacrificers (*yajamāna*), some maintain that the sequence must be performed one by one for each individual: first above the necks of all the sacrificers, then below the necks of all the sacrificers, and finally below the navels of all the sacrificers. Likewise, in the case of the handfuls of grain, the placing of the potsherds (*kapāla*), the portions of the offering (*avadāna*), the ointments (*añjana*), the unguents (*abhyañjana*), the shavings (*vapana*), and the purifications (*pāvana*), the sequence must be performed one by one for each individual; such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
The word "ca" (and) serves as an illustration for the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, such as the *upākaraṇa* and other rites.
Just as the ritual duties beginning with the *upākaraṇa* apply to each individual animal, so it is with the handfuls of grain and the rest.
However, all [the acts] constitute a single performance because they share a common purpose and possess those same qualities.
This is the sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhānta).
The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
All [the rites] indeed must be performed in succession, and not just one by one.

Because each of the four handfuls, the vessel beginning with the *kapāla*, the sacrificial portion (*avadāna*), the ointment substance, the single unguent, the shaving, and the purification with twenty-one blades of *darbha* grass has a single purpose—namely, because it possesses a single transcendental result (*apūrva*)—there is a single conceptualization (*ekabhāvanā*) due to their being subordinate to that [single result].
This remains the same meaning even if the reading is *ekaikam*.
Or, in the phrase "of these" (*eṣām eteṣām*), it is because of the singleness of the state [of the four handfuls] through their being qualities thereof.
The same principle should be applied to the placing of the potsherds (*kapāla-upadhāna*) and so forth.

Therefore, there is no sequential performance (*anusamaya*) by means of a single handful, a single placing of potsherds, a single portioning (*avadāna*), a single application of collyrium (*añjana*), a single application of ointment (*abhyañjana*), or a single purifying act (*pāvana*). Rather, the sequential performance must be carried out by means of four handfuls and so on.
And thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) here is that there is a collective performance (*samudāyānusamaya*).
Ke.: In the *nirvāpa* (offering) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the four handfuls constitute a single ritual act (*padārtha*). Vi.
5.2.3: The measure of the handfuls in the *nirvāpa* belongs to both [the New and Full Moon sacrifices] together.
*Saṃkarṣa.* 1.4.12. See *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 2377, under the entry "The measure of the handful (*muṣṭi*) in the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*).

Due to the omission of the handful, there is an omission of the number [four] in the case of the *caru* of seventeen *droṇas* at the Vājapeya sacrifice; [this is because the number is subordinate to the handful].
10.2.28.65–68. *Oṃ*: But due to the omission of the handful, there should be an omission of the number, since that [number] is its quality.

In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is stated: "He offers four handfuls (*muṣṭi*)," whereby both the handful as the instrument of offering and the number four are prescribed. Now, regarding the *vājapeya*, there is the injunction: "A seventeen-vessel offering of wild rice (*naivāra*) on a skin. Here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) expressed in the Sūtra is that while the omission of the handful should not be made, the omission of the number four should indeed be made.
He negates that position with the word "not" (*na*).
The omission of the handful (muṣṭi) should not be performed;
for if the number four were a quality of the handful, such an omission would be possible,
but the number is not a quality of the handful.
Because the number [four] is subordinate to the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*), the two phrases "he pours out four" and "he pours out handfuls" have separate syntactical connections.
Therefore, it is not the number that should be omitted, but rather the handfuls that must be omitted; this is the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

He establishes this very position as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) later on. As for the number, it is a modification of that [original] because of its similarity to the injunction and because of its connection with the subsequent scriptural statement. The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Now the third prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is stated: "There is the omission of both.
It is not merely the omission of the handfuls;
because of the commonality regarding the injunction, the number is a modification of that.
Furthermore, because of the conjunction [of the number seventeen], one should know that the *śarāva* measure of the *naivāra* oblation is a modification of the original number four;
the number seventeen sublates the number four.
Moreover, because of the conjunction—that is, the conjunction with the substance that measures the material—the *śarāva* substance sublates the *muṣṭi* (handful) and is a modification of it.
And thus, the modified number sets aside the original number, and by the modified *śarāva* measures, the original handfuls (*muṣṭi*) are set aside.
Therefore, there is a sublation of the number of handfuls when the handfuls are omitted; this is the third prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
[The Siddhāntin replies: No, because of the connection with the injunction and because of the application of the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is stated: "He pours out four handfuls," whereby both the measure—the handful—and the number are prescribed as the means for the pouring out (*nirvāpa*). Now, in the Vājapeya sacrifice, there is the injunction: "The *naivāra* [grain] is seventeen *śarāva* measures, placed upon a hide. In that case, the omission of both those two—the measure and the number—is obtained [by implication].
This being the case, rather than abandoning the handfuls (*muṣṭi*), it would be better to abandon the number (*saṃkhyā*), because the former is subordinate to the latter.

Thus, the first prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been stated as being foolish due to its abandonment of the handfuls. He refutes that with the word "no" (*na*) and states the second prima facie position itself as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
There is no contradiction of both [the injunction and the perception],
because of the connection with the *codanā*.
By "codanā," we mean the sacrifice.
For the number seventeen and the two *śarāva* measures are connected to the sacrifice;

whereas in the archetype, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the number four and the substance of handfuls are connected to the preparatory act (*saṃskāra*) because of their connection with the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*).

Indeed, that which is performed in place of an element obtained through the *codaka* (extended injunction) by means of a directly heard [textual] statement should be set aside by that very [statement].
In this case, because it accommodates the number four, the omission of the *muṣṭi* (handful) is more logical.
Therefore, the omission of the *muṣṭi* should be performed, but the omission of the number four should not be performed.
If so, how is the ritual to be carried out? It is said:
Having filled a *śarāva* with four *kuḍava*s and so forth, its offering (*nirvāpa*) should be performed; again this [is done], and again in this very same way, until there are seventeen *śarāva*s.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Regarding the statement, "But because of the omission of the handfuls, there should be an omission of the number, since that [number] is subordinate to them" (Ke. 3.1.6.12), it will be explained that in the case of the rule "he offers four handfuls," the number four becomes a qualifier of the handfuls as indicated by the context; therefore, when seventeen-pitcher rice-offerings (*caru*) are involved, the number is maintained so as not to obstruct the primary handfuls. (Kau. 3.1.6.12). The act of clenching the fists (*muṣṭīkaraṇa*) belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

(Vā. 3.1.14.24). The clenching of the fists, expressed by the injunction "he clenches his fists," serves the purpose of the entire context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, and not merely for the purpose of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) or the piercing of the skin (*veda*).
Bhāṣya 3.1.14.24–25: By the act of clenching the fist, restlessness is prevented during the initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

Vi. 3.1.14: The pestle (*musala*) is a sacrificial implement (*yajñāyudha*), as in the statement, "They thresh with the mortar and the pestle. Vi. 3.1.5: In the Rājasūya, during the sacrifice of various grains (*nānāvījeṣṭi*), the pestle is used according to the *tantra* (the common ritual procedure).
The Apūrva (transcendental result) is the prompter of the sprinkling of the pestle. (Bhāṣya 9.1).
The word *musala* is well-known in the sense of a staff (*daṇḍa*).
For example: "How indeed might the boys carrying staffs not descend into the Gaṅgā?
(Bhāṣya 4.2.2).

"A *muhūrta* is the sky-mind, whose fruit is the transcendence of parts, and which consists of the accumulation of descriptions regarding the movements of the sun and other [planets]"; thus say those who maintain that time exists as a substance distinct from action. (Su. pṛ. 170).
"One should instruct a fool using the very language of a fool"—this is a well-known maxim.
This is clear.
The Thousandfold [Verse]. 742.
The Maxim of Serving Fools; 3164. The Maxim of the Deer, the Hunter, and the Wolf;
the Maxim of Serving Fools.
The sense is that its application occurs where the action would otherwise be fruitless. [This refers to] the reckless person. 307.
The root is not the motivator for the cutting of branches, the fetching [of fuel], and the enclosing [of the altar] in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Bhāṭṭa 4.2.3:
The sprinkling of water on the root is a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) for the sacrificial grass (barhis).

In human statements, the establishment of certainty regarding the meaning occurs solely through the door of the foundational source (*mūla*); thus, in the absence of a foundation, even a certainty that has arisen instantaneously dissolves immediately, resulting in a lack of reliability.
Vaidyanātha, 1.2.12, p. 16.
Sublation characterized by the total eradication of the root is called "non-attained sublation" (*aprāptabādha*).
Bāla., p. 13.

[The injunction] "having stripped a branch from its root, he makes an under-layer" (*mūlataḥ śākhāṃ parivāsyopaveṣaṃ karoti*)—this is the applicatory *śruti* (scriptural statement) in the form of the suffix *-ktvā*, which possesses the characteristic of being both prior and subsequent [to the action], according to the opinion of Someśvara.
Bāla, p. 45:
Like the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti), [the sacrifice] is desired for the sake of the Agnihotra and other rites;
Ci. 8.1.3, varṇaka 2.
Bending [the mind] is performed by means of a price;
that becomes much easier with many substances.
(Bhāṣya)

Regarding the phrase *dup-megha*, there are four positions: (1) the use of both [words] without modification; (2) a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) such that the dual ending refers to the two deities and the singular utterance refers to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); (3) both refer to the owners, with the dual referring to them in relation to their husband (*pati*), while the singular refers to them in relation to their common designation (*saṃjñātṛ*); or (4) both refer to the deities, with the singular referring to them in relation to their common designation. Regarding these, he states the fault in the third position in Sūtra 36: "There would be a displacement (*utkarṣa*) in the case of the deity. For whomsoever the word denotes a deity, for him a displacement occurs; since this [singular] ending is singular, it would apply only to animals that have a single deity.
"In that case, it is simply because of the word *pāśyā* [meaning 'cord'] and the word *anya* [meaning 'other'].
(He shows the meaning of *pāśyānya*: "Where the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is the primary factor, there the number (*vacana*) is led as a subordinate factor.
(He states another reason for the displacement: "The status of being a deity belongs to the aggregate (*saṃghāta*), not to the individual parts.")
Alternatively, when there is a connection with the meaning, there may be an application according to the respective number in the case of a dual conjunction.
The Bhāṣya says: "Or rather, it is not so;
for here there is a conjunction of those two—the singular ending and the dual ending."

The singular ending is prescribed for those [texts] where it is handed down as "svāmin" (master), while the dual ending is prescribed for those where it is handed down as "rāma. He will explain that in their case, the deity is dual.
Therefore, in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) involving multiple deities, the dual ending proceeds by way of modification (*ūha*).
When there are many sacrificers, the singular form is employed;

thus, the application will be according to the respective number. However, because the master is one, there would be an elevation [of the singular] regarding the deity; as for the wife, the word "second" (dvitīya) would apply.

The Commentary: The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that [the term] denotes both the owner and the deity. Since there is a dual number and since there is a singular number, it is that very same term "medhapati" which will be the denoter, and it will not denote both the owner and the deity.
[Objection: But surely even a single "lord of the sacrifice" (medhapati) is perceived as two distinct entities; how then can he be said to be non-expressive?
[Reply: It is said:
when [the word] refers to the owners, then the connection is: "O sacrificial doors, bring that which is the cloud for the lord of the sacrifice."

When it refers to the deity, the connection would be: "Lead [the victim] to the lord of the sacrifice; lead the sacrificial doors. This single utterance cannot possibly be connected with both sets of words simultaneously;
for due to the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*), a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would result.
Therefore, it is determined that [the word] denotes the owner (*svāmin*).
Now, for what reason is it not assumed to denote the deity? For if it were so assumed, the singular number would have to be displaced from its context when there is only one deity.
In that case, the *prakaraṇa* (context) would be contradicted.
Furthermore, if the word were interpreted as referring to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), it would not be displaced from the dual number;
in that very context, it would denote the two sacrificers, namely the husband and wife.
Therefore, for the sake of maintaining its connection with the ritual context (*prakaraṇa*), it is interpreted as denoting the owner (*svāmin*).

There will be a modification (*ūha*) for the owner (*svāmin*), but the deity (*devatā*) would be purposeless because it is already attained through the benediction (*āśis*) directed toward that [owner]. The Commentary: the word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position.
It is not a word denoting the owner; rather, it will refer to the deity. Why? Because it is a benediction for that [deity].

In the instruction regarding the oblation for the deity, it says: "Aiming for the victim for the Lord of the Victim (medhapati), bring it near for those two. Thus, it refers to the two Lords of the Victim.
The recitation of blessings directed toward the sacrificer is purposeless, for its purpose is already accomplished.
Since the rain-cloud has already reached the master [the sacrificer], why should it be wished for?
Furthermore, there is no need for a constant connection with the master by means of that [blessing].
For the sacrifice itself does not coalesce [with the animal].
Therefore, the term *medhapati* denotes the deity. [Dūṣaṇa:
But the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is the position that it refers to the deity and so forth.

In the case of the master [as the referent], the meaning of the sentence itself is not even possible, because the word *āśāsāna* would be meaningless. Furthermore, "bring the sacrificial doors (*medhyā duraḥ*) to the victim for the sacrificer, who is the lord of the sacrifice (*yajamānāya medhapataye*). Since it asks "for what purpose?", the sentence-meaning is untenable because it lacks a stated purpose.

And nothing is enjoined with reference to the sacrificial portion (*medha*). Otherwise (in the case of the deity), the meaning of the sentence is appropriately established as: "Bring the sacrificial portions, desiring thus: 'May [the portions] be for the sake of the Lord of the Sacrifice (*medhapati*) so that he may perform the sacrifice. Furthermore, since what belongs to another cannot be performed for the sake of a deity, it follows by implication that this [sacrificial portion] belongs to the sacrificer himself.

And because of its relinquishment through devotion, there would be ownership in that [recipient]. The Commentary states: "Once it has been relinquished by the sacrificer with the thought 'this is not mine,' it is protected as belonging solely to another."
"It is at the proper time that one is connected with the deity.
But what is this connection with the deity? It is that for whose sake the acceptance of this [gift] is relinquished. And that sacrifice has already been performed.
Therefore, in that sacrifice, the substance intended for another does not remain after it has been relinquished.
That which has the self as its primary purpose is "one's own" (*ātmīya*); it is not that toward whom the self has become subordinate.
In such a case, however, the state of being a wife (*patnītva*) exists figuratively (*bhaktyā*).
Therefore, in those two cases alone, there is the status of "cloud" (megha) and "lord of the cloud" (medhapati), as well as "servant" (bhakta) and "master" (svāmin).
Since elevation [of meaning] is impossible when a dual number is joined with a single entity,
that which was stated in the Bhāṣya must be refuted.
"But [the term applies] to one [animal] because of their co-inherence (samavāya), since that is its defining characteristic.
The Commentary states: "Regarding this, it is said:
for those two who are these [animals], the word 'Lord of the Sacrifice' (medhapati) [applies] to the group of them."
And here, he is associated with the deity alone.
In that ritual act, it is said, "Offer the oblation to one group.
Therefore, the word *medhapati*, which denotes a group and ends in the singular number, is not to be extracted [from its compound].
And from that contact, there would be a conceptual construction (vikalpa).
The Commentary states: This is another resolution. That which is in contact is this very deity named [the object].
When two objects are combined, they become a single deity.
If some substance is intended for two [deities], then there are two deities therein;
the two objects, having been joined, have attained oneness.

Therefore, even that which ends in the singular number enters into the context and is optionally combined with the preceding [term], because there is no loss of the quality even in the case of singularity. The Commentary states: "This is a statement regarding the subsequent connection (*anvārabdha*)."
Granted that oneness may not be the meaning here;
nevertheless, the singular ending would still enter into the context,
for the nominal stem (prātipadika) possesses its own inherent meaning.
And the singular number is intended to signify its connection with the initiation ceremony;
or else, singularity is not intended to be expressed.
Therefore, it is not displaced from its context.
It is replied: the case-ending expresses a relation belonging to that which is qualified by oneness.
Even so, the position that [the universal] is non-existent is all the more appropriate;
for everything is indeed connected with oneness.

Now, [the opponent] argues that it establishes a connection and expresses oneness, yet it does not qualify [the object] with it because that [oneness] is not intended to be significant; thus, there will be no contradiction. Or, it might be said: even though the expression of oneness is not intended to be significant, the singular number occurs when there is a connection with oneness and not otherwise; likewise, this oneness will belong to the "Lord of the Sacrifice" (medhapati), and therefore it is merely restated. Consequently, there is no fault.

Śā—The dual number [is used] by virtue of the number of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and the singular number by virtue of the number of the deity; thus, it must be modified according to the specific ritual form (*vikṛti*). Soma—It is stated that even though there is singularity, because the word *medhapati* refers to what is inherent (*samaveta*) [in the two], there is no modification (*anūha*); this is the connection.

In this regard, after first presenting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) in the passage, "The animal is the sacrificial essence (medha), and the sacrificer is the lord of the sacrificial essence; thus he endows the sacrificer himself with his own sacrificial essence" (AitBr. 6.16), it continues: "But on the other hand, they say that the speech of a Vaiśya is to be spoken [thus]: 'The animal is sacrificed for the deity; she herself is the lord of the sacrificial essence.'"

Regarding the statement in the *Tantraratna*: "The status of being the 'Lord of the Sacrifice' (*medhapati*) belongs to the owner, because the sacrifice is connected to all three [the sacrificer, the wife, and the deity]; and since the word 'lord' (*pati*) is used for sovereignty in all cases, and since the singular number is appropriate for all three, there is no modification in any of the ritual variations (*vikṛti*),"—this was stated as a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintya*), on the grounds that the following recitation from the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* does not exist: "If the animal is dedicated to a single deity, he should say 'to the Lord of the Sacrifice'; if it is dedicated to two deities, 'to the Lords of the Sacrifice'; if it is dedicated to many deities, 'to the Lords of the Sacrifice'" (*AitBr.* 6.16–6).
The Vi [rtika] states: "Regarding the two words *medha-pati*, there may be either no modification or a modification.
If it is a modification, does it mean 'lord and deity' (*svāmi-deva*), or is it a single meaning (*ekārtha*) even in the latter case?
Or are there two lords and two deities? Since there is a difference [in these views], the former [position] is correct."
Now, due to the difference [in meaning], there are two meanings here for these two words.
Because of the unity of the mantra, there is one [meaning] here; O Lord, [the distinction arises] from the wife being a second.
From the perspective of the deity, there is one [meaning]; however, regarding the substratum, there are two, as there is a doubling of the movement.

In that very *praiṣa* (the *agnipraiṣa*), it is heard in the scripture: "Bring forward the sacrificial doors, desiring the sacrifice for the Lord of the Sacrifice (*medhapati*). According to some teachers, it is "for the Lord of the Sacrifice, the sacrifice" (*medhapataye megham*).

In this regard, there is no difference in the mantra due to the difference in schools (*śālābheda*); for even with a discrepancy in a single part, the oneness of the mantra is understood through the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), according to the principle established in the section concerning other scriptures (*śāstrāntarādhikaraṇa*, 2.4.28–33).
Consequently, its referent (*artha*) must also be expressed as one only.
Therefore, it is either the sacrificer or the deity who is the "lord of the sacrifice" (*medhapati*), but not both.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault even if both are denoted under the condition of being delimited by that [status], because the delimitor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—namely, the state of being the lord of the sacrifice—is one.

Nevertheless, in this context, it is untenable for the other words to possess the quality of being produced by both [the speaker's] intention and the momentary cognition whose object is the sentence-meaning constituted by their respective referents. To explain: if the passage were intended to refer to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the meaning would be as follows: "O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), becoming pure (*medhyāḥ*), bring forward through the doors—that is, toward the *cātvāla* pit—the cloud which was the means of enjoyment for the husband of the sacrificer; doing so while desiring either your own sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) or the fruit for the sacrificer."

In the case of the deities, the meaning is: "O Doors, bring him toward you, [him] who is becoming fit for sacrifice (*medhya*), aspiring for a husband as his sacrificial portion (*medha*) for the deity.
In every respect, since it is illogical for a single word to produce two distinct cognitions, the denoted object must be of a single form.
Furthermore, there is no rule that a word uttered once can convey two meanings simultaneously.
In the section concerning the master of the clouds (*meghapati-adhikaraṇa*),
the state of being the master of the clouds is indeed a flaw, and its very nature constitutes the reason for its being a defect.
And it should not be argued that this [repetition] does not exist here because there is no single hearing of what has been heard twice due to the difference between the two treatises (*śāstra*);
for even so, by reason of the burden of assuming an indicative mark (*liṅga*), only a single meaning is to be expressed.

Thus, when considering what the purport of this [passage] is here, since it is untenable for the deity to possess ownership— which is synonymous with lordship— by virtue of having a physical body, the purport must be the sacrificer himself.
Nor does the use of the dual number contradict his singularity,
for that is justified by the principle of the *pāñcanāyya* (PMS 9.3.14).

In reality, however, because the husband and wife are distinct agents of the act of going forward (*prasthāna*), there is a singular number as in the case of *yajeta*; and because of the intention to include the wife along with the sacrificer, there is a dual number as in the case of *vasānau*.
For this very reason, when a single wife is employed, the mantra ends in the dual;

but elsewhere, it ends only in the singular. Thus, according to this view, there is no option at all. This being the position reached, [we reply: if the mantra were intended for the sacrificer alone, then the prayer for the prosperity of the animal would be redundant, since that [prosperity] is already established.
Furthermore, since it would require the postulation of unmentioned items such as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), even the injunction for that [offering] would not be possible.

Therefore, because the connection between the deity and its own ownership was established in the third book (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 3.1.25–29) for the sake of establishing the conventional usage of "the god" and so forth, and because the status of being the "lord of the clouds" (*meghapati*) is logically consistent upon accepting the deity, the view that the passage refers to the deity alone is correct.

As for the statement [of the opponent], it is indeed consistent with my position as well; for, according to the method stated there, since the nature of being a deity (*devatātva*) resides distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) across both the *agniṣṭoma* and the *ukthya*, its unity is established, and its duality is established through the difference in substrates (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Thus, it is perfectly reasonable.

Just as in the case of agency, even in the status of being a deity, the state of being the "Lord of Clouds" (Meghapati) is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*); thus, there is no defect whatsoever.
Furthermore, even the option (*vikalpa*) is not a fault, because it pertains to the result (*phalamukhatvāt*).
The purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there would be a modification (*ūha*) of the two [names] in a sacrificial session (*satra*).
And *vikalpa* (option) occurs when two meanings are pursued together;

however, this will be discussed in the section on fire (*agnimādhikaraṇa*) in the Siddhānta. Maṇḍana [states]: "There may be modification (*ūhana*) of the term 'lord of the clouds' (*meghapati*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)."
Śaṅkara says: "Because he is a deity, [the term] is *meghapati*.
[This is] the *ūha*.

[The argument is: Since the status of being the lord of the clouds (*meghapati*) is inherent in the nature of the presiding deity (*svāmidevatva*), and since it is employed everywhere, and because that [status] is not restricted to anything else, there should be no modification (*avikāra*) anywhere.

In the fire-houses (*agnigṛha*) of certain reciters (*śākhin*), it is thus: "To the lord of the clouds, the cloud"; but for other reciters, it is "To the two lords of the clouds, the cloud," due to the dual number.

Regarding these two mantras, there arises an inquiry: is there application without modification (*avikāra*) in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) involving a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), or is there a modification (*ūha*) of the dual number to refer to the deities, while the singular number refers to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); or rather, do both refer to the sacrificer; or finally, is there a modification of both to refer to the deities? In this discussion, he states the first position.

In all modified sacrifices (vikṛti), there should be the application (adhikāra) [of this rule]. Medha means sacrifice; because it is the means for that, it is called "paśumedha" (animal sacrifice). The lord of the sacrifice is "meghapati."
And the state of being the master of the cloud is due to its being the master and the deity;

for Agni and Soma are both the master—the sacrificer—and the deity. Therefore, it possesses the nature of the master and the deity in their entirety. This is because of their coexistence—that is, their connection.
The sacrificer is connected [to the sacrifice] by way of being the giver,
and Agni and Soma are connected by way of being the recipients.
Furthermore, in all regions from the Himalayas to the land of the Kumārīs, the word "lord" (pati) is employed in the sense of sovereignty.

Furthermore, since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself, there is no fixed rule regarding whether the mantra is composed of the word *meghapati* in the singular or in the dual, it is impossible to express the status of three *meghapatis* by means of either the singular or the dual.

This being the case, because singularity or duality is non-distinctive and the application of the two mantras in the archetype is accepted based solely on the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is no defect even when they are applied in the same manner in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*).
Therefore, one view is that the two mantras should be used without modification (*anūha*) even when there is a group of animals.

Since the word *pati* is employed everywhere in the sense of lordship (*ādhipatya*), and because the status of being the deity of the owner is inherent (*samavāya*), there should be the status of "lord of the clouds" (*meghapati*).

Furthermore, since the mantra ending in the singular and the mantra ending in the dual are not restricted to other [specific] cases, and because there is a desire to express merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), there should be a modification (*vikāra*) of both mantras in every instance, whether in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*).

Thus, there is a different meaning for these words of the Sūtra. Alternatively, when two [words] are combined, if the meanings are distinct, their application should be according to their respective numbers.
In the *agnigṛha* texts, the word *meghapati* is recited in some places with a singular ending and in others with a dual ending, as in *meghapatibhyām*.
The first position—that there is an application [of the term] to groups of animals without modification—has been stated; he refutes that with the word "api vā" (or rather).
Now he states the second position:
the word *meghapati* will apply when there is a dual co-occurrence (*dvisamavāya*), namely, in the sense of both the owner and the pair of deities. Thus, there is a co-occurrence of two.
For those for whom the word *meghapati* ends in the singular, it would refer to the master (*svāmin*);
but for those for whom it ends in the dual, it would refer to Agni and Soma.
Thus, when there is a difference in meaning—that is, a distinction between the two meanings of "master" and "deity"—the application [of the term] would be according to their respective numbers.

In the archetype (prakṛti), there is the use of the owner's mantra in the singular; in the archetype, there is the use of the dual-form deity-dvandva; in the archetype, there is the use of the dual-form deity-dvandva for the cloud (megha); and when there are many deities, there is the use with modification (ūha)—thus, according to the respective order, there is the state of being the lord of the cloud (meghapati-tva), the state of being the lord of the cloud.
The application would be as follows:

the singular ending is used in relation to the owner (*svāmin*), and the dual ending is used in relation to the deity (*devatā*), according to their respective numbers. Now, the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Due to the distinction of the master, there would be superiority in the deity; the word "second" would apply to the wife.
The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of rejecting the second position.
The term *meghapati* ("lord of the sacrifice") in the context of Agni-Soma would be indicative of the master.

The distinction that the singular-ending form refers to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) while the dual-ending form refers to the deity (*devatā*) is not tenable; for it is improper for a single word, even within a single sentence, to have multiple meanings simply because of its singular number.

If it is asked, "Why could both forms of the word *meghapati* not refer to the deity?", [the answer is: the singular-ending word *meghapati* would have to be displaced (*utkarṣa*) to a modified sacrifice (*vikāra*) consisting of a single deity, and that would contradict the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, it does not refer to the deity.
But it refers exclusively to the master.
[Objection: What then is the status of the dual number if it refers to the master? It is replied:
the word "second" is a dual form; it is appropriate as referring to the wife, with the wife in mind.

Likewise, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the singular form "to the lord of the cloud" (*meghapataye*) is used with reference to the sacrificer alone, while the dual form "to the lords of the cloud" (*meghapatibhyām*) is used with reference to both the wife and the sacrificer.

In a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*) where the sacrificer is absent, their application occurs through modification (*ūha*). The third position is that the word "lord of the cloud" does not refer to the deity at all;
for if it were the deity, then because the deity is already established and possesses the desired blessing, the ownership [implied by the term] would be redundant.

By the word "tu" (but), having set aside the third position, he states the fourth, which is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "The deity would be the meaning of the word 'lord of the clouds' (*meghapati*). Because it contains a benediction for that—this mantra contains a benediction for the oblation by means of those two deities; its state is "containing a benediction for that" (*tadāśīṣṭva*). Therefore, the mantra has the deity as its primary referent, specifically through the word 'lord of the clouds'.
"Desiring the state of being the lord of the clouds, bring forward the cloud, O cloud-like doors.

However, if the word "lord of the clouds" (*meghapati*) refers to the owner, then that benediction would be purposeless because it has already been attained; for the animal was already previously obtained by the owner. Thus, a further benediction would be redundant.
Therefore, the word "lord of the clouds" must refer exclusively to the deity.

Therefore, modification (*ūha*) occurs only when [the term] refers to the deity itself. Furthermore, because of the act of offering (*utsarga*), the status of being a "lord" (*pati*) would apply to it figuratively. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) states that in the *agnigṛha* formulas, the word "lord of the sacrifice" (*yajñapati*) refers to the deity.

That which constitutes the state of being the "lord of the sacrifice" (*medhapati*) or the "lord of the victim" (*paśupati*) in that sacrificer is [only] through figurative or secondary usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*).

Because of the act of relinquishment—since the sacrificer performs the renunciation of the animal with the formula, "This is for Agni and Soma; it is not mine"—the sacrificer possesses the status of "lord of the sacrifice" by virtue of this quality of being the agent of relinquishment. However, the primary status of being the "lord of the sacrifice" belongs to the deity alone.
It would have to be displaced because, when joined with that [singular], it is impossible for it to be dual;

for, since the word *meghapati* (Lord of Clouds) refers to a deity in the fire-houses, if it were dual—meaning in a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*) characterized by duality—the singular form of the word *meghapati* would be impossible, as it could not apply. Thus, one would have to effect the displacement of the word *meghapati* to a single-deity animal, as stated in the sūtra: "There would be displacement regarding the deity" (9.3.12.14). This objection is refuted by the following: "This is a restatement. (anuvādaḥ).
But it is one [word] because of its inherent connection (*samavāya*), since that is its defining characteristic.

In the fire-chambers, the word *meghapati* is singular; it refers to that group which consists of Agni and Soma. This is because of the inherent connection, that is, because the word *meghapati* has a denotative relationship with that specific group.

It is said: "O you who desire [rain], bring forth the cloud for the host of deities headed by Meghapati. Because that host possesses that characteristic, it means that since the host has that as its defining mark—namely, being of a singular nature—it is appropriate for it to be expressed by the word *meghapati* in the singular number, given the oneness of the host.
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
Furthermore, the term *meghapati* ending in the dual number is also appropriate as it denotes a group (*gaṇa*).
Therefore, the term *meghapati* ending in the singular number, which signifies a group, should not be displaced when the animal sacrifice is dedicated to a single deity.
And because of that association, there would be a conceptual differentiation.

In the *agnigṛhas*, the term *meghapati* is also read in the dual number as *meghapatibhyām*. Even though it refers to a deity, there is no contradiction due to the association with the group of deities consisting of Agni and Soma.
This referent, namely the deity, is a composite;
having become unified through its association with two [entities], the word *meghapati*—whether ending in the singular or the dual—pertains exclusively to the context.
Therefore, since there is no contradiction, there may be an option (*vikalpa*) between the singular-ending and the dual-ending forms within that very context.

In a modified ritual (vikṛti), however, where there are multiple deities, the mantra must be applied with modification (ūha); for even though the number is one, the quality [of plurality] does not depart. In the Agni-gṛhas, the word *meghapati* is recited in the singular.

In that case, even though singularity is intended by the singular number, because the quality of singularity does not depart when it is included within the group of deities consisting of Agni and Soma—since there is no departure (or loss) of singularity with respect to each [deity] in the *amedhya* section and in the *soma* ritual—it is possible to say, "It is made un-sacrificial; bring the sacrifice. Therefore, by virtue of that rule, there is modification (*ūha*) of the mantra ending in the singular number according to the context.

Because it possesses the form of the deity, the singular number of the word *medhapati* is appropriate; and because it possesses the dual form of Agni and Soma as deities, the dual number is also appropriate. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the modified ritual (*vikṛti*), the modification (*ūha*) of the word *medhapati* follows the deities, not the sacrificer.
Some [say]: "The term *medhapati* means the state of being both master and deity" (*devatya*;

*devatyasya* is the correct reading). Thus, there is an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), which was omitted, following the word *medhapati* from the first *sraja*-formula as it is supplied (*anupakta*) in the subsequent sūtra, "Or that of the master" (*svāmino vā*).
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 647). Regarding the word *medha*, which occurs in the *abhigupraiṣa* in the singular, there is a modification (*ūha*) to the plural form when used in the context of the *ekādaśinī*.

Bhāṣya 9.3.14.44. See the discussion in Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 340, under the heading: "Regarding the word *medhapati* occurring in the *abhigupraiṣa*, ending in the singular, in the context of the *ekādaśinī*. There is an option for the word *medhapati*, occurring in the *abhigupraiṣa* and ending in the singular, when the animal has multiple deities, [to be replaced] by the dual form.
9.3.12.3.42-43. Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 340: "Regarding the word *medhapati* occurring in the *abhigupraiṣa*, ending in the singular, when the animal has multiple deities."
In this context, the locus (adhikaraṇa) should be examined.
The attainment of intelligence (*medhā*) occurs through the consumption of *vacā*.
(Sudhā, p. 59). Expressions such as "the wisdom of Medhātithi" appear like statements from the *itihāsa* (ancient lore).
If there were a historical account (itihāsa) as a means of proof, the defect of having a beginning would attach to the Veda.
If it is argued that let it be so, [we reply: in that case, because of its lack of authority, the statement "the sacrifice belongs to Medhātithi Kāṇvāyana" would not be established.
Bhāṣya 9.1.16.44. The section concerning the sacrificial animal (medhya-adhikaraṇa).

The *ābhri-gu-paiśa* formula found in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, which is composed within the *praiṣa*, should not be recited during the *sārasvatī* animal sacrifice belonging to the *atirātra*. This has been considered:
because of the specification of gender (*liṅga-viśeṣa-nirdeśa*), the *sārasvatī* [animal] is not included among those for whom the rule of prescription applies, as it is female.

Commentary: There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. In that context, animals are prescribed: "A sacrificial cake for Agni is to be offered; a bull for Indra-Agni at the Upaśad; a ram for Indra at the Ṣoḍaśin; a ewe for Sarasvatī at the Atirātra.

However, there is also the *abhry-upaveśana* (the placing of the spade) in the rite for Agni-Soma: "Bring forward the sacrificial animal to the doors of the sacrifice, O eager ones, toward the victim belonging to the Lord of the Sacrifice."
In this regard, there is a doubt: should the *abhiguvacana* (the recitation of the *abhigū* verses) be performed at the *sārasvatī* sacrifice when it is pure (*medhyā*), or not?
Now, one might argue that since it is for the sake of the *aindrāgnīya* sacrifice, it is extended here by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
To this, it is replied:
The inquiry is conducted on the basis that the procedure is common to all.
What, then, is the prima facie position? Regarding these animals whose procedures are common, the *sārasvatī* ewe is not included in the *abhri-gu* formula.
Why? Because of the mention of a specific gender mark (*liṅga-viśeṣa*).
A word with a specific gender mark is indicated by the dual number, as in "Bring fire for him" (*prāsmā agniṃ bharata*), which has a masculine form, yet her [the animal's] nature is feminine.
And it is not a masculine expression.
The word ought to denote a female;

therefore, the ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī is obtained through the plural number. [Durga says: Regarding the four animals, the word *prāsmedha*, being in the masculine gender, is simply incapable [of denoting a female].
It is said: because it is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is twofold;
just as the nominal stem is not [merely] that which has been expressed by the word, so too is the sentence, as established in the section on the *pāśa* (9.3.14).
Therefore, it denotes that which is inherent [in the object], because the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) is possible [therein].
However, the feminine gender cannot be expressed by means of the masculine gender. In this context, gender is not the meaning of the case-ending (vibhakti), as is the case with number.
However, it has been stated that gender is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Therefore, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) considers it logical that there is no absence of the female [animal], because the meaning is not inherently connected [to the male], on the grounds of the "specification of a particular gender.
Or rather, because it denotes the animal (*paśu*); for that [term] constitutes the injunction, whereas the state of being an animal pertains to the male.
Commentary: The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that the Abhrigu formula is unobtained in the Sarasvatī sacrifice;
rather, the Abhrigu formula should also be present in that [Sarasvatī sacrifice].
Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Since it is considered that the context is common to all the animal sacrifices, it follows that [the rule] applies to the Sārasvatī sacrifice as well.
Regarding that which is stated as "in it," namely that which is joined with a specific gender-indicative word: therein,
because of the denotation of the animal,
the state of being an animal (*paśutva*) is present.
Intending this, one should say, "O cattle, bring Agni to him";
for that [referring pronoun] is an injunction regarding the masculine gender of the pronoun,
and it is expressed by the word "cattle" (paśu).

And that [animal] exists as something fit for sacrifice; with reference to it, the pronoun will be uttered in grammatical apposition with the word "animal" (paśu). In this way, the context (prakaraṇa) will be upheld.
Therefore, it follows that the statement of Abhṛgu applies to the Sārasvata [sacrifice].

Dvivedagaṅga says: But the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) thinks that there will be grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) here with the word "animal" (paśu), as in the phrase "for our animal" (*prāsme paśave*).
That which is the subject of the sacrificial rite is denoted by the word *paśu* (animal), and it is also pierced in the sacrificial post (*medhya*);
therefore, this *nigada* formula is capable [of expressing that meaning].
He establishes this with the statement, "Or because of the designation of the animal.
Or there is a distinction because of the specification of its purpose.
The Commentary states: The word "or" (vā) sets aside this position.
This is not so; one would not obtain the statement of Sarasvatī and Bhṛgu.
This is the position here: that one would not obtain it.
Why? Because there is a distinction due to the specification of its purpose.
For this word is capable of denoting the male object;
however, the meaning "sheep" is feminine, as in "ewe.
Thus, the first position was stated: that a masculine word is not able to denote a female.

This is solely because the opponent's position is neither stated nor refuted. Thus, by the Siddhānta-sūtra, "Or rather, there is a distinction, because of the specification of its purpose," the very meaning of the first sūtra is recalled.
And the state of being an animal [is established] from the singular number.

Commentary (Bhāṣya): Now, as for what was said—that this [term] "cattle" (*paśu*) intends the owner of the cattle, since the single word "cattle" can refer both to the owner of the cattle and to the cattle themselves, and thus the connection will be "the cattle are for us"—that must be refuted. Dūṣaṇa (Refutation): Regarding the statement "and the state of being cattle [is indicated] by the singular number," this word *paśu* is masculine.
The word *asme* also refers to that which is expressed by the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of those two;
or, as it has been stated, because of proximity.
The Bhāṣya says: "As it has been stated, the mention of the *abhriyu* [verse] does not apply to the *sārasvatī*."
Why? For the very same reason previously stated, namely, because of the indication provided by the gender.
As for what was said—that a pronoun will be employed in grammatical apposition with the word "animal" (paśu)—that is not so.
Why? Because of proximity.
For a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) denotes that which is proximate (*saṃnihita*).
It refers to whatever object is brought into proximity by the word as soon as it is uttered.
Now, when that [object] exists—being proximate in its form as qualified by all particularities such as gender and so forth—it is employed [by the pronoun].
In proximity, a single qualifying attribute is unable to denote an individual as qualified by that attribute alone.
Due to proximity, a single universal (*sāmānya*) is resorted to therein, and nothing else such as "cowness" (*paśutva*) or the like.
When the word "animal" (*paśu*) is uttered there, once the individual has been extracted from its cowness by means of the word, the connection can be established as "for this animal."
But when it is being recited, a word expressing a specific gender would result;
therefore, the mention of the Sārasvatas and the Bhṛgus is not applicable [in that context].
This is a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvā-cintya*).
In this case, the purpose need not be stated.
This deliberation is for the sake of the purpose in this section: whether the animal-rites are intended for the Āgneya and Aindrāgna sacrifices alone, or whether they are common to all.
If they are common—

From the *paśu* ritual, the *sārasvata* [animal] obtains the *abhri-gu* procedure; from this [same source], the *āgneya-upāṃśuyāja* rituals obtain the *abhri-gu* procedure through the principle of modification (*ūha*). Furthermore, one need not state the purpose of a purpose.

[Dvivedagaṅga says: By this, that which was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin)—namely, "or rather, it is as previously stated, because of proximity" (*yathoktaṃ vā saṃnidhānāt*)—is refuted.
It is the inherent nature of pronouns that they denote what is proximate.
As soon as a pronoun is uttered, it is quickly connected with whatever other word brings it into proximity;
however, the word "animal" (paśu) has not been uttered here, by which a connection could be established.
When that [word] occurs, the mode of its relation [to its referent] is determined by observing other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

What is the meaning of the statement: "It is employed when the form is present as qualified by all qualifiers such as gender and so forth" (the question being: what is the meaning of the word *paśu*, etc.)?

The meaning is that it denotes the individual (*vyakti*) as qualified by the specific genus (*jāti*), gender (*liṅga*), and number (*saṃkhyā*), by way of its own form—that is, through its inherent capacity (*svasāmarthya*).
This is precisely the capacity of all names: that they denote even the opposite of what they appear to signify;
however, the actual manifestation varies.
Alternatively, by the word "rūpeṇa" (by form), an existing entity is denoted.
And that [universal], being present and brought forward by the context,
cannot— while in proximity— denote an individual as qualified by only one qualifier;
rather, wherever it is qualified by proximity, they denote it as such.
Therefore, their proximity is the common cause.
And the masculine gender is proximate;
even though the feminine gender is also proximate, the word is nevertheless incapable of functioning there, because it is masculine.
"In that case, when the word *paśu* (animal) is uttered...

When the word *paśu* is pronounced—as in "for this animal" (*asme paśave*)—the masculine word can be connected with a masculine [referent]. In this view, the word *asme* ("for us/this") is connected with the generic property of "animality" (*paśutva*) extracted from the individual, and not with the individual itself.
This too is indeed a high point [in our argument]: that even when the word *paśu* (animal) is uttered, this [objection] does not arise.

Śā—Because of the specific context, and because the word *asme* in the phrase *prāsmā agniṃ bharata* (bring fire for him) is masculine, and since the word *asme* has a fixed gender, it is intended to refer to the animal (the object denoted) which possesses that gender; thus, it can apply to a female animal as well in the form *prāsme paśave*, and there is no contradiction regarding gender. Therefore, the statement regarding the two Sarasvatīs and the Bhṛgus [applies here].
This being the position reached, the following is stated in reply.

"In this case, such [a cognition] would occur only upon hearing the word 'animal' (paśu); however, that [word] is not heard here. Therefore, at the time of usage, that which exists as something immediately present—"
In that context, this [word] is capable of expressing the masculine gender when applied to a substance (*dravya*);
it does not denote "what kind of substance" (*kiṃ-dravyam*), and therefore it functions through the [suffix] *medhya*.

Therefore, in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the common application of the rule, the procedure proceeds from the words *agni* and *mepī*. It should not be argued that the procedure proceeds [only] because the gender denoted by the case-ending—just like the plurality in the word *pāśān*—is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣā*). This is because, according to the principle that "the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of three factors," gender is also the meaning of the nominal stem. Furthermore, even under the view that gender belongs to the expressed meaning (*vācya*) of case-endings such as *sme* and so forth, or of suffixes such as *tātr* and so forth, since it is possible for gender to be intended (*vivakṣā*) through its inherent connection (*samavāya*) in animals other than the ewe (*mepī*), it is improper to assume that it is not intended to be significant. This is the underlying sense.
This is what must be understood here: one view is that there are four animals at the Atirātra sacrifice, characterized as those dedicated to Agni, Indra-Agni, Indra, and Sarasvatī;
another view is that there is only one animal, characterized by Sarasvatī.
Thus says another [author].

Bhāṣya 10|6|15|4. Liberation: it arises from knowledge. How so? For he who knows the Self—which is distinct from the body, infinite, unborn, undying, and imperishable—becomes detached from the union with the body. Through the exhaustion of previously performed actions by the experience of their fruits, and because future actions do not exist due to their non-performance, no further body arises; thus, there occurs an absolute cessation of connection with the body.
In that state, for those who have realized the Self, because of the exhaustion of prior actions through experience and due to the absence of further effort, the body is not produced again;
the body does not manifest for the sake of experiencing the fruits born of karma.
In the absence of that [desire], no motive whatsoever remains there;
one who seeks liberation does not engage in rites performed for desire or those prohibited. One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites out of a desire to avoid transgression.
A desired fruit is not attained by one who lacks the desire [for it];

since this [desire] exists in the case of the Self, that knowledge is useful. (Ślokavārttika, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra, verses 108–111; and Ratnākara). Liberation (*mokṣa*) is the cessation of the ignorance regarding Brahman through the cessation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
*Rahasya*, page 1. Liberation (*mokṣa*): Bondage is the connection with a body;
its absence is liberation.

That which is the non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of bodies already produced, and that which is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of those not yet produced—that is liberation.
Bondage has karma as its cause, and it ceases only through the destruction of karma.

*Ratnākara*, in the section on the refutation of the connection [between self and bondage], states (p. 106): "Liberation is mentioned separately even from the specific dharma [that leads to it], just as the Brahmin is mentioned separately from the wandering ascetic (*parivrājaka*). *Sūtrabhāṣya*, p. 127: "One who seeks liberation does not engage in [actions] that are either optional (*kāmya*) or prohibited (*niṣiddha*)."

"One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to avoid sin" (Ślokavārttika, Saṃbandhākṣepaparihāra 110). By this principle, because one avoids actions performed for specific desires (*kāmya*) and prohibited actions (*niṣiddha*), the production of a body occurs for the sake of experiencing their fruits.

[Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 329]. For one who does not desire heaven because it consists of bondage, and who seeks liberation (*mokṣārthin*), the duty lies in the very nature of the action itself (and not in its fruit).
*Ṭup-ṭīkā*, 6.3.112, p. 1106: Even by one who seeks liberation (*mokṣa*), the destruction of evil (*pāpa-kṣaya*) must necessarily be desired; for in its absence, there is no liberation.
[This concludes] the discussion on liberation. But what, then, is this so-called liberation?

Some maintain that for the stream of consciousness—which flows with various forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth, driven by the force of diverse latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—there occurs, through the total eradication of all latent impressions, a state of abiding in pure consciousness alone after abandoning the diversity of blue, yellow, and the rest. Others, however, hold that there is the cessation of the stream of consciousness, like the extinction of a lamp.
Both of these views, being rooted in the non-existence of external objects, have been refuted by the very statement of the Knower of Reality (*tattvajña*).
Others, however, declare that liberation (*apavarga*) is the dissolution of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*).

For phenomenal proliferation is constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*); like the proliferation of a dream, it dissolves of its own accord once ignorance has dissolved through the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), even while one is still alive.
Thus says the Scripture (*śruti*): "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see?"

This [objection] is also already refuted by the demonstration that the ultimate reality consists in the fact that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), and by the teaching that the previously arisen body, senses, and objects are [unreal]; for [the scripture says],
"The Self alone is all this."
Destruction, and the absolute non-arising of those things not yet arisen. How is it "absolute"? It means that the Self is the enjoyer of everything. As in: "He who should desire... [etc.]

What is non-arising? It is the complete exhaustion of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the two causes of arising. "I would be the kingdom" means "I would be the enjoyer of the kingdom," just as [in the phrase] "he who desires...
This connection with the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is bondage; liberation from that is release (*mokṣa*).
"May I become all this"—that is, "may I be the enjoyer of everything."

Now, if this were so, it would mean that for one liberated through the exhaustion of all phenomena (*dharma*), nothing exists at all; likewise, if "the Self is everything" meant that the Self is the owner of everything, then there would be pleasure [for the Self], and consequently, liberation would not be the supreme human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), because it would be something to be enjoyed.
This is the meaning.
This is not a fault.

For the bliss of the liberated one is not produced by dharma; rather, as for the absence of duality expressed in the passage, "For where there is, as it were, duality," if that [bliss] were subject to origination while duality exists, it would be perishable.
In that regard, the statement concerning non-return and the absence of delusion is merely figurative;
otherwise, there would indeed be a contradiction with the scriptural teaching on the manifold nature of dreams.

Intrinsic bliss, however, having been obscured for some time by the illusion of saṃsāra—like a mirage in the desert—and being overwhelmed by it, becomes manifest as an object of enjoyment once one is liberated from saṃsāra; subsequently, it remains as an object of enjoyment even when the body has dissolved. Thus is the meaning.

Furthermore, since bliss (*ānanda*) is intrinsic, such scriptural passages as "Brahman is bliss" and "The phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is the object of the senses, [is for the sake of] this Self for some time," serve as evidence from thousands of *śrutis*.
Now, one might object: even if there is an absence of pleasure, that which is enjoyable for a certain period of time becomes unenjoyable after its destruction.
"There is indeed no touching of pleasure and pain for one who is bodiless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1).
By this similarity with "it exists," he is figuratively called "deluded.

This is true; however, such a statement is intended with reference to the pleasure derived from sense objects. Otherwise, by failing to turn people away from the enjoyment of sense objects, there would be no inclination toward liberation.

There is a contradiction with the scriptural passage concerning bliss (*ānanda*). Now, one might attempt to produce [the idea of] bliss by the force of the statement regarding the absence of pleasure.
As for the passage: "But where for him everything has become the Self alone..."
Why should the statement regarding liberation not be explained as intending the absence of suffering—that is, the non-duality (*advaita*) of the self? That too is not correct;

for statements concerning the absence of pleasure are few, whereas those concerning bliss are abundant. Therefore, it is more reasonable that those [few] statements serve another purpose—namely, to negate the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) while affirming its existence—rather than the numerous statements of bliss negating the existence of the self.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of negating any connection with a self, because of the use of the word "his" (*asya*).

If the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) were intended to mean the absence of suffering, there would be a complete abandonment of its own primary meaning; for it is not stated here that "where everything has become the Self alone.

This might be so in the case of the word "pleasure" (*sukha*), which, being a general term, can apply even to a specific instance; but what is actually said here? "But where for him everything has become the Self alone."
Therefore, since there is no loss of its own meaning in this explanation, that alone is correct.
This is its meaning: "in whichever [state] of liberation for whichever self," such is the sense of "of this."
Surely, even if bliss exists, if it is not experienced, it is of no use at all—whether as an object of sight for the self, as a means of seeing, or as the locus of seeing.
Nor is it logical that there exists any other connection for the bliss of the one who possesses all the senses; rather, the self alone is its [connection].
If it is argued that experience occurs because this bliss is self-luminous, [the response is: "then nothing else exists; at that time, who would see what?
Just as: [it is said].
In the state of saṃsāra, it is unmanifest.
But surely even there its nature is bliss; for in the world, even that man who possesses neither kinsmen nor wealth is indeed manifest, because love arises toward his own self.
For one who is not happy does not speak thus: "I have nothing; I alone am everything.
Nor can the arising of love occur with respect to happiness that is unknown.
(The answer: In this context, just as in the case of a relationship, what is intended to be expressed is merely that "there is nothing [else]."

Now, is the self experienced by the wise in its own essential nature? Indeed, it is so; for liberation consists in the realization that "the self alone is everything for the self," based on direct experience.

Nor should it be said that even at that time there was no such experience; for if you argue that this is because [the bliss] is obscured, we reply that it is impossible for that bliss to be obscured, since its self-luminosity is established by the scripture, "In this state, this person is self-luminous," and because the bliss that is the very nature of the Self does not depend on any other cause well-known in the world.
As it has been said: "Since the Self is its own innate consciousness, bliss itself,
and that which is eternally liberated and so forth, the Self is never truly released."

Therefore, they say that liberation is the eternal manifestation of bliss. To this [we reply]: No, because there are scriptural passages that establish the absence of cognition at the time of liberation, such as: "By what means could one know the knower? When everything has become the Self for him, whom could he see and by what? Thus, there is a contradiction between these scriptural statements.

Furthermore, the nature of the self as consisting of consciousness, bliss, and so forth is contradicted by the perception of difference found in such scriptural passages as "Knowing the bliss of Brahman" (*ānandaṃ brahmaṇo vidvān*) and "That is the one bliss of Brahman" (*sa eko brahmaṇa ānandaḥ*).

Moreover, there is the experience: "I have no happiness at all, only suffering. Finally, there is the scriptural passage establishing the similarity between deep sleep and liberation: "These [individuals] go day after day to the world of Brahman, and day after day they return," which indicates that [the self] is not [pure] bliss.

219). According to the principle stated in *Yajatiṣu dravyaphalabhoktṛsaṃyogāt* (2.3.5.14), [the term "sacrifice"] does not apply to the mere relinquishing of a substance and a deity in the absence of an actual sacrifice.
