Bhāṣya 1.1.2.13: Wherever the root *yaj* is heard, there the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) in its non-interrupted form (*ahīna*) is applied.
8.1.5.25: The root *yaj* denotes a collective: "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa."

For what purpose, then, is the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* used? It is merely a restatement of what is already established (under the view that the Vedic text enjoins the meaning of the word). [ŚBh 1.1.1.13] The root *yajati* has the sense of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
[ŚBh 2.3.1.10] The root *yajati* denotes either the worship of a deity or the act of giving. [ŚBh 2.3.1.10]
*Saṃkarṣa.* 2.4.14: There is no intention [to express] the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) when there is the conceptualization of a quality as a fruit.

*Bhāṣya* 4.3.12.3: The root *yajati* denotes a fruit consisting in the destruction of ownership (*svatva-dhvaṃsa*). The verbal meaning of *yaji* is the relinquishment of a substance intended for a deity, as characterized by the fruit consisting in the destruction of ownership.

*Maṇi*, p. 102: "In the *yajati*s one performs the *ye yajāmahe*, but not in the *anuyāja*s"—this is an injunction of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) regarding a qualification of the object (*uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa-paryudāsa-vidhi*), which serves the purpose of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*). *Bāla.*, p. 20: "'In the *yajati*s one performs the *ye yajāmahe*, but not in the *anuyāja*s'—this is an injunction of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vidhi*) having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). p. 21:
The mantra "ye yajāmahe" is established for the *yajati*s by means of a general statement (*anārabhyavāda*).
And regarding the statement "not at the after-sacrifices" (*nānuyājeṣu*), there is a prohibition concerning the after-sacrifices.
In that case, with respect to the sacrifices excluding the after-sacrifices, the rule "he performs the *ye yajāmahe*" is a preclusion (*paryudāsa*), not an option (*vikalpa*).
The meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is the sacrificer.

Regarding the meaning of *yaj*: even when the mental renunciation in the form of a resolve—“I shall employ this substance for some purpose of my own, beginning with its transport”—and the verbal renunciation in the form of uttering the words “not mine” have been performed, the sacrifice is not completed without a physical renunciation consisting of taking [the object] with the hand or another limb and depositing it in a certain place.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 1627). That which is the effect of the meaning of *yaj* is the primary element (*pradhāna*).
For that [duty] is indeed called "that which is to be performed" (kartavyatā).

Bhāṣya 9.1.12.1, Section 2. Soma is characterized by the injunction *yajati* (he sacrifices), whereas the *dadhi-homas* (curd-offerings) are characterized by the injunction *juhoti* (he offers oblations).

Bhāṣya 8.4.1.9. The *ahīnas* (non-sacrificial sessions) are characterized by the injunction *yajati*, while the *satras* (sacrificial sessions) consist of the cutting off of the *āsana-upāyi* (the preparatory sitting).
VI. 10|6|16: Because of the injunction to sacrifice (*yajati-codanā*) and because the number [of priests] for the masters is not fixed, it is an *ahīna* (non-deficient) sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 10|6|17/6|1: The injunction to sacrifice consists of the action involving a substance and a deity, since its purpose is fulfilled in the aggregate.
In this sūtra, either the definition of sacrifice (*yāga-lakṣaṇa*) is stated, or the performance of sacrifice (*yāga-prayoga*) is described.

The injunction to sacrifice (*yajati-codanā*)—expressed as "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) or "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*)—denotes the verbal root *yaji*, as well as the substance (*dravya*), the deity (*devatā*), and the action consisting of renunciation (*tyāga*) in the form of "not mine. The aggregate of these—the substance, the deity, and the action—is what is called the "substance-deity-action" (*dravyadevatākriya*); this much constitutes the meaning of the term "sacrifice" (*yāga*). This is because the injunction to sacrifice finds its purpose and reaches full completion in that aggregate, namely, the aggregate of substance, deity, and renunciation. Regarding the statement, "The injunction to sacrifice [finds its purpose] in the aggregate, because it has achieved its aim," it will be explained that sacrifice (*yāga*) is the act of renunciation directed toward a deity, while that same act, when accompanied by the act of throwing [into the fire], is called an oblation (*homa*).

Ku. 3|4|18|4|7: However, if one were to enjoin a quality for that which has already been produced (*utpannaśiṣṭaguṇavidhi*), then the word *ādi* (etcetera) found in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) would become redundant, since it refers to the substance in general.

This is because the substance in general is already obtained through the pronoun *tat* in the sense of the nominal suffix (*taddhita*), and by the mere injunction of sacrifice according to the maxim: "The injunction of sacrifice consists of the action involving a substance and a deity.
Advaita. 2|9|40-41: In the injunctions of sacrifice, [the rite] ends with the act of throwing [the offering into the fire].

In passages such as "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni" (*āgneyo'ṣṭākapālo bhavati*) and "The pap is for the Viśvedevas" (*vaiśvadevyāmiṣkā*), since there is no mention of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) and only the presence of a material substance and a deity is established, one might argue—just as in the case of the *āghāra* libation or the *utsarga* rite—that the purpose is fulfilled by the mere act of relinquishment (*tyāga*), and not by an offering (*āhuti*). This being the position, we reply: Since the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) signifies either the worship of a deity or the giving [of a gift], in instances such as "the deity is worshipped with perfumes and so forth" (*devatā gandhādibhir ijyate*) or "it is given to a Brahmin and others" (*viprādya dīyate*), there is no perception of the act ending in the casting [of the substance] into the fire. Therefore, because the deity possesses a physical form (*vigraha*), the casting [into the fire] occurs only after the transition to the ownership of another (*parasvatva*) has been effected.
For this very reason, the scriptural injunction is established: "In the middle, he offers the oblations to the immortals, then the five oblations, and then the cake-oblations" (Saṃkarṣa.

2.4.1). Furthermore, in cases where the originative injunctions enjoin *yajati* (sacrifices), since the acts of relinquishment (*tyāga*) and dedication to a deity (*devatoddeśa*) are already established, the term *juhoti* (offers) is understood to signify merely the act of pouring into the fire (*prakṣepa*). (Vārttika 3.4.14; 4.1, p. 986).
When there is an originative injunction of *yajati*, the state of being an *ahīna* sacrifice consists in its not being accomplished by the qualities of a single day (*ahargaṇa*).
10|6|16|60-61: This is to be seen under the section beginning with "The nature of a *sattra* consists in the application of sitting and the presence of an injunction.

In cases such as *yajati* (he sacrifices) and *juhoti* (he offers oblations), the difference in words (*śabdāntara*) is a means of proof for the distinction between ritual acts. 2|3|1|9: The relevant section is to be found under the heading "The Section on Difference of Words" (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*).
From [the roots] *yajati*, *dadāti*, *juhoti*, and so forth, both the meanings of the sacrifice (*yajyādi*) and the sense "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*) are understood.
Bhāṣya 2.3.1.9.

From the difference in the verbal roots of the sacrifices, there is a distinction between ritual acts (*karmabheda*), as in: "He sacrifices to the *samidhs*," "He sacrifices to *tanūnapāt*," and so on.
Bhāṣya 2.3.12:
The word *yajati* (he sacrifices) applies to the substance, the deity, and the action.
Bhāṣya 6.1.1.

They record that Dharma is precisely what is denoted by the word *yajati* (he sacrifices), as in: "The gods sacrificed with sacrifice; those were the first dharmas" (Bhāṣya 1.1.2.12). Furthermore: "If on the day of sacrifice the moon is seen in the western quarter, one should offer oblations with the Vyāhṛtis and give a staff to a twice-born man."
"This prohibition is to be understood as a penalty" (Bāla. pṛ. 30). Regarding the statement "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the sacrificer is only one" (Vi.

3.1.14), and in the case of "The sacrificer is the cake on one potsherd," the word *yajamāna* is a praise (*stuti*) of the cake on one potsherd; it is neither a name (*nāmadheya*) nor an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*).

In a *sattra* sacrifice, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is specifically the *gṛhapati* (householder) who performs the duties of the sacrificer, such as the commencement of the *śukra* cup; it is not just anyone. Bhā. 12.4.13.4. The sacrificer is taught [in the texts] as having two wives or many wives. Bhā. 9.3.16.20. It is recorded in the sacred tradition: "The sacrificer is the *prastara* (grass-bundle)."

In this regard, when there arises a doubt as to whether this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that such a passage is an *arthavāda*, not an injunction. [As in the case of] "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*); here the word "sacrificer" is a praise of the grass-bundle, because both are means for accomplishing the ritual action.
Sacrificer:
23-1. See under the section "Tatsiddhyadhikaraṇam" on page 1910 of the Mīmāṃsākośa.
At the Mahāvrata, the sacrificer puts on a heated garment.
There is a combination with the ordinary garment (*ahava-vāsas*). 10.4.7.12–15.

Where the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is enjoined as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), that injunction is accomplished by any sacrificer whatsoever; for example: "The *audumbarī* post is of the same height as the sacrificer," and "The sacrificer touches the *śukra* cup. Bhāṣya 9.1.13.40:

Regarding the statement "The sacrificer is the sacrificial post" (*yajamāno yūpaḥ*), there arises a doubt as to whether this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that this is a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda) and not an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi). (Sūtra 2.4.12.22–23). According to Vi. 5.2.5, "The sacrificer shall not let go of the sacrificial post (yūpa) until the end of the process beginning with its anointing. By such statements as, "The sacrificer [is present] in the cakes baked on a single potsherd (ekakapāla) and in the omentum (vapā) of the Vaiśvānarī [offering]," the death of the sacrificer through the act of cutting the portion (avadāna) is mentioned.
Saṃkarṣa 2.2.16: The sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is so called because he performs the sacrificial acts, such as the purchase of services (*parikraya*), and thereby sacrifices.
Bhāṣya 6.2.1: The sacrificers are those who remain alive of this very [sacrifice].
10.2.17.48–49: The sacrificers themselves should be the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Regarding the *sattra*: see Śābarabhāṣya on Jaiminisūtra 10.6.15.51–59, which states: “In a *sattra*, the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)."
There are many sacrificers (yajamāna).

[See Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.6.14.45–50. Regarding the statement "In a sattra there are many sacrificers," it should be understood that in ritual acts, the renunciation (tyāga) must be performed by the sacrificer himself, while other duties are performed through the medium of the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
This is to be seen under the section titled *Śāstraphalādhikaraṇa* (3|8|8|18–20).
The sacrificer, having resolved upon rice (*vrīhi*), must not offer barley (*yava*), because of the prohibition: “One should not speak what is disregarded” (Vārttika 3|4|14|13, p. 143).

Furthermore, based on the statement “by the sacrificer [measuring] with his own *aratni*,” the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and other items must be measured by the sacrificer’s own *aratni*, even if they are five *aratnis* long.

*Saṃkarṣa* 1.4.19: In the performance of the ritual with its constituent parts (*sāṅgakarma*), the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) must perform only the act of renunciation (*tyāga*); everything else is to be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because they have been hired for that very purpose. Since the sacrificer alone is the agent of all actions, whether directly or through intermediaries, his status as the enjoyer of the fruit is not contradictory.
This is the section concerning the fruit of the scripture (*śāstraphalādhikaraṇa*).
VI. 3|17|8: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [the rule] beginning with "by the sacrificer, whether it exists or does not exist," etc., [is applied].

Bhāṣya 10|3|12|150: Just as the ritual acts (*padārtha*) are to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest, so too must they be supervised by the sacrificer to prevent negligence.

Or [as stated in] 3.8.7.17: even when the *hotṛ*’s *yājyā* is removed, the portion (*bhakṣa*) is not removed from the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) in the *jyotiṣṭoma* during the *ṛtugraha* offerings, provided the sacrificer performs the recitation himself. 3.12.8.144–46: The sacrificer’s *anumantraṇa* occurs in certain rites among the twelve rituals of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

Bāla, p. 97: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the sacrificer indeed has the consumption of the *iḍā* and other portions in the *aiṣṭika* rites.

Mīko., p. 1243: See under the entry “In the *ṛtuyāja*s, when the recitation is performed by oneself.”
The sacrificer has two characteristics: being the agent of the action and being the enjoyer of the fruit.
Of these two, his status as the agent is established by the performance of the rite; however, the enjoyment of the fruit is not [directly] seen [at that time].
Vi. 3.7.2. By means of the ritual purchase (parikraya), the sacrificer’s own agency is established in all cases.

Vārttika 3.8.1.19: There is no substitute for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Even though one who is appointed to take his place upon the death of any one of the sacrificers in a *satra* functions as a substitute and possesses the duties of a sacrificer, he nevertheless does not partake in the fruit of the *satra*. Vi.
6.3.7–9: The sacrificer is the primary cause of the transcendental result (*apūrva*).
Or [it may be so]. 3|8|1|27: Even for a sacrificer who has gone abroad, the status of being a sacrificer is established through the renunciation of the sacrificial materials.
3|8|16|16: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and in the Agnyādheya, the fruit is to be prayed for by the sacrificer, not by the Adhvaryu priest.
For the sake of luster.

3|8|326–28. The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are hired solely for the purpose of performing those rites which belong to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Vi. 3|8|10. In the event of the sacrificer vomiting Soma, the expiation is the *somendra-caru* offering; however, this does not apply to the officiating priests as well (the *somendra-caru* applies only when the fault occurs in the drinking of Soma by the sacrificer).
3|14|13|34–36. This should be understood from the passage: “The *caru* offering to Soma-Indra [is prescribed] in the event of an accident befalling the sacrificer.
The primary rites intended for prosperity belong to the sacrificer.

The morning oblation must be performed by the sacrificer and the officiating priest, or by the sacrificer's attendants in any manner whatsoever, for the sake of avoiding the fault incurred by failing to complete what has been commenced.

12|4|12|32. And that one [performer] is unrestricted.

Soma. 6|3|4. For the ritual action for the sake of the sacrificer must be complete with all its constituent parts.

in the absence of either of these, there is a deficiency (vaiguṇya).

Bhāṣya 6.1.9.82: There is a father-son relationship between the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and the *āhavanīya* fire. Saṃkarṣa 3.4.2: A mantra prescribing a fruit that accrues to both the sacrificer and the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is: "What is auspicious here, may that be with us there. Bālakrīḍā, p. 63: Singularity of the sacrificer applies in the Jyotiṣṭoma and similar rites; duality of the sacrificer in the Kulāya sacrifice; and plurality of the sacrificers in the Sattra.
VI. 3|13|4. The giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has the sacrificer as its agent. VI. 3|8|19–2. The *Yajamāna-kāṇḍa* is an intermediate section within the *Yajurveda*.
VI. 3|8|10. Regarding a rite performed for a group of sacrificers, the rule "the *audumbarī* post is equal in size to the sacrificer" means it is equal to one sacrificer alone, not to all of them.
And that [sacrificial post] belongs to a single householder alone in a *sattra* sacrifice, and to some one sacrificer in an *ahīna* sacrifice, not to all [the participants].
(Vi. 12.4.11–13). The measurement of the sacrificial post and so forth pertains only to the sacrificer.

*Saṃkarṣa* 1.4.9: Regarding the statement “the measurement of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth is by means of the *aratni* and other units,” one should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*).
