*Saṃkarṣa* 1.4.10: See the section (*adhikaraṇa*) under *Mīko.* p. 34, regarding the phrase “in the measurements of the layers (*citi*) in the *Agni-cayana*.”

The fruit manifested by the ritual formula (*karaṇamantra*) accrues to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). [Śābarabhāṣya on Jaiminisūtra 3.8.13–26–28]. The injunction regarding the fruit accruing to the sacrificer is the mantra: “May my luster increase at every sacrifice” (*mamāgne varco vihaveṣvastu*). Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 62. The status of being a sacrificer belongs to one who has studied the Veda and understood its meaning.

VI. 3|8|19. In the *kulāya* and other sacrifices, as well as in the *ekāhas* and *ahīnas*, there exist two or more sacrificers (*yajamāna*) as explicitly prescribed by scripture: “Two should sacrifice with the *yajus*-prescribed [rite],” “One should cause two to sacrifice with this very [rite],” “One should cause three to sacrifice with this very [rite],” and “One, two, or many should sacrifice with the *ahīnas*. Vārttika 3|13|17. In a *satra*, a substitute (*pratinidhi*) takes on the duties of the sacrificer. 6|3|10|26. The mention of the sacrificer’s name in the *sūktavāka* recitation is mandatory, not optional.

*Saṃkarṣa* 4.3.21: "The wives of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) eat the *iḍā*," because this is a refinement of the substance (*dravya-saṃskāra*), the sacrificer—who was not previously established—is enjoined by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and name (*samākhyā*).
*Ḍupū* 6.4.15: "The wives of the sacrificer, having come together, eat the *iḍā*"; thus, there is also eating for the sacrificer in the *darśa* and other sacrifices.
*Vi* 10.2.9: The collective joining (*saṃhanana*) of all the wives of the sacrificer occurs in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites.

In the injunction, "She [the wife] should perform the binding at the sacrifice," because singularity is intended as a qualifying attribute of the subject (*upādeya-viśeṣaṇa*), it follows—as in the case of the *audumbarī* post—that there should be only one wife bound, whether she be the specific wife of the sacrificer or any other single wife. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as binding must be performed for all wives; because there is no distinction in their status as agents (*kartṛtva*), and because these rites are brought together as being prompted by the portion of the result that accrues to them. Furthermore, since they are equally purificatory rites like the *graha* vessels, the number is not intended to be significant.

And because the nominal stem *patnī* (wife) refers only to the sacrificer's wife (*yajamānī*). Saṃkarṣa 1.2.1, Section 2. [The term] *yajamāna* (sacrificer) is intended [to include the wife] in the case of a modification where the bearer is the agent, such as in the *sūktavāka* at the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle. 9.1.14.40. And these (*camasādhvaryus*) are distinct from both the persons who are sacrificers and from the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
The Camasādhvaryus are not to be chosen by the sacrificer;
they are to be chosen by the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Bhāṣya 3.10.25.

The ancestors of the sacrificer (yajamānapūrvajāḥ) are indeed the seers (ṛṣayaḥ) belonging to the various divisions of the Yajurveda; they are referred to by the statement, "He chooses his ancestral lineage" (ārṣeyaṃ vṛṇīte).
(Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 3.4.4)
See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1004, under the entry "ārṣeyaṃ vṛṇīte.

Since the sacrifice is intended to prevent the loss of the sacrificer's fruit and so forth, and because the sacrificer's status as the agent of the sacrifice is established by the mental impression (*vāsanā*), and because the word *yat* indicates that the sacrifice and the mental resolve have a single agent, the sacrifice must indeed consist of the sacrificer's mental resolve.
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha, p. 15.2).
The plurality of sacrificers is the defining characteristic of a *satra*.
The portions for the sacrificers (*yajamāna-bhakṣas*) certainly exist in the *jyotiṣṭoma* as well as in the *iṣṭi*-type rites.
Demonstration that the sacrificer’s friend acts as the agent.
Even after the death of the sacrificer, the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice must be completed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
This is to be understood from the statement: "The *sarvasvāra* [is to be performed] after the death of the sacrificer.
The word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is equivalent to "single-cup vessel" (*ekapāla*), as in the expression: "the sacrificer is the single-cup vessel."

On the grounds that the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) expresses its own number when denoting a single sacrificer, an adaptation (*ūha*) is made in a performance involving two sacrificers, because it occurs in a context where its own number is to be expressed.
Bhāṣya 9.1.1.10.
The disposal (*pratipatti*) of the fires and the sacrificial vessels within the body of the sacrificer occurs during the concluding rite (*paridhānīya-karma*).
For the meaning of the term *dīkṣā* is indeed a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer.

Bhāṣya 10.6.15.52: Purificatory rites for the sacrificer (*yajamāna-saṃskārāḥ*). In the Jyotiṣṭoma, [it is said]: "He shaves his hair and beard, cleanses his teeth, clips his nails, and bathes"; "He anoints him; he anoints him with a reed-shaft. These purificatory rites for the sacrificer, such as shaving and so forth, benefit the primary sacrifice and do not benefit the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*); this is to be understood from the section titled "The Authority Connected with the Master" (*svāmiyuktādhikāra*). The purificatory rites for the sacrificer are for the sake of all sacrificers.
Regarding the *sattra*:
this should be understood from the statement, "In a *sattra*, there are purificatory rites for the sacrificers" (*yajamāna-saṃskārāḥ*).

And since these purificatory rites for the sacrificers serve as instruments for making [the performers] fit to receive the fruit—rather than being subordinate elements (*guṇabhūta*) of the sacrifice—it will be stated later (3.7.16) that even those who fall on the side of being enjoyers (*bhoktṛtvāṃśa*) possess the status of being knowers of the sacrifice (*yāgajña*).
Or [it may be as follows]: Vārttika 3.1.7.4, p. 718.

Regarding the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer, their form is such that they must occur prior [to the main act] because there is no release [of the obligation] beforehand; this is established in the case of the fire-piling (*cayana*).

It has been stated in the section "The injunction (*codanā*), moreover, is the commencement" (2.1.2.6) that the sacrifice (*yajati*) accomplishes the *apūrva*, and that subsequently, from that *apūrva*, the fruit arises at a later time.
Bhāṣya 7.4.12:
*yaji* denotes an act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) qualified by a specific recipient (*uddeśya*).
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 749: *yaji* denotes the collective whole consisting of the relinquishment of a substance intended for a deity (*devatoddeśa-dravyatyāga*).

p. 748 | Regarding the statement that in the case of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), there is a subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) toward the visible fruit—that [subordinate status] is understood to be impossible unless it brings about the *apūrva*.
Bhāṣya 7.1.3.
The meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is the connection between the substance and the deity. Bhāṣya 10.1.10.42:
The meaning of *yaj* is [the act] because it consists of a substance being offered with a dedication (*praśipya*) toward a deity by means of a sacrificial verse (*yājyā*).

The establishment that [the Agnihotra] is an injunction for a ritual act involving sacrifice (yajimat-karma-vidhānatva) is based on the established conclusion (siddhānta) of the section concerning the Animal and Soma sacrifices (paśusomādhikaraṇa).
Su. pṛ. 125.

Regarding the term *yaji* (the act of sacrificing), even in the case of that which is called the *agnīṣomīya*, one must accept its status as denoting an action (*karman*) denoted by *yaji*, as established in this very section (2.1.6).
This constitutes the discussion concerning injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) in the section on the Animal and Soma sacrifices (Paśusomādhikaraṇa).
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha, p. 925.
Certain *yajus* formulas are recited in all three Vedas, and likewise certain *ṛc* verses.
According to Vārttika 3.1.1, those very *yajus* formulas are designated as *nigadas* by virtue of the quality of being recited in a loud tone (*uccaiḥ*).
Bhāṣya 2.1.3.43: In those *yajus* which are not addressed to another, the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is established.
"The *yajus* indeed [are characterized by this], because they possess that form" (2.1.3.40); thus it is stated that *nigadas* are simply a specific variety of *yajus*. Bālakrīḍā, p. 58.

The oneness of the *yajus*: as many words as constitute a *yajus* by definition, which serve as a means for the sacrifice and yet remain syntactically expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) when separated, that many form a single *yajus*.
(Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.46).
"For the purpose of expiation for a deficiency in the Yajus, one should offer an oblation in the Dakṣiṇāgni with the formula, 'Abhūḥ svāhā.
The character of being Yajus belongs to the Nigadas."
The section concerning the *nigada*;
the section concerning the measure of the *yajus*;
and the distinction between *yajus* formulas among those that are equal in being mutually independent (*parasparanirākāṅkṣatva*).

In the section concerning *yajuryukto dakṣiṇā* (10.1.3.21–74), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established that, like the *prākāśya* lamps, the *yajus*-joined [gift] also excludes the portion belonging to the *adhvaryu*. However, the conclusion is that since two new items (*apūrva*) are being enjoined as the *prākāśya* lamps, it is logical that they should set aside the *adhvaryu*'s share (10.1.3.17–64).

In this case, however, seventeen sets of seventeen [cows] are prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) collectively, by way of setting aside the ordinary sacrificial fee. Among these, the giving of the one yoked with the *yajus* formula is already established; it was settled that while its distribution to either the Adhvaryu or another priest was initially obtained, it is restricted specifically to the Adhvaryu (Bālambhaṭṭī, p.
17). Thus, the one yoked with the *yajus* formula shall be the Adhvaryu’s entitlement as the sacrificial fee.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, seventeen chariots, gold neck-ornaments (*niṣka*s), and other such items—numbering seventeen each—are given to the seventeen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*s).
Regarding this, the scripture states: "He gives the chariot yoked with *yajus*-verses to the Adhvaryu.
This chariot yoked with *yajus*—that is, the chariot joined together by means of the *yajus* mantra—should serve as the substitute for the Adhvaryu’s share of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
"The chariot yoked with the Yajus belongs to the Adhvaryu alone, and nothing else"—
this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Alternatively, since all [the verses] have become part of the revealed scripture (*śruti*), his specific share is restricted.
The word "api vā" (or rather) sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Since all seventeen chariot-forms constitute the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) as established by scripture—being enjoined by the scriptural statement "seventeen chariots"—there must indeed be one horse for the *adhvaryu*.
By that means, his portion is restricted: it is the chariot yoked with a sacrificial formula (*yajuryukta*).
"To the Adhvaryu alone, and not to another"—just as [the ritual duties] belong to the Hotṛ alone among the priests, or to the Udgātṛ alone.

On whichever chariot the two horses are yoked by means of the *yajus* formula, that chariot which has been made yoked by the *yajus* and harnessed with horses is indeed "yoked by the *yajus*" (*yajuryukta*); likewise, there are those "yoked by the *ṛc*" (*ṛyukta*) and "yoked by the *sāman*" (*sāmayukta*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is no replacement of the Adhvaryu’s entire share of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) by means of the chariot.

In the section concerning "that which is yoked by the *yajus*" (*yajuryukta*) (10.1.2.74–75), it is stated that in the Vājapeya sacrifice, the chariot prescribed for the "yoked by the *yajus*" is to be combined with the Adhvaryu’s share as extended by analogy (*atideśa*).
Bāla, p. 177: The chariot yoked with the Yajus-mantras is the chariot of the sacrificer at the Vājapeya sacrifice, prepared with the mantras beginning with "Thou art the thunderbolt of Indra" (Vi.

"In the Vājapeya sacrifice, one gives a chariot yoked with Yajus-formulas to the Adhvaryu priest. This constitutes a prohibition in the form of a restriction regarding what was otherwise obtained as an unrestricted option.
Bāla. p. 17.
This is the section concerning the chariot yoked with Yajus-formulas (Yajuryuktādhikaraṇa).
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, because it is enjoined by a Yajus mantra, there is a combination of the Adhvaryu’s other portions, such as those consisting of female slaves and so forth.
"The chariot yoked with a *yajus* formula should belong to the *adhvaryu*; this is his entitlement.
Commentary: There is the *vājapeya* sacrifice.
In that context, it is recited: "He gives the chariot yoked with a *yajus* formula to the *adhvaryu*."

In this regard, the meaning of the three [points] is as follows: Is that which is joined with the *yajus* a substitute for the portion of the *adhvaryu*, or is it a restriction regarding the portion? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That which is joined with the *yajus* should be the entitlement of the *adhvaryu* to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of setting aside doubt.
Indeed, there is no doubt.
It is understood that one gives the chariot yoked with a *yajus* to the *adhvaryu*, and not anything else.
That chariot, having set aside the portion belonging to the *adhvaryu*, is unable to effect the exclusion of any other specific items that are obtained through the general rule (*codaka*).

The connection is not made in this way—that one gives [the chariot] at the Vājapeya when it is joined with the Yajus—by which a connection with the sacrifice (*ṛtu*) would be understood. Why? Because the Vājapeya is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), whereas the Adhvaryu is mentioned by means of a distinct syntactical statement (*vākya*).
Furthermore, the sentence is more authoritative than the context;
therefore, the *rayi* excludes the portion belonging to the Adhvaryu.
Alternatively, because it is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), his portion is restricted.
Commentary: The word "api" (even/also) serves to exclude the alternative view.
For all the chariots are indeed mentioned in the revealed scripture (*śruti*) by way of a general statement: "He gives seventeen [of each];
seventeen chariots, seventeen gold coins, seventeen female slaves, seventeen young women, seventeen hundreds of cows, and seventeen of each kind of bird."
Therefore, seventeen chariots have been obtained for all [the priests] without distinction and must be distributed;
in that regard, it is not known which chariot belongs to whom.
Therein, the Adhvaryu priest—who is connected with the Yajus formulas—is obtained as an option, and he is now restricted [to a specific one].
He gives that which is joined with the Yajus to the Adhvaryu, and not another, nor to anyone else;
likewise, that which is joined with the Ṛc to the Hotṛ, and not another, nor to anyone else.
In this regard, the mention of "joined with the Yajus" in that context is for the purpose of prescription; it is not intended to exclude the Adhvaryu's share.
And upon its non-occurrence, that which is obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) will come into effect.
Therefore, the *rayi* is restricted to the portion of the Adhvaryu; it does not exclude that portion.
This concludes the section on those joined by the *yajus* (Yajurveda). [3186] In the Yajurveda.

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, after prescribing the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) with the words, "Sixty chariots for the priests, sixty female slaves," it is heard: "He gives the chariot harnessed by a *yajus* to the Adhvaryu priest" (*yajuryuktaṃ ratham adhvaryave dadāti*).
[The term *yajuryukta* means "prepared with *yajus* mantras," such as "Thou art the thunderbolt of Indra.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: does the chariot harnessed by a *yajus* exclude the share of the Adhvaryu?
In this regard: "The *yajuṣ* connected with the *prākāśa* would be its sublater;
however, this is not a sublater of that which is already established, for this is merely a restrictive rule (*niyama*)."—Soma:

If there is a sublation of the portion (*bhāga*) through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) even when the word *dakṣiṇā* is present, then what need be said when it is absent? This is the connection [of the argument].
Vi— "The *yajuryukta* [chariot] sets aside the portion of the *adhvaryu* and also restrains it;
the setting aside is like that of the *prākāśa* [vessels]; thus, in this case, the morning [portion] is restricted.

Bhaṭṭa—In the *Vājapeya*, it is heard in scripture: "He gives seven hundred sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*): seven hundred chariots, seven hundred female slaves, seven hundred gold neck-ornaments (*niṣka*), seven hundred weapons, seven hundred hundreds of cows, and seven hundred youths."

In that case as well, the original (archetypal) gift itself is enjoined as qualified by a specific substance for the purpose of receiving [the guest] first; thus, there is the displacement of the original substance.
And in that context, it is heard in scripture: "He gives a chariot yoked with a *yajus* to the Adhvaryu," and so forth.

Even there, just as in the case of "he gives two *prākāśa* mirrors to the Adhvaryu," the chariot yoked with a *yajus* displaces the portion belonging to the Adhvaryu that would otherwise be given, because when there is a modified (variant) substance, the original substance is set aside, and the distribution of the original purpose and so forth is also sublated by the distribution of the modified substance.

This being the position reached, it is not the case here that a chariot yoked with a Yajus-mantra is enjoined as something distinct, like the *prākāśa* [vessel], such that the exclusion of other portions could be asserted. Rather, the chariot yoked with a Yajus-mantra, already established by the preceding sentence, is obtained for any priest whatsoever; however, out of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is restricted specifically to the Adhvaryu. Furthermore, since its acquisition occurs only in conjunction with other items such as female slaves and the like, it is restricted precisely in that form. Therefore, there are two restrictions (*niyama*) in this case.

For just as there is no restriction regarding the recipient (*prāpta*), such that it could be anyone at all—resulting in no restriction on the form of the recipient and so forth—likewise, there would be no restriction on the form of the Yajus-mantra associated with the Adhvaryu priest, such that it might be applied sometimes and not others.
Furthermore, because both types of restriction would constitute separate results, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

However, in the cognition produced by the word, since the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) cannot be logically connected as the intended object (*uddeśyatva*), the instrumental case (*caturthī*) indicates the status of being an object (*karmatva*); thus, a mantra associated with the Yajus is enjoined for the sake of the Adhvaryu.
However, since the gift (*dāna*) is the substratum (*āśraya*) for that which has reached its storage, there is a disparity with the *prākāśa* [offering].

For this very reason, it is not appropriate to accept [the gift] as having the restriction (*niyama*) as its result—just as one does not accept that the number [of vessels] has the *yava* and other grains as its result.
Therefore, there is no exclusion of other portions here.
Maṇḍana: "The Yajurveda approaches the Adhvaryu priest, and no other. Śaṅkara: "He is not considered [to be so] when joined with the Yajus;
he is the Blessed One (Bhagavān)."
Mantra is of three kinds: that which has the form of *yajus*, that which has the form of *ṛc*, and that which has the form of *sāman*. (Bālam Bhaṭṭī, p. 58). The definition of *yajus* is as follows:
the term *yajus* applies to what remains [after the other two].
Commentary: Now, what is the definition of a *yajus*?
The definition of a *yajus* need not be stated separately;

it is understood through the very definitions of *ṛc* and *sāman* by way of contrast. That which is neither a chant (*gīti*) nor composed in metrical feet (*pādabaddha*), but is recited in prose (*praśliṣṭapāṭha*), is a *yajus*.

Or rather, it should be explained as a compound, in accordance with the rule: "The word *brāhmaṇa* [is used] in the sense of the remainder. Vi: When it is suspected that there might be a confusion (*sāṃkarya*) regarding the measures (*lakṣa*) of the *ṛc*, *sāman*, and *yajus*, [the author] states: "The measure of a quarter (*pāda*) is [defined by] a sung [verse] or a recited [verse]; thus there is no confusion."
Yajus-mantras are those mantras taught as prose, being devoid of metrical structure and song.
According to the Bhāṭṭas, the nature of a Yajus is the state of being a mantra distinct from Ṛk and Sāman;
thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to the *stobha* syllables, as they also possess that same nature.
Maṇḍana: "A mantra that is distinct from the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda is indeed a Yajus.
Śaṅkara: "The definition of the Yajuses is likewise [stated].
(The word "has been stated" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.)
The Yajurveda is known as the *Ādhvaryava-pravacana* (the instruction for the Adhvaryu priest).
Su. p. 757. Whatever is enjoined by the Yajurveda, whether it be optional (*kāmya*) or occasional (*naimittika*), all that must be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Vā. 3.3.2.9. The tone of the Yajurveda is *upāṃśu*.
Bhāṣya 3.3.1.12: In the Yajurveda, the ritual details (dharmas) regarding milking and pouring out [the oblation] are recited.
Vi. 3.3.16: In the Yajurveda, the entire procedure—including the substance, the deity, and the action—is traditionally handed down;
however, in other Vedas, after merely mentioning the action, the hymns (stotras), recitations (śastras), and so forth are recited.
Consequently, because [the sacrifice] possesses both a material substance (*dravya*) and a deity (*devatā*), it is impossible to enjoin an independent action as something distinct.
In the Yajurveda, however, since the complete form [of the sacrifice] is prescribed, the sacrifice can be accomplished even without the *stotra* (hymns) and other such elements.
Vārttika 3.3.4.10: In the Yajurveda, there is a subordinate section concerning the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), while the major section pertains exclusively to the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*).

VI. 3|8|10, in the Yajurveda, specifically the Soma-Yajurveda (3186): "One should sacrifice"; the acquisition of the sacrificial materials and [the worship] of deities such as Indra and Agni—this is the injunction therein.
Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma:
the wearing of a golden garland prescribed in the Yajurveda for the Vājapeya belongs to all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), not to the Adhvaryu alone (Vi.
3.8.5). Because they are prescribed as primary characteristics ordained by the Yajurveda, the *sāmans* of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) are to be recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Pāṇini 3.3.12, p. 813. In the expression "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), there are two parts: the verbal root *yaji* and the suffix.
Within that suffix, there are also two parts: the quality of being a verb (*ākhyātatva*) and the quality of being an optative (*liṅtva*).

In this context, because of its *liṅ* suffix, there is the verbal productive energy (*śābdī-bhāvanā*), and because of its verbal inflection (*ākhyātatva*), there is the objective productive energy (*ārthī-bhāvanā*). In the expression "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the meaning of the verbal inflection is "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*). Regarding this productive energy, there is a threefold expectancy: "what? refers to the result to be accomplished, which is the goal; "by what? refers to the instrument, which is the means; and "how? refers to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), that is, the collection of auxiliary parts—the collection of supportive factors.

In that context, the objective productive urge (*arthabhāvanā*) connects with heaven and so forth due to the expectancy for an end (*bhāvya*); with sacrifice and so forth due to the expectancy for an instrument (*karaṇa*); and with the entire collection of auxiliary parts—such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*), the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and the threshing (*avaghāta*)—due to the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
The intended meaning is that heaven is attained by performing the sacrifice after having performed the fore-sacrifices and other such acts. (Vi.

2.1.1, Varṇaka 2) In the expression "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the suffix denotes the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) by way of its form as a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*); and because it is a prescriptive suffix (*liṅpratyaya*), it possesses the quality of impelling a person toward action by virtue of being an injunction (*vidhi*).
And since a person does not engage in action without a fruit, the Sūtra and its Bhāṣya on that point [state]:
"In the case of 'one should sacrifice' (yajeta), the sacrificial act is what is to be enjoined; and the singularity residing in the verb is its qualifier. (PMS 6.1.1)
Since an action implies an agent, the agent as well must be enjoined by way of the action.
Furthermore, the number residing in the enjoined agent ought to be intended to be expressed.
In the case of *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"), the verbal *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is understood through the *liṅ* (optative) portion of the suffix.

That [injunctive suffix] has three parts: the *bhāṣya* (the verbal expression), the *karaṇa* (the instrument), and the *itikartavyatā* (the procedure). Among these, according to Mīmāṃsā, the *arthabhāvanā* is to be understood through the *ākhyātatva* (verbal nature) aspect residing in the suffix; the *karaṇa* is the knowledge of the *liṅ* (injunctive suffix) which brings about the object to be produced by the *bhāvanā*, as well as the excellence (*prāśastya*) obtained from the *arthavāda*; and the *itikartavyatā* is the manner of performance. In the case of "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), this very self [of the injunction] is merely a restatement of what is already established by the injunction. (Soma. 6.1.2). In "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and so forth, there are two parts: the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).
The suffix *pratyaya* has an unprecedented meaning (*apūrvārtha*),
and that meaning is what is called *bhāvanā*. The word *bhāvanā* is derived from the root *bhū* with the causative suffix *ṇic*.

One performs [the action] in cultivation (*bhāvanā*); from "to perform" (*karoti*), one desires "to be" (*bhavati*). Thus, by means of the sense of "performing," the meaning of "cultivating" (*bhāvayati*) is established in all verbal forms (*ākhyāta*).
(Commentary on Vārttika 2.1.12.1): The agent is implied by the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*);
that agent is further specified by the term "desirous of heaven" (*svargakāma*).

As in the case of "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. And the qualification becomes a constituent part of the ritual action (1.1.12). Having heard the word "should sacrifice," which expresses the productive urge (bhāvanā), it implies a human goal.
And that [expectancy] is anticipated: which part does it fulfill first?
In that regard, the sacrifice is enjoined as the means (*upāya*).
At *Jaiminīyasūtra* 1.1.12, by the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the necessity of the triad—consisting of the result, the instrument, and the procedure—is expressed.
5|1|5|8. The meaning of "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is: "one should perform a sacrifice" or "one should act by means of a sacrifice.
Only the mere expression of existence is understood, not the agent of the fruit nor its substratum.
The meaning of the root *yaj* is either the instrument or the object.

Bhāṣya 6.2.16: In the expression "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), the preceding part expresses the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), while the subsequent part [expresses] "he should bring about" (*bhāvayet*). Similarly, in "dadāti" (he gives), the preceding part expresses the meaning of the root *dā* (to give), while the subsequent part restates that very [action] as "he should bring about. Likewise, in "juhoti" (he offers oblations), the preceding part expresses the meaning of the root *hu* (to offer), while the subsequent part restates that very [action] as "he should bring about. The final part [of each verb] is the expression of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
It is the same everywhere.

In the case of "he gives" (*dadāti*), it is understood that one should accomplish [the result] through giving; thus, giving alone is perceived as the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the meaning is that one should effect [the result] by means of the sacrifice (*yāga*).
For sacrifice (*yāga*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*).
"One should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is the injunctive scripture (*viniyoga-śruti*) consisting of a single word ending in a verbal suffix.
Bāla. p. 42. When "one should sacrifice" is stated, there arises a threefold expectancy: what [is to be accomplished], by what [means], and how.

In that context, once the requirement for "what" and "by what" has been satisfied by the result and the instrument respectively, and while the requirement for "how" remains unobstructed, because no procedure (*itikartavyatā*) has been mentioned in close proximity, a sentence of equal status presents itself to the mind; that presented sentence brings its own meaning into proximity. By this means—namely, through the laying of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) and so forth—the procedure becomes connected.

In this way, O Caitra, properties (*dharmas*) are obtained through similarity; in the absence of similarity, there is no acquisition of properties. (Duṣa. 8|1|2|12). When it is said "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), it must be understood that this does not contradict the acts of *juhoti* and *lāti*. (Vā. 3|4|14|1, p. 982). When the word "one should sacrifice" is uttered, the expectations (*ākāṅkṣās*) arise as to what [is to be sacrificed], by what means, and in what manner.
In that regard, what is it? It is the constant desire for the human goal, whether directly or indirectly;
thus, the production of the verbal root occurs.
Even in the case of "one should cook rice," there exists the expectancy of "what? (kiṃ).
There, at the cooking,
he should sacrifice the sacrificial implements.
The procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is indicated by perception and other means of knowledge;
here (in the case of Vedic ritual), it is indicated by the scripture (*śāstra*).
However, the threefold expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the same [in both cases].

*Ḍupa* 7|8|1|2: Expressions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) arise with expectancy (*sākāṅkṣā*), [asking] "what, by what means, and how?"; they become free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣā*) through the purpose expressed by the phrase "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*).

*Bhāṣya* 2|1|1: By the verbal root (*dhātu*) in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) or "one should offer oblations" (*juhuyāt*), the action (*kriyā*) is expressed; by the suffix (*pratyaya*), the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.
Of these two, the agent is the primary element,
while the action is subordinate. The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together.
1.1.4.122: "One should sacrifice," "one should offer oblations," and "one should give"—these [words] constitute a difference of action due to the difference in verbal roots (*śabdāntara*).
"One should sacrifice" means that one should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice; the sense is that one should exert oneself for the sake of heaven.
However, this remains to be known: what exactly is this exertion?
And in its proximity, the laying of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) and other rites are heard [in scripture].
Because it is required by that [sacrifice] and because of its proximity, this operation belongs to that which possesses it—namely, that by which the sacrifice produces heaven—as in the injunction:
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*). (1.1.2.10)
There is a distinction regarding their application to the performance [of the sacrifice]; otherwise, the statement would be merely a meaningless utterance.
Furthermore, in the term "sacrificial implements" (yajñāyudha), the offering of these [implements] is supported.
"Whose weapons are the means of accomplishing the sacrifice.

Otherwise, by direct hearing (*śravaṇa*), the weapons would belong to the digging out of the ground and so forth, while [their connection] to the sacrifice would be through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And in this way, the number is appropriately accounted for, because it is heard as one in relation to the sacrifice.
Otherwise, because various meanings are heard, the number [of deities] would not be appropriate as a specification.
Therefore, they should be offered.
Since it is enjoined without distinction within the context, it must pertain to the primary sacrifice.

"dup—" (Now, since their purpose for the acts such as *udvāhana* [lifting] is already established in the third book through application according to their respective connections, why is anything further considered here? To this he says: Since the status of being a "thing to be offered" (*pradeyatva*) has been refuted here, the consideration in the third book [is relevant]. (The question is: should all acts such as *udvāhana* be performed by all [the substances], or according to their specific connection?
However, here the very status of being a "thing to be offered" is first taken up and refuted.)

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states: "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhāni*)—this is an injunction regarding the *sphya* and other items as means for the sacrifice, because [the word] has its own primary meaning (since the term *yajñāyudha* refers to its literal sense). Otherwise (if it were a restatement of those things already obtained through their roles in digging and so forth), there would be a secondary sense (i.e., it would function by implication). If these (the *sphya* and others) bring about the sacrifice when they are being offered, then they become the instruments of the sacrifice.

This term *yajñāyudha* (sacrificial implement) denotes a means of accomplishment; therefore, in that case [the view that they are to be offered], the word *yajñāyudha* is used in its primary sense. Otherwise [if it were not stated that they are to be offered], it would be used in a secondary sense [by treating them as instruments for accomplishing the sacrifice through an indirect process]. [It is thus expressed by a figurative term.]
The printed reading "yāgasādhanatvāviśeṣe'pi" (or "yāgaviśeṣe'pi") is incorrect.

[The correct reading is] "pradhānasādhanānyeva. How so? Regarding the words "etāni vai daśa yajñāyudhāni," [the printed edition contains the additional phrase: "(atra 'darśapūrṇamāsayorāmnātān pradhānasyaiva aṅgaṃ' iti adhikaṃ mudrite" (here, the phrase "these [items] recited in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa are indeed the subsidiary parts of the primary sacrifice" is an addition in the printed edition).

Furthermore, this is not found in the *Tannaratna*. Sentences that are syntactically expectant (*sākāṅkṣāṇi*) within a context attain syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the subject matter at hand—the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Therefore, these have no connection with the *prayāja* offerings and other such subsidiaries (*aṅga*).

Alternatively, because of the scriptural statement "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements" (*etāni vai daśa yajñāyudhāni*), which is recited in the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, they are a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the primary sacrifice itself, and not of the *prayāja* offerings and the like.

(Now, since the word *yajña* denotes sacrifice in general, it is logical that the substances prescribed by reference to that [sacrifice]—by overriding the context (*prakaraṇa*)—should serve both the subsidiaries and the primary rite, just as the altar and its components do.
To this, he says: In the statement "that which he places for the Vaiśvānara," the act of placing, which is already established by the sense of the matter, is restated, and the altar is enjoined.
The placing of the oblations for the subsidiaries and the primary rite is already established by the general rule (*adhi*).

Therefore, in that case [where there is a conflict with the context], the sentence establishes that the accessory belongs to both the primary and the subsidiary acts; however, here in the statement "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements," nothing is being restated (such that, by restating everything, the substances being enjoined would become applicable to all acts).
Indeed, it is not possible for one of the two compounds to be the subject of reference while the other is the injunctive element.
(This being so,) the number [of ten] is also justified through its connection with a single action.
"But because substances have distinct purposes, they are connected with their own respective purposes; therefore, they should be used according to the scriptural injunction.
The Commentary states: "And this is not the case that there is an injunction [to use them] as offerings (*pradeya*).
It is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because they are already established by other means."

"One digs with the *sphya*," "they cook on the potsherds," "he pours out [the grain] with the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle," "he winnows with the winnowing-basket," "he spreads the black antelope skin under the mortar and pestle," "with the winnowing-basket he places the grinding-stone upon the *śamyā*," "he threshes with the sprinkled mortar and pestle," and "he grinds with the sprinkled grinding-stone and millstone"—in this manner, the acts of digging and so forth are obtained through their respective sentences.
The restatement of what has already been obtained is an *anuvāda*.
Furthermore, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the sentence (*vākya*).
It is logical that the word *yajñāyudha* (sacrificial implements) functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*), not as an injunction (*vidhi*).
For that word "implement" is used figuratively with respect to the wooden sword (*sphya*) and other such items.
Furthermore, the number [of implements] will be intended merely as a recitation (*pāṭha*).
And this is clearly established by acts such as digging, whereby the wooden sword (sphya) and other implements are enjoined;
for there exists an injunction therein, such as "he digs with the wooden sword," and so forth. But there is no injunction that the sacrificial implements themselves must be produced.

Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those [instruments] already obtained through the sentence concerning digging and so forth. When the expectation arises—"Something must be done with the *sphya* by means of the instrumental case ending"—and that [expectation] for a purpose is satisfied by another word (*udvanti*), which provides the act of digging, then [the *sphya*, etc. no longer have an expectation toward that [act]. Consequently, they expect a purpose; thus, digging and so forth constitute the purpose of these [instruments, such as the *sphya*].
Through the context, there may or may not be a connection with the seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtu*).

Furthermore, while the word "weapon" (*āyudha*) is well-known in its primary sense as referring to weapons such as arrows and the like, it occurs in reference to the *sphya* and other implements only through figurative (secondary) usage (*lakṣaṇā*);
for both of them are indeed means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Furthermore, when a direct injunction (*vidhi*) is present, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not logical;
therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) because it serves as praise.
For there exists an injunction: "They collect the sacrificial implements."

Since it is understood as a single syntactical unit by virtue of being a cluster [of words], it does not require a separate injunction, for that would entail the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*).
Furthermore, the number refers to the means of accomplishment.
And they are enjoined for the purposeful rites (*arthakarman*).

The Commentary states: "In the purposeful rites, such as the *puroḍāśa* cakes and so forth, they [the implements] are enjoined; these too would be subject to option (*vikalpa*), and in that case, there would be sublation (*bādha*).
There is no combination (*samuccaya*), because the *puroḍāśa* cakes and so forth are independent due to their connection with the sacrifice, as are the *sphya* and other implements."
Or rather thus:
they are enjoined for ritual acts involving material objects;
they are enjoined for the rite of donning [the garment] with the words, "Those who have established the sacred fires strike this [post] with the sacrificial vessels."
If they were offered there, they would not exist [as distinct entities].
Therefore, for this reason as well, they should not be offered.

Duh—(In this regard, the Commentator states that in the case of purposeful rites (*arthakarma*), such as the *Āgneya* and *Āgnīṣomīya* sacrifices, the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and other such items are not mentioned; therefore, there is no optionality between them.)

Having stated that there can be no combination because of the injunction being independent [of other rules]—lest there be the contingency of partial sublation (*pākṣikabādha*)—he then states another interpretation (*varṇakāntara*): "In the ritual of wearing [the garment], the observation of the vessels is appropriate as the object to be offered.

With the intention that the objection raised against the option (*vikalpa*) regarding partial sublation is not sound, he says: "This option is improper, because the injunctions are unequal (*viṣamaśiṣṭatvāt*).
There is indeed the same inconsistency even in the second interpretation."
How so? (In the prima facie view: because of the injunction, "He cuts twice from the middle and from the front half," only that much is offered in the oblation, and thus a remnant remains.
By means of that, the sacrificer will be able to eat.
This is not so.
(Why? Because death is uncertain; for even if one dies after a long time, [the implements such as] the *sphya* and others would have their forms destroyed.
It might be argued that this is not so because of the offering of abundant materials.
In that case, sacrificial vessels (*yajñapātra*) would not be possible [to maintain], for a sacrificial vessel is defined by its material belonging to the class of the *sphya* and other such items.)
Upon the disappearance of the genus, that [usage] is no longer possible.
Alternatively, because there is the relinquishment of a substance intended for a deity, they are independent;
therefore, they must be employed at each performance (since it is impossible for another sacrificer to relinquish again those things already used in one performance).

In that interval, when one is dying, it is impossible for those [materials] to be taken up by the body even if they have not been used [in a sacrifice], precisely because they have not been used. (For materials that have been used in a single ritual do not perform their function in another.)

Alternatively, when the gift of the substance has been set aside for the sake of the sacrifice, that which was previously a sacrificial vessel (in its entirety) due to the setting aside of the substance becomes such no longer at the time of death (because it is now deficient); thus, [the status of] being a sacrificial vessel is not applicable.
However, if it is for the purpose of carrying away the remains and so forth, there is nothing contradictory, as this is seen from the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states: "And because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*): 'Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day; thirteen on the new moon day.
For this reason also, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
[Here follows the difficult question (*duppraśna*), which is printed in the Ānandāśrama edition and others under the preceding sūtra.]

Since the *Tantraratna* introduces [the discussion] with the words, "It implies the sūtra 'And because of the observation of an indicative mark' (*liṅgadarśanācca*)," it appears that this sūtra is necessary here.

(The phrase "and because of the observation of an indicative mark" implies the sūtra. In both cases (both in the prima facie view and the established conclusion), the numbers fourteen and thirteen are the same.
(Why? Because there is no difference in the substance, the fuel, or the oblations.
Because there is a single deity, a single oblation shall be offered by all.
Regarding this, some say:

since [the implements such as] the wooden sword (*sphya*) and so forth are set aside by the substance (*dravya*, such as the *puroḍāśa* cake) due to the division of the sentence concerning the material, they postulate a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*). Thus, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it follows that a separate ritual action alone must be enjoined by this sentence; therefore, the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga-darśana*) is appropriate.
He refutes this position of the proponent of a single part: "This is not tenable.
For a distinct ritual act does not arise merely through the connection with a substance [or a different deity].
Therefore, it must be explained otherwise."

The rule "he offers fourteen times" prescribes the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) for all oblations within the context. In this regard, ten substances each have been mentioned as the means for these other oblations (for they are not merely *vrīhi* and *yava*, since they are enjoined together). Consequently, when the offering of each substance is performed, many fourfold portions result.
And it is heard that there is one *caturvatta* (fourfold portioning) at home.
If that were taken from only one [of the four fires], the status of the others as means [for that portioning] would be lost.
(If, for the sake of favoring them, it were taken from all and offered, then the singularity [of the portioning] would be lost.)
Therefore, the sacrifice is performed by offering that [substance] once for each fourfold portion (*caturavatta*).
But surely, having taken many portions, one should offer them all at once because the deity is the same,
just as in the case of the *sāṃnāyya*, where two fourfold portions are taken and offered together once?
It is said:

In that case, because the acts are distinct, when an offering is made together with another, one's own fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) is taken separately, and the other is also taken separately; thus, there is no violation of the rule regarding the fourfold portion.

Here, however, because the act is a single one, when performed together, [the ritual] is repeated out of fear of violating the rule regarding the fourfold portion, as in the case of the Soma sacrifice.
In that case, because [the implements] have not been consecrated by the *āhuti* offering, their being seen [as sacrificial tools] is not tenable.
For the Śruti, having enumerated "The wooden sword (*sphya*) and the potsherds (*kapāla*s)," states: "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudha*s). Is this...?
The section concerning the sacrificial implements;
the section concerning the lord of the sacrifice;
[regarding the formula] "Iḍā, invited! Invited Iḍā! May we partake of the Iḍā! Let the Iḍā be invoked! The Iḍā is invited," he says.

From this it is understood that this is the commencement, and that "the mantra of the iḍā" refers to what falls within its middle, beginning with "the humans are invited" (upahūtā manuṣyāḥ) and ending with "may he increase the lord of the sacrifice" (yajñapatiṃ vardhāt). Therefore, it is understood from the statement that one should say "the iḍā is invited."
Regarding the removal of the capable Śreḍī:
there is no scriptural statement that one must speak in order to encourage the sacrificer;
rather, there is merely the capacity to speak.
Nor do applications arise from a sentence merely by virtue of its inherent capacity; rather, in this way, the context of the *iḍā* will be upheld,
and there will be syntactic unity with the *iḍā*.
Therefore, this is the correct interpretation of the statement: "The humans who have been invoked are those capable of increasing the lord of the sacrifice.
In that context, it is the increase qualified by the lord of the sacrifice that must be expressed; thus, when a single sacrificer is mentioned, the function of the qualification is fulfilled.
Therefore, there is [only] one entitlement.
It may be so, like a primary injunction (*vidhi*).
Just as in a case where the sacrificer is enjoined as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), that injunction is accomplished by whichever sacrificer happens to perform it.
For example: "The *audumbarī* post is equal in measure to the sacrificer," and "The sacrificer touches the white [post].

Regarding the mantra "May it increase the lord of the sacrifice" (*yajñapatim vardhāt*), the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that since the increase is directly stated in relation to the lord of the sacrifice (*yajñapati*) through the word *iḍā*, it is direct (*pratyakṣa*); whereas in relation to the *iḍā* itself, it is indirect (*parokṣā*).
However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the word *yajñapati*, the "increase" (*vṛddhi*) is merely an attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*).
The increase [of the sacrificer] is equal to that of the *iḍā*,
because it forms a single syntactical unit with the *upahūta* (invocation) of the *iḍā*.
Now, as for what was said— that the statement regarding the increase of the sacrificer is understood as independent of the word *iḍā*— [that is not so].
It is said:
by the statement, "He who, knowing thus, moves with the *iḍā*," it is enjoined that one should move with the *iḍā*.
In that context, this mantra beginning with "The *iḍā* is invoked" and ending with "invoked by Brahmā and the gods" is for the purpose of the performance of the *iḍā*.
The purpose is for the invitation of the *iḍā*.
The passage beginning with "the lowly ones, the swift ones" (*dainyā acyarvayaḥ*) is for the invitation of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

All the officiating priests are indicated by the word "adhvaryu" through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, they alone are referred to [in the text] by the phrase "the humans have been invited" (*upahūtā manuṣyāḥ*).
"What are they like? It is said:
those who protect the sacrifice and who are capable of increasing the lord of the sacrifice—such men are invited.
Therefore, because it is a qualification of the human [sacrificer], the term *yajñapati* (lord of the sacrifice) is not set aside by that [general rule].

Śā—Regarding the text, "The humans who are invited, may they increase the lord of the sacrifice," since this serves to consecrate him by means of providing encouragement for the manifestation of the increase of the lord of the sacrifice, should it be recited in rituals involving multiple sacrificers, or should the word *yajñapati* not be recited in the same manner as the *iḍā*? And for that purpose, is this for the sake of consecrating the sacrificer who is denoted by the word *yajñapati*, or...
The extraction of the doubt is as follows:
"Since the *iḍā* is syntactically connected with the mantra, it should have the same purpose as the mantra;
its function for the sake of the master's nourishment is understood through its inherent capacity."
Moreover, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than a syntactical connection (*vākya*), and a visible purpose is observed here:

because it generates enthusiasm, [the mantra] would otherwise result in being for an unstated purpose (*aṭaṣṭārtha*) through mere praise. This is so that, when there are many sacrificers, all the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) may be accomplished.

When it is argued that [the mantra] should be used thus, "O Lord of Sacrifice, may you increase," it is replied: By virtue of the direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-vacana*), the mantra is subordinate to the offering of the *iḍā* portion; therefore, that which falls within the middle of that *nigada* is likewise [subordinate].
It is not possible for it to exist separately; therefore, its purpose as a praise is preferable.
An indicative mark (*liṅga*) must be postulated as the means of application (*viniyojaka*) for the manifestation of prosperity (*vṛddhi*).
Furthermore, by the word *yat*, the subservience of prosperity is enjoined through direct statement (*śruti*).
Furthermore, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is the manifestation of the increase for one's own purpose by the elder [priest].
However, in the *sattra* sacrifice, since the praise of the *iḍā* is accomplished by the manifestation of the increase of a single sacrificer, there is no modification (*ūha*).

If even the word "grain" (*dhānya*), which is used figuratively in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*) for Soma, were subject to modification, then what need is there to mention the word "sacrificer" (*yajñapati*), which is primary in the model sacrifice? Such is the connection of the points already stated.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Even though the word *yajñapati* (lord of the sacrifice) is addressed [to the sacrificer], because it exists for the sake of another (*parārthatva*), and because it is similar to the *iḍā* [invocation], there should be no modification (*avikāraḥ*); that is, there is no substitution (*nohaḥ*). This is according to the rule.

Just as in cases where the sacrificer is enjoined for the sake of another—such as in "the sacrificer touches the white [horse]" (*aśuklaṃ yajamāno 'nvārabhate*)—there the purpose is accomplished even by a single [sacrificer], so too here, the praise is accomplished even by the manifestation of the increase of a single sacrificer.
Regarding the modification (*ūha*): "The sacrificer is indeed the *yajñapati*; it is for the sake of increase," so says the first [view].

Since the mantra has been specifically prescribed for the purpose of the *iḍā*-offering, there is no modification (*nohana*) from that. Because the mantra has been specifically enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) for the purpose of the *iḍā*-offering, there is no modification (*ūha*) in the *satra*.
In the Bhaṭṭa school, this is now heard in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices:
"The Pitṛs have been invited, the Ṛṣis have been invited, the humans who have set out to increase this sacrificer—the lord of the sacrifice (yajñapati)—have been invited," and so forth.

Regarding that, in the case of a Sattra sacrifice, there arises the consideration whether the word *yajñapati* (lord of the sacrifice) should be modified (*ūhya*) because it is in the singular, or not. It is not the case that there is no modification because the meaning is already complete; for the lord of the sacrifice and his prosperity are connected to the ritual through the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), who are the agents of the action and are expressed by the words of the mantra.

Nor can there be modification (*ūha*) on the grounds that this [mantra] serves the purpose of another, despite its meaning being connected to the ritual act, because—unlike the *iḍopahāna* mantra—it lacks syntactic unity with the sentence and words of the *yajñapati-vṛddhi* (increase of the sacrificer) section, and thus does not manifest the increase of the sacrificer. This is because the sentence within the mantra, "asyonaṃ te" ("this pleasant seat for you"), is established by its indicative power (*liṅga*) as having the purpose of manifesting the increase of the sacrificer.
Nor is there the case of the "section concerning the sacrificer" (*yajñapatyadhikaraṇa*).

Having prescribed [the rule], "Knowing the invocation, he proceeds with the *iḍā*," the Brāhmaṇa passage—"Then he begins: 'The *iḍā* is invoked; we are invoked; let the *iḍā* call us; the *iḍā* is invoked'"—indicates through the citation of the opening words (*pratīka*) that the entire *nigada* is to be employed. Therefore, it must be argued that the mantra's own indicative power (*liṅga*) is set aside by the sentence within the mantra itself, as assisted by that [Brāhmaṇa]. However, this is not so; for while the Brāhmaṇa passage establishes the application of the mantra up to that point, there is no authority for the citation of the opening words [to apply to the whole].

Or rather, let there be the assumption of a comprehensive application (samastaviniyoga) based on the perceptible sentence itself for the taking up of the ritual portions (*pratīka*), out of fear of the cumbersome assumption of another application.

For this very reason, in cases such as "syonaṃ te," since there is no perceptible sentence enjoining the application, there is no harm even if the required application is assumed from the context (*arthavādakalpanā*).

Furthermore, in passages such as "ye yajñapatiṃ vardhān," by the force of the word *yat* alone, the human priests who are the agents of the sacrificer's increase are understood to be the objects of the invitation (*āhvāna*).
Therefore, by the force of the word *yat* (which), this [mantra] is subordinate to the offering of the *iḍā*.

For this very reason, even in the case of "syonaṃ te," if the word *yat* were present for the sake of the preceding portion, then there would indeed be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) there; however, since that is not the case, a division of the mantra is accepted.
In the present instance, however, because of the existence of the word *yat*, it is precisely subordinate to the offering of the *iḍā*.

Nevertheless, even though it is a remnant of the spreading [of the sacrificial grass], the mantra "May the lord of the sacrifice spread your thighs" must be employed for the purpose of encouraging the lord of the sacrifice; thus, its application as such is justified. In the case of a *satra* (a sacrificial session), that very [mantra] undergoes modification (*ūha*).
For in the case of mantras used for encouragement, such as "O Agni, give life to this one," there is neither modification nor repetition in a *satra*.

And therefore, although this is not the primary fruit [of the sacrifice], nevertheless, by means of a mere incidental encouragement (*ānuṣaṅgika-protsāhana*), even though this mantra is a subordinate part of the *iḍopahāna* (the offering of the *iḍā*), it serves the purpose of incidentally encouraging the patron of the sacrifice (*yajñapati*); thus, the modification (*ūha*) is indeed justified.

In reality, however, since the passage beginning with "He desires long life" (*āyur āśāste*), which forms a single syntactical unit with the words expressing the majesty of the striking and so forth, serves to indicate the fruit of the striking—as will be explained in the counter-example sūtra regarding the *satra* sacrifice where there is modification (*ūha*)—so too here, even though this [passage] is an injunction for the invocation of the *iḍā*, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the words for the invocation of the *iḍā*, it indicates the fruit of the invocation of the *iḍā*; therefore, modification (*ūha*) in the *satra* is indeed appropriate.

Indeed, there is no authoritative basis for the restriction that the fruit mentioned by a mantra must be indicated only by the instrumental case (tṛtīyā) and not otherwise; for even a mantra enjoined for a specific purpose, such as its application to a particular place, can—as in the case of the construction of a deity—likewise imply a fruit, provided there is no sublation. Nor is it the case that even when implying a required factor, a mantra cannot imply a fruit without the instrumental case, as seen where the *iḍā-upahāna* and so forth, though serving the purpose of consecrating the *iḍā*, have their function fulfilled therein.

It must be stated that even in the case of what is called the third [instrumental case], since the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is to be understood as the object of the instrument, there would result the necessity of establishing a deity solely on the basis of the words of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*) by virtue of its being expressed by the *sūktavāka*; for the instrumental case-relation thus understood could be fulfilled by the mere mention of the deity, just as the words "this heaven and earth" (*idaṃ dyāvā*) are fulfilled. Furthermore, the words "long life" (*āyuḥ*) and so forth are justified as being merely explanatory (*anuvādaka*), like the words "this heaven and earth," and there is no evidence for their being the originators of a fruit (*phala-kalpaka*). Therefore, the preceding mantra, "May my strength increase" (*mamāgne varcaḥ*), is what is taken up [as the relevant text].

Thus, because [the word] "iti" is employed to indicate a result, it brings about the postulation of a result; and even in the case of the offering of the *iḍā*, since it too is employed with the word "iti," it is logical that it should bring about the postulation of a result.

Furthermore, even in such cases, since the status of the sacrificer (*yajñapati*) as the object to be given away—and its qualifying attributes and so forth—is in every instance not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*) according to the actual state of things, it is unfit for manifestation. Moreover, if [the singular number] were established in every respect, then, just as in the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), the meaning would be understood by the nominal stem alone. It should not be asked: "How can the singular number, which serves the purpose of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), be modified (*ūha*) in the ectype (*vikṛti*)? For although it is not intended to be expressed in the archetype, the existence of that singular number is merely a conventional designation (*upacāra-kalpamātra*) for the sake of a greater referent; and since the manifestation of oneness is accomplished by that much alone, there is no evidence for assuming it serves the purpose of grammatical correctness.
Therefore, in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the modification (ūha) indeed succeeds for the purpose of manifesting that [increase].

This being the position reached, we reply: first of all, the fruit is not the increase of the sacrificer (yajñapati), because that which has already fulfilled its purpose through being the consumption of the *iḍā* does not, by its very nature, require a fruit.

Even this being the case, if there were an application toward the action by means of the third [case-ending] as the instrument (*karaṇa*), then the entire mantra would be an instrument for the action by way of manifesting the action; thus, in the first instance, its function would simply be the manifestation of the action. If that were impossible, its function would be the manifestation of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) in connection with that [action]. If even that were impossible, then the mantra would effect the action even though its own manifestation is not required. Otherwise, the entire mantra would fail to fulfill the purpose established by the Vedic text (*śruti*).

And in that case, because there is no separation from the departure [of the result], just as [the attainment] of the deity expressed by the mantra in the *sūktavāka* is to be postulated, so too is the fruit such as longevity (*āyus*) and the like.
However, where it is in every way impossible—as in the case of "This heaven... (*idaṃ dyāvā*) and so forth—it is indeed accepted that [the passage] has the nature of a praise (*stāvakatva*).

Furthermore, by the direction of the fire [mantras], it should be understood that even [qualities] such as luster (*varcas*) and the like constitute fruits in passages such as "My luster... (*mama agne*) and so forth.

Because even in that case, the fact of being enjoined by means of the particle *iti* has been established in the *Kaustubha*. For this very reason, a staff and the like do not possess causality toward a jar and the like by virtue of being a substance (*dravyatva*); nor does the sense organ possess causality toward that which is delimited by perceptibility (*pratyakṣatvāvacchinna*) by virtue of being a sense organ (*indriyatva*), because [the latter] is non-existent [in the case of the former]. The *putrakāmeṣṭi* here [is an example of] a *jāteṣṭi*. The author of the Sūtras (also) desires the *itikartavyatā* (procedural details) for obligatory rites, as he says: "It may occur even in the performance of a single [rite]" (6.1.15), and by citing the example "possessing offspring" (*prajāvattva*) in the passage: "In the sacrifice, because there are eight [results] such as possessing offspring, its commencement [is justified]" (referring to 6.2.31). By taking up the example "possessing offspring," he shows this as an established fact.
Furthermore, the injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*), which expresses the sense of "what ought to be done," does not deviate from the status of being for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārthatā*).

For a person does not engage in activity without a result—whether directly, as in the case of certain rites like the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, or indirectly, as in the case of others like the procreation of offspring (*prajā*); indeed, there is no injunction that is fruitless.

Moreover, if the meaning of the verbal root were to abandon its status as the instrument (*karaṇa*) when no result is heard [in the text], then names such as "procreation" (*prajā*) and so forth would not exist.

Because [the subjects and so forth] have become the field of action, they do not require this thought, "What must be done by me? (for, due to their state of equanimity, they do not require any other duty). And since they do not require it, how could they be connected with the *itikartavyatā* (the ritual procedure)? (Therefore, the accomplishment of the result occurs here [in the subjects]).

Furthermore, if the verbal root-meaning were to function as the instrument (*karaṇa*) only where the word for the fruit (*phalapada*) exists (otherwise it would be the object), then— since the verbal root-meaning is an object in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) due to the absence of a mention of the fruit, and since heaven (*svarga*) is an object in the performance injunction (*prayogavākya*)—

there would be no connection [between them] because both are equally objects (*karman*). And in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of [heaven] being a separate object in the fruit-injunction.

However, this fault does not arise when [the verbal root] functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, wherever there is an injunction (*vidhāyaka*), there the verbal root-meaning must be accepted as an instrument.
Since this [injunction] exists even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), the verbal root-meaning is indeed an instrument there as well; thus, the obligatory rite certainly exists.

The designations "optional" (*kāmya*) and "obligatory" (*nitya*) are appropriate respectively because of being something to be performed [only when desired] and because of being something that must necessarily be performed; therein, that which must necessarily be performed is the obligatory, while the other is the optional.
However, if they were both for the sake of a result, there would be no distinction between them.

In this case, the fruit arises from that which is designated as the *agnihotra* and that which is designated as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

Therefore, the cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni is [performed] together with the two *agnihotra*s, and the clarified butter (*ājya*) for Agni-Soma and the others on the full moon day;

As for what was stated—that because of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Full Moon [sacrifice] on the full moon day, and with the New Moon [sacrifice] on the new moon day," the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* denotes the sacrifice together with its subsidiaries—this is not so.

For when the two purposes— the purpose of the Full Moon sacrifice and the purpose of the fruit together with its subsidiaries— are established, then [the procedure] is enjoined as being with its subsidiaries.

It is not so even in the case of what is eternal (*nitya*). The section on "according to one's capacity" (yathāśaktyadhikaraṇa) establishes that the connection with "according to one's capacity" applies as a counter-correlative to the performance of the primary rite itself, and not to the subsidiaries.
For this very reason, even the *nimitta* (occasioning condition) is subsumed under the injunction of application (*viniyoga*) alone.

For this same reason, application (*viniyoga*)—being of the nature of a property that constitutes the object of the knowledge which generates activity—is common to both [the *nimitta* and the *uddeśya*].

For this very reason, the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) also belong to the primary rite (*pradhāna*) only subsequent to this [application], because they depend upon the cognition of that [primary rite] as possessing a fruit.

In this regard, however, there is this distinction: in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), the application of the subsidiaries occurs only after the knowledge that they possess the status of being means, as implied by the injunction. In the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), however, even when the knowledge arises that the non-performance of the sacrifice—which is based on the occasion (*nimitta*) and conjoined with the injunction—is the counter-positive of the non-existence [of the result], there is no connection with the subsidiaries, because such a connection is not required. Rather, it should be understood that subsequently, when the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) whose instrument is the primary act requires an end (*bhāvyā*), the destruction of previously committed sins is understood to be that end. Since everything from the *avadāna* (cutting) up to the *prakṣepa* (offering) constitutes a single unitary act, this [act] is characterized as a single action; therefore, even though there is no absolute identity of time between the *yāga*—which consists of the relinquishment of the substance for the sake of the deity and is performed immediately after the *vaṣaṭkāra*—and the *prakṣepa*, which includes the subsequent acts of pouring into the ladle, placing it upon the *āhavanīya* fire, and other such operations, their simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is nonetheless established.

At the very moment when the placement of the substance for the gift (dravyadāna) into the Āhavanīya fire is commenced by means of the characteristic double-portioning (dviravadāna), at that same moment, through the two sacrificial invitatory verses (yājyā-anuvākyā), the consecration of the entire sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is performed by way of recollecting the deity who is the object of the offering.

Su. Pṛ. 1536: Because the memory produced by the impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the exertion of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is stable, there is no possibility of an absolute temporal gap even for the sacrifice (*yāga*). At the moment of approaching the *āhavanīya* fire, there is the dedication (*uddeśa*) to the deity; at the subsequent moment of placing [the oblation] upon it, there is the relinquishment of the substance (*dravyatyāga*); and immediately thereafter comes the casting-in (*prakṣepa*). Thus, although the sacrifice and the casting-in do not occupy the exact same moment, an absolute temporal proximity (*atyantāntarya*) is possible. Furthermore, since it would be contrary to reason (*nyāyavirodha*) for destruction to occur in the interval between them, such a gap does not arise. Moreover, the simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is established because we observe common usage such as, "A cognition that arises with absolute temporal proximity is a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*).
p. 1536. In rites other than the sacrifice, such as the *cayana* (piling of the altar), there is no *svāhākāra* sacrifice (the fifth *prayāja*).
Bhāṭṭa 8.1.7. The definition of a sacrifice.
The impulsion of the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) pertains to the aggregate [of the act] involving the substance, the deity, and the action, because it achieves its purpose in that totality.
Bhāṣya: The application of the subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*) has been stated.
Now the definition of the primary element (*pradhāna*) is being stated: what is that primary element of which these are the subsidiaries?
It is said:
[the definition] is simply "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers.
Now, what indeed are the characteristics of sacrificing, offering, and giving?
The root *yajati* (to sacrifice) denotes a substance, a deity, and an action.
A substance is relinquished with reference to a deity, and there is an action belonging to that [relinquishment], by which the connection between those two is established.
The word *yajati* applies to this collection when these elements are combined.
Because it is desired in the world by means of this [sacrifice] together with the sacrificial animals (*paśu*),
we therefore conclude that the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) conveys the meaning of a substance, a deity, and an action. Thus, there is no need to state a further purpose for defining the definition.
"Knowledge alone is the purpose here. [Duhkha: This passage is intended to show that the purpose is fulfilled by the aggregate;
for the word "sacrifice" (yāga) does not denote all three—the substance, the deity, and the action—collectively.
What then? It is that which is expressed by the verbal root *yajati*.
As for the objection that "if the denotation belongs to the whole [root], then only one part would be denoted," this is not a fault, because the whole is well-established as the denotatum.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that the root *juhoti* involves the addition of pouring (*āsecanādhika*).
Some [hold] that because the verb *juhoti* (he offers) is present even in the case of the *puroḍāśa* cake, one should offer those cakes baked on a single potsherd;
for it is said, "He offers them," and "He offers the cakes baked on a single potsherd.
To this, it is replied:
This is not a definition of the category of "substance" (*padārtha*).
What then? It is the performance of the sacrifice as it is enjoined as a means by the injunction, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice.

He who relinquishes a substance while dedicating it to a deity has performed the sacrifice; the sacrifice does not come to be through mere relinquishment alone. Why is that? Because [the sacrifice is defined by that dedication].
Therefore, this is simply a non-statement of the performance (*prayoga*).
And the author of the Sūtras states that from the injunction of the sacrifice (*yajati-codanā*), there is an inference of the performance of that which is enjoined for the sake of the fruit;
and therein, the addition of pouring (*āsecanādhikya*) is the counter-example (*prātika*).

The statement regarding *dadāti* (to give) is likewise merely a description of its performance. Viśvarūpa states: "Whether not distinguished or distinguished, the acts of sacrifice (*yajati*), oblation (*juhoti*), and giving (*dadāti*) consist of renunciation and so forth; sacrifice is defined as renunciation, while oblation is intended to be the act of casting [the offering] into the fire."
The expectancy of the word "sacrifice" (yāga) is satisfied by the act of relinquishment alone.
Upon the sacrifice, the characteristic of the oblation (homa) belongs to the sacrificer (yājamāna). 3237. Yājamāna.
The completion of an injunction occurs at the point of its execution.

Giving (*dāna*) consists in the performance of an act such that one’s own property is relinquished and comes to belong to another; even though there is relinquishment (*tyāga*) in both cases, this is the distinction between them.
Bhaṭṭa: By way of digression, we shall investigate which entities such as sacrifice (*yāga*) are to be performed based on injunctions (*vidhi*).

That entity in which the renunciation (*tyāga*) of a substance, preceded by the dedication to a deity (*devatoddeśa*), is enjoined along with the act of throwing into the fire (*prakṣepa*), is the meaning of the term "sacrifice.

In the case of the *prayāja* offerings and others, the first qualification [the mention of throwing into the fire] is for the purpose of establishing that act of throwing; for in those cases, the act of throwing is established simply through the implication of the sacrifice itself.

And it has already been stated that the delimitor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is a universal (*sāmānya*), either in the form of a genus (*jāti*) or an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), which is co-extensive with and pervaded by the state of being arrived at through the aforementioned procedure.
An oblation (*homa*) is the act of renunciation (*tyāga*) characterized primarily by the act of throwing [into the fire] according to the aforementioned procedure.
A gift (*dāna*) is the renunciation of a substance preceded by the production of ownership in the recipient.

In both cases, the delimitor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is a generality (*sāmānya*) that coextensively pervades (*samavyāpaka*) each respective property, just as before. Other interpretations of this sūtra have been omitted as their meaning has already been covered. Maṇḍana [Miśra] states: "Sacrifice (*yaji*) would be an abandonment (*tyāga*) conjoined with a scripturally enjoined objective (*uddeśa*)."
Śaṅkara: "The definition of sacrifice has been stated.
The word *svāhākāra* is synonymous with sacrifice, just as *samit* and the others are. Bhāṣya 10.1.7.14."
There is no injunction for sacrifice in the absence of a connection with a deity;
therefore, in the passage "one should touch the calf," there is an injunction for mere touching. This is within the context of the Agnihotra-hotrā.

Here, the injunction for sacrifice arises from the connection between the substance and the deity, as in "One should immolate a white animal for the sake of Yaṣṭi" and "One should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya.
