Bhāṭṭa 4.1.7:
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the begging [of wealth] is obligatory even for one who possesses riches.
"Requesting and purchasing [are to be performed] when [the required items] are not available, as in common worldly practice.

Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, based on the scriptural injunction, "For twelve nights, the initiated one should seek prosperity," it is stated that wealth consists of requesting two things, and "he purchases Soma," which prescribes the purchase of Soma. "Requesting and purchasing" (*yāccākrayaṇam*) is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of these two; it is to be performed when one's own wealth and one's own Soma are not available.
One who is himself wealthy should not make a request for wealth;
and one who possesses soma within his own forest-retreat should not perform the purchase of soma.
This is as in common worldly practice.
Just as in the world a poor man begs, and one who does not possess a certain object for himself buys it— that is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Or rather, it must be fixed, because it serves a purpose.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), which suggests that there should be begging and purchasing when one's own wealth and *soma* are not available, is set aside by the word "or" (*vā*) in the sūtra; the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
begging and purchasing must be mandatory (*niyata*) and obligatory (*nitya*), because they serve a purpose—that is, they are for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*).
If that were not performed, there would be a deficiency in the sacrifice;
therefore, it must be performed even when [the materials] are already present.
Who?
The status of a sacrificer (*yājakatva*) is subordinate; the teacher (*adhyāpaka*) is [primary].
Ratna. 6|1|6|24, Section 2.

"Wealth is to be acquired by this very means and no other. (Vi.

Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), in one instance [it is said]: "He lets loose the calf and causes the cow to drink" (*vatsam copāvasṛjati, uttām nātvijā adhidadhāti*); thus there are seven pairs (*dvandva*). This should be seen in the section on the "Benediction" (*āśīr-ādhikaraṇa*) at Mīmāṃsākośa, page 1012. In another instance, [the same applies]. 3|8|16–16. See Mīmāṃsākośa, page 1012. It should be observed in the section titled "The Topic of Benediction" (*āśīr-ādhikaraṇa*).
The five pairs [of rites] beginning with "the sacrificial vessels are clearly visible" (*spaṣṭaṃ kapālāni*) are desires arising from specific qualities (*guṇajanyakāmāḥ*).
Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1436. Twelve pairs are recorded.

These actions in the form of pairs should be examined under the section titled "The Section on the Kāṇḍas" (*kāṇḍādhikaraṇam*); for they are actions belonging to the *Yājamāna-kāṇḍa*, as stated: "Because they are mentioned together in the *Yājamāna-kāṇḍa*, and because they are recited there, the *Yājamāna* [rites] belong to that [section], being primary like the ritual acts themselves" (3.8.14). They are indeed ritual acts.

Just as in the statement "the Vedas are the authority," the ritual acts are for the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), not for the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*)—such as the *samidh* offerings and so forth that conclude the sacrifice—as seen in the application of the *sautrāmaṇī*.
The meaning is that the ritual acts belong to the sacrificer.

Furthermore, according to the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), the recitations (*japa*) and other such acts are purificatory rites for the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*). Because of the specific designation (*viśeṣasamākhyāna*) "belonging to the sacrificer" (*yājamāna*), these ritual acts would indeed belong to the sacrificer.

Vārttika 3.4.14.3, page 942: "The prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is that [the term] *yāja-* refers to the *yājamāna* (rites performed by the sacrificer). By the statement, 'In this context, the *yājamāna* rites are the authorities,' it follows that [the performance] is accomplished by him (i.e., the sacrificer; there is also a reading in the *Kutūhala* as *yajamānakartṛkatā*, meaning "the state of having the sacrificer as the agent" regarding the management of the Soma)."
"The qualification [for the office] consists in the capacity; for the designation [of 'Adhvaryu'] is based on reason, as it signifies one who performs that function.
Since the status of being a priest (*ṛtvij*) is established through study and hearing [the scriptures], it need not be established again. (20)

This is to be understood as follows: and he will state in the section beginning with "But those pertaining to the sacrificer... that in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, actions such as "he lets loose the calf" are to be performed by the sacrificer.

P. 1098, lines 3|7|6|13: There are seven [mantras], such as "clearly the potsherds" (*spaṣṭaṃ kapālāni*) and so forth, and five others; thus, twelve actions in the form of *dvandva* compounds are recited in the *Yājamāna-kāṇḍa*. By this principle—that because they are subordinate to that [the sacrifice] they are like the ritual action itself (*yājamānāstu tatpradhānatvāt karmavat*, 3|8|14)—since they produce the fitness for receiving the fruit, that [transcendental result, *apūrva*] belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). Thus, by the specific designation (*viśeṣasamākhyā*), it is understood that these are "belonging to the sacrificer" (*yājamānāni*), as previously established. Vārttika 3|8|127, p. 284:
This is the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*), whereas the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) had been reached by means of the previous sūtra.

One might object: "Even though these rites are established as purificatory acts for the seasons (*ṛtu*) and the person (*puruṣa*), they should be performed by the *adhvaryu* priest and not by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), because the purpose of the sacrifice is served even by the purification of the priests. For the *adhvaryu* is hired for the sake of the sacrificer; therefore, he alone should perform them.
Anticipating this objection, the author states another principle: "But [the rites] belong to the sacrificer" (*yājamānās tu*). Thus, one should indeed perform them.

Even if the designation *yājamāna* (pertaining to the sacrificer) is a specific designation (*viśeṣa-samākhyā*), as stated on page 320 regarding the prohibition of what has been mentioned [elsewhere], nevertheless, that [specificity] is not based on reasoning (*nyāya-pūrvā*). While the designation *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu priest) applies to the duties of the person, the general designation *yājamāna* is supported by reasoning through the principle "But those [acts] pertaining to the sacrificer... (*yājamānās tu...*) and the principle "And in case of conflict between a subordinate and a quality, [the former prevails] because it is for the sake of that" (*aṅga-guṇa-virodhe ca tādarthyāt*), since otherwise there would be the consequence of the [act] falling upon the enjoyer [of the fruit], and because [the act] lacks the status of being a constituent part of the means (*sādhana-aṃśatva*). Thus, it is favored by reasoning.

The discussion on the *yājamāna* (the sacrificer's duties): regarding the statement "there is no exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the *yājamāna* mantras," one should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*). It is observed that even for pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses assigned according to their sequential order, they serve to determine the deity for the *upāṃśuyāja*.
Su. Pṛ. 467: When the *yājyā* (offering verse) is removed, the *bhakṣa* (consumption of the remnant) is not removed, just as in the case of the *pravara*.
This occurs in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice.

Regarding the *ṛtuyāja* offerings therein, it is heard in the scripture: "He gives the command for the sacrificer’s *yājyā*, saying, 'O Hotṛ, recite this offering verse,' or he himself, having set it aside, performs the sacrifice."

When one performs the sacrifice oneself, a doubt arises as to whether there is a consumption [of the offering] for him or not. Herein lies the clarification of the subject matter: in the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is a repetition of the cup-drawings for the seasons (ṛtugraha), and there are indeed offering-verses (yājyās) present therein.

And although, according to the traditional designation (*samākhyā*), these [recitations] are to be performed by the Hotṛ alone, nevertheless, in this case, the selection (*varaṇa*) of the sacrificer and the assistant priests (*sadasya*) is for the purpose of their performance. Having removed them from the Hotṛ, they may also be performed by others. Regarding the sacrificer’s own *yājyā*, two alternatives are prescribed: either its performance by the Hotṛ or its utterance by himself.

When he himself pronounces [the *vaṣaṭ*], a doubt arises as to whether the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance should be performed by the *hotṛ*, and consequently, the consumption based upon it should also be performed by the *hotṛ* alone, or rather by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) himself.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: Indeed, the *yājyā* has been taken away from the *hotṛ* by the [transfer] to another; however, the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance and the consumption have not [been taken away].
Nor does the removal of the *yājyā* entail the removal of both the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance and the consumption, because these two are distinct matters from the *yājyā*.

Therefore, just as even when the *yājyā* is removed, the *varaṇa* (the act of choosing), which is a distinct entity denoted by the term *pravara*, is not removed, so too are the *vaṣaṭkāra* and the *bhakṣaṇa* (the drinking).
Consequently, the mere recitation of the *yājyā* must be performed by the one who does not incur the interruption of the others;
however, the *vaṣaṭkāra* and the drinking are to be performed by the *hotṛ* alone.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"If [the portion] were high, because of the arrival of the cause.
This is the intention: this would indeed be so if, upon the removal of the *yājyā*, the *vaṣaṭkāra*—which constitutes the cause for the consumption—were not also removed.
For instance, it is not merely heard that "the sacrificer has the *yājyā*";
rather, it is stated that "having himself placed [the offering], he sacrifices.
And these [results] do not follow from the mere recitation of the *yājyā*.
What then? [The recitation continues] up to the *vaṣaṭ*-call, because that alone serves the purpose of offering the oblation (*havis*).
Furthermore, it is heard in scripture: "He sacrifices without interruption.

Or, if he wishes to recite it himself, it is heard in the scriptures that the sacrificer, having set [the implements] aside and sat down in the place of the Hotṛ according to the rule, performs the sacrifice and recites the *yājyā*.

This being the case, when the sacrificer himself recites the *yājyā*, there arises an inquiry: when the removal of the *yājyā* from the Hotṛ occurs, is the consumption (*bhakṣa*) also removed from the Hotṛ or not?
In that regard, concerning the removal of the *yājyā*:
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) states, by means of the sūtra,

If it is because of the arrival of a higher cause:

This is a sūtra of established doctrine (siddhāntasūtra).

When the *yājyā* verse is removed from the Hotṛ, the *vaṣaṭkāra*, which is inseparably connected to it, is also removed from the Hotṛ; and the consumption [of the soma] occasioned by the *vaṣaṭkāra* is likewise necessarily removed from the Hotṛ.
This is what the sūtra expresses: "If, however, there is consumption."
Whoever is the reciter of the *yājyā* verse that is invariably accompanied by the *vaṣaṭkāra*, for him alone is there also the consumption (*bhakṣa*).

This is because of the arrival of the cause—that is, because the cause of consumption, the *vaṣaṭkāra*, arrives from the *hotṛ* priest and reaches the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that when the *yājyā* is recited by the sacrificer, the *vaṣaṭkāra* must also be uttered by the sacrificer himself, and the consumption must likewise be performed by him alone.
Because it has already commenced, there is no removal from the position of the *pravara*.

This sūtra is intended to refute the objection raised by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*). Because the *pravara* has already commenced, there is no "departure" (*apāya*), meaning no departure and no removal.
Since the *bhakṣa* (consumption) has not yet commenced, there is indeed a removal. That which has commenced is already commenced from the very beginning.

Furthermore, there is an observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "Indeed, he who, being a performer of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, should let the full moon or the new moon day pass by, is cut off from the heavenly world. For if the ritual action were a property of the person (*karmadharma*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) would not be completed within the duration of one's life, and there would be no lapse of time therein. *Saṃkarṣa* 1.4.9 states, "One fixes the post within the altar (*antarvedi*), and [then] outside the altar (*bahirvedi*). This is a definition of location; it does not mean that [the post] exists simultaneously both within and outside the altar in the *Agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

The Upavedinaya [states]: 1.7.6.13–14. At the time of production, as in "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*), and at the time of the daily application, as in "he binds [the animal] to the *khadira* tree," the excellence of the sacrificial post (*yūparatna*)—though not yet understood—is subsequently realized through the observation of the reversed word-order: "that which is prepared by the rites of cutting and so forth from the *khadira* wood for the sake of the animal sacrifice is the sacrificial post.
(Su. pp. 1102–03). The sacrificer should not neglect the sacrificial post, even down to ignorance and other such errors.

VI. 5|2|1. Regarding the injunction "he anoints the sacrificial post with clarified butter" (*ājyena yūpam anakti*), the ritual properties (*dharmāḥ*) pertaining to the original model (*prākṛta*) clarified butter need not be performed.
This applies to the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya paśu*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Mā. 3|8|16|31: "Having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted [cord]" (*trivṛtā yūpam parivīya*) prescribes a second encircling with a triple-twisted cord in the Savanīya animal sacrifice.
11|3|3|4: "He cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) during the initiations, or when the Soma has been purchased.

12|4|13|3: Regarding the phrase "for the sacrificial post belonging to the sacrificer," there is no modification (*ūha*) of the word *yūpa* in the animal-related *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices when the duties of the sacrificial post are performed upon the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*).
9|2|13|1–43: From the untying from the sacrificial post until the separation of life, this constitutes a single ritual act (*padārtha*) regarding the animal sacrifice.
Saṃkarṣa 1.1.4: Regarding the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, its application is both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*).

The statement "He binds [the animal] to a *khadira* [post]" indicates its obligatory nature; the statement "One desiring virility should make the sacrificial post of *khadira*" indicates its optional nature.

Mīmāṃsā 4.3.13–17: In the passage "Having churned fire near the sacrificial post, he offers the *yūpāhuti*," the act of churning is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*), whereas "near" (*antika*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).
The churning [of fire] is prescribed not in the vicinity [of the sacrificial post].

(12.2.27, 29). Having churned the fire in the vicinity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), one offers the *yūpāhuti* (post-oblation). In that case, having established the fire at such a distance that the sacrificial post does not become visible to the *havirhotṛ*, the oblation should be performed according to the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the eleven posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*) in that very same location.
(Vi. 11.2.17). There is a rule regarding the sacrificial post being made of *khadira* wood in the *Vājapeya* sacrifice, because of a subsequent scriptural injunction.
*Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 10.7.16.1–57: The measurement of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), such as its five-cubit length and so forth, is to be understood as excluding the upper portion.
*Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa* 1.4.8: "The measurement of the sacrificial post, such as its five-cubit length and so forth," is the subject matter.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the measurement of the sacrificial post, such as its five-cubit length and so forth, includes the upper portion as well.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this measurement is indeed to be seen as given by the donor;
the same applies to the *audumbarī* post.
(Saṃkarṣa 1.4.8) The five-cubit length and so forth of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) are measured according to the span of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) himself, not of anyone else.
Because it forms a single syntactical unit with another scriptural statement, namely, "It is commensurate with the sacrificer" (1.4.9).
Regarding the measurement of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), eleven lengths ranging from twenty to thirty-two *aratnis* are optionally prescribed (1.4.26).
In the case of the eleven posts (*ekādaśinī*), the sacrificial post is encircled eleven times on both sides by two ropes (*raśanā*).

1|4|12–15: Regarding the measurement of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), when there are two ropes for the modified *dairaśana* (encircling), the rule is that one should be wound around at the prescribed spot and the other as space permits. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that, according to the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the encircling should be performed simultaneously with both ropes.
1|4|14: In the encircling of the sacrificial post, the Adhvaryu’s instrumental mantra is "Thou art encircled" (*parivīr asi*).
The Hotṛ’s mantra recited while the action is being performed (*kriyamāṇānuvāka*) is "The youthful, well-protecting one" (*yuvā suvāsāḥ*), in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice within the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Those two [rites] are not obtained in the *kuṇḍapāyinām ayana* sacrifice.
Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.8.10.22. Regarding the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there is a repetition of the Adhvaryu’s mantra, "Thou art encircled," in the case of the *ekādaśinī*.
Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 1.4.16. The sacrificial post consists of five jewels.

Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.7.6.3, page 1083: The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is motivated solely by the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the animal sacrifice, and not by the ultimate *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma. Consequently, for an animal that is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is no fruit [accruing from it], nor is there an extension (*atideśa*) of the properties of the Agniṣomīya [animal]. (Bhāṣya 1.1.2, Vārṣika 2): Because the archetypal sacrificial post is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the tethering of the archetypal animal.
There is a sublation by the prescribed *paridhi* in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices belonging to Soma.

Bhāṣya 10.3.4.18–22. Regarding a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), two posts, or many posts, when there is contact with something mundane, there are expiations consisting of the recitation of specific mantras.
For example, if one should touch a single post, one should say, "This is your Vāyu"; if two, "These two are your Vāyus"; if many, "These are your Vāyus."
Bhāṣya 9.1.3: When a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is placed in a worldly (non-Vedic) context, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), but not when it is raised by one who is ignorant of the Vedic rites.
The recitation of mantras such as "This for thee, O Vāyu" constitutes the expiation.

According to the natural sense of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya, this expiation—which serves the purpose of the person—is to be performed outside the sacrifice only after the completion of the sacrificial post's function.

However, according to the natural sense of the Vārttika, there is indeed a fault regarding worldly contact occurring in the midst of a sacrifice; for the Smṛti states: "One should bathe upon touching those [things] beginning with the gup (to protect) and the ci (to gather)," which includes touching [impure things].
(1.3.13). As for the width of the sacrificial post (yūpa), it should be made at the very place where the animal is bound, because that is where its purpose lies.
But it is not [the case] at the upper part, because the eight-cubit measurement is absent there.

(Āpastamba Sūtra: "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is broad; whatever is prescribed for the girdle (*raśanā*) applies to its dimensions; when above, both branches are eight-cornered and possess side-branches.
(Saṃkarṣa 1.4.8). The sacrificial post has its own independent ritual procedure in the Jyotiṣṭoma animal sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 12.1.5.18–12: "He makes the *svaru* of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Here, the genitive case in "of the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya*) has the sense of indicating a part.
Thus, the *svaru* is a part of the sacrificial post.

Vārttika 4.3.1.13: The measurement of the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) that support the fire-altar takes place on the day of the purchase [of the Soma]. And those eleven posts should be measured on the very day of the *aupavasathya* (the day of preparation), according to the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the correct conclusion is: because the time for the subordinate acts (*aṅga*) is determined by the time of the principal act (*pradhāna*), their measurement occurs on the very day of the *sadyaskrī* sacrifice itself.

In the archetype, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the primary constituent of the animal-sacrifice apparatus; although it was previously measured by the height of the sacrificer for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, due to the requirements of the ritual purpose, there is no observed division of vessels even when they constitute a single vessel for the sake of the animal sacrifice.

For this very reason, by the passage beginning, "They should measure out the sacrificial post on that day, for on that day one is about to offer a small portion," the measurement of the middle sacrificial post is made the reason for the immolation of the animal at that place. Therefore, even when the measurement of the posts is performed together with that [immolation], since those respective consecrations (*saṃskāra*) are performed only at the time of the primary rite (*pradhāna*), the censure found in the text—"As if they were cutting up their own bodies, they should not measure them out"—is consistent [with this view].
Saṃkarṣa. 1.4.14. The sequence of the sacrificial posts begins from the [preparation of] the wood and ends with the [immolation]; this is because of the scriptural injunction.
Bhāṣya 5.2.17: When many sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) are encircled, the *hotṛ*-mantra "yuvā sutrāsāḥ" is performed as a single ritual act (*tantra*) and is not repeated.
Saṃkarṣa 1.4.16: Where there is a set of eleven sacrificial posts (*ekādaśinī*), the oblation for the posts (*yūpāhuti*) should be performed as a single ritual act (*tantra*).
Vi. 11.2.7: The properties such as the encircling (*parivyāṇa*) do not extend by analogy (*atideśa*) to the secondary post (*upaśākhya-yūpa*).
"He lies down right upon the ground" (Pāṇini 7.3.13). "He erects a single sacrificial post (*ekayūpa*)"—this is an injunction regarding number.

Regarding the *Sāmidhenī* verses in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is heard in scripture: "This horse-sacrifice is indeed built for the sake of the heavenly world; as for the set of eleven posts (*ekādaśinī*), if one were to erect the eleven posts [for the horse], he would not provide [the horse] with the Agneyī [verse] for the heavenly world; he should erect them with the [Agneyī] verse, but not with the mantra for the heavenly world; he does not deprive the animals of their *svaru*-chips."

In this context, since both the set of eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*) and a single post (*ekayūpa*) are obtained by virtue of the original injunction (*prakṛti*), if the single post were merely being restricted, then—by the very logic of the *pāśukajāghanī* passage—the exclusion of the other would be established; consequently, the prohibition of the *ekādaśina* would be redundant.
Therefore, the statement "the sacrificial post for binding the animal is that which is used for tying the *āhuti*" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the post.
And in the case of a restatement regarding another sacrificial post, the figurative sense is not a defect;
furthermore, the prohibition applies only to the general nature of being a sacrificial post.

Or, if it is argued that an extraordinary (aprākṛta) sacrificial post (yūpa) is being enjoined, then there would be no ritual properties (dharma) other than those constituting the body of the post itself. This being the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa), we reply: since the prohibition is understood through its specific portion by the phrase "one should not measure [the post]," and since existence and non-existence cannot coexist in a single performance, the injunction proceeds by reconciling both; it prescribes merely a modified number with reference to distinct sacrificial posts, as in the statement: "He recites one *sāmidhenī* verse."
For this very reason, the combination of both [methods] is not stated in the two occasional (naimittika) passages (Saṃkarṣa.

2.4.16). Regarding the sacrificial post: when eleven animals are tied to a single post, then according to the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa), the sprinkling (samajana) belongs to only one animal, whereas according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), it belongs to all of them.
Bhāṣya 4.14.1028: Binding to the sacrificial post (yūpa) is the characteristic of the animal sacrifice.

3.6.178: When the sacrificial post stands as a surrounding enclosure (paridhi), the injunction "one should bind the animal to the paridhi" is a prescription of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi), not a separate ritual act (karmāntara).

The principle regarding the spreading of sacrificial grass at the base of the sacrificial post (yūpavaṭastaraṇabarhirnyāya) applies here; the difficulty regarding the sacrificial post and so forth remains exactly as it was. Because the animal sacrifice is known to be for the purpose of consecrating Agni and Soma through the general injunction among the animal rites, the animal-cake offering (paśupuroḍāśa) does not apply to another deity.
Furthermore, the perception of these two would be contradicted.
Therefore, it is a matter of providing assistance and so forth.

Śā—Since, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the properties of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) are for the sake of both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*), therefore, even in the modified rite (*vikṛti*), they must be performed upon the sacrificial grass used for strewing the base of the sacrificial post (*yūpavaṭastaraṇabarhis*).
This being the prima facie position, the sūtra of the final conclusion states: "But that designation [of the grass] in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) is an application to a new place.

The ritual properties of the sacrificial grass (barhis), which are connected to the function of the grass in the archetype (prakṛti), proceed to the modified sacrifice by way of that function, not by way of their own essential form.
Therefore, the ritual properties are to be performed in the modified sacrifice only when they serve to accomplish the archetypal function.

Furthermore, the spreading [of grass] upon the sacrificial post-base (*yūpavaṭa*) is not the function of the original *barhis* (sacrificial grass). Therefore, the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the *barhis* do not apply to that which accomplishes it.
Soma says: "This deliberation concerns the scope of non-extension (*anideśa*); it is relevant here by way of incidental connection (*prasaṅga*)."

(First Sūtra: In the *prakṛti* (archetype), the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that [the ritual details] serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rite (*pradhāna*); and the reason "because there is no distinction in the context" (*prakaraṇāviśeṣāt*) is connected to their serving the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the primary rite in the *prakṛti*. Since the ritual properties (*dharma*) are prescribed in the *prakṛti* as means for accomplishing specific effects, the application of those properties to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) which is not a specific effect of the *prakṛti*—such as the spreading of grass on the sacrificial post-base (*yūpavaṭa*) or the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)—is an extension (*atideśa*), yet it lacks authority (*anadhikāra*), meaning there is an absence of connection with the ritual properties. This is the meaning of the second Sūtra. As stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "The properties residing in the *prakṛti* are extended to the *vikṛti* (ectype) by way of transfer (*atideśa*)."

There is no specific application for this because its particularity has not been determined. One should not perceive the function of the *prakṛti* (archetype) in the *vikṛti* (modification), as in the case of the sacrificial post and the pit; for the function is not the original *barhis* grass.
Bhaṭṭa: It has been stated that the properties of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) apply commonly to both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice in the archetype (*prakṛti*) (3.1.1).

Consequently, even in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), when it is enjoined that "one strews the sacrificial pit with sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣā yūpavaṭam astṛṇāti*), the properties of the sacrificial grass belonging to the southern altar (*dākṣiṇāgnika-barhis*) should apply to the grass used for strewing the pit for the sacrificial post (*yūpavaṭa*).

This being the prima facie view, we reply: because of the scriptural statement in the archetype, "He places the oblation upon the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi havīṃṣy āsādayati*), the properties of the sacrificial grass serve only for the purpose of placing [the offering] upon the grass common to both subsidiaries and the primary, and not for the sake of the mere act itself; this will be explained in the subsequent section.

Even if they were intended solely for ordinary purposes, like common utensils and the like, nevertheless they would not serve as the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the covering of the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpavaṭa*), which is an extraordinary purpose.

This is because, through the extension (*atideśa*) of ritual elements by virtue of their being substances that provide assistance, it is logically impossible to assume a function other than their ordinary one in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

For in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), no relationship whatsoever serves as the delimiter of the oblation designated as *apūrva* (the new), by virtue of which even a non-archetypal [sacrifice] could be made to take up the ritual properties (*dharma*) through that same relationship; rather, because the entry [of the sacrifice] occurs precisely through the specification of that particularity by the force of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the specific name, that general [category] which is not present [in the archetype] cannot enter into the scope of the delimiting condition of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).

And yet, even so, the altar-ground for the sacrificial post (*yūpavaṭa*) does not acquire ritual properties (*dharma*) through the principle of "that which is clear and fruitful" (*phalavatprasannayāya*) [PMS 3.1.2] when there is an expectancy for such properties; for once that expectancy is satisfied by the adoption of worldly properties, there is an absence of both direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*). However, in the case of the *phalacamasa* (the cup of fruit-juice), there is a distinction: because it occupies the place [of the Soma-cup] and because it is a modification of food, an assumption of extended application (*atideśakalpanā*) occurs. Maṇḍana states: "The ritual properties do not apply to the clarified butter (*ājya*) due to its knowledge as a sacrificial post."
Śaṅkara says: "Not [the case] of the sacrificial post, the base, and the *barhis* grass" (where *barhis* refers to the sacrificial grass).
This is the principle of the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti-nyāya*), as seen in the context of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*).

It must be stated that there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the *yūpāhuti* (the offering at the sacrificial post) due to the loss of its purpose (*arthalopa*), because the force of the *lṛṭ* suffix indicates that the action has the sense of "reaching" (*prāpta*), and since the root *iṇ* has the sense of "going," the *lṛṭ* directly reveals that the action has the purpose of the going which reaches the sacrificial post. Furthermore, since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the going has the purpose of cutting, and in the archetype the *yūpāhuti* is understood to have the purpose of the going directed toward the cutting, the sublation follows from the absence of cutting when the *lṛṭ* indicates no such cutting.

This is because, even though the going incidentally produces the cutting, the phrase "he shall go to the sacrificial post" (*yūpamaccheṣpatā*) is understood as having the purpose of a going whose sole fruit is the reaching of the sacrificial post (*yūpaprāptimātra*).

In the present case as well, since *lṛṭ-balā* (the force of the future tense suffix) occupies the position of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the invocation of the post is justified even in the absence of cutting, because it is possible for her to go there with the intention of reaching that [post].

For there is no absence of going there for the sake of *lṛṭ-balā*; where there is *lṛṭ-balā* in a barley field, one must necessarily go there for the purpose of preparing the *śāla*, precisely because that [preparation] is the intended object of reaching that place. Furthermore, according to your own view, the invocation of the post would result in the case of the injunction "one should tether the animal to the *paridhi*," because going there for the purpose of cutting the *paridhi* is likewise necessary.

This being the position reached, the *yūpāhuti* (the offering for the sacrificial post) is not prompted by the act of tethering the animal; rather, based on the scriptural statement "one should cut the sacrificial post," it is that which produces the state of being a sacrificial post (*yūpatva*), consisting of the acts of cutting and so forth. For *yūpatva* is indeed a collection of visible and invisible consecrations belonging solely to the wood intended for the post; otherwise, since the definition of a whole depends upon its constituent parts, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate multiple powers (*śakti*).

Therefore, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), it has been stated that [the term *yūpa*] applies by way of secondary figurative indication (*ahantarā*)—just like the terms *āhavanīya* and so forth—or else that "post-hood" (*yūpatva*) is a subordinate element of its injunction; furthermore, even that [post-hood] is produced solely by certain properties such as the cutting [of wood] performed at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), and not by [properties] such as anointing (*añjana*).

For this very reason, since those [properties] would otherwise be purposeless with respect to the essential nature of the post itself, it has been stated in the ninth book (5.1.1) that, like the cleansing of the fire (*agnisāṃmārga*) and so forth, they serve the purpose of binding the animal (*paśuniyojana*) through an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*).

Therefore, even the *yūpāhuti* (the offering for the sacrificial post), by virtue of the verbal suffix *lṛṭ* in the injunction "one should go to fetch the sacrificial post" (*yūpam accheṣyatā*), has as its purpose either the act of going for the sake of obtaining the sacrificial post or the act of going conducive to the felling of the sacrificial post; it thus serves to produce the status of being a sacrificial post (*yūpatva*).

For this very reason, the name *yūpāhuti* is also justified. Furthermore, since the force of the *lṛṭ* suffix overrides the literal meaning of the words "felling" and so forth, the status of being a sacrificial post cannot be established due to the absence of the entire collection of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*); thus, the *yūpāhuti* occurs precisely because the original purpose has been lost.
Likewise regarding *paridhi*:
Maṇḍana says, "There is no invocation (*āhuti*) for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), because it is not a victim (*medya*).
Śaṅkara says, "One should perform the invocation for the sacrificial post."
In the digging of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there is indeed a combination (*samuccaya*) of the Adhvaryu’s and the Hotṛ’s mantras, not an option (*vikalpa*).
This is because there is no identity of purpose due to the mixture of both types of recollection—namely, "it must be done" and "I am doing it.
[The mantra] "Oḍhivam" is for permission.
"Stabhāna... and so forth;
the four Hotṛ-mantras beginning with "Ucchrayasva vanaspate... and so forth. Vi. 1.2.16.

The time for the production of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*): In the case of the *abhīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, it is said, "One cuts the sacrificial post during the initiations (*dīkṣā*), or when the King (Soma) has been purchased," but the production of the post does not occur at the time of the animal sacrifice itself.
For this very reason, like the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the sacrificial post serves the purpose of all animal sacrifices. (Vi. 1.1.13)

The touching of the sacrificial post (yūpa) is an expiation only in the worldly context, not in the Vedic; Bhāṣya 1.3.12.9. The group of eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī) is not mentioned at all in the Agni sacrifice.

But in the case of the *Vācastoma* and other such rites, because this [rule] regarding the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*) is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*), the intervals between the posts will not even be as much as a *vyāma*.
The eleven sacrificial posts occur in a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*).

In the archetype (*prakṛti*), since the cutting—which is common to all animals—is single, the fixing [of the animal] also occurs at the very time of the cutting; thus, even though it lasts only for that duration at the time of the animal-sacrifice, its status as a *tantra* (a common procedure) is not contradicted by the scriptural statement.
In the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well, it is likewise extended and remains a common *tantra*. (Saṃkarṣa 1.4.20).

In the case of the *yūpaikādaśinī* (the set of eleven sacrificial posts), in a space measuring twenty-four *prakramas*, because the eleven posts are to be measured according to the capacity [of the site], the wings (*pakṣa*) and the tail (*puccha*) are each one *vyāma* in measure; this is because it is prescribed that the two wings are to be one *vyāma* in measure (*su.
Wherever the *yūpaikādaśinī* is ordained, there the distance between them is to be one *akṣa*.
There is the *yūpaikādaśinī* (the set of eleven sacrificial posts) in the *vācaḥstoma* and other rites. Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 998.
In the ritual of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), the posts to the south and north of the central post are to be measured out; they are not arranged facing east.
Saṃkarṣa. 1.4.22.
In the ritual of the eleven sacrificial posts, the fire-pit and the ropes for the posts are common to all (*tantra*).

Because the time for the rope of the *abhīṣomīya* animal sacrifice is different [from the time of the *savanīya*], even though the *tantra* (the common ritual procedure) must be performed in a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), the time for the *savanīya*—since time is the occasion for the rite—repeats every day.

As for the post (*yūpa*), although it is permanently established once at the time of the animal sacrifice and cannot be re-established, it is possible to encircle it with a rope each day using a different one.

This being the prima facie view, we reply: since the act of encircling the post is subject to the same principle as the previous section, even if the time for cutting is postponed to the time of the animal sacrifice, the status of the *tantra* (commonality) is not lost; therefore, there is no evidence for a difference in the ropes.
Therefore, in the case of the fire-preparation (*agnipraśana*) and the animal-sacrifice (*paśvaparaśana*), they assist through a single performance (*tantra*).

Regarding the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), when the actions beginning with the anointing (*añjana*) are obtained for each post, there is a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) starting from the anointing up to the encircling (*parivyāṇa*), but not by performing each action such as the anointing individually for each post.
"From the time of anointing until the completion [of the rite], the sacrificer shall not release the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," according to the scriptural statement (Bhāṣya 5.2.15–19). Therefore,
in the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), the entire sequence from anointing up to the encircling with the cord must be performed for each one.
Having performed the collective rite at one sacrificial post (yūpa), the collective rite must be performed at the second sacrificial post. (Vi. 5.2.15).
Even in the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī), the two ropes are to be wound around simultaneously.
Even when there is a vision of Vaikuṇṭha, one [meditation] is prescribed for a specific place while the other is performed as before—just as in the case of "immersion" (avagāha).
This being the prima facie view, the conclusion is that both meditations are to be performed simultaneously, as in the original model.
Saṃkarṣaṇa-kāṇḍa 1.4.14.
In the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), there is equality in length among the upper parts (*upara*), but not in their horizontal dimensions.

According to such scriptural injunctions as, "One desiring the world of the ancestors should measure [the post] level with the chest; one desiring the world of men should measure it level with the middle or level with the girdle (*raśanā*); one desiring sensory power should measure it level with the base," the equality prescribed for the eleven parts—the upper parts and so on—according to these various desires, would otherwise appear to be of a single uniform type due to their proximity in the text.

This being the prima facie view, we reply: in order to respect the specific scriptural statements, one must disregard the proximity of the text and accept that each part possesses a distinct characteristic different from the others.

The length of the *upara* stones is prescribed according to the measurement of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). However, for the post, measurements ranging from one to twenty-three *aratnis* are provided as optional alternatives.

Consequently, since a disparity in the dimensions of the *uparas* would result from these differences in the post, it is ordained for the sake of the ritual fruit that they be equal in length, not in their transverse width.
The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is not a part [of the wood] below the notch;
for, since the carving of that portion is prohibited by the injunction "it is to be without grass and with a smooth top," such [carving] is impossible there.

As for the middle portion, its uniformity in length is already established by its being measured by three *vyāmas* and by the piercing of the cord; therefore, the injunction regarding its equality refers only to its width in relation to the cord.
And likewise in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifice: *Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa* 1.4.24.
In the *Yūpaikādaśinī* (the set of eleven sacrificial posts), the eleventh post is called the *upaśaya*; it is not raised up, but rather lies upon the ground itself to the south.
In that context, the word "sacrificial post" (yūpa) is used figuratively because it possesses certain characteristics such as being unaddressed and being subject to cutting and so forth;
Vi. Mī. Ko. 409.

In the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), the yoking of the eleven animals is transferred to the *ahīna* sacrifices according to the manual of Kāpeya; however, the other manual applies to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).

Having prescribed eleven animals for Agni, Sarasvatī, Soma, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, Viśvedevas, Indra, the Maruts, Indra-Agni, and Indra-Varuṇa, and having stated, "That which these creatures and waters move upon is indeed the *yūpaikādaśinī* (the set of eleven sacrificial posts)," he then proceeds with the animals in reverse order, prescribing them as: "For Agni, for Indra, for the kindled [fire], for Indra, for Indra-Agni, for Sarasvatī, for Soma, for the Viśvedevas, for Pūṣan, for the Maruts, for Bṛhaspati, and for Varuṇa. It is heard [in the scripture]: "The Kāpeyas know this; one should employ this at the end of an Atirātra sacrifice."
In this context, the term "final atirātra" refers to the *ahīna* sacrifice,
because it has an *atirātra* on either one side;
it does not, however, refer to a *satra* that has *atirātras* on both sides.

Since the *ekādaśinī* (the group of eleven sacrificial animals) is prescribed as being of two kinds by the scriptural statement "this very one," it follows that the *ahīna* sacrifice is to be extended to both.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because the phrase "this which" refers to the first [type] as belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*) through its connection with many performers, and because it is associated here with the word *kāpeyya* (the descendant of Kapi) in relation to Sarasvatī, and because the phrase "this very one" also refers back to what is proximate, the *ahīna* status applies specifically to the *kāpeyya* alone.

As for the Kalpasūtra statement, "The *āgneya* [animal] is on both sides of the *aindrī*," that is merely a designation based on the combination of the eleven animals of the *aindrāgna* [set]; thus, [the opponent's position] is a lack of learning.
Saṃkarṣa 1.4.25:

In the *yūpaikādaśinī* (the ritual involving eleven sacrificial posts), the *yūpāhuti* (oblation for the posts) obtained through the *codaka* (extended injunction) serves as the *tantra* (common framework) for the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
In the *yūpaikādaśinī*, there is an exchange between the tenth and eleventh [posts]: the tenth is in the south-eastern corner, and the eleventh is in the north-eastern corner.

Regarding the rules for the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), the *iṣṭakā* bricks, and the mountain-altars (*parvata*) and so forth: starting from the southeast corner (*āgneyakoṇa*) up to the northeast (*īśāna*), there are ten sacrificial posts because of their occurrence at Agni and Bhadrata. Alternatively, even if the primary location for the fire-hearth (*agnyādhāra*) is unavailable, there is no evidence to justify abandoning a site situated near it; therefore, to avoid conflict with the sequence of the principal animal sacrifice (*pradhānapaśu*), one should measure the second post to the north of the fire-hearth (*agniṣṭha*), and the third post to the north of that.
In this manner, the pairs of the fourth, fifth, and subsequent posts are to be measured to the south and north.

Since the statement, "The sacrificial posts (yūpas) are oriented toward the north," is thus established as valid, by this the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—"That which belongs to Agni and that which belongs to Bṛhaspati are on both sides of the one belonging to Soma"—is also justified.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), [the following is stated]: Since the binding of the animals is established according to the sequence of the deities—namely, that "the animals are oriented toward the south"—and since that same sequence would apply to the sacrificial posts as well by virtue of attaining proximity to the primary elements (*pradhāna*), when such a commonality is reached, [the following applies].

The procedure for measuring the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) as set forth by Gālava in the *Udaka-parva* must be understood as being applicable only where it does not conflict with the proximity of the posts.

Thus, according to the sequence of the animals, one should not measure the tenth post by bypassing its position; rather, having measured the tenth at the corner of the altar (*vedi*), one should measure the eleventh in the space adjacent to its center.
The author of the *Bhāṣya* maintains that if this were done, there would be a violation of the sequence only for the two—the last and the penultimate—posts.

Although it is possible—even after the post has been leveled—to proceed with the tethering of the animals by first performing the rites on the posts in the order from the northward joint up to the northeast (starting with the Aindrāgna), and then tethering nine animals according to the sequence of the posts, while the tenth and eleventh are tethered upon their displacement; nevertheless, this is stated as it accords with the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "the tenth [is tethered] after the last.

This observation of indicative marks, being supported by logical reasoning (*nyāya*), is established in the archetype (*prakṛti*) because it contradicts other statements; the other [sequence], however, is for the sake of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

However, because there is no difference in their being based on explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanikatva*), the teachers have accepted that in the archetype (*prakṛti*) there is indeed no option (*vikalpa*).
Saṃkarṣa. 1.4.23.
In the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), the *hautra* mantra "The youth, well-clothed... is the common ritual procedure (*tantra*).
Regarding *Saṃkarṣa* 1.4.15, "The mantra for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) [is used] in the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*)," this should be consulted.

In the case of the eleven sacrificial posts, the distance between the posts is to be the measure of a chariot axle; however, there is no restriction on other measurements, nor is there an option based on the size of the altar (*vedi*) or the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), because in that case, it is the altar itself that must be enlarged.
*Saṃkarṣa* 1.4.23–24.
In the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), there is a common ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the offerings to the posts.
At the end, the offering to the posts is likewise [common].
Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the "eleven posts" (*yūpaikādaśinī*), as stated in the injunction: "He cuts eleven posts."
However, in the Agnīṣomīya animal sacrifice, which is the archetype, there is the oblation for the sacrificial post (yūpāhuti).
Should that be performed separately, or as a single common rite (tantra)? What is the prima facie view?
The oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*) is likewise.
The meaning is that just as the offering of the fat (*vasāhoma*) is performed separately among those [oblations] dedicated to various deities, so too this one must be performed separately.
Why? Because it is heard in scripture: "Having churned fire near the sacrificial post, he offers the oblation for the sacrificial post."
Furthermore, the ends of many sacrificial posts (yūpa) are distinct.
If one were not to offer [the oblation] at the end of a particular post, that specific post would be excluded by virtue of that very quality.
Therefore, the rite must be performed at the end.
Or else, it is the negation of the other; that is to say, it should not be performed separately. What then? It is a *tantra* (a unified ritual procedure).
Why? Because this is a prohibition of the other—the prohibition of the *āhavanīya* fire—and not an injunction for its non-existence.
How is this known? Since there is a general rule stating "one offers into the *āhavanīya*," the *āhavanīya* is established for all oblations.
In that context, it would have been necessary to say, "having churned the fire."
Furthermore, since the ritual action has already commenced in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, that churning would logically take place in the *prāgvaṃśa*.
Even so, it must be stated that "the fire is to be churned near the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
If both [locations] were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Because churning serves both its own purpose and the purpose of another, one or the other— either the churning or the proximity— is not intended to be expressed. In this regard,
we maintain that it is the churning which is intended to be expressed, while the proximity is not intended to be expressed.

Why? Because the sentence is devoted to another injunction, namely the churning. It should be understood thus: "Having cut the sacrificial post (yūpa), one should offer [the wood] into the fire. For one who is consecrated (dīkṣita) does not offer into the fire; he considers there to be a fault in offering into the fire of the consecrated. To avoid that, an alternative procedure is stated: "Having recited the verse addressed to Viṣṇu, one should cut [the post]."
Nevertheless, as if it were like churning without fire, he says again, "It must be offered.
[He states that] for a person alone there is the locus of the *juhoti* offering.
Having rejected both of those as impossible in that context, he states a third alternative.
The fire should be produced by friction near the sacrificial post (yūpa) and the oblation offered there;
both of these are possible, as it is stated that "one offers" and "one does not offer in the consecrated fire.

In that case, if the intention were simply that the offering is made near the post, then it would follow that one must take the Āhavanīya fire itself to the vicinity of the post and perform the offering there.
Because of the restrictive rule, "One offers in the Āhavanīya fire," the statement "One does not offer in the fire of the consecrated" (dīkṣitāgni) is not connected to that context. However,
if the phrase "having churned the fire" (agniṃ mathitvā) is repeated, then there follows a prohibition regarding the Āhavanīya fire.
This Āhavanīya fire is different from that which is churned;
therefore, it becomes established that one offers oblations [into it], and yet one does not offer oblations into the Āhavanīya.
Consequently, the churning is what is enjoined, not the proximity.
It is merely a restatement of what is proximate.
Why is it a restatement? Because it is easily understood.
Seeking sacrificial posts with fire is difficult;
however, having churned [fire] near the sacrificial post, the oblation is easy to perform.
This is a restatement of what is established by logic.
This being the case, if one offers the oblation in the ānīkīya fire, there is no fault.
Now, why is it not offered in the āhavanīya fire itself after merely performing the churning?
[Because] an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) would have to be postulated.

Therefore, the oblation for the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*) is part of the *tantra* (the common ritual procedure). Furthermore, because locations do not possess fixed boundaries, it is impossible to restrict them to specific areas, since "proximity" is a relative term.
If, on the other hand, it were left until the end of the rite, then the sacrificial post would burn;
and that is prohibited.
Furthermore, it is not possible to perform the churning at a location far removed from the fire.
Therefore, the final [act] is not intended to be proximate.

Śā— Regarding the doubt as to whether the *yūpāhuti* (post-offering) in a *yūpaikādaśinī* (a set of eleven sacrificial posts) should be performed separately or collectively (*tantra*), since the locations near those [posts] are distinct, there must be repetition, just like the *vasāhoma*.
Not so;

for churning is possible at a relatively near distance. Therefore, at whatever place one has reached and considers oneself to have reached the vicinity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—that is, where the sacrificial post comes within the range of vision—it is there that the churning and the oblation (*homa*) take place. And since such a location is possible for all [the performers], it is a *tantra* (a common procedure), because no distinction is perceived.
Soma: By the phrase "like the *vasā-homa*," the meaning of the sutra indicating the connection is suggested.
Vi— "Is there a difference between the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and the oblation for the post (*yūpāhuti*), or is there a common ritual procedure (*tantratā*)?
Since proximity is observed [as the basis], the last [post] has proximity due to the difference in location.
Bhaṭṭa—In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni (*daikṣa-paśu*), there exists the position regarding the oblation for the sacrificial post.

First, there is the view that because of the injunction "one should go for the purpose of obtaining the sacrificial post (yūpa) and [the fact] that it must be offered," one should offer [the oblation] in the Gārhapatya fire even before that; and second, the view based on the statement "for one who is consecrated (dīkṣita), they do not offer in the fire.

Regarding this, the position that there is no offering is presented by first pointing out the fault [of the former view] and then stating, "having recited a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, he cuts [the post]."
It has been stated:
"He goes to reach the post" means he goes so as to obtain the post.
The third [alternative], however, is the option of an oblation, stated as: "After going, having churned fire near the post, he offers an oblation."

In that regard, concerning the set of eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), in the first two positions, the *tantra* (common procedure) applies to both the oblation (*homa*) and the cutting (*kṛpāṭha*).

However, in the third position, due to the instruction regarding proximity (*antika*), there is a distinction between the oblations for the posts. This being the prima facie view (*prāpta*), it is replied: there is no injunction regarding proximity; for if one were to enjoin both the location and the time of churning (*mathana*) by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the already established ritual action, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is reached by means of the *yūpāhuti* offering, the proximate location is already established through the fact that the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*pradhāna*) share the same location.

In reality, however, even if there were no injunction regarding the proximate location, since the oblation would logically occur in the house itself—given the option (*vikalpa*) between the churning-stick and the *āhavanīya* fire—it is necessary to enjoin the proximate location as well, in order to establish that it must take place after one has departed [from the house].

Furthermore, because there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) due to the prescription of proximity qualified by place and time, even when "proximity" (*antika*) is prescribed, it is impossible for the fire that has reached the highest point to be subject to burning. This is because the word "proximity" intends that degree of closeness by which one can say, "I have reached the vicinity of the sacrificial post" (*yūpa-deśa*); and since that [degree of proximity] is one, it is indeed a single performance (*tantra*). However, it should be understood that if there is a difference [in the degree of proximity], then there is a repetition (*bheda*).
Maṇḍana states: "The oblation near the sacrificial post (*yūpāntika-āhuti*) is a single performance."
Śaṅkara says: "At the end, there is the oblation to the sacrificial post (yūpāhuti) in the same manner; this is the meaning in the ritual system (tantra).
In the case of the set of eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī), as many as are the locations for those posts, so many Gārhapatya hearths are to be constructed.
(Saṃkarṣa. 1.4.24)

Regarding the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), there is no option between the measurement by the axle of a chariot and the rule "he measures them commensurate with the altar" (*vedisaṃmitān viminoti*).

Since, by an equal principle, the other statement "he measures them commensurate with the altar" also refers to the intervening space (rather than the altar itself), both measurements would naturally be optional. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: there is no option because there is no contradiction; for the other statement is justified by the intention that the altar should be measured as many times as there are intervals between the sacrificial posts. Thus, there is no conflict.
Saṃkarṣa 1.4.22:
In the case of the "eleven sacrificial posts" (yūpaikādaśinī) and similar rites, the sacrificial posts other than the central one (agniṣṭha-yūpa) are to be measured out to the north and south.

Since the location characterized as "half within the altar and half outside the altar" has already been occupied by the central post, the remaining posts at the end may be placed anywhere without restriction.

Regarding the statement "he measures out in front," since it is established that the measurements should follow the sequence of eastward orientation when reaching the location of the fire-altar (*agni*), this is the prima facie view.

However, since the specific location at the edge of the altar—which is extended toward the north and south—is still maintained even at its extremity, and because there is no injunction such as "he measures them crosswise" that would contradict it, the measurements must indeed be made on the northern and southern sides of the fire-altar.
Furthermore, because everything remains situated in the eastern part of the altar, the statement "he measures in front" is also not contradictory.
Saṃkarṣa 1.4.20:
In the case of the "eleven sacrificial posts" (yūpaikādaśinī) and similar rites, the intervals between the sacrificial posts are equal to the axle of a chariot;
that is, the ten spaces between the posts are of equal measurement.

By the principle that "it should be equal," even if a gain [of measurement] occurs, since there is no evidence for a specific quantity, an absence of restriction would result; however, because the statement "he measures the axle of a chariot" is meaningful only as referring to the intermediate space, the intervals between the sacrificial posts (yūpas) must be made to be the size of a chariot axle.
Saṃkarṣa. 1.4.21.
In the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī) and so forth, the ritual refinements associated with the term "yūpa" do not extend by analogy to the *upaśaya* post.
In the case of the *ekādaśinī* (the set of eleven sacrificial posts), that which is common and elevated remains indeed a *tantra* (a single performance for multiple purposes).

This *ekādaśinī* is considered by the ancients to be a subsidiary (*anūṅga*) to those [main sacrifices] for whom it is intended; however, because it occurs at the final time, even though it provides assistance within the *tantra*, there would be a repetition (*āvṛtti*)—just like the sweeping of the *āhavanīya* fire—at each distinct main sacrifice (*pradhāna*), despite its being common to the time of the *sutyā*.

This being the case, since in the archetype (prakṛti) the acts such as cutting, which are common to all animals, are performed at the same time [as the measuring], even the measuring is established as occurring at the very time of cutting; however, although by virtue of the scriptural statement (vacana) there is a displacement (utkarṣa) of only that much [the measuring] to a later time,
it is not contradictory for the acts intended for the preparation [of the post]— namely, the mere work on the sacrificial post— to remain non-repetitive (atantra), unlike the cutting and other acts.
It has been stated similarly even in the *Vikṛti* (modified sacrifice) that the *tantra* (the common ritual framework) remains the same.
(*Saṃkarṣa.* 1.4.18).

The consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the felling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-āhuti*) and so forth, which are intended for the purpose of preparing the post, ought to be omitted in the *matīṣṭi* sacrifice because their purpose is lost there.
Bhāṣya 10.1.5.9.
The Principle of the Post-Erection (Yūpakarman-nyāya):

In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the cutting of the sacrificial post (yūpa), which is drawn forward during the initiatory rites (dīkṣā), does not cause the displacement (apakarṣa) of the carrying forward of Agni and Soma and other such rituals.
"But because of the lack of connection, that very modified [act] is drawn forward.
Commentary: In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, which has the Darśapūrṇamāsa as its archetype, there is a modified rite regarding the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
That is drawn forward by the injunction: "He cuts the post during the initiations" (*adīkṣāsu yūpaṃ chinatti*).

In this regard, when there arises a doubt as to whether the subsequent elements—such as the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of Agni and Soma—are also postponed along with that [element] which is being postponed, or not; the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are postponed because of the purchase (*saṃkraya*).
To this, we reply:
in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), that which is additional, when it is postponed, cannot cause the postponement of those elements preceding it, such as the carrying forward of Agni and Soma.
How so? Because there is no connection.
The ritual concerning the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) pertains to the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*);
that which precedes it pertains to the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*).
There is no mutual relationship between the two;
nor is a ritual element belonging to the Soma sacrifice a benefactor of that which pertains to the animal sacrifice.
Or rather, it belongs to the animal.
For if it were beneficial to those two [the sacrificer and the patron], then by assisting them while performing its own duty, it would become auspicious;
but this is not the case.

Therefore, there is no fixed rule regarding their mutual sequence. Consequently, only the post (*yūpa*) is brought forward. Moreover, by bringing forward only the post, the purpose of the word is fulfilled, and thus there will be no subversion of the own-order (*svakrama*) of the Soma-related rites.

*Duṣa*: The acts such as the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which are recited after the carrying forward of Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomapraṇayana*) and are drawn forward by a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*), do not draw forward the Saumika rites.
Why? Because they are encompassed by a distinct injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*).
For it is only with respect to those things encompassed by this injunctive statement that the sequence is required.
And in sequence, the preceding item presents the succeeding one;
therefore, when the preceding item is withdrawn, it withdraws the others as well,
because they are connected by the order of recitation.
Śā—The cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpacchedana*), being deferred from the initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*), defers the *āghāra* offerings and other elements, just as the *prayāja* offerings do.
This being the prima facie view, it is said:
"There is indeed no sequence between a ritual element belonging to the Soma sacrifice and one belonging to the animal sacrifice."
"That displacement of the subsidiary does not displace the Soma [rite].

Regarding "Soma": here too, as before, the connection arises from the determination that because the sequence exists in which the meaning of the preceding word brings about the presentation of the meaning of the subsequent word, there is no difference in their being bound by a fixed order.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, after the Vaiśarjana oblations, the sacrificial horse (vahiḥ) has gone outside to the east of the hall;
the Āgnīṣomīya animal is being observed;
and the Soma, previously established to the east of the hall, is present.
Now, [the fire] is to be led forward at the *iṣṭi* sacrifice. After leading forward both of those, the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is prescribed.
All of this is obtained on the *aupavasathya* day, which precedes the day of the *sutyā*.

In this context, the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is shifted forward from its original time—three days before the initiation (*dīkṣā*)—to the time of the initiation itself. Since that [cutting] has been shifted forward, according to the principle of the *prayāja* offerings (*prayājanyāya*, 5.1.12), the entire series of days ending with it must also be shifted forward; thus, the leading forth of the fire (*praṇayana*) should likewise be shifted forward. This is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). Is the shift from the cutting of the post merely as heard at the end of that [series], or [is it otherwise]?
Because it concludes with that [final element], it is like the *prāyāja* offerings; furthermore, let another [element] be drawn forward.
The carrying forth of Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomapraṇayana*) belongs to the Soma sacrifice, while the cutting [of the sacrificial post] belongs to the animal sacrifice.
Due to the presence of the *prāyājas* as a substratum, there is a drawing forward of only what is explicitly heard in the scripture.

Bhaṭṭa: Following the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) of Agni and Soma for the Soma sacrifice, the felling of the sacrificial post (*yūpacchedana*)—which arises from the injunction "he cuts the post after the five-fold carrying" (*pañcahṛtyā yūpaṃ chinatti*)—is drawn back [to an earlier time] by the rule "he cuts the post during the consecrations" (*dīkṣāsu yūpaṃ chinatti*). According to the logic of the *prayāja* offerings (5.1.12), this draws back not only the subsequent items but also the preceding ritual elements, such as the carrying forward of Agni and Soma.

This being the case, since the sequence [of the items] is not established here because the recitation is governed by distinct performance-injunctions (*prayogavidhi*), and because even the great performance-injunction (*mahāprayogavidhi*)—at the time of the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*)—has no requirement for sequence as it concerns the performance as a whole, and because the recitation lacks a fixed sequence as it does not establish a specific order; furthermore, when the time for initiation (*dīkṣākāla*) is reached by the injunction, that very point requires a sequence; therefore, even though the ritual elements pertaining to the time of initiation and the Soma sacrifice are governed by separate performance-injunctions, their sequence is determined by the recitation. Consequently, immediately after the *samahotṛ-homa*, one should perform either the mere cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) or merely the preparatory rites for erecting the post, having extracted them from their place.
But it does not extend to the end of the *akapatha*.
By this, the claim of certain [authorities] that the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) occurs at the conclusion of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is refuted;
for the injunction "he cuts the post during the initiations" is recited immediately after the *samahotṛ-homa*.

Śaṅkara: "There would be a postponement of what is prescribed for the sacrificial post.

Regarding the mere act of the sacrificial post in the consecrations (*dīkṣā*), because of the injunction for postponement in the statement "he cuts the sacrificial post," it is postponed, but not the carrying forward of Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomapraṇayana*) and other such rites.

Bhāṣya 3.1.7.14, p. 616: There is no extension (atideśa) of the properties of the sacrificial post (yūpa) to the *upaśaya* (the wooden wedge).
