In the case of the digging of the sacrificial post, there is an injunction regarding a specific location characterized by the rule: "half within the altar (*antarvedi*), half outside the altar (*bahirvedi*)."
3|7|6|13–14. This should be seen under the "Yūpavedinyāya" (the principle of the sacrificial post and the altar).
The Yūpanyāya (the principle of the sacrificial post). The section concerning the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
In the Agniṣoma sacrifice, there is a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) pertaining to three animals, because it consists of the essential properties of the post.

Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are three animals—the Agniṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Anubandhya. Regarding them, the sacrificial post is prescribed in the scripture: "He binds [the animal] to a *lādira* tree," "He binds [it] to a *palāśa* tree," and "He binds [it] to a *rohitaka* tree."
In this regard, it is deliberated: is the sacrificial post (yūpa) distinct for each of the three animals, or is it common (tantra)? What is the prima facie view? That it is distinct. For what reason?

In the case of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, the sacrificial post (yūpa) is indeed included by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*); it is also obtained for the two subsequent [sacrifices] through the extended application (*codaka*).
Since the *codaka* and the injunction of performance, which apply to specific ritual acts, bring about the sacrificial post without distinction, there is therefore no difference [in its application].
This being the case, it is replied: the sacrificial post (yūpa) should also be a common feature (tantra). Why? Because it does not occur at the time of the ritual action.
Its origin does not lie in its being for the purpose of animal sacrifice.
What then? It is at a different time, as stated: "He cuts the sacrificial post during the initiations, or when the Soma has been purchased.
Therefore, no distinction is perceived regarding this sacrificial post used for the animal sacrifice, such that it would not apply to the *yūpa-dhvaja* (the sacrificial post).
And it is employed for all [of them]; therefore, it serves every purpose. Furthermore, it indicates a single sacrificial post (*ekayūpa*).
The Commentary states: This [text] shows that a single sacrificial post (yūpa) is common to all three animals.
Regarding the Savanīya animal, it enjoins the act of encircling with a triple-stranded rope, saying, "having encircled the post with a triple-stranded rope.

If there were separate posts for each, then, since the rule for the first post would already apply to the subsequent one by virtue of the general injunction (codaka), the injunction to encircle it with a triple-stranded rope would not need to be stated.

Now, if the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is common to the entire ritual (*tantra*), then its consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) must also be common. Consequently, since the act of encircling (*parivyāṇa*) has already been performed for it, the encircling would not apply again to the *savanīya* animal;
yet that [encircling] must be prescribed, and indeed it is so prescribed.
Therefore, it is also a tantra.

The principle of the sacrificial post (*yūpanyāya*): In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the sacrificial post is taught in connection with the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*); however, it is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to the *savanīya* and *anubandhya* sacrifices.
Is that sacrificial post (*yūpa*) common to all three animals, or is there a distinct post for each animal?

To determine this, it must be considered whether the injunction "he cuts the post during the initiations" refers to the displacement [of the cutting] of the *agnīṣomīya* animal alone, or of all the animals.
In this regard, it is just as in the case of the *adhvarakalpā*, where there is a displacement of the *ātharvaṇa*.

In the same way, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) for the *nirvāpa* is postponed to the very beginning; therefore, it is postponed until the conclusion of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. Separately, at the *savanīya* and subsequent rites, the collection of the sacrificial post takes place at its own proper time.
That is not so, because there is no distinction here due to the drawing forward of all the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*).
Nor is it appropriate here to draw forward the first [post], as in the case of the *adhvarakalpa* and other rites;
for the time of the principal act (*pradhāna*) is established here in that very same way, and thus the [time for] the cooking of rice (*odana*) is likewise not obtained [by anticipation].
Even in the case of the initial displacement, there is a principle of dependence (*tantratā*) because of the displacement of everything;

for in the *Adhvarakalpā*, when the first pouring of the oblation is displaced, one obtains a restrictive injunction regarding the time of the primary rite, and thus only its displacement is resorted to. But here, even upon the displacement of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) for the *Agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, there exists the principle of the time of the primary rite.
This is a case of non-attainment (*aprāpti*).

Therefore, since there is no distinction [among the stakes], when all the sacrificial stakes (*yūpa*) are brought forward, because they do not occur at the time of the ritual action (*akarmakālatvāt*), the specific stake belonging to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice serves as the common procedure (*tantra*) for all of them.

Regarding Soma: it is stated that, like the fire-installation (*ādhāna*), because there is an absence of a specific mention here, there is no status as a common procedure; this constitutes the connection (*saṃgati*).

In the Sūtra, the word "tantra" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Vi— "In the case of the sacrificial post for the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there is a distinction; yet there is *tantratā* (commonality).
It is distinct by virtue of direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*), but not due to a difference in time."
Bhaṭṭa: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the sacrificial post (yūpa) is prescribed for the Agniṣomīya animal; however, it is extended by analogy to the Savanīya and Anubandhya animals.

In considering whether this rule applies to all three [sacrifices] collectively or individually: since the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*) prescribed by the injunction "he cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) during the initiations" is enjoined with reference to the cutting of the post, and because instruction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*) regarding the post apply equally to the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*) respectively, the injunction of the initiation-time pertains specifically to the cutting of the post for the *āgneya* animal sacrifice—just as in the case of the *Gṛhya* rites. Furthermore, according to the principle of the "arrangement of the Adhvara" (JS 5.1.10), since that [post] alone is the one to be erected, its extraction [from the original place] occurs at the time of initiation; thus, since that [post] is completed at the end of the *āgneya*, another post must be prepared for the *savanīya* and subsequent sacrifices.

This being the case, the time for initiation (*dīkṣākāla*) is not connected with the initiation as a preliminary (*dīkṣāpūrva*), because there is no means of establishing it through performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). Rather, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is connected with the displacement (*apakarṣa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma; thus, since it applies directly to that [sacrifice], it is placed upon its sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
And since that [post] is common to all [the parts of the sacrifice], its application to all purposes is established.

In reality, however, since the time prescribed with reference to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) can serve the purpose of indicating the location—by means of the principle of non-repetition (*dviruktanyāya*) aided by the inclusion of the various sacrifices despite their deviation from the archetype—it is not possible for it to belong to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* alone, as in the case of the *vāraṇa* wood. Even if the instruction were given specifically for the *daikṣa* (initiation) sacrifice, that [time] could still apply to the *savanīya* and other offerings through extension (*atideśa*). Therefore, because the time is common (*tantra*), the sacrificial post is also common. Indeed, one must necessarily maintain that the sacrificial post is common due to the commonality of the time resulting from the original instruction (*upadeśa*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of three sacrificial posts even at a single point in time.
In the case of animals dedicated to Vāyu and others, however, there is no lapse of time precisely because the initiation (*dīkṣā*) has already been performed for another purpose.

As for the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and other such acts, they must indeed be performed according to the principle: "Even when a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is omitted, the primary action (*mukhya*) should still take place" (Jaimini Sūtra 10.2.17).
Maṇḍana [states]: "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) should be common (*tantra*) to the three animals."
Śaṅkara: [There is] the identity of the Soma, the sacrificial post (adrīyūpa), and the stake (yūpa).

If it is argued that in the multi-day sacrifices (ahargaṇa), the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā at the time of the Upasad rites differs due to the difference in the primary acts, we say no; because, by virtue of occurring at a prior time, it is common (tantra) according to the principle of the sacrificial post (yūpanyāya).
Even though the word *yūpa* and its referent are non-worldly (*alaukika*), their linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) is possible through co-occurrence with well-known words.
In the *pāśuka-cāturmāsya* sacrifices, there is the performance of the non-conflicting properties belonging to both the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
[Bhāṣya: The length of the other [the enclosing stick] is determined by the measurement of the sacrificial post.
Saṃkarṣa:

While the wrapping of the sacrificial post (*yūpaparivāṇa*) is being performed by the *adhvaryu*, the *hotṛ* recites it in response with the mantra, "The youth, well-clad... (*ayuvā suvāsāḥ*). [End of] section.

3|8|11: The Adhvaryu performs the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-parivāṇa*) with the mantra "thou art the encircler" (*parivir asi*). 3|8|12: The encircling of the sacrificial post is a property of the post (*yūpa-dharma*), not a property of the animal (*paśu-dharma*). 3|8|16, 4|3|4, 5|2|5: The encircling of the sacrificial post is the binding of the post with a rope (*raśanā*).
The mantra for wrapping the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is to be recited by the *hotṛ* priest during the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) dedicated to Agni and Soma in the *kauṇḍapāyinya* rite.
Regarding the wrapping of the post in the *kauṇḍapāyinya* rite, the *hotṛ* priest should perform the ritual action belonging to the *adhvaryu*,
while some other assistant of the *hotṛ* should perform the duties belonging to the *hotṛ*.
Or perhaps some external factor [is the cause].
[Objection: No; for by the statement regarding all three classes of officiating priests—the *kuṇḍapāyins* and the others—it follows that they are indeed occupied with other duties.

In the *Ṭippaṇī*: Regarding the *yūpavedinyāya* (the principle of the sacrificial post and its rope) at 3271—the rope is for the purpose of binding the sacrificial post (*yūpaparivāṇa*), and the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the rope are heard in the texts; these are for all purposes, not exclusively for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, at the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma:
[the commentary] states that it is a foot of the sacrificial post (yūpa).

In the *Saṃkarṣa*: when a substitute sacrificial post (*yūpa-pratinidhi*) has been accepted and the tethering of the animal (*paśu-niyojana*) has taken place, even if that [substitute] is lost, the tethering must be performed using the substitute itself. *Vinduka*.
Regarding the *yūpamantra* "yuvā suvāsāḥ" in the *yūpaikādaśinī* sacrifice, the *hautra* mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ" constitutes the *tantra*.
Since the subordinate element (*guṇa*) must be repeated for each primary element (*pradhāna*), it follows that the *hautra* mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ" should be recited eleven times.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the established conclusion is: because the mantra is a descriptive recitation (*kriyamāṇānuvāda*) and is not detached from its context, it applies only there [once].

The principle that "it applies to each primary act" refers to mantras that have a visible purpose, such as "aparivirasi," because they serve as instruments for that purpose; [this is stated] in the Saṃkarṣa.

The postponement of the *yūpa* mantra occurs during the *dīkṣā* rites due to its connection with the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, but not for those subsequent [rites] such as the bringing forward of the fire (*agnīṣomapraṇayana*) and others belonging to the Soma sacrifice.
[Bhāṣya: The specific locations characterized by the inner and outer altars (*antarvedi* and *bahirvedi*) belong to the measurements of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Bhā:
This is generally the *yūpa-raśanā-nyāya* (the principle of the sacrificial post and its rope); this is the *śālīya-nyāya*.

And so says the Śruti: "Because one winds two ropes around a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*), therefore one man obtains two wives; and because one winds a single rope around two sacrificial posts, therefore one woman obtains two husbands" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.6.1.2).
The *Sāhasrī* [section] states:

"In the case of the sprouting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the ritual rule is: 'He whose sacrificial post sprouts shall sacrifice a hornless goat that is hairy, tawny, brown, and multicolored'"; this applies both to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) and, as in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), to the *Saṃkarṣa*.
The expiation for the sprouting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) applies even to the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Regarding the injunction: "If one's sacrificial post sprouts, he should offer a ram that is lordly, with testicles, hairy, tawny, brown, and multiform"—this rite, performed on account of the emergence of a shoot from a perforated post, applies only to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

For these [modified sacrifices] involve the pressing of Soma (*sutvā*), which entails perforations and long durations; whereas in the archetype, at the time of consecration (*dīkṣā*), it is impossible for a post—whether cut or uncut—to sprout within such a short period of time.
This being the position reached, [we reply]: even for a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) that has not been cut down, growth is possible; thus, it is not contradictory even in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

For even a *palāśa* tree possessing only a portion of the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) does not enter into the category of those things that serve as the basis for the specific designation "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) at the time of its ritual application.
(Saṃkarṣa)
The principle of the sacrificial post (yūpa) and the altar (vedi):

regarding the digging of the sacrificial post for an animal sacrifice, it is enjoined that "half [of the post] shall be within the altar and half outside the altar," thus fixing a specific location characterized by this division.
In the same way, there is the altar for the sacrificial post.

The Commentary states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal for initiation, according to the text: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Indra and Agni. In that context, with reference to the sacrificial post (yūpa), it is heard: "The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt. If one were to fix it within the altar, it would burn [the sacrificer]; if one were to fix it outside the altar, it would not be secured. Therefore, one fixes it half within the altar and half outside; thus it is both secured and does not burn."

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the phrase "within the altar" (*antarvedi*) indicate the interior of the altar as the location for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or is it stated for the purpose of defining a location such that "half is within the altar and half is outside the altar"?
How is it by way of the absence of the post, or how is it by way of defining a location?

If the intended meaning were a connection between the half of the post and the interior of the altar, then the altar would have to be made twice over; thus, [the phrase] is by way of the absence of the post.
Now, that place where half of what is being measured is within the altar (vedi) and half is outside is taught as the defining characteristic of the location.

What is the prima facie conclusion? That the altar belongs to the sacrificial post (yūpa), just as the initiation fee (dīkṣā-dakṣiṇā) belongs to the principal sacrifice. Just as the initiation fee belongs to the principal, so too does the altar belong to the sacrificial post.
In that manner the sacrificial post (yūpa) is to be measured, so that half of it being measured remains within the altar (vedi).
In this way, the established position of the altar will also be maintained; otherwise, there would be a cutting away of the altar at the designated spot.
Between a direct scriptural statement (śruti) and an implied indication (lakṣaṇā), the direct statement is the proper rule, not the indication.
Therefore, by means of the absence of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the altar (*vedi*) is indicated.

Or rather—regarding the statement, "He fixes half [of the post] within the altar and half outside the altar"—is it the end of the post that is enjoined as being within the altar, or does it indicate a portion of the space mixed with the area outside the altar?
But surely, since its applicability to all purposes was established previously in this section (Sūtra 3.7.17, *cikīrṣayā ca saṃyogāt*), the present discussion is now stated.
While this subject matter remains unsettled, that non-duality [of the two] exists;

for if the status of being for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) were established through syntactical connection (*vākya-saṃyoga*), then how could there be an occasion for an investigation into the *kaimarthyam* (the purposefulness) at that time?

However, once it is established that [the term] has the sense of indicating a location (*deśa-lakṣaṇārthatva*), then the distinction between being for its sake (*tadarthya*) and not being for its sake (*atadarthya*) is appropriate.
What is established? Setting aside the context (*prakaraṇa*), the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is connected by the direct statement (*vākya*);
otherwise, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, the literal meaning of the location within the altar (*antarvedi*) does not fail to apply, such that one would have to resort to figurative indication.
Therefore, even the general rule "thus we are able" is restricted to the subject of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) alone, thereby establishing that the altar (*vedi*) is all-encompassing.

Alternatively, since the status of being for the sake of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice with its subsidiaries was established by the preceding section, it is now considered whether it also serves the purpose of the sacrificial post or not.
It should not be argued that its status as being for the sake of the post is already established by that [previous section] and thus need not be investigated.
It is not established by that [reason], because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is a subsidiary of the animal (*paśu*).
For the altar (*vedi*) belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice along with its subsidiaries;
[but] surely the animal will also provide it from its own constituent parts?
If it were to be given by its own greatness, the altar would exist;
however, by means of the primary [sacrifice], that which leads across remains only in its own essential form.

And when the function of the altar is reached, the Soma-related altar (saumikī vedi), arriving through extended application (atideśa), sets aside the New and Full Moon altar (darśapūrṇamāsikī vedi) and becomes established in the animal sacrifices and others.
That [measurement] is to be employed in the Vedic rites belonging to the archetype (prakṛti).

Nor is this measurement of the sacrificial post (yūpa) archetypal, because it would otherwise extend over the altar (vedi). Therefore, since the sacrificial post is already established by general rule, and since its measurement would otherwise—due to common worldly understanding—be taken as being either inside or outside the altar, the meaning is restricted to "inside the altar" by this specific statement.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
"Or rather, it is the mere location [that is indicated], because of its syntactical unity with the injunction.
The Commentary states: "Or rather, by the word 'vedi' (altar), only the location is indicated by secondary implication (lakṣaṇā), not the altar as a subordinate part of the sacrificial post."
Why?
Because it is part of a single sentence with what is not an injunction.
If that [measure] were to indicate a location by way of being enjoined, it would be so because of its syntactical unity with the sentence: "He fixes half within the altar and half outside the altar."
Now, if the altar is indicated by the absence of the sacrificial post (yūpa), then the area outside the altar does not need to be taught.
When the altar is being taught by way of the absence of the sacrificial post, half of it is [implied to be] outside the altar;
thus, when it is being uttered, nothing remains that is not already established.
Furthermore, if one were to teach even the location outside the altar by means of the absence of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, when the altar is indicated by the absence of the sacrificial post, the location outside the altar must not be taught at all.
However, if there is an indication of a specific location (*deśalakṣaṇā*), then, since a particular location is being characterized, the location outside the altar must necessarily be mentioned.
If it were not so stated, it would be understood that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is to be placed at some unspecified location within the altar (*vedi*).
However, when it is heard [in the scripture] that it is to be measured such that half is inside the altar and half is outside the altar, it is intended that this specific location be indicated;
and since that location cannot be indicated without reference to the area outside the altar, it must necessarily be taught.
Therefore, regarding the definition of the region (*deśa-lakṣaṇa*):

by both [the inner and outer altars], the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*) is defined through the regions both inside and outside the *uttaravedi*; it is not a prescription for the manifestation of something previously unknown.
Why is this so?
In the case of a connection between two things that have already achieved their purpose, there is an indication of place and time, as in the case of the *sarveṣṭi* sacrifice;
for both [the sacrificer and the post] have already achieved their purpose by approaching the altar from elsewhere.

Indeed, if there were a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), the altar would necessarily belong to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Yet neither of these is tenable: because [the post] has no further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*), because it would involve an improper assumption (*adṛṣṭakalpanāt*), and because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
First of all, there is no requirement on the part of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which has already been purified by the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), toward the altar (*vedi*).

Nor is there any requirement on the part of the sacrificial post—even one related to a thousandth part of the altar—which is occupied by the maintenance of the sacrificer, the oblation, and its accessories.
Furthermore, it is not possible for a visible benefit to accrue to either of them [through such a connection].

Furthermore, why would it be unnecessary to teach that "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*)? For in your view, it is impossible for this to be either an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*).
In my view, however, since it is impossible to indicate a specific location without both [inside and outside], this must be taught as a locative specification.

How so? When the measuring of the entire sacrificial post (*yūpa*) would naturally occur either inside or outside the altar, the rule "half inside the altar" (*ardham antarvedi*) is established as a restriction; for otherwise, there would be the contingency of no restriction regarding the second part [of the post].
The statement "half outside the altar" (*ardhaṃ bahirvedi*) must also be considered.

Consequently, because it would have multiple meanings, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), as well as the undesirable consequence of it not being connected with the verb "he digs" (*minoti*). Furthermore, one would have to assume that this is a restatement of something optional as if it were obligatory, which is purposeless.

But surely, since one half [of the measuring] is prescribed as being within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*), the other half will necessarily be outside the altar (*bahirvedi*) due to the nature of the injunction?
This would indeed be so, if it were the case that measuring the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) were invariably applicable either exclusively within the altar or exclusively outside the altar.

For, since the entire area of the altar would otherwise be occupied, the repeated mention of "one half" serves as a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), from which it is understood that the measuring of this [other half] takes place outside.

Alternatively, if it were understood that the whole [altar] must be entirely outside, then the rule "half is not prescribed" would remain in force, and thus the other half would necessarily be inside the altar.
However, neither of these two cases is the case.
Therefore, this restriction means that one half is indeed inside the altar, but it does not mean that it is *only* the half that is inside the altar.
That being the case, since the other half is not restricted, it might at some time fall inside as well; thus, its existence outside would not be established.
Now, if one were to measure the whole within the *vedī*, then one should simply do so by the injunction "half within the *vedī*" itself.
Why does one not do so? If the purpose there were already accomplished, then one would necessarily measure [the whole] inside; however, this is what is enjoined, and nothing else is prohibited.
Therefore, a location qualified by both [the interior and exterior of the altar] is indeed what is designated; thus, there is no split in the sentence (*avākyabheda*).

Śā—By the statement, "He plants half within the altar and half outside the altar," one should plant the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) at that place where half of the post being measured is within the altar and half is outside the altar;
this refers to the consecrations of the *yūpa* (3274), namely its joining and releasing (*yogavimokau*).

Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 118: Regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni-Soma (*abhīṣomīya-paśu*), some maintain that because it is a sacrifice, even a desire for a result (*kāmanā*) is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) in the accomplishment of the injunction (*niyoga*). For that [Prābhākara] as well, the intention to express the optative suffix (*liṅ-vivakṣā*) is indeed unavoidable. Furthermore, there is this other distinction here: whereas in other cases a person desiring a fruit (*phala-kāma*) is not explicitly heard, here the fruits themselves are indicated by a word ending in the dative case, and the ritual action is enjoined as being for their sake.
The mention of "bondage to desires" (kāmopabandha), however, is for the purpose of indicating their status as results; it is not itself an independent factor.
Furthermore, those things that are desired simultaneously would necessarily arise at once.
Therefore, they would indeed occur simultaneously.
This being the case, we reply:
"With reference to desire, it is the action itself that is enjoined as the means;
and for those [actions] being thus enjoined, their simultaneity is not intended."

This action is enjoined as the means for the accomplishment of each individual desire independently; and that [independence] is contradicted by dependence. For whatever cause is the producer of a particular effect independently, it produces only one at once—just as a lump of clay produces only a single water-pot at once, not many.
And there is a distinction regarding desire (*kāmanā*).

For an injunction (*vidhi*), which consists in the instigation of a conscious agent, establishes the status of being a fruit only for that which is desired, not for something resembling a goat or similar [unwanted] things.

Even in cases where desires occur simultaneously, because multiple actions cannot occur at once, whatever [action] is undertaken with reference to whatever [desire] at a given time, only that [desire] becomes the fruit at that time, and no other.

For just as actions that have a single fruit—being enjoined as the means for achieving a specific result such as heaven or cattle—produce only one such fruit simultaneously and not many; otherwise, since the desired fruit would be accomplished all at once, the performance of a single optional rite (*kāmya-karma*) would not be appropriate, yet repeated performance is indeed intended. Likewise here too, there is only a single simultaneous fruit. Nor should it be argued that the fruits here consist of the desires collectively and not individually; for it has already been stated that collectivity (*sāhitya*) is not intended to be expressed.
Therefore, desire (*kāma*) is [the basis for] the sequential arrangement. This connection with Soma is incidental.

For here, even though the word "all" (*sarva*)—as in "the Jyotiṣṭoma is foremost among all"—is primary, it is not coextensive with the subject (*uddeśya*), because it is dependent; rather, it is the word "desire" alone that is independent.

Furthermore, because "allness" (*sarvatva*), like the act of grasping, lacks the purpose of concluding the cognition of the subject (*uddeśya*), it is merely a qualification of the subject; thus, like singularity (*ekatva*), it is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), and therefore the result does not consist in their performance together. As stated in the *Vṛtti*: "The Jyotiṣṭoma is for all purposes; everything [is performed] once because of the single performance.
One should give separately in the case of separate performances, but once for that [sacrifice], since there is no distinction."
Since each individual position is enjoined as the means for its own specific result,
these desires arise in succession;
therefore, there must be a separate performance for each.

The Bhaṭṭa [position]: In the deliberation as to whether all results (*phala*) arise from a single performance (*prayoga*), or only one, [the conclusion is that] all arise. This is because, since "allness" (*sarvatva*) serves as the delimiting factor for the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*), it also serves as the delimiting factor for the effect (*kāryatā’vacchedaka*); and by rule, an effect delimited by that [delimiting factor] must necessarily arise when its cause is present.

Alternatively, even if "allness" is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*)—because it functions merely as a qualifier of the objective, just as "sonhood" (*putratva*) is in expressions such as "that word" (*tacchabda*)—nevertheless, since the cause exists in a single performance, there is no obstacle to the arising of the entire set of effects.

For it is not the case that a single cause does not produce two effects, since we observe the production of multiple things—such as color, taste, and action—from a single entity like a jar. While we observe that when there is the production of something delimited by a specific delimitor of effectness (*kāryatā’vacchedaka*), there is no production of something else delimited by a narrower delimitor (lest another son, for instance, be produced), there is no contradiction whatsoever in the simultaneous or sequential production of things such as a pot, which are delimited by other distinct delimitors of effectness.

Nor is it the case that there is no simultaneous production of everything for everyone from the very beginning due to desire, because there is no evidence for desire being produced by karma or for its being the generator of a result; thus, even in the absence of such [karma], there is no obstacle to its arising. Since the desire for a result is the cause of activity, once activity has occurred through even a single desire for one particular result, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the production of all effects, given the presence of the cause. For this very reason, the status of being a means to a desired end as understood from an injunction is also justified by the teaching, since it is acquired with respect to at least one of the results.
Nor does it follow that liberation is impossible because those [impurities] persist even when all fruits arise;
thus, what is stated in the *Tantrasāra* is correct, since through knowledge those *apūrvas* (unseen potencies) are destroyed.

However, when one adopts the position stated in the *Tantrasāra*—that because the scriptural injunction regarding heaven would otherwise be rendered purposeless, that alone constitutes the primary fruit, while the other sacrifices are secondary fruits based on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "for each single desire," and that this is not inconsistent since the understanding derived from the passage is that they are for "each one" rather than for "only one," but for all desires as well—then there is no contradiction whatsoever in the case of a son [attaining results] like longevity and so forth, even in the absence of a specific desire for them.

In reality, however, since the statement regarding heaven is logically consistent as having prosperity (*abhyudaya*) as its head, and because it is possible for an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) to indicate both the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the primary status [of the means], this view should be disregarded; thus, the aforementioned explanation alone accounts for everything.

Or, let it be that there is no production [of the sacrifice] when there is no desire for the result; nevertheless, where there is a desire for two types of results, the production occurs by means of those [two]. By whom can this be prevented?

Nor is it correct to say that "this alone is the established tenet" as stated in the *Tantrasāra*, because that would constitute an abandonment of the established tenet (*apasiddhānta*) due to its not being mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* and other such works.
For this very reason, although [the status of] being a son and so forth is present...

The delimitant of the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*) is both "allness" (*sarvatva*), because the word "all" requires a specific referent, and [the object of desire]; however, since the word "desire" (*kāma*) was introduced in the preceding sentence, it is that very [object] which is referred to by the pronoun "all. Therefore, being the object of desire alone is accepted as the delimitant of the objective, and likewise as the delimitant of the effect (*kāryatā’vacchedaka*). Nevertheless, where there is a desire characterized by a collection of many forms, the production [of the result] for all of them is precluded. This being the position reached, it is established by the aforementioned reasoning that the delimitant of the objective is simply being the object of the desire that motivates the activity.

In order to prevent the arising of a desire that occurs subsequent to the performance [of an action]—which is delimited by not being an object of desire—one qualifies the desire as "that which motivates activity" (*pravṛttiprayojaka*), so that it may enter into the scope of the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) for that very desire already established as the motivator of activity. Consequently, at the commencement of the performance, the arising of a desire that is delimited by non-desirability must be prevented.

Furthermore, there is no possibility of the production of a [cognition] whose objective status (*viṣayatā*) resides in more than one [individual] in the case of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), because even as in a collective apprehension-cognition, so too in a collective apprehension-desire, the objective status must necessarily reside in each individual member; otherwise, since a collective apprehension alone would be produced from such a cause, there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the production of a memory. For this very reason, since the rule of production applies only to that which is delimited by the delimitor of the effect-status (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), another jar is not produced from a single lump of clay and so forth, and likewise, no other fruit is produced.
Thus, in a single application, there is only one fruit.

And since that [desire] alone serves as the motive for engagement when it functions as a causal sign (*nimitta*), there is no fault even if the fruit such as heaven arises along with the destruction of sin during a performance of a desire-based rite where multiple fruits are simultaneously desired; for the desire for the destruction of sin lacks that status [of being the primary motive], and thus the destruction of sin is not delimited by the "effectness" (*kāryatā*) defined by the injunction for the production of the destruction of sin.

For this very reason, in cases where beings perform sacrifices and other rites according to various injunctions for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord through threefold types of worship, and when the production of heaven and so forth as a result is thus implicated, its validity is established either because the Smṛti—beginning with "having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action"—prescribes even that which is known from other sources as a fruit by way of being an unimpeded factor therein, or because the Smṛti itself, such as "whether free from desire or having all desires," declares that very [injunction] characterized by the absence of other fruits to be the actual fruit.

The Topic on the Chariot and the Drum.

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, there is a doubt regarding whether the original ritual duties and mantras are set aside by the sound of the chariot and the drum, which are prescribed as the means for the consecration of the Mahendra cup. [The prima facie view is: Because of the connection with the indicative mark of the archetype, the purificatory rite pertaining to the action should be additional in the modified sacrifice.
Commentary: Or it is thus. There is the Vājapeya sacrifice, [enjoined] by the text: "One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Vājapeya in autumn.
In that context, it is heard: "With the sound of the chariot..."
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *dabhra* grass serves as the means for the service known as "issuing commands," and the mantra "upāvartadhvam" is also a means.

When the archetypal [mantra] is set aside by the directly taught (*aupadeśika*) sound of the chariot—which functions as a constituent part—there arises the following inquiry: Is the chariot the displacer of the *dabhra* grass due to the commonality of being a substance (*dravya-sāmānya*), and is the sound the displacer of the mantra due to the commonality of being sound (*śabda-sāmānya*); or rather, is it the sound of the chariot itself that displaces both? Upon reflection, because the formation of a *tatpuruṣa* compound would be untenable due to the consequence of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the first member of the compound, this [term] must be a *dvandva* (copulative) compound.

Nor should it be argued that even in a *dvandva* compound, since a dual ending would result from an *itaretarayoga-dvandva* when [the singular] is not heard, one must assume a *samāhāra-dvandva* in order to conform to the singular;
for in that case, since both words would have to undergo secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the collective sense—just as in a *bahuvrīhi*—it would be better simply to accept a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
This is because, even in a *samāhāra-dvandva*, secondary indication must be admitted for both words.

For in expressions such as "wash the hands and feet" (*pāṇipādaṃ vādaya [kṣālaya]*), no specific collective entity (*samāhāra*) is perceived; otherwise, if the hands and feet were treated as a collective whole serving as the qualifier, it would be impossible for them to be the objects of the actions of playing or washing.
Therefore, there is only one type of *dvandva* compound.
And regarding that, by the rule "every *dvandva* may optionally be singular," the singular number is optional.

For this very reason, even the designation "non-collective dvandva" (*asamāhāra-dvandva*) for a dvandva compound ending in the singular number is merely a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule). Consequently, since nothing at all is to be indicated (*lakṣya*) in a dvandva, it is more laborious (*prayatnatara*) than a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Even if one were to suggest that the singular number indicates duality or other numbers, such an indication would still be subject to the principle of being the "last mentioned" (*jaghanya*), and thus, by the logic of the *pāṣāṇa-adhikaraṇa*, it remains less laborious than the *tatpuruṣa*.

Nor does the prescription of both [the *dhava* and *khadira*] result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because by means of a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the instrumentality is prescribed for the two only as they are mutually associated. Nor can it be argued that even so, since in a copulative compound denoting mutual association (*itaretarayoga-dvandva*) there must necessarily be a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the two words as being mutually associated, how can such [a compound] be accepted? For in that case, the syntactical split is avoided even without prescribing the connection between the *dhava* and *khadira*, since there is no evidence for secondary indication. Indeed, the *dhava* is construed with the objecthood of the action through its non-separation from its own associate [the *khadira*] when duality exists; likewise, the *khadira* is construed with the objecthood of the action through its non-separation from the *dhava* when [duality] exists.
And therefore, it is established that the sound of the chariot is what causes [the deer] to turn back, while the sound of the mantra is what causes [the enemy] to turn back.
Thus, the purpose is that this sound does not belong to anything other than the chariot itself;
nor is there any doubt regarding this, since their mutual association is understood through the copulative compound (*dvandva*).
Since the two young red horses are restricted to each other by logical necessity, why should it not be said that the sound belongs to the chariot alone?

For whatever [quality] is possible for the two objects—even down to cowherds and women—just as it is understood for those two objects, when such [qualities] arise in the production of the two others, there is a mutual restriction between the two.

In this way, in cases such as "two-year-old reddish-brown [oxen]," there is indeed a relationship of delimitation and delimited between the members on the level of external reality (*pārthika*), characterized by their mutual connection.
In expressions such as "to Agni and the Kṛttikās," there is simply a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

For this very reason, in the final view (*siddhānta*) regarding compounds like "hand and foot" (*pāṇipādam*), since the mutual dependence of the *itaretarayoga*—which consists in the single syntactic integration of the members—is manifested solely within the resonance of the words (*śabdaghoṣa*), there is no external reality-level connection whatsoever, nor is the relationship of the qualifier and the qualified (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*) an object of cognition.

Thus, when it is argued that the mere sound of any [mantra] whatsoever serves to effect the ritual application (*nivartaka*), we reply: this is not a *dvandva* compound. For it cannot first be an *itaretara-yoga* (conjunctive) *dvandva*, because in that case the dual number would necessarily follow.

Nor can it be a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective); for, in the absence of a word denoting the collective whole, both members of the compound would have to undergo figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the aggregate.

Nor should it be argued that there is no authority for the *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compound) because the rule "every *dvandva* may optionally be treated as singular" (*sarvo dvandvo vibhāṣaikavad*) prescribes optionality only for the singular number in the case of the *itaretara-yoga-dvandva* (mutual copulative compound).

This is because the *Mahābhāṣya* itself serves as authoritative evidence by way of an *jñāpaka* (indirect indicator), stating: "The rule *dvaika-vac-cāśvo na paṭhitavyo bhavati* need not be recited, since that [singular form] is established through the oneness of the collective."

For this commentary, being intended as a refutation of the rule "sarvo dvandvaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.2), implies that the mention of the collective (samāhāra) serves to indicate the use of the singular ending in a *dvandva* compound.

Consequently, by the force of this very grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the collective—which is synonymous with the aggregate—within the two constituent words, just as in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*.
Nor is there any impossibility of connecting the action [to the compound] there; for such a connection is established in instances such as "pāṇipādaṃ paśya" ("look at the hands-and-feet").

In cases such as "wash the hands and feet" (*pāṇipādaṃ vādaya*), however, one should understand that either there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through the collective sense alone, or else there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the two items being collected.

Therefore, since a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) is not produced by those [individual meanings], it is better to accept a single secondary indication; for, due to the absence of hearing a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it is simply the sound of the chariot itself.

In reality, although it is maintained that the optionality of the singular number applies only to the *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction) type of *dvandva* compound, and that in no case does a *samāhāra* (collective) *dvandva* appear, nevertheless, there is no *dvandva* in the present context. This is because the recourse to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the singular number when [the referent] is actually a duality or more is equal even in the case of the *dvandva* alternative. Nor can it be argued that such [indication] is not a fault because it is a secondary mode of operation (*jaghanya-vṛtti*); for since the term "grove" (*ghoṣa*) is dependent upon a qualifier, and in order to obtain the required injunction, it necessitates primary indication (*mukhya-lakṣaṇā*), it is more appropriate to rely on the [compound] *tatpuruṣa* rather than the *dvandva*.

For when even the abandonment of the primary (śrauta) meaning is accepted—as in the case of *prajāśara* and so on—in order to obtain the intended injunction, then what need is there to mention the case where both [meanings] possess secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sake of obtaining the intended injunction?

Furthermore, even in a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga-dvandva*), since the indication of association (*sāhitya-lakṣaṇā*) resides in both words, a determinative compound (*tatpuruṣa*) alone is appropriate.
Nor does that [association] appear as a mode of relation (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*), because if that were the case...

for otherwise, there would be the consequence of cognizing even objects such as actions (*karman*) as being that very [nature].
And for this reason, the sound of the chariot sets aside both the ritual duty (*dharma*) and the mantra.
Nor should it be argued that, because it is a mere sound in general, it should set aside the mantra alone.

For similarity functions as a regulator only when there is a need for a regulating factor; however, in the present case, the sound of the chariot—which is enjoined as the producer of the effect consisting in the communication of the *upakarana* and *saṃdhyā*—excludes the mantra that serves as the communicator by means of enjoining its own literal meaning. Section on the Rathantara (First):

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the injunction "He draws the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava" and so forth is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the precedence of the cups (*grahāgratā*).
But a quality, by virtue of its connection with a particular season, should occasion a distinct ritual act, because that connection itself constitutes a subordinate element [of the act].

Commentary: There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [established by the injunction]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. With reference to that, it is heard in scripture: "If the Soma sacrifice has the Rathantara as its *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; if it has the Bṛhat as its *sāman*, [those] beginning with the Śukra; if it has the Jagat as its *sāman*, [those] beginning with the Āgrayaṇa."

In this regard, a doubt arises: is a specific precedence of the cups (*grahāgratā*) enjoined for the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, or for a different ritual characterized by either the *rathaṃtara* or the *bṛhat* sāman?
If the Jyotiṣṭoma is denoted by the mention of the *rathaṃtara* sāman or the *bṛhat* sāman, then the specific precedence of the cups belongs to it;
if, however, it is not so denoted, then it belongs to a different ritual.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That it belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma because of the context.
To this, it is replied:
"But it is a subordinate element (guṇa), because of its connection with the sacrifice."
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
This is not the case for the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Why? Because of its connection with the ritual season (ṛtu).
How then? [It refers] to another ritual action.
But surely this statement—“having the Rathantara-sāman” or “having the Bṛhat-sāman”—is a description of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself. We say: no.
If there were no connection with the entire *ṛtu* sacrifice, this would be a statement regarding the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. However, this is indeed a connection with the entire *ṛtu*.

How, then, does the connection with the entire *ṛtu* come about, or how does it not? If either the *Rathantara-sāman* or the *Bṛhat-sāman* were the cause for the specific priority of the cups (*grahāgratā*), then there would be no connection with the entire *ṛtu*.

If either the *rathaṃtara* or the *bṛhat* *sāman* exists, then the sequence begins with the *aindravāyava*, followed by the *śukra* and *manthī*; this is the injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) for the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
Now, if the presence of the *rathaṃtara-sāman* or the presence of the *bṛhat-sāman* is not the condition (*nimitta*), then there is a connection with the entire sacrifice (*ṛtu*).
If it is said, "that which has the *rathaṃtara-sāman*," what then? This—
Martha says: If the *rathantara-sāman* is a qualifier of the sacrifice (*kratu*), how so? Because of the semantic power of the compound word;
for a compound occurs only between words that possess mutual semantic capacity (*samartha*).
And there exists a functional capacity for the relationship between qualifier and qualified;
furthermore, a qualifier must be unique.
In this context, the meaning is as follows: if the *rathantara* alone is the *sāman*, or the *bṛhat* alone, and not any other.
Furthermore, there are many *sāmans*, such as the *gāyatra* and others, belonging to the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
Therefore, these two words are denotative of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

Consequently, although it might be understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) that this is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) for the *jyotiṣṭoma*, nevertheless, setting that aside, it must—by virtue of the syntactical connection (*vākya*)—pertain to the *rathaṃtara-sāman* and the *bṛhat-sāman*.
[Objection: But surely, just as the Jyotiṣṭoma is not one that has the Rathantara-sāman, so too there is no other [sacrifice] whatsoever that has the Rathantara-sāman.
[Reply: It is said:
this sentence establishes a distinct ritual action (karmāntara) characterized by the Rathantara-sāman, namely: "If the Soma sacrifice were to have the Rathantara-sāman..."
[Objection: But surely there is no injunctive word here. [Reply: It is said: there is, namely this word "syāt" (should be).
He said:
"This cannot be an injunction, because it arises from the word itself.
A word of this kind exists for the purpose of indicating a cause (nimitta), not for the purpose of an injunction."

To this we reply: regarding this sentence, "If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman," there exists within it a subordinate sentence, namely, "The Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman.
The meaning of that subordinate sentence is one thing, while the meaning of the whole sentence is another.
The primary injunction is not able to enjoin [the entire act];
rather, it will be that intermediate sentence which shall enjoin it.
Furthermore, even though the existence of the *rathantara-sāman* or the *bṛhat-sāman* is mentioned as a condition (*nimitta*), it would not be meaningful [if it were merely a subordinate element].
Therefore, the inclusion [of the sacrifice] is undifferentiated.

And since that is undifferentiated, this pair of words—"the Soma sacrifice having the Rathantara-sāman"—is capable of enjoining a ritual (*kratu*) characterized by the Rathantara-sāman, provided it is understood in this way.
Alternatively, "if it should please" is the construction.

Alternatively, just as it is said, "One should eat rice with milk; if one eats *śāli* rice, one should pour curds over it," by such a sentence the eating of *śāli* rice is enjoined, so too here a substance is enjoined:
"If the Soma sacrifice should have the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu."
But how, then, is the eating of *śāli* rice enjoined by that statement? It is said:
the connection would have to be supplied by [the word] *vyāsa*, as in: "If one should desire the addition of curd, one should eat *śāli* rice."

Is it not indeed the case that we do not perceive a subsequent instrumental case-ending [for *sicyate*], since they recite a subsequent [form] for the root *sic*? Indeed, the section concerning the *rathantara* pertains to the root *sic*.

The section concerning the *Rathantara*: "That [particle] being uttered as a reply (*parā*), what does this lead to? We consider it to be for the purpose of expressing a desire (*kāmapravedana*)," according to Pāṇini 3.3.153: "In the sense of expressing a desire (*kāmapravedana*), the optative (*liṅ*) shall be used when a question is understood, but not with *kacit*.
Thus, here too, in the phrase "if one should take the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu," the meaning is "if one should wish to take them."
"Therefore, one should perform a sacrifice whose *sāman* is the *rathantara*.
Now, if this were the case, it would be a matter of mere whim, rather than a specific injunction regarding the cups (*graha*). It is replied: [this is not so].

Just as in this worldly sentence, "If one should desire curd as a condiment, one should eat rice," it is understood from the mention of curd as a condiment that one should eat rice with curd as a condiment—because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with that [desire]—so too here, because of the mention of the specific cups (*graha*) and the *rathaṃtara* chant, they form a single syntactical unit, and thus it is understood that the *rathaṃtara*-chanted Soma is for the cups where the *aindravāyava* cup comes first. Alternatively, according to Pāṇini 3.3.156 (*hetuhetumator liṅ*), the meaning is that the Soma sacrifice characterized by the *rathaṃtara* chant must be performed as the cause (*hetu*) for the cups beginning with the *aindravāyava*.
Therefore, because of its connection with the entire sacrifice, this accessory (guṇa) should bring about a distinct ritual act (karmāntara).
In this way, the connection with the entire sacrifice will be meaningful.
Furthermore, there must be a prior occasioning cause (nimitta), followed by the subsequent contingent rite (naimittika).
How so? For the effect (naimittika) exists only when the cause (nimitta) exists, not when it does not.

And that which is yet to come is not [already] existent; and since the Rathantara-sāman is something yet to come, how can it serve as the cause for the previously existing general act of drawing the cup (grahagrahaṇa)?

Furthermore, it is beyond doubt that the Jagatsāman constitutes a distinct ritual action; and by analogy with that, it is understood that the other [Rathantara-sāman] is also a distinct ritual action.
Therefore, this is not an injunction of a quality for the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Alternatively: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are first enjoined as optional means for accomplishing the Pṛṣṭha-stotra.

Subsequently, it is heard again: "If the Soma sacrifice has the Rathantara as its Sāman, one should draw the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava; if it has the Bṛhat as its Sāman, [one should draw] those beginning with the Śukra."

In this regard, a doubt arises concerning the mention of the "complete ritual" (*saṃpūrṇaṃ karma*): is it a separate ritual from the Jyotiṣṭoma, or is it a specific injunction regarding the cups (*graha*) for that very same ritual, where the hearing of the term refers to the occasion (*nimitta*) when the Rathantara [Sāman] has not been interrupted? Therefore, to establish this, it must be deliberated whether this connection of the Rathantara is with the entire sacrifice, or merely a connection with its existence. To establish that as well, this must be considered: is the Rathantara qualified by the sacrifice, or is the sacrifice qualified by the Rathantara that is being enjoined?
But surely, if the word "yadi" (if) introduces a condition here, then because that [condition] is being pointed out as the subject, a relationship of qualifier and qualified would not be possible.
This would constitute its status as a condition only if some prior attainment of such a thing were known from elsewhere;
however, in the case where there is no such attainment, it necessarily results in an injunction.

Furthermore, the nature of the occasion (*nimitta*) is heard [in scripture] as being of a specific kind; if the Jyotiṣṭoma is of that kind, then it is understood that the scriptural statement is for the purpose of prescribing an accessory (*guṇa*) for that very sacrifice.

But if it is not of that kind, then one must bring about such a state, and the rite must be performed on that occasion. Moreover, that which was previously not even an occasion because of its absence becomes a qualification of the occasion itself, as will be stated in the section concerning affliction (*ārtyadhikaraṇa*) in the Bhāṣya.

"We tolerate the qualification by means of the oblation. Therefore, there is no fault of restating something already qualified. What, then, is the prima facie view? Because the possession of the *rathantara* sāman and the *bṛhat* sāman are established through the context and by another scriptural statement; because the word "if" (*yadi*) indicates that [the action] depends on what is obtained as its cause; because the non-distinction regarding the cups (*graha*) is grasped by the injunction of performance; and because there is no obstruction by another stronger conflicting quality, there is no separate ritual action, according to the principle: "Due to proximity to that, the repeated mention is for the sake of enjoining a quality."
Thus, having set aside the established conclusion (siddhānta) indicated by the word "tu" (but), the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) stated in the Sūtra—that it is a different ritual action—is adopted.
Why? Because a compound occurs when there is semantic capacity (sāmarthya), and that [capacity] exists here only when there is a qualifier;
furthermore, in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is no such thing to be excluded by a qualifier.

Regarding the rule "In connection with a new quality, there is a distinction [of the act]," it has been stated that a quality connected to a previously established action is what effects the distinction.

Here, however, through the bahuvrīhi compound, it is understood that the presence of the *aindravāyava* [cup]—qualified by the word "if"—is the occasion (*nimitta*), and not the mere existence of the *rathantara* [sāman], because the latter is a subordinate member of the compound.
Furthermore, the *rathantara* as qualified by the sacrifice is not perceived here, such that it alone could be postulated as the occasion.
And that [connection] cannot be delimited by the season (*ṛtu*), because it exists elsewhere as well due to its manifold nature.
For it could only be so delimited if it were the case that "the *rathaṃtara* alone is its *sāman*," but this is not possible.
Therefore, it must necessarily be performed with the thought, "the *rathaṃtara* alone is its *sāman*."
Furthermore, the nature of the Jyotiṣṭoma or any other rite as being thus [characterized by the Rathantara] is not understood such that it could serve as the cause [for the interruption].

Therefore, setting aside the scriptural mention of the cause, and because it would otherwise be inexplicable, it is determined that there is a distinct ritual act characterized solely by the Rathantara-sāman which effects the interruption.
For that [distinct act] can indeed be performed prior [to the main sacrifice].
Furthermore, the *rathaṃtara-sāman* alone cannot be the qualifier, because it is too broad.
There is no semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) without a qualifier;
nor is a compound possible without semantic capacity.
Or rather, since that [compound] is seen here, there is a lack of recognition (*apratyabhijñāna*) of the preceding one in this context.
Now, why is it not simply made to apply to the *kevalarathantara* option? It cannot possibly be done, because the *stotra* is directly prescribed—
The section concerning the Rathantara:
[the rule applies] because of the conflict with other related Sāmans.

For this [rule] is heard in connection with the seasons (*ṛtu*); by the principle "because of meaninglessness, it applies to its subsidiaries," it descends to the *stotras*. However, the *gāyatrī* meters and so forth are directly enjoined in the *stotras*, and therefore they are stronger. But in another season, the *rathantara* which is directly enjoined becomes stronger than those obtained through extended application (*codaka*); thus there is no fault.
And in this way, because another word-meaning is being enjoined, a *bahuvrīhi* compound in which that [other meaning] is predominant is understood here.

Otherwise, the status of being subordinate (*upasarjana*) would have to be accepted as a last resort, as in the case of sentences such as "red-turbaned" (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*). Furthermore, if this [sentence] were a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) together with the injunction regarding the cups (*graha*), then the injunction of the *rathaṃtara* melody there too—due to its multiplicity—would be resolved by the very injunction of the prior efficient force (*bhāvanā*). Moreover, because of the immediate proximity, "there should be Soma" (*somaḥ syāt*) is understood precisely as that which is to be performed; however, the necessity of performing the *rathaṃtara* melody would only arise through the assumption of an intervening element (*vyapahita-kalpanā*).
And by means of the word "Soma," which serves as an indicator of the archetype (*prakṛti*), this [rite] will be of the nature of the Jyotiṣṭoma as its archetype.
Therefore, it is an injunction for a ritual action (*karmavidhi*).
The author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates this very point with the words: "What is the meaning of the phrase 'if it has the Rathantara-sāman,' etc."
Furthermore, the specific application of this very sacrifice will be established through the syntactical connection (*vākya*) or the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

Even though intermediate sentences within great syntactical units (*mahāvākya*) are not independently authoritative, nevertheless, because the sense is possible, the injunctive power (*vidhiśakti*) is not obstructed here by resorting to the intermediate sentence within the remaining great syntactical unit.
Thinking that it is better to fill the gap by supplying an ellipsis than to abandon the word "if" (*yadi*), he shows [the alternative] with the words, "Or rather, if it should please."

Furthermore, since the inclination (ruci) implied by the necessity of performing that [act] must be supplied from a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), what has been stated is not merely a product of one's own imagination.

Considering that even more than supplying a word, the assumption of a remote [word]—which functions as its own term—is lighter [in terms of cognitive effort] than assuming a mere property (*dharmamātra*), he assumes another word even in cases such as "if one were to eat śāli rice.
But the opponent, because the example is unestablished (*asiddha*), asks: "How, then?"

"There would be a connection with the word *ityatvena* [if one were to assume] 'the addition of curd,' etc., as stated in the Bhāṣya. For it is an established principle (*siddhāntādhikaraṇa*) that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the sense of "making known a desire" (*kāmapravedane*) conveys a wish.

In that very context, the meaning of the sentence becomes: "If one should wish to draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu, one should perform the sacrifice having the *Rathantara* as its *Sāman*.
Consequently, the two words "it would be Soma" (*somaḥ syāt*), being devoid of the word "if" (*yadi*), are injunctive.

Although the phrase "one should take the cups" (*grahān gṛhṇīyāt*) is not itself injunctive, nevertheless, because it is based on desire, the result of an injunction is obtained through the principle: "for whoever desires something, he does that.

Alternatively, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) will enjoin the state of being a cup-taker (*grahātratva*) as it is presented, conjoined with mere desire, by means of the word "should be" (*syāt*). Thinking that this position is even stronger—even without the assumption of a remote [injunctive force]—he introduces [the next rule]: "The optative suffix is used for cause and effect" (*hetuhetumator liṅ*).
In this context, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in "somaḥ syāt" (there should be Soma) expresses a reason (*hetu*), whereas in "gṛhṇīyāt" (he should take) it expresses an injunction (*vidhi*).
By this, the following is stated: "One should take the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava, which have Soma as their cause, when the Rathantara-sāman is used.
And since that [taking of the cups] cannot attain the status of being a reason if it is not performed, it will therefore be enjoined by implication (*arthāt*).
Alternatively, the optative suffix in "one should take" (*gṛhṇīyāt*) may express the cause (*hetumat*).

In the injunction "there should be Soma" (*somaḥ syāt*), even though the causality of the Soma is not explicitly stated, it will be established by virtue of its being the basis for that which possesses the cause (*hetumat*). In that case as well, the meaning is: "The Soma sacrifice, which serves as the non-specific cause for the taking [of the cups], must be performed."
"The abandonment of the word *yadi*, the assumption of conventional usage,
the connection through mediation, and the indicative mark (*liṅ*) of the cause and its effect"—
this is the summary verse regarding the various alternatives of the position (*pakṣa*).
All of this will be utilized precisely in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the section concerning the *aveṣṭi* sacrifice, as has been explained here at length:
"That which is to be accomplished is promised by means of a cause that is already accomplished;
however, the existence of the *rathaṃtara* chant is not yet accomplished, whereas the existence of the sacrifice is."

For at the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana), there are indeed the cups (graha); at the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina), there is the Rathantara [Sāman]. And it is not logical for that which is unaccomplished to serve as a causal condition (nimitta), since the word "condition" (nimitta) is synonymous with "cause" (kāraṇa). For me, however, there is no condition whatsoever.
Or rather, it is the season (ṛtu).
And that [sacrifice] exists from the very beginning;
moreover, the Jyotiṣṭoma has the Jagatī as its *sāman*, for it will be stated later that "because there is no *sāman* in the Jagatī-sāman.
Therefore, by the principle that "the same applies to others because of that commonality," it is a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).
However, because of the difference in indicative marks (*liṅga*), this is stated for the sake of a specific purpose: it is a statement of qualities (*guṇavākya*).
Commentary: By the word "but" (*tu*), the position is otherwise.
It is not as was said—that this is a different sacrifice (*kratvantara*).
How then? [The answer is: The cups belong specifically to the Jyotiṣṭoma without distinction.
Why? Because of the power of the context (prakaraṇa).
But was it not said that, by the power of the sentence (vākya), they belong to another sacrifice characterized by the Rathantara-sāman or the Bṛhat-sāman?
Furthermore, because the Jyotiṣṭoma consists of many *sāmans*, a qualification by means of either the *rathantara* or the *bṛhat* cannot be established. To this it is replied:
the qualification is indeed established.
Because the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans] are optional alternatives.
The section concerning the *rathaṃtara*. Section 3294: The section concerning the *rathaṃtara*. The section concerning the *rathaṃtara*.
The Section on the Rathantara (Section 3295): The Section on the Rathantara.
This is because it is logically consistent [to apply the *rathantara*] by cutting off its own intermediate function as the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*;
otherwise, it would not be so.
Even in your view, it is not possible because of their distinctness;
for sound does not reside in sound.

Furthermore, it is impossible [to apply such properties] directly to the sacrifice, as well as to the acts of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and threshing (*avaghāta*), according to the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).
It occurs together, yet it stands separately in the verses "abhi tvā" and "kyā naḥ. Therefore, it is indeed appropriate that the *rathantara* serves as the occasion for the *kratu*.
However, in reality:

For there would have to be a connection between the action—namely, the act of singing—and the word; but there is not, because there is no purpose for it, as the [word] does not serve as a cause for any other ritual act.
This is understood from the context.
[This applies] to the word! Therefore, there is no extended application (*atideśa*) even by way of being something to be contained (*ādheyatva*).

Consequently, this is not [the case], because otherwise, due to the force of being a subsidiary element of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅgatva*), the connection with another referent would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
Regarding the phrase "the application of the *ṛc*s":
since there is no modification (*vikṛti*) of the other referent—the nature of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice—there is no [application] to the subsidiary status of the *śukra* cup and so forth.
Alternatively, it would apply to its own primary meaning; for that is the purpose of the ritual action, as it is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of that [sacrifice].
Because it would lead to a contradiction;
therefore, even by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), the *rathantara* alone is the occasioning factor (*nimitta*),
as they would be taught by way of their presence.

But the occasional (*naimittika*) [rite] is a specific modification (*amatāviśeṣaḥ*) [of the archetypal rite], being enjoined with reference to the oblation that serves as the means for the *apūrva* under discussion.
The Commentary states: "Or rather, the *abhivatti*s, proceeding toward their own purpose, are enjoined."
Nor can the restriction regarding the precedence of the Aindravāyava cup be established from the mere recitation [of the text], nor can it be taught through the non-existence of the *kavatī* verses.
How then? "Kava..."
If [the Sāman] were already obtained, the injunction for it would be purposeless; therefore, it must be performed as an occasional (naimittika) duty prior to that.
Is it possible to teach its status as a subordinate element (aṅga) in the statement "he sings over the *tīr* syllables"? It is possible, because of the injunction.
And that purpose [is realized] when the cause is absent, whether in the archetype (prakṛti) or the ectype (vikṛti);
as in the rule: "With whatever rite this [defect] occurs, there one should offer the Jaya oblations," and thus there is an omission.

And although in all cases the object of knowledge is merely the necessity of the effect's existence when the cause exists, nevertheless, that [necessity] is established from the very recitation of it. What, then, is the purpose of the *kavatī* verses? [They serve to establish] their non-existence.
It is said: An unseen purpose must be postulated. Why? Because of the action.
The object of knowledge (*prameya*) to be understood is that in the absence of that [means], there is necessarily an absence of that [result].
Therefore, it is not [the case that the means is established by the result]; for the action is explicitly heard [in the scripture]: "He sings the *Rathantara* on the *Kavati* verses."
For example:
the injunction for another ritual action;
the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is the performance of the action.
It is said:
this very [point].
Maṇḍana [states]: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the state of being the cups (grahas)."
In this view, there is a fault: that one must postulate a purpose for the ritual action.
Śaṅkara says: "It is the state of being intended as equal to the *Bṛhat-sāman*," such as the *Bṛhat-sāman* and so forth.
Therefore,
for this reason as well, the position that the Jyotiṣṭoma [is the archetype] is flawed.
The meaning is that it is not so in another ritual action.
If it is argued that it is merely a word,
this is the second section concerning the *Rathantara*.
The commentary on the Rathantara: If you hold that,
by virtue of their being parts of the sacrifice, the words [denoting the Sāmans] signify specific melodies.
"The designation of the *vati* suffixes is poorly taught.
Therefore, in that case, it is merely a word;
the application of the name "Sāman" would occur through its denotative word, just as is traditionally taught.
Let it be granted: one should employ the word *rathaṃtara* with respect to the *kavatī* verses;
that is, one should designate the *kavatīs* by means of the word *rathaṃtara*.
What is the reason? Because [the word] is a sound.

Commentary: This is heard: "One sings the Rathantara on the two [verses] beginning with uttarayoḥ. Upon its utterance, there is first of all a comprehension [of it] as primary. Regarding the function in the word—
Passages such as "He sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses" are recorded in the tradition.
Since the purpose is understood through the possibility [of its application], just as in the case of the command "Bring the cow," there arises the consideration:
what is it that is being extended here?
Now, [one might object]:
"In this case, however, the effect occurs in the word itself, not in the meaning;
therefore, here [the modification applies to] the word."
It is expressed by words such as "tarat" and so forth; that is extended [to other cases].
Certainly;
it is that very same thing.
We wish to investigate this;
however, it is not yet known what is expressed by these words.
[Objection: But is it not established—?
Because it is not something produced [by convention].
This refers to the statement: "The designation *sāman* applies to the *gītis* (chants)" (Pāṇini 2.1.166).
The Commentary states: This argument is even more flawed than the previous one.
Why?
Because an objection will be raised against that which is not established in such a manner;
indeed, that alone shall be the final determination.
Because it is innate;
for the relationship between a name and the named is indeed innate.
It will come to pass.

If that itself is the established conclusion, for what purpose is there an objection? [It is because] a word is not well-known in a particular sense through an innate relationship (*autpattika-sambandha*),
such as the meaning of "dādi" or the meanings of "sthūṇā," "akhila," and "navana."
In this regard, what is established?
He is able to cause another to understand that [meaning] other than [the one previously stated].
Indeed, it is not by means of the word "cow" [that he does so].
That is stated as follows:
for it is possible to designate [the word] "horse" as having the *hiṃkāra* [syllable], the *stoma*, the musical accent (*svara*), and the *kālī* and *āsava* modifications.
In a verse possessing the *praṇava*, *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratihāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana* [sections],
the treatise would likewise be rendered meaningless;
yet the word "Sāman" is used by those who are proficient in it.
Therefore, that very point is stated.
The Commentary says: "This being the case, the rule of extension (*atideśa-śāstra*) would be purposeless.
[Objection: But surely, since there is a state of being sung (*gīta-satya*), there exists the purificatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*) called singing."
It might be so;
however, because it would be purposeless,
there is no application of the word either.
It has been stated that these words are denoters;
this very point is now explained as follows:
it is logical.
But the author of the Vṛtti considered that the science of grammar is being challenged [by this view]:
"These [suffixes] are not denoters of refinement (*saṃskāra*)."
What is the reason?
It would be purposeless.
Thus.
The intention regarding that [Sāman] is as follows: provided there is a way [to explain it].
Why? Because it is employed at a time when there is no ritual action (*akarmakāla*).
At a time when there is no ritual action, the Sāman is employed.
It is not logical that the learned (śiṣṭas) would accept such great effort for the sake of a fruit [in this case].
Nor are the purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarmāṇi*)— such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), looking at (*avekṣaṇa*), and carrying fire around (*paryagni*)— [meant to produce a result].
