If it is argued that [the name applies] to the tone (*svara*), [we reply:
the instruments and so forth are employed at times when there is no action, because there is no purpose [for them then].
The Commentary says: If you view it thus, then there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the name.

But if these are indeed mantras, then it would be improper [to say] that "one's own Vedic study (svādhyāya) must be recited daily. Therefore, in that case, let there be an extension (atideśa) of the accent.
Because of the rule "it is the tone," its employment at a time when there is no ritual action is appropriate;
therefore, [the application] of the *ṛc*s...
In common usage, it is expressed by the word "name" (sāman), as in "Sāmā, Devadatta, and so forth"— these are names. Furthermore, because of the distinction in designations.
And there is a difference in designation, such as "the *rathaṃtara*," "Sukhara," or "Devadatta.
These are [designations for] tone (*svara*), resonance (*ghoṣa*), and sound (*nāda*). They are identical.
The passage beginning with "bṛhat" and so forth is purposeless because the preparatory rite (*saṃskārakarman*) is a single act;
there are no distinct purposes.
That is expressed by the word *sāman*, and the *rathaṃtara* is a *sāman*; for in that case, it is sufficient as a single unit, just as a melody is.
Now, regarding the *ṛcs*:
therefore, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of that [rule] to them.
As for the names, it is appropriate that the direct perception of the designation (*saṃjñā*) follows immediately from that.
Moreover, there is no lack of connection for the Vedic text because of the absence of an object;
for if the Rathantara is singing and the Bṛhat is also singing, then this is the Rathantara and this is the [Bṛhat].
Commentary: This is not so; it is an extension (*atideśa*) of the accent.
The application of the distinct designation "Bṛhat" would otherwise be untenable. [This refers to] the *ṛc*.
Why? Because of the absence of meaning.
For there is no sense of the future *svarita* accent in the *kavatī* verses;
however, it is appropriate [to apply it] when they function as names.
Furthermore, because of the distinctness of modifications;
[and] because of the absence of [a separate cause].

But is it not the case that this [Sāman] is brought into being through extended application (*atideśa*), even though it does not exist [there]? And the Sāman is distinct from its modification; and for each Sāman, there is a distinct modification.
It is said:
it cannot even be cultivated,
for it is not [an object] that can be expressed in words.
It is observed;
however, because the singing is a single act, that [distinction] is untenable,
given the difference in the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
The *nāda* (nasal sound) of the *kṣara* syllables can be brought about in the *kavatī* verses;
for a distinct modification is observed there,
just as, for example, the transformation of rice grains through the act of threshing.
If one should think that they would not be *kavati* verses, [it is so] if they are not cultivated; [otherwise], it is not so. Grinding is pulverizing.
But it is not the case that there is both the bringing of rice and its grinding for a single person. This is established by the Vedic scripture: "He sings the Rathantara over the *kavatī* verses."
Now, if these were the names of the *ṛc*s, then, due to the difference between the *ṛc*s, there would be no mutual connection between the words of the modification (*vikāra*).
Therefore, it is not [the case that] the accent—
Separateness is logical;
therefore, [they are] the names of the *ṛc*s. To that, the following [is said]:
There is an extended application (atideśa). He recites: "The application [of the term] to the *sāman* should be by means of a denotative word (*abhidhānaśabda*), as for example—"
The accent would belong to the productions [of the chant], because it is not distinct from the measures (mātrā) and the syllables (varṇa).
Regarding the word "as taught" (śiṣṭam): the application of the Sāman by means of its designating term occurs exactly as it has been taught.
Commentary: The word "tu" (but) is used to adopt an alternative position. If it were... [the sentence continues].
That which has been taught by the learned masters to their disciples. Furthermore, what is it that remains?
The application of the *vatī*-svarita accent to the *kavatī* verses is not appropriate, as it would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
The *ṛc* distinguished by *stobha* and so forth is the *sāman*.
That [sāman] proceeds.
What is the reason?
Let it be that the Rathantara is sung over the *kavatī* verses.
How so? That is explained:
its name is "Rathantara" and so forth.

In this context, there are two statements regarding the sentence "He sings the Rathantara on the Akvatī verses": first, because [the word] *rathantaram* is a term denoting a specific entity (*nāmadheya*), it does not apply to other entities; second, because it is an injunction of meaning (*arthavidhi*) through its verbal forms, it functions as two distinct utterances.
In the *kavatī* verses, he sings that which is the *rathantara*;
for there is a connection with the action because of their distinctness.
This is one [view].
"That which is the *rathaṃtara*, one sings that upon the *kavatī* verses"—this is another [view]. The commentary says: this is for the purpose of excluding the bird;
however, it should not be so.
As has been stated, this is not possible in the case of their being *sāman*s;
for there is no application of *ṛc* verses [to them].

How so? Here, [it is argued that] the *rathaṃtara* [sāman] is in the *kavatī* verses; thus, the accent of the *kavatī* verses can be made to enter into the *kavatī* verses. But the former [view holds]:...
The phrase "he sings" is extended by analogy to the function of the *kavatī* verses of the *abhilava* sacrifice;
it is possible [to understand] that he sings the *rathantara* which exists within the *kavatī* verses.
But surely...
Or [it might be argued that it applies] by way of being the substratum for the *kavatī* verses;
in that case, the effect would have to occur there. But even that is not possible, for the *rathantara* chant does not exist within the *kavatī* verses.
Therefore, for that long, extension [of application] is not possible. Why? Because the meanings are enjoined by words.
It is said that the accent (svara) should occur at the points of origin; however,
the determination of the meaning of words must be performed according to the accent.
And the Rathantara [Sāman] is not [to be sung] upon the *kavatī* verses;
the *vatīsvara* (the accentuation of the *vatī* verses) would apply to the *kavatī*s in their originations—that is, in their recitations.
How so?

"He sings with the *kavatī* verses"—this refers to that which is designated by them; for they possess both measure (*mātrā*) and phonemes (*varṇa*). Indeed, many measures and phonemes belong to the *abhilavī* verses.
They are able to speak [thus].
Therefore, there is no extension of the effect (*kāryātideśa*). [Regarding] the thing to be placed (*ādheya*)—
The *abhivatī* verses also exist as distinct from the *kavatī* verses, and the *kavatī* verses also exist [as distinct].
That aforementioned *abhivatī* accent exists in the *kavatī* verses as being accompanied by common phonemes.
Therefore, this restatement is appropriate: "He sings the *rathantara* on the *kavatī* verses."
Therefore, it is a restatement of the accent.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The Commentary states: "And an indicative mark is seen regarding this matter, namely: 'The *rathaṃtara* [sāman] is in the two later [verses].'"

What is that indicative mark? It is stated thus: "I do not see the *Rathaṃtara* in the two subsequent verses," so Viśvāmitra performed penance; "I do not see the *Bṛhat* in the two subsequent verses," so Vasiṣṭha [performed penance].

And when something exists but is not seen, an effort is made for the sake of seeing it—just as one makes a lamp because one says, "I do not see the jar," but not because one says, "I do not see the horn of a hare.
Therefore, the *Rathaṃtara* exists in the two subsequent verses.
"It is a restatement of those two.
And because the subsequent modification is not heard, it is according to what is heard.
Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
This is not a restatement of the accent. Why? Because if that were the case, no modification of the subsequent [verse] would be heard;
therefore, the subsequent verses should be employed exactly as they are heard in the text.
Just as they were heard at the time of Vedic study,

in that context the statement "one proceeds with the *Rathaṃtara* as the latter [melody]" would become a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), which— failing to produce any specific activity— would result in being purposeless. Therefore, a restatement of the accent is not tenable.
And there would be an inconsistency regarding the words [denoting the Sāmans].

The Commentary states: "There would be an inconsistency regarding the words *sāman* such as *rathaṃtara* and others, in the case of the injunctions ‘the *rathaṃtara* on the two following verses’ and ‘the *bṛhat* on the two following verses.
How so? That is explained."
This word *rathaṃtara* or the word *bṛhat* is employed for a specific tone (*svara*) when the term *sāman* refers to a collection of tones arranged in a particular sequence.
It would be inconsistent if applied to a single part [of that collection] or where the sequence is different.
Therefore, it is appropriate that the word *sāman* refers to the tone, and that this [application of the names *rathaṃtara* and *bṛhat*] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of it.
Here he says: "In this way, you have refuted all positions. What follows from that? Is it non-occurrence?
It is replied:
Let the *ṛc* itself be the locus.
But was it not said that it is not possible for one *ṛc* to have its locus in another *ṛc*? Certainly; there will be an indication by way of location (*deśalakṣaṇā*).

It is stated, "One sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses," yet it is not possible to sing the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses; therefore, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of place, meaning "in the place of the *kavatīs*.
This is like saying, "He stands in the fire" or "He stands in the well.
Alternatively, it may be an indication of property (*dharma*).
Alternatively, the properties of the *rathaṃtara* are extended by implication to the *kavatī* verses through the word "etc.
(*ādi*), such as: "While the *rathaṃtara* is being chanted, one should meditate on the earth with the mind," and so forth.
Just as when a teacher has gone abroad, the service due to the teacher is extended to the teacher’s wife by the statement, "The teacher’s wife is your teacher."

Furthermore, the word *karman* might indeed mean "object," because it is understood in its conventional sense; however, the modification (*vikāra*) is distinguished from others by the oblation (*havis*). Commentary:

But this cannot be so—that the word *sāman* refers to the *ṛc* (verse) and that there is a "placement" (*pradeśa*) of it—because one would have to resort to an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of either place or quality (*dharma*). Resorting to such an indication is only taken when there is no other way.
What then? It would be a word denoting an action (*karma*).
The term *rathantara* and so forth is a designator of the purificatory action (*saṃskārakarma*) known as singing.
Why? Because the principle has already been stated in the sūtra: "The designation *sāman* applies to songs" (2.1.36).

In this context, the word "this" (eṣa) is observed [to refer] to a ṛc distinguished by its singing (gīti). And a cognition of the qualified object is not possible without the qualification having been apprehended;
therefore, the qualification is first denoted.
Furthermore, because there is a cognition of the qualified [object] through the cognition of its qualifier,
there is no contact with the word "ṛk" itself.
By that very reasoning, we maintain that it is the name of the melody.
Furthermore, because it refers to what is well-known:
this word "he sings" (*gāyati*) is well-known in the sense of the act of singing.
What, then, is that? It is a particular kind of vocal utterance; as in, "he sings" means "he performs singing."
And the words *rathaṃtara* and so forth denote that [melody],
because they are uttered together with it and because of the force of the accusative case,
as in "he sings the *āsāritaka*" and "he sings the *vardhamānaka*."
But surely, there is also utterance by means of the word "recitation," as in "he sings a gāthā" and "he sings an ṛc.
True;
however, this is after the word has been modified, meaning that he consecrates the ṛc by means of singing.
Just as a song is not connected with the meaning as it happens to fall [into the mind],
therefore it is a term for "singing.
Thus, it is a term for "singing."
Why? Because modification remains as the distinguishing feature from others;
and modification is observed in the case of the *ṛc*:
the lengthening of short syllables and the shortening of long ones.
The opening of those that were closed and the closing of those that were open;
this is no different from other acts of preparation (*saṃskārakarman*),
just as rice grains are turned into rice-powder by threshing, or flour is produced from rice-grains by grinding.
Therefore, the refinement of sounds known as "singing" (gāna) is expressed by words such as *rathantara* and so forth;
this is its application, such as "one sings the *rathantara* on the two [verses] beginning with *uttare*" and so on.
A.
*Bṛhat*: The practice for the purpose of training occurs during non-performance time;
however, for the *Rayaṃtara* chant, there is only one objective. When that has been practiced in its original form (*yoni*), it need not be practiced again later on.
In those cases, the employment [of the word] at a time other than the performance of the action is justified as being a *saṃskārakarma* (an action of consecration).
Therefore, the word *sāman* refers to the consecration (*saṃskāra*).
This established proposition is determined by the Sūtra.
It may be indeterminate with respect to other meanings, as in the case of the word *pāka*.
The Commentary states: "There may be dissimilarity (vairūpya). Why is this? Because it is not restricted to other meanings."
In the case of different *ṛg*-verses, it differs due to the difference in substrata,
just as in the case of cooking.
For example, the single meaning called "cooking" [is the same].
In that case, there is a difference in form regarding another object.
The cooking of rice has one characteristic, while that of molasses has another.
One who has mastered the cooking of rice does not know how to cook molasses without being instructed.
Therefore, its employment even at a time when there is no ritual action is appropriate, and there is consistency among the words.
The Bhāṣya states: "And in this way, there is consistency between the words *sāman* and the words *ṛc*."
"One sings the *Rayaṃtara* upon the *kavatī* verses. The word *kavatī* will refer to the *ṛc* (verse) itself, and the word *rayaṃtara* will refer to the *sāman* (chant).
Otherwise, there would be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of location in the word *kavatī*, or an indication of properties (*dharmalakṣaṇā*) in the word *rayaṃtara*.

Therefore, the word *sāman* refers to the chant (*gīta*). Śabara [says]: Regarding the statement, “He chants the *ṛc* verses with the *Rathantara* melody,” it must be determined for the sake of understanding what is being extended (*atidiśyate*) to the *kavatī* verses by means of the word *rathantara*: do words such as *rathantara* denote the *ṛc* verses—such as “*Abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ*”—as qualified by the chant, or do they denote the chant alone?
Furthermore, while defining the characteristic of a mantra, it was merely stated that “the chant is the *sāman*,” but this was not yet established.
In this case, however, for the sake of establishing the scope of the extended application (*atideśa*), it is logically reinforced that the subject matter is indeed the *gīti* (melodic chant).
In that regard, because the term is used for the *ṛc* (verse) as qualified by the *gīti*, it denotes the *ṛc*.

Since the denotation of the qualified entity necessitates the denotation of the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*), and since the comprehension of the *ṛc*—which is invariably concomitant with that [attribute]—is established through that very [denotation of the attribute], it is illogical to postulate a separate denotative power; therefore, the *gīti* alone is their denoted meaning.
Therefore, that specific mode of chanting which exists in the *abhidhā* [verses] is extended (*atideśa*) to the *kavatī* verses.

Since the investigation into whether the term "Soma-chanting" refers to the word itself or to the mode of chanting serves as the purpose for the extension, it is the extension itself—viewed through that lens—that must be investigated; thus, there is a logical connection with the chapter.
Setting aside the actual form of the *ṛc*, the application of the *āyī*-modification and so forth [occurs].

Then, at the time of its conjunction, the syllables of the mantra— which constitute its original form through processes such as *āyībhāva*— are brought to mind. Consequently, because all the syllables are recognized, it is logical that the *ṛc* is a single unit.

Otherwise, at the time of employing the *āyī*-substitution, if there were no recollection [of the specific melody], the Sāman would lack the capacity to manifest the *ṛc*, and its purpose would become merely transcendental (*adṛṣṭārthatā*).
According to the maxim that "one does not grasp a qualified object without grasping the qualification," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the term refers only to the melody itself.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: the application—that is, the linguistic usage—should proceed without transgressing that which is taught by teachers to students by means of the designating words such as *Rathantara* and so forth, namely, the form of the mantra characterized by the melody, exactly as it has been instructed.

The *viniyoga* (application) is as follows: "One sings the *rathantara* on the *kavati* verses"—here, the word "sings" (*gāyati*) denotes either the act of singing itself or words associated with singing.
"Thus is the doubt; however, it is well-known from established usage that [the *abhilāvya*] is connected with singing (*gāna*).
Due to parsimony (*lāghava*) and because of its suitability for extension (*atideśa*), it should be understood as being connected with *cintā* (reflection).

Bhaṭṭa: In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the *Abhilāvya* is produced; the *Rathantara* is heard as something to be performed among the *Kavatī* verses in a specific modification (*vikṛti*), such as the *Avikā*, by such [injunctions] as "He sings the *Rathantara* on the *Kavatī* verses."

Likewise, it is heard in scripture: "Where one sings the *ṛc* in the *ṛc* [of the *rathaṃtara*], there one should sing the *uttarā* [verse] in the *sāman*. In that context, since words such as *rathaṃtara* are used to denote a *ṛc* qualified by a specific chant, it might initially appear that they denote the qualified entity. However, according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, what is denoted is merely the specific chant, or simply the state of being a chant distinct from others.
Similarly, the word *sāman* also denotes merely the chant, or the state of being a chant, but not the chant as qualified by the *ṛc*.

Since its primary meaning is absent, as in the case of the term *aruṇā*, understanding [the meaning] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is established by means of an inconceivable logic (*acintyanyāya*).
However, the sūtras following the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (1.3.10) are intended to state the purpose [of the discussion].

For if it were denotative of the *ṛc* verse itself, then, because the movement of the *ṛc* would be possible [in that case], the word *kavatī* would have the purpose of indicating the function (*kāryalakṣaṇārtha*).

The *kavati*-action should be performed by means of the *abhivati* verses through the transfer (*atideśa*) of the characteristics and so forth; this is the transfer of the *ṛk* of another [verse] to perform the function of the *kavati*.

Alternatively, it means that one should recite the *abhivati* in the place of the *kavati*, or that the secondary term *rathantara*—serving to indicate its properties (*dharma*)—should serve to indicate the locus of those properties, meaning that one should apply the properties of the *rathantara*, such as *saṃmīlana* and others, to the *kavatis*.
Other alternative views found in the commentary have not been recorded here because they lack logical coherence.

In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, because there is no evidence for secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and because there is an absence of any comprehension of the *ṛc* verses here, the extension (*atideśa*) applies to the melody alone in the case of the *kavatī* verses; this is the purpose [of the discussion]. Incidentally, this is the section on *rathantara* and other *sāmans*, which establishes that the term denotes the melody itself, as already proven in the section on "Form" (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*).
It should be understood that certain *sūtras* which reveal exceptions (*chidra*) serve as corroborative factors (*upodbalaka*).

Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as “He sings the *gāyatra* on the *yoni*,” because it is enjoined in the form of a connection with the *yoni*, the definition of extended application (*atideśa*) is appropriate; whereas in cases such as “He sings the *rathantara* on the *kavatīs*,” because the *rathantara* itself is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of what is enjoined, extended application is inappropriate.
For even there, in order to obtain the assistance for grasping the ritual properties (*dharma*), the proximity to the *abhivatīs* serves as the delimiting factor of what is enjoined.

In reality, however, since the injunction regarding the *ājyabhāga* offerings in the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice lacks the character of an extended application (*atideśa*), there is no deficiency whatsoever in this [sacrifice] also lacking such an extended application.

For, by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), when the form of assistance rendered in the *abhivatī* verses is accepted as the very same form of assistance in the *kavatī* verses, the modification (*ūha*) is logically established.
Maṇḍana [states]: "Only the melody (*gīti*) would be extended."
Śaṅkara says: "The *gīti* is considered to be the *sāman*, but not the *ṛc*.
In the section concerning the *Ṛyantara*, there is an apavāda-type connection with the section concerning the *Aveṣṭi*."

In the Kauṣītaki section (Kau. 2.3.13), under the discussion concerning the *Rayaṃtara*, it is established in the Kaustubha that, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, since there is no contradiction in the *Saṃsava* and similar rites, there is an absence of a motive (*nibhisā*), and thus the occasional (*naimittika*) ritual duties do not apply.
Consequently, in that context, the number of vessels to be taken is unrestricted, and any vessel whatsoever may serve as the *pratipad*.
Bhaṭṭa 10.5.16:

According to the commentator on the *Saurya* sacrifice, by the principle of the *Rathantara* section, since it is a modification of the *Āgneya* and other offerings, both mantras are obtained; because there is the possibility of their conjunction (*samuccaya*) as independent means for the act of strengthening (*abhiśardhana*), the lack of fixed restriction (*avyavasthā*) resulting from optionality (*vikalpa*) is established.
There is a fixed acceptance of the *ṛk* verses for the *ṛc*-based melodies such as the *Rathantara*.
Maṇi., p.
170: "The words *rathantara* and so forth, as well as the word *sāman*, denote the melody (*gīti*)."
It should be understood in this context that the word *sāman* refers to words such as *rathantara* which denote the act of singing;
for it is well known that words like *rathantara* signify what is sung.
(Śabara-bhāṣya, p. 862).

The words *ṛgantara* and so forth denote specific types of chanting. This is the section concerning *ṛgantara* and others: the singing of the *sāmans* such as *ṛgantara* over a triplet of verses (*tṛca*).
In a sacrifice, those [Sāmans] that reside in a single verse should be treated like the *svādhyāya*.
Commentary: This is an illustration based on analogy: namely, the *Rayaṃtara*, the *Bṛhat*, the *Vairūpa*, the *Vairāja*, the *Śākvara*, and the *Raivata*.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should the singing (*gāna*) of these Sāmans be performed upon a single verse (*ekarcā*), or upon a triplet of verses (*tṛca*)?
What is established? They should be performed as a single unit in the sacrifice;
they should also be sung as a single unit;
thus they are sung in the private recitation (svādhyāya).
Just as songs are sung during Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), so too should they be sung during ritual action (*karman*).
It is logical that there should be a distinction between ritual action and Vedic recitation;
for they regard Vedic recitation as the means for performing ritual actions.
Therefore, one should apply [the chant] there exactly as it has been practiced. Consequently, the examples are those produced from a single ṛc, not those produced from a triplet (tṛca).
As it has been said: "The *agāpati* and *śākvara* [chants] have their color [determined] by the continuity of the *sīmā*.
Or rather, [the color applies] to the triplet (*tṛca*), because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
The Commentary states: "And this is not so; they are to be sung upon a single [verse]."
Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). There is an indicative mark;
for it says thus: "One chants the prelude (prastāva) of the first verse with eight syllables, and that of the two following verses with two syllables each."
For there is no connection between a first [verse] and a subsequent one within a single ṛc;
therefore, they are to be sung upon a triplet (tṛca).
Now, here is another indicative mark: "The Ṛc and the Sāman said, 'Let us become a couple.'"
He said, "Indeed, you two are not my wives; the Veda is my greatness.
They two became three; he said, "Become one. Therefore, a single *sāman* is performed as a *stotrīya* on a triplet of verses (*tṛca*).
He said:
"This is an indicative mark; let the attainment be stated. That is now explained.

In the entire Ṛgveda, there is no such thing as a verse called "the first," nor likewise one called "the subsequent. Rather, "firstness" and "subsequentness" are established by convention. Thus, it is said that the first verse should be chanted with an eight-syllable *prastāva*, while for the two subsequent verses, it should be done with a two-syllable *prastāva*.
When this statement exists, the verse attains the status of being threefold.

Likewise, although this statement—"Therefore, one *sāman* is performed on a triplet (*tṛca*) as a hymn"—is of the nature of a restatement (*anuvāda*), nevertheless, it is understood that it enacts an injunction through the prior commendation found in the passage "The *ṛc* and the *sāman* spoke.
This has been stated: "Because [the injunction] is preceded by [a commendatory] speech."

Śabara: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are Sāmans such as the Rathantara to be sung as stotriyas. Regarding the doubt as to whether these are to be sung on a single Ṛc verse or on a triplet (tṛca) of verses: since they were sung on a single Ṛc during the time of Vedic study (svādhyāya), for the sake of consistency with that, they should likewise be sung on a single verse in the sacrifice; furthermore, the statement "one Sāman is performed on a triplet" is a description of an existing state and is not capable of being an injunction. Thus, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) regarding the singing of the Rathantara and other Sāmans is that they should be sung on a single verse.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The Ṛc and the Sāman said," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the Sāmans are to be sung over a triplet of verses (*tṛca*), based on the scriptural statement: "One Sāman is performed upon a triplet.
As for the *Soma* [section], some say that its status as a separate section (*pādāntaratā*) arises because the Ṛcs obtained through Vedic study are here set aside by another injunction.

Alternatively, they say that its status as a separate section is due to the fact that here the sublation (*bādha*) of the Sāman is primarily investigated; furthermore, there is an internal connection (*antarasaṃgati*) such as: since in the previous section there was a mention of the form "You are a Suparṇa, having the Gāyatrī metre," even though there was no actual application (*yathāstavyatva*) there, here there is indeed such application, and so forth.

In reality, however, it should be understood that this section constitutes a separate *pāda*, as it establishes here the sublation (*bādha*) concerning the *Soma* sacrifice, which consists of a single day's performance.

In the Sūtra, the phrase "referring to the *Rathantara* and others" indicates the chapter. According to the Bhāṭṭa school: The *Sāmans* produced in only one particular *Yoni* (melodic source) must be sung at the time of the ritual in that very same *Yoni*, because they were practiced in that manner during the period of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), and because otherwise there would be the logical fallacy of producing a specific *Sāman* in a different *Yoni*. Furthermore, scriptural statements such as "one *Sāman*" are appropriately explained as restatements (*anuvāda*) referring to those [specific *Sāmans*].
Thus, although the root *dṛś* (to see) would [otherwise] be understood as having the status of an agent when accompanied by an upapada, it is here understood as being subordinate;
the agent, however, is the primary element.

Nor can an agent, being made known by the inferential mark of "looking," be postulated, because the act of seeing is entirely dependent [on an object]. Furthermore, this [agent], even if it were enjoined, would not establish a coherent connection with the act of looking. If, first of all, this meaning were taught as "one should look at one's own reflection," [then the injunction would be redundant].

If we do not understand what this "self" (*svārtha*) is toward which the act of looking (*vīkṣaṇa*) is enjoined, we would certainly not determine the performance of the action. Even if the meaning were "one should effect the act of looking for one's own sake," the same fault would remain due to the lack of clarity regarding that very object.
Thus, when such a relationship is accepted through direct injunction (*ājñāsena*), neither the indicative mark (*liṅga*) nor the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is favored.

However, in the case of a relationship based on indication (*lakṣaṇa-sambandha*), there is a logical connection with the act of looking (*vīkṣaṇa*) at the time of uttering this [formula], such that "one should look. Furthermore, a relationship with praise (*stuti*) is not incompatible even with the injunction regarding the agent (*kartṛ-vidhāna*).

By virtue of the common subject matter (*sāmānyādhikāra*), one accepts the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between "the Ruler" (*īśāne*) and "from Him" (*tataśca*); [it is said] "the Ruler, the self-ruling.
Therefore, state the arrangement (*racanā*).

And it is called *raśanā* (girdle). Although here the word *raśanā* is not explicitly heard [in the primary injunction], but rather [the act] is obtained from the very act of encircling the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as in "he encircles the post," nevertheless, because words such as *darbhamayī* ("made of darbha grass") are etymological (*yaugika*), they denote specific types of encircling materials; therefore, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that "the *raśanā* is heard."

Just as the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpapariṣyāṇa*) is prescribed for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice by the injunction "he encircles the post," so too is it prescribed for the *savanīya* sacrifice by the injunction: "Having taken up the *āśvina* cup and gone out, he encircles the post.

Consequently, since the encircling of the post and other such acts apply to both sacrifices, and because the cord (*raśanā*) is already established in both cases, a doubt arises regarding the properties (*dharmāḥ*) of the cord that are being heard in the texts: do they apply only to the cord of the *agnīṣomīya*, or to the cords of both the *agnīṣomīya* and the *savanīya*?

On this point, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: In the sequence of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, the properties of the rope, such as being made of *darbha* grass and so forth, are heard [in the scripture] on the fourteenth day, but not for the Savanīya.
Therefore, like the properties of the animal itself, these rope-properties apply only to the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) belonging to the Agniṣomīya.
But is it not the case that, by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), they are understood to pertain to ropes in general?
And direct statement (śruti) is stronger than syntactical connection (vākya).
True;

however, because the relationship with the nature of the sacrificial post (yūpa) would otherwise be purposeless, its application must be stated by means of a direct statement that indicates [the post] as a means to the transcendental result (apūrva).

Therefore, just as by direct statement (*śruti*) aided by context (*prakaraṇa*), the properties of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) apply only to the grass situated within that specific context, so too—even though the direct statement is common [to both], the properties of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* do not apply to its grass; likewise, by direct statement aided by sequence (*krama*), the properties of the rope (*raśanā*) apply only to the rope used for encircling the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, which is presented by that sequence.
This being the prima facie view, the following is established:

this would indeed be so if the encircling mentioned in the Agniṣomīya context—namely, "he encircles the post"—were to serve, through the medium of the post, to accomplish the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the primary sacrifice, just like the sprinkling of rice grains.

However, because the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is transcendental (*alaukika*), it requires a means for its accomplishment that serves as an undesirable end (*aniṣṭopāya*). In this context, by the force of the accusative case in the scriptural injunction "he encircles the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ parivyayati*), it is understood that the act of encircling has the sacrificial post as its purpose, specifically for the sake of the post's consecration (*nirvṛtti*). Likewise, regarding the *savanīya* sacrifice, although the act of encircling is heard in scripture as having the sacrificial post as its purpose in the statement "having gone out, he encircles the sacrificial post," it is nevertheless common [to all sacrifices], since the sacrificial post is actually produced only at the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.

Although it is not useful for the actual production of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) itself, nevertheless, according to the principle that "it is useful for both its own form and its function," it serves the purpose of the post’s function—namely, the tethering of the animal—and thus it becomes [the means] by generating excellence.
Furthermore, because there is no distinction in their being ropes used for encircling for the sake of the post, these ropes belong in common to both [ropes].

Nor, this being the case, is it understood through the direct statement (*śruti*) aided by sequence (*krama*) that they apply only to the rope encircling the *agnīṣomīya* post, since that post is presented in its proper order.

It should be stated that, as if aided by the context (*prakaraṇa*), the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) establishes that the properties of the *barhis* belong to the *barhis* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
For the very same sacrificial post (*yūpa*) that belongs to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice also belongs to the Savanīya sacrifice.

Consequently, the properties enjoined by way of connection with the rope used for tying the post of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice become enjoined by way of connection with the rope used for tying the post of the Savanīya sacrifice as well.

It is stated that the rules regarding the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) used in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* do not apply to the grass used in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, as they are distinct; however, even so, in the originative injunction for the *Savanīya*, the restatement "he encircles the sacrificial post with a triple-stranded cord" (*trivṛtā yūpaṃ parivīya*) would be inexplicable if the rules for the cord were not common [to all three], and thus this serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, by the observation of this indicative mark, it is established that the rules for the cord are indeed common.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the restriction regarding the use of *darbha* grass and so forth applies to the rope of the *savanīya* animal;
according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the restriction regarding the properties of being made of *darbha* grass and so forth applies to the rope of the *agnīṣomīya* animal alone.
As for the *sūtra*, the word "rope" (*raśanā*) is intended to indicate the properties pertaining to all ropes.

Therefore, this is the meaning: just as the properties of the cups (*graha*) are common to all the cups occurring in the three pressings (*savanatraya*), so too the properties of the cords (*raśanā*) are common [to all].
And the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga-darśana*) has already been stated. Thus says the Tautātita school.

Regarding the statement "And the girdle [is common] because of the observation of an indicative mark," the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) must state the resolution that the girdle is common to both methods of binding.
Vārttika 3.6.22, p. 1049: "And the girdle [is common] because of the observation of an indicative mark.
(The word *tulya* [common] is carried over from the eighteenth sūtra. And the girdle is common to the two animals, the Agniṣomīya and the Savanīya.
Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Thus it says: "Having taken the Āśvina cup, having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-stranded rope, he prepares the Savanīya animal dedicated to Agni. This indicates the rope at the time of encircling the Savanīya [post].
If that [rope] were common to all [the animals], then this [textual] statement becomes possible.
Bhāṣya 3.6.13:
The rope and its properties, which belong to the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, are extended by analogy to all animal sacrifices;
the rope and its properties [are taken] from the Agniṣomīya sacrifice according to the sequence.

This being the prima facie view, it is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) that [the ropes] are for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). It is said: "The properties of the ropes, such as being made of *darbha* grass and so forth, are understood through syntactic order (*krama*) to belong to the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice]; however, they have attained the status of being for the sake of the sacrificial post through direct scriptural statement."
For this rope is heard in scripture as belonging to the sacrificial post;
it goes along with the ritual action (dharma) until, in due order, it reaches the status of being a remnant for the animal.
Scripture is more authoritative than the sequential order.

Vārttika 3.3.7, page 836: The rope (*raśanā*) and its properties are indeed properties of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), not properties of the animal (*paśu*). [The text continues: "One should tie the sacrificial post with a threefold rope..."

In the section concerning the girdle (*raśanā*), by virtue of the third-case hearing (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) in the word *parivyaye* and by syntactical connection (*vākya*), [it is established that] the girdle (*raśanā*)—indicated by the second case—is not for the purpose of seizing the animal, but rather for the purpose of consecrating the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Vi. 3.6.10.
4|4|126–24. The rope (*raśanā*) is for the purpose of binding the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); it is threefold (*trivṛt*) and possesses the property of being twisted to the right (*pradakṣiṇāvarta*).
Bhāṣya 3|6|13:
[Regarding] the ropes.

In the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, there are two sets of ropes for the sacrificial posts on the two sides; in a series of days (*ahargaṇa*), they serve their purpose through a single common procedure (*tantra*).
Saṃkarṣa 1.4.16:
the ropes belong to the set of eleven (*aikādaśina*).
"Agni envelops you with a cord and causes you to dwell," this refers to a specific consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the cord (*raśanā*).
*Saṃkarṣa* 1.4.12; *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 78. "Agni causes you to dwell with a cord"—this is the consecration of the cord.
Thus it should be understood.
The Adhvaryu performs the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with the girdle (*raśanā*) using the mantra beginning with "thou art encircled" (*parivīr asi*). [Vi.
3.8.11] There is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the girdle for the purpose of the sacrificial post.

Vārttika 4.4.122, p. 1279. In a sacrifice involving the *sāgnika* [fire-altar], when eleven animals are bound to a single sacrificial post (*ekayūpa*), there is no division of the girdle (*raśanā*) intended for the consecration of the post; thus, there is indeed a twofold nature [of the girdle].
Bhāṣya 3.6, Section on the Girdle (*raśanādhikaraṇa*).

The properties of the rope (*raśanā*) in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice are common to both the Agniṣomīya and the Savanīya sacrifices. And that there is a rope [in this context] is established by the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
The Bhāṣya states: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, as it is said: 'When one who is initiated sacrifices the Agniṣomīya animal...'"
In this context, the girdle is mentioned, as well as the properties of the girdle: "It is threefold, it is made of darbha grass, and it must be covered.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: are these properties common to both the girdle of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice and the girdle of the Savanīya animal sacrifice, or do they belong to the girdle of the Agniṣomīya alone? What is the prima facie view? On account of the context, they belong to the girdle of the Agniṣomīya.
This being the case, we reply:
they are common to both. Why? Because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga).
There is an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Thus it says: "Having taken the Āśvina cup, having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-stranded rope, one prepares the Savanīya animal dedicated to Agni. This shows the rope (*raśanā*) in connection with the encircling of the Savanīya post.
If that [rope] were common [to all three animals], then this [indicative mark] would be consistent.

If it belongs to the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice], then it would exclude the non-archetypal wrapping (*pariṣyāṇa*) of the Savanīya [animal]. And in the case of the Savanīya, there is another non-archetypal wrapping in which the *trivṛt* [cord] is seen.
How so? "Having taken the Āśvina cup and gone out, he wraps the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)."
In that case, if the girdle were not common [to both], it would follow that it should be wrapped with a cloth; however,
the text actually shows the use of a girdle.
Therefore, the girdle is common [to both].
And because it is common, its properties are also common. This commonality of the girdle is established by this indicative mark (liṅga).
What indeed is the logic here? It is said:

[the rule] applies to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa), whereas it applies to the sacrificial post (yūpa) in general by virtue of the syntactical connection (vākya). Or rather—having prescribed the encircling of the sacrificial post for the Agniṣomīya, it is further stated regarding the Savanīya: "Having taken the Āśvina cup... and so forth; and because of this repetition of the action devoid of specific qualities (nirguṇa-punaḥśravaṇāt), it constitutes a distinct ritual act (karmāntara).
And there must be some substance for both.
That substance which serves as a means of binding is well known in the world and in the Veda as the *raśanā* (girdle).
Therefore, because it serves that same purpose in both cases, the *raśanā* is obtained [as the required item].

When it is asked what that [rope] is made of and what its properties are, a specific detail is understood from the scriptural injunction—"A triple-stranded rope made of *darbha* grass is to be used as a cover"—within the context inferred by the position of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, and not for the binding of the *savanīya*.
Therefore, just like the other properties of the animal, the procedure regarding the rope belongs to the *agnīṣomīya* alone.
This being the prima facie view, the author says that it is common to both, because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

For the reference to the threefold nature (*trivṛttva*) and so forth in the originative injunction of the *savanīya* [animal sacrifice] is not justified by the commonality of the properties of the rope, such as its being made of *darbha* grass.

If it is asked, "What is the basis for this?", he states it: on account of the connection with the direct statement (*vākya*), it applies to the rope in general; on account of the position (*sthāna*), it applies to that of the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice].
And he will state the answer later in the sūtra: "And because of the direct statement" (3.6.14).
Therefore, because it is prompted by the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, there would be a fixed restriction;
but this is not so,
for this [quality] is not directly connected with the animal.
What then? He will state [later], "Or rather, it is the sacrificial post (yūpa), because of its connection with that" (4.4.123).
Therefore, this constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) of such a kind:
that these ritual properties (*dharma*) are common to both the sacrificial post and the enclosing rope (*parivyāṇa*).

And likewise, because the sacrificial post (yūpa) is one and the same, the girding of the post belonging to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice is [identical to] the girding of the post belonging to the Savanīya sacrifice.

Furthermore, the substance here is understood as a means for the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), and it will not be like the *barhis* grass used in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña in relation to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Therefore, just like the properties of the *barhis*, the properties of the rope (*raśanā*) are common to the animal sacrifices.
The properties of the girdle (raśanā-dharmāḥ) pertain, in sequence, to the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice.
This being the prima facie view, we reply:
by virtue of direct scriptural statement (śruti), these [properties] have attained the status of being connected to the sacrificial post (yūpa) through the act of encircling it.

The properties of the *nāmīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] would not apply [to the *savanīya*], for it is only by virtue of its being a *tāvat* (that much) that they are applicable. Furthermore, this encircling with a rope (*pariṣyāṇa*) belongs to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Therefore, in that case as well, the rope is introduced along with its associated properties.
Thus ends the section on the girdle (raśanādhikaraṇa).
The section on the girdle.

Since there is no *prakaraṇa* (contextual section) for the [sacrifice] following Soma—which would have been reached by sequence—the connection [of the discussion] arises from the fact that the properties of the rope (*raśanā*) pertain to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.

This is because, as will be stated in the eleventh book (11.1.13–14), the unity of performance (*tantratā*) applies to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) used for the animal sacrifices belonging to the Soma ritual; thus, the encircling (*parivyāṇa*) of the Savanīya animal also pertains to the post associated with the Agniṣomīya.
As for the meaning of the *sūtra*: the rope and its properties are common to both instances of encircling.

"Having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted rope, he dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni"—because in this originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) of the Savanīya, there is observed the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the rope endowed with the property of being triple-twisted. [Objection: "In all cases, the wrapping of the rope and so forth apply to one and the same [post].
[Reply: These [properties] belong specifically to the Agnīṣomīya; the first [set of properties] follows from the sequence, while the last [set] follows from the indicative mark.

Bhaṭṭa: Since the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is enjoined by the designation "for the tethering of the animal" and so forth, its purpose is the tethering of the animal which serves as a means for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, due to the requirement of performance; and through extension (*atideśa*), it serves the purposes of the *savanīya* and *anubandhya* sacrifices.
The same applies to the preparatory rites such as cutting, which bring that [post] about.

Although there is a scriptural statement of futility regarding the mere form of the post, nevertheless, because that which is being referred to (*anuvādya*) must apply to what is proximate, its placement is within the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.

In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), however, the movement is like the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward). Since their piercing and so forth would otherwise be required to arise separately, it will be stated in the eleventh book (*11.1.13*) that because the time for initiation (*dīkṣākāla*)—which is enjoined through both direct instruction and extended application (*atideśa*)—is one and the same, it is performed once by way of a single ritual framework (*tantra*); thus, a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*) serves as the benefactor for all.

Furthermore, those rites such as the encircling (*parivyāṇa*) which are purificatory acts (*saṃskāraka*) for the post already produced, possess the nature of being both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*) due to the sequence of their performance, based on both direct instruction and extended application.

Because the essential nature of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) arises even apart from that [specific ritual], and because the post is one and the same, there is no repetition [of rites]; for even though its specific characteristics are being grasped, the purpose is accomplished through incidental application (*prasaṅga*), according to the logic of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) at the *Ātithyā* and other rites (12.1.19). However, it does not follow by that same logic that the Agni-praṇayana and other such rites belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices would also apply incidentally to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

Just as in the case of the sprinkling of rice (*vrīhiprokṣaṇa*) and similar acts, even if a certain thing arises for the sake of a specific set of effects (*kāryakūṭa*), there is no such contingency [of its destruction] because it has been established that the final effect of that set of effects is the destroyer of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) arising from those things that have ceased to exist.

For in this case, the residual impression resulting from the attainment of fire (*agniprāpti*) and so forth—which arises for the sake of a specific set of effects—is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of that set of effects, since the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) belongs to a different category than the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and other such rites.

Therefore, because destruction occurs by way of a specific causal relationship—namely, that the final effect, which is the fruit of the action, acts as the destroyer with respect to the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) delimited by being produced by that [specific] speech and action—the destruction results from the fruit residing in its counter-correlative. Such is the distinction.

And thus, although the girding with the rope (*parivyāṇa-raśanā*) is performed on the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*), it serves the three purposes through both direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*).

By the injunction, "Having taken the Āśvina cup at the Savanīya [offering], having gone out, one encircles the sacrificial post," a second act of encircling is prescribed through repetition; this follows from the textual sequence (pāṭha) which places it after the time of the Āśvina cup, and the act of going out is obtained by implication.
Furthermore, that [act] is an auxiliary (aṅga) to the Savanīya alone due to the context (prakaraṇa).
Moreover, it does not serve the purpose of the original (prākṛta) function, because—like the gift of the *prākāśa* ornaments—that would result in the redundancy of the injunction.
For this very reason, its effects—such as the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) or the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth—are distinct matters.

Therefore, in this context, the rope and its properties, such as being threefold (*tribhṛtva*) and belonging to the *bhīṣya* [the sacrificer], do not apply to another act of encircling (*parivyāṇa*) that serves a non-original purpose, just as they do not apply to the spreading of grass around the pit for the sacrificial post (*yūpavaṭ*).

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: by virtue of the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*) in the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*), which takes the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the threefold nature, and on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), the delimiting factor of the referent (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) is simply the state of being the encircling of the sacrificial post that serves as the means (*sādhana*) in the present context, and not the state of being the encircling of a sacrificial post of a different class.

If that were the case, since the state of being threefold (*tribhṛtva*) is not already established in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), its prescription would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*).
Therefore, because the defining characteristic of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka-rūpa*) exists there as well, the rope (*raśanā*) serves the purpose of that [binding] too.

However, we do not understand the intention behind the commentary which—out of a desire for consistency—accepts that all three (the cutting of the sacrificial post, the binding, and the purpose of the rope) are common to the triad through direct instruction (*upadeśa*) alone, and then asserts that the requirement for the other binding of the *savanīya* animal is obtained through direct instruction as well.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The girdle has the same purpose as the three sacrificial animals.
Śaṅkara [states]: "There is [a commonality] between the girdle and the cake;
there is a commonality in their serving all purposes."
The section on the girdle.
The girdle belongs to the sacrificial post.
The girdle should be an accessory of the animal, because it is prescribed upon the arrival of that [animal].

Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "Having taken the Āśvina cup, having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted rope, he dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the rope an accessory (aṅga) of the animal, or is it an accessory of the sacrificial post? What is the prima facie view? It is an accessory of the animal.
Why? Because it is prescribed upon the arrival of that [animal].
For it is prescribed upon the arrival of the animal;
the connection between the animals and the *assā* (rope) is heard in the originative injunction: "Having performed the encircling (*parivyāṇa*), one removes the animal, and not otherwise."
Thus the scriptural statement occurs.
If it were a statement of time, there would be figurative indication (lakṣaṇā);
the time of the encircling (parivyāṇa) would be indicated.

Ḍuṣa [says]: "Having encircled the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with a triple-stranded rope" (*tribhṛtā yūpaṃ parivīya*); because the sacrificial post is that which is most desired to be reached (*īpsitatama*), the rope is for its sake alone.

However, the second case ending (*dvitīyā vibhakti*) following *yūpa*—which denotes the object of the act of encircling (*parivyāṇa*)—indicates that the encircling is for the sake of the post, not that the rope is for the sake of the encircling.
And as for that [encircling]...
The section concerning the girdle;
the section concerning the girdle,
O Lord.

What then? By this [text], the connection between the *āgneya* (the cake for Agni) and the rope is established, and therein it serves a purpose. The rope belongs to the *āgneya*, as it is for its sake;
for it assists that [cake] by means of preventing its displacement.
But surely another [rope] is prescribed for the animal to prevent its escaping?
It is said in reply: just as there is a combination of ropes for the sake of the sacrificial post (yūpa), so it is here as well.
[Objection: But surely, because the sacrificial post (yūpa) is indicated by the accusative case, the rope must be for its purpose.
[Reply: It is said in response:
In the other case as well, the accusative is indeed prescribed in the word "āgneyam."

Alternatively, the accusative case in the word "yūpam" (the sacrificial post) in the phrase "parivyāṇasya yūpam" expresses that it is for the sake of the act of encircling (*parivyāṇa*), not for the sake of the rope (*raśanā*).
[The opponent] says: Because it serves the purpose of encircling, the rope also has the sacrificial post as its purpose.
It is said:

because the rope has a purpose in preventing the animal from escaping, the act of encircling (*parivyāṇa*), even though it is being performed as a subordinate action (*bhāvyamāna*), is for that purpose; the capacity of the rope is produced by the act of encircling.
[Objection: But surely the act of encircling is also purposeful insofar as it pertains to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and its purpose, and thus the rope is for that [encircling] as well.
It is said:
this must be carefully considered.
Is the rope intended for the purpose of encircling [the sacrificial post] and thus subservient to the post, or is the relationship of subservience the reverse?
The encircling is for the sake of the animal; since it serves as the substrate for the encircling of the sacrificial post, it is for the sake of the animal.
In this regard, what is appropriate?
The rope has a purposeful function in preventing the animal from escaping.
The encircling (parivyāṇa) also has that [the post] as its purpose.
The sacrificial post (yūpa), too, while serving as a substratum, serves the girdle (raśanā) for that same purpose.
As for the accusative case used for the post in relation to Agni, it will indicate the sense of the locative case.
Furthermore, for that which is being established as a substratum, its purposefulness (*tādarthya*) will be investigated by way of context.
Or rather, it is for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), because of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) thereof.
The Commentary states: "For in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the injunction is indeed a refinement of the sacrificial post."
For the girdle produces for the sacrificial post whatever degree of firmness it may have, and the sacrificial post has a need for that firmness;
therefore, the girdle should belong to the sacrificial post itself for the sake of its firmness.
Furthermore, the accusative case-ending occurs only when that [the post] is the primary object.
And the third [case-ending] is used for the girdle;
and that third case is used because of its being an accessory (guṇa).
Therefore, it belongs to the sacrificial post (yūpa).
As for what was stated—that [the quality] belongs to that [substance] because of its prescription in the scriptural injunction—that must be refuted.
It is replied:

the prescription regarding that [substance] arises from the syntactical connection (*vākya*), whereas the accusative case-ending is a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and is perceptible; therefore, the syntactical connection must yield to the direct statement.
As for the point regarding "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*): when a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is impossible, even indication is logically permissible.

[Durga says: "In the case of the text, 'having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-stranded rope,' because the post is that which is most desired to be reached, the rope is for its sake alone.

However, since the act of encircling has the post as its object, the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā vibhaktiḥ*) refers to the post; it establishes that the encircling is for the sake of the post, not that the rope is for the sake of the encircling."
And that (encircling,
which is obtained by implication) is restated.

In the case of [the injunction] "he dedicates the animal" (*paśum upākaroti*), the accusative case ending on *paśu* establishes that the act of dedication (*upākaraṇa*) is the primary ritual element (*padārtha*), and not the rope.
Furthermore, the girdle does not obtain as a means [for the sacrifice] merely by virtue of being an accessory implied by the purpose;
rather, the girdle is implied by the act of encircling (*parivyāṇa*).
In this regard, there is no insistence on whether that which is enjoined by this [text] is followed here, or whether that which is enjoined by that [other text] is followed here.
In every respect, the rope is for the purpose of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

Since eleven animals are to be bound to a single post, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), a separate rope should be used for each animal. In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, there is indeed a dual arrangement [of ropes]; this is the purpose [stated in the Bhāṣya]. Those who hold a partial view, considering the prima facie position otherwise, do not accept this.

(How so? Even though it serves the purpose of a single animal, the rope (raśanā) is not [repeated] because it provides assistance through direct application (*saṃnipatyopakāritvāt*). Since it is made upon a common sacrificial post (*yūpa*), it will assist all the animals with just one instance.
Just as the *prayāja* offerings, when performed once, assist all the sacrifices beginning with the *āgneya*, therefore there is a twofold classification in both positions.
(For they describe it thus:
Even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the encircling (*parivyāṇa*) is not for the sake of the rope; rather, the rope itself is for the sake of the encircling.

Furthermore, the encircling is not for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), but—by virtue of the gerund suffix (*ktvā*) in the word *parivīya*—is for the sake of the animal's presentation (*upākaraṇa*), and through that medium, it is for the sake of the animal.)
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that even though the girdle (raśanā) is applied to the sacrificial post by way of that [encircling], it serves the purpose of the animal.

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is that according to direct scriptural statement (śruti), the encircling is for the sake of the post alone; it is not an accessory (upakaraṇa) for the animal by virtue of syntactical connection (vākya).
(He refutes the objection regarding the purpose: This too is incorrect.
Even though it serves the purpose of the animal, the rope (*raśanā*) assists the animal directly by preventing its escape.
Just as a second rope is combined with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) [in the final Siddhānta], so too [in the Pūrvapakṣa] it is combined with the animal (i.e., the animal is bound with two ropes).
Therefore, this purpose is indeed appropriate; and the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is meaningful for that reason.
The Commentary states: "And in this way, the mantra and the explanatory passage will be meaningful."
"The youth, well-attired and girt with the sacrificial cord, has arrived; he becomes even more excellent as he is born.
Wise poets, seeking the divine with their minds and intent on meditation, lead him forth.
Thus it is said.
Therefore, [the rule is] "the rope belongs to the sacrificial post.
What is the purpose of this deliberation?
It is heard in the context of the Agni sacrifice: "Eleven animals are to be bound to a single sacrificial post."
A separate cord must be made for each animal, if the previous section on cords (raśanādhikaraṇa) 3308 is the position regarding the properties of the cords.
In the established conclusion (siddhānta), there is indeed duality.
They also cite this verse: "If the rope were a limb of the animal, one would employ many ropes in this sacrifice;
if there were a rope for each animal on the sacrificial post, there would be duality."
Śabara says: "The two posts are for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and the two ropes are for the purpose of binding the animal.
Because they do not depart [from their original place], the rope must therefore be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the animal."
This being the case, we reply:
If it were for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) in relation to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), such an assumption of an invisible result (*adṛṣṭakalpanā*) would indeed be necessary;
however, even though it serves the purpose of the sacrificial post, it has a visible purpose (*dṛśyārtha*) because it produces firmness (*dāḍhryajanman*).

For the act of encircling is understood from the accusative case to have the sacrificial post as its purpose; and the rope, being subordinate to the act of encircling, is indicated by the instrumental case.
If the rope were for the sake of the animal, all that would be the opposite;
therefore, the rope must be for the sake of the sacrificial post, and not for the purpose of binding the animal.

Just as in the case of the Soma-pitṛyajña, where there is a sublation of the word denoting time because it occurs on the new-moon day (darśa), here, since there is no such sublation of anything and because the "rope" (raśanā) is directly perceived, there is a logical connection. As for the meaning of the sūtra: the rope is an accessory of the animal sacrifice; it is not [merely] for the sake of the person, as might otherwise be assumed.

In the case of the expression "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*) being employed, it is understood that what is intended to be expressed is precisely the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) based on the factor of providing assistance.

Even in cases where the status of being a subordinate is absolutely non-existent in the owner of a cow, a slave, or the like, it should be seen as a metaphorical designation (*upacarita*) due to the relationship of being a benefactor.

*Rājapuruṣa*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he who is both a king and a man. The form *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king's man) is used for the sake of explaining the meaning, even though the actual form [of the compound] is different; this is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning. (Soma. 6.1.2)

In the expression "rāja-puruṣaḥ śobhanaḥ" ("the king's man is handsome"), there occurs a compound even though the word *puruṣa* (man), being a subordinate member (*śeṣa*), is a substantive (*viśeṣya*) that requires the word *śobhana* (handsome). See Ratnākara, p. 347. In the case of *rājapuruṣa*, the subordinate element *puruṣa* does not undergo qualification by another word.
For it does not happen that [the word] *ṛddha* [is used] as "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*).
(An attributive word is not connected with another word [as its primary referent], just like "the king's man"—*Bṛhatī*, *Kraju.* p. 70).

"Two persons—the king and the royal priest—desiring union (sāyujya) should perform the sacrifice," [it is said] regarding the Kulāyayajña; thus, there is joint entitlement for the king and the royal priest even though they follow different ritual manuals (kalpa).
However, concerning the second fore-offering (prayāja), since both are equally primary, this should be examined under the section on the Nārāśaṃsa and Tanūnapāt in the Rājasūya.

In the Rājasūya, the forms of sacrifice such as the Anumati offerings and others, as well as non-sacrificial acts such as the Vidēva offerings and others—all these are not fruit-bearing; they are all equally principal preparatory rites (*pūrvāṅga*). However, those that are non-sacrificial are for the sake of the ritual act (*kratvartha*), whereas only those that are sacrificial in form are the principal acts.
4|4|11–2. In the Rājasūya, the *iṣṭis* such as the Anumati, the *soma* sacrifices such as the Pavitra, and the *homās*—all are principal.

Bhā. 1112|3112. In the Rājasūya, the sacrifices beginning with the Anumati are prescribed; since the commencement (of these) is omitted, the Ārambhaṇīyā [introductory offering] should not be performed.
Vi. 10|1|13. In the Rājasūya, the release of speech occurs only at the final time of the *haviṣkṛt* call.
Vṛ. 1113|17|4. In the Rājasūya, the *vidan* and other [formulas] occur prior to the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

Bhāṣya 5.12.10.21: In the Rājasūya sacrifice, following the sequence of wooden vessels (kāṣṭhāṅga) obtained through the force of the archetypal rule (*codaka*) in the Abhiṣeṇīya Soma-sacrifice, the Videvana, Śaunaḥśepa, and other rites are to be performed.
If this is argued, [the reply is:

since the Abhiṣeṇīya has the character of being a single performance unit (*eka*) because "one is consecrated at the Māhendra-stotra," therefore the Videvana and other rites preceding the consecration must also constitute a single performance unit.
VI. 5|12|10. In the Rājasūya sacrifice, the Abhiṣeṇīya and Daśapeya rites have distinct ritual frameworks (tantra).
11|2|14|17–62. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 563; consult the entry "abhiṣeṇīyadaśapeyayorbhinnaṃ tantram" (the Abhiṣeṇīya and Daśapeya have distinct ritual frameworks).
In the Rājasūya sacrifice there is the Aveṣṭi.
Regarding that, it is said: "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, having placed the offering for Bṛhaspati in the middle and having offered the oblation, he should cause that to be moved forward;
if a Rājanya, [the offering] for Indra; if a Vaiśya, [the offering] for the Viśvedevas."

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the terms "king" (*rājā*) and "royal" (*rāja-*) can apply to Brāhmaṇas and Vaiśyas as well through their association with sovereignty, this [Rājasūya] may be performed by them too. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the Rājasūya has a Kṣatriya as its performer alone; whereas the *Aveṣṭi* is enjoined as a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*) with specific qualities, which may be performed by Brāhmaṇas and others.
And likewise, the Aveṣṭi is both a subsidiary of the Rājasūya and independent;
it should be understood as independent in that very context (Vi.
2.3.12). In the Rājasūya, regarding the Aveṣṭis, the subsidiaries are to be performed separately; there is no *tantra* (common performance).

Bhāṣya 1.4.4.18–10: In the Rājasūya, there are sacrifices (*iṣṭis*) such as: (1) "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Anumati," (2) "A cake on one potsherd to Nirṛti," (3) "He offers a pap (*caru*) to Aditi," (4) "A cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu," and so forth.
There are animal sacrifices (*paśus*), such as: "He immolates a pregnant cow for Aditi," "A speckled cow for the Maruts," "A he-goat for the Aśvins," and so forth.
There are Soma sacrifices, such as: the Abhiṣecanīya, the Daśapeya, and so forth.
Regarding the *homās*: the *darvihomas* are those such as "the offering in the mound of an anthill" (*valmīkavapāyāṃ homaḥ*) and so forth.
All of these are of the nature of sacrifice (*yāga*) and are primary (*pradhāna*).

Those that are not of the nature of sacrifice—such as "he plays with a four-year-old heifer," "he plays with dice," "he defeats a Kṣatriya," and "he causes the Śunaḥśepa story to be recited"—these, however, are subsidiary acts (*aṅga*).
VI.4.4.1 | In the Rājasūya, the iṣṭis, animal sacrifices, Soma sacrifices, and oblations (davihomas) are the primary rites.
Among these, the Ārambhaṇīyā [iṣṭi] need not be performed for the sake of the iṣṭis.

(Since) they perform the Agniṣṭoma first. Bhāṣya 10.1.13.6: "In the Rājasūya, regarding the two [offerings] connected with the latter [part], namely the Soma-pauṣṇa on eleven potsherds and the Aindrā-pauṣṇa, both have the sacrificial fee.
In that context, the grinding of the offering to Pūṣan (pauṣṇa-peṣaṇa) should not be performed for a dual-deity offering, but only for a *caru* dedicated solely to the deity Pūṣan.

3|13|15|16–46. Regarding the *rājasūya*, there is a doubt as to whether the performance of the *videdanā* and other rites occurs at the end [of the sacrifice] or prior to the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). The conclusion is that it is prior to the consecration. Bhāṣya 5|12|10|21. In the *rājasūya*, the subsidiaries of the principal acts—such as those connected by the phrase "two [are] joined" (*atisaṃyukte dve*)—are to be performed individually (*anu*), not collectively (*tantra*). 11|4|11–3. In the *rājasūya*, during the sacrifice named *daśapeya*, ten cups (*camasa*) are drunk from, each by ten persons respectively.

Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the cup belonging to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is to be drunk by ten [persons], and those must be Kṣatriyas alone. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: a Kṣatriya has no right to consume the Soma at all, and this applies to the sacrificer as well. Since the Brāhmaṇa text prescribes, with reference to the ten cups numbering one hundred, "One hundred Brāhmaṇas drink," it follows that just like the other cups, the sacrificer’s cup too is to be drunk by ten Brāhmaṇas alone.

VI. 3|5|20. In the *rājasūya*, regarding the *daśapeya* sacrifice, it is said: "He gives two *prākāśa* [mirrors] to the *adhvaryu*. These two *prākāśas* are the displacers (*nivartaka*) of the *adhvaryu*'s share alone, but not of the entire sacrificial fee (*kratudākṣiṇya*).
10|1|13|63–64. In the *rājasūya*, there are two Soma sacrifices, the *daśapeya* and the *abhiṣecanīya*.
"He purchases the Soma together for both the *abhiṣecanīya* and the *daśapeya*."

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the injunctions for the *daśapeya* sacrifice—which occur prior to the purchase [of Soma]—are brought forward, there is a single performance (*tantra*). [The reply is:
There is no single performance; the commencement of the *daśapeya* occurs in the afternoon following the ten sacrifices known as the *saṃsṛps*.
Prior to those, at a time separated by a great interval, is the *abhiṣeṇīya* sacrifice.
"In the Daśapeya sacrifice, they are consecrated immediately and purchase the Soma immediately"—this indicates the immediate timing (*sadyaḥkālatva*).
"He purchases the Soma together"—this indicates mere simultaneity (*sāhitya*) of the purchase and the formal agreement (*krayārthopasaṃvāda*).
Consequently, there is no *tantra* (common ritual procedure).
VI. 11.2.14. In the Rājasūya, regarding the offering to the quarters: "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; gold is the sacrificial fee.
He offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra; a ram is the sacrificial fee."
"A *vaiśvadeva* oblation of boiled rice (*caru*), with a *piñjalī* bird as the sacrificial fee; a *maitrāvaruṇī* oblation of meat, with a ram as the sacrificial fee;
and a *vārhaspatya* oblation of boiled rice, with a *kṣitipṛṣṭha* [a white-backed animal] as the sacrificial fee."
Regarding these [rites], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are to be performed as a single common procedure (*tantra*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a common procedure for the external performance (*vahiṣparyāya*), but there is a distinction (*bheda*) for the internal performance (*antaḥprayoga*).
(Vi. 11.4.3). In the Rājasūya sacrifice, the gambling and other such rites are auxiliary to the entire Rājasūya, and not merely auxiliary to the Abhiṣecanīya Soma-sacrifice alone.
The performance, however, takes place at the time of the *māhendra* stotra during the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice.

(4.4.2). In the *Rājasūya*, there is a difference of location: "A pap for Bṛhaspati in the house of the Brahmin; a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra in the house of the King; a pap for Aditi in the house of the Mahiṣī," and so forth.
(Bhāṣya 11.2.13–14). In the *Rājasūya*, there is the *Nānābījeṣṭi*: "He offers a cake on eight potsherds of black rice to Agni Gṛhapati; a pap of millet to Soma Vanaspati," and so forth.

In that context, the sequence beginning with threshing consists of: the spreading of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), placing the mortar (*ulūkhala*) upon it, sowing the seeds therein, threshing, winnowing by form, and the separation of the rice grains from the husks; all these taken together constitute a single ritual act named "threshing.
In this regard, the performance of the entire collection—beginning with the spreading of the black antelope skin and so forth—must be carried out simultaneously for each individual seed.
Thus, there is one black antelope skin, one mortar, and so on.
VI. 5.12.7. In the Rājasūya sacrifice, there is the Nānābījeṣṭi (the sacrifice with various seeds).
In that sacrifice, the application of the mantra by means of pouring [the oblation] is obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction).
In that case, there is a repetition of the mantra for each seed.

Bhāṣya 11.4.13.43: In the Rājasūya sacrifice, during the Nānābījeṣṭi, the release of speech (vāgvisarga) occurs at the very time of taking the portions of the oblation associated with each different seed-grain (*anyatvīja*).
See Mīmāṃsākosa, page 2313, under the entry "nānābījeṣṭau anyatvīja...".
In the Rājasūya, regarding the *caru* for Nirṛti, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) must be performed upon the pestle and mortar among the stakes used as means for the fourfold release.
VI. 4.12.2: In the Rājasūya, there is a state of equal importance (*sampradhānya*) among the many distinct sacrifices—*iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices (*paśu*), and *soma* sacrifices.

VI. 4.4.21: In the Rājasūya, regarding the rule "they proceed with the *saumya* [offering] prior to the *upasad*s," this is a connection for the purpose of time (*kālārtha-saṃyoga*). The *saumya* sacrifice is already established as being prompted by the fruit of sovereignty (*svārājya*); it is obtained as something to be performed as another ritual action (*karmāntara*) due to its position in the textual sequence (*pāṭhakrama*). Therefore, the presence of the *upasad*s—which would otherwise be obtained through extended application (*atideśa*)—is what is enjoined here.
