Bhāṭṭa 4.4.3: In the Rājasūya, the word *vaiṣṇava* occurring in the *tri-kapāla* offering to Viṣṇu—which is connected with the preceding [rites]—does not extend the ritual details (*dharma*) from the *atithyeṣṭi* (the guest-offering) belonging to the Soma-sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 7.3.6.17: In the Rājasūya, the performance of the rites such as those dedicated to Agni-Viṣṇu, which are associated with separate sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), is carried out separately.
Because the *codaka* (the rule of extension) is one, the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) are performed collectively (*tantra*) when their place and time are not specifically mentioned in the Rājasūya.

Commentary: In the Rājasūya sacrifice, those principal rites for which place and time are not specified—such as the two [sacrifices] connected with the Trisaṃyukta—are here considered. Is there a common performance (tantra) of the auxiliary rites (aṅgāni) for them, or is there a distinction? What is the prima facie view? In the Rājasūya, for the principal rites whose place and time are not specified, there is a common performance of the auxiliaries.
Why? Because of their combination (*samavāya*).
Their combination occurs in the production of the result.
These [factors] accomplish the result when combined, not individually.
How is this known? Because it is an impeller (*codaka*).
By means of the word "rājasūyena," ending in the singular number, the connection with the fruit is established for those primary acts that have been mentioned;
therefore, the aggregate is what possesses the fruit.
And that which possesses a fruit is what is intended to be performed;
that is the purpose to be sought. And the procedure consists of the injunctions.
Therefore, it is a *tantra* (common performance).

Or rather, because of the connection with the agent at each individual circumambulation (*pratidakṣiṇa*), it is like the subsidiaries here; for the whole (*samudāya*) would indeed, through the cessation of that [performance], receive a single designation by virtue of its unity.
The Commentary states: "And this is not so; the subsidiaries are not a *tantra*."
What then? By way of distinction. Why? Because of the connection with a distinct sacrificer for each dakṣiṇā.
In these rites, a difference in the dakṣiṇā is heard in the scripture.
"A cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, and one for Indra and Viṣṇu; or a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu, with a dwarf as the sacrificial fee.
A cake on eleven potsherds for Soma and Pūṣan, and one for Indra and Pūṣan, and one for Pūṣan; a ram is the sacrificial fee.
Because of the difference in the sacrificial fees, the connection with the performers occurs for each respective fee.
Those purchased from the dwarf are the performers of the first *trisaṃyukta*;
those who are bodiless are [the performers] of the subsequent *trisaṃyukta*;
and those not purchased from heaven are the performers of the latter *trisaṃyukta*.
Those [subsidiaries] also belong to the former [principal action] as its subsidiary;
therefore, due to the difference in the agent, there is a difference in the subsidiaries,
just as in the case of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice.
It is just as the full-moon sacrifices performed at different times are distinct from one another;
therefore, they must be performed separately. As for the argument that, because the injunction refers to a single entity, the collection [of parts] is intended [as a whole]:
It is said:
for it is the collection that [is so designated] because of the production thereof;
the collection is intended [as such] by virtue of the production of the fruit.
The mention [of them] together is due to their unity and the unity of their result, not due to the unity of the performance, as in the case of the *iṣṭi* sacrifices.

For example, although there is a difference in the performance of the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there is a collective statement—namely, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*"—because of the unity of their result. This is also the case in the *rājasūya*.
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose in the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Commentary: Another purpose is also shown in this very same way:
"The former is connected with three; the latter is connected with three."
In that case, there would indeed be a sequence of priority and posteriority.
Now, one might argue that even if they belong to a single ritual procedure (*ekatantra*), the sequence could still exist in relation to the primary act (*pradhāna*).
This is not so.
However, it will be established by means of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) that this sequence refers to the two principal things to be accomplished.
For thus it is here: that which is the first triad is the production of heroes, and that which is the subsequent triad is the production of cattle.
Furthermore, the connection with the fruit belongs to the two together with their constituent parts (*sāṅkhya*), not to the two alone.
Therefore, this is merely a request for wealth.
As stated in the Śāstra: "Due to differences in place, time, and fruit, there may be a commonality (tantratā) among the Vedic branches;
nor is there even a difference of performers, since the only distinction lies in the sacrificial fee."

It is said that because of the difference in the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the status of being the performer (*kartṛtva*) also differs. This is because for those who have not received [the fee], there is a lack of independence regarding the performance due to the distinctness [of the recipients]. Therefore, with each individual sacrificial fee, there is a distinction of the ritual procedure (*tantra*).

Soma—the meaning of the sūtra is as follows: in the Rājasūya, because the rites whose times are prescribed by subsequent injunctions are performed simultaneously under the impelling force (*codaka*) of the statement "one sacrifices with the Rājasūya," their constituent parts (*aṅgāni*) constitute a single performance (*tantra*); thus, they are the constituent parts of the Rājasūya.
At the commencement of the Rājasūya...

"But they proceed with the *saumya* [offering] when [the dice] are difficult to obtain"—this conjunction has the purpose of indicating time; thus, the *saumya* [offering] is for the sake of the fruit.
Bhāṣya 4.4.3.5–6. The gambling and so forth are subordinate to the *rājasūya*, because of the context.
Vi. (Vivaraṇa).
The exclusion of the *anvārambhaṇīyā* [introductory offering] from the *anumati* and other sacrifices included within the *rājasūya*.
Mīko., p. 937; see the section titled "Exclusion of the *ārambhaṇīyā* from the *anumati* and other sacrifices occurring in the *rājasūya*.
In the *daśapeya* sacrifice, which is part of the *rājasūya*, only Brāhmaṇas are the consumers of the portions of the sacrificer's cup (*yajamānacamasa*).
Bhāṣya 3.5.2.52–53: In the Rājasūya and similar rites, there is the emergence of knowledge through the performance of the principal [sacrificial] acts as taught by those words.
1.2.1.3–19: For the priests chosen at the commencement of the Rājasūya, their duties extend until its completion.

"If it be argued that there would be no restriction," the Bhāṣya states: "In that very context it is deliberated: whether those who are the performers at the commencement are the same [throughout], or if there is no restriction—this is the *rājasūya* principle regarding the *abhīṣeka* [consecration] within the *rājasūya*."

The subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) of the *āvaiṣṇava* cake-offering and others belonging to the *rājasūya*, which are associated with separate sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), must be performed separately; they do not constitute a single performance (*tantra*).

Bhāṣya 11.4.1.1–2. Regarding the *āvaiṣṇava* cake on three potsherds belonging to the *rājasūya* and the *āvaiṣṇava* cake on nine potsherds belonging to the *ātithyeṣṭi*, there is no relationship of original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) between them, nor is there any extension (*atideśa*) of ritual properties (*dharma*).
VI. 7.3.6. There is no extended application (*atideśa*) of the ritual details (*dharma*) belonging to the *Ātithyeṣṭi* and the *Vaiṣṇaveṣṭi* within the *Rājasūya*.

See the section titled "The Vaiṣṇava Principle" (*Vaiṣṇavanyāya*) at VI. 7.3.6.188. Since the terms [denoting the specific sacrifices] are absent from the sentences concerning the Brāhmaṇas and others, the injunction for the *Rājasūya* is not weaker than them; therefore, the fact that it is to be performed by a Kṣatriya as stated therein cannot be sublated.
Su. P. 910. The Principle of the Rājasūya:
By the word *rājasūya*, it is established that the sacrifices alone are for the sake of the fruit;
and because of the commonality of the context and the word, they are subordinate to the injunction.
Commentary: There exist [rites] such as the *anumaya* and others belonging to the *rājasūya*, which is an *aiṣṭika* (sacrificial) rite; regarding the three-night period, it is said:
"One should sacrifice with the *rājasūya*."
Mīmāṃsā. The traditionalists hold that the term *rājasūya* is a conventional designation (*abhyutpanna*), just like words such as *adhvara*.

In the Mīmāṃsā section concerning the *rājasūya*, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that because the acts of gambling and so forth—expressed in the passage “He plays with dice, he conquers the Kṣatriya”—occur within the context of the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, they are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the *abhiṣecanīya*.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that, due to proximity (*saṃnidhi*) or because the larger context (*mahā-prakaraṇa*) is more powerful than the intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*), these acts of gambling and so forth belong to the *rājasūya* as a whole. The distinction, however, is that their performance takes place at the time of the *māhendra-stotra* during the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice.

VI. 4.3.10, 4.4.2. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: just as in the *rājasūya* sacrifice there is a connection with the fruit through the term *yajati* (the act of sacrificing), so too, in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, let there be a connection with the fruit common to all the subordinate offerings (*prajājah*). Bhaṭṭa 4.1.12: Just as in the *rājasūya* all the sacrifices have a connection with the fruit and possess primacy, so too in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, because all [parts] beginning with the *prāyaṇīya* are connected with the fruit, all of them possess primacy. This is the prima facie view.

4|4|12. Since the *rājasūya* sentence prescribes the various rites (*prākṛta-karma*) as qualified by the status of being performed by a king (*rājakartṛtva*) in relation to the result, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), even when there is a connection between the qualities and the result through the restatement of the rites already established.
Bhāṭṭa 2|1|1. The word "king" (*rāja*) is the name of that collection of many primary rites consisting of the *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, *soma*, *darśa*, and *havir-yajña*.
Vi. 10|1|3. The word *rājasūya* is the name of a sacrifice, because, while its meaning is not otherwise well-known, it stands in grammatical apposition with the word "sacrifice."

4|1|1: In the passage "A king desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the *rājasūya*," the word *rājasūya*, functioning on account of its connection with the king, serves as the name for all the sacrifices read within a single context that have the king as their performer.

4|4|11: Only those sacrifices denoted by the term *rājasūya* are for the sake of the fruit [of the ritual], and not non-sacrificial elements such as the *videvanā* and others. 4|4|12–2: The inclusion of the *saumya-caru* and other elements occurs only at the time of the *rājasūya* resolution (or at the commencement of the *saṃsthā*), and not at the time of the *upasat* resolution.
The sacrifice known as the Rājasūya, involving Soma, is enjoined as the means for one desiring sovereign rule:
"One desiring sovereign rule should sacrifice with the Rājasūya."
Sūtra 1.4.12.5: It is observed that even all four castes (varṇas) perform the act of ruling;
therefore, all are kings.
[Objection: But surely sovereignty has been prescribed as belonging to the Kṣatriya class; thus, the other two, performing the act unjustly, would not be kings.

This is not a fault; for in every respect, kingship was indeed obtained by those two through the act of governing. Vārttika 2.3.12, p. 580: "For the defining characteristic of a kingdom (*janapada*) is the unique royal function; therefore, that is called 'kingdom' (*rājya*). 2.3.13, p. 586: "The kingdom is the king's function; one should not, however, assume by implication that the king is the agent of the kingdom, because [the meaning] is already known in other regions (among the Dravidians)."

Page 585, 2|3|13: Regarding the word *rājya*—when the relationship between word and meaning is eternal, and that very eternal relationship is understood through the treatise (*śāstra*), then at the time of comprehending grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), the word *rāja* is explained; and while being so explained, although it appears to have an etymological origin based on those [causes], because its causes are eternal, it does not acquire the quality of having a beginning (*ādimattva*).

Vārttika 3|7|140, page 1105: The word *rājya* is used by the inhabitants of Āryāvarta in the sense of protecting the realm (*janapada-parirakṣaṇa*) and in the removal of various thorns (*kaṇṭaka-śodhana*).
Those learned in the tradition teach that "the act of a king is kingship" (*rājñaḥ karma rājyam*).
It was stated in this context (2.3.12) that even for the word *rājya*, its application is not beginningless; see Vārttika 2.3.163, p.
821. Manu and others record in their legal codes that the duty denoted by the term *rājya* consists of the protection [of subjects] and so forth, which belongs to the Kṣatriya.
Vārttika 2.3.13, p. 584: “The maxim of the beauty of a lamp-flame at night when the sun has risen.

Just as a lamp-flame does not shine at sunrise, so too this maxim is employed when the intended meaning is that one possessing qualities is not honored in the presence of one who possesses even greater qualities. Sāhasī 798: The section concerning the night.

Regarding the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) as both the substance and the time [of the sacrifice], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the fast (*upavāsa*) occurs on the preceding day, the sacrifice (*ayāga*) occurs on the following day, and even on that following day, the sacrifice takes place specifically at night. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it occurs during the day itself.
Saṃkarṣa.

3.1.16: Regarding the night-sessions (*rātriparyāya*), there is indeed a combination (*samuccaya*) of the *graha* and *camasa* vessels, not an option (*vikalpa*). Concerning the subject of the *rātri*, there is a statement regarding a single part: “One should sacrifice with a two-night [rite], one should sacrifice with a three-night [rite], one should sacrifice with a four-night [rite], one should sacrifice with a five-night [rite], one should sacrifice with a six-night [rite], one should sacrifice with a seven-night [rite], one should sacrifice with an eight-night [rite], one should sacrifice with a nine-night [rite], one should sacrifice with a ten-night [rite], one should sacrifice with an eleven-night [rite].”
An example of taking [the term] in its entirety is: “One should cause one desiring offspring to sacrifice with the Dvādaśāha.
Bhāṣya 10.5.1.1. The word *rātri* [is used in this sense]; this is the principle of the *Rātrisattra*.
The word *rātri* denotes a day-and-night (*ahorātra*), as does the word *aha*.
The *dvirātra* and others are *ahīna* sacrifices;
[an example is] the *dvādaśāha*.
Bhāṣya 8.1.9–10, 17: The word *rātri* (night), when occurring within compounds such as *dvirātra* (two-night sacrifice) and so forth, refers to a day consisting of six *ghaṭikās*.

Vi. 8.1.10: The word *rātri*, in the sense of a *satra* (sacrificial session), is used with a singular ending by virtue of the primacy of the collective whole, as in *trayodaśarātraḥ* (the thirteen-night session).
In some instances, however, by virtue of the primacy of the individual nights, it is also used with a plural ending, as in *ya etā viṃśatiṃ rātrīrapaśyan* (those who saw these twenty nights).

4|3|8. There is no specific sacrifice called *rātrisatra*; rather, those sacrifices such as the thirteen-night (*trayodaśarātra*) and fourteen-night (*caturdaśarātra*) rites that are *satras* are designated by the term *rātrisatra*.

Vi. 4|3|8. In the *rātrisatra*, the fruit is that which is stated in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), consisting of stability (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth; heaven (*svarga*) is not to be assumed there. The explanatory passage is: "Those who perform these nights indeed become established; they perform these nights possessing spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)."

4|3|8|17–19. Just as in the Rātrisattra sacrifice, the "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) heard in a supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) as an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) is postulated as the fruit [of the action], so it is here as well.

Vi. 4|3|22. The Principle of the Rātrisattra Sacrifice (*rātrisattranyāya*): Where no fruit is heard in the injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*), the fruit is extended from an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*); this is the "extension of the eulogy" (*arthavādādeśa*), and this alone is the scope of the Principle of the Rātrisattra Sacrifice.

For this very reason, in the section concerning the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice, regarding the passage “Those who perform these *rātri*sacrifices indeed become firmly established,” it is stated that since a fruit is heard in the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), and since an injunction cannot be valid without a fruit, when a fruit must necessarily be postulated, the fruit of "firm establishment" mentioned in the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is to be accepted; such is the direction [of the argument].
This is the *Sāhasī Rātrisatranaya*.
Regarding the ritual (*kratu*), Ārṇajini [holds that] there is a statement of fruit (*phalārthavāda*) for the sake of auspiciousness.
The Commentary: The teacher Ātreya, however, maintained that in such cases there is indeed a fruit, and not merely a statement of fruit.
Why? Because even though no fruit is explicitly heard, there must be an injunction of a fruit for these [acts], which serves as a supplementary part (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the sentence.
Therefore, while another [sequence] being separated would have to be assumed as separated by something else,
this one, however, is already established as being without separation.
The co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of these— namely, "foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*), "Brahman-splendor" (*brahmavarcasa*), and "existence" (*sattva*)— is directly perceived.
Therefore, only the injunctive suffix (*vidhi-vibhakti*) must be accepted here. He asks:
how can it be that only the injunctive suffix is to be accepted here?
It will be connected with the meaning of the verbal root through the effort consisting of the installation and so forth.
It is said: it will exist together with the meaning of the verbal root, not by itself alone.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Alternatively, the same injunctive suffix that enjoins the nights will also enjoin this specific excellence, such as stability (*pratiṣṭhā*), within the statement of performance (*prayogavacana*).
Or else, the praise, together with the [mention of] stability and so forth, will serve as the injunction.
An action must have a fruit.

In this regard, should one supply the word "heaven" (*svarga*) and form a single syntactical unit with it, or should one modify a portion of the word "firm foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*) and treat "firm foundation" and so forth as the fruit?
Since the proximity [of the latter] is already established, the syntactical unity of "firm foundation" and so forth is what must be inferred.
For if one were to assume heaven and so forth as the result, both proximity and syntactic unity would have to be postulated;
in that case, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*). Therefore, the text beginning with "Hence, only the injunctive suffix must be accepted" is connected precisely to the means (*sādhana*).
By the former [section], the goal to be accomplished, such as installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth, has been established.

However, by the latter, through the present-tense indication in the word "they approach" (*upayanti*), the injunctive force (*liṅ*) is set aside for the purpose of understanding [the acts] as means of accomplishment.
He asks: "How can there be merely the injunctive suffix alone elsewhere, by which it is indicated as being connected with the meaning of the verbal root, such as installation and so forth?"
Being thus questioned, he said: "We shall supply that very root which has the relationship of means and end (*sādhya-sādhana*) to be performed at the proper time, namely *upa-yu*.

Alternatively, just as the statement regarding the procedure for the production of nights requires a connection with the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*), so too will that very statement establish the relationship between the goal and the means.
Just as from the statement, "Other sacrificial rites are undertaken for the sake of a single desire,
but the Jyotiṣṭoma is for the sake of all desires," the Jyotiṣṭoma becomes the means for attaining all desires even in the absence of the optative suffix (liṅ),
so too here: the optative suffix occurring in the originative injunction (utpatti) enjoins the Jyotiṣṭoma as a means, and it is the same in this case as well.
Alternatively, the explanatory passage (arthavāda), through its inseparable connection, indicates the two [factors];
once indicated, it will establish the relationship between the means and the end. Therefore, the injunction is derived from the explanatory passages.
And those very same [actions], as they undergo transformation, attain the state of being results.
Therefore, there is an exception to the rule that "it would be heaven.
The praise regarding the auxiliary elements (aṅga) is for the sake of another purpose.

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): Now, as for what was said—that just as in such passages as "He whose sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) is made of *suvar* wood," there is a mention of a fruit (*phalaśruti*), so it might be here as well—it is appropriate that there be a mention of a fruit in those cases. This is because a fruit is possible there, and because a commendatory statement regarding a fruit (*phalārthavāda*) is also possible.

As it has been said: "In the case of substances, preparatory rites, and actions, because they are for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit should be regarded as a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda). And from the Śābarabhāṣya: "In that case, like the verse concerning the 'sinless fame,' because it is stated in the present tense and lacks the capacity to enjoin a fruit, it is an arthavāda subservient to that [injunction]."
Since no specific fruit has been enjoined, it follows that heaven is the purpose;
however, because of the explicit mention, *pratiṣṭhā* (firm foundation) itself is bent toward being the fruit.
They did not perform ritual acts with a desire for results;
in that regard, a result must be imagined through meditation, as it cannot be attained by other means.
(Vināmaḥ means transformation.

Soma—As for the meaning of the sūtra: the teacher Kārṣṇājini considers that in sacrifices such as the Rātrisatra, where a fruit is mentioned, this is a *phalārthavāda* (a declamatory statement regarding the fruit), just as [the mention of fruit] in the case of the *parṇa*-wood [used for ladles] is merely a subordinate element (*aṅga*).
Vi— "Whether for the sake of heaven or for stability, the Rātrisatra is the first [example] here."
The installation should be as before; since it is so heard in the scripture, I have stated it thus.

Bhaṭṭa: After enjoining the Saurya rites established by such sentences as "The light [is for] the bull," the scripture states, "Those who perform these Rātri-sacrifices indeed become firmly established.

In that context, regarding the Rātri-sattras and similar rites, rather than postulating heaven (svarga) as the result—as was done previously—there would arise the fault of complexity (gaurava), because one would have to postulate both the presence of heaven (implied by the word *svarga*) and the presence of desire (kāma) implied by the word *tadācakṣata*. Therefore, by the principle of parsimony (lāghava), one should postulate the very "firm establishment" (pratiṣṭhā) mentioned in the scripture itself as the result to be attained (bhāvya).

In this regard, there is a twofold determination: where, in the case of words heard [in the text] themselves, there is a connection with the result through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For example, in the cited sentence, having postulated that the suffix *-vipra* has the sense of the periphrastic future (*lṛṅ*), and thus understanding it as being in the future tense, its status as the "to-be-accomplished" (*bhāvya*) is established because it is desired as something to be accomplished, such as *pratiṣṭhā* (firm foundation) and so forth; or else, having postulated that the verbal root itself is followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*), and thus understanding it as the object of desire, one understands its status as the "to-be-accomplished" just like heaven (*svarga*) and the like.

In that regard, when the expectancy for the primary fruit is present, once it is established through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that the heard sentence itself has the fruit as its purpose, then subsequently, when there is an expectancy for praise (*stuti*), the very nature of the praise is obtained through the force of what was not previously established [by direct denotation]. However, in cases where the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) heard do not find justification through the mere purpose of the fruit without the assumption of a praising function—
as in "Whatever is on the potsherd, by that very *gāyatrī* he purifies him with Vedic splendor" (*brahmavarcasa*) and so forth— therein their function is solely that of praise.

However, when there is an expectation of a fruit, one must assume another word of the same class as the word standing nearby (upasthita) that is connected with the word "kāma" (desire); thus, it is never the case that [the fruit] is not connected with heaven (*svarga*).
Maṇḍana states: "In the Rātrisatra, the fruit is for the sake of praise. Śaṅkara states: "The fruit of the Rātrisatra is from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)."

By the logic of the *rātrisatra* [sacrifice], qualities such as "purity" (*pūtatva*) mentioned in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) may serve as motivators for engaging in [the worship of] Vaiśvānara. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 890).

According to the logic of the *rātrisatra*, although it is possible to interpret these explanatory passages as having results such as purity, even if one assumes they are intended for another purpose or that they aim at a result, there is no result with respect to [the number of bricks] being eight and so forth.

By the principle of the *rātrisatra* (the "night-sacrifice" rule), it is proper to postulate that the satisfaction of the deity—known from the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) and the wording of the mantras—is the very means (*dvāra*), and not the postulation of an entirely unknown and unprecedented (*apūrva*) entity (as maintained in the *pūrvapakṣa*).

By this, the Vedāntic position is also refuted; for, by the *rātrisatra* principle, the favor of the deity itself—as conveyed in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "Indra indeed satisfies him with progeny and cattle"—is logically established as the means, and thus the postulation of an unmanifested *apūrva* is not appropriate.
Furthermore, one should not expect [the result] by way of being a subordinate element (*upasthitatva*) alone, according to the principle of the *rātrisatra* sacrifice (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 2.1.3, p.

47). From the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), "By dharma one dispels evil," and so forth, it follows by the principle of the *rātrisatra* that the fruit belongs specifically to the obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*).
*Bhāṭṭa* 2.4.9:

Regarding the statements "The *caru* is made of wild rice" (*naivāraścarurbhavati*) and "He places the *caru*" (*carumupadadhāti*), in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), in the sentence concerning the wild rice, there is a connection between the substance in the form of the *caru* and the deity Bṛhaspati mentioned in the *Atharva* [text], according to the principle of the *Rātrisatra*. Thus, even though the word "Brahman" is understood from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) as an established fact, when there is a requirement for a specific person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the specific person to be enjoined—namely, Brahman—is obtained through the principle of the *Rātrisatra*. *Bhāmatī* 1.1.4, first section: [This refers to the same argument.]
"In the passage, 'It consists of ten potsherds; the Gāyatrī indeed purifies him,' by means of the *rātrisatra*-principle,
when there is an expectation of a fruit, qualities such as purification (*pūtatva*) and so forth are postulated as the fruit according to the *rātrisatra*-principle."

In a context where there is a contradiction with the gender [of the word], since the purpose for another is already known, the capacity of the statement to bring about a result can be inferred according to the *rātrisatra* principle; this is capable of being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the case of the passage "vaiśvānaraṃ dvādaśa-kapālam," since the term *aṣṭakapāla* lacks the status of a name (*nāmadheya*), and because the status of being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—such as "gāyatryevainaṃ"—is accepted, it is admitted that this [passage] has the purpose of indicating a fruit (*phala*) according to the principle of the *rātrisatra*.
This refers to the first position in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
(Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 1.4.12–17).

When there is an expectation for a result, the attainment of that result for acts such as threatening (apagoraṇa) is achieved through the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa), "He should be fined a hundred [paṇas]," etc., according to the principle of the Rātrisattra sacrifice (rātrisatranyāya).
(Ku.

3.4.10.23) Regarding the injunction "One's own Veda (svādhyāya) is to be studied," one should bring about something by means of the study of one's own Veda; in that case, the status of being the fruit of the Viśvajit sacrifice is not to be postulated.
Nor can the fruit [of the injunction] be derived from an explanatory passage (arthavāda) according to the "logic of the Night-sacrifices" (rātrisatranaya). Furthermore, there must be a fruit.
Therefore, that which is understood through the study of one's own Vedic recitation (svādhyāyādhyayana) is the fruit in this context.
The purport of the *rātrisatra-nyāya* is as follows.

In the sūtra stating the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), "Kārṣṇājini [holds that] in a sacrifice there is a statement of fruit which is merely commendatory" (4.1.8.17), he considers that in the case of the sacrifice mentioned as the subject, the fruit is indeed nothing other than that which has come down in the commendatory passage (*arthavāda*)—namely, "Those who perform the *rātri-sattras* certainly attain a firm foundation."

He will state that its action [is connected] together with the indication of the relationship between quality and qualified, because the general relationship has been established; as it will be said at Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1849:
"Like the *pratiṣṭhā* [fruit] of the *Rātrisatra*."

Nor can it be argued that, when there is an expectation for a result, because [the Vaimṛdha] is present as being intended for another purpose, one must assume another word denoting that [result]—just as in the case of the *pratiṣṭhā* (firm foundation) in the *Rātrisatra*—on the grounds that the Vaimṛdha is for the sake of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) alone.
(The prima facie view, *pūrvapakṣa*:
Bhaṭṭa 4.1.19).

According to the principle of the *Rātrisatra* (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 4.1.8.17–19), since there is no cessation of the expectation for a fruit through the context (*prakaraṇa*), even an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that merely provides praise—as in the case of Agastya—may serve to provide the fruit.
(Soma.
1.1.2) "The battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa belongs only to Rāma and Rāvaṇa."
Praise becomes even more effective through non-difference, because it cannot arise from anything else.
For in the world, such praise occurs by relying on a conceptual distinction that has not been apprehended as real;
it would not be appropriate if a real difference actually existed.
The performance of a sacrifice like that of Rāma [is an example of] the transgression of dharma by Bhīṣma, who was without a wife. (Vākyapadīya 2.3.3.7, p. 204; Cāndra-vyākaraṇa 1.4.4.8, p.

By the phrase "like Sudhā and Rāma," it is indicated that even so, there was a transgression of dharma due to the performance of a sacrifice by one who was alone through the abandonment of his wife (p.

185). [To this, the following reply is given: For Rāma, because of the power of affection, the success of the sacrifice was achieved despite the grief caused to his father by his offspring; furthermore, the making of a golden Sītā was for the purpose of removing suspicion, as he had lost faith in Sītā due to public scandal and sought to dispel doubt.
Or [as stated on] page 208:
Because of his affection for Sītā, Rāma— having undertaken a vow not to approach another wife—
was followed by his two sons, Kuśa and Lava, who were his own wives in person.

One might object: "Since Rāma possesses another wife who is the source of his dharma and wealth, and since the sacrifice currently being performed is one that requires [a real] wife, the making of Sītā out of gold would be purposeless. Anticipating such a doubt, he says: "She is golden" (*hiraṇmayī*).

The meaning is that this is intended to dispel the suspicion of a lack of excellence (*anaiṣṭhya*) regarding her—namely, the internal deficiency caused by the fact that Sītā was previously abandoned out of fear of scandal.

"She was abandoned merely out of fear of public scandal—that Rāma is consorting with Sītā who was defiled by her abduction by Rāvaṇa—and not because of any fault in Sītā, nor due to any lack of constancy in Rāma toward her. To demonstrate that the act of abandonment is invariably dependent upon the fear of public scandal, a *sāpekṣasamāsa* (compound involving a word requiring an external factor) has been formed between the words *tyaktā* and *sītā*.
(Page 192).
Furthermore, the rule "one should perform the *brahmasāman* for the *rātrīvājīya* sacrifice" is purely occasional (*naimittika*) within the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and not obligatory (*nitya*).
Bhāṣya 4.3.14: "The Rātrovājīya is the Brahmasāman of the Veda at the Dvādaśāha sacrifice.
The oblations called Rāṣṭrabhṛts are clarified-butter offerings (dravahomas).

These *homās* are prescribed for the sake of various results, as follows: (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.4.8)—for one performing sorcery (*abhicaran*), for the purpose of self-exaltation, for the avoidance of insanity, for one desiring vigor (*ojas*), for one desiring a village, for one desiring preeminence, and so forth.

Regarding the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*, there is an extension (*uddeśa*) of the instruction concerning their performance, based on the statement: "He offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*.
(Bhāṣya 7.1.1.12). There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* into the acts of raising the ladle (*udgrāhakarma*), because of the scriptural injunction.
The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations: [performed by] one who is ignoble, unlearned, and ignorant of Vedic rites. Vi.
3.4.13. The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations are those performed with mantras such as "The Gandharva Ṛtāpāt, whose abode is truth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.4.7).
And these [oblations] are for Vedic rites alone, not for worldly activities such as agriculture and the like.
Regarding the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations for Rudra: "To these *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations for Rudra, svāhā!"— this is the second mantra.

Even in the mantra: "Ṛtāpāṭ, Ṛtadhāmā, Agni is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the plants, named Ūrjas; may he protect this Brahman and Kṣatra; may they protect this Brahman and Kṣatra; to him Svāhā! To them Svāhā!"—one should separate the words accompanied by their respective gender-markers (*saliṅga*) as appropriate and form two mantras: "Ṛtāpāṭ, Ṛtadhāmā, the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the plants, named Ūrjas; may he protect this Brahman and Kṣatra; to him Svāhā! is the first mantra.
"May these protect this *brahman* and *kṣatra*; to them, *svāhā*. This is the second [offering]; thus there is an application in two oblations (*homadvaya*).
In the case of the two mantras beginning with "yā te agne," although the portion beginning with "tanuḥ" is recited only once, it is observed to be applied through repetition.

In the application of the mantra "namo rudrebhyo ye pṛthivyāṃ ye'ntarikṣe ye divi" to the oblation, because the designations of earth, atmosphere, and heaven are not fixed, it is observed that even those [terms] which are intermingled by the *parvan* [sections] are to be divided separately.

This being the case, because the word *svāhā* is recited once [in each instance], because of the presence of other mantras [such as] *agnaye*, because of the determination of the number of oblations (*homa*) in various places, and because the mantra "to them, svāhā" is rendered complete in its expectancy by the act of pausing twice, that much alone constitutes a distinct mantra.

Because of the presence of the word *tat* [in the mantra], when the portion beginning with "these are these" (*etā idam*) is excluded, then by the very fact that the word *tat* pervades all parts, the recitation as "to him, to them, svāhā" (*tasmai tābhyaḥ svāhā*) would render the other *svāhā*-utterances redundant; thus, on the basis of this very redundancy, there is proof that those portions constitute distinct mantras.
(Some ritualists, however, do not accept this.

This is the maxim of "Rāhu’s head.
This maxim was cited by Kaiyaṭa and Nāgojībhaṭṭa in their works, the *Bhāṣyapradīpa* and the *Bhāṣyapradīpodyota*.

Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa states: "Just as in the case of the entity 'Rāhu’s head,' there is a conventional treatment of non-difference due to the difference between the word and its referent, so too here, by the word 'grammar' (*vyākaraṇa*), the status of the science as an instrument in the act of grammatical derivation (*vyākṛti*) is expressed."
"But by the word *sūtra*, it possesses the nature of a composite whole (*samudāya-rūpatā*); thus, the linguistic usage of distinction (*bhedavyavahāra*) is justified.

Regarding this, Nāgeśa, taking up the phrase "due to the difference between the word and its meaning" (*śabdārthabhedāt*), states: "The meaning of the word *rāhu* is a head endowed with multiple states (*anekāvasthāyukta*); the meaning of the word *śiras* (head) is a head endowed with some particular state (*yatkiñcidekāvasthāyukta*).
The sense is that the meaning of such a word *śiras* is a 'constituent part' (*avayava*) of the meaning of such a word *rāhu*; thus, the use of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) is justified."
The impulsive one. 460.

The fire, which was situated in the *ukhā* (fire-pan) and placed upon a stand, is to be held around the neck in such a manner that it does not burn the chest; this act of holding is what constitutes the "wearing of the gold ornament" (*rukmadhāraṇa*).
And this should be performed after the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the *vacana* and others. (Vi.
5.2.122). The wearing of the gold ornament is prescribed in the *Agnicayana* ritual after the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rites.
Following the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) such as shaving the hair and so forth, which are obtained through the force of the general injunction (*codaka*), take place.
Among these, first the purificatory rite is performed, and afterwards the wearing of the gold plate (*rukma*) should be done.

Regarding the "fastening of the gold plate" (*rukmapratimocana*): when the gold plate—a specific type of twenty-one-fold gold ornament—is fastened to the neck by hanging it from a sling (*śikya*) upon the sacrificial altar (*cayana*), the phrase "the gold plate is fastened in between" is prescribed for the purpose of creating an interval to prevent burning of the chest region; this wearing of the ornament is understood from the term *rukmapratimocana*.
The fastening of the gold plate (*rukmapratimocana*) and other such rites in the fire-piling (*agnicayana*) must be performed after the purificatory rites for the initiated (*dīkṣita-saṃskāra*).
5.2.1223. This is to be seen under Mīmāṃsākośa 9446, in the entry "In the fire-piling, the fastening of the gold plate and so forth."
The marriage of Rukmiṇī is explained by [the example of] the marriage of Subhadrā; Vākyapadīya 1.3.17, p. 210. *Ruci* means an intense desire.
Rudra is Agni.

This is because we observe such usage as "O Agni, you are Rudra, the Asura of the great heaven," and because we observe explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "This Agni is indeed Rudra," and because it is seen in the *Āraṇyaka*—in the section known as the *Kumārasambhava*—that "the twice-born call Agni Rudra."
Su. Pṛ. 56–57. Regarding *rudra*: because the word is observed to be based on the act of weeping (*rodana*), it is said, "That which he wept" (*yadrodīt tat*).
Bhāṣya 1.2.1.10. [The statement] "One should give one cow to Rudra," and so forth, is like the word *rudra* being used as a designation for a cow (*gavānuvādena rudraśabdaḥ*).

From the mention of "form" (rūpa), there is a prescription of mere number; thus, regarding the statement "he offers four," the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that there is either a prescription of number with reference to the handfuls (muṣṭi), or a prescription of the handfuls with reference to the number.

The word *rudra*: it is derived from the root *rud*, meaning "to weep" (*rodana*), and since the suffix *-ra* has the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*), grammar establishes that it denotes the agent of weeping. (Sukhabodhini, p. 56). A conventional (*ruḍha*) word: *kuśala*, *pravīṇa*, *aśvakarṇa*, *aparimita*.
Bhāṣya 6.1.2.22:
Conventionalness (*rūḍhatva*) [of a word] consists in its having a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) and thus being non-etymological (*ayogika*),
as in the case of "ghaṭa" and so forth.
Maṇi, p. 78:
Conventional usage (ruḍhi), when not established by etymological derivation (yoga), overrides it;
as in the case of the word *prokṣaṇī*.
There is a maxim that "conventional usage (rūḍhi) sets aside etymological derivation (yoga).

For example, this maxim applies in cases where—while considering the individual word-meanings that might otherwise lead to over-extension—the intention is to assert the predominance of the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) over the etymological meaning.

Just as in cases such as "cow" (*go*), where one relies on the observation of the primary meaning of the word to exclude over-extension to other things, and thus sets aside the etymological meaning (*yogārtha*)—such as being an agent of motion—and instead grasps the individual (*vyakti*) possessing a dewlap, tail, hump, hooves, and horns by virtue of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*); so too, in the passage "During the rains, the *rathakāra* should establish the sacred fires," the term *rathakāra* denotes a specific caste born from a *vaidya* father and a *trātyā* mother, and not a member of the twice-born (*dvijāti*) based on the etymological derivation "one who makes a chariot. This is the summary.

Conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), however, operates in the relationship between a name and the named object when that object is fit for designation by way of its own form, genus, or quality—as in "Ḍiṣṭha," "Ḍavittha," "cow," or "white. Regarding "Ḍiṣṭha": it is a wooden elephant, and "Ḍavittha" is a deer made of the same material.

Yoga, however, refers to a word whose secondary synonym is "derivative" (yaugika), which denotes a meaning derived from the combination of a base (*prakṛti*) and an affix (*pratyaya*). For example, words such as *āditya* are derivative. In this case, [the derivation is as follows]: from the word *āditya*, meaning "the offspring of the Ādityas," one applies the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ* to form the feminine stem ending in *ī*; then, by the rule *saumyo ḍhak*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied. Thus, in the study [of grammar], there is only the derivative meaning.
The rash one (sāhasī). 233.

According to the maxim "conventionality sets aside etymological derivation" (ruḍhiyogamapaharati), there is only one Udgātṛ; and for the sake of justifying the plural number [in the text], those closely associated with him are indicated by implication.
Vi. 3|15|8. Conventionality (ruḍhi) has less force than etymological derivation (yoga), because the latter depends upon the consideration of the meanings of the constituent parts.
Conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is a cause for quicker understanding than etymological derivation (*yoga*).

3|16| 6|17. "Or rather, it is the form [of the fire], because [the consecration] is not a subordinate element (*aśeṣabhūtatvāt*)... Just as in the case of a cart or a garment produced by action, only the form of the cart or garment is obtained, and not the action that produces it; for since the words "cart" and "garment" do not have their application based on the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the action is not a subordinate element (i.e., it lacks subordination). Similarly, although the *āhavanīya* and other fires are prescribed as being produced by action, the consecration (*ādhāna*) which generates the latent impression is not subordinate to the *agnihotra* and other rites. Therefore, by the scriptural mention of the *āhavanīya*, when the *āhavanīya* and so forth are enjoined as produced by action, only the form of the *āhavanīya* that is produced is attained, and not the producing consecration itself. Thus, there is an equality of reasoning.

Su. Pṛ. 917: Even by means of the *sūtra* alone, the taking up of the liquid is established; for it is illogical to assume that the effort (*āyāsa*) is an auxiliary factor. Vārttika 2.3.3–4, Page 590: By the principle that "the application and purpose [of a mantra] occur after its form has been perceived," since the difference or non-difference of unseen results (*apūrva*) follows from the difference or non-difference of mantras, and that in turn follows from the difference or non-difference of the rites, it is not proper to assume a single sentence even when there is a mention of a distinct *apūrva*.

On page 493: even when there is a difference of form (rūpabheda), the distinction between the injunctive and the non-injunctive is caused by ignorance and knowledge.

For example, when those sacrifices belonging to the *puroḍāśa* class—which have *pṛṣadājya* as their substance—are permitted, those belonging to the same class that have *ājya* alone as their substance are also accomplished by that same permission.
