Bhāṣya 2.1.123: Words such as *rūpa* (form) and others are [classified as] words denoting qualities alone (*kevalaguṇavacana*).

When they are employed with reference to substances, they do not function without a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*). Vārttika 3.1.612, p. 681: In the proximity of things possessing form, a word for that which lacks form, being the remainder, takes on the sense of the subject under discussion (*prakṛtagrāhaka*).
*Ṭup-ṭīkā* 7.1.13: "Because there is no distinction from the word *rūpa* (form)" (6.1.3.12).

For it has been stated under the [sūtra] beginning with "*rūpa*" that we do not perceive form through action, because it is designated as something perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). *Vārttika* 2.1.2.5, p. 400: The principle of the commonality of form (*rūpasāmānyanyāya*).

Likewise: "We wear those very same garments that [were worn] in Mathurā; we eat those very same śāli rice grains that [were eaten] in Magadha; this very same kārṣāpaṇa coin is what was received in Mathurā," and so forth.

Regarding this very point, it is stated in the Mahābhāṣya on the sūtra *aḍuṇ* (Pāṇini 5.3.70): "Because of the commonality of form (*rūpasāmānyāt*), there arises the cognition 'this is that very same thing.
Sāhasī. 602. Furthermore, those qualities of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) which reside in the objects of perception...
"Those bodies are also the causes of experience for each individual self. (Vākyapadīya 3.1.7.13, pp. 702–03). The maxim of the line-drawn gavaya:
For example, a certain forest-dweller was asked, "What indeed is a wild gavaya like?"
Having drawn it, he showed it to him, saying, "This is a gavaya.
Because of his straightforward intellect, he took that line-drawing to be the actual gavaya.
Later, having gone to the forest and seen a real gavaya, he realized that his cognition based on the drawing was false; for there is a worldly proverb: "The mind follows the object."

Likewise, according to the Śruti passage beginning with "This person," one who is ignorant of the previously mentioned effects perceives what is not the Self as the Self; however, when the Self is known through the instruction of the venerable True Guru’s teaching, one then abandons that notion of identity with the non-Self. [Sāhasī 48] The maxim of the line-drawn cow (rekhāgavayanyāya):
in a syntactical formulation devised for the purpose of instruction according to the maxim of the line-drawn cow, there is indeed the elision of case-endings.
Thus, since the genitive case-ending (*ṅas*) itself does not exist within a compound, it cannot function as that which establishes the nature of the *saṃvara* (restraint).
Soma. 6|1|12. "The Vāravantīya [chant] is upon the Revatī verses."

Since the *vāravantīya* cannot function as a qualifier of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) without being connected to a verbal root-meaning that delimits that *bhāvanā*, and since the *sāman*’s status as a means for the sacrifice remains intact—thereby allowing its connection with the verbal root-meaning called "sacrifice" (*yāga*), which is the primary element—it would be illogical for the word "having performed" (*kṛtvā*) to delimit the *bhāvanā* of the sacrifice by means of the phrase "having made the *vāravantīya* on the *revatī* verses a means for the sacrifice. Rather, because there is a requirement for a verbal root-meaning to delimit that [primary *bhāvanā*], it is understood through extension (*atideśa*) that the *vāravantīya* is a qualifier of the *bhāvanā* of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*. Consequently, since it is known that the *revatī* verses, being conjoined with the *vāravantīya*, are also qualifiers of that [stotra-*bhāvanā*], it follows that the *vāravantīya* based upon the *revatī* verses also attains the status of being the *sāman* for the *agniṣṭoma*.
Su. Pp. 860–61. The Section on the Revatīs; the Section on the Revatī-Vāravantīya;
the Section on the Vāravantīya.
In the case of identical [sacrifices], it would be connected with the ritual action.

The Bhāṣya states: "The Agniṣṭoma has three *dhṛt*s; its *vyāya* is as follows: having made the twenty-one-fold [stotra] the *agniṣṭomasāman*, one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with it.
Having made the *vāravantīya* on the *revatī* verses the *agniṣṭomasāman* of this very [sacrifice], one desiring cattle should indeed sacrifice with it."

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: there is a doubt—whether, in that very same manner, cattle are the fruit resulting from the *ārbhavīya* chant as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) of the *agniṣṭoma*, and thus the phrase "one should sacrifice with this" (*etena yajeta*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*);
or rather what?

Regarding the statement "one should sacrifice with this," it might be argued that this constitutes a different ritual action. What is the prima facie view? That it is not a different ritual action, because the fruit results from a subordinate factor (guṇa). Why? Because this is a statement concerning what is already known through the injunction "one should sacrifice with this," and not concerning something unknown.
Therefore, it is not a separate injunction.

It is stated that "one desiring cattle should sacrifice in this manner," not simply "he should sacrifice. How so? Because it says, "having performed the Vāravantīya [chant]. Furthermore, the phrase "of this very [sacrifice]" is a clear statement of a distinct ritual action. Therefore, the conclusion reached is that the fruit results from the accessory (guṇa).
This being the case, we reply:
in such similar instances where the sentences are distinct, the fruit must be connected with the ritual action.
Regarding the statement, "Having performed the Vāravantīya on these very Revatī verses": it is not the case that he possesses Revatī verses upon which another Vāravantīya might be performed.
In that context, the Revatīs would have to be supplied, and the Vāravantīya would have to be enjoined for them; thus, the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (vākya-bheda).
Now, it might be argued: "Having taken the *revatī* verses from this [context] and having performed the *vāravantīya* upon them, one should sacrifice with this"—thus it is said.
However, in that case, the designation "the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*" would not be appropriate.
Or, if it is said that it serves the function of the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*, [then the objection remains].
The phrase "of this very [act]" would be intended here; otherwise, the sentence would be contradicted if both were the objects. Therefore, it is a different ritual action.

Now, how is there non-division of the sentence (*avākyabheda*) in another instance of ritual action? In the case of "Having performed the *vāravantīya* chant upon the *revatī* verses, one desiring cattle should sacrifice," a new sacrifice (*apūrva-yāga*), qualified by all the qualifiers, is enjoined.
Therefore, since there is a single purpose and mutual expectancy when separated, the status of being a single sentence (*vākyatva*) is established.
But [it may be argued]: is there not a difference in meaning, such that both the sacrifice and the unprecedented result (*apūrva*) must be performed?
[The opponent claims: "In the Revatī verses, the Vāravantīya [sāman] is something unprecedented. We say: no.
A sacrifice characterized by the Revatī verses as its quality and having the Vāravantīya [sāman] already accomplished is what is enjoined; it is not the introduction of the Vāravantīya itself.
That is to say, "the Vāravantīya [chant] is to be produced upon the Revatī verses. And it is possible for that to be produced.
It is said:
In that case, no connection between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* would have been prescribed; consequently, other *sāmans* might occur in the *revatī* verses,
and the *vāravantīya* might occur in other verses as well.
This is not a fault.

By the word "having performed" (*kṛtvā*), a connection that has been brought about is expressed for the sake of the sacrifice; by that, the connection is understood. In the case of the substance and the deity, this word "having performed" is capable of expressing both the accomplishment [of the action] and its priority in time.

Just as in the case of the command "Bring the horse that is red," the horse is enjoined by the word itself as being connected with the quality of redness, so that no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) occurs; the same should be understood here as well.
[Objection: Even so, there are many things: the *revatī* verses, the *vāravantīya* chant, the connection between them, and the sacrifice for one desiring cattle.
[Reply: This is not a fault.
Many [factors] are heard [in the text].
Here, however, only one qualified sacrifice is enjoined.
But is it not the case that both the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant are also enjoined?
If they were not enjoined, the sacrifice qualified by them would not be understood at all;
for it is not possible to enjoin that which is qualified without first enjoining the qualifier.
Therefore, when many things are being enjoined, there is no single purpose.
To this it is replied:
the word "atha" (now/then) denotes the production of a purpose.
As many words as accomplish a single purpose, that many constitute a single sentence.
And there are not many purposes here;
for in this case, multiple words do not enjoin multiple intended things.
The phrase "in the Revatīs" does not function in this way as an injunction of the Revatīs.
In the expression "vāravantīyam [is sung] in the Revatī verses," even here, within these two words, the word *vāravantīya* ends in the accusative case;
from this, no intended relationship is understood,
because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is distinct [from the action].
The word "having done" (*kṛtvā*) does not terminate in a mere connection with the verb "to do" (*karoti*);
rather, it expresses a connection with a purpose for another.
Thus, the act of sacrificing (*yajati*), when thus qualified, is for the sake of another.
Therefore, there is a single purpose regarding the two objects;
hence, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*).
However, when a fruit is attributed to a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), the *vāravantīya* chant becomes the function of the *agniṣṭomasāman*.
Furthermore, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) regarding the phrase "the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* of this [sacrifice].
If it were argued that a sacrifice qualified by all the qualifiers beginning with "the *revatī*" is enjoined as belonging to this *agniṣṭoma*,
even so, the sentence would be split due to the connection with the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*).
Now, if it is argued that "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vāravantīya performed during the Revatī verses," this cannot be so.
It would be [invalidated] by defects such as the measure of the *naḍanta* interval and so forth, due to the absence of those qualities.
But was it not just stated that "it is indeed possible to perform the *vāravantīya* on the *revatī* verses"?
It is possible only when there is an explicit scriptural injunction (*vacana*).
In the absence of a statement, they would not be taken up even when the Vāravantīya is being employed. However, there will indeed be a statement:
"One desiring cattle should perform the Vāravantīya upon the Revatī verses."
Therefore, the phrase "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the act of sacrificing.

If the statement establishes the connection between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant, then a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) is established; it is not a prescription of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).

[Objection: But since "one should sacrifice from that" (*tato yajeta*) is a restatement of a sacrifice, there will be a connection between this [chant] and the sacrifice through the act of sacrificing itself.
This is not possible;
for if the sacrifice were enjoined as being for its own sake, it would have no connection with one who desires cattle.
If it were connected to both, the sentence would be split.
Now, the connection with the sacrifice will follow; thus,
in the section concerning the Revatīs, there will be the word "anu" used in a figurative sense (lakṣaṇā).

Therefore, it is established that from such a quality (*guṇa*), the result arises as a distinct action (*karmāntara*) characterized by such properties; thus, in all such similar cases, it is appropriate that the result is connected to the action. [Durmādhava: Now, the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced for the purpose of providing an exception (*apavāda*) to this.
Therein, he first shows the subject matter (*viṣaya*): "The *Agniṣṭoma* is threefold (*trivṛt*)."

Having introduced the mixed injunction, "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with that [rite] which has the *Vāyavyāśvekaviṃśa* as its *agniṣṭoma-sāman*," and having prescribed the quality, "The *Vāravantīya* is the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*," it further states: "Desiring cattle, one should sacrifice by performing the *Vāravantīya* on the *Revatī* verses of this very same [rite].

Regarding this also, there is the same doubt as before: is a sacrifice qualified by these qualities being enjoined as distinct from the previous one, or is it the same previous sacrifice where cattle are the fruit—just as sensory power was [the fruit] of the quality?
Is it merely that? Indeed, according to the entire previous section, the result arises from a subordinate element (*guṇa*).

For instance: "In the injunction concerning the connection between the *Revatī* verses and the *Vāravantīya* chant, the result is heard; since [the result] was not previously established, the sacrifice itself is not being enjoined."
And it will establish the connection between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant. Even without [the word] *pratyaya*, the word *āgūḥ* is heard separately as a distinct term.

As for the objection that a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by a double injunction might be suspected—namely, because of the injunction establishing the connection between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant, and then the injunction of that [connection] with respect to the result—that too should not be apprehended, since the means and the result are already established by the Veda itself.

For when it is established that "one should perform the Vāravantīya on the Revatī verses," the [words] being implied by implication do not cause a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because they lack injunctive force. However, when there is a further injunction regarding a qualifier of another action, and that action is not implied as being devoid of connection with it, the injunctive word must necessarily be repeated; thus, a syntactical split inevitably results.
This is not a fault.
For when the meaning of the word "having done" (*kṛtvā*) is grasped, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) follows;
it too will take as its qualifier that which has come within its own scope.
When the subsequent *grahaṇa* (seizing) has been performed by means of this sacrifice (*kratu*),
the *sāman* residing in the ritual manual (*kalpasthāna*) itself effects the connection with the *revatī* verses through its own power.
Having thus accomplished the connection with the *revatī* verses, it remains awaiting the subsequent *bhāvanā* (efficient force).
The meaning of the word is precisely the implication of its own qualifiers;
it is grasped by the sacrifice.
And therefore, the implication of its own qualifiers belongs to the sacrifice itself.

However, because it is subordinate (*guṇabhūtatva*), that connection—which is the direct means of subsistence—is placed among those who are ignorant; thus, by means of the word *āgnīdhra*, which is well-known through extended application (*atideśa*), he imagines even the *revatī* verses as being its object.
Therefore, although the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* is not enjoined in this sentence, nevertheless, the qualification of the sacrifice (*kratu*) also transfers there; hence, there is no fault.
And consequently, the *āgnīdhra* has no requirement for a substance connected to the sacrifice under discussion (*prakṛta-yāga*).
Padya:
"Action is supported by the qualities (guṇas) which consist of the activity of the self;
what, then, is the purpose of the action of singing the Vāraṇtīya hymn?"
Substances such as curd and cows for milking, being incapable of functioning as instruments (*karaṇatva*) without an action, require such an action.

However, the *vāraṇtīya* [sāman], because its nature consists of the action denoted by the verbal root *gāyati* (to sing), is capable of producing a fruit just like a sacrifice even without another action; this is the position [of the opponent]. Therefore, if it were not connected with a sacrifice, it would produce the fruit independently while being sung over the *revatī* verses for the sake of the *agniṣṭoma* performance.

Consequently, the words "of this very [sāman]" (*etasyaiva*), "of the *agniṣṭoma*" (*agniṣṭomasya*), the term "having done" (*kṛtvā*), and the verb "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) would all become incoherent.
Therefore, the fruit arises from that sacrifice;
and because it is distinguished by qualifiers different from those of the previous [sacrifice], it is a distinct action (*karmāntara*).

The phrase "among equals" (*sameṣu*) intends to refer to the requirement for a relationship between substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) due to the unsuitability of the sacrifice and the quality [to stand in such a relation].
Or rather, because it consists of action (*kriyātmakatva*), it is said to be independent of other actions, as in the phrase "just like one who begs.

In both views, since the connection between the quality and the fruit—or the subject matter of a different sacrifice—is a distinct matter, syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) will indeed be established by definition; however, when there is a connection with the previously mentioned rite, a certain form of sentence remains intact.
The intention is that when there is a connection with another sacrifice (*kratvantara*), there is an absolute difference.

[The objection is: "For he does not possess the *revatī* verses"—this mode of expression appears due to the infinite number of sacrifices; it means that the *vāraṇtīya* chant is performed upon those *revatī* verses which belong to this [sacrifice].

In that case, although the qualification "of this" (*etasya*)—being obtainable through the context (*prakaraṇa*)—does not split the sentence, nevertheless, since the very nature of the *revatī* verses to be employed is not yet perceived, nothing else can be understood.

In that case, the *revatī* verses would have to be employed; and regarding those verses, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in the sentence "and upon them [is] the *vāraṇtīya*," as well as the redundancy of the word "this" (*etad*). If, however, for the sake of supporting the word "this," it is maintained that "these *revatī* verses are to be performed, and upon them the *vāraṇtīya* [chant is to be sung]," and that this [chant] is what is desired because it is being inquired after—that too is untenable. For even so, since the syntactical split arises from the fact that the purpose is not established, it is impossible either to enjoin or to exclude the connection with the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*; thus, neither way is feasible.

Now, if that [agniṣṭomasāman] were also enjoined, then because the previous injunction would be set aside, there would be the contingency of it being merely the agniṣṭomasāman; thus, the phrase "of this very one" (*etasyaiva*) would be redundant, or else, if it were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This is one way of construing the text. Alternatively, this word *etad* (this), remaining in its sequential position, is accepted as a qualifier of the *revatī* verses; and in that case, the statement is understood as follows: "The vāravantīya is made the agniṣṭomasāman upon those *revatī* verses which belong to this [sacrifice]."

To what ritual act [does this refer]? Because there is no qualifying attribute for it, and because the word *etad* (this) is already exhausted as a qualifier of the *revatī* verses, the phrase "the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* of this" cannot be established. Alternatively, if that were the subject, there would again be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Having thus refuted all the modes of expression for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) right here, when it ought to be asked how there is no syntactical split in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the proponent of the prima facie view asks in astonishment:
Thus, when that name has been established, he has shown as many syntactical splits (*vākyabheda*) as he desires, like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*).

Therefore, I ask: how is it that there is no syntactical split in this case? The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntavādī*), however, maintains that an unestablished ritual act (*aprāptakarman*) is being enjoined.
"Since the establishment of a qualified injunction is possible, [the two] have a single effect"—

this is because it is intended to show that there is no difference between them, as it is impossible for a single sentence to enjoin two distinct *bhāvanās* (efficient forces) when they are already included within the same context.
"We say no"— this is intended to mean the injunction of another primary *bhāvanā* qualified by subordinate *bhāvanās*.

"Otherwise, there would be no prescribed relationship between the *revatī* verses and the *vāraṇtīya* chant"—thus, [the connection] is enjoined by means of a qualifier and the qualified, and so forth. Furthermore, the word "having done" (*kṛtvā*) is not remembered as being part of an injunction.

Therefore, although the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is denoted, nevertheless, because human activity is dependent upon an injunction, a person does not undertake it even when it exists [if it lacks an injunction].

Since the *revatī* verses and the *vāraṇtīya* chant are merely qualifiers of the sacrificial *bhāvanā*, they are to be employed simply by virtue of their non-existence [elsewhere]; for there is no authority for a mutual restriction (*anyonyaniyama*). In that case, if one were the object [of the injunction], and there being no restriction to a single part thereof, the *gāyatra*, *mahīyava*, and other chants would also apply to the *revatī* verses.
Likewise, the *vāraṇtīya* chant would also apply to the *gāyatrī*, *bṛhatī*, and *anuṣṭubh* meters which constitute its own insertion (*āvāpa*).
In that regard, concerning the *revatī* verses, [the objection] "But even so... is raised.

Since there would be a multiplicity of meanings due to the assumption of injunctions for as many subjects as there are, it would be for the sake of perceiving a connection that [the verse] is called the *vāraṇtīya*.
Therefore, he considers that there is no unity of sentence (*naikākyatva*) regarding the *vāra*.
This is not a fault.
For it has been stated that this [suffix] is not enjoined as *revala* specifically with reference to its actual location;
rather, because it denotes multiple things, it possesses a manifold meaning.
Now, as for the objection: "This is not a fault;
even if one has heard what is enjoined, one might think it was not actually performed because the person to be enjoined did not act upon it"—to this it is replied:
He says this:
even so, in this manner, its fruit according to the rule is that many objects [are implied], yet only one is enjoined as qualified.

"In every case where it is heard, 'Having done this, one should do that,' if it is the *bhāvanā* [productive operation] that is intended, and that is characterized as a sacrifice (*yāga*), then— even though the action expressed by the verbal root has already been obtained from elsewhere— the *nairṛta* and *vaiśvadeva* offerings are also enjoined. If one adheres strictly to what is literally heard, then the hearing occurs for that specific purpose.
But if [the subsequent action] has not been reached, then because the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) arises from that very [subsequent action], there would be a resolution [of the objection].

However, all these [actions] are enjoined as instruments (*karaṇa*) by virtue of occurring after the cessation of the preceding [action]; since they are enjoined while permitting that [preceding action], they function as its auxiliaries (*yojanabhūta*). Therefore, their purpose is indeed one and the same.
It is said that because it cannot be performed otherwise, it must necessarily be performed; thus it is "enjoined" (*vihita*).

It is stated here that even that which is merely to be enjoined (vidheya) is not the [sole] meaning; rather, it is understood that the meaning connected with the primary injunction— such as the connection between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* chant— is what is enjoined here, and that is a single thing.
Because it has already been accomplished, that by which it might be resorted to as a cause [is not required].

Therefore, he says: "For here, there is no word intended as the purpose for what is to be understood. If, then, the connection were as something to be understood (*anujñeya*), [it would be so]; [but it is not].
It is an injunction;
for, since actions are intermediate acts, it is connected with the [principal] sacrifice itself— because it must be performed and because it is to be permitted—
and thus there is no completion prior to the efficient-force (bhāvanā) of the sacrifice.
He states that [the word] "kula" is subsequently understood through a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*): this word "kula" is able to express a certain meaning;
therefore, because each has a single meaning, it is established that they form a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*). Thus it is said.

If it is asked how there can be comprehension of multiple meanings by means of a single [word], he says in response: "In the case of a variety of qualities (*guṇa*), syntactic splits (*vākya-bheda*) are observed and stated.
This is what is meant by "it might be argued" (*athocyeta*);
for indeed, this is also a way of understanding.

For example, [in the injunction] "bring the red one" (*śoṇam ānaya*). This is for the purpose of supporting this word. Even though it is established that there is a separate action (*karmāntara*), and even though another action is obtained when connected with the act of bringing, the red axle being enjoined is refuted as not being an alternative to the result of the red [color].
In that very context, the mode of expression is as follows: the word "aśabda" (non-verbal), when employed, produces a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Likewise, in the case of "Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman on the Revatī verses," by means of this [injunction], there is here the accomplishment (*nirvṛtti*) and the state of being prior in time (*pūrvakālatva*) taken up by the word "anu.
Alternatively:
"One should sacrifice. What will follow from this? First, the context (*prakaraṇa*) will not be sublated.
"In that very [context], the qualifier of the qualifier is not enjoined."

In a case where a substance is understood through the word *etasyaiva* ("of this very [sacrifice]"), which grasps the subject under discussion and favors a proximate connection, it is not perceived as being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the ritual action.
Regarding that, it is said: "In that case, there is the cognition of the sacrifice consisting of this.
To this, it is replied:

No, because it would follow that the word "desiring cattle" (paśukāma) is meaningless. Since [the substance] is already established, it is subordinate; thus, if one were to abandon the injunction regarding the qualifiers of the substance, there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (vākya-bheda). For it is not possible for a single [act] to be enjoined as both a ritual procedure and a fruit.

The connection between the *revatī* verses and the *vāraṇtīya* chant is established; thus, the simultaneous injunction of the specific [elements] is logically possible. Now, if it were argued: "When the *revatī* verses have been performed, because the sense of the root *kṛ* (to do) is already present as a general factor, its status as something not to be enjoined does not apply here."
First, he returns to this very position in order to state another objection;
thus, some suggest that he sets forth [the view] with the intention of expressing, "We accept the qualification by means of the oblation.
Or rather, it is not so.

How then is there the twofold view among ritualists (*yājñika*) regarding the meaning of "performing" (*karoti*), which qualifies the act of meditation (*bhāvanā*), in the case of the *Revatīvārantīya* and other desires for specific qualities (*guṇakāma*)? For some, it is accepted as being qualified by a relationship; thus, according to the Mīmāṃsakas, the fruit belongs to the quality (*guṇaphala*).
For others, however, it is the quality itself [that is the fruit].

Furthermore, the qualifications of the subjects and so forth—such as the substance and the deity—as well as the status of being performed on the new and full moon days, belong to the sacrifice; therefore, it is that [sacrifice] which is connected with another fruit.

In this case, these [qualifications] will be mentioned in the context of the month and so forth. Consequently, the syntactical expression is qualified by a connection that is not [already] established.

First, one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with this [rite] constantly. Regarding the cultivation of the mental impression (*bhāvanā*), there is no restriction on the season or the sacrificial materials. Because it is true, one should have faith in it; however, if one should desire cattle, then one should perform the rite according to the specific injunctions for that purpose.
The purpose [of the negative particle] is precisely to exclude the performance of the *pratipad*, not to exclude its authorization.

If that were the case, the negative particle (*na*) would first enjoin the proximate object; however, since the *agniṣṭomasāman* is not employed prior to the sacrifice, it will not be enjoined in this manner.

Nor is it subordinate to anything else, for it is distinguished by its injunction of origination, as in the case of "Having employed the Vāraṇtīya on the Revatī verses, [one should sacrifice] with the *yadi-yāmī*.
What then?
It is established that, while enjoining the sacrifice for the sake of a fruit, it is not separated from the proximate [element].
Having formed the intention, "I shall do thus," the sacrifice is to be commenced.
Furthermore, that which has not yet arisen does not even conceive of its own arising.
This concludes the section concerning Revatī.

Regarding the section on the Revatīs and the injunction of multiple meanings, he speaks thus, considering that just as in a subsequent injunction the occasion for enjoining an action is obtained, so too in an injunction of a result, the action is enjoined by way of the result: "Now, one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Vāravantīya performed upon the Revatī verses.
This is because its status as an instrument (karaṇatva) is established through its being a means of accomplishing the sacrifice by virtue of its importance in the stotra.
Alternatively, it is the indicator of a particular state (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*);
for by this very [act] being in such a state, one desiring cattle should sacrifice.
To that, the answer is as follows:
It cannot be so;
for there would be a deficiency (vaiguṇya) due to the loss of the specific quality of being chanted on a different *ṛc* verse and so forth.

If this were indeed the same ritual action (*karman*), then because its substance (*dravya*) is the *vāyavya*, the *sāman* prescribed for it must be chanted upon the *ṛc* verses known as the *revatī*s; otherwise, by losing the specific quality of the previously prescribed substance, a deficiency would result.
But has it not just now been stated by you yourself regarding our own position that, in that case, the *ṛk* verses belonging to the *revatī* meters would also necessarily apply?
This is not a fault.
The word "performed" (*kṛta*) refers to the connection having been accomplished for the sake of the sacrifice.

"This word ['kṛtvā'] is capable of expressing these two meanings. However, thinking that in the Siddhānta view—where there is an injunction of a new act—it is possible to enjoin multiple things, whereas in the other case it is not, [the opponent] says: "If there is a direct statement (*vacana*), it is possible in my view; but in your view, since the *revatī* verses are obtained merely by the mention of the *vāravantīya*, it is impossible.
The opponent replies again: "In that case, there will be a direct statement."
It is for that very reason:
because a specific action is enjoined with respect to the fruit, and because a restatement (*kṛtvā-vāda*) is not injunctive;
furthermore, even though there is an injunction regarding the fruit, the phrase "it is a restatement of the sacrifice" is intended to mean that it does not enjoin anything else.

The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntavādī*) states the result of the impossibility of his intended injunction of meaning: "If the statement is already established, then there can be no injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhāna*) regarding what is already present. [The opponent objects: "But surely, because of the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sacrifice by the word *yajeta*... [The proponent replies: "This cannot be so," which is the exposition of the established conclusion, as it has not yet been refuted by that statement; thus, even now, he considers his own position to be stronger. This is the explanation of the established conclusion.

For if the *vāravantīya* song, characterized by the *revatī* verses, were enjoined as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) with respect to the sacrifice, then that [sacrifice] would be its objective (*uddeśya*).

Consequently, precisely because it is being pointed out as the objective, the word denoting the fruit could not be connected either to that sacrifice or to the subordinate element; thus, the mention of the fruit would be entirely meaningless, or the sentence expressing such a connection would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Alternatively, if there were an injunction of a ritual action qualified by a subordinate element, then, because the action is intended as something new, it would necessarily constitute a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).
Furthermore, it is not possible for the statement "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" to be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
By this, its status as a *nimitta* (condition) with respect to the injunction regarding the *revatī-vāravantīya* is established.

Consequently, the *vāravantīya* is not connected with the *revatī* verses by any stronger means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for that would involve abandoning the qualified [injunction] and result in a doubling of the [textual] burden.
Now, [the opponent claims] that "the connection with sacrifice is a restatement" (*anuvāda*).

This means that since the result arises from the accessory (*guṇa*) itself, the fact that the sacrifice is the substratum—already understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*)—is merely restated in this sentence.
But what is the distinction between this case and the previously refuted notion of the relationship between substrate and superstrate (*āśrayāśrayitva*), such that it is brought forward again?
It is said in response: for in that case, the principle "on account of meaninglessness, [the result applies] to its subsidiaries" has been refuted.
However, the intention is that in place of being a subsidiary (aṅgatva), the connection with the *dhūma-sāman*—which asserts a relationship with that—is easily established.
He refutes those [objections] with the statement: "The sentence [of direct injunction], due to its context and so forth, is more powerful.
For a relationship between substrate and superstrate is possible through another means because it is conducive to the connection with the fruit;
however, it has already been stated that such [a relationship] is not possible here.
The relationship between part and whole (*aṅga-aṅgin*) would indeed exist if there were an apprehension of the "how-to-be" (*kathaṃbhāva*), but that is not the case;
for [the author] will state later: "It is not connected because of the context."
It is connected with the four fruits;
therefore, because there is no contradiction, there is an injunction of an action qualified by both qualities and fruits.
In this regard, it might be argued as follows:

Even though there is another action, he refutes [the opponent's view] by showing that the connection between the fruit and the sacrifice is understood from the quality itself as favored by that [action].
Therefore, it is an injunction of an action (*karmavidhi*).
"But then, when the sacrifice is being enjoined as something remaining [to be performed], how can there be a connection with another action—the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*—by way of a qualification?"
Regarding this, the reply is: "Because of the statement.
By the principle previously stated, this should be understood as a transference (atideśika) statement:
"The Agniṣṭoma-sāman is to be performed."
There exists no *ṛg* verse whose mouth is the *girdhoma*, established as such, for which the *vāravantīya* is said to be the fifth in its function.
Therefore, it is stated that [the *vāravantīya*] serves as the fifth in the function within the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛtayajña*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that the function of the *stotra* itself—namely, that which has the *girdhoma* as its "mouth"—must be performed for that purpose.

Therefore, it is established that the fruit must be connected with the sacrifice. Śābarabhāṣya: "In this case as well, as before, only a subordinate quality (guṇa) is enjoined for the sake of the fruit; there is no injunction of the sacrifice itself, because that would entail excessive complexity (vidhigaurava)."

Although the sacrifice has a direct connection with that which serves as its substrate, it nevertheless becomes possible through the mediation of the performance of the *stotra* chants. Thus, the enjoined accessory (*guṇa*) takes up the ritual action under discussion for the sake of the fruit.
In that case, a sacrifice intended for a specific quality (*guṇakāma*) cannot be accomplished by means of a *sāman*.

Therefore, it is possible to enjoin the very sacrifice under discussion for the sake of a result, provided it is qualified by having the *revatī* verses as its basis, the *vāravantīya* as its *sāman*, and the *agnidhoma-stotra* as its measure of performance.
This constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*) because it serves as a refutation of the preceding [view regarding] Soma.
Thus [it is said].

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: when the qualities are equal, because of the distinction in the ritual action and due to the dependence upon the substratum, the fruit resulting from the rite would belong to that [rite] in which the qualities are heard, and not to that in which the qualities are merely present. As Viśvarūpa says: "Having stated, 'For this [rite], the Vāravantīya-sāman is indeed the iṣṭi... "
It is heard in scripture that "the Ṛk was made during the Revatī [nakṣatra]" for the sake of obtaining cattle as a fruit; thus,
it possesses the quality of beginning with Revatī and has Revatī as its substratum.
The action in the section concerning the Revatīs is distinct; as in the previous case, it is a subordinate element (guṇa).
The connection between the Revatī verses and the Vāravantīya chant is that which bestows cattle.

In this context, there is a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) regarding the connection between the result and the ritual action. Therefore, the result is connected to the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice as qualified by the previously mentioned attributes. The Bhaṭṭa [view] is as follows: When the connection of the result is established for the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice prescribed by the injunction "The *trivṛt* is the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice" through the sentence, "Desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), one should sacrifice with this, having performed the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* on the *vāyavyā* verses twenty-one times," then subsequently the following is obtained: "Desiring cattle, one should sacrifice with this, having performed the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* Vāravantīya on the *revatī* verses."

In this regard, as before, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument is as follows: according to the principle of the Rājasūya sacrifice, since there exists a connection with the performance that is inseparable from the time, agent, and so forth—which constitute the meaning of the *iṣṭi* and other rites qualified by the *āgnīdhra-homa-stotra-bhāvanā* and qualified by their own respective factors—it is possible for there to be an injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) characterized by such application (*viniyoga*).
Furthermore, this very method is accepted even by the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) in the case of the *vāyavyā-vākya*.
The second [position], however, is that the principle of the Rājasūya does not apply here.

Since the performance of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice and its occurrence subsequent to the *stotra* are already established by the *vāyavyā* injunction, a prescription for the *revatī* verses by way of restating those [elements] while prescribing them for a specific result would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), as it would involve a prescription for the *agniṣṭoma* itself.
For in the *vāyavyā* injunction, through the principle of extension (*atideśa*), the occurrence subsequent to the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* and other such details are already possible;
