Regarding the definition of *stobha*: "And that which is additional" (6.1.13). The nature of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*)—which is a pervasive property that distinguishes [an object] from others—and its variegated color, should be consulted in the Sūtra [9.2.10.9].
The nature [of the sacrifice]:

Su. Pr. 1080. Regarding the definition of the *lakṣaṇa-homa*: "Because it is heard as being so stated, there would be an additional [act] due to the excellence of the quality-offering; this is the principle that the establishment of a thing occurs through both definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

When that [meaning] has been expressed by the root *yajati*, the meaning of cloth and so forth is indicated (*lakṣyate*)—[the root *lakṣ* being used in the sense of "perception" or "manifestation"]? Because the root *juhoti* is heard in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), the meaning of *juhoti* is the act of pouring (*āsecanādhika*), as it is derived from the root *hu* (to sacrifice).
This is a common characteristic (*lakṣaṇasādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*). Its injunction would be for the other [root].

"The Naiyāyikas hold that every characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is known, and the characterized (*lakṣya*) is that which is characterized; it is that which leads to the inference of distinctions and is employed in linguistic usage. [Objection: It is not possible. Vārttika 3.1.2, p. 657. [Response: A definition (*lakṣaṇa*) has been stated because it is impossible to teach, through exhaustive questioning in various instances, that which distinguishes a thing from its own class (*sajātīya*) by means of its very nature as a characterized object.
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that dharma, as established in the Veda, is the defining characteristic [of authority].
"The knower does not reach the end of objects through their individual distinctions;
for even the sages, by whatever means they cognize an object, that is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

Regarding the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), it is said in the *Vārttika*: "But when a desire for knowledge has arisen concerning the established conclusion through a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), the wise, having set aside the knower (*pramātṛ*), determine that [object] by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (Bhāṣya 2.1.73). Thus it proceeds. And so: "Just as one who desires perception and the like [of smell] would have 'smell-ness' (*gandhatva*) and so forth as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), that by which the object to be defined is characterized is called a 'definition' (*lakṣaṇa*)."

Or [it is said]: "And by means of a proof (pramāṇa), the establishment of earth and so forth occurs; likewise, wherever there is a desire to speak, there its [nature] is observed. That by which something is characterized is a 'definition' (lakṣaṇa); smoke is a definition—such is the application [of the term].
And thus, in the case of Agni, Indra, Āditya, Īśvara, and so forth, there are various discourses.
The word *lakṣaṇa* [is used in this sense]. (Lakṣaṇa, 3340).

Lakṣaṇa 3341: Lakṣaṇa. The defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) consisting of being the cause of creation and so forth, as well as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as scripture (*śruti*), are observed here and there to establish [the existence of] Godhood (*īśvaratva*). (Sāhasī. 72)

As in examples such as "ayathīḥ praveśaya" ("cause him to enter in an improper manner"), where even the literal meaning (*śakyārtha*) is connected with the action. The theorists of poetics (*ālaṃkārikāḥ*) maintain that this very [type of indication] is *upādānalakṣaṇā* (indication by inclusive transfer).

The word *lakṣaṇa* is seen in the Mīmāṃsā treatise in the chapters on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as in the aphorisms: "Dharma is a purpose characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ*) and "Now, therefore, the definition of the subsidiary" (*athātaḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam*).
(Bāla. pṛ. 1). By conventional usage, the word *lakṣaṇa* denotes a unique property that distinguishes an object from those of its own class and from those of other classes. (Su. pṛ.

*Jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication) is that which causes the connection [of a word] with a meaning that does not have its own primary sense as the qualificand, as in "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is preferable to the postulation of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭakalpanā*). Bhāṣya 9.12.3, 11.15.43; Dūṣaṇa 10.8.8.4; Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 546. (The discussion concerning *lakṣaṇā* is primarily found at Mīko. p. 2229; it should also be consulted in the entry "dvitīyārthaḥ" [in the *Bhāṭṭarahasya-tā*]).

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is another function of words. Indication is the presentation of that which is not directly denotable (*aśakya*) by means of a relationship other than similarity with the denoted meaning (*sādṛśya*).
Indication by indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) is also included within this very category.

This is because, in words such as *dve-repha*, there exists a relationship consisting of being denotable by a word composed of two phonemes that constitute the word denoting its own referent; thus, this is a case of *lakṣita-lakṣaṇā* (indication of the indicated).
By this, the view that the word *dve-repha* indicates the word *bhramara*, and that the cognition of "bee" arises from that [word *bhramara*] through primary denotation (*śakti*), is refuted.
Because the meaning of the case-ending following the word *dvārepha* cannot be otherwise [established],

indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consists in possessing a relation with that which is denoted by the word itself. And its status as residing in the word is through the relation of being the denoter of that which is related to its own denotation.

For example, in expressions such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the relation with the flow (pravāha), which is the primary denotation (*śakya*) of the word "Gaṅgā," constitutes the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of that [indication] is the nature of being a verbal cognition whose qualifier (*prakāratva*) is the state of being related to the Gaṅgā and whose qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) is the river.

The relation with the Gaṅgā appears either as a generic relation-ness (*saṃbandhatva*) or as a specific relation such as conjunction (*saṃyogatva*), because there are two types of experience: "the hamlet is related to the Gaṅgā" and "the hamlet is on the bank conjoined with the Gaṅgā."
Similarly, in the case of "Devadatta is a lion" as well, there is indeed indication (lakṣaṇā) in the cognition "Devadatta is one related to a lion" through a mediated relationship.

Furthermore, the meaning of the phrase "in that which is invariably concomitant with the denoted object" is that the mode [of signification] therein is indication (lakṣaṇā), by virtue of its connection with the denoted object.
[This occurs] by means of indication.

The recourse to secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is also established as a fixed convention (*nirūḍha*) due to its having functioned since beginningless time, as in the case of words such as "white" (*śukla*).
In some instances, it is applied [by choice], as when one says "the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*) on the dark fire."

Furthermore, in some cases it is not even possible to perform [the action], as in the case of sound, touch, taste, and smell. (Vārttika 3.1.6.22, p. 683). The restatement of a definition is appropriate;
it occurs for that which is already known.

Bhāṣya 11|1|12|64: Even when figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is assumed, it becomes valid when the primary meaning of the word cannot be logically established. In such cases, as in "he stands on the fire" (*agnau tiṣṭhati*) or "he stands in the pit" (*avaṭe tiṣṭhati*), the conventional usage results in the understanding: "he stands near the fire" (*agni-samīpe*) or "he stands near the pit" (*avaṭa-samīpe*). For even figurative indication is indeed worldly (*laukikī*). 2|1|16: Furthermore, figurative indication is possible when there is syntactic unity with the action (*karmaikavākyatā*).
4|4|8| 19. Even indication (*lakṣaṇā*) constitutes an injunction, as in common usage: "Let these balls of flour be made into lions. In the Veda as well: "He worships with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras].
And since the word "lion" is not seen there to denote a physical likeness, here too [the word] denotes a likeness.
"By diminishing [the world] with his splendor while it was already being diminished, he truly desires the earth for himself from another"— this is the maxim.
Thus says Bhāravi.
*Sāhasrī*.

When a light means has been adopted, even though recourse to a heavy one would otherwise be impossible, one resorts to the heavy even when a light [means] has been adopted, in order to avoid purposelessness.
*Sūtra-pṛṣṭha* (Su. pṛ.), pp. 50–51. *Laṭ* (the present tense suffix).
The suffix *laṭ* has the power (*śakti*) to denote the present tense, according to the grammatical rule:

*‘vartamāne laṭ’* (Pāṇini 3.2.123). And that "presentness" consists in either: (1) being proximate to the time that serves as the locus for the employment of *laṭ*; or (2) subsisting within the temporal adjunct (*upādhi*) that serves as the locus for the employment of the word *laṭ*; or (3) being related to a time other than past and future times.
And thus, the present time is precisely that time during which the operation of the performance of that action is being carried out;

it is the usage of the term "presentness" with respect to the efforts (kṛti) belonging to that time. Although there is no underlying commonality [among those efforts], there is a unification by means of verbal expression alone.

Just as the referent of that and other such pronouns is not a commonality [shared by all], so too, if there were a commonality through the nature of cognition (*buddhitva*), then cognition itself would lack commonality; and if there were a commonality even for that cognition...

Thus, even in cases where there is the time of the performance (*prayoga-adhikaraṇa-kāla*), the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth exists because of the presence of the knowledge of the performance produced by writing and other means;
this is according to the sūtra [Pāṇini 3.3.161]: "The optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others [are used] when there is a desire to express the meaning of the root. (3346)
An injunction (*vidhi*) is the instigation or impelling of a subordinate person, such as a servant.

An invitation (*nimantraṇa*) is the necessary impelling of a daughter’s son or others to a Śrāddha feast and similar occasions. A request (*āmantraṇa*) is permission for acting according to one's own will.
"Adhīṣṭa" means setting something in motion preceded by an act of honor.
In this regard, there is no capacity [in the word] in its true sense,
because it would entail the postulation of various capacities.
However, [the nature of *pravartanā*] consists in being that which sets in motion the operation of these four [factors].
And "being a motivator" (*pravartanātva*) is the state of being a property of a motivator that is the object of a cognition which generates an activity directed toward another.

By this, those who assert that the status of being the meaning of an injunction (*vidhyarthatva*) belongs to "being a means to a desired end," "being achievable through effort," and "the non-connection with an undesirable consequence"—on the grounds that these lack the status of being a motivator—are refuted.

Maṇḍana, however, maintains that since the knowledge that an action such as sacrifice is to be accomplished by an effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is established through worldly experience alone, the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) has no denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to it, as it is obtainable from other sources.

Furthermore, the knowledge that an action is not followed by a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvajñāna*) is otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*) by its production of the absence of aversion (*dveṣābhāva*), and thus is not a direct cause of inclination (*pravṛtti*).
For this very reason, the inclination of a seeker of liberation who is an *āstika* remains unimpeded even when he possesses the knowledge that a particular act is a means to hell.
Therefore, he states that *pravartanā* (the impulsion to act) is simply the state of being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).
The teachers [hold] that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is the "task" (*kārya*), while the desired [end] is...
Endowed with the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth;
the mark is the state of being something else to be proven (*sādhyatā*).
However, in the world, that which is apprehended as the cause for the possibility of comprehension— of that which is to be accomplished as an action by virtue of being a means to the highest good—
is "comprehension" (gamaḥ).
And by that form, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote the action to be performed (*kārya*). Or rather:

Page 584, 2|1|125: In the case of a human-authored statement (*pauruṣeya-vākya*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—which consists solely in its capacity to convey a task that requires dependence [on other factors]—must be understood as having been derived from another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). However, with respect to all things, it is the efficacy (*sāmarthya*) that is to be understood; and the status of being a "task" (*kāryatā*) belongs only to an action (*kriyā*) that serves as a means to the highest good (*śreyas*).

It should be understood [as stated at] PMS 3.1.14, p. 841: "The indicative mark (liṅga) and the sequence; therefore, in common worldly usage, it is action itself that is denoted by the word as something to be accomplished (kārya).
But in the Veda..."
And it is able to set aside the conventional designation (*samākhyā*).

Bhāṣya 2.1.20: By means of the implication (*paryudāsana*) of the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), [the word] possesses a gender (*liṅga*) that persists through another time in accordance with the means for attaining heaven; thus, gender is stronger than order (*krama*).
Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.1.7, page 836: "The capacity to denote an effect is determined;
and that is not [derived from] another means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara)."

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) derived from the injunction (*codanā*) is an internal factor. Bhāṣya 8.1.31: "Being understood" means that its independence consists precisely in its being for the sake of the task (*kāryārthatā*); nor is there [dependence] on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).

The *liṅga* (indicative power) residing in an injunction (*codanā*) is that which brings about [the action], while that residing in a mantra is that which illuminates what has already been brought about. Since the purposeful nature of the action is understood as it is being perceived, it does not deserve to be abandoned.

8|1|16|31. Indicative power (*liṅga*) is of two kinds: the capacity of the word (*śabdasāmarthya*) and the capacity of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*). This is because, even when the word’s own expressive power depends on a further purpose, it is observed in common usage that such dependence is logically consistent. (Bālakrīḍā, p. 9). [Objection: But surely, if that is the case, then the Veda would not possess meanings established through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).
It pertains both to the word and to the meaning.
[If it is argued that] in rites such as the two-night or three-night sacrifices, it would apply to the twelfth day— do not say so.
The object is indeed well-established by worldly convention;
however, it proceeds according to rule through other means of valid cognition and scriptural authority.

In this regard, it is established that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) residing in the word is "independent" (*nirapekṣaḥ*). (Ṛjuvimalā, pp. 15–16). [The words are] the word *ahaḥ* and the word *rātriḥ*.
The word *ahaḥ* (day) also denotes a day-and-night (*ahorātra*), and because it is a property of words such as gender (*liṅga*) and so forth, it is called "verbal productive energy" (*śabdabhāvanā*).
The word *rātri* (night) is likewise [denotative].

Gender (*liṅga*) and number (*gaṇatva*) reside in the object; the collection (*gaṇa*) itself is the aggregate (*saṃghāta*), and that alone is the injunction (*vidhi*), the mandate (*niyoga*), and the instigation (*preraṇā*).
The child (bāla), page 75, is capable of following the collection of dharmas.
Bhāṣya 8.1.10: A gender mark (liṅga) does not [indicate] the other [meaning], because it resides in Vedic words such as "gender" (liṅga) and so forth; it is not of that very form.
It is twofold: that which depends on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as the general possibility, persistence, and so forth, and that which does not depend on them. *Rahasya*, p. 15.

The first example is the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*). Because this mantra contains words such as "cutting" (*lavana*) which possess indicative power (*liṅga*), it makes known an action that is not the object of any other means of knowledge. Thus, it brings about the understanding of the meaning for the performance of the ritual.
Furthermore, other words also [indicate] the status of being an auxiliary to the ritual action through their capacity for effectuation; this is the second [type].
Indicative power (*liṅga*) is of two kinds: because they do not have another purpose, they denote their own meanings by being intent upon that [action].

Therefore, the investigation into whether [an object] is non-worldly (*alaukika*) or scriptural (*śāstrīya*), and so forth—[as discussed in the *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. ...]: those objects as well are the objective domains of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). By that...

In the *Vṛtti*, it should be understood that "the meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārtha*) is [the basis for the application of the suffix]. However, upon examining the nature of the meaning itself, there is no dependence [on other factors]. (*Rjuvimalā*, p. 35).

The logical mark (*liṅga*) is a means of valid cognition that indicates the knowledge of a property (*dharma*). Maṇi, p. 13. The nature of being a logical mark does not exist without necessity (*niyatatva*).

The *liṅga* suffix— nor indeed, by relying on the fact that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, do the grammarians [assert] the capacity of the *liṅ*, *leṭ*, *tavya*, and the fifth mood (*pañcamalakāra*) for injunction (*vidhi*).
Or [as stated in] Pāṇini 3.1.14, page 700:
"The manifestation of groups of words that have become names and of forms [of words] is the masculine gender.
An example of a scriptural (śrauta) rule for gender is: "By means of the Jyotiṣṭoma [one attains] heaven..."
The concealment of these is the feminine gender; their equilibrium is the neuter.
"One who desires this should sacrifice.
(Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 30).
And although every entity possesses gender, nevertheless, in the absence of a logical rule (*nyāya*), gender is not a cause [for ritual application].
Bhāṣya 7.2.17.
Since it has been stated that a certain gender is manifested by the word, gender is the authority for extension (*atideśa*) in the case of trees.

[The word] *maṇi* [is used as an example]. On page 13, regarding the gender (*liṅga*): since both masculine gender and so forth exist even in [words like] *vṛkṣa* (tree), and since masculine gender and so forth possess the capacity to denote meaning even in such cases, it would follow that they serve as subordinate elements (*śeṣabhāva*) within the mantras. [If one objects that] because [gender] exists [in all nouns], this [objection] is untenable, it must be said in reply: [The objection is: "Since masculine gender and so forth exist even in [words like] *vṛkṣa*, and since masculine gender and so forth possess the capacity to denote meaning even in such cases, they would therefore function as subordinate elements within the mantras. To this, it must be stated: "This is incorrect because [gender] exists [universally]."

Because it is based on what is well-known in the world (lokaprasiddha), as stated in [Sūtra] 1.1.1, the specific application of mantras has been set forth as the cause in accordance with the following traditional teaching: "One who possesses breasts and long hair is a woman; one who is hairy is known as a man."

Su. pṛ. 1169. [The gender] is to be understood through the indicative mark (liṅga). Since it is stated that "that which is the interval between the two [masculine and feminine] is the neuter when both are absent," there ought to be an inference of the gender after [observing] the breasts;
however, it is not [determined] through the arrival of the indicative mark.
In the case of *keśadeva*, "hastinī," and "vaḍavā," the cognition of "femininity" (*strītvabuddhi*) and the apprehension of gender (*liṅgāvagama*) occur at the very same time.
Śābarabhāṣya 4.1.5, p. 78.
[This is] the connection.

Therefore, they maintain that "that genus [is inferred]" because the very mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the presence of breasts and hair is observed as the pervaded (*vyāpya*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), while the pervader (*vyāpaka*) [the genus] exists elsewhere;
or rather, it is because a specific genus indicated by these marks is the probans (*liṅga*), whereas the manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and so forth are merely the marks.
For grammarians, *liṅga* is merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣāmātra*) for the purpose of teaching grammar;
it refers to any one among [the properties] such as being the agent (*kartṛtva*) associated with the action (*kṛti*).
In the case of "he cuts with the *luva*," there is no possibility that the meaning of the word is accessible through worldly linguistic usage; thus, it is not [the same] here.

In this instance, since the status of being the instrument of the sacrifice (*sūtrakaraṇakatva*) arises through the postulation of a word expressive of the state of being the object of offering (*uddeyatā*), there is no fault in considering such an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
For this very reason...

Since those whose fitness is certain lack [the quality of] being the agent (*kartṛ*) or any other [participant] denoted by a word crowded with [such] designations, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) because of the absence of that [quality]; therefore, the inclusion of "being intended for another" (*paroddeśyatā*) is necessary. [This is based on the established doctrine: "The marks [of gender] are the shape and the procreative capacity. Thus, due to the absence of [that quality], there is an over-narrow definition; hence, the inclusion of "being intended for another" is introduced.

The purpose of assigning [the status of] a *liṅga*—characterized by disappearance and manifestation—to the modifications of the *parikṛti* and the *kāraka*, etc., has been clearly stated by the grammarians (*śābdika*) themselves in the context of the rules for refinement (*saṃskāra*).

By the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (presumption otherwise impossible), since the meaning of the *saṃskāra* (consecration) is already established in the *śeṣavākya* (subsidiary sentence), the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*)—whether neuter, masculine, or feminine—is not expressive of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), but rather of the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*). There is no application (*viniyoga*) through the assumption of a separate word for the object (*uddeśya*) or the predicate (*vidheya*), nor is there any modification of the *suv*-suffixes; rather, it is merely the instruction (*anuśāsana*) of the word itself. This is the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*). For example: "If [one does] not [offer] Soma... [and so on].

In cases such as "siṃhaḥ" (lion) and "siṃhī" (lioness), there is gender [variation]; and in passages such as "one should find pūtīka plants, one should press them," although the pūtīkas are not the primary substance, because the function of being the object of pressing would otherwise be untenable, it must be stated that even those which are modifications of the base word— such as the *soma* mentioned in the injunction "one should sacrifice with soma"— are denoted [as the primary substance] in certain instances.

In the very same sentence, "In the absence of Soma, [one should use] *pūtīka* plants," there is the use of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyānta*). Therefore, that [number], like the number [in the injunction] "with an animal" (*paśunā*) and so forth, is a construction of the word-meaning (*padakalpanā*); in that context, it serves as the indicator of the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvācaka*) regarding its applicability to the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so on. And in some cases, it is intended to be expressed solely as the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*).
However, where there is a contradiction, [the former applies].
The exclusion of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is achieved by the absence of suitability for the construction of word-meanings (*padakalpanā*).
In that context, the use of the pronoun "that" (*tat*) is for the sake of establishing grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) regarding the modified form (*vikṛti*). (Bhāṭṭa 4.1.6).

In a case where there is no inherent capacity for accomplishment (*niṣprakṛtisādhya*), by means of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) such as the *aprakṛtisaṃdhi*, that which is called the "indicative mark" (*upaliṅga*)— namely, the capacity of mantras to convey meaning—

is not found in any way, whether primary or secondary, in a word denoting either the objective (*uddeśyatā*) or the instrumentality (*kārakatā*) expressed in the phrase "one should perform" (*kuryāt*).
Or [it may be defined as such] because it is conducive to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). The term "capacity" (*yogyatā*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*);
see page 112, lines 475–476.

According to the reasoning stated previously, since the property of being any one of [the categories] such as the object-to-be-indicated (*uddeśyatā*), the agent (*kartṛtva*), and so forth, is cumbersome, the gender (*liṅga*) is now defined. The ancients maintain that "capacity (*sāmarthya*) is gender. This is because it is any one of the following: the state of being an agent, the state of being an object, the state of being an instrument other than those two, the state of being a recipient (*sampradānatva*), the state of being a point of departure (*apādānatva*), and so on. As it has been said: "The capacity of all entities is understood to be gender."

The intended meaning is as follows: the definition under discussion consists simply in the fitness conducive to the postulation of a word expressive of either an injunction (*vidhi*) or a qualification (*viśeṣya*), such as "one should sacrifice with *soma*. However, let there be no [such fitness] for those two—namely, the object (*uddeśya*) characterized by being a constituent part (*aṅga*) and the factor of action (*kāraka*)—which are already established. Now, the fitness that is not yet determined is that which is conducive to the postulation of a word expressive of either an injunction or a qualification in the manner of "one should sacrifice with *soma*."
The indicative mark (*liṅga*) consists in the capacity for the postulation of a favorable qualification, based on the impossibility of [the statement] being otherwise [explained].
For example, in the case of "He cuts with the *sruc*," there is the over-extension (*atiprasakti*) of the intended object (*uddeśya*), namely, "two substances."

[Objection: "Durvā grass and so forth do not have a status as an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) based on indicative marks (*liṅga*); for there is no certainty regarding their suitability for the act of cutting with a sharp instrument, which would be conducive to the postulation of the required words [in the Vedic text].
If this is argued, it is not so.
For [the word] *soma* and so forth serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*).

Or, for example, in the case of injunctions regarding purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as "he chooses the *adhvaryu* priest," even though the status of being an auxiliary is established by the authority of the indicator, the word *soma* and others—under the view that they indicate a thing to be accomplished (*bhāvya*)—are described with an instrumental ending because it would otherwise be inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*) [that the substance could serve as an auxiliary]. Therefore, that which is [so described] is [an auxiliary].

The meaning of the sentence is that [the soma] is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*). According to the view of others— such as those who hold that the instrumental case endings (*nayana*) express predominance (*prādhānyena vyapadeśāt*)— there is the conceptualization of a connection between the instrumentality of the *soma* and the *bhāvanā* through a mediated sequence, such as "one should effect [it]," which involves the conceptualization of the application of the object to be refined (*saṃskārya-viniyoga-kalpanā*), and the conceptualization of suitability conducive to the conceptualization of the word ending in the third case.

Or rather, by the maxim "they exist [as such]," the term *vākyāṅgatva* (syntactic subsidiarity) refers specifically to *śrautāṅgatva* (direct scriptural subsidiarity), as in the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods," and not to *laiṅgikāṅgatva* (subsidiarity based on indicative power). Even though the cutting of the grass (*barhirlavana*) is manifested [by the mantra], the indicative power (*liṅga*) consists in the fitness conducive to the assumption of words expressive of its own function—such as being the instrument (*karaṇa*)—which is favorable toward the intended object to be expressed, as in the rule: "If the animal belongs to another deity, the *manotā* hymn must still be addressed to Agni."
They say that even the statement of a Brāhmaṇa possesses greater authority due to its indicative power (*liṅga*);

for instance, in the passage, "With the remainder of the *prayāja*, he sprinkles the oblations," they maintain that this serves as the means of proof for the status of the meaning of the pronoun (*tat*) as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) toward those respective objects, by way of postulating the direct Vedic hearing (*śruti*) of that word.

Even while accepting the injunction for sprinkling the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings onto the clay and other materials for the sake of producing jars and so forth, [the *prayāja*] is conducive to the sacrifice and the like through its capacity (*yogyatā*).
By means of the instruction regarding the remnants of the *prayāja*, one accepts that the act of sprinkling possesses conduciveness through its supporting nature.
In that regard, the definition of the *kṛtikāraka* word is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) with respect to the *naya*.

However, as for the over-extension with respect to the fitness conducive to the postulation of an additional injunction (*adhikavidhikalpanā*), there is no need for concern, because its being an auxiliary to inference (*laiṅgikāṅgatva*) is accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Nor is it the case there...

Since the injunction for the disposal (*pratipatti*) is inferred solely from the requirement for a disposal of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings, it lacks the status of being "based on indicative power" (*laiṅgika*), as it does not arise from indicative power itself.

When an injunction is inferred based on the suitability for sprinkling and placing, the indicative power serves as a corroborative factor through its role in fulfilling that requirement; thus, indicative power is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the fact that those [remnants] are indeed the leftovers of the *prayāja* offerings used for sprinkling and placing.

In that regard, if expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) were the means of valid knowledge for subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*), then because it would conflict with the classification of the means of valid knowledge for subsidiarity, Devadatta—who, though capable of cooking, lacks the expectancy for cooking—would not be seen to be employed in the act of cooking; and since there is no instance where *liṅga* (indicative power) functions as a means of application without expectancy, and since expectancy alone is the means of valid knowledge for subsidiarity in all cases, *liṅga* would fail to attain the status of a valid means of knowledge.

Now, if the sprinkling with the remnant of the *prayāja* were enjoined by a scriptural injunction (*śrutavidhi*) as being performed upon the sacrificial oblation (*haviraddeśena*), then because the remnant of the *prayāja* would have already been employed in that sprinkling, there would be no requirement for its disposal (*pratipattyākāṅkṣā*). Consequently, the postulation of an implied injunction (*ārthikavidhikalpanā*) would be untenable.

Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of "he cuts off [the portion] for Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half" (*uttarārdhāt sviṣṭakṛte samavadyati*), where the northern half—though employed as a subordinate element (*guṇatvena*) as the source (*apādānatayā*)—is nevertheless to be disposed of through the postulation of an implied injunction, so too should it be here.

In that case, even though the latter half [of the verse] has been enjoined with respect to the portion of relinquishment (*tyāgāṃśa*), because there is an expectancy for the purpose of the portion of casting-in (*prakṣepāṃśa*), an implied injunction (*ārthikavidhi*) is postulated. Only when the attainment of the object to be conveyed (*pratipādya*) with respect to the portion of casting-in is established does it apply; however, in the present instance, since there is no division of parts, that [attainment] is impossible.

By this [it is shown that], for example, in the case of "He gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa," the injunction is for the purpose of the Maitrāvaruṇa regarding the staff which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Thus, according to the Siddhānta, since it is impossible to apply the consecrated staff—which has already been utilized as the emblem of initiation—to the act of giving, the scriptural injunction must enjoin a different staff. Therefore, in order to avoid the fault of [the staff] being [merely] for Maitrāvaruṇa, the giving of the staff is established as a *pratipatti* (disposal) by virtue of being an implied act of giving. Furthermore, since the restriction of the function [of a disposal] will be explained in the case of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*), the fact that this refers specifically to the consecrated staff is established through such a restriction of its function; thus it was stated in the *Natyā*.

Likewise, it is refuted [by the opponent] that the explicit injunction (*śruta-vidhi*) enjoined here for the act of pouring (*abhidhāraṇa*), in order to avoid the burden of postulating a power to imply another act (*dhāraṇākṣepa-śakti-kalpanā-gaurava*), might instead have the status of being something to be accomplished by postulating an implied injunction for the act of presentation (*pratipatti-vidhi*)—arising from the requirement for the subsequent half [of the vessel]—on the grounds that there is no fault in this according to the maxim "there is no fault when one has already bowed. This is because, in the case of an implied injunction for presentation, the capacity to motivate the act of pouring would still have to be postulated, and thus no advantage is gained.

In that case, since the benefit for Maitrāvaruṇa is accomplished by the mere act of dedication (*samarpaṇa*), the requirement that the staff be accepted through the element of relinquishment (*tyāga*) does not apply here; for while such a requirement exists in subsequent cases, it is impossible in the present context.

Furthermore, because a restrictive injunction (*viśeṣaṇavidhi*) regarding the sprinkling with the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings is necessary, it is appropriate to characterize that very injunction as having the capacity to imply the holding [of the staff]; thus, there is no room for the complexity of assuming an unmentioned injunction of the literal text (*śrutavidhi*).
If it is argued that there is a disparity because, in the case of "to Maitrāvaruṇa," it is simpler to assume a rule prescribing an attribute (*viśeṣaṇavidhi*),
whereas in the Taittirīya recension, such an assumption is not made there because the disposal rule (*pratipattividhi*)— "that he gives the initiation-staff"— is explicitly heard in the scripture.

In the case of the scriptural injunction (*śrutavidhi*), although the status of being part of the *prayāja* remnant context exists even within the *bhāvanā*, the understanding that it serves the purpose of the sacrifice depends upon the subsequent injunction regarding the qualification (*viśeṣaṇavidhi*). Therefore, prior to that, there is no undesirable requirement for the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prayāja* remnant; for just like the injunction regarding the qualification, the injunction regarding disposal is also logically established through the presence of the causal complex consisting of indicative marks (*liṅga*) assisted by the requirement for disposal.

Nor should it be argued that, since even the injunction regarding the specific [remnant] must be inferred, there is no basis for determining which one [the remnant] is intended, and thus it would follow that a capacity to retain [the substance] must be postulated; for if that were so, it would follow that the remnant must be retained for the purpose of sprinkling over the heart and other organs in the *daikṣa* sacrifice, and for the purpose of sprinkling over the *prājāpatya* cups in the *vājapeya* sacrifice.

Furthermore, if one were to accept that the disposal (*pratipatti*) itself is the motivator for retention, then the statement in the fourth book (*Bhāṭṭa*, 4.1.44, the *prayājaśeṣābhidhāraṇa* principle) regarding the completion of the remnant in the proximate injunctions would be contradicted. This is not a valid objection.

There is no possibility of a middle position based on the intention that there is no contradiction—since the burden of procuring another vessel for the purpose of holding the oblation (*havis*) at a later time serves as the decisive factor (*vinigamakara*), and thus the injunction for disposal (*pratipattividhi*) itself can be assumed to include the act of holding.
Furthermore, this indicative mark (*liṅga*) is of two kinds:
that which depends on a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a general relationship, and that which does not depend on such a means.

In the first case, the dependence on a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that conveys the relationship of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*)—consisting precisely in being delimited by a property that pervades the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*)—is what constitutes dependence on a means of knowledge conveying a general relationship.
And this [dependence] exists in the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*).

Here, in the Vedic injunction (*śruti*) inferred from the indicative power of the mantra, the cutting is not the objective in its capacity as mere "cutting," because even without the mantra, the connection with cutting could be established through other means such as memory (*smṛti*), which would render the mantra purposeless; rather, it is the cutting as a constituent of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result).
Furthermore, the status of being a mantra cannot be established by that form [of the word], because it conveys meaning merely through the act of cutting (*lavana*).

Nor is it possible to assume the hearing of a word denoting that which is delimited by the aforementioned objective (*uddeśyatā*), namely, "this mantra manifests the cutting related to the *apūrva*," without first having a cognition of that cutting as being related to the *apūrva*.
Therefore, for the sake of such a cognition—namely, that the cutting is related to the *apūrva*—one must rely on means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as the context (*prakaraṇa*).

In this regard, because this mantra is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is first understood that "something related to the New and Full Moon sacrifices is being manifested by this [mantra]. When the expectation arises as to "what is that?", it is understood from the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra itself to be "the act of cutting" (*lavana*). Therefore, since this indicative power (*liṅga*) depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes known the relationship of the mantra with that which is delimited by the nature of being related to the New and Full Moon sacrifices—which pervades the state of being the cutting related to the New and Full Moon sacrifices as determined by the indicative power—it follows that this indicative power depends upon a means of valid cognition that makes known the general relationship.

Thus, regarding the rule "the mantra is for the consecration of the sacrifice" (*yāgānumantraṇam*), once it is understood from the designation that "something related to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) common to sacrifices is manifested by this [mantra]," and when the expectation arises as to "what is that [something]?", it is understood from the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra as being "Pūṣan.

Therefore, because the indicative power (*liṅga*) depends on a general means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that conveys the relationship between the mantra and the object of injunction—characterized by being delimited by the status of being a means to the transcendental result common to sacrifices (which pervades the delimitor of the objective, namely, the status of being a means to the transcendental result of a specific sacrifice not established by other means)—the indicative power possesses a dependence on the aforementioned means of knowledge.

However, where the very nature of the subject matter (*uddeśya*) does not render it purposeless, its status as the subject matter—such as being a means to the *apūrva* (unseen potency)—does not depend on context (*prakaraṇa*) and the like; this is as in the case of the knowledge of meaning, which by its own capacity leads to the performance of the ritual. In such cases, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) does not require any other means of proof (*pramāṇa*) to establish its general connection. Furthermore, because an indicative mark is non-verbal and thus not itself injunctive, its authority is mediated by the assumption of an injunctive scriptural text (*śruti*) based on a general connection defined by the fact of being enjoined. Consequently, the authority of a scriptural text whose validity is not so mediated is superior to that of one whose authority is mediated.

For this very reason, in the case of the verse "kadācana starīrasi," which reveals Indra, its purpose of revealing Indra is inferred from its indicative power (*liṅga*); yet, its purpose of being for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire is established by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) "he worships the Gārhapatya with the verse addressed to Indra" (*aindrī*), as determined in the *Aindrī-adhikaraṇa* (3.2.12). Nor should it be argued that because the knowledge of Indra is understood through the direct scriptural mention of the word "that" (*tad-it*) situated in the opening [of the section], the verse cannot be a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) for the worship of the Gārhapatya.

Due to parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more appropriate to accept that the *taddhita* suffix—which is capable of denoting "divinity" (*devatātva*) as an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) invariably concomitant with the state of being a substance to be abandoned—possesses a secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "that which is primarily intended to be conveyed," specifically regarding divinity as an adjunct of the locative case; for otherwise, in the present context, the *taddhita* suffix would lack its primary denotative power (*śruti*), and there would arise the fault of violating the principle of "single thrust of expression" (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*) in the injunction directed toward Indra. Furthermore, the injunction "by means of the [verse] addressed to Indra" (*ainyā*), which is recited within the section on the fire-altar construction (*cayana*), cannot logically serve as an injunction if it were merely intended to manifest Indra as a subordinate element of the construction.
Although the Gārhapatya fire is connected to the piling (cayana) by virtue of being its means, it is nonetheless possible for it to be the object of the piling's ritual action.

Therefore, since the Gārhapatya is present through its capacity (*śakti*), one should understand that the designation "Aindrī" is applied to this verse by taking its power of manifestation; thus, by the force of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) supported by secondary capability (*gauṇa-sāmarthya*), this verse has the function of manifesting the Gārhapatya fire alone.

When there is a conflict with an indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of primary capacity, a secondary capacity—even if supported by direct statement (*śruti*)—does not possess inherent applicative power.

For this very reason, it was stated in the *Liṅgādhikaraṇa* (3.2.16): "In the case of the mantra *barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*, which is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, its syntactic connection (*vākya*) is to the state of being a seat for the gods through the *barhis* grass; it does not, however, have a secondary application as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) for the cutting of the lotus-stalk purifier.
This concludes the definition of indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Murāri says on page [x]:

"Whether it be the *liṅga* (indicative mark) or the *prakaraṇa* (context) that is to be favored, activity does not occur toward that which has already been determined. One engages in that which is understood to be 'this is fruitful.'"
Bhāṣya 3.1.8.2, p. 778: Indicative power (liṅga) is stronger than context (prakaraṇa).
Vārttika 3.1.7.
Page 836: Indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*).
The fact that a mantra, which by virtue of its context is established as being for the sake of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, is sublated by its indicative power as being subsidiary to Pūṣan.

Mīmāṃsā: Indicative power is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). When they recite a certain meaning in proximity to a matter already possessed of context, it is understood that "this [meaning] is an instrument for that [matter]."
How indeed is one "standing above"? When there is doubt, the determination arises through functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Where a thing is capable with respect to a purpose, it can be employed for that purpose. (Bhāṣya 3.1.7.4, p. 882). *Liṅga* (indicative power) is the factor that assigns a word-meaning whose general relationship [to a rite] has been established by another means of knowledge.

Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.1.4.11 states that *liṅga* (indicative power) among mantras is the capacity of the words [to indicate application], as seen in the lack of explicit injunction in the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*).
*Liṅga* is the factor that applies a mantra; it applies it only to its primary meaning, not to a secondary one.
Thus, the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" is an auxiliary for the cutting of *kuśa* grass, not for the cutting of *ulapa* grass.

Indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*); therefore, in the case of the two mantras beginning with "asyonaṃ te," they are respectively applied to the act of settling and the act of seating within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. (Bhāṣya 3.6.7.14; Vṛtti 3.1.8). Indicative power is stronger than syntactical connection, because syntactical connection effects application only by postulating an indicative power which in turn postulates a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), whereas indicative power effects application by merely postulating a direct Vedic statement.

In the mantra "syonaṃ te sadanam," the phrase "syonaṃ te sadanam" serves the purpose of preparing the seat (*sadanārthatva*), but it does not constitute a subsidiary element for the act of placing the offering (*sādanāṅgatva*) by virtue of the syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Mīmāṃsā: *Liṅga* is the capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting in being the object of application.
Sūtra-pu. 1111. *Liṅga* is weaker than *śruti* because it involves a delay [in the process of application].

VI. 10|8|8. The indicative mark (*liṅga*) is intended [as the basis for differentiation], as in "In spring, one should sacrifice a black-necked [cow] to Agni in the morning," and so forth; "The pregnant ones are the indicative mark;
by the indicative mark..."
This is because of the specific injunction: "They become [so].

Furthermore, in the passage, "The horse, the two bulls, the bull, the ram, and the man," the masculine gender is intended to be significant, because of the specific injunction: "They are with testicles."
Bhāṣya 4.1.6.17: *Liṅga* is the capacity to denote a specific meaning.

Śābarabhāṣya 3.1.7.14, p. 824: Vedic *liṅga*, in the form of the observation of another purpose (*anyārthadarśana*), being unestablished otherwise (*ananyathāsiddha*), is stronger than a *śruti* inferred from *smṛti*. Kauṇḍinya 3.1.7.14, p. 363: Vedic *liṅga* is more powerful than *smṛti*.

Vārttika 3.1.7.14, p. 841: "The indicative mark (*liṅga*) [of the Gavāmayana] would belong to the aggregate because it serves that purpose, like the two [days]," according to this sūtra (7.4.3.16), the view of the opponent is stated as follows: since the Gavāmayana—which consists of an aggregate of days—takes on the function of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which also consists of an aggregate of days, the properties of that [twelve-day sacrifice], such as the twelve *upasads* and the ritual distribution (*vihāra*) of the eleven [cattle], are obtained in the case of wild rice (*nīvāra*) and so forth, just as the properties of *vrīhi* [rice] apply; thus, the occurrence of these two indicative marks is established. Sūtrārthadīpikā, p. 731: "The indicative mark is stronger than the similarity of form (*samākhyā*)."
Vārttika 3.1.7.18, p. 837: Indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than common name (*samākhyā*).

The status as a subsidiary to the act of eating, which would be assigned to the sentences recited in the *Bhakṣānuvāka*—such as "O, eat," "the three-eyed one," and "impel me"—by virtue of common name, is set aside by their indicative power, which establishes them as subsidiaries to the taking up, the inspection, and the correct swallowing [of the Soma].

In the section on the *kāmya* (optional) *ājyānuvākyā* verses, following the *ājyānuvākyās* for the *āmiṣāruṇī* sacrifice and preceding those for the *saumāraudrī* sacrifice, there are verses addressed to Manu. The status as *yājyā* (offering verse) and so forth, which these verses would acquire by virtue of their designation (*samākhyā*) as belonging to the optional *saumāraudrī* sacrifice, is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), namely their being intended for the *sābhimarśana* (touching) rite. *Bhaṭṭālaṃkāra*: "Indicative mark" (*liṅga*) means capacity (*sāmarthya*).

*Bhāṣya* 3.1.7.14; 6.5.9.32; *Ṭupṭīkā* 9.1.3.4. As for "indicative mark," while gender (*strītvādi*) and the like are understood merely through the verbal form (*śabdatanumātra*) in cases other than qualities pertaining to living beings, in the case of words such as *padvān* (having feet), they are understood through the actual form of the object (*artharūpeṇa*).
Vārttika 3.1.8.3, p. 328: Indicative power (liṅga) is stronger than position (sthāna).

Regarding the two mantras recited in sequence—"Upahūtaḥ" and "Upahavyasa"—the application of these mantras to the acts of requesting permission and granting permission, respectively, as suggested by their order of recitation, is set aside by the indicative power which effects a reversal of that assignment.
According to the Bhāṭṭālaṃkāra, indicative power is indeed stronger than context (prakaraṇa).
He said:
"When there is a conflict, the context (prakaraṇa) is set aside by the indicative mark (liṅga), but there is no conflict between these two.

In this context, by the word *liṅga*, a derivative (*yaugikī*) scriptural mention (*śruti*) based on its connection with a deity is intended, not mere capacity (*sāmarthyamātra*). For instance, in the case of the collection of words such as "Indra, the king of the moving [waters]," which serves to denote a quality, there exists a *liṅga*— consisting of the capacity to satisfy the expectancy for a quality within a sentence— acting as a support for that sentence.

Su. Pṛ. 662: It is stated here that gender (*liṅga*) is not the meaning of a case ending as a word-form (*vacana*) is, but rather that gender is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself (as explained by the author of the Bhāṣya in [Pāṇini] 1.2.51–52, beginning with the words "for the word *strī* is a qualifier of the nominal stem"). T.D. 9.1.16, p. 692: Gender is the sign (*liṅga*) for the appropriate connection of preceding words with subsequent words according to their respective meanings.
Bhā. 3.4.1.131: "Capability (*sāmarthya*) is one intended sign (*liṅga*) of the action."
Furthermore, the power of the statement [is understood] by examining the preceding and following [parts].
Vākyapadīya 3.4.1.131, p. 965: It has been stated that whatever is present in the intellect is the *liṅga* (inferential mark).
Bhāṣya 8.2.17.33–34: The expressive capacity (*ukti-sāmarthya*) of the word "yat" (that which) is the *liṅga*.
Vākyapadīya 3.1.7.14, p. 824: The capacity of all entities is designated as the *liṅga*.

Mīmāṃsā: When a general relationship exists and is understood, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) finds its scope of application. *Ṭup-ṭīkā* 10.1.2.1: 42. Subordination by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*): For example, the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*) has subordination to the act of cutting (*lavana*). For that mantra is capable of manifesting the act of cutting.
From the context (*prakaraṇa*), the general connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is understood.

When the general connection of the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantras with sacrifice is established through the designation (*samākhyā*) "sacrifice-consecration," their specific connection with the Pūṣan-sacrifice is understood by virtue of their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Thus, in Mīmāṃsā, the order of sequence (*krama*) is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "He clenches his fists" and "He restrains his speech. Immediately thereafter, it is heard: "He announces the consecrated one.

In that context, by virtue of the sequence, the clenching of the fists and so forth are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) of the consecration (*dīkṣā*). However, by means of indicative power (*liṅga*), the one-pointedness of the mind is established as a subsidiary element of all ritual acts, in the form of its fitness for all ritual acts.
VI. 3.1.14. By the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside in that case (the *sūktavāka*).
"When there is a reference to a substance by means of an indicative mark, there should be a cognition of all [substances], because the indicative mark applies to everything."

Regarding the statement, "The *sāmidhenī* verses are those of Manu," since the substance in the form of the *ṛc*s is indicated by the mark (*liṅga*) of "Manu," and because that mark—the connection with Manu—is all-pervasive, being present in all *ṛc*s composed by Manu, there would be a cognition of all of them; that is, there would be the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of all the *ṛc*s belonging to the *Daśatayī* collection that are composed by Manu.
The meaning is that all *ṛc*s composed by Manu are to be employed as *sāmidhenīs*, not merely seventeen. This is just like the case of the *Āgneyī*.
"One should remain for a year performing the placing [of bricks] with the *Āmeyī* hymns"—
this is [an example of] inference from a characteristic mark to a characteristic mark.
Thus, as many *āgneya* hymns as there are in the *Daśatayī*, with all of them the bricks are laid;
such is the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*).
Or rather, it should be according to the purpose, because they are subordinate to that purpose; therefore, the measure should be small, and in that case, the indicative power (*liṅga*) is effective.

Regarding the statement, "The *sāmidhenī* verses are those of Manu," it does not mean that all the verses belonging to the *Daśatayī* [the ten maṇḍalas of the Ṛgveda] must be taken as being by Manu; rather, because they are subordinate to the purpose—that is, because they are subordinate to the function consisting of kindling—their number should be small, limited to exactly fifteen according to the requirement for the purpose.
The meaning is that only a few verses by Manu are to be taken, not all of them.
And in that small collection of verses, the capacity—meaning the efficacy or connection—of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), which consists in its relation to Manu, is indeed present.
Even the seventeen verses belong to Manu alone and are not non-human;
thus, the connection with the gender is the same.
Therefore, only as many as are required for the purpose should be taken, not all of them.
(69) Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Regarding the *āmeya* [offering], there is a complete injunction (*kṛtsnavidhi*).
The proponent of the conclusion (*siddhāntin*) demonstrates the disparity between the example of the *āmeya* presented in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) [at 10.6.1.9–73].
In the example of the Āgneya [rite], there is a rule for the whole; that is, a rule for all the hymns (sūkta). This is because it has been stated: "with the Āgneya hymns."
However, because the *sāmidhenī* verses are limited in number, it is not appropriate to include all the verses of Manu.
Since the *ṛjīṣa* (the dregs of the Soma) is the primary element, its inclusion would result in the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the entire substance.

If it is argued that—just as in the case of the guest-offering where the rule "he throws the *ṛjīṣa* into the fire" implies that whatever *ṛjīṣa* there is of all the cups is thrown without distinction, so too all the verses of Manu should be included by virtue of being *sāmidhenīs*—to this the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) replies:

Since the *ṛjīṣa*—the remnant of the Soma whose juice has been extracted—is the primary substance, it should be disposed of by all [the priests] together during the *arhaṇa* rite; however, at the *avabhṛtha*, there should be its casting into the water.

But regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses of the Mānava school, because they serve as a subordinate part of the action consisting of kindling the fire, not all of them are to be taken [as the object of the disposal]; such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
(Ke.)

Those mantras that are enjoined by means of indicative power (*liṅga*) must be employed in the ritual exactly as they are known [to be], and in that regard, there is no function for the Brāhmaṇa at all. (Ṭupṭīkā 12.1.8.21). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the measure of the mantra is that those [mantras] which are connected by indicative power do not apply to the transcendental result (*apūrva*), as stated in the sūtra "And because of the fruit and the deity" (1.1.6.13).

Ratna. 3|1|12. A *liṅga* (indicative power) is sublated by another *liṅga*, as in the mantra "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee" (*syonaṃ te sadanaṃ kṛṇomi*). In this case, both meanings lack the capacity to manifest the sense of being connected to the ritual action (*karmasamavetatva*).
The *liṅga* consisting in the capacity for the acceptance of a single sentence is "sit upon that" (*tasmin sīda*).
Bāla. p. 135. A *vākya* (syntactical connection) is sublated by a *liṅga* because of the remoteness of its meaning.
Vārttika 3.1.7.12, p. 1126: It has been stated that a restriction is established by an indicative mark (liṅga). Bhāṣya 3.1.2.12; 3.1.16.28:

An Indicative Mark (liṅga) is not to be set aside by Direct Assertion (śruti), as in the cases "he cuts with the *sruva* ladle" and "he cuts with the *svadhiti* axe," where the *sruva* and other implements are indicated.

In the case of a single remnant, when multiple principal acts (śeṣins) are indicated by direct statement (śruti) regarding either the offering of liquid or other offerings, the restriction to the offering of liquid alone—by virtue of indicative power (liṅga)—sublates the status of the remnant [in the other cases]. Similarly, when there is a single principal act such as the offering of liquid, although multiple remnants are indicated by direct statement through the ladle (sruva) and other implements, the restriction to the ladle alone by virtue of indicative power sublates even the scriptural (śrauta) mention of the other implements. Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 180. For everything studied as an unattached injunction (anārabhyādhīta) becomes an auxiliary (aṅga) through syntactic connection (vākya-sambandha) or through some non-deviating indicative power (liṅga).

Vārttika 3.4.8.24, p. 954: From the indicative mark (*liṅga*), this much is understood: "This [word] is capable of accomplishing this particular meaning. Bhāṣya 3.1.7.14, p. 843: From the indicative mark, the cognition is accompanied by doubt; from direct audition (*śruti*), it is free from doubt. Bhāṣya 3.1.7.14, p. 842: From the indicative mark, there is the possibility [of application]; the aggregate consisting of the indicative mark, the order, and the position is stronger [than the others].

Vārttika 3|1|7|14, p. 880: Scriptural testimony is stronger than an indicative mark.

Bhāṣya 3.1.7.14, p. 823; 9.1.12.37: Indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than name (*samākhyā*) when it is dependent on [the latter]. 3.1.7.20: The remoteness of meaning of indicative power regarding the application of the *aindrī* verse—when both direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative power set out together toward the application, and the letters that constitute the applicatory direct statement are perceived, then those [letters] are capable of bringing the [mantra] to mind through indicative power; thereafter, while one begins to postulate applicatory [words] for them based on the requirements of context and other factors, the application has already been communicated by the other [means], namely, the directly perceived [direct statement].

And in that case, the mantra is also independent of the context (prakaraṇa) regarding its application; this is established under the section on Indicative Power (liṅga), specifically at Mīmāṃsākośa 4.2.0, sūtra 3.3.54, the section on Indicative Power (liṅgādhikaraṇa).
Even in the case of context (*prakaraṇa*), it applies with respect to the mantra.
That being so, by the power of the context, there is primacy of the primary meaning.

However, regarding subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*), since the authority for a single [subsidiary] can be established otherwise, the two mantras should not be cited as examples based on the power of the primary and secondary meanings in relation to the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) denoting Indra as the principal element.

In the case of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is effective; however, without direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the application (*viniyoga*) is not established. Therefore, direct scriptural statement is more powerful.

From the transfer of gender and so forth, the transfer of name is stronger; [this is because] it is quicker—page 830, 7|4. An example of the modification (*ūha*) of gender: "You are clothed," because it is the cause of cognition. Furthermore, the transfer of gender is stronger than the transfer by lineage (*paraṃparā*).
Regarding the one-year-old heifer (*ekahāyanī*), [the mantra] is "Thou art Rudra" (*rudrāsi*).
Regarding the castrated bull (*sāṇḍa*), it is "Thou art Vajra" (*vajrāsi*) and "Thou art Rudra" (*rudro'si*).

As for the gender, first of all, a Vedic text inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) becomes the meaning of the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*) of the action by virtue of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

Su. Pṛ. 739. It is known from the fact that the *liṅga* (indicative power) has its application restricted solely to manifestation. Vā. 2.2.4.36: "The state of depending on a weaker means of proof" (this refers to the sense of *adhikāra*). Pṛ. 153. Bhā. 3.2.120: "The *liṅga* culminates in the word alone"—this is the *Liṅgādhikaraṇa*.

The gender (liṅga) of the animal, such as its masculinity, must be determined through syntactical application (vākya-viniyoga), because it cannot be established by the indicative power (liṅga) alone. And so forth. Vākyapadīya 3.3. Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (liṅga).

This is extended by analogy to the section on number and the section on gender, as demonstrated in the *Bhakṣānuvāka* (Sūtras 3.2.125–26).
Or [it may be argued]: the indicative power (*liṅga*) is not intended to be significant, because the sentence (*vākya*) is heard as being sublated.
Nor is it the case that the capacity for application (*viniyoga-sāmarthya*) of the indicative power is not intended; for this is what constitutes "indicative power" when it is heard as such.

In the case of "the female cow (strī gauḥ) belongs to whom? because there is no occurrence of the word in isolation, but rather through its placement alongside another word, the statement "she is necessarily the *somakrayaṇī* (the cow for purchasing Soma)"—due to the fact that the status of being a *somakrayaṇī* is not intended [as a primary meaning]—the sentence itself is essentially subsumed within it; thus, only the gender (*liṅga*) is perceived. Now, why is it not the case in "bring the doe (*mṛgīm ānaya*)"? On page 817, the meaning of the direct statement (*śruti*) is mediated by the inference of the gender from the direct statement alone.
Is a deer being brought? Not so; for that would be an impossibility.
"The former [indication] of the sentence is again separated by the inference of indicative mark (liṅga) and direct statement (śruti)."

As in the example "He runs" (dhāvati), the gender is intended to be significant. [This is because] the meaning of the sentence [depends on it], whereas gender is superseded by more specific means of proof such as direct statement (śruti) and syntactical connection (vākya). This is because, having heard [the word], [the gender] is not understood [otherwise].

And likewise there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "In the *hāna-mantra*, they are pregnant women, [with the words] 'who may protect this sacrifice and who may prosper the sacrificer. And likewise: "They are males. This portion must be treated separately.
Regarding the application (*viniyoga*) stated for the recitation (*japa*) of the *abhidhru* verse in the sense of "purchase," as in the example "The female cow is the *somakrayaṇī*":
therein, the term "female" (*strī*) is the subject;
however, it is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*) by virtue of direct statement (*śruti*), syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), or the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *iḍā*.
Likewise, in the case of the injunction "He should sacrifice men to Prajāpati," it is impossible to do so because of the contradiction with the [male] gender;
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Thus, the mention of "men" (*puruṣa*) in the phrase "he sacrifices" (*ālabhate*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).

For it has been clearly stated [in Vi. 9.1.14] that, because of a conflict with direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), there is in some cases a logical principle (*nyāya*) regarding the intentionality of gender (*liṅga-vivakṣā*).
Therefore, even when gender is intended, its sublation does not necessarily imply sublation in all instances. (Su.
3.8.2.12) Thus it is said.

Soma. Because of the word-meaning [principle], the cognition of a word leads one to infer its denotative power (8.1.12). Section on Indicative Power (Liṅga): 3355. Regarding the relative strength of indicative power (*liṅga*) and order (*krama*):
according to the Bhāṭṭa school, let it be granted that number is intended because it is the denotation of the word.

Recollection arises from both inferential signs (*liṅga*) and from the meaning (*artha*). However, even though the inferential sign is most worthy of being adopted, it is not intended [as a primary factor] because it is not the direct meaning of the word.
