this is a case of non-sublation of what was not previously established.

Or rather, that [gender] is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), because it is not perceived from words such as "lion" (*siṃha*) and the like; for, as stated in [Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī] 3.3.14 (p. 860), gender is common to all three genders and thus deviates from any specific gender. Nor is gender the meaning of the suffixes, according to the rule *liṅgopadeśaś ca tadarthavat* (1.2.14), precisely because of that same deviation. Nor is gender the meaning of the case-endings (*sup*), such as those in the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* (7.1.19) and others, nor of the feminine suffixes (*ṭāp*, etc.), nor of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). Thus is the explanation of the gender in the Sūtra.

Su. Pṛ. 112: Because of the deviation [of gender] even when applied to things like trees—which possess contrary gender—and because gender and sequence are established by authoritative instruction (*upadeśapramāṇatvāt*), they are absolutely useless.

Therefore, this is merely an instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*); it is not the case that "gender" (*liṅga*) is something to be obtained through incidental application (*codaka*). (Soma. 10.7.15) Thus, the meaning of any particular word is not intended to be expressed here.
Thus, there is a conflict between gender (*liṅga*) and word-order (*krama*).

This has been demonstrated in the *Sūtra* and the *Adhikaraṇa* regarding the established rule: when there is the cognition of a gender that cannot be otherwise accounted for—as in "siṃhaḥ" (lion) or "siṃhī" (lioness)—the principle applies: "But by the meaning, [the suffix] should be drawn back.

An example of this established case is as follows: just as gender is sometimes accepted through the addition of suffixes such as *ṭāp*, and sometimes not, so too in the case of the well-known sequence of permission and non-permission, one must state the forms of the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) such as "upahūtaḥ" and "upasṛtāḥ."
Therefore, these two mantras, "tat" and "havyasya," are recited in the tradition.

Due to the commonality of location, they apply to something possessing a certain number in one case, and in another case, they apply by means of the nominal stem's meaning alone; thus, they are obtained as a pair. In the case of the performance [indicated by] "upahūtaḥ," the requirement is fulfilled. However, where there is a sublation (bādha), there the use of that word occurs for the sake of grammatical correctness (sādhutva).

Having been authorized by the statement "of Upahavya," there is no such capacity [to be primary]; rather, as Maṇḍana says, "the gender of the root is intended to be significant," the status of being a subordinate element (śeṣatva) is the opposite.
For as long as [the application] is determined by position (*sthāna*), O Śaṃkara, the indicative power (*liṅga*) is thus held to be [the stronger authority].
Likewise regarding number (*saṃkhyā*):

when a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) is postulated by taking up the context (*prakaraṇa*), then the direct statement (*śruti*) is [determined] by the indicative power. In the section concerning indicative power (*liṅgādhikaraṇa*), the application (*viniyoga*) is established by first postulating a direct statement based on the indicative power—such as [the application of] the *vahis* [verse] to the *havina* [rite] for another [deity]. Thus, the application occurs in the primary sense through a direct statement whose indicative power has not been postulated.
3|3|16–2. Mīko., p. 2993: Only the sequence of the word (*padakrama*) is sublated.
This should be seen under the *avahinyāya* (the logic of the carrying-away) in the context of the performance of the ritual action following the inquiry (*paripraśna*).

Vārttika 3|2|1: Regarding the two disputants, whether [the verses] "parīrirasi" or "yuvā sutrāsāḥ" are applied according to their indicative power (*liṅga*) during the taking up of the portions for consumption (*bhakṣānvākya*), and so forth—having been divided [accordingly]—when the state of being an inquiry (*paripraśnātva*) is reached, there is a secondary application (*viniyoga*) based on the indicative power and the sense of the *sanīya* [verse] in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
VI. 3.2.1. There is also the question of inquiry:
"How is there no sublation of the sequence of the *manotā* belonging to the *āgneya*, and because of the absence of indicative marks (*liṅga*) for the permanent [rite]? (1.3.18.8).
If it is argued that, by virtue of a capable indicative mark, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) of the *savanīya* belonging to the *āgneya*.
No;

this is a more powerful scriptural aphorism (*śruti-sūtra*) intended to set aside the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of those [passages] that appear to be established by such signs as "na" and so forth—just as in the case of the statement "there might be a non-factual meaning due to the word. This is because, through the constant practice of established usage, the fixed agent [the *āgneya* offering] possesses the character of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatva*), thereby subverting the indicative marks imagined from the application of the action.

Because of the absence of a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) that serves as an indicator [of the agent], even though it was stated [by the opponent] that "the *manotā* belongs to Agni alone, even if the animal is dedicated to another deity"—since that mark is absent, and because what is otherwise possible becomes impossible, it must be understood as a mandatory injunction (*kārya*). For by this scriptural statement (*śruti*), the *manotā*, which would have been displaced from its context by the characteristic mark (*liṅga*), is restricted to all ritual duties. (Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 251). Thus, the *manotā* is precluded from being displaced.

Even though there are two deities, [the offering] belongs to a single deity alone; it is not merely by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and so forth that the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is set aside, for the inferred statements (*ānumānika*) such as *śruti* and the rest are sublated by the fact that the deity is Agni, resulting in its being performed after the *Āgneyī*.

Alternatively, there is sublation (*bādha*): just as in the case of black rice (*kṛṣṇala*), by virtue of its capacity, the phrase "one threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) sets aside the restrictive particle (*evakāra*) from its own context and establishes that [the action] must indeed be performed according to the sequence, because of the Vedic statement inferred from the location.
Bāla. pṛ. 146, vā. 3|3|14: it is determined that "the connection must be made."

Vārttika 3.3.7.4, p. 841. There is no independent authority for *liṅga* (indicative power) and the like without having postulated a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Vārttika 3.2.134. When there is a conflict between *liṅga* and *krama* (order), as in the case of the two [mantras] "upahūta" and "upahvayasva," which by their sequence of recitation belong respectively to the question and the answer, they are subject to sublation by *śruti* and the other means of proof.
When [the order] is understood through the sequence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is a reversal based on the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
Thus, when there is a contradiction with another sequence, the status of the means of valid cognition, the inferential marks, and so forth, remains established;
for even though a substance may be contradictory with the preceding [elements], [the sequence is not thereby sublated].

But in the case of being a remainder (*śeṣatva*), when there is a modification (*vikṛti*) dedicated to another deity in proximity, the consecration formula (*anumantraṇa*) recited for that [other] deity is set aside by the consecration formula dedicated to the deity [of the original sacrifice]. (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 3.3.17)

On page 360, in the passage beginning with “Because of the sequence of the indicative marks and the name, the recitation is connected with optional rites,” it is established that Indra and the other deities exist even outside of ritual action.
Because of the designation according to the sequence of the *liṅga* (indicative mark), the recitation is connected with optional rites (*kāmya*).
Here, the section containing the optional *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses serves as the illustration;
for example, the verses beginning with “O Indra and Agni, the luminous realms of heaven,” “The most excellent leaders,” “O Indra and Agni, the ninety forts,” and “He seized the vulture.”

And in the Brāhmaṇas, optional rites (kāmyā) are heard of here: "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"; "One desiring to drive away rivals should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"; "One desiring prosperity should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara"; "One who desires to overcome his enemies should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara"—and so forth.

Regarding these *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, a doubt arises: should this pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* dedicated to Indra and Agni be employed in every ritual action for Indra and Agni whatsoever, or only in this specific optional (*kāmyā*) sacrifice to Indra and Agni? The same applies to the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for Vaiśvānara.

Thus, having established through general rules and exceptions (*utsarga-apavāda*) that indicative power (*liṅga*) is the means of application, it is now considered here how the applicative force of indicative power depends upon other means of proof (*pramāṇa*). This is the specific point under investigation.

Herein is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): although here the rituals such as those dedicated to Indra-Agni and others are recited in a specific sequence, and in that very same sequence the pairs of optional *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses associated with those deities and bearing the designation "optional" (*kāmya*) are also heard;
nevertheless, since both the sequence and the designation apply to them, it is proper that the application of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses follows that very sequence.

Nevertheless, because *liṅga* (indicative power) is stronger than *samākhyā* (name) by virtue of its sequence, and because *liṅga*—possessing the capacity to manifest Indra, Agni, and so forth—sublates both *liṅgakrama* (sequence by indicative power) and *samākhyā*, it is proper that the *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses should be subsidiary only to the duties pertaining to deities such as Indra and Agni.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
this would indeed be so if *liṅga* were the applicator independently of a general connection.
For *liṅga* (indicative power) is the capacity to manifest fire and so forth;

however, an application (*viniyoga*) in the form of fire and so forth is not possible, because that would result in futility. But such an application is possible in the form of the sacrifice’s *apūrva* (unseen potency).
Moreover, the nature of the sacrifice as an *apūrva* cannot be attained without a general connection [to a specific fruit].

Therefore, where a sentence or a context exists that establishes such a general connection, it is only in dependence upon that [sentence or context] that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) possesses the power of application (*viniyojakatva*).

In this case, however, since there is an absence of both syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), if there were no dependence upon order (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*), then the indicative power (*liṅga*) would not have any means of application at all. Therefore, by means of order, the general connection of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses with the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) dedicated to Indra-Agni and others will be stated. In that regard, there arises an expectation for a specific object—namely, "performing what does one attain this?"—and thus [the verses] are applied to the manifestation of that which is inherent in the desired result belonging to the sacrificer.

Furthermore, where even after a sequential connection with the general [context] has been established, there remains a requirement—since a mark (*liṅga*) that is common to both the effect and the state is ambiguous and thus alone incapable of effecting application—in such cases, the name (*samākhyā*) is also resorted to for the sake of establishing the mark. For example, in the ritual dedicated solely to Agni, the *ṛc* verse addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*) is recited in sequence; and by its mark, the function is understood to be the illumination of the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and the illumination of the fire (*agni*).
In this regard, if the designation "yājyā" were not relied upon, then, due to its position as the first [verse], it would serve solely to illuminate the *samit* (fuel-stick) oblation.
However, the designation "yājyā" is indeed intended; by means of it, the mantra's capacity to illuminate the deity to whom the sacrifice is offered (*ijyānamāna-devatā*) is postulated.
Even though the capacity for denotation does not pertain to the deity itself, but rather to the mere generic form common to all sacrifices.

For instance, in accordance with the capacity [of the mantra] for the sacrifice determined by its name (*samākhyā*), it is applied by means of its indicative power (*liṅga*) specifically to the manifestation of the deity being worshipped.
As it has been said: "The status of being for the sake of a desired result is not evident as long as no connection has been established" (Vākyapadīya, p. 331).
Therefore, in all cases, the application of a mantra based on its indicative power (*liṅga*) is necessarily preceded by a general connection.
The purpose [of this discussion] is as stated in the previous section.

As for the Sūtra: the meaning is that the recitation of mantras connected to the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) occurs only through indicative power, sequence (*krama*), and name (*samākhyā*), and does not apply everywhere.
[The opponent says: "It is [the order] of the sequence; the recitation is joined with optional rites (kāmya) because of the indication (liṅga), sequence (krama), and name (samākhyāna).

'One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni'; 'One whose kinsmen have departed should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni'—thus the optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi) are prescribed."

Thus, in the *Kāmyayājyānuvākyākāṇḍa*, the pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the sacrifice to Indra and Agni—beginning with "indrāgnī rocanā divaḥ"—is recited. In this regard, there arises the question: must this very pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for Indra and Agni be used in every ritual action dedicated to Indra and Agni, or is this pair restricted to the first mentioned sacrifice to Indra and Agni, while other pairs are used elsewhere? This is the section concerning the relative weight of indicative power (*liṅga*), order (*krama*), and name (*samākhyā*). [The conclusion is that] based on the indicative power (*liṅga*), the order (*krama*), and the name (*samākhyā*), this pair of verses applies specifically to that particular sacrifice. Therefore, it is not mandatory that this same pair be used in all rites for Indra and Agni; rather, it belongs only to the specific rite mentioned in the context. Thus ends the section on the relative authority of indicative power, order, and name. (Sūtra 3.3.5–7)

In this inquiry, the question is whether the pairs of *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* mantras—associated with specific deities and designated as "optional" (*kāmya*)—should, by virtue of their indicative power (*liṅga*), override the sequence and apply to any ritual action for those respective deities regardless of order; or whether they should be applied to those very optional sacrifices (*iṣṭi*) according to the sequence in which the rituals such as the *aindrāgna* and others were originally prescribed.
Regarding this inquiry, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

From the sequence supported by indicative power (*liṅga*), and from the name (*samākhyāna*) supported by indicative power, the recitation—the recitation in the section of *kāmya-yājyānuvākyā* mantras—should be connected as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) specifically to the sacrifices performed for specific desires (*kāmyeṣṭi*).
Therefore, its application (*viniyoga*) is only in the *kāmyeṣṭis*. Now, why are both "from sequence" and "from name" taught? Because there exist therein the *pāthikṛtīya* and *prātaḥpatīya* rites.
This applies both to the function of the *sāmidhenī* verses and to the function of the *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses.
If only "by means of indicative power (*liṅga*) and order (*krama*)" were stated, then their application even to the function of the *sāmidhenīs* would occur by virtue of indicative power alone.

Therefore, for what purpose are both indicative power and order mentioned? [It is so that] they may all be applied specifically to the function of the *yājyā-anuvākyās*, while their application to the *sāmidhenīs* remains established [by other means].

The Bhāṣya states: "Just as, when the sequence has passed by [the *abhidāruṇī* sacrifice] which was desired, and the *soma-arādi* [sacrifices] have arrived, those [verses] marked with the word 'manas' are called *dhāyyā*s among the *sāmidhenī*s; therefore, both [the *manonka* and the *dhāyyā*] must be designated. Regarding this, the verses beginning with "Agni is placed in front" (*agnir hotā purohitaḥ*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.23.16), whose mark is the word 'manas', and the verses "O you who are born of the *pṛyuja*" (*pṛyujāḥ*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.12.5) and "Him, the one who is pressed" (*taṃ savādhaḥ*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.12.6), which possess the words 'pṛyuja' and 'java', are employed for the function of the *sāmidhenī*s by virtue of their indicative power (*liṅga*) because they are *dhāyyā*s in the *yājyā-sāmidhenī* section; this is stated in the sūtra "On account of indicative power, order, and name" (*liṅgakramasamākhyānāt*).

Sūtra 12.31: From the *liṅga*—which consists in the capacity to illuminate the meaning—the mantra’s status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) pertains solely to its own expressed object, and not to the status of being a subordinate element by way of that [object], because the status of being a subordinate element is established merely from the capacity to illuminate the meaning, even in the absence of an actual performance.

Therefore, since the general relationship of subsidiary and principal has been established by means of the season, the specific door, and the mantra and tantra, there arises an expectation for a door as to which one fulfills the status of being a subsidiary that has already been performed. In response to this expectation, it was determined in the section beginning with "On account of indicative power, order, and name" (Soma. 10.5.8) that indicative power (*liṅga*) is the authority for the mere status of subsidiarity through the door characterized by the meaning of the mantra's primary expression.

In cases such as "O Indra and Agni, both of you... (*ubhā vām indrāgnī*) and so forth, where a general connection is established through both sequence (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*)—as in the injunction "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni" (*aindrāgnaṃ ekādaśakapālaṃ nirvapet*)—the application (*viniyoga*) occurs only there, and not in every ritual action merely related to Indra and Agni, because the general connection does not exist in those other cases. Thus concludes the section concerning the relative strength of indicative power (*liṅga*), sequence (*krama*), and name (*samākhyā*).
This is the Section on Indicative Power, Sequence, and Name.
The application of the mantras contained in the sections of the *yājyānuvākyās* for optional rites (*kāmya*) is restricted solely to those optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*).
Because of the designation according to the sequence of the *liṅga* (indicative mark), the recitation is connected with optional rites (*kāmya*).
Commentary: Here, the section containing the optional *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses serves as the example.
Such verses as “O Indra and Agni, the luminaries of heaven,” “O Indra and Agni, you who have shattered the ninety forts,” and so forth, are the examples.

There are also other optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*): "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"; "One [desiring to overcome] rivals should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"; "One who has a desire should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara"; "One who is suffering from a disease should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara"—and so forth.

Regarding these *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, there is a doubt: should every ritual action for Indra and Agni be accompanied by this pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Indra and Agni, or should they be used only in this specific optional (*kāmyā*) sacrifice to Indra and Agni?
The same applies to the two verses for Vaiśvānara;
the same applies everywhere.

What, then, is the prima facie position? Whatever belongs to Indra-Agni, whether it be an *iṣṭi* sacrifice or an *iṣṭīya* offering, in all those cases there ought to be a pair of *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Indra-Agni.
Why?
[One might argue: "But surely the sequence (*krama*) and the name (*samākhyāna*) will serve as the qualifiers."
True;
nevertheless, *liṅga* (indicative power) is capable of subverting both *krama* (order) and *samākhyā* (name).
This being the position reached, we reply:
From the indication of the sequence by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*), it is understood that these two alone are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras for the optional sacrifice;
for whatever is the sequence of these ritual acts, that same sequence applies to these *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras.
Therefore, they are subordinate to those very acts.
But was it not said that indicative mark (liṅga) is more powerful?
True, this is so;
however, in this case, name (samākhyā) is more powerful.
And this [result] does not belong to these optional rites (*kāmyakarma*).
Why?
Because [it is established] even without a designation (*samākhyā*).

In the section concerning indicative mark (liṅga), order (krama), and name (samākhyā), it is not even known that these [verses] are *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* [invocatory and offering verses]; how then could they be the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for distinct rituals? Furthermore, this name [of theirs] indicates that they are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* only for the optional (*kāmya*) rites, not for all.

If the designation [of these mantras] were not established, they would not possess the status of being *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. If it were to depend on the [general] beginning [of the section], then it would apply only to the optional (*kāmya*) rites;
for it is thus designated as the "Section of Optional *Yājyā* and *Anuvākyā* Verses."
Now, for what purpose are both taught—namely, "by means of the indicative mark" (*liṅga*) and "by means of the sequence" (*krama*), as well as "by means of the designation" (*samākhyāna*)?
In that context, there exists the ritual action pertaining to Pāthikṛt and the ritual action pertaining to Vratapati;
furthermore, there exists the function of the *sāmidhenī* verses as well as the function of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses.

If it were stated merely that [the application is] "by virtue of indicative power and order" (*liṅgakramāt*), then those verses would be applied by indicative power even to the function of the *sāmidhenīs*.

Now, for what purpose are both indicative power and order mentioned? [Otherwise], all [verses] would be applied only to the function of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, and there would be no application to the *sāmidhenīs*.

Furthermore, when the purpose of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses is set aside by means of direct designation (*samākhyāna*) and the sequence of indicators (*liṅga-krama*), their application to the *sāmidhenī* verses becomes established.

For example, although the *manasvatī* verses are mentioned in the sequence of the *āgnivāruṇī* sacrifice, they are stated to be used as *sāmidhenī* verses when the *somāraudra* sacrifice has not yet arrived.
Likewise, two verses beginning with "pṛthupājāḥ" are designated as *dhyāya* (to be meditated upon).
Therefore, both must be specified.

Or rather: in whatever order the optional rites (kāmyakarma) such as the Āgneya and others are prescribed, in that very same order are the pairs of *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* mantras dedicated to those same deities and designated by the name "optional" (*kāmya*).

Do these [mantras], disregarding the sequence, apply to any rite dedicated to those deities on the basis of their indicative power (*liṅga*), or are they applied according to that sequence specifically to those optional sacrifices (*iṣṭi*)?
For this [example] is cited as an illustration for the purpose of conceptualizing a specific qualification from the Sūtra.

In that case, although the status of being for all purposes (*sarvārthatva*) is initially suggested by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), since the role of the *agnīdh* priest is established, it is held that "capacity (*sāmarthya*) does not function as a means of application (*viniyojaka*) when there is no connection with a ritual (*kratu*).
And by whatever [means] there is a connection with a ritual, by that its status as being for the sake of a desired result (*kāmyārthatā*) is made clear."
For the *liṅga* (indicative power) would indeed establish a connection with a deity;
however, there is no result in [the mantra] being merely endowed with that intrinsic form.

Whether it is a connection with a sacrifice or a connection with a deity associated with it, neither of these can be established by such [a *liṅga*] alone when it is devoid of syntactical context (*vākya*), thematic context (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not known in which specific part [of the ritual] the application lies;
therefore, one must necessarily rely upon the name (samākhyā) for the time being.
For by means of that, both the connection with the sacrifice and the specific function are established.
When it is said, "it goes elsewhere," there is a connection with the sacrifice.
And since that [offering] is for the purpose of double presentation, a specific effect must necessarily follow.
Consequently, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that "it is connected with whichever [deity] in whatever manner," it is understood that it belongs to that deity.
But even so, it is not established.
How is it not established? Because by this title, "The Section on Optional Yājyās" (*kāmya-yājyākāṇḍa*), its application to the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) is fixed.
Furthermore, even if the title were to establish a connection with sacrifice in general, it would still be sublated by the stronger order (*krama*).

Therefore, this designation is appropriate only for the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*). [Objection: For what purpose are both [the name and the indicative mark] stated in the Sūtra? [Response: Because the status of being the subject matter of the optional sacrifices is established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) supported by the order (*krama*).
Alternatively, one might think that everything is established by the mere fact that this section of *yājyā* verses is designated as "optional" (*kāmya*).
To this, it is replied:

True; in the case of the offerings to Indra and others, the application would indeed be established by indication (*liṅga*) and sequence (*krama*) alone, because these *ṛc* verses function as *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, and thus cannot be applied otherwise.

Regarding those rites such as the Āgneya, which are enjoined by such injunctions as "to the Āgneya, to Vratapati," there are two positions [for the verses]: being *sāmidhenīs* and being *yājyā-anuvākyās*.
Due to similarity and because of the authority [of the text], there is an expectation for the *sāmidhenīs* toward two *ṛcs*.

In that case, if the designation (*samākhyā*) "yājyā" were not established as the means of application (*viniyojikā*), then [the application] would be possible for the *sāmidhenīs* as well through indicative power (*liṅga*) and order (*krama*).
Since there is no reason for bypassing the first [possibility], the application would naturally fall upon that very [first] one;
however, that is set aside by the name (*samākhyā*).
Therefore, let that alone suffice, and there is no need for indicative power (*liṅga*) and sequence (*krama*).
This is explained as follows:
If, in this context, the *iṣṭi* were intended exclusively for the Āgneya [offering], then it would indeed be so.

However, here, in the sequence of a ritual action dedicated to another deity—which is already supplied with its own appropriate *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses—those *ṛc* verses belonging to the Āgneya that are observed, if they were applied solely by means of their name (*samākhyā*), would be employed for the function of the *yājyā*.
And there is no possibility [of such application], because the indicative power (*liṅga*) has been set aside by those two [other] indicatives;
therefore, there would be no application at all.

However, when the application occurs through those two [indicatives] once the operation of the name (*samākhyā*) has ceased—by means of indicative power and order alone—the employment [of the mantra] in the *sāmidhenī* verses becomes established.

He shows that subject: having recited the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses for the *iṣṭi* dedicated to Agni-Vāruṇa, when the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses for Soma-Rudra-Manor-dau-manasidhana have arrived, the verses of Manu are recited.
It is said that these [verses] become the *sāmidhenīs* in meditation (*dhyāna*).
The same should be understood regarding the *pṛthupāja* verses as well.

Even there, because the [mantras] are recited after the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* by bypassing the sequence of the preceding *sāmidhenī* verses, it is understood that they belong to the subsequent [verses].

Furthermore, if the sequence were not established, then by the mere force of indicative mark (*liṅga*) and name (*samākhyā*), the first pair addressed to Indra-Agni would be applied to the second verse, and the second pair to the first.
This constitutes the section concerning the conflict between indicative mark, sequence, and name.

Regarding the section on Indicative Power (liṅga), Order (krama), and Name (samākhyā): when order exists alongside name, order takes precedence because it establishes the connection with the ritual sacrifice more quickly; thus, indicative power, being in closer proximity to that [order], postulates a direct scriptural statement (śruti), and so the application according to order is observed.
Therefore, it is correctly aphorized as follows:

In the section on Mantras, there is a doubt: should mantras be applied everywhere wherever their semantic capacity exists, setting aside the constraints of *krama* (order) and *samākhyā* (name), or should they be applied only to those rites for which they are intended by that specific location, such as the *kāmyeṣṭi* sacrifices?

For this purpose, one must determine whether the *liṅga* (semantic capacity) alone is an independent means of application like *śruti* (direct statement) and the rest, or whether its authority regarding the specific function arises only after depending upon the means of knowledge that establish the mantra's connection with a particular ritual (*kratu*).

In this regard, they maintain that even an independent indicative mark (*liṅga*) possesses the power of application; however, since that [indicative mark] is weaker than both position (*krama*) and name (*ākhyā*), it would follow that [the mantra] serves all purposes.
For a mantra, which is encompassed by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*), must necessarily have a purpose through its meaningfulness.

In this regard, the notion arises that since this [mantra] reveals the visible purpose solely from its own verbal form, it must therefore be employed here. It is not the case that the manifestation of the object to be employed is the sole purpose; rather, by means of that [manifestation], the unseen purpose (apūrva) and other such goals related to it are also understood from that very source—what need is there for another means of knowledge here?
And that [application] is more powerful due to direct statement (*śruti*) and name (*ākhyā*);
thus, by virtue of its presence, the *liṅga* (indicative power) has a universal application.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"It is true that there is a dependence on a purpose for the mantra; such a purpose is possible [for it].
For even if a purpose is required, it cannot be obtained through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor is any purpose established merely by the fact of being understood."
It is understood through the capacity [of the mantra] that its purpose is merely to reveal the form of the fire and so forth;
yet there is no fruit in revealing only that much.

Furthermore, the purpose of revealing the form of the means for the prior sacrificial act (*karmapūrva*) is not established by capacity alone, without even the authority of a direct syntactical connection (*samanvaya*).

However, in the case of the statement "the qualities are the *pradībhāga*," because the word *bhāga* denotes a sacrifice (that is, it indicates a sacrifice), the connection with the ritual (*kratu*) is established;
this we shall explain [at 3.3.15].
Nor is there any deviation from the ritual in the case of Agni, Sūrya, and so forth, because they possess the nature of deities (*devatā*).
By which [means] a sacrifice (*kratu*) might be undertaken.

Since that [existence] is present even in the world, and since Indra and the others are understood from mantras, *arthavādas*, and so forth to be engaged in ritual action—even outside of the ritual—because they are heard of as lords of all things and as guardians of the world (*lokapāla*), and because they are presented as such in all [scriptures], it is understood that Indra and the others are possible even beyond the ritual; thus, the meaning is that their existence in the world is established.
Therefore, a means of knowledge for the connection with a sacrifice must also be required.
There is no authority other than sequence (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*) for the section on mantras;
and since these two apply only to the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), their application (*viniyoga*) is restricted to those alone, not to other rites.
Nor is the application of these mantras to the optional sacrifices based on the requirement for *śara* grass, because the recollection [of the grass] can be accomplished by other means as well.
Because it absolutely does not depend upon mantras.

However, where there is absolute dependence, there the status of being for that purpose (tādarthya) exists even by virtue of mere capacity, as in the case of the knowledge of the meaning [of a mantra] having the nature of an injunction for performance;
for without that, the performance is not accomplished.
And just as the knowledge of the Self is useful for the performance of rites that have results pertaining to the future world,
so too, because of the absence of any absolute [incompatibility], there is no application [of the mantras] to other rites.

However, by means of order (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*), they are applied as *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses respectively and according to their names, specifically to the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*).
Whether [the verses] are applicable or not applicable, their application in the *sāmidhenī* and other rites occurs through the indicative power (*liṅga*) accompanied by sequential order (*krama*).
(And "inapplicability" occurs in some cases due to the absence of the capacity to manifest the deity of the primary sacrifice (*pradhānadevatā*).

For example, in the sequence of the *Soma-iṣṭi*, although the *mānavī* verses recited in that order are incapable of manifesting the deity of the primary sacrifice, they are applied because of their plurality. In another case of inapplicability, for instance, regarding the verses beginning with "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ," which are recited in the sequence of the *iṣṭi* "one should offer the *pṛthupāja* cake to Agni Rathodhā," [they are inapplicable because they do not manifest that specific deity].)

Kau: Having previously established that verbal testimony (*śruti*) depends upon other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its production, the immediate connection (*anantara-saṃgati*) here is incidental (*prāsaṅgikī*), as it proceeds from the determination of inferential mark (*liṅga*) as well.

Soma: As for the meaning of the Sūtra: because of the respective inferential marks (*liṅga*) and because of the name (*samākhyāna*), the *kāmyeṣṭi* sacrifices are measured by the *Indra* and other sections (*kāṇḍa*).
Vi: "The *aindra* and other optional (*kāmya*) *yājyā* verses have also been declared in their proper sequence."
Regarding those [verses] in the two sections (*kāṇḍa*), there is a rule for their application according to their indicative mark (*liṅga*); as it is said:
"The indicative mark is more powerful than both sequence (*krama*) and name (*samākhyā*);
therefore, even in the absence of desire, that [mark] prevails everywhere in the application. This is the exception.
From the traditional designation (*samākhyāna*), there is a connection with the *kāṇḍa*; in the case of the sacrifices (*iṣṭi*) [of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*], their application follows the sequence.
The capacity [to effect results] depends solely upon the deity, being restricted exclusively to those sacrifices performed for specific desires (*kāmya*).
[Bhāṭṭa: In the *kāmyeṣṭikāṇḍa*, there are sacrifices for specific desires having Indra and others as their deities.

The section concerning the relative strength of indicative mark (*liṅga*), order (*krama*), and name (*samākhyāna*) [establishes that] the application of mantras is justified by their capacity for manifestation.

Nor should it be argued that, because [mantras] would be purposeless when applied literally to those similar to Indra, they must also depend upon the ritual action in order to signify the status of being a means to the *apūrva*.
This is because the definition [of a deity] is applicable through the possibility of deviation in the act of offering to deities such as Indra and Agni;

or, even if there were such deviation, since it is possible to exclude worldly fire and the like, the fact that [the deity] has the *apūrva* (transcendental result) as its purpose is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).
Therefore, by the mere indicative mark (*liṅga*), the sequence (*krama*) and the name (*samākhyāna*) are set aside.

This being the case, since the indicative power (*liṅga*)—which consists of semantic competency (*yogyatā*)—cannot function as a means of application (*viniyojaka*) in the absence of a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*), and because all mantras have their requirements satisfied by being applied [to their respective rites], it is not possible for them to serve all purposes based on indicative power alone. Therefore, through sentence-meaning (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), order (*krama*), and other such means of knowledge that establish a general connection, the specific requirements of each mantra are fulfilled; thus, the distinction regarding the sublation of indicative power lies precisely in the specific connection with this or that particular sacrifice (*kratu*) via its respective medium (*dvāra*).

Nor should it be said that there is a sublation of context (*prakaraṇa*) and the other criteria by the *taumīya* sentence; for those [criteria] which concern specific mantras are deliberated upon at the time of the recitation of the mantras, when there is a requirement for the purpose of the mantra—[a time] when they have not yet ascended to the status of indication (*liṅga*), sentence (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), or name (*samākhyā*). "The power inherent in all constituent parts is designated as indication (*liṅga*)."
It was stated previously that a sentence is merely a collection of words.
The expectancy regarding "how it is to be done" (itikartavyatākāṅkṣā) constitutes the *prakriyā* (contextual procedure), and that is of two kinds;
furthermore, *krama* (sequence) is of two kinds, distinguished as textual (pāṭha) and performative (anuṣṭhāna).
Experts in the Bhāṣya know that there are four types of application: etymological designation, worldly nomenclature, and likewise Vedic nomenclature; this much constitutes the means of application.
In that context, the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra "vahnimantra" depends upon the *prakaraṇa* (context), because it lacks the qualification of being a means for the unestablished (*apūrva*).

Regarding these [mantras], the power of indicative mark (*liṅga*) functions as an applicator only in cases where a visible result (*dṛṣṭa*) is possible, not in cases where an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*) is required.
And just as with direct statement (*śruti*), here too, within the *prakaraṇa*, [the application] occurs for the sake of establishing the specific status of the means.

Moreover, there is this further distinction: in the case of a mantra being applied through its indicative power (*liṅga*), a connection with a sacrifice must first be established by some means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) prior to that application;

for in the absence of such a connection, the application by indicative power itself would not be possible. This has been demonstrated therein [in the *Tantravārttika*] regarding indicative power, order, and name.

As for application by syntactical connection (*vākya*), however, it has been explained in detail at the very occasion of the discussion on application by direct assertion (*śruti*), for the sake of distinguishing it from the others.

Regarding the indicators (liṅga), the sentence (vākya), and the context (prakaraṇa): first, there is the previous alternative. Thereafter, since the animal sacrifice of the Dīkṣā (daikṣa-paśu) lacks any natural expectancy (*svābhāvikākāṅkṣā*), the very existence of an expectancy for the procedure of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-vidhyanta*) is inferred by the observation of the *prayāja* and other such elements; thus, it is not established that it is a modification (*vikṛti*). Consequently, an investigation into its specific archetype (*prakṛti-viśeṣa*) is not tenable.

When only the general form [of a rite] is perceived, there is no consideration regarding its specific archetype (*prakṛti*), because it is already complete in itself. However, when its status as a modification (*vikṛti*) is inferred through the observation of elements such as the *prayāja* offerings, then there arises an occasion for inquiry, since the determination of its specific archetype is precisely what is required.

Nor should it be argued that in the sūtra "And in the case of the animal sacrifice, because of the observation of indicative marks" (*paśau ca liṅgadarśanāt*), the purpose is merely to establish—by refuting the theory of a new transcendental result (*apūrva*) for the animal sacrifice—that the animal sacrifice follows the same procedure as the previous one (the *savanīya*), and that the question to be deliberated is simply whether or not certain ritual properties (*dharma*) are extended from somewhere; for in the first instance, the reason for the inquiry concerns the extension of specific properties.

And this [section] is not concluded such that an inquiry into the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the *darvihoma* would be undertaken; therefore, only the transfer of specific details (*viśeṣātideśa*) is considered.
Thus, the author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates precisely the deliberation on the transfer of specific details:
"In the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), are the rites of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* performed, or those of the Soma sacrifice?"

Even in the Siddhānta, having raised the objection regarding the indicative mark (*liṅga*) as a means of bringing about [the application], it is stated that [application occurs] "due to the similarity of the injunction" (*codanāsāmānyāt*). And that [similarity] is possible only when the status of being a modification (*vikṛti*) is established in a general sense, not otherwise. Now, if—[in order to avoid this fault]—one were to assume, by the observation of the indicative mark, a mere expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and then [conclude] that there is an extension [of details] due to the similarity of the injunction, then the same objection would apply: since one would have to assume an expectancy based on the capacity of the instruction regarding the *abhikramaṇa* and the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the case of the *prayāja*s and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of the entire Soma ritual procedure applying [to them]. Thus, the challenge remains equal.

This objection must be refuted as follows: it is appropriate to speak of "unmanifestness" (*avyaktatva*) regarding those sacrifices for which there is no deity specified by a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), a dative case ending, or the wording of a mantra;
however, since the *prayāja* offerings and others are connected with deities through the wording of their respective mantras and so forth, they do not possess unmanifestness.

If, on the other hand, "unmanifestness" were defined simply as that for which no deity exists in its originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), then it would follow that even the *upāṃśuyāja* is unmanifest.

For, having deliberated that "it must belong to a deity for that purpose," [the author] will later state the connection with a deity based on the wording of the mantra: "Or it may be Viṣṇu, because of the act of saving.

Furthermore, since the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice also expresses the deity by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in the injunction "He takes the draught for Indra and Vāyu" (*aindravāyavam gṛhṇāti*), it would not be indistinct.
It is not the case that the deity is enjoined in the sacrifice by the secondary derivative, but rather in the act of taking; therefore, there is no fault.

Furthermore, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the *saumika* (Soma-sacrifice) details to the *prayāja* offerings and the like, because of the impossibility [of such an application]. For it is heard in the ancient traditions that the completion of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, together with their subsidiaries, must occur within two days; therein, the common elements (*tantra*) such as the *paristaraṇa* and the *hastāvanejana* are to be commenced and concluded only once. In that context, if the entire sequence of the *saumika* rites—from the *dīkṣaṇīyā* to the *udavasānīyā*—were to be extended to each individual *prayāja* offering, then while that sequence was being performed for each one, there would be a displacement of the time for the principal sacrifice.

Nor is simultaneous performance possible by way of *tantra* (common procedure) or *prasaṅga* (incidental application), because of the difference in time and because there is no injunction for them within the middle of the *tantra*. For the *prayāja* offerings conclude before the principal sacrifice, while the *anuyāja* offerings follow after it;
even further removed from them, separated by subtle requirements and other factors, are the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

This being the case, there can be no extension (*tantra*) of the Soma sacrifice's ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, as there is in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites within the *iṣṭi* ritual procedure.
Nor can it be asserted that one may perform some auxiliary elements while omitting others according to one's capacity, because there is no specific knowledge of such a distinction.

Therefore, there is no extension of the Soma sacrifice's ritual procedure to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; consequently, this [Soma sacrifice] itself possesses its own intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).
How, then, is it maintained that the *videvana* (gambling) and other such acts do not constitute auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the *abhiṣecanīya* (consecration rite)?
Because the requirement of the *abhiṣecanīya* is already fulfilled by the very *dharma*s transferred by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), the rite reaches its conclusion beforehand.

For, as the author of the Bhāṣya will state in the *Gṛhamedhīyādhikaraṇa*, modifications (*vikṛti*s) have a pre-established need for assistance; therefore, they first connect with the archetypal elements (*prākṛta*) which are situated nearby before connecting with others.

In this way, even for a modification (*vikāra*) that has reached its conclusion at the end of the night, its non-conclusion must be assumed on account of the proximate subsidiary elements (*aṅga*); from that, a sequence (*krama*) arises.
Even among modifications, that which is recited in the midst of the archetypal subsidiaries (*prākṛtāṅga*)—such as the *āmanahoma*—is included within the context (*prakaraṇa*).

If that is so, then for the gambling and other such acts (*videvanādi*) performed at the time of the *māhendra-stotra* in the midst of the archetypal subsidiaries, there would be an extension (*prasaṅga*) to the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice by virtue of the context.

Their occurrence there is not possible; rather, for those [rites] that have arisen elsewhere as subsidiaries of the Rājasūya understood from the context, there is a displacement [to this point], since it is prescribed at the time of the stotra. Therefore, it is not a subsidiary of the Abhiṣecanīya.

As for the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) of the *rājasūya*, the group of sacrifices beginning from the *pavitra* and ending with the *kṣatrasya dhṛti* is grasped by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) within its own sentence and presented as the instrument (*karaṇa*) through the principle of *tantra*. Thus, whatever archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiary (*aṅga*) exists prior to the *pavitra*, and whatever exists up to the *kṣatrasya dhṛti*, all that constitutes the archetypal subsidiary of the *rājasūya*; the gambling (*videvana*) and other rites situated in the middle of these fall within the scope of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, even if one accepts the existence of a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), there is no fault whatsoever.
Context is of two kinds.
In that context, it is the purpose of the meditation alone that serves as the remote instrument of application (*viniyojaka*), and not the substances and so forth, nor even the incidental factors;
for their application occurs through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means according to their respective roles, while the context (*prakaraṇa*) is merely an auxiliary.

Even in the case of mantras, they are not grasped by the context in their own form, but rather the context applies the verbal cognition of the sentence-meaning produced by them—which is of the nature of an action; and that too is [based on] indicative power (*liṅga*).

It has been demonstrated in the *Mantrādhikaraṇa* (the section on mantras) by the passage beginning with "The cognition of the sentence-meaning [is] fulfilled" (*vākyārthapratyayasya kṛtārthaḥ*) that [the mantra] functions through the combination of indicative power (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), and context (*prakaraṇa*).
However, for those who maintain that the effect is something unprecedented (apūrva) and falls within the scope of the sentence,
the status of the *prayāja* and other such rites as being auxiliary to the *darśa* sacrifice is not established.

In their view, it is held that the *apūrva*—which is the primary object (*pradhāna*) to be accomplished, denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), and in which all other constituent elements are subordinate—is conveyed by the sentence as a whole. According to this position, the status of the *prayāja* and other such rites as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to the *darśa* sacrifice and others would not be established. Why? Because "the primary object indeed does not require connection with another primary object."
By means of which there may be a connection of the subsidiary apūrva with the principal apūrva.

According to the logical principle of *anvaya*, the *apūrva* of the *prayāja* offerings does not become subordinate to another effect; rather, being its own primary element, it does not require any other purpose.
And since it is independent, there is no connection with the *darśapūrṇamāsa-apūrva*, even though they are recited in conjunction.

As for what has been said by someone here—that the sentences concerning the *prayāja* and so forth, being recited in proximity to the *apūrva* associated with the qualified injunction (*sādhikāra*), do not lead to the understanding of a separate *apūrva*—how can that be possible? For it would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), like the case of *avaghāta* (threshing) and similar acts.
However, [the words] present the very nature of the sacrifice as qualified by its own constituent factors (*kāraka*).

Consequently, since the mantra— which does not have anything else as its object— becomes purposeful through its connection with the prescriptive injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*), which constitutes its purpose, the investigation into qualification (*adhikāra-vicāra*) becomes possible.
Even when a doubt exists, a subsequent determination through contradiction occurs even in the case of the *samit* sacrifice and others.
If one should think that there is no initial doubt regarding the *samit* and other [offerings], [the following applies].

Rather, due to proximity, there arises the misconception that this [injunction] pertains solely to the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the primary rite; because there is no contradiction in that regard, it is apprehended by the grasper [the injunction].

Nevertheless, that [misconception] is set aside by the observation of contradictions, just as when a specific word (*pratipada*) has been determined through the logic of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) to be included within the context (*prakaraṇa*), its application is revoked upon the appearance of a contradiction with direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) according to the logic of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Furthermore, if another injunction were not understood [in these cases], just as in the case of threshing and so forth, then why would it not be accepted that words such as "sacrifice" occurring in sentences like "one desiring wisdom" (prajñākāma) denote their own meaning—which culminates in the primary apūrva—just as words such as "threshes" occurring in their respective sentences do?
For this is the reasoning there:
that these [words] must denote their own meaning as connected with the primary apūrva.
That being the case, that which is understood as non-distinct from the very act of origination could not be the object of another *niyoga* (injunction),
because it is impossible for two effects to be related to a single [subject].
For it is not possible to cognize a single entity as simultaneously related to two distinct effects.
And this is understood: a word is not able to express its own meaning within another injunction.

Therefore, if it were to convey another injunction, then—due to the absence of contradiction—the word *ājya*, occurring in the context of the *samidh* [offering], would possess the quality of expressing its own meaning as connected to the primary apūrva, just like the word *avahanti*.

On the other hand, if it does not convey [another injunction], then, given the conflict with direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the acceptance by the grasper (*grāhaka*) is untenable. Thus, this is a rope with a noose at both ends.

Now, in the case of the first performer, even where there is the denotation of its own meaning as connected with the *apūrva* of the primary injunction (*adhikārāpūrva*), that [denotation] is subsequently sublated by the comprehension of another injunction; therefore, even the "grasping by the recipient" (*grāhakagrahaṇa*) must be sublated because it contradicts the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Consequently, the status of being a name for the *praiṣa* (direction) and so forth is not possible in any way whatsoever. Furthermore, as for the statement, "that which is not enjoined does not become an auxiliary (*aṅga*)," this was said with reference to the prohibition against speaking untruthfully (*anṛtavadana-pratiṣedha*).

However, regarding the statement that [the injunction] pertains to the subordinate (ārādupakāraka) auxiliaries because it is an injunction for the recitation of mantras when they are being produced (*jajñyamāna*), this was said merely by considering the literal meaning of the words.

Otherwise, how could the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) have stated—specifically with reference to the subordinate auxiliaries in the passage "In the case of their omission, the rites [are to be performed]"—that the human effort is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*)? Thus, it cannot be explained in that way. How, then, should it be explained? It should be explained thus: the mention of the injunction (*vidhi*) refers to the application (*viniyoga*), while the other [mention] refers to the performance (*prayoga*). This is how it must be interpreted.
For indeed, in the absence of an injunction (*vidhi*), the status of the *samit* and other [subsidiaries] as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) cannot be established.

But is it not the case that, even without an injunction, the status of the *samit* and others is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*) just as by direct statement (*śruti*), as in the case of "one should sacrifice with soma" (*yajeta... somena*)?

Even though there is no separate injunction for the *soma* beyond the verbal root *yaji* (to sacrifice), its status is established by the primary injunction itself, since it is employed as an instrument by the instrumental case ending.

If it is argued that, likewise, when the *prajāyas* and other such elements are applied within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, their injunction as subordinate elements is already established by the injunction of the qualified primary sacrifice itself, and thus there is no purpose for a separate injunction—this is true; the qualified injunction indeed encompasses the qualifiers, yet their status as qualifiers is not established merely by that [qualified] injunction. If it is argued that this status is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), [we reply:]...

No, because that very [injunctive force] is dependent upon the injunction (*vidhi*). For the meaning of *prakaraṇa* (context) is the application (*viniyoga*) of that which has an expectancy toward that which likewise has an expectancy; however, there is no expectation for a purpose (*prayojana*) on the part of root-meanings devoid of an injunction. This is because, in the absence of a verbal root-meaning brought forward by the same word, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is satisfied even by the abstract noun (*bhāṣya*), especially since it is derived from a compound. But when the efficient force is underpinned by an injunction, it is not satisfied by that much alone, and thus an expectation for a purpose arises.

And since that [injunction] exists, the status of the *samit* and other [subsidiaries] as being subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the New and Full Moon sacrifices is established through their context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, for the sake of establishing that subsidiary status, there must indeed be an injunction regarding the *samit* and others.

Thus, since the performance of those things which have become subsidiaries is accomplished by the very injunction of the qualified principal (*pradhāna*), the injunction regarding the subsidiaries is said to be a restatement (*anuvāda*) with respect to that aspect. Consequently, both [the injunction and the restatement] are logically consistent; everything is thus clarified.
That very context (*prakaraṇa*) is the means of application for the *prājāpatya* offerings and so forth.

Order (*krama*), however, is characterized by commonality of location (*sāmānya-deśa*), and it is of two kinds: commonality of location in the text (*pāṭha-sādeśya*) and commonality of location in performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*). First, regarding the former: where there is a textual recitation in the same location for both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*liṅga*), such as the *yājyā* verses of the southern *Agnihotra* and those of the northern [Agnihotra]; and where there is a common performance for both the subsidiary and the principal (*śeṣi*), such as between the sacrificial animal of the *Dākṣāyaṇa* sacrifice and the ritual duties pertaining to the animal.

Through both types of proximity (*sādeśya*), there occurs the application (*viniyoga*) of the *tantra-mantras* and the animal-rites (*paśudharma*), such as the *upākaraṇa*, to the *gomīya* [offering].
*Samākhyā* (name) is a derivative designation;
it is both worldly and Vedic.

Just as there is the application [of the rule] "the office of the Hotṛ" and "the office of the Adhvaryu," so too is there the application of the Hotṛ in drinking from the *camasa* cups and of the Adhvaryu in performing the ritual acts (*padārtha*).

As for one who considers the seventh means of proof (*pramāṇa*)— namely, the mention of inclusion (*upādāna*) which is the operation of an injunction— to be the applicator (*viniyojaka*) in those two cases, [it is argued that] their applicatory power is secondary.
Indeed, no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "appropriation" (upādāna) is possible, because there is no object to be cognized (prameya) for it.
As for what is said—that the status of sprinkling and so forth as being for the sake of the sacrifice (ṛtvarthatva) is established by that [appropriation]—that too has been answered:
it is established by the Vedic revelation (śruti) itself through the application [of these acts] to the form of the means for the transcendental result (apūrva).
For this indeed is the nature of being a means to the realization of reality—that it serves as a prerequisite by way of that [realization].
Nevertheless, how is it said to be for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*)?
[It is because] of the rice grains, the rice-powder—

3367. By means of indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), and context (*prakaraṇa*), there is the status of being a means to the *apūrva* through the mediation of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth.
Likewise, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) enjoined for such a purpose becomes an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice, which stands in the relationship of the door and the thing to be entered.

And how, by means of *upādāna* (incidental mention), can sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the like be for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*)? If it is thought that, within the context of the *niyoga* (the mandate), at the very moment of being grasped by the *grāhaka* (the apprehender), the sprinkling and so forth are not yet understood as being for the sake of the sacrifice; and that since they cannot function as the *karaṇa* (instrument) due to their being subordinate (*pāriśeṣyāt*), their subservience to the sacrifice is established only through their being auxiliaries to the instrument; and thus, the *niyoga* itself, having been apprehended as connected with that [sprinkling], postulating its status as an auxiliary to the instrument, implies the purpose of the instrument—then, in this case, this is simply *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting), which has been described under a different name.

If it is argued that, for its sake as well, in your view, the primary intention regarding the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is established precisely through their being apprehended as instruments (*karaṇa*), and since such [instrumentality] is impossible [otherwise], the conceptualization is mediated by the assistance (*upakāra*) provided by the instrument;

thus, the very nature of the assistance is what is contextually primary (*prākaraṇika*), while the fact that the *prayāja* offerings and so forth produce that [assistance] is merely derivative (*aupādānika*).
Then, the application (*viniyoga*) of the *prayāja* and so forth would have to be contextually primary.

For the application of a rite through context (*prakaraṇa*) is not established merely by the production of assistance imagined through that context; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all subsidiaries (*aṅga*), whether they are directly contributing (*saṃnipātin*) or those named after the principal act (*anāmnya*), would be applied by context simply because they produce such assistance.
Therefore, the status of *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) and other rites as subsidiaries is established solely through their connection to the context.
But surely, that which is not connected by context (*prakaraṇa*) is applied [to a purpose], whereas sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is indeed connected.
This is not a fault;

for even those things that are connected depend upon a means (*dvāra*), and that very dependence is the basis for it. Thus, even when there is a difference in the nature of the means of knowledge, "appropriation" (*upādāna*) is what establishes the means for those things that are connected.
And the statement that "the section [deals with] unconnected [elements]" is merely a conventional designation.

It has already been discussed previously that even for [factors] such as the singularity of the animal, the application is established by direct audition (*śruti*) itself, while the fact that the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other rites serve the purpose of the fruit is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*) and so forth.
Therefore, these alone are the means of proof regarding the distinctness of the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*).

The Topic Concerning the Conflict Between Indicative Mark and Syntactical Connection.

In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya has employed the term *liṅga*—in the sense of the capacity of a word—to denote that meaning which constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with a mantra; and he has done so because it is distinct from the previously mentioned *liṅga* (inferential mark) and *vākya* (syntactical connection).

Regarding the example of the contradiction between indicative mark (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*) in the passage "asyonaṃ te sadanaṃ... (O Agni, this is your pleasant seat...): if it is held that the two mantras have separate things to be manifested—namely, the seat and the sacrificer—as being inherent in the ritual act, then since both require manifestation and the objects to be manifested also require manifestation, once the application (*viniyoga*) has commenced, that which possesses an established capacity for a particular purpose will reach it more quickly than anything else; thus, it cannot be led elsewhere by virtue of syntactical connection (*ekavākyatā*), nor does it yield room for others who might arrive there later.
