Su. Pṛ. 1209. In the *Mantrādhikaraṇa* of the *Bhāṣya*, it was refuted that the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa-prathana*), which belongs to the section on the application by indicative power (*liṅga-viniyoga*) of the mantra "the fame of Yaśaspati," is the result [of the spreading]. [This is] the *Parākrama*. 4819.
"Because of the mention of a specific gender, [the mantra] is connected with a male, according to Aitiśāyana."

Because of the mention of a specific gender—the masculine form—in such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," Aitiśāyana, the son of Itiśāyana, held that the status of being a sacrificer belongs to a man;
that is, the teacher [Aitiśāyana] considered that the entitlement to perform the ritual belongs to a man alone, not to a woman.
This is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position.
And because of that statement, the scriptural mention of a defect is understood.
This sūtra provides another reason for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that "only a man has the entitlement to perform ritual acts, not a woman.
"Because of that statement" means because of the mention of masculinity; the meaning is that masculinity is intended to be significant.

Precisely because masculinity is intended to be significant, the scriptural statement regarding the fault incurred when an embryo is killed while its sex is unknown is logically consistent; however, if masculinity were not intended to be significant, that scriptural statement— namely, "By killing an embryo whose sex is unknown, one becomes a bhrūṇahan"— would not be logically consistent.
The male is the performer of sacrifice;

it is heard in scripture that the destruction of a sacrifice occurs upon the killing of a man, and thus the sin of *bhrūṇahatyā* (the killing of an embryo) is attributed to one who kills an embryo whose sex is unknown.
If women were also entitled to perform sacrifices, then the killing of a woman would likewise constitute *bhrūṇahatyā*.
Therefore, in the phrase "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*), the masculine gender is intended to be significant;
thus, only a male has the qualification for ritual action.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

"But the birth [is the means], according to Bādarāyaṇa, because there is no distinction; therefore. For the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), it is "because it is enjoined, as per the scriptural text.
The meaning of the words, however, is evident from the commentary itself.
Thus,
having set aside by means of the word "but" (*tu*) the prima facie view reached through the two preceding sutras— that the entitlement to sacrifice belongs to the male alone and not to the female—
the teacher Bādarāyaṇa states the established conclusion: he considers that women are entitled to [sacrificial] acts according to their caste.

Because there is no distinction— since both man and woman belong to the genus *manuṣyatva* (humanity) and there is no difference between them— the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) denotes the woman just as it does the man. The referent of the genus *manuṣyatva* is either heaven itself or the desire for heaven that is being sought.

Since there is no distinction [regarding the meaning of the word *jāti*] whether it refers to a male or a female, and because the desire for heaven is common to both without difference, the female also is understood [as eligible].
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the female also has the right to perform ritual acts (*karmādhikāra*),
because she is enjoined [to do so] according to the scriptural injunction.
The present sūtra is intended to refute the reason stated in the previous sūtra: "And because that [act] is mentioned as such, there is no fault, due to the specific scriptural injunction.

Since the rite is enjoined as applicable to both males and females (*coditatvāt*), in accordance with the scriptural mention of the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), even when a fetus whose gender as male or female is not yet known is killed, one still possesses the qualification for sacrifice. The statement "by killing a male, the sin of *bhrūṇahatyā* (killing an embryo) occurs" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to express extreme censure. Thus, it is understood that "the fetus must not be killed."
Therefore, a woman also is entitled to perform ritual acts;
such is the meaning of the Sūtra according to the Halābhāṣya. Now follows the interpretation according to the Bhāṣya.

If it is argued that just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*), both masculinity and singularity are intended to be significant, so too in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), masculinity must likewise be intended—this is answered as follows: In the case of "animal," one may intend masculinity and so forth by overriding the literal hearing of the text, because it is enjoined as something to be taken up (*upādeya*) due to being prescribed. However, in the present case, since the status of being human applies equally to women as to men, and the desire for heaven is likewise no different for a woman, it is impossible to maintain that masculinity is intended in the term "one desiring heaven."

"The scriptural mention of the fault of concealing the pregnancy is a restatement for the sake of praising it"—this is the refutation of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of a statement that deviates from the sūtra.
Thus [it is said].
However, in the *Vṛtti*, the phrase "If it be argued that [the suffix] is due to the case-ending" (6.1.3.8) is the sūtra expressing the doubt of the prima facie opponent.

"Just as in the injunction *paśunā yajeta* (one should sacrifice with an animal), the third case-ending indicates that both singularity and masculinity are intended to be significant, so too in the term *svargakāma* (desirous of heaven), masculinity should be intended.

To this, the reply is given: "Because they possess the nature of being property (*dravyatva*), [the rite] would belong to men, for it is connected with property; women possess the nature of property through buying and selling, because they share the same connection with property.

Since ritual action is accomplished by means of property, and since women are themselves connected with property, they have no entitlement to perform the ritual"—this is the sūtra intended to present the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) once again.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the position of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
Women have no ritual action (*karman*).

For ritual action is heard in scripture as being connected with material substances (*dravya*), such as "one should sacrifice with rice-grains" and "its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is one hundred and twelve," and so forth.
It is not like the case of "substance-ness" (dravyatva) belonging to men.
Since substance-ness belongs to men, the action connected with a substance would belong to men alone;
however, for women, there is no substance-ness, and thus no connection with a substance.
Therefore, action does not belong to them.
Furthermore, the lack of ownership over property on the part of women is established by two reasons: purchase and sale;
for women are purchased by their father and sold by their husband.
Because they have been sold, they have no ownership over their father’s property, and because they have been purchased, they have no ownership over their husband’s property.

Furthermore, the sale [of women] is heard in such scriptural injunctions as: "He should give a hundred [cows] to the one who has a daughter," and "In the Ārṣa marriage, he should give a pair of cattle to the one who has a daughter.
And just as articles such as clothing are subject to purchase and sale, so too are women equal to such goods in this regard.
The application [of the rules] regarding women is the same as that for goods such as clothing, by virtue of their being subject to purchase and sale.
Thus, because women are objects of purchase and sale, and because they share the same status as material goods (*dravya*), they lack the nature of a [legal] person (*adravyatva*).
And because they lack the nature of a legal person, women do not have [the right to perform] ritual action (*karman*).
"But [the capacity for knowledge belongs] to men alone.
This is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose.

This sūtra is intended to establish the gender [of the subject] in the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that, because women are objects of purchase and sale, they are property (dravya), and therefore they do not have the right to perform ritual acts.

The statement in the explanatory passage (arthavāda), "She who, having been purchased by her husband, behaves otherwise," shows the fact of being purchased; this is the indicative mark (liṅga) for the fact that women are objects of purchase.
And because they are objects of purchase, they are not property; and because they are not property, women do not have the right to perform ritual acts.
Because it is for that purpose, there is the status of being an object (*karmatā*) due to being for that purpose.
This *sūtra* is intended to dispel the doubt raised in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that women have no entitlement to perform ritual acts because they lack property.
In that regard, the doubt is as follows:

"Is it not the case that women lack the status of being property (*dravyatva*)? Rather, they possess the status of property through the wealth acquired by means of the husband's surplus or by spinning and other such activities; and because they possess the status of property, they have the entitlement to perform ritual acts. To this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) replies:
Because women are purchased by their husband, they exist for his sake; that is, they are for the purpose of the husband.
Because they exist for his sake, even in matters such as the duty of spinning and so forth, they exist for his sake—that is, they are for the purpose of the husband.
Whatever property is acquired by women through spinning and other such means belongs to the husband alone.
For this very reason, it is said: "The wife, the slave, and the son—all these are indeed without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong."

Thus the Smṛti is consistent. Therefore, since women lack property, they have no entitlement to perform ritual acts; this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). [The Siddhāntin replies: Because there is no difference in their enthusiasm for the fruit [of the action].

When the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) has been reached through the sūtras that "women have no entitlement to perform ritual acts because they lack property," [the author] states the established conclusion (siddhānta).
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the position that women lack property.
Women are not destitute of wealth.

Women are connected with property; consequently, they are entitled to perform ritual acts, because there is no difference in their enthusiasm for the fruit. Enthusiasm regarding the fruit is the desire for the fruit.
Since there is no distinction—that is, no difference—between the enthusiasm for the fruit in a woman and that in a man.

Therefore, because of the specification of particular gender markers, the consumption associated with the cups dedicated to Varuṇa and the others would be without a mantra— that is, it would be devoid of a consumption mantra.

One prima facie view is that the *bhakṣa-mantra* belongs to the Soma [offering] because of the mention of a specific gender in the phrase "of what was drunk by Indra" (*indrasya pītasya*), which serves as a qualification of the Soma;
and because that qualification cannot be connected to [the Soma] in offerings not dedicated to Indra.
This is one position.

This sūtra belongs to the eleventh section (adhikaraṇa). Following this, the subsequent sūtra, which forms the remainder of this section, would be: "But there is a prohibition of the vowel [in the case of] chandas" (3.1.129).
It should be understood that, however, there are intermediate internal sections (*antarāgarbhi*) within the middle.
Or rather, it follows the respective deity, for its nature as a prototype (*prakṛti*) is observed.

The word "vā" (or) indicates an alternative position. The first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), as previously stated, is that in the *aindrāna* and *aindra-soma-graha* offerings, the consumption of the non-*aindra* soma-cups must be performed without a mantra. Now, he states the second prima facie view.

The consumption of offerings not dedicated to Indra is not to be done without a mantra; rather, according to the principle "of that which was drunk by Mitra and Varuṇa," there should be the presence of a mantra through modification (ūha).
Modification must be performed according to the deity, without overstepping the specific divinity.
For this reason, the status of being the archetype (prakṛti) belongs to those offerings not dedicated to Indra, because they have the offering to Indra as their primary archetype.

Regarding gender and number (liṅgasaṅkhye): the principle of the inherence of gender (liṅgasamavāyanyāya) holds that [gender and number] are intended because they are subordinate to the action; thus, gender and number apply everywhere by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). (Durgasiṃha on Pāṇini 10.2.17.63, p. 1898). Gender and number function everywhere through figurative indication.
12|1|2|1, p. 2267: There is a traditional rule (*smṛti*) that a *sup*-suffix denoting gender and number must follow a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
Su., p. 958: The "inherence of gender" (*liṅgasamavāya*) is one of the causes for figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*).

In the case of the statement "he places the breath-bearers" (*prāṇabhṛta upadadhāti*), since they possess the gender [of being "bearers"], the application of the word occurs solely through the inherence of that gender.

Although only the first mantra contains the word *prāṇa* and no other does, nevertheless, here we observe a combination of that which possesses breath (*prāṇabhṛt*) and that which does not possess breath (*aprāṇabhṛt*). Śā. 2.1.18: "Combination of indicative marks" (*liṅgasamavāyaḥ*).
(The "combination of indicative marks" refers to those qualities which serve as the basis for [the application of] the term.)
It is heard in the scripture: "He lays down the *prāṇabhṛt*s.
In the piling of the fire-altar (*agni-cayana*), certain bricks to be laid down are named *prāṇabhṛt*s.
In the mantras for their preparation, the word *prāṇa* is recited: "This one is the one who exists in front; his breath is the blowing wind."
second

Because it is connected to an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the capacity of the single sentence to produce a scriptural injunction (*śruti*) is untenable; furthermore, even if by some logic the entire [mantra] does not serve the purpose of eating, the capacity of the *bhakṣānuvāka* (the section on eating) remains established. Since there is no contradiction with the name (*samākhyā*) regarding the capacity to denote the act of taking up (*grahaṇa*), it is logical that it produces a scriptural injunction. Thus, because it is required as something to be manifested through performance for the sake of taking up (*grahaṇa*), its status as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) is established; whereas, if it were equal to the unrequired act of eating, it would result in an unseen purpose. This is another interpretation of the portion of the sūtra: "Because the meaning is enjoined" (*arthasya coditatvāt*).
By means of both indicative mark (*liṅga*) and name (*samākhyāna*), the section [of the Veda] has the purpose of consumption (*bhakṣa*).

The mantra for consumption is heard as follows: "Enter me for long life, for health, for the increase of wealth, for splendor, and for good progeny. Come, O Vasu, O Purovasu; you are dear to my heart. Through the arms of the Aśvins, I have attained union with you. O divine Soma, you who look upon men, may I, being well-eyed, gaze down upon you."

"Enter my limbs, O Lord of Bay Horses; do not cause me pain. As one auspicious, attend upon the Seven Sages; do not go beyond my navel. O delightful and victorious banner of glories, Vāk, being pleased, release that [portion] of Soma: of the Vasudrava, the Rudradrava, and the Ādityadrava—O God Soma, your portion for the sake of the thought [of the sacrifice], of the morning pressing, of the midday pressing, of the third pressing, of that which has the Gāyatrī metre, the Triṣṭubh metre, and the Jagatī metre, of that drunk by Agni, drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, and drunk by the Pitṛs—of the honeyed [Soma] that has been invited, I partake of the invited [portion]. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.2.15), and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should this entire section (anuvāka) be applied to the act of consuming, or is some part of it to be applied elsewhere? Having established, as a corollary to the demonstration that the application of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) depends upon a general proximity of parts, and having further demonstrated that even direct assertion (*śruti*) applies by depending on a general proximity of parts, we shall now determine—on the basis of the indicative mark alone—the specific point of whether the application of an indicative mark occurs in cases where [the action] is directly enjoined or where it is merely implied by the sense (*arthākṣipta*).

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: although it is perceived that the section beginning with "bhakṣehi" and ending with "sadhyāsam" has the purpose of taking up [the cup], the section beginning with "nṛcakṣasam" and ending with "avakhyeṣam" has the purpose of looking down, the section beginning with "hinve me gātrā" and ending with "mā meḍvā'nābhimati gāḥ" has the purpose of proper digestion, and the section beginning with "mandrābhibhūtiḥ" and ending with "bhakṣayāmi" has the purpose of consuming; nevertheless, since only the consumption of Soma juice is enjoined, and because the indicative power (*liṅga*) applies mantras to what is specifically enjoined, and since taking up, looking down, and proper digestion are already implied by the act of consuming, they are unfit for application through indicative power. Therefore, this entire mantra is applied to the act of consuming.

Furthermore, at the beginning it is heard: "Do not eat," and at the conclusion: "I eat. Therefore, because eating is mentioned both in the opening and the conclusion—just as in the case of the Vaiśvānara section—and because the entire Anuvāka constitutes a single syntactical unit, and also due to the designation of the *Bhakṣānuvāka* (the "Eating Section"), the whole [text] has the purpose of eating.
Furthermore, since acts such as taking up [the food] are already established by their very purpose according to worldly practice, a purely worldly procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is appropriate.
Therefore, since that eating is accomplished even through worldly words, there is no requirement for Vedic mantras.
Consequently, even the mention of specific details such as "taking up," "examining," and "properly swallowing" serves only to clarify the particular manner of eating.

Therefore, since the mantra forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the mention of "eating" found in both the opening and the conclusion, and because of the designation (*samākhyāna*) as the *bhakṣānuvāka*, it follows that the entire mantra is for the purpose of eating. To this, it is replied: "Because its form and the instruction [of the ritual] enjoin a restricted meaning.

The general principle is this: this would indeed be so if the application of the mantra were not based on its indicative power (*laiṅgika-viniyoga*) regarding a matter already established by other means.

For instance, even if drawing [the cup] (*grahaṇa*) and so forth are not explicitly enjoined here, nevertheless, since the act of consuming (*bhakṣaṇa*) is impossible without drawing and so forth, drawing and inspection (*avekṣaṇa*), being implied by the injunction for consumption itself, must necessarily be performed.

Furthermore, "proper digestion" (*samyagjaraṇa*)—because it is prescribed as the final stage of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the substance that constitutes the act of consumption—is enjoined by the very injunction for consumption; yet, because it is to be accomplished through a distinct effort, it must be performed separately.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for those [Vedic texts] to be non-remembered (asmṛta) when they are not being performed, and because they possess the capacity to function as Vedic injunctions through their own power, there is no need for them to depend on Vedic means as a cause for remembrance.
Moreover, the mantra is capable of manifesting the acts of taking up [the vessel] and so forth in accordance with its literal meaning.
Therefore, like the *sūktavāka*, the mantra is to be employed in the acts of taking up and so forth by virtue of the injunction itself, according to its indicative mark (*liṅga*).

As for the claim that because the opening and the conclusion both mention eating, they constitute a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatva), and therefore the entire passage has eating as its purpose— that is incorrect,
because of the remoteness [of the connection].

For instance, the status of a sentence as something to be understood is established through its opening and concluding parts; and in accordance with that, an indicative mark (*liṅga*)—consisting of the capacity of the sentence in the form of secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*)—must be inferred. Even further from that is direct audition (*śruti*). Thus, there is remoteness [in the case of *liṅga*]. In contrast, because the capacity for expressing the act of taking [the vessel] exists directly, the inference of *śruti* occurs immediately; therefore, the application (*viniyoga*) occurs through division based precisely on the capacity for expressing the act of taking.
This concludes the section on Indicative Mark and Name (*Liṅgasamākhyānādhikaraṇa*).
And conventional designation (*samākhyā*) is weaker than indicative mark (*liṅga*); moreover, being worldly, it can be established even by means of a single part, so nothing is inconsistent.
The purpose [of this discussion] is as stated regarding the previous position (*pakṣa*).

As for the Sūtra: because that mantra is divided into parts through the consumption (*bhakṣa*) and the wiping (*kaṣarpaṇa*), and because the taking up (*grahaṇa*) and other acts are taught by way of its indicative mark (*liṅga*), how can there be an instruction for that which has not yet come into being?
Regarding this, he says: "Because the eating of the substance has been enjoined.
This concludes the section on Indicative Mark (*liṅga*) and Name (*samākhyāna*). *Tautātita*.

The Section on Consumption (Bhakṣādhikaraṇa). In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the section concerning consumption (bhakṣānuvāka) is applied to the acts of consuming and so forth by distributing its parts according to their indicative marks (liṅga). By means of both indicative mark and name (samākhyā), this section is established as being for the purpose of consumption.

The commentary states that the mantra for consumption is heard as follows: "Enter me for long life, for health, for the increase of wealth, for splendor, and for good progeny! Come, O Vasu, O Purovasu; you are dear to my heart. With the arms of the Aśvins, may I hold you fast.
O divine Soma, you who look upon men, may I, being of clear sight, behold you.
You stir my limbs, O Lord of Bay Horses; do not satiate my limbs."
"May Śiva protect my seven seers; do not go beyond me, nor against my will.

O delightful one, the overcomer, the banner of glories, Vāk (Speech), being pleased, release that [portion] of Soma—of the Vasu-drava, of the Rudra-drava, of the Āditya-drava, O divine Soma, you who know the mind, belonging to the morning pressing, the midday pressing, and the third pressing; of that which has the Gāyatrī metre, the Triṣṭubh metre, and the Jagatī metre; of that drunk by Agni, drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, and drunk by the Pitṛs; of the honeyed [Soma], being invited, I partake as invited," and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this entire section (anuvāka) to be applied to the act of eating, or is some part of it to be applied elsewhere as well? What is the prima facie view? On account of both indicative mark (liṅga) and name (samākhyā), the entire section has the purpose of eating;
thus, the whole anuvāka is to be applied to the act of eating.
Why? Because the word "bhakṣayāmi" (I eat) is to be applied to the act of eating as a manifest action; this word is capable of expressing eating and nothing else.
And its other words [the accompanying mantras] are subordinate to the eating, since they qualify it.
Therefore, wherever the word "bhakṣayāmi" occurs, those [mantras] are employed there.

Indeed, the portion beginning with "Ehi vaso" and ending with "sadyāsam" is a distinct sentence for the act of taking [the draught], consisting of a collection of words that possess mutual expectancy and a single meaning; it is separate from the sentence regarding consumption.
The portion beginning with "nṛcakṣasam" and ending with "avakhyeṣam" is the statement regarding the act of looking.
And the portion beginning with "hinve me gātrā harivaḥ" and ending with "mā meḍvānābhimati gāḥ" is for the purpose of proper digestion.
There are many statements from numerous authorities on this matter.
How can it be said that all of this constitutes a single statement enjoining consumption?
It is replied:
It has been stated that all these are qualifiers of the act of eating.
[The opponent] says: Even so, the sentence remains incomplete, because it is impossible for the qualifiers and the qualified to be joined simultaneously.
It is said:
the qualifiers are not intended to be expressed.
Rather, a single object qualified by the qualifiers—such as grasping, looking at, and so forth—is what is intended to be expressed.
This is not correct.
It is understood that there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on two points: that the qualifying words do not intend their literal meaning, and that they are intended to qualify the act of eating.
And when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the direct statement is the explanation, not the indication.
And therefore, it is a single sentence. To this it is replied:
although many meanings such as "purpose" and so forth, as well as "grasping" and so forth, are understood from this, not all of them are intended [by the speaker].
One should strive for eating alone;
for that is explicitly stated in scripture, whereas the qualifications are not heard [in the text].
There is no purpose served by their [individual] comprehension. Furthermore, as many words as constitute a single collection, so many form a single sentence.
Therefore, since this is a single sentence for the purpose of a qualified consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*), it must be applied to that act of consumption.
Furthermore, there is the designation "the *bhakṣa* recitation" (*bhakṣānuvāka*).
This refers to the entire recitation as heard in its entirety, not to a mere part thereof.
Now, it may be objected: "But this designation is a worldly term; how can it restrict a Vedic mantra?"
Although it is worldly, it is nonetheless beginningless; its connection is with the Anuvāka. What follows from this being so? This is what results from it.
He states that what is brought forward through verbal expression is equivalent to being consumed; and co-utterance occurs when there is a relationship,
as in the case of "cook" and "reaper."
We shall infer the relationship from their co-occurrence.
He says: it is not to be apprehended through inference.
In such cases, the status of being a constituent part is understood solely from the injunction itself, and not otherwise;
nor does the name (samākhyā) serve the purpose of an injunction.
To this it is replied: The name (samākhyā), existing in the intellect, will bring about proximity; and the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) is the prescriptive authority.
Therefore, the entire anuvāka must be employed for the act of consuming.
The citation of the entire Anuvāka is for the purpose of distinguishing the subject matter to be explained later—namely, which words belong to which [sections] and what their boundaries are.
Now, the terms "Prātaḥsavana" (Morning Pressing) and so forth function as substitutes for the Sūktavāka.

Consequently, the terms of common grammatical core (*samānādhikaraṇa*), such as "Vasubhadra" and others, as well as "Gāyatrachandas" and so forth, and "Indrapīta" and so forth, should be extracted and employed in sequence according to the respective pressing (*savana*).

This, however, is to be considered: should the entire anuvāka be employed solely for the act of consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*), or should it be applied according to its respective indicative marks (*liṅga*) even to the acts of taking up (*grahaṇa*), looking at (*avekṣaṇa*), and proper digestion (*samyagjarana*)?
In this regard, there is the section concerning the indicative mark and the name (*samākhyāna*) of the consumption.

Because [the act] has been enjoined, and because the word *bhakṣya* (to be eaten) possesses the capacity to manifest that [act], and because the remaining words—connected with the word *āyāta*—are not brought in from elsewhere; just as it is said, "Therefore, the statement of those [words] is employed for the sake of the others" (9.2.11.137), since the acts of taking up (*grahaṇa*) and so forth also serve as qualifiers for the enjoined eating, they constitute a single sentence with a single primary purpose, and thus their application (*viniyoga*) is to that very [act]. This being stated, the objection is raised: even in the case of eating, the phrase "O food, come to me" (*bhakṣehi mā āviśa*) is appropriate; however, the portion beginning with "Come, O Vasu" (*ehi vaso*) and ending with "may I sit together" (*sadyāsam*) is intended for the act of taking up [the vessel].

Although it is not explicitly clear from the reading "sadhi hiṃsāyām" that the root *sadhi* has the sense of "seizing," nevertheless, because it is frequently used in that sense, there is the understanding of its inclusion as "seizing.
Furthermore, verbal roots possess multiple meanings;
or rather, the act of seizing itself may be intended here as "violence" (*hiṃsā*), and thus there is no fault.
Likewise, in the case of *anunakṣasam* and so forth, the root has the sense of "entering.
Although it is recorded in the grammatical tradition that *cakṣi-kṣa* means "distinct speech," nevertheless, in actual usage, it is understood to have the general sense of "manifestation.

Therefore, regarding the form *nṛcakṣāḥ*—meaning "one who is renowned among men"—with the intention "I shall speak to him," the augment *śvij* is added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) to the rule *cakṣi-kṣaḥ khyāñ*.
Therefore, it has the sense of "observing.

[In the mantra] "hinva me gātrāṇi" (stimulate my limbs), one who has been properly digested is able to gratify the limbs; thus, because it does not mean "I am struck by this," it has the sense of "anointing.
Consequently, due to the contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the status of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) is untenable.
This is explained as follows: all of these—both those that preceded the eating and those that are present—are qualifiers of the act of eating.

Therefore, since they serve to qualify the eating for its intended purpose, there is no contradiction in their having a single referent, because the qualifiers are implied by the object [of the action].

And although it is appropriate to enjoin the acts of seizing (*grahaṇa*) and so forth separately—since they do not relinquish their own primacy and since they are directly stated in the Veda (*śrauta*)—nevertheless, there is no fruit whatsoever in enjoining what has not been enjoined; therefore, it is more logical that they serve as subsidiaries (*śeṣa*) to what has been enjoined.
This has been stated in the *nirvāpa-mantra*.
Therefore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is unobstructed.
And thus, the designation (samākhyā) will be accepted [as authoritative]. Regarding this, they raise an objection:
that designation is indeed fit to be the allocator (viniyoktrī) which is recited within the Veda itself.
But as for the designation "Bhakṣānuvāka," since it is not recited [in that context], how can it be applied?
To this it is said: "Whether worldly or Vedic, a means of knowledge that is free from defects [is authoritative]."
Everything is relied upon for its own sake, and no fault arises in this regard;
just as the Veda possesses authority because it is free from the defects of a speaker, so too does a worldly word, since there is no difference in their lack of beginning.
Nor does the logic of an infinite regress apply here.
Because both the designation and the designated object are entirely perceptible;
for the Anuvāka is not imperceptible in the same way that the relationship between the means and the end—such as the Agnihotra sacrifice and its results—is [sometimes considered].
Therefore, the fact that this is denoted by the word "Bhakṣānuvāka" is itself the proof.
Therefore, having reflected upon the section (*anuvāka*) being recited in this context, the designation (*samākhyā*) comes to mind;

and that designation, being analyzed as *bhakṣyānuvāka* ("the section on eating"), causes one to fix in the mind the connection with the act of eating. Then, through the observation of the mutual proximity of the two [the eater and the food], that very general connection becomes a specific connection.
For even the *bhakṣa* (the act of eating) requires a reminder (*smāraka*),
and the *anuvāka* (the recitation) also serves to illuminate [the meaning];
furthermore, both possess the requisite capacity [for this function].
The injunction of the formula for application pertains to the object to be manifested and the manifestor as they exist in that state.
By that [formula] also, there is the purpose of eating.
There is a displacement [of the formula] due to its form and the instruction, because the meaning has been enjoined.
Commentary: This is not so; the entire section (anuvāka) is not enjoined for the act of consuming.
By virtue of its form, the sentence concerning the taking [of the cup]—beginning with "ehi" and ending with "sadhyāsam"—is enjoined for the act of taking.
And the passage beginning with "tṛcakṣasam" and ending with "avakhyeṣam" is enjoined for the act of looking.

Why? Because in this way that sentence possesses its primary meaning; otherwise, there would be recourse to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And the primary meaning is logical, not the indicated meaning.
It is said:
it has been stated that there is no purpose whatsoever in denoting the qualifiers. To this, it is replied:
These are not merely qualifiers;
rather, these acts such as the *grahaṇa* (taking up) and so forth are enjoined separately by their respective individual sentences.
Why? Because there is indeed a purpose served by them.
For these have indeed been enjoined;
some by separate sentences, and some as they were already established.
These must necessarily be made manifest.
These words will illuminate those [meanings];
their form consists in that capacity for illumination.
Therefore, because they have different meanings, it is not said that there is a single sentence.
[Objection: But surely the form of these [words] in the sentence concerning eating is twofold.
[Reply: It is said: their form is that of a statement (vāda).
But these are not postulated as qualifiers of that [object].
For what reason? Because they would be of unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Whether with the stated qualifiers or without them, the object remains exactly the same.
Otherwise, they would manifest the acts of grasping and so forth;
thus, they would have visible purposes.
Therefore, by means of these two instructions, there would be a displacement of certain [elements].
Or rather— by this very method of objection, a demotion [of the mantra] must be made,
because it favors the primacy of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*),

and because the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*)— whether by way of its form, its capacity, or the context (*prakaraṇa*)— just as in the case of the taking up of the cups and so forth.
But is it not the case that being a sentence concerning eating is also a very strong inferential mark (*liṅga*)?
True;
nevertheless—
The section concerning Indicative Power (liṅga) and Name (samākhyā): [Name] is weaker due to its remoteness from direct Vedic statement (śruti).
For, by means of the capacity to denote the act of taking up [the vessel], one infers a direct Vedic statement and thereby performs the application quickly.
By contrast, the other [alternative] forms a single syntactical unit;

thus, there is a remoteness [of connection], because the capacity for the act of eating arises through the medium of indication (lakṣaṇā), and from that, the inference of direct Vedic statement (śruti) follows.
Consequently, since the act of eating is already occupied by another mantra and so forth, these [mantras] must be displaced even though they themselves possess the status of being mantras.
But surely, the manifestation of things already obtained through implication is purposeless.
How is it purposeless?
Because even those [things] cannot be performed if they are not manifested.
That which is already established by its very nature and accomplished without effort need not be explicitly stated;

however, all actions such as the taking up [of the cup] and so forth must be achieved through separate efforts, and since they cannot be performed if they are not remembered, they must necessarily be recalled.
Furthermore, even the injunction for consumption cannot fulfill its own purpose without prompting those actions; therefore, it too prompts them.

Therefore, because they consist of the nature of mantras, because of their injunction, and because of the instruction regarding both the *samyañjana* and those mantras, there is a displacement [of the action] solely on the basis of that instruction; for it is the purpose itself that is enjoined.
Thus, although a direct instruction cannot be asserted here because it has not been cited as an example, nevertheless, there is no fault.
As for the *samyañjana*, however, it refers to emesis and purgation.
"He who vomits *soma* is indeed deprived of sensory power and vigor;
therefore, one who has vomited *soma* should offer a sacrificial cake (*caru*) to Soma-Indra"—
this and other such passages are to be understood as direct injunctions regarding expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
Śabara: "The entire [mantra] is subsidiary to the act of eating, because the acts of taking [the cup], and so forth, are not enjoined [by the mantra].
An unaccomplished purpose cannot serve as the means for a mantra. Furthermore, the Saṃhitā of the Bhakṣānuvāka is intended to convey knowledge regarding the act of eating."
And the efficacy of the mantra lies in its consumption, because of that specific qualification.
Therefore, the entire section (anuvāka) is a single sentence as a subordinate element of the consumption.
This being the position reached, we reply:
"Through its indicative power (*liṅga*), this [mantra] is applied to the act of taking up [the cup] and so forth by way of distinction.
For the two designations of *vākya* (syntactical connection) and *saṃjñā* (name) are not capable of subverting the indicative power.
And although the act of taking up and so forth is not explicitly enjoined by the scripture,"
Nevertheless, because it must be performed according to the enjoined purpose, it is brought forward [into the context].
Therefore, there is a distribution of application (*viniyoga*).

Soma: Just as in the previous case, the natural force of the direct statement (*śruti*) was set aside by the context (*prakaraṇa*) which expresses a general connection, so too here, the natural force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) must be set aside by the name (*samākhyā*) which expresses a general connection.
Thus, the connection [of the mantra] is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).
In the Sūtra, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it refers to the capacity for a specific act of consumption (*viśiṣṭa-bhakṣaṇa*).
As stated: "This entire section beginning with *bhakṣehi* is connected to the act of consumption."
Just as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) determines the distribution [of a mantra] at the time of the taking up [of the cup] and so forth, so too,
when the taking up and other acts are not directly enjoined,
that entire [mantra] is distributed according to rule among those very acts implied by the sense, such as the eating.
(Bhaṭṭa:
In certain instances, a mantra is heard that is designated by the name *bhakṣānuvāka* (the section on consumption), such as "O food, eat me; enter me," and so forth.
Among those [mantras], that portion which teaches the act of eating itself is employed for that very purpose.)

Regarding the portions [of the mantra] that enjoin seizing (*grahaṇa*), looking (*avekṣaṇa*), and straightening (*saṃmārjana*), there arises the inquiry: is their application (*viniyoga*) restricted to seizing and so forth, or—by virtue of syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the act of eating (*bhakṣaṇa*)—is it for eating alone? In this deliberation, [it is concluded that they serve eating]. For seizing and the rest are not themselves enjoined; thus, since they do not produce a perceptible result, they lack even the status of being a producer of an *apūrva*. Although seizing might subsequently apply by way of being a means to eating (*bhakṣāṅgatva*), the seizing performed by both arms—as stated in the phrase "I grasp with both arms" (*bāhubhyāṃ sadhyāsam*)—is in no way established [otherwise]. Furthermore, looking is not established except through its syntactical connection with the sentence concerning eating. As for straightening or the activity conducive to it, because these occur subsequent to eating, they do not produce eating and thus lack even the capacity to motivate an *apūrva*. Consequently, if they were for the sake of seizing and so on, they would result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*); therefore, by virtue of syntactical unity with eating, they must indeed be for the purpose of eating.
And in this way, even the traditional designation becomes justified.

This being the position reached: although there is no direct injunction for the acts of taking up (*grahaṇa*) and so forth within the perceptible injunctions, once the connection with the act of consuming (*bhakṣaṇa*) is understood through the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) aided by the name (*samākhyā*), it is possible to establish the acquisition [of those acts] because injunctions for taking up and so forth can be inferred from the wording of the mantras themselves by the force of their indicative power (*liṅga*). Thus, the application of the mantras is logically justified as being for that very purpose. It is not tenable to assume—either by some forced construction of syntactic unity between the two verbal words—which are inherently independent and possess distinct intensities—that they have a secondary sense (*gauṇī*) directed toward consumption, or to assume that they manifest the acts of taking up and so forth merely as qualifiers of the consumption through their primary denotative power (*śakti*).

Even so, there can be no injunction regarding the act of *samyañcaraṇa* (proper swallowing), because it is already established as something to be accomplished; for what is to be enjoined and performed is specifically the particular posture (*āsana*) that is conducive to the activity of proper swallowing.

Furthermore, since the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by vomiting or purging applies only up to the point of proper swallowing, it follows that the act of swallowing serves as the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the substance.

Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*).

there is no option; rather, it must be restricted.

As for what is stated here in the *Tantraratna*—namely, that the suffix *-luṭ* (future) in the word "intending to sacrifice" (*yakṣyamāṇa*) occurs when one action is the object of another, as in "one who is about to sacrifice with Soma"—that too is intended merely to establish the syntactical application by showing that the use of *-luṭ* is grammatically correct only when there is a connection with another action. The *leṭ* [mood].
Regarding the *leṭ*: its status as the fifth [letter] is to be understood in two ways.

Although the vowel *e* (ekāra) is recited when the suffixes beginning with *ac* are introduced, nevertheless, because there is no letter *la* (lakāra) among those having *la* as an indicatory mark (*anubandha*), the *leṭ*, which has *e* as its indicatory mark, is the fifth among the letters that have *la* as their indicatory mark; for among the characters that possess the indicatory mark *la*, the vowel *e* is the fifth.

Alternatively, under the third [section] concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*), within the governing rule "suffixes [occur] when there is a connection with a root" (*dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ*), the *leṭ* suffix is prescribed by the rule "the *leṭ* [is used] for the intensification of action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre leṭ*).
Following that, two *lakāra*s (tense/mood markers) are prescribed by the rule "in the Veda, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [are used]" (*chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*).
Then, the *leṭ* is prescribed again by the rule "the *leṭ* [is used] in the sense of the *liṅ*" (*liṅarthe leṭ*).
Therefore, within the context of the third chapter on verbal roots (*dhātu*), this is the fifth mood (*lakāra*), because it is prescribed after the four preceding moods; moreover,
its application is seen in common usage even without regard for formal grammatical rules.

According to the *Lokavākya-subodhinī*, however, this is its own meaning: "Upasaṃprāpti" refers to the attainment of building a house and so forth; it is "unscriptural" (*aśāstrā*), meaning it is not pure.
The sense is that scripture does not support such things as building houses, nor does it support one's own [worldly] perception.

When a person has not yet attained [purity] and is devoid of cleanliness through acts such as house-construction, the scripture is meaningful and effective. The sense is that one who is unable to perform [purification] by his own power should act after having consulted the scripture.
Thus:
the view of the partisan (ekadeśin), which imagines that "once an action has been commenced, it must necessarily be brought to completion," is not pleasing.
This is because, when it is possible for the word *kāma* to refer to the fruit required by the injunction (*vidhi*), it is improper for it to refer to a cause (*nimitta*) that is not so required.

Furthermore, if the motive for sacrifice were the desire for a result, then the instruction to perform a rite consisting of hardship—such as the cultivation of pleasure and pain—would be untenable, and it would entail the unwarranted assumption of some other result.

VI.1.1.7. Just as in the world it is said that for people who have arrived from another village, an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭa upakāra*) is produced by the act of circumambulation (*paryatrikaraṇa*), and there is no inconsistency in this worldly usage;
so too, it should be understood that those words which are well-known in the world must, if possible, retain their very same meanings [in the Veda].
Their meaning should not be postulated through methods such as *adhyāhāra* (supplying ellipses), nor should they be assigned a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). (Bhāṣya 2.1.4.12)

In the world, objects already previously known are expressed by such terms as "yielding much milk" (*bahukṣīrā*); for example, [in the statement] "this cow is to be purchased because she yields much milk. For those [objects], the mere cognition of them is not the purpose [of the statement].
Therefore, praise is understood;
for people would not have faith in a discourse on what is unknown, just as they do not in previous statements,
and it is precisely because [the subject] is known that they are inspired.
In the world, indeed, an equal division among sons regarding the father's property is observed (Vi.
In the world, such a practice is also seen being carried out.

Furthermore, there is no room for questioning in the world [regarding linguistic usage], because it is beginningless (*anāditva*). According to the principle that "a word whose capacity is understood in common worldly usage is also expressive in the Veda," the meaning of the Veda must be described in accordance with [worldly] linguistic proficiency. *Vivaraṇa* 1.1.2 (in the view of the Guru).
The means of knowledge known as worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) is indeed included within perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This principle is to be seen under the rule "Because it is obtained from the *bhāvanā*" (Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 3030).
As in common worldly usage.
For example: "This cow should be purchased by Devadatta, for she yields much milk, is beautiful, and has a prolific offspring."

It has also been stated that people proceed to act because of the mention of qualities, as in "she should be purchased," where the mention of the quality is understood from the words "one who yields much milk.
In the same way, this will also apply in the Veda, as in such passages as, "The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood; it is for the sake of strength and prosperity."

Commentary: "Now, regarding words such as 'cow' (gauḥ) and so forth, there is a doubt: do they have the form (ākṛti) as their referent, or the individual (vyakti)?
It is said:
first, this must be examined—whether those very same words used in common worldly usage are the same as those in the Veda, or whether they are different."
When those very same [words] are used then as well, there arises the doubt: "Are these the same meanings that exist in common worldly usage, or are they different?
To this we reply: "The worldly words are one thing, the Vedic words are another, and their meanings are yet another.
Why? Because of the difference in designation and the difference in form.
The distinction in designation is that "these are worldly" and "these are Vedic.
The form [of the word] in the expression "one who destroys the dullness of fire" (agnivṛṃvāṇi jaḍaghnat) is different from the worldly word *agni*.
And because the words are different, the meanings are not the same.
Moreover, they recite: "The divine cows indeed carry [the offerings] on their backs.
When it is stated that those which are the cows of the gods carry on their backs, it is understood that those which carry on their backs are denoted by the word "cow.
Therefore, the meaning of a Vedic word is different [from its common usage].

Likewise, in the Veda it is said: "O Vanaspati with golden leaves, from of old your purpose is for the gods, O bringer of oblations"; thus the Veda knows the golden-leaved one as the divine Vanaspati.
And in the Veda it is said: "Clarified butter is indeed that which belongs to the gods"; thus the word *madhu* (honey) is used for clarified butter.
Therefore, these [words] have other meanings.
This being the position reached, we reply:
those very words that are worldly are the same as those that are Vedic, and their meanings are the same as well.
Why? Because there would be an absence of an injunction for performance (*prayoga-nodanā*).
Such an injunction for performance is possible only if those very words denote those very same meanings;
otherwise, if the words were different, the meaning would not be understood.
Therefore, it is said that there is a single word. This is explained as follows: this is the application.
"Because they are designated as causes. Therefore, "due to the non-distinction in the functioning of the cause," we do not perceive any distinction between those [elements] and these [effects].

For this very reason, we understand various distinct meanings from the single word "you" (tvam), and therefore we do not claim that there is any difference [in the word itself]. As for what was said—"Those who carry on their backs are the divine oxen (devagava); that which is clarified butter is honey; that which has golden leaves is the lord of the forest (vanaspati)"—there is no such statement that would assert that those who carry on their backs possess the nature of a cow.
"That those oxen carry while lying on their backs" is exactly what that [text] means.

If, by this statement, "ox-ness" (gotva) were being enjoined, then "they carry while lying on their backs" would be a mere restatement (anuvāda). Furthermore, there are no well-known oxen that carry while lying on their backs.
Those [other qualities] must necessarily be enjoined;
while they are being enjoined, it is not possible to enjoin "cowness" (gotva),
for in that case the sentence would be split.

And if they were other than Vedic, then the meaning of [the words] *uttāna* and so forth would not be understood; in that case, it would be even more impossible to understand the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*), whose characteristics are unknown.
Nor is the statement regarding "carrying on the back" (of the earth) purposeless; it will be meaningful as a form of praise (*stuti*).
The same applies to the honey-nature of the clarified butter and the golden-leaved quality of the tree.
Therefore, those very things are words and meanings. Here, among nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles, nouns are selected.
Among those, from the category of words consisting of genus, quality, action, substance, proper names, and pronouns, words denoting genus are taken.
Taking even one of those words, "cow" (*go*), as an example, it is investigated whether this denotes the form (*ākṛti*) or the individual (*vyakti*).
Therefore:
"Having set aside this [preliminary] matter concerning renunciation, that which is to be discussed shall now be addressed."

[The meaning is as follows: Having set aside for one's own mind—as if in a secure deposit—the fact that the subject matter to be explained (the unity of form) is fit for renunciation (*sāṃnyāsika*), another point is now considered at the outset for the sake of establishing the means and the fruit. He said: "What is the purpose of establishing the identity between words of common usage and those of the Veda, such that it is being established first?"
It is said: "The fruit of this inquiry will pertain to the Vedic [tradition], and in the world as well, by means of this method of determination, one strives for unity."

"If there were non-difference between the words and meanings in both worldly and Vedic usage, then it would be possible— by means of this investigation into the expression of transposed [words] and by following the manifold applications of the linguistic practice of the elders— to determine what is denotable and what is not denotable.

However, no purpose whatsoever for the world is accomplished by the definitive determination of the ultimate truth regarding whether the class (*ākṛti*) or the individual (*vyakti*) is the denoted meaning."

For a word is employed when many meanings are present in a state of commingling; it produces a cognition regarding a certain range of objects. And thus, it is employed when the accomplishment of a purpose is being carried out by means of all the properties falling under a category whose denotable objects are not clearly distinguished.
"If it is argued that [the word] is used [in the Veda] because its meaning is understood through the genus (jāti), as in the *Lokavedādhikaraṇa* (Mīmāṃsākośa 4.24)..."
Everything is rendered [as such].

If it should be argued that here too, as in the case of the Veda, the very accomplishment [of the goal] is the purpose because of the nature of general and specific characteristics;

This is stated: "For everything in the world, such as the giving of curd and so forth, is characterized by action" (11.1.26). However, when that which is performed is characterized by what is heard [in scripture] and is to be contemplated, this worldly deliberation becomes purposeless.

The suffix *-lyap* and *ktvā* are substitutes [for the gerundive]. Regarding the direct scriptural injunction (*viniyoktrī śruti*) according to the opinion of Someśvara, it is as in: "His teacher [should shave] his hair," and so forth.
Bāla, p. 45:

Although [suffixes] such as *lyap* convey the state of having a single agent (*ekakartṛkatva*) and priority in time (*pūrvakālatva*), it is not established that they convey the absence of ignorance (*ajñābhāva*).
This is because even in the absence of a causal relationship between cause and effect (*nimittanimittikabhāva*), the state of having a single agent and so forth can be accounted for.

As in the case of [the injunction]: "Having concluded from the *sattra*, they should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma* characterized by a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇa*) as the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*";
here, one first intends to express the qualification, and only then follows the utterance of the word.
Furthermore, the listener first hears the copula (*dvandva*), then the qualifier, then the qualificand, and thereafter proceeds to other things that serve as its logical support (*upapatti*).
Therefore, even if the speaker has already considered the relationship beforehand, the listener will nevertheless grasp it only later. Vākyapadīya 3.6.12, p. 676.
Inference of the Speaker’s Knowledge.
It is now established that human utterances convey their meaning only through the mediation of an inference regarding the speaker’s knowledge.
Why is it that the comprehension of meaning does not arise from the mere hearing of words that are logically consistent?

[Objection: "The cognition of the speaker is inferred [from the word]. [Reply: If it is argued that this occurs by means of the speech, no; for even when a sound is produced through mere brilliance (dyuti), there is a determination of the speaker's intention, and from that, the denotation of the object follows. Therefore, the cognition of the speaker's intent (*tātparya*) is also postulated as a constituent factor of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
And the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya-jñāna*) consists in the reflection: "Having understood this meaning, this sentence was uttered in order to convey that very thing.
Consequently, [the testimony of scripture] is included within another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, one might object: "Let it be that mere sentences do not denote [meaning]; why is it not accepted that the words of a trustworthy person (*āpta-vākya*), being free from defects, possess the capacity to bring about the understanding of an object? This is not so. Trustworthiness consists precisely in being free from defects such as greed and the like; yet even for one who possesses such [trustworthiness], there are instances where a statement is seen to be directed toward something else, as in the case of the sentence "Eat poison," which is intended to effect the cessation of eating.

Therefore, once the intended meaning (*tātparya*) has been understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is the ascertainment of the meaning. The ascertainment of the meaning follows from the ascertainment of the intention, and the ascertainment of the intention occurs by way of inferring the speaker’s cognition; thus, it is established that only the statement of a reliable person (*āpta-vākya*) possesses the nature of a logical mark (*liṅga*). This remains so even in the case of a sentence such as "one should eat brāhmaṇas," because [the inference] does not deviate, since it is preceded by the cognition of a possible meaning.

Now, how is cognition inferred? It is certainly not an inference of cognition in general, for since there would be no determination of the specific nature of cognition in general, such an inference would be redundant. Nor is it an inference of the cognition of a positive injunction (*vidhi*), because the specific character of a cognition is determined solely by its object; thus, one might argue that the inference of a qualified cognition occurs through the determination of the object, and once that determination has occurred, the inference is indeed redundant. [Objection: Is it not rather the inference of the speaker’s cognition? [Reply: Not so. Upon hearing a sentence, the word-meanings are first recalled even before the act of expression. Once the word-meanings have been recalled, a deliberation arises as to whether they can be connected in this way or not. Therefore, through the deliberation produced by this logical process (*nyāya*), the object is apprehended in its qualified form; it is by means of that very qualified object that the qualified cognition is inferred.

Now, what indeed is this so-called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness)? Furthermore, we do not know whether it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not. It is said in reply: You yourselves have already accepted *vimarśa* even prior to the verbal expression; otherwise, a qualified object could not be known through the word-meanings that have been expressed, because since word-meanings are common to many objects, which specific object would they cause one to understand? If you argue that they cause one to understand an object endowed with expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*saṃnidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*), then that very thing is the meaning of the term *vimarśa* which you have accepted.

And that [inquiry] consists of the procedure for valid cognition (*pramāṇa-itikartavyatā-rūpa*), being neither valid cognition alone nor mere recollection (*smṛti-mātra*). Furthermore, if inquiry were not admitted, there would be no investigation into the expression of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the process of making something perceptually evident. Some, however, hold that because it is obscured by the suspicion of contradiction, a definitive determination of the object does not arise. As stated in the *Mīmāṃsākośa*: "But in the case of human speech, that [determination] is obscured by the suspicion of contradiction" (Mī. Ko. 425).
They say that this is because it has been stated thus.
That is incorrect; for when the causal complex for verbal expression (*abhidhāna*) is present, even a conventional usage (*saṃjñā*) can serve as its subverter.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the existence of a determination of a result would act as an obstacle, and such a consequence would also apply to the ascertainment of an inference.
Therefore, this expression [of meaning] occurs precisely because of the absence of the complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Now, it may be argued that since linguistic usage is established in this manner, the acquisition of knowledge (*vyutpatti*) arises from human utterances; yet it has been stated that a sentence is not a direct denoter (*abhidhāyaka*), but rather a mere indicative mark (*liṅga*).
This is not so, for there is no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the scope of the expressive power (*śakti*).
And by means of the inferential mark (liṅga), there is the determination of the object at a later time.
Therefore, it is established that the determination of the object occurs through the mediation of inferring the speaker’s cognition.
(Praviv. 7–11)

Because of the statement "by the word," the *aindrī* verse— composed of the word "Indra" and containing the instrumental case-ending— would be non-literal; that is, having set aside its literal primary meaning, it would exist in a figurative sense,

The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude other alternative views.
Alternatively, there may be designation based on a quality (*guṇa*), because the relationship [between the deity and the mantra] is the cause for such designation.

If it is argued that—just as in the case of "one succeeds through Agni"—the injunction of an impossible matter, namely the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire with the *aindrī* verse, is untenable, to that he replies:
Or rather, the word "api" here serves to dispel doubt;
it is not the case that there is an injunction for an impossible matter,

In the case of the *Haviḥśravaṇa* [mantra], it is possible for the word "Indra" to denote the *Gārhapatya* fire due to its connection with the swift hearing (*śruti-laghuna-yoga*). This is because the relationship of denoter and denoted (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*) is beginningless and thus cannot have the Veda as its cause; consequently, there is no possibility of it being a function of the scripture (*śāstra-kārya*).
Furthermore, this is also logically consistent with the word having a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) established in common worldly usage.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *ṛc* addressed to Indra is to be employed for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire.

This is because, in the section concerning the rule "The *aindrī* [verse] may be used in three ways due to a scriptural statement," it was stated that the application of the *ṛc* by direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*) cannot be sustained unless its secondary application (*gauṇa*) is justified; specifically, by the *guṇasūtra* "Or there is denotation through a quality" (*guṇādvāpyabhidhānam*), it is explained that the word "Indra" occurring in the mantra denotes the Gārhapatya fire through its connection with qualities such as the mention of the oblation (*haviḥ*). Thus, the secondary sense is established.
This is precisely the section concerning the Aindrī [verse].
According to the rule: "By virtue of the scriptural statement, there would be a threefold application of the Aindrī" (Ku. 3.1.7.13), such is the logic.
In this very case, the principle of the *aindrī* [verse] applies.

Now, if in the sentence "and if [the deity] is Agni" (*yady agnīś caiva*), the [deity] were not enjoined by direct denotation (*abhidhātṛtā*), then because the statement would apply immediately, Prajāpati alone would be the deity.
And thus, for the mantra "Agni is light" (*agnir jyotiḥ*), which is applied by the statement, there would be a "deviation from its purpose due to the statement" (*vacanāt trayathārthyam*).

If it is argued that, according to this principle, [the mantra] must refer to Prajāpati in a secondary sense, and thus Agni’s status as the deity cannot be established from the wording of the mantra (Soma. 4.4.4, p.

Regarding the two mantras, "vratam kṛṇuta," it was stated as if established that "because of the statement, the [mantra] would be for Indra" by accepting its purpose as being for the Gārhapatya fire; this we shall now establish here with the intention of emphasizing the superior force of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). By the sūtra "On account of the statement, the Aindrī [verse] may be used for its true purpose" (3.1.2.13), the status of the Aindrī verse as a means for the worship of the Gārhapatya fire is enjoined on the strength of the scriptural text (śruti): "He worships the Gārhapatya with the Aindrī. In response to this expectation, the first part [of the sūtra], "Or there may be denotation through a quality" (*guṇād vāpy abhidhānaṃ syāt*), states that it is by virtue of a shared quality.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Why does this statement not serve merely to demonstrate the proximity of the word *indra* to the designation of the *gārhapatya* fire? As it is said: "On account of the scriptural statement, the *aindrī* verse would be used otherwise than its true sense" (3.1.2.13).

"By virtue of the scriptural statement, the Aindrī mantra may be used otherwise [than its primary sense]"—according to this principle of the third book (*tātīyādhikaraṇa*), the application of the two mantras (which possess the capacities for illuminating the sun and Prajāpati respectively) by the force of the scriptural injunction (*vācanika-viniyoga*) makes the mention of their identity with Prajāpati logically consistent.
This is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Because of the scriptural statement, there is a dual conjunction; therefore, for one [family], it is like the hand.
Regarding the sacrifice performed for the sake of the family, the suffix is stated [in the rule]: "By this, the king and the domestic priest, desiring union, should sacrifice.
The word *tu* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.

By virtue of the scriptural statement "the king and the two domestic priests," precisely because of that statement, there would be a dual connection for a single king, namely a connection with two domestic priests.

Even though in common practice it is impossible for one king to have two domestic priests, nevertheless, by virtue of the scriptural statement, there would be a dual connection for one, that is, a connection with two domestic priests, as in the case of the hands.

According to the rule that "it must be performed with the right-hand manner," the left hand would not be applicable; nevertheless, because of the statement "one offers with the *añjali*," both hands—the left and the right—come into play here. "Like the hands" means as in the case of the hands. And likewise, in the compound *rājapurohitau*, [the analysis is: *purohitaśca purohitaśca* (the priest and the priest), and *rājñaḥ purohitau* (the two priests of the king); such is the compound.
The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that for the *kulayāga*, the entitlement belongs to one king and two domestic priests (*purohita*).
The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) found in the sūtra, however, is not found anywhere else;
nor has it been commented upon by anyone.
We have accepted this because it is recited everywhere.
It could not be so on account of the absence of meaning.

[The author] refutes, by means of a sūtra, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) reached regarding the Kulāya sacrifice—that "the King and the two Purohitas, desiring union, should sacrifice," whereby two Purohitas would be authorized for a single King.
In this way, it would not be the case that one king has two domestic priests (*purohita*),

because of the absence of purpose— that is, because there is no need for two domestic priests. Therefore, the compound *rājñaḥ purohitau* is not formed by taking *purohitaś ca purohitaś ca* (the domestic priest and the domestic priest).

If it is argued that "rājñaḥ purohitaḥ" forms the compound "rājapurohitaḥ," and that "rājapurohitaśca rājapurohitaśca" forms the dual "rājapurohitau"— and thus the position may be taken that the *kulāyāga* belongs to those two priests who serve two kings— then the author replies to that.
"It would not be so because of the absence of meaning"— but even so, it would still not be so because of the absence of meaning.
In this view, there is an absence of meaning— that is, an absence of purpose— for the word "king."
This is because the injunction "the two domestic priests (purohita) should sacrifice" establishes this as a settled rule.

If it is argued that, by the compound *rājānau ca tau purohitau ca* ("and those two are both kings and domestic priests"), the qualification belongs to those who are kings and are also domestic priests, we say no;
for it is heard in scripture that only a Brāhmaṇa is eligible for the office of domestic priest (*purohita*).
Since the meaning of "the state of being the domestic priest of the king" is absent [in this case], it could not be so even in that way.
Therefore, the compound must be accepted as a *dvandva* (copulative) compound: "the king and the domestic priest" (*rājā ca purohitaśca rājapurohitau*).
There is one king and one domestic priest for him.
Thus, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that both [the king and the priest] have joint authority over the *kulāyāga*.
Furthermore, because the objects [of the action] are distinct, there is a connection with what is heard in the text.

Regarding the passage, "The king and the domestic priest, desiring union, should sacrifice," he states that neither of the two following positions is possible: that there are two priests for one king, or two priests for two kings, or that the king and the priest [are two separate persons].

If it were the remainder of the *kulāya* sacrifice, there would be no connection between that which is heard and the fruit heard for those two—the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya—since both are Brāhmaṇas. [Objection: "Svāhā! Because the purposes are distinct; for it is heard that the qualities of the purposes, in the form of *tejas* (brilliance) and *vīrya* (valor), are distributed: 'Brilliance belongs to the Brāhmaṇa from the mantra, and valor belongs to the Rājanya from the mantra. Thus, indeed, the distribution of the qualities of the purposes, consisting of brilliance and valor, is declared in the scripture.
In this regard, it is stated in the Siddhānta that "the king and the domestic priest" [are meant];
therefore,
the king and the domestic priest have a joint entitlement to their common abode.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Because there is no reciprocal relationship between the two hands, a lack of connection is perceived.

Regarding the statement, "The king and the domestic priest should sacrifice," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that two priests belong to a single king and have joint entitlement (*adhikāra*) in the *kulāya* sacrifice; [the author] now refutes the example "like the two hands" (*pāṇivat*) cited therein.
Regarding the statement, "One offers with joined palms (*añjali*)," what was said— that a single person has two hands— is indeed correct.
Because the hand is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*),
when the *añjali* is to be performed, the left hand is the counter-correlative of the right hand.
The right hand is the primary agent (*añjabhūta*), while the left is its counterpart (*pratyajñabhūta*).
Otherwise, they would be perceived as unrelated, and there would be no effort toward the connection of the *añjali* (the hollowed palms).
Indeed, the *añjali* is not formed by a single hand, nor does it arise from two right hands belonging to two different persons.
Thus, it is appropriate that one person should take hold of both hands in that case;
however, regarding the expression "the king and the domestic priest" (*rājapurohitau*), it has been stated that there is no purpose in one king taking two domestic priests.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that both the king and the domestic priest are jointly entitled (*adhikāra*) to the *kulāya* sacrifice.

In the Agniṣṭoma, regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) dedicated to Agni-Soma, the ritual acts such as the anointing and the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) are prescribed in the scriptures.
These [rites], such as anointing and so forth, are obtained by extension (*codaka*) in the case of the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*).

Regarding the inquiry as to whether there is a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) with each individual act starting from anointing, or whether there is a sequential performance with the entire group of ritual acts (*dharmakāṇḍa*) beginning with anointing and ending with the binding of the cord (*parivyāpa*), the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
in the case of the eleven sacrificial posts, the group of subordinate acts (*guṇakāṇḍa*) beginning with anointing and ending with the binding of the cord must be performed sequentially for each post.

Because of the statement, "One should not release the sacrificial post from the ointment and so forth until the end of the *parivāpa*," it follows that this constitutes a single ritual act (*ekapadārtha*) up to the conclusion of the *parivāpa*.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) up to the end of the *parivāpa*.
Alternatively, there may be non-release due to a specific cause, as in the case of the increase in the number of vessels.

Regarding the *yūpaikādaśinī* (the ritual of eleven sacrificial posts), when the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) has been stated—that there is a simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) from the anointing (*añjana*) up to the encircling with the cord (*parivyāpa*), because of the scriptural injunction: "The sacrificer shall not release the post from the anointing until the encircling"—the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) speaks as follows.
The word "vā" indicates a shift in position.
This non-releasing (*anavasarga*), which consists of the state [of the post] beginning with the anointing—
From the statement,

it follows that there is no absence of the simultaneous cutting-off (apaccheda), and the act of taking hold (anvārambha) has been mentioned; that [act] would exist because of a specific cause, serving as assistance for the two [sacrificers].

however, by that [erection], the end of the surrounding enclosure is not accomplished.

Just as in the case of the injunction, "He performs the after-sacrifices with speckled butter," there is the purification of the vessel for the purpose of holding the speckled butter, and thus the vessel becomes a sacrificial offering (*pātramedha*); so too here, by implication, there is no relinquishment, yet that [implication] is not a restrictive rule.

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, it is explained that because of the cause—namely, the cause consisting in the mutual dependence of the two [the sacrificer and the wife]—there would be an *avasarga*, which is the postulation of someone other than the sacrificer;
thus, another person would have to be postulated for the act of taking hold (*anvārambha*) on behalf of the sacrificer.
Furthermore, the reading *avasargaḥ* itself should be accepted.

It has been explained that even in the case of *kutūhala*, there should be an *avasarga* (conclusion) here because of the reason that it would otherwise violate the rule of sequential enumeration (*padārthānusamaya*). However, the reading in that [text] is "the *avasarga* would be an *anvārambha* (recommencement)," and that is not tenable.
"Avasarga" means relinquishing, abandoning, or cutting off;
"anvārambha," however, is non-relinquishing.
Or rather, because it is effected by sound, it is merely a formal act; otherwise, there would be purification of the vessel.

When the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) has been stated—that for the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*), there is simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) by means of the group of subordinate acts (*guṇakāṇḍa*) beginning with the anointing and ending with the meditation on the enclosing sticks (*paridhyāna*)—the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) raises a doubt based on the sūtra: "There is no relinquishment [of the procedure] without a specific cause" (JS 5.2.1). The respondent (*siddhāntin*) dispels this doubt; the word *vā* serves as the dispeller.

It is not that there is simultaneous performance of individual items (*padārtha-anusamaya*), but rather that there should be simultaneous performance by means of the group of items (*padārthakāṇḍa*) ending with the meditation on the enclosing sticks.
