Non-release (*anavasarga*), however, is not due to a causal necessity, but rather because it is established by scriptural injunction (*śabda*); for there is the specific statement: "One should not release the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) until the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) have been placed.
Indeed, even in the absence of the sacrificer, the Adhvaryu is capable of erecting the post;

as for the other [requirement], namely the status of being the sacrificer's property (*yajamānatva*), the injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavacana*) is merely a matter of logical principle (*nyāyamātra*).
The injunction of the archetype (codaka) is stronger than the injunction of the application (prayogavacana).

In the animal sacrifice, however, there is the purification of the vessel for the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), because the *upabhṛt* ladle is occupied with taking the clarified butter (*ājya*) and thus cannot hold the speckled butter.
Ke.

Even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that "there is a combination because of the scriptural statement" (*vacanāt samuccayaḥ*, 3.6.16.45), he will state the combination by treating the very *darśana* as a scriptural statement out of necessity.

Vārttika 3.6.16.42, p. 1064: "Because of the scriptural statement," meaning because of the injunction regarding [the grass] that has lost its potency (*yātayāma*). "The *kuśa* grasses, the *darśana*, the mantras, and the Brāhmaṇas who are deeply learned..."
They do not become like discarded offerings when they are employed again and again.
Thus, according to the Smṛti (Vārttika 2.2.8.24; Sūtrabhāṣya, p. 1121).

On account of the scriptural statement regarding the *rathakāra*, his [right] to the *ādhāna* (the establishment of the sacred fires) is to be understood as a qualification for that specific caste among the three higher varṇas; for there is the scriptural injunction: "The *rathakāra* should establish the fires in the rainy season.

This is because this *ādhāna* performed by the *rathakāra* is a "remainder of all" (*sarvaśeṣatvāt*), meaning it remains as a residual option after the *ādhānas* prescribed for all members of the three higher varṇas.
Alternatively, because this chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) remains distinct from all those belonging to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*),
such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Here, the prima facie position is that the chariot-maker is indeed one who does not belong to the three [higher] castes.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) will be that [the Rathakāra] is slightly inferior to those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), but is not entirely outside the caste system (*anairvarṇika*).
Or rather, it is logical that he belongs to a caste because of his connection with specific rituals, since [other rituals] are prohibited for a Śūdra.

Regarding the statement, "In the rainy season, the Rathakāra should perform the fire-consecration (*ādheya*)," which establishes the Rathakāra as eligible for the consecration, someone says this in response to the position that the Rathakāra is outside the three castes (*atraivarṇika*), which was suggested by the Sūtra.

The word "proper" (*nyāyyaḥ*) means one who has not deviated from justice; [it refers to] a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who is endowed with the principle of eligibility for ritual action. The meaning of the particle "or" (*vā*) is that the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) must be such a person, and not one outside the three castes (*anairvarṇika*). Furthermore, even for a member of the three castes, the term "chariot-maker" is applied because of his connection to the work—that is, because of his connection to the task consisting of the construction of a chariot.
Since the Śūdra is prohibited from [Vedic] rites, the Śūdra is not the *rathakāra*.
Therefore, the *rathakāra* must be someone belonging to the three higher castes who occasionally performs the work of a chariot-maker.
According to some, his consecration (*ādhāna*) takes place during the rainy season.
The reading "or it would be *nyāya*" appears in the *Kutūhala*.
It is called *nyāya* because it is led (*nīyate*); the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The meaning is that the term *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) should be applied here to those of the three [higher] castes by relying on the connection with the activity of making chariots as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
The rest is the same.
[Objection: This cannot be so, because it is not a [proper] action (*akarmatvāt*).

The word "tu" (but) serves to refute the position stated previously: the *rathakāra* mentioned in the injunction "In the rainy season, the *rathakāra* should perform the consecration (*ādadhīta*)" would not be a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). This is because he lacks the [Vedic] ritual duties, as he is engaged in the craft of a chariot-maker, and because of the prohibition: "One who lives by mechanical arts is not [eligible for Vedic rites].
Furthermore, [the injunction] would otherwise be purposeless due to its connection [with a specific caste].
When it is stated, "The chariot-maker (rathakāra) should establish the sacred fires during the rainy season," the term "chariot-maker" [is used] because of the direct statement;
for there is no [contradiction] with the statement.
The aphorism is intended to establish another argument for the position that [the Veda] is not composed by a person (*pauruṣeya*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used to indicate an additional reason:
because of the connection between the Brāhmaṇas and others with the spring season and so forth.
If the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) were a member of the three [upper] castes (*traivarṇika*), then the mention of the rainy season for him would be purposeless.
Therefore, the chariot-maker is distinct from the three castes.
If it is argued that this is for the sake of a specific quality (*guṇārtha*), [we reply: no.

Regarding the statement, "A *rathakāra* should establish the sacred fires during the rainy season," it was argued that the *rathakāra* is distinct from the three *varṇas*, because the practice of crafts is forbidden for those of the three *varṇas*. To this, he replies:

Although the practice of crafts is forbidden for the twice-born (*dvija*) for the sake of livelihood, nevertheless, for the sake of excellence—namely, for the purpose of acquiring various kinds of knowledge to increase one's qualities—even a member of the three *varṇas* may construct a chariot.
Furthermore, in times of distress, even a twice-born person may construct a chariot for the sake of livelihood.
If someone should say, "Therefore, the *rathakāra* is not at all distinct from the three [twice-born] castes," [we reply:
it has already been stated that [caste] is not the determining factor.

When someone asserts that the injunction, "A chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) should perform the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) during the rainy season," prescribes the *ādhāna* for a chariot-maker who is already a member of one of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), on the grounds of his occupation as a chariot-maker, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) offers this reply: Because of the scriptural declarations—"A Brāhmaṇa should perform the *ādhāna* in spring, a Kṣatriya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn"—these are not intended as contingent conditions (*nimitta*), but rather as established rules of application. This was stated in the section [of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra*] beginning with "On account of the distinction of the four castes" (6.1.17–28). Thus, it has been declared that those scriptural declarations do not function as contingent conditions.

Therefore, the scriptural statement, "The chariot-maker (rathakāra) should perform the fire-consecration during the rains," serves as the injunction for that very consecration which was previously unestablished.
Consequently, this consecration belongs to the chariot-maker who is outside the [three] social classes (anairvarṇika).
However, it is understood from the wording of the mantra that they are the Saudhanvanas, because of their low status.

Regarding the statement, "A *rathakāra* should establish the sacred fires during the rainy season," who indeed is this so-called *rathakāra*? To this, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to refute the two previously mentioned positions.
By the term *rathakāra*, the specific caste known as the *Saudhanvana* is to be understood.
Because he is slightly inferior to those belonging to the three [higher] castes, his placement is at the end.
However, from the wording of the mantra, it is understood that by the term "rathakāra" (chariot-maker) only the Saudhanvanas are meant;
for the mantra for the rathakāra’s establishment of the sacred fires is: "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Ṛbhus, the gods."
In the mantra, "The Ṛbhus lead the rim as [if they were craftsmen]," it is stated that those who lead the rim are the Ṛbhus.
Furthermore, in the mantra, "The Saudhanvanas are the Ṛbhus," it is made known that the Ṛbhus are synonymous with the Saudhanvanas.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that the initiation of these rites belongs to one who is not of the [three] varṇas and is distinct from the Śūdras.
Some say: "Because of the scriptural statement regarding the *rathakāra*’s fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), and because it is subsidiary to all [Vedic rites].

Regarding the text, "In the rainy season, the *rathakāra* should consecrate the fires," there arises a doubt: does the word *rathakāra* here denote one of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) based on its etymological meaning (*avayavaprasiddhi*), or does it refer to another person of a distinct caste based on conventional usage (*samudāyaprasiddhi*)? Since the word *rathakāra* can apply to a member of the three castes who constructs chariots through its etymological meaning, it is not appropriate for a non-Ārya—who is excluded by the section concerning Śūdras (6.1.126)—to have the entitlement [to perform this rite].

This being the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), it will be stated that because the conventional meaning of the whole (*samudāya-prasiddhi*) overrides the conventional meaning of the parts (*avayava-prasiddhi*), by the force of the scriptural statement, the entitlement belongs exclusively to one who is not of the [three] castes (*anairvarṇika*).

In that context, it has been demonstrated that the conventional meaning of the whole is stronger than the conventional meaning of the parts. However, if the superiority of the conventional meaning of the whole were established through some other means, then since the entitlement of even one who is prohibited by logic—namely, one who is not of the [three] castes—would be determined by the force of the scriptural statement, there would be no doubt; consequently, the commencement of the section on the *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) would be unjustified.
Furthermore, the strength of a conventional meaning based on a collective whole (*samudāya-prasiddhi*) is never seen to override [etymological derivation] elsewhere.
Nor is the entitlement (*adhikāra*) of a non-tri-varṇika established through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) in the absence of such etymological derivation.

Even for a tri-varṇika, since it is possible for the word *rathakāra* to denote him through the application of its constituent meanings, and since he would obtain the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) by virtue of the sentences concerning spring and so forth, the scriptural statement can be explained as being for the purpose of prescribing the rainy season for the fire-laying on the grounds of his status as a *rathakāra*. Thus, it is illogical to assume the entitlement of a non-tri-varṇika when one has not yet reached a conclusion.

Having explained the primary reason with the words "precisely because of this statement," the reason stated as "this injunction for the fire-laying (*ādhāna*),"— namely that because the fire-laying is not subordinate to everything, it remains applicable to all Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who are connected to it, while those of other castes are excluded—

is further explained in the Bhāṣya by the use of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the fire-laying is subordinate to everything," as being an interpretation based on figurative application (*upacara*).

Su. Pṛ. 166: "Because of the statement, 'Some perform the Atirātra first,' the Atirātra—a single Jyotiṣṭoma—is to be performed first. Bhaṭṭa 5.1.12: A scriptural statement has independence regarding its purposeful meaning. Bṛhatī Pṛ. 23: There is no overburdening for a scriptural statement."
Bhāṣya 3:
For there is nothing at all that is "insignificant" in speech;
in speech, [everything is significant].
When there is a direct statement regarding the calf, there is no room for inference.
When there is a direct statement possessing the necessary capacity, [an inferential rule] does not apply.

Vārttika 2.3.3–4, p. 589: Regarding the term *vacanātideśa* (extension by statement), the "statement" (*vacana*) is of two kinds: that which is directly heard (*pratyakṣaśruta*) and that which is inferential (*ānumānika*). Bāla., p. 118: Because a statement would otherwise be purposeless, it is better to assume a secondary figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) for a single word.
Soma., 7.3.8: Prosperity [arises] from a statement (prosperity occurs through three modes: through activity, through the result, and through a statement).
The excess of the *āśitambhava* is the subject of the scriptural statement.
That substance which is the *āśitambhava* is the prosperity (*bhūti*), and that is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Since it is established as being the sacrificial fee, anything in excess of that exists by virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement.

In the modified *ṛtapeya* sacrifice, by virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement (*vacanaprāmāṇyāt*), even a small amount [of wealth] is prescribed in place of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), namely, a *soma*-cup.
(Bhāṣya 10.3.16.14). By virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement, the prohibition will set aside the injunction;
and the injunction likewise sets aside the prohibition.
The position that "there is no other course" is for the most part false;
it will be postulated [only] when there is a prescription and not a prohibition.

"Then there is a prohibition when there is no injunction. (Bhāṣya 10.8.3.6). Regarding modification (*ūha*) of the mere wording: in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is "of the goat's omentum and fat," whereas in the case of the *prājāpatya* offerings, it is "of the goats', the omenta', and the fats'."

Vāla-pṛ. 127: Between the number (vacana) and the case-ending (vibhakti), the case-ending is primary because it expresses the grammatical relation (kāraka); the number, however, is secondary because it denotes the count of the kāraka. Vi. 9.3.5: *vacanavyakti* (the mode of expression).

For the mode of expression is one when something is being enjoined, and another when it is being connected with a subordinate element (guṇa). An object being enjoined is made known as if it were unknown; however, for the purpose of connecting it with a subordinate element, it is understood as if it were already known. And that which is uttered only once cannot simultaneously be both "as if known" and "as if unknown."
Bhāṣya 3.1.6.12, p. 650: "Even with a hundred statements, it is impossible to effect an application [of a term] that is unfit for such application. Sūtra-bhāṣya, p.
1089: "Indeed, even with a hundred statements, the word *indra* cannot be made capable of denoting the *gārhapatya* fire."
Or [as stated] on page 754, line 3.2.4:
"Even by a hundred statements, it is not possible to make one understand that Agni is to be indicated by the word 'Indra'; one who asserts this would be contradicted."
"Just as one might say, 'It should be accomplished by fire,' or 'One should kindle it with water' (Bhāṣya 3.2.4).
Indeed, even by a hundred statements, an impossible matter cannot be enjoined."

For if someone were to say, "One should burn with water; one should moisten with fire," would he be following the efficacy of the purpose of that statement? (3.1.6, p. 691). The fruit of actions such as consuming *vacā* is the attainment of intelligence (Su., p. 59). The maxim of adamantine glue (*vajralepananyāya*).

This [term] is employed when one intends to express that the substance is not firmly established as a friend. Regarding the bricks named *vajriṇī*, they are a remainder of the [overall] structure (*adhiśeṣa*), but not a remainder of a specific layer (*citi*).
Therefore, they are to be laid down once at the end, and not with every layer.
The section concerning the *graha* (cup).

Bhāṣya 5.3.6.15–16: The bricks named *vajriṇī* are prescribed in the context of the *akaraṇa* rite. Since they also serve the purpose of the fire-altar (*agni*), their characteristics—being unbroken, not black, and contact with ashes—must be performed, because the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is more powerful than the context (*prakaraṇa*).
3|6|12|35: The placement of the *vajriṇī* bricks occurs in the middle layer (*madhyamaciti*). 5|3|17–19: And that [placement] should take place prior to the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick.
5|3|18|20: The *vajra-jula* grows in the waters.
The statement "the reed (*vetasa*) is born from water" shows that the word *vetasa* applies to the *vajraju* [variety].
Bhāṣya 1.3.4.
This is the principle of the Yakṣa in the banyan tree (*vaṭe yakṣanyāya*).

It should be understood that if there is no foundational experience for the instruction passed down through a lineage of speakers, then that [instruction] is of this same nature; however, if such an experience exists, it is distinct.
Some say that this very [instruction] is what they call "attaining a specific means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇaviśeṣalabdhi*).
"He should be one whose religious duties are performed by others.
(Mānava Dharma Śāstra 10.3.136).
However, my child, cooking must not be done [by him].
In that case, even the pouring over would not take place.
The Vatsas (those of the Vatsa lineage) are performers of the five-fold cutting.

In the injunction "one should touch the calf" (*vatsam ālabheta*), the touching of the calf serves as a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*) for the purpose of [obtaining] milk, because it directly assists the milking which is itself enjoined. Therefore, this Vedic ritual—consisting of the activity of performing the touching—is a directly-contributing auxiliary (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) that has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), intended to purify the substance (the calf) that is not otherwise useful for the directly enjoined assistance. This point was stated by Bhavadeva in the section on the Animal and Soma sacrifices (*Paśusomādhikaraṇa*). Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 82. The phrase "one should touch the calf" is heard in the context of the milking of the cow for the Agnihotra sacrifice.
In that context, there is the section concerning the touching of the calf by means of the calf at the Vatsaspadī sacrifice.
This is an injunction regarding the measure [of time], not an injunction regarding a sacrifice.
This is the section concerning the touching of the calf.
It is the prescription, for the purpose of the vow during the New and Full Moon sacrifices, of the time characterized by the calf and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

O Vatsa, even though they have taken the place of the *anvāhārya* (the sacrificial fee), there is no pouring of clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*) upon them during the performance of the *Āgneya* sacrifice. See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 885.

Regarding the passage, "In the case of the *āśrayaṇa* [mixture], there is the attainment of the pouring of clarified butter for the *vāsas* (garment) and the *vatso* (calf), even though they have taken the place of the *anvāhārya*," one should consult that specific section (*adhikaraṇa*).
In the case of the *vatse* [offering], even though it occupies the place of the *anvāhārya*, there is no performance of the cooking at the *āgrayaṇa*.
Regarding this, one should consult the section in the *Mīmāṃsākośa* (p. 853) stating: "In the case of the *vatse* occupying the place of the *anvāhārya*, there is a sublation of the cooking.
In the *vatse*, which takes the form of the *āgrayaṇa-dakṣiṇā*, the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the original *anvāhārya* are to be performed.

Regarding the statement on page 855 of the *Mīmāṃsā-kośa*: "In the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, the properties of the ordinary gift (*anyāhāryadharma*) must be performed for the cloth and the calf which serve as the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)," one should consult that specific section (*adhikaraṇa*).
This is the *Vatsādhikaraṇa*;
it is the very same as the *Vatsālambhādhikaraṇa*.
Only the removal of the calf (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) is the motivator for the cutting of the branch and so forth, not the placing of the potsherds (*kapālopadhāna*). See *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p.
1674, under the section "Upavepādhikaraṇa."
The driving away of the calves is a duty of the milking;
and that indeed occurs in the evening and in the morning.

The driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) is the motivator for the cutting of the *palāśa* branch, but the throwing [of the branch] together with the *prastara* bundle is not the motivator. (5.1.1) Regarding the *prastara*, the driving away of the calves is performed with the branch, as in: "That which he drives away the calves with the *palāśa* branch" and "He drives away the calves with the branch. (4.1.2, 3) The driving away of the calves is the means for the milking of the *sāṃnāyya* offering, and the fetching of the *palāśa* branch is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that.

The connection with the vow occurs at the time of driving away the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*), even though there is no continuity (*asaṃtanyatva*) in the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*). See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2022.
Regarding the statement "the connection with the vow at the time of driving away the calves [occurs] even in the absence of continuity," one should consult the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The time for the driving away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) is common to both the *Saṃnaya* and the *Asaṃnaya* sacrifices. (Vi. 6.4.12).

Regarding the statement, "At the time of the driving away of the calves, one should undertake the vow; this is the injunction for the time characterized by the driving away of the calves at the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*)," the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.
Mīmāṃsākośa 426: The driving away of the calf, milking, and so forth are the ritual duties (dharma) pertaining to the *sāṃnāyya* offering.
The section concerning the touching of the calf (*vatsālambha*).
The Topic of the Calf: The touching of the calf is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) consisting of mere contact, pertaining to the qualification for milking for the Agnihotra;
this is because it is observed in the majority of cases within the context of doubt.
The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) asks: What is the example here?
It is not something already encompassed by the Sūtra itself, such as [the case where] "in the Aveṣṭi, because of its connection with sacrifice, it is said that the sacrifice is primary" (2.3.12–13).
Nor is it a thesis to be established, such as "there is another injunction regarding the Agnis" (2.3.14–15).
It is merely indicated that "the observation of what is generally seen" is the reason when there is doubt regarding the object;

yet we do not understand for what this is the reason. Nor do we perceive that the statement "this ritual action consists of sacrifice," which was introduced as the subject at hand, is even connected [to the present context].
Thus, this very indicative sūtra is first of all meaningless.
Now, it must be stated: what is the basis here, and how does the doubt arise?
We understand the basis and the doubt from the words of the author of the commentary (Vṛttikāra).

Regarding this, the Blessed One said: having cited the example, "One should sacrifice a calf, for cattle are fond of their calves," he raised this doubt: "Does this verb *ālabhati* denote a ritual sacrifice (*yajimat*), or does it merely signify the act of touching (*ālambhamātra*)?
And this example is appropriate for such a doubt.
And therein he sets forth the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), namely: "it denotes that which possesses sacrifice.
This, however, is a sūtra providing a counter-example to the prima facie position;
there is not much purpose in this prima facie argument here.
Nevertheless, having considered the various differences in the intellects of people, this [notion] has arisen even among the dull-witted through mere general observation;
that too must be refuted.
For one bitten even by a scorpion with mild venom would not die, nor should medical treatment ever fail to be applied with care in such a case.

Therefore, in order to refute that [view], he sets forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "The root *ālambhati* is observed to denote a sacrifice when connected with a living being; this *ālambhati* here is likewise connected with a living being. Consequently, someone might suspect that this too is indeed a word denoting a sacrifice. Alternatively, since the root *ālambhati* is observed to denote a sacrifice when connected with a living being, this [instance] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of enjoining the calf."
And thus, no fruit will need to be postulated.
This being the position reached, we reply:
regarding this doubt, the mere touching is the purificatory act (saṃskāra).
Why? Because it is observed as the general rule.
Where other purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*) are also obtained, there this section concerning the touching of the calf (*vatsālambhādhikaraṇa*) applies as well.
It is heard that even from a preponderance [of evidence], there arises a determination of the meaning;
for example, when something is written in a context primarily concerning fire, it is understood to mean "fire."
But surely, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is a matter of general observation; how, then, can there be proof by means of it?
It is said:
one must explain how it is established through general observation.
And how is "observation of common occurrence" (*prāyadarśana*) a reason? It is not because [the word] applies to whatever is obtained.
What, then, is the logic? Because there is no connection with a deity, it does not denote a sacrifice.
Furthermore, because it serves a visible purpose, the calf, when being touched (*ālabhyamāna*), will cause the cow to flow with milk.
Therefore, since this is established by logic, the observation [of the term] "mostly" (*prāya*) serves as an indicator.
Consequently, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) consists merely in the taking hold (*ālambhana*).
(Or rather: "For indeed, everything that is in the *Vṛtti* and everything that is in the *Vārttika* is contained within the *Sūtra* itself.")
To those who say, "The source is in the Sūtra; everything is established in the Sūtra," it is replied:
No means of knowledge (sādhana) establishes its own object without having its scope demonstrated.
Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras has not provided a logical reason here.
Nor is any one of the [required members], such as the example, the proposition, the doubt, or the reason, to be found even through the *arthakaraṇa* and other means.
Therefore, since the Sūtra is thus deficient in its components (*agamaka*), the authors of the commentaries (*vṛttikāra*) and others must necessarily strive to rectify this defect.
It has been stated in the *Bhāṣya* at the beginning of the *Śāstra* that when a meaning is possible [within the text], one should avoid supplying words (*adhyāhāra*) and so forth.

In every case, among the various refinements of the wisdom of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) that are in operation, one should accept only that which is performed in accordance with that [meaning], and one must not practice non-acceptance (*asagraha*).
This was not explicitly included by the author of the *Sūtra*; this was not included by the author of the *Vṛtti*. To demonstrate this point, this [rule] must be described.
In this regard, the venerable Upavarṣa has cited this statement heard in the section concerning the bamboo-milking vessel in the Agnihotra rite: "One should touch the calf.

And regarding that, as before, he has presented a threefold doubt: Is it the original act of touching (*ālambha*) that is enjoined there? Or is it merely the act of touching? Or is this a sacrificial act (*yajati*)?

In this regard, because there is no distinction [from the previous case], it was not introduced in the Bhāṣya as something already established by the preceding section—that there is no ordinary (*prākṛta*) cognition.
Following that very sequence, once the notion of denoting an act involving sacrifice (*yajimat*) has been raised, an exception (*apavāda*) is now made.

Therein, based on the example of the connection with the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-saṃyoga*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the *gātra* [mantras] is also presented due to the interruption of the two-fold Vedic revelation (*śruti*).

It is demonstrated here that for one who, due to the latent impressions of a logician (*tārkika*), would seek to determine the meaning of the Veda by means of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), such a determination cannot be established unless it is first shown [to be possible].

In this regard, some hold that in the section concerning the son (*putrādhikaraṇa*), the root *ālabhati* is well-known as a synonym for *yajati* (to sacrifice), while others hold that it merely indicates the act of sacrificing; both of these views are maintained here as well.
In that context:

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a duality of positions: either it is the injunction of a previously unknown sacrifice (*apūrvayāgavidhāna*), or, since [the sacrifice] is already established, it is the injunction of the calf (*vatsavidhāna*).

The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that because the connection between the substance and the deity is otherwise untenable, we previously postulated a sacrifice; this was not done on the basis of some unprecedented or impossible designation, nor by means of a fallacious inference involving deviation.
Since such [an alternative] does not exist here, the matter is limited to what has been stated.

And thus, the observation that such acts are primarily purificatory rituals, such as milking, becomes intelligible; their visible purpose is established by their being the cause for the birth of cows,
and because the explanatory passages (arthavādas) are thereby rendered consistent.

The commentary states: And there is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) which says, "For animals are fond of their calves" (*vatsānkāntā hi paśavaḥ*). [Here, *kānta* means extremely dear; those for whom the calf is most dear are *vatsānkāntāḥ*.
Since animals are fond of their calves, therefore the calf should be sacrificed. This statement is appropriate only if the cow is sacrificed in order to cause her to flow with milk.
Furthermore, in that context, a statement of such a nature as "to make [the animal] understand" would not be appropriate.
Therefore, it is established for this reason as well that the *saṃskāra* (consecration) consists merely in the taking up (*ālambha*).

Or rather, because of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "for they [the cows] are fond of their calves," which serves as the reason for the injunction regarding the touching of the calf during the ritual procedure, it is logical that the *saṃskāra* consists merely in the taking up.
If, however, the purpose were slaughter, then the statement that "cattle are dear to their calves" would be utterly incredible.
For since that calf is dear to its mother, the claim that it should be slaughtered for the sake of being killed (saṃjñapana) would be equally incredible.
In the other case, however, it is logical: the mother is fond of her calf because she coos to him, or because she is gratified by the cooing he makes, and out of affection she will yield milk.
Therefore, it is established that this is also an injunction for the touching (*ālabha*) of a consecrated object (*saṃskāra-bhūta*) which possesses a purpose.
In the section concerning the milking for the *Agnihotra*, the scripture states: "One should touch the calf.

Therein, because of its connection with a deity and because of the commonality of being the touching of a living being (*prāṇi-dravya*), one considers this also to be an injunction for a sacrifice (*yāga*).
The answer to that is as follows: "Touching" (ālambha) means mere contact; it does not stand to reason that this [act] cannot occur without a sacrifice.
Furthermore, because it is observed even in common worldly practice, what is prescribed here is merely the touching, which serves as a consecratory rite (saṃskāra) for the calf.
In this case, because the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is extremely weak, it serves merely as a counter-example.
The purpose [of the discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view, some animal sacrifice might be permitted alongside the *agnihotra*;
however, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the calf is used as the means of performance.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: when there is a doubt as to whether [the act] is an injunction for a sacrifice (*yāga*) or an injunction for a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), only that which is explicitly stated—namely, the mere preparatory rite—is to be enjoined, because it occurs in a section primarily consisting of preparatory rites such as milking. The section concerning the touching of the calf (*vatsālambhādhikaraṇa*): "Is the touching of the calf a sacrifice or a mere touch? It is a sacrifice, like [the offerings to] Vāyu and others."
The *sparśa* [initiation] would apply because of the absence of a divine [preceptor], while the *saṃskāra* [initiation] applies because of its position in the general enumeration (*prāyapāṭha*).
Bhaṭṭa: But where there is no mention of a deity, there is no assumption of a sacrifice; rather, there is merely an injunction for a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
For example, in the Agnihotra, regarding the statement "one should touch the calf," only the touching is enjoined as a purificatory rite for the calf.
This is because the root *ā-labh* denotes mere touching.

Maṇḍana [states]: "The sacrifice is not the touching of the calf. Śaṅkara [states]: "The sacrifice is not the touching of the calf. The section concerning the touching of the calf (2.3.16–17) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the section concerning the touching of the *īpā* (2.3.12–16).

Kau. 2|3|16|16, the section on the touching of the calf (*vatsālambhādhikaraṇam*). The *Nyāya-śarīra* states: "The quality of the sacrifice of the calf, which has an unmixed object, is the cause of differentiation [from the main sacrifice], because it occurs in a context primarily consisting of preparatory injunctions (*saṃskāra-vidhi*). This is the *Vatsavatsī-nyāya*.

The Sāṅkhyas maintain that just as insentient milk flows forth for the sake of nourishing the calf, so too does insentient *prakṛti* proceed toward the liberation of the *puruṣa*. And it has been said: "Just as the flow of milk occurs for the purpose of nourishing the calf, so the activity of *pradhāna* occurs for the purpose of the liberation of the *puruṣa*."
Thus [it is said].
The calf-knee and so forth of the Veda (serving as the means for the cleansing of the *darbha* grass) exist solely for the sake of the human purpose.
Commentary (Bhāṣya) 4.1.2.12, Section 2:
Calfhood (*vatsatva*) is a subordinate genus of youth (*bālya*) that inheres in the same object as cow-ness (*gotva*).
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1411.

The calf-skin (*vatsatvak*) is to be used as both an upper garment (*uparivāsaḥ*) and a lower garment (*adhovāsaḥ*); there is a conjunction of both, not an option, nor is there a sublation of the [ordinary] garment. [This is stated in] Āṣṭra-tre. The calf-skin will serve the function of an upper garment, while the [ordinary] garment will serve the function of a lower garment. Bhāṣya 12.3.11-2. In the *viśvajit* one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), the calf-skin is prescribed for the purpose of wearing: "Having emerged from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), he puts on the calf-skin."
In the Viśvajit sacrifice performed with the *aṣṭrā* (plow-handle), there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the calf-skin and the unwashed garment.
Mīko., p. 759.
One should consult the section titled "In the Viśvajit performed with the *aṣṭrā*, there is a combination of the calf-skin and the unwashed garment. (12.3.1.1–2).
"Beloved of their calves":
those animals for whom the calf is exceedingly beloved and dear. Which ones?
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) associated with the *vatsara* [year] in the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice sets aside the ordinary *āhārya* dakṣiṇā.
The word *vatsa* denotes a specific age of a cow.
Or [it may be]. 3|4|4| 13 pṛ. 120.
Regarding the connection with the calf:
"In the case of the connection with the calf, there should be an injunction for the vow."

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is revealed in scripture: "With *barhis* (sacrificial grass) they undertake the vow at the full moon; with a calf at the new moon. In this context, a connection with a calf is heard.
When both that connection with a calf and the connection with *barhis* are revealed, the injunction regarding the vow (*vratacodanā*) would be an injunction for a vow whose instrument is *barhis*.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that on the day preceding the fast (*aupavasathyāhni*), the consumption of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the calf should be performed during the night.

[The author] refutes this first prima facie view with the word "but" (*vā*) and states the second position: "Or rather, the time [for these acts] is connected with their production, as previously stated."

In the statement, "They undertake the vow with *barhis* at the full moon sacrifice, and with a calf at the new moon sacrifice," the time for the vow is prescribed by another scriptural injunction which states, "He undertakes the vow consisting of much ghee and coming from a cow that has recently calved. This is because the vow itself has already been established [by other means], whereas its timing was not previously established.
It is not, however, an injunction for a vow whose instrument is *barhis*, because [the *barhis*] is connected to something already produced.
This is a connection with a vow that has already arisen and been prescribed, not a connection with its origination.
Because of this connection with what has already arisen, this [act] is enjoined at the time of the aforementioned vow.
The meaning of "he performs the vow" (*vrataṃ vratayati*) is that he consumes what is to be consumed.

And thus, the meaning is that the consumption of the vow-food (*vratabhakṣaṇa*) occurs at the time of bringing the sacrificial grass (*barhirāharaṇa*) during the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*), whereas the consumption of the vow-food occurs at the time of making the calf (*vatsākaraṇa*) during the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*).
This is for the purpose of determining the scope of the matter. 136.

In the sentence, "They undertake the vow with *barhis* at the full moon sacrifice, and with a calf at the new moon sacrifice," the proponent of the second position states the defect in the alternative view: that the time for taking the *barhis* and the time for separating the calf are being prescribed for the consumption of the vow.

This means that if one accepts the injunctions "they undertake the vow with *barhis*" and "they undertake the vow with a calf," there would be no determination of the meaning (*arthasyāparimāṇāya*), because of the absence of a measure of the meaning (*arthaparimāṇābhāvāt*), which results in the impossibility of knowing the determined meaning (*niścitārthajñānābhāvaprasaṅgāt*).

Is it that the calf itself is to be consumed as the vow-food (*vrata*) here? Or is something else to be consumed as the vow-food while the calf, acting as a hand-like instrument, is present? Or is something entirely different to be consumed as the vow-food after having placed the calf nearby? The meaning of the scripture is not established in this way.
It has been stated that "one should perform the vow using the calf as the means (*sādhana*). How [is this] in connection with the calf?
The claim that this is a forest-dweller's doctrine is uncertain;
therefore, the connection [of the words] also has the sense of time.
Thus ends the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Vatsa, however, maintains that because of its connection with the scriptural injunction, the calf (*vatsa*) should be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that [rite].
Regarding the statement, "With *barhis* grass one undertakes the vow at the full moon; with a calf at the new moon," the vow (*vrata*) in the binding of the calf should consist of the *barhis* grass.

When the vow has been obtained from another source, it is prescribed for the calf because of its connection with the Vedic revelation (śruti), as in the text: "They approach with the calf and the sacrificial grass (barhis). However, if it were applied to a specific time, there would be a metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).

Therefore, the second position is that the *barhis* grass is prescribed for the calf due to ignorance of the vow; the word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude the second position. However, the time [of the rite] would not be [prescribed], as there is no injunction [for it].

Regarding the statement, "One undertakes the vow with sacrificial grass at the full moon sacrifice, and with a calf at the new moon sacrifice," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is no injunction here for the sacrificial grass as a means for that [vow], nor is there an injunction for the time, nor is there an injunction for the sacrificial grass or the calf by way of being subordinate to the vow; rather, the time for the taking up of the sacrificial grass and the driving away of the calf is being specified.
The alternative view is a mere explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*).
And here too, that cognition [of "forest"] is the universal; it is called "that cognition" because there is indeed a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in all forests as "forest, forest.

For he says that the universal exists even in many things that are not connected [as parts], just as [the universal] "whirling-ness" (*bhramaṇatva*) and so forth exists even in the constituent parts [of a whirling firebrand].
It is evident that even when based on various substrata, the state of being a "forest" is perceived in the same way.
(Even though it consists of separate parts, its commonality is manifested; how much more so when it is not broken apart!

One might think that this cognition of "forest" is produced solely by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of the trees situated in one place and perceived as polished [as a whole]; therefore, for one who holds that forest-ness is non-existent, he states another position: "Where, because they are the cause of a single effect, it is like the word 'cow' applied to many."

Just as the phonemes *ga*, etc., while performing a single effect characterized by the comprehension of a meaning, are denoted by the word *go*—which expresses a collection—as "word" (*padam*), because the collection is a unity; likewise, trees, while performing a single effect based on cognition regarding their own objects, are denoted by the word *vana* ("forest"), which expresses a collection and ends in the singular number. And the state of being the cause of a single purpose is mentioned merely as an illustration. Alternatively, those things that have attained the status of a collection by virtue of performing a single effect, or by occupying the same place and time, are denoted by a word expressing a collection such as "forest," which ends in the singular number. For among the members of a collection, when they are characterized by a single adjunct, there exists a specific quality called a "collection" (*samudāya*) which, though distributed across its parts, serves as the basis for a single cognition.

He says that this is not tenable: "Those trees which are perceived individually are certainly not accepted as a forest. (This means that those things perceived individually, which are the causes of multiple moments and do not abide in a single place or time, are not called a "forest.
He states another alternative: "Or rather, there is unity through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by way of place, time, action, and so forth."

It is also accepted [that the singular number] applies by virtue of the oneness of the substance (*dravyaikatva*) and so forth, as in the case of "a cluster of mud" (*paṅka*) or "a row of trees" (*vṛkṣapaṅkti*). Previously, it was established that the singular number is justified merely by referring to the collection (*samudāya*), while now, having admitted that the words refer to the individual members (*samudāyin*), even though they are many, that which is their common substratum—such as place, time, or action—is unitary; because of that unity, it is called "one forest. Thus, the justification is established either through the oneness of the substance or through the oneness of the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇaikatva*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the universal of "treeness" (*vṛkṣatvasāmānya*) is included.

Thus, since the forest is real, it has been stated by way of that example that the configuration (*ākṛti*) is false. If it is further argued: "Just as the cognition of a forest [is based on a collection], let the cognition of a cow also have the collection of individual bodies as its object; what is the use of a universal (*jāti*)?"—to this he says: "Just as the cognition of a forest arises with respect to a collection of trees..."

In the same way, the cognition of "cowness" does not arise with respect to a collection of cows in the manner that the cognition of "tree" arises there; rather, the cognition of cowness is exactly like that [cognition of tree].
The conceptualization of a "forest" [arises] because trees are not established as separate [from the forest];

since the cognition of a forest is established based on trees that are not distinct [from one another], it is logical that it has a collection as its objective support (*ālambana*). But the cognition of a "cow" is not like this.

Now, if it is argued that it has a collection of *sākṣa* and other parts as its objective support, to this he says: "And the aggregate of *sākṣa* and so forth could not be the objective support of that cognition."
(He states the reason: "When these [individuals] are perceived as discrete bodies (*piṇḍa*), the cognition of 'cowness' (*gotva*) indeed arises with respect to their commonality (*sāmānya*).

For it is the dewlaps and other [features], when combined, that produce the cognition of a discrete body; however, the cognition of a 'cow' takes as its object only the universal (*sāmānya*) which persists through many discrete bodies.

Therefore, since you must admit that this [cognition] has a composite as its object, the [universal] must be excluded from being merely another instance of the cognition of a discrete body; rather, the universal is distinct because it follows after a plurality of composites. Thus he says: 'Therefore, even in the absence of parts, the universal is distinct.'"

(But from the perspective of ultimate reality, even parts and words do not exist; thus he says: "By the very same reasoning stated previously, its substantiality and its state as a whole are established.

(Just as a universal is established because a single cognition occurs despite the difference between [individuals], so too, because there is the appearance of a single substance—such as 'This is Devadatta' or 'This is a jar'—among distinct parts, the whole is distinct from its parts.
Is the whole absolutely distinct? No, he says: "It could not be absolutely distinct from its parts."
(Why? Because) this universal is not perceived as established apart from the individuals.

For it is the very threads themselves, having attained the state of being a single substance through a particular conjunction, that are apprehended by the cognition "this is a cloth" as having a single form; therefore, the whole is nothing more than a particular state of the parts, and there is no absolute difference [between them].

He says: "By some [it is held] to be non-different, by others to be different"—thus, those who resort to either absolute difference or non-difference regarding the whole have themselves established this doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*).
Whether it is refuted or established, force has no role therein;
rather, some consider the conclusion regarding the universal alone to be preferable.
(For this very reason, because it possesses the character of both assertion and negation, there is the establishment of both.

Furthermore, since the pair of otherness and non-otherness cannot be shown as being either existent or non-existent, he states that even its acceptance as having a manifold nature—like a painting—is false: "Therefore, its otherness and non-otherness are said to exist and not to exist. Consequently, its state of having a single form must be false, just like a painting."

(Now, if this were so, for those who maintain the doctrine of mutual difference, since no one among them could be definitively determined, there would be doubt—such as "Is it a post or a person?"—and thus nothing at all would exist; therefore: The cognition that arises in the midst of forests, "This is indeed a forest," [is explained as follows:]
That very tree-nature belongs to it; we do not know a tree-nature that resides in a single [tree].

For our notion of "tree" has multiplicity as its universal (*sāmānya*) and takes a collection as its objective support (*ālambana*). Therefore, it is logical that in all forests, the cognition of a "forest" is the state of being a collection of trees produced by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of the multiplicity inherent in the trees.

It might be argued that when expressing the multiplicity residing in trees, whether one is denoting many substrates or denoting their collection, the word "forest" (*vana*) would necessarily be used in the singular; for if the position is that "many trees are the forest," then why is the singular form not untenable? To this he replies: "Even in the case of unity, there is a dual or plural state due to the [inherent] capacities [of the words], with respect to the individual instances."
For while plurality exists in that way [in the individuals], there is unity in the individual with respect to the genus;

(just as the genus has plurality when considered distributively, so too the individuals have unity by virtue of their nature as the genus. The mention of the "genus" is intended to include place and other factors as well). This may be so; however, why does the expression of plurality not also occur by virtue of its own specific configuration? Consequently, even in the case of a single collection of trees, the usage "forests" (*avanāni*) might occur. Therefore, he says: "And words have restricted powers in denoting both the one and the many."

(For words possess fixed capacities: some express an object delimited by singularity, others by plurality, and still others express it in both ways depending on the difference in usage; he shows examples therein: Some convey a meaning possessing its own number, as in the case of "amarāḥ" (gods) and so forth; [others convey] a genus through its own state, as in "one rice-grain is well-prepared."
In the case of the *patnīsaṃhanana* and other such [physical constitutions], the individual is perceived through the configuration of its form;
whereas in the case of the Kapila and other lineages, it is perceived through the configuration of the individual itself.
Others say that the individual and the genus [are designated] by the number of the parts of a substance,
just as one says "we" when there is only one person, or "the noose is twofold" (naditi) even when it is a single object.

The mention of *vrīhīn* (rice grains) is intended as an illustration for other genus-words (*jātiśabda*) such as "tree" and the like. Regarding the word *patnī* (wife), although it functions through an adventitious attribute (*aupādhika*) in reference to one who is associated with the sacrifice, it denotes an individual (*vyaktivacana*). Furthermore, that [individual] is delimited by the number of the genus; for instance, in the injunction "slaughter the wives" (*patnīḥ saṃjñapaya*), since both the dual and the plural are used, the word expressing the number of the genus refers to the state of being associated with the sacrifice (*yajñāsāmitva*) based on the substance, for there is no such thing as a "genus" called *patnītva*. This is because [the term] is a designation for the *vanaspati* sacrifice.
[The term] refers to the genus (*jāti*) as inherent in the ritual application (*prayoga*), and not merely to the genus itself like the *kapiñjala* bird;
nevertheless, having accepted the genus [as the referent], it is said that it expresses both the genus and the substance.

And regarding these words such as "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so forth, he states that they may take different numbers according to one's preference through different modes of application: "In that regard, the connection or non-connection of words such as 'rice' with [specific] numbers is according to one's preference."
(He says: "But words such as *vana* (forest) and *dārāḥ* (wife) function according to established convention (*vyavasthā*)."
(He establishes this very point by means of an illustration: "Just as [terms such as] 'herd' or 'forest' apply to both individual entities and to the class;

(but what, then, is the specific application of words such as 'wife'? He demonstrates that: in that regard, words such as 'wife' (*dārā*) are employed with reference to both the individual and the class."
And [words] function by taking up the number of the individuals [they denote].

For instance, when a word such as *dāra* (wife), which is always plural, is employed with reference to a single individual, it then brings about a distinction among the individuals based on the arrangement of its parts; however, when the distinction between individuals is not intended and it refers merely to "wife" in general, then there is no distinction between individuals.
As for the word *vana* (forest), however, [it denotes a single individual].

Section on the Vanishṭhu (3.4.14): Section on the Shaving. Because of the scriptural statement, "Of that *iḍā*, the *vaniṣṭhu*," it serves solely as a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) for the *iḍā*, just like the under-spreading of butter (*upastaraṇa*).

Consequently, since there is no evidence for its being intended for consumption (*bhakṣa*), the original carrying away (*haraṇa*) dedicated to the *āmīkṣā*—which is for the purpose of consecrating the *vaniṣṭhu*—is not otherwise established. Therefore, there is also an exclusion of the original consumption of the *iḍā*.

For this very reason, it should also be understood that the *vaniṣṭhu* [omentum] undergoes the acquisition of properties such as purpose (*artha*) and so forth, just like the archetypal (*prakṛta*) case.
Maṇḍana states: "One should perform the offering of the *vaniṣṭhu*.
Śaṅkara states: "The *vaniṣṭhu* is also a sublater (*bādhaka*)."

"Oṃ: By proximity to the *vaniṣṭhu*, the term *uruka* denotes the omentum (*vapā*). Regarding the intended meaning, the text reads: 'Do not cut the *vaniṣṭhu*, thinking it to be the *uruka*. In this regard, there is a deliberation as to whether the meaning is 'do not cut the *vaniṣṭhu*, thinking it to be similar to the *uruka*,' or rather 'do not cut the *vaniṣṭhu*, thinking it to be the omentum (*uruka*'). In response to this inquiry, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):"

By the word *uruka*, there is a designation of the omentum (*vapā*); it would be a designation of the omentum. [Regarding] the cutting of the omentum, the locus of the cutting is the *vani*. 3416. [The cutting of the omentum is not...]
In that very context, there is a restriction regarding the designation of subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*).
However, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) belong to the sacrificer.

Since the act of measuring is to be enjoined as a primary operation, and because there is a scriptural statement regarding an operation performed by another, these rites also pertain to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), as in the case of "the priests wearing golden garlands."
Because it is not subject to command (*avidheya*), there is no restriction to the *adhvaryu* priest.
Nor is there a connection here through the use of the *parasmaipada* ending, as in the case of the *soma-pūrvavadha*, because of the counter-positioning [of the argument].

The meaning of the Sūtra is that there is a restriction to another agent; for the root *snā* has a *svarita* accent, and due to its presence, its meaning—namely, the purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*)—is established as being like the ritual action itself, pervading the respective place and time.
Therefore, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are performed by the master alone.
Since they reside in the agent, they are useful for generating capacity in the person who acts as the agent.

As for the purificatory rites—such as wearing a golden necklace and so forth—which are prescribed generally for all, [the question arises]: "Are the purificatory rites, such as shaving and the rest, for the Adhvaryu priest or for the master alone?"

However, since they are specifically prescribed for those [priests] alone, it is not the case that even there— alternatively, because the Adhvaryu is capable, those [rites] belong to him in that location; thus,

the designation (*samākhyā*) is a restrictive rule, and having reached the state of being connected to the preparatory acts that bring about [the result], the priests perform their own respective duties through that restriction.
It will be stated that [one] purchases [the priests] because of the absence of [other] means;
their activity is the consecration (*saṃskriyā*) performed for the sacrificer. According to Maṇḍana, acts such as shaving (*vapanādi*) reside in the master (*svāmin*).

Bhāṭṭa: The acts of shaving and so forth are purificatory rites for the sacrificer (*phalisaṃskāra*), according to the traditional designation (*samākhyāna*). Śaṅkara: "The purificatory rites for males belong to the sacrificer. However, by virtue of a specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*), they are performed by the Adhvaryu priest.
Therefore, the Adhvaryu [performs them] for the priests as well, using a razor, a wooden staff, and water.

And having taken [the hair], the shaving of the sacrificer's hair and so forth, the cleaning of the teeth, the bath, and the actions for the purpose of shaving—such as the shaking [of the head]—are to be performed by the sacrificer, just like the anointing and smearing, according to the context of the piling (cayana). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the established conclusion is: the mantras recited at the time of shaving are to be employed according to their heard number without restriction; thus, by means of the word "he shaves" (*vapate*), the agency for that act belongs to the sacrificer who is the recipient of the fruit of the shaving. (Bhāṣya 10.5.14.8)

It is understood that for him [the sacrificer] as well, there are acts such as shaving, which—by virtue of being the substratum for the acts of cutting and shaving—are purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the sacrificer that assist the primary ritual. Just as in the expression "the pot cooks," his status as the agent is established; taking that into account, these acts do not merely assist the officiating priests.
(Vi. 3.7.2) Acts such as shaving are purificatory rites, as seen in the formula: "Therefore, I shave my hair."

As for the practice where, by the injunction of the sacrificer himself, all the priests wear golden garlands and [the text says] "having had themselves shaved, they shave," and so forth— this applies to the Vājapeya sacrifice because of the cutting [of hair], as in the case of the *kulakṣura* (family-shaver); and the wearing of red turbans applies to all the priests,
based on their status as performers of the ritual action.

Because the barber is the agent by virtue of being the instigator (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) of that [act], there are purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as shaving and so forth; hence the usage "he causes the sacrificer to shave" (*yajamānaṃ vāpayati*), etc. And thus, in the statement "he shaves" (*vapate*), since the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is justified by taking the [barber] as the locus (*ādhāra*) rather than the agent, the purificatory rites such as shaving with a razor are prescribed in the Yajurveda.

Even if one were to assume that the intention (*tātparya*) is for [the sacrificer] to be the agent of the grasping, there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*). Therefore, regarding the omission of the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as sowing the seeds, since there is no evidence for a restriction that the sacrificer must be the agent for one who has bones or one who is authorized by a substitute (*mutādhikārin*), the position of the Karman [is maintained]. As for the question, "What occasion is there for a restriction that the Adhvaryu priest must be the agent?"—in the case of the barber (*nāpita*) being the agent, even for those who have bones or are authorized by a substitute, there is likewise [an absence of such a restriction]. However, in the *Soma* sacrifice, because of the form "he sows for the gods" (*pravapati devabhyaḥ*), which uses the *parasmaipada*, there is an omission [of the agent's role].
This is to be understood from the following:

because of the use of the word [in the text], after the Adhvaryu has performed the giving and the shaving, he hands over the razor to the barber, as prescribed by the injunction: "He gives the razor to the barber," who is the one performing the service of the preparatory rites such as shaving; therefore, that [action] indeed has him as its agent.

Thus, for one who thinks in this way, agency does not exist in the form of the agent (*kartṛtva*), but rather in the form of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*); this should also be understood as expressed by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Therefore, it is said: "Darkness alone... (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.7.2).

In such cases as "they shave [him]," "he cuts with a razor," and "he initiates him with a staff," the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending is heard as an additional indication that the agents are the barber (*niṣanta*) and the hair-cutter (*tanāpita*), even though there is a requirement for the act of cutting. (Sūtra 3.8, p.

54). Since the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) ending is justified by taking the agent to be the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) on the basis of the substratum [of the action], the prohibition of shaving applies to him. However, in the case of the *āghāna* (fire-consecration), because another intervening operation not previously mentioned is also enjoined, it is indeed intended that the Adhvaryu priest be the agent.
The prohibition of unseen action (*adṛṣṭakriyā*) performed by another [is established].

However, in the proper place, it is indeed one's own activity; for even the *parasmaipada* form "he bathes" (*snāti*) is used in reference to shaving, fasting, and austerity within the modifications of the *āmīṣomīya* sacrifice and others, whereas when the agent is another, the usage is simply "he causes to bathe" (*snāpayati*). Thus, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is no going [to a different location].
Or [as stated] at Vārttika 3.7.16, page 1078:
regarding the section on vomiting (vamanādhikaraṇa) concerning shaving (vapana),
purifying (pāvana), anointing (añjana), and smearing (abhyañjana), it should be understood that these apply when there are many sacrificers (bahuyajamāna).

The *vapāśrapaṇī* (the two omentum-roasting spits) do not constitute a *tantra* (common procedure) among animals of different species; rather, in certain *ahīna* sacrifices, there is a common time for the sacrificers regarding each individual ritual act (*padārtha*) characterized by [repetition] three times or more, as in the *sautrāmaṇī*. (Mīmāṃsākośa, p.
1936; Soma. 5.12.4). There is no *tantra* for the *kumbhī* (pot), the *śūla* (spit), and the *vapāśrapaṇī*.
In this regard, the *vapā* (omentum) is offered in its entirety.
(Bhāṣya 10.7.8.23; though the formal discussion [*adhikaraṇa*] should be consulted).
At the *Vājapeya*, although the sacrificer is one who takes four portions (*caturavattin*), the *vapā* must nevertheless be prepared as five portions (*pañcāvattā*).

The sacrificial animal (paśu) for Prajāpati is similar to [the norm]. Mīko., p. 164: "At the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana), they proceed with the omentum (vapā) and the entrails (pā). Regarding the statement in *Abhiṣoma* 1935, "'The pot (kumbhī), the spit (śūla), and the omentum-cooking ladle (vapāśrapaṇī) constitute a single performance (tantra),' this refers to the Savanīya animal."
The section concerning the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) at the morning pressing (*prātaḥ-savana*) should be consulted.

They proceed with the *caru* at the morning pressing, with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), and with the limbs (*aṅga*) at the third pressing; [the text] will state that "at the Vājapeya, at the *Prājāpatya* pressing," three pressings are to be performed. Thus, it indicates that for the animals, the procedure (*tantra*) for the offering of the limbs and so forth is common to all.
Dvaidhasūtra 12.2.132:
"The vessels for vomiting are for the purpose of vomiting.

In the case of vomiting the Vedic Soma, they proceed at the morning pressing with an offering to Soma-Indra, at the midday pressing with a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and at the third pressing with the limbs [of the animal]; this is the expiation."

In the case of the phrase "at each pressing" (*savane*), although there is only one Savanīya animal, it is prescribed at different times. The same applies to the rule regarding the consumption [of the Soma]. (Vi. 12.2.13)

The cooking of the omentum (*vapā*) is prescribed in the *Āhavanīya* fire; the Bhāṣya states: "They recite this: 'One should offer a pap (*caru*) for Soma-Indra... [for one who has vomited Soma]'; there is a prohibition regarding this cooking of meat in the Vedic fire. In this regard, there is a doubt (Bhāṣya 12.2.16).

Regarding the omenta—specifically the omenta of the Vājapeya sacrifice—if there is vomiting of the Soma drink, whether that drinking of Soma be worldly (*laukika*) or Vedic, the offering to Soma-Indra (*somendraścaruḥ*) must be performed; furthermore, there is no sprinkling with the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings.

(See Mīmāṃsākośa). What is worldly drinking of Soma, and what is Vedic? This is to be seen under the principle of "sprinkling with the remnant of the *prayāja*" (*prayājaśeṣābhidhāraṇanyāyaḥ*), page 2785.
It is said:

The Vedic drinking of Soma occurs in the Jyotiṣṭoma and its modifications. However, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual properties (*dharmas*) belonging to the original model (*prakṛti*) to the offering of the omentum (*vapā*).
Saṃkarṣa: The drinking of Soma in the worldly context occurs in the *sattras*, *atirātras*, and *daśarātras* due to the power of the constituent elements (dhātu-sāmarthya). See Mīmāṃsākośa, p.

653, regarding the section on "the original *avadāna* [cutting] on a single potsherd" (*avadānaṃ prākṛtaṃ eka-kapāle*) when the Soma is being pressed; one should consult that section for what the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is. Regarding the "disorder of drinking" (*pānavyāpac*), see the relevant discussion there.
It is the same in this case: the *iṣṭi* should apply to worldly vomiting, not to Vedic vomiting;
for the term "omentum" (*vapā*) refers to the *ūrūka* by way of its being a synonym for fire.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is indicated by the word *aditi*.

Just as in that case— where, as stated on page 344 of the *Doṣasaṃyogī* [of the *Mīmāṃsā-kośa*], it was said that because the word *urūka* is heard in the context of the *agnipraṇayana*, its meaning cannot be understood in a worldly sense— so too here, in this section concerning the designation of the omentum (*vapā*), the relevant *adhikaraṇa* should be consulted.

Due to the combination of defects, there occurs the hearing [of the following]: "He who vomits Soma is deprived of his sense organ or his vigor; this contradicts the science of self-preservation regarding the excision of the omentum. (Sūtra, p.
4). In the world, [this is known] through the efficacy of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

When emesis has been improperly practiced, there occurs a disorder of the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātusāmyavyāpad*). Through the improper performance of the ritual, the time for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is missed;
thus, a transgression arises.
For according to the scripture, there would be no fault in the Vedic rite.
In that regard (at Jaiminīya Sūtra 12.1.16 and 12.1.4–5), the remainder is to be recited; thus, when [the rule] is enjoined by the word "iti" and then ceased, there is no fault.

Just as with the omentum (*vapā*), even if only the heart and other parts are offered as the five-fold portion (*pañcāvatta*) in the *jyotiṣṭoma* animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, nevertheless the act of drinking (*pāna*) is accomplished therein. Why? Because it is performed.
Since the meaning of the statement is [as explained], there would be no fault.

Therefore, regarding the worldly [practice], in the case of the *paśu* sacrifice to Agni and Soma, just as with the omentum (*vapā*), when all the limbs are damaged, the offering should be made to Soma-Indra; this is to be seen in the section concerning "the five-fold cutting" (*pañcāvattatva*) on page 120.
Or— this too is indeed an *anārabhyavāda* (independent injunction).
"The Pratiprasthātṛ prepares the *caru* for Soma-Indra and the two omentum-spits" (*Viṣṇu-dharmottara* 10.7.8).
"One who vomits Soma should offer [the sacrifice]";
in that case as well, just as before, the procedure (*tantra*) regarding the omentum-cooking spoons (*vapāśrapaṇī*) applies to the eleven animal sacrifices (*aikādaśina-paśu*).
Furthermore, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is also examined.

Regarding the drinking of worldly *soma* (as a medicinal elixir), Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1306, states: "In the case of the eleven sacrificial animals (*ekādaśina-paśu*), when vomiting occurs after [the *soma*] has been prepared, is there a sacrifice to Soma-Indra (*somendra-yāga*) for the worldly [case], or for the Vedic [case], or is there a common procedure (*tantra*) for the pot (*kumbhī*), the spit (*śūla*), and the omentum-cooking vessel (*vapāśrapaṇī*) in both cases?
In this regard, the general position is indicated by the term "tadvat" (in the same manner).
Mī. Ko. 428: Section on Emission (vamanādhikaraṇa) — Section on Emission (vamanādhikaraṇa)

The principle "But because of a defect, there should be an *iṣṭi* sacrifice in the case of worldly [liquor]" (*doṣāt tviṣṭilaukike syāt*) is extended [by analogy]. Alternatively, both sections are extended as established conclusions (*siddhānta*) even to the two other sections, because they possess a prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by virtue of some specific distinction.
In that very context, since the substance has already been offered through Vedic drinking, there is never again a need for a remedy; such is the meaning of the injunction for the *iṣṭi*.
In the worldly case, however, when emesis has failed due to the absence of the qualities of an elixir (*rasāyana*), a decline in the sensory faculties and vitality is possible;
it is not as utterly impossible as in the case of dropsy (*jalodara*).
Furthermore, the sacrifice heard to be performed upon such a conjunction is understood from the *Atharvaveda*.
Therefore, it should apply there. Because of the fault [in the other case], it should apply to the Vedic [act] by implication; there would be no fault in the case of the worldly [act].
Commentary: It may occur in the event of an accident involving the drinking of the Vedic [liquor], but not in the case of the worldly [liquor].
Why? Because of a defect.
Here, a connection with a defect is heard in the text: "He is indeed deprived of his vigor by means of the sense organ.
But when [the rite] is performed for the sake of balancing the bodily humors (dhātu) in the worldly context, nothing is defective.
For indeed, in the world, people drink that [medicine] for the very purpose of inducing vomiting and so forth.

Even if this were a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), nevertheless, in order to avoid the assumption of a separate result, it is logical to assume that it pertains specifically to the Vedic context.

Or rather, why is it said that these two [rites] occur in the Vedic context by virtue of those very reasons, such as their commonality with Vedic elements? For Vedic character is not possible in the case of vomiting, since it is not enjoined by scripture (*acoditatvāt*).

Therefore, whatever fault constitutes a reason for [the rite] being directed toward worldly purposes would likewise apply in the case of Vedic subjects; for it is said: "The performance [of the consumption] is enjoined as ending with complete digestion;
if that [consumption] fails, the result of the primary act will not occur, just as before.
Yet, there is no fault in the failure of the worldly drinking, because the drinking is intended solely for the purpose of vomiting.
Even if that were the case, its remedy would be found in medical science (*vaidyaka*), and thus there would be no need for the Vedic injunction.
However, regarding the drinking prescribed by the Veda, since the text mentions "proper digestion," the ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) must be understood as ending with digestion;
and that [digestion] is frustrated by vomiting.
Consequently, due to the deficiency of the primary result, the sacrifice is understood to belong to the branch [of the Veda] that shares that same basis.

Now, however, since this [act] is for the sake of a result, its cessation from the merely worldly—based solely on the assumption of a result—is even more clearly understood. But in the case of the Vedic [act], the drinking is indicated by the vomiting; therefore, the sacrifice belongs to one who is situated within the ritual (*ṛtu*), which makes the application (*saṃcara*) easy.
Śā— "In that case, since both [options] are equally defective, it should be done in a worldly manner;
for here there is the defect that vomiting leads to the loss of the senses and virility.
This being the position, the following is the sequence.

"In the world, indeed, no fault is found in drinking for the sake of vomiting; however, in the Veda, drinking is prescribed up until the point of complete digestion. But in the Veda, due to a deficiency in the ritual, it arises as a means of expiation."
In that case, the injunction for expiation has a required purpose,
because it is an injunction of what is required rather than a mandate for what is not required.
Therefore, the sacrifice is indeed for the sake of the ritual union, and its fruit is not to be conceived in this [other] way.

Soma: As for the meaning of the sūtra—[it is that] even the mishap of drinking Soma is merely a worldly [event], like the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the acceptance of a horse-gift, which serves as the occasion (*nimitta*).

Ke: What is the connection of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) here? Ci: "Is there a doubt regarding the sense-faculty (*indriya*) in the worldly [case] or in the Vedic [case], based on the vomiting of Soma?"
Therefore, in the world, vomiting is prescribed for the sake of removing visible defects;

drinking [liquor] is for the purpose of vomiting itself and is not considered a defect in worldly practice. However, in the Veda, it is for the purpose of digestion; thus, one vomits in order to eliminate the defects.

Bhaṭṭa: Even though it was not specifically commenced [in that context], the sacrifice heard in the scripture—“Verily, he who vomits Soma is deprived of his senses and vigor; for one who may be a vomiter of Soma, one should offer this two-oblation pap of cooked rice to Soma and Indra”—should apply to the vomiting of Vedic Soma, and not to that of worldly [Soma].
For, due to the fear of [scriptural] inconsistency and other defects, it is first of all untenable that the *jyādi*-oblations serve both purposes.

Nor can it be assumed that this rite serves to remove a defect, as in the case of the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi* sacrifice, because that [latter] pertains solely to the secular domain; for while the destruction of sensory power (*indriya*) and vigor (*vīrya*) mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) results from vomiting, the fact that this [vomiting] is for the purpose of removing that [defect] is directly perceived. Furthermore, since medical science prescribes the drinking of Soma specifically for the purpose of inducing vomiting, it is illogical for that [Soma] to cause the destruction of the senses and so forth. Therefore, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the term "destruction of sensory power and vigor" refers to the deficiency of the ritual itself; thus, it is proper that this sacrifice has the purpose of remedying that deficiency.

Furthermore, because the consumption [of the Soma] ending with proper digestion is for the purpose of the disposal of the remnant—as indicated by the words of the mantra, "May this speech of mine not pass beyond my navel"—there is a deficiency of the sacrifice (*ṛtuvaiguṇya*) in the event of vomiting.

Consequently, just as in the case of the gift of a horse, although vomiting is not prescribed by Vedic injunction, there is no contradiction in the *iṣṭi* being a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the intended specific sacrifice.
Maṇḍana says: "If one vomits after drinking what is enjoined by the Veda, there shall be a penance."
Śaṅkara says: "The sacrifice [is prescribed] for vomiting after consuming the Soma.

Regarding the *vamaneṣṭi* (the sacrifice for vomiting), as stated in [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.3.2–3]: "He who vomits Soma should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Indra," the use of the relative pronoun *yaḥ* indicates that the sacrifice and the vomiting have the same agent; therefore, the sacrifice is to be performed only when the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) vomits.

Su. Pṛ. 1512: The *vamaneṣṭi* (the offering for vomiting). The ritual dedicated to Soma and Indra (*saumendra-karman*), by virtue of being an auxiliary to the act of vomiting, benefits the one who has vomited the *soma*; furthermore, it is capable of benefiting the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) alone without obstacle. Consequently, since the ritual for Soma and Indra is performed by the sacrificer as it is intended for his sake, and because it is prescribed as having the same agent as the vomiting (in the injunction: "He who vomits *soma* should offer"), the ritual for Soma and Indra occurs only upon the vomiting of the sacrificer.
