p. 1512: In the *vamaneṣṭi*, the fact that it is occasioned by the vomiting of Vedic *soma* depends upon the authority of the *arthavāda*. p.
There is a scriptural injunction for an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the case of the vomiting or purging of *soma*.
Or:
"A pigeon today is better than a peacock tomorrow"—this is the maxim. (Vārttika 3.1.2.6, p. 785).

*Sāhasī*. 676 | ⚑ Regarding the term *vara*: "A cow is indeed a *vara*, an excellent *vara*; another, a milch cow, is an excellent *vara*; another, a bull, is an excellent *vara*. This meaning of the word *vara* should be understood as stated by the teacher Āpastamba. *Soma*. 3181 |
⚑ The maxim of the assembly of excellent cows (varagoṣṭhīnyāya).
*Goṣṭhī* means many cows or many voices standing together; according to Amarasimha, "goṣṭhī" means an assembly. It refers to a specific place for mutual conversation.
A *varagoṣṭhī* is an assembly for choosing a bridegroom;
just as in such an assembly a single task—such as the marriage ceremony—is accomplished by bowing before the lotus-feet of the chosen bridegroom, so it is in the present case as well.
[Sāhasī 20]

The maxim "choosing a bride for the sake of killing the groom" (varaghātāya kanyāvaraṇam) means that one does not marry off a daughter for the purpose of slaying the groom. These two maxims share the same scope and the same meaning; they clearly intend to convey that when there is a possibility of falling into an undesirable consequence, even if a thing is desired, it should not be accepted.

The impetuous one. 153, 154 | ✱ Regarding the granting of boons as the duty of the Adhvaryu priest during the Abhicayana sacrifice at the laying down of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks: "Whoever should lay down this brick, he shall grant three boons."
The grain called *varaka* is unwholesome; it should be substituted for that [other grain].
Bhāṣya 6|3|6|20.
*Varaṇa* (the act of choosing) is a request for the purpose of engaging those who are extremely eminent.
Vārttika 3.7.1.24. *Varaṇa* should produce those [priests (*ṛtvij*)] required for the ritual, just like the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration); it will thus serve a visible purpose.
For those whose scriptural statement is, "The choosing [of the priests] is desired with the *ṛtu* and *traipāda* [mantras]," their choosing is performed with those very mantras.
(Saṃkalpa 3|4|12; Mīko, p. 1243).
For those [whose view is] that "it is performed with the *ṛtu* and *traipāda* [mantras]..."
In this regard, the governing principle (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.

Since the selection (*varaṇa*) of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is for the purpose of addressing them, there should be no such selection in a *sattra* sacrifice, because [the participants] are one's own kin.
Thus, in the *sattra* form of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there should be no selection of officiating priests.

In the case of the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*), the formal selection (*varaṇa*) of the priests is for the purpose of propitiation (*ānamana*), because in a sacrificial session (*satra*), the performance of the ritual is one's own duty;
since in a *satra* all participants are both sacrificers (*yajamāna*) and priests (*ṛtvij*), the performance of the ritual is exclusively one's own duty and not that of another.
However, in the Full Moon sacrifice, the performance of the ritual is not one's own duty for the priests; therefore, it is logical that the selection there is for the purpose of propitiation.

Therefore, the established conclusion is that there is no formal selection (*varaṇa*) in a sacrificial session (*sattra*). [Kumārila states: "The selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is for the purpose of honoring them" (Jaimini Sūtra 10.2.1.35).

Since the Adhvaryu and others are mentioned in the initiation (*dīkṣā*) formulas, both selection and maintenance (*bharaṇa*) would have to be performed; therein lies the "selection of the officiating priests."
Thus it is contradicted.
Vārttika 3.7.16.33, page 1098:
"The choosing [of priests] is for the purpose of honoring the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)."

In the *satra* sacrifice, there is no formal selection (*varaṇa*) of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because such a selection would result in the loss of their status as one's own agents (*svakarmatva*), and because both prayer and selection are impossible with respect to oneself. (Sūtra 3.7, p. 35). Regarding the selection of the officiating priests: is it directed toward each individual part or toward the collective whole? What, then, is the correct view here? It is directed toward the collective whole.
That being so, the action is accomplished by the agent without interruption (Bhāṣya 11.8.12.5).
As for what is said— that the selection is made with reference to the collective— that is incorrect.
The selection (*varaṇa*) must also be performed individually;
that is, the selection of each [priest] separately.
In the archetype (the *Jyotiṣṭoma*), the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) serves a visible purpose, namely, for the sake of securing their consent (*ānamana*).
Bhāṣya 10.2.1.0.135; Saṃkalpa 2.3.1.
Choosing is the choosing.

The selection (*varaṇa*) is prescribed for the sake of accomplishing the presence of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) denoted by the word *ṛtvik* (Sūtra 3.7, p. 36). And this selection takes place prior to the commencement of the ritual action;
because it does not remain as a residual element (*avaśeṣa*) for subsequent [actions], it is common (*tantra*) to all.
By that, all purposes are accomplished in the Rājasūya sacrifice;
such is the opinion of the Bhāṣya.
The view of the Vārttika, however, is that the Vedic selection (*varaṇa*) must be performed separately for each ritual act, whereas the worldly selection may be common (*tantra*).
Bhāṣya 1.4.15:
"The sacrificer, desiring to perform the rite, should announce the Soma to those Brāhmaṇas who are to be selected."
"‘He announces the Soma to them,’ so says Āpastamba.

And the manner of announcing the Soma is shown in the Kalpa-sūtra: ‘I shall sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma, which has the Agniṣṭoma as its final form, the Rathantara as its Prṣṭha-stotra, and a gift of one hundred and twelve cows; in that sacrifice, you be the Udgātṛ,’ and so forth.
The selection (*varaṇa*) may be performed as a single ritual act even for the purpose of a thousand *yajyās*, and when it serves an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
(Vārttika 3.5.186, p.
1016). "Selection" (*varaṇa*) means [the act] preceded by hospitality, such as [addressing someone] with the words "O Agnihotṛ," and so forth.

Because the word *varuṇapraghāsa* is well-known in common usage as denoting dropsy (*jalodara*), one whose abdomen swells due to the influx of water is said to be "seized by Varuṇa" (*varuṇagṛhīta*) on account of being afflicted by that disease called Varuṇa. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1493). The deity Varuṇa is the bestower of the disease of dropsy.
VI. 3.4.15. Varuṇapāśa is the disease of dropsy.
VI. 3.4.16. Varuṇapraghāsas is the second section among the Cāturmāsyas.
VI. 7.1.3. One should sacrifice with the Varuṇapraghāsas during the rainy season (Cāturmāsya).
The performance of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices is a single-day rite, because they occur at one time and have a common beginning and conclusion.

Regarding the performance of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices prior to the *upti*, there is the injunction: "Having spread [the under-layer] once, one should pour [the clarified butter] twice" (Saṃkarṣa. 3.1.22; Mīko. p. 1693).

Demonstrating the relevant section concerning the statement, "If one should sacrifice in the Cāturmāsya rites prior to the *upti*," the re-enactment of the kindling of the fire (*agnimantha*) and other rites in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices should belong to the southern sacrificial area (*dakṣiṇavaihārika*).

Bhāṣya 1.1.15: In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, there is a difference of location between the primary rite and its subsidiary, because of the scriptural statement: "They perform the Avabhṛtha in the waters.
Bhāṣya 1.1.15: [This refers to] the injunction of another distinct rite possessing the characteristics of the Avabhṛtha within the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices.
1|1|15|63–66. See the section *mīko.* p. 603, "The injunction of a separate rite possessing the characteristics of the *avabhṛtha* in the Varuṇapraghāsas.

In the Varuṇapraghāsas, the word *avabhṛtha* enjoins a separate rite connected with those characteristics by means of the extension (*atideśa*) of the characteristics of the Soma-sacrifice *avabhṛtha*.
Vi. 7|1|4: In the Varuṇapraghāsas, the performance of the offerings to Agni and others is distinct from that of the offering to the Maruts.

1|1|15|34–42. In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, the Adhvaryu places the oblations in the northern sacrificial area (*vihāra*), while the Pratiprasthātṛ places them specifically in the southern one. This is a scripturally enjoined (*vācanikī*) arrangement based on location (*deśataḥ*). Bāla. pṛ. 18. Regarding the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) in the Varuṇapraghāsas, there is the statement heard as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*): "They scatter [the earth] here" (*upātra vapanti*).
This refers to the northern altar in the Varuṇapraghāsas.
Due to the absence of *medhā* (the sacrificial animal), the auxiliary rites (*aṅgāni*) are performed according to the *tantra* (common procedure).

It should not be argued here that the original *āsādana* (placing) itself is [the locus], because a difference in location is heard [in the text]; for since that [original placing] is intended for the *āhavanīya* fire—which is suitable for *homa*—it lacks the required purpose [for the present context]. Furthermore, since a difference in location is perceived even in the *homa*, it is understood through the force of the context that the injunctions for the performance of those [auxiliaries] pertain specifically to that location; thus, there is a difference in the auxiliaries due to the difference in location. This is not the case, however, because if one were to enjoin multiple qualities such as location and agent by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the placing, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Likewise, if the specific placing were qualified by the number of the oblations (*haviḥ*), there would be a syntactical split due to the qualification by a specific location.

Therefore, in that context, immediately after the act of placing (*āsādana*), a subsequent act of placing qualified by a specific location is enjoined with reference to the Maruts in the latter sentence; whereas in the former sentence, having accepted that the vessels containing the *vigraha* are the objects of reference through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there is a subsequent act of placing qualified merely by location. This is because the participation of the Adhvaryu is established solely by the force of the name (*samākhyā*).

Consequently, since two acts of placing—which do not have their archetypal functions (*aprākṛta-kārya*)—are enjoined with different locations, this does not constitute an injunction for the performance of another purpose (*anyārtha-prayoga-vidhitva*).

Or, let there be an injunction for placing [the offering] within the very context of the original action (*prakṛta-kārya*), or let the original placing itself be enjoined by extension (*atideśa*) according to its prior nature; even so, this is not an injunction for the performance of the sacrifice (*yāga-prayoga-vidhi*). For while it is possible to enjoin the location with respect to the mere act of placing, there is no evidence for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the sacrifice. Or, even if the location were enjoined with respect to the sacrifice itself, since there is an indication in the nominative case—as in "those [offerings] are to be performed in a low voice" (*tā upāṃśu kartavyāḥ*)—this injunction of location applies only to the principal act (*pradhāna-mātra*) and not to the act together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*); thus, there is no authority for the repetition of the subsidiaries.
This being the position reached:

It is true that in both these sentences, according to your own reasoning, there is an injunction for the specific placing (*āsādana*), and according to your own reasoning, it has the nature of a primary function (*prākṛta-kāryatva*) or simply the character of being archetypal (*prākṛtatva*). Nevertheless, since in the archetype that placing is for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice residing therein, if it were performed in a different sacrificial enclosure (*vihāra*), it would result in a non-archetypal function; therefore, by implication, this is indeed an injunction for the performance of the sacrifice.
Furthermore, the act of placing (*āsādana*)—by virtue of its being a form of offering (*nirvāpa*)—is a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of those respective sacrifices.

In this way, even for the nine [offerings], the distinction between two abidings (*vihāra*) and the mutual redundancy of the others are avoided; there is also brevity, because the established order of one follows from the mere establishment of the other.

The statement "eight oblations" (*aṣṭau havīṃṣi*) and "the *māstīm*" cannot be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the objects of action that are already possible, as it would lack the capacity to indicate the intention regarding their abandonment.

Consequently, since there is no hearing of the accusative case in the word "places down" (*āsādayati*), unlike in "he offers in the evening" (*sāyaṃ juhoti*), the injunction must pertain to the very performance of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) characterized by the sacrifice and its accessories—specified by place and so forth—and thus there is no need for repetition.

Furthermore, here in the Varuṇapraghāsas, there is no separate injunction for the performance of the subsidiary rites apart from the injunction for the performance of the primary rite together with its subsidiaries.
Regarding the Varuṇapraghāsas; regarding the Varuṇapraghāsas.

Nor should it be argued that even so, since the result is accomplished by a single performance of the *prasaṅga* (extension) for one who has performed the act once, there is no basis for repetition because the benefit (*upakāra*) for another sacrifice is already established by that very act; and furthermore, since the benefit is obtained, there is no further requirement for the injunction (*ajñā*) for that purpose, and since *prasaṅga* will be explained as applying even when the place is prescribed. For, due to the absence of a restrictive factor regarding which act is the *tantra* (principal) and where the *prasaṅga* occurs—given that the acts are recited within the same *tantra*—the contingency of *prasaṅga* would arise indiscriminately.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the principle "the nature of that [subsidiary] belongs to many," the restriction of the location alone is the indicator of the intent for the subsidiaries to be performed as a *tantra* (once for all) across multiple instances;

for even if that were so, in cases where there is equality—as in the *Sarvatomukha* sacrifice and the like, where four *vihāras* are performed in the four directions by four different *vihāra*-officiants and others—there is no *vinigamanā* (decisive factor) to establish a single *tantra*, and thus, since *prasaṅga* (extension of benefit) is impossible, the repetition of the subsidiaries (*aṅgāvṛtti*) is necessary due to the differences in location, performers, and so forth.
In the present case, however, although *prasaṅga* would apply to the *Māruti* offering by virtue of following the majority, [the situation differs].

Nevertheless, it should be understood that because the statement "Whatever the Adhvaryu does, the Pratiprasthātṛ does the same" indicates an absence of *prasaṅga* (incidental performance), and because the injunction for the performance of the Mārutī sacrifice—qualified by its specific location and performer—is restricted to the mere act of throwing the Mārutī offering and so forth, there is no repetition of the subsidiaries (*aṅgāvṛtti*).
Maṇḍana states: "In the two sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*), there is a difference in the *tantra* (the common performance of subsidiaries);
[it is not the case that there is no difference at all]."
Śaṅkara: "The rule regarding the two sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*) is as follows:
in the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, in the southern enclosure, the mantras of the Pratiprasthātṛ possess distinct qualities from those of the Adhvaryu."
And the mantras, because of their simultaneous occurrence (*saṃnipāta*).

The Commentary states: Since there are two sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*) in the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, there are certain mantras that occur simultaneously—such as those used for taking the clarified butter (*ājya*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and touching (*abhimarśana*). Is their performance (*prayoga*) by way of a single common procedure (*tantra*), or is it distinct (*bheda*)?
This is an inquiry into *tantra*, not an inquiry into incidental application (*prasaṅga*).
In this regard, although the principle of *tantra* (common performance) would apply in order to favor the injunction of the ritual procedure (*prayoga-vacana*), it is stated:
the mantras, such as those for taking up the clarified butter (*ājya-grahaṇa*) and so forth, must be performed separately. Why? Because they are *saṃnipātin* (directly contributing factors).
These mantras, which assist the collective [rite], denote the ritual acts as they arise;
however, in the case of separate rites, the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ perform them separately.
Therefore, they should be employed separately.

Moreover, he will state that the commencement of the ritual action with the instruments [of recitation] occurs at the end of the mantra, according to the rule: "Because the mantras serve the purpose of the instruments, the commencement of the action should occur at the end of the mantra, since this applies to all.
This being the case, the specific distinction is understood as follows: whichever ritual action the mantra has joined with, that action is the one [to which it belongs].

Therefore, there is repetition. Regarding the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, there arises a doubt: should the mantras for the offering (*nirvāpa*) and so forth be recited by either the *adhvaryu* or the *pratiprasthātṛ* together as a single performance (*tantra*), or should they be recited separately by both? In this doubt, one might think that even if recited by only one, they would be capable of producing the memory [of the rite] for both. However, because the mantra beginning with "I offer" (*nirvapāmi*) is a self-addressed invocation, a single performance is not possible; thus, there must be a separate application for each of the two.
Because there is the possibility of performing [the rite] either once or repeatedly, this consideration of *tantra* (central performance) and *āvāpa* (repetition) is also undertaken here.
The connection [of this section] arises from the objection that, as in the previous case, the accomplishment of the purpose is not achieved here [in the *soma* sacrifice].

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: the mantras for the pouring out (*nirvāpaṇa*) and so forth must be employed separately, because they are *karaṇa-mantras* (instrumental mantras) and thus come into contact with the action and other factors; and because, since both types of performers can possibly perform the rite, when one has performed it, it is impossible for the action and other factors to come into contact with the other performer.
Is there a difference in the ritual manual (*tantra*) regarding the location and the mantra for extinguishing [the fire] when the monastery is divided?
Since the *tantra* is established by the recollection of both, the one spoken and the one to be spoken should be separate.

Bhaṭṭa: In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, because of the difference in location between the southern and northern sacrificial enclosures (*vihāra*) and the difference in the performers (*kartṛ*), it is established that there is no *tantratā* (commonality) among the ritual acts (*padārtha*).

In that context, regarding the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and so forth, since it is proper to favor the majority [of the rules], the *prasaṅga* (extension of performance) that would otherwise apply to the Māruti offering by the rule of logic is set aside by the scriptural statement: "Whatever the Adhvaryu does, that the Pratiprasthātṛ does. Therefore, those [acts] must indeed be performed separately.
As for the mantras, those whose meaning is identical to the purpose at hand should be recited by the Adhvaryu alone.

Consequently, they consider that when the Adhvaryu has already performed his own ritual action and the Pratiprasthātṛ subsequently performs his own action, because the sequence of the actions of the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ is prescribed, the action performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ is brought to mind by the action performed by the Adhvaryu. Thus, since the requirement for the mantra is fulfilled through *prasaṅga* (incidental fulfillment), there is no separate recitation of the mantras by the Pratiprasthātṛ.

This being the position reached, there is no room for *prasaṅga* (incidental performance) because, in mantras such as "I offer" (*nirvapāmi*), the act of offering is remembered as having the self as its agent due to the first-person address; since such a recollection cannot be obtained from any other source, it must be performed by both. In reality, however, the statement "Whatever the Adhvaryu does" does not enjoin a sequence, as its purpose is merely to indicate the state of incidental performance (*prasaṅga-bhāva*) by prescribing the mere execution of the ritual items (*padārtha*). Furthermore, because the performers are different, even the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) lacks restrictive force.
Therefore, the ritual items accompanied by their respective mantras must be performed simultaneously by both; thus, there is scope for *prasaṅga*.
Maṇḍana: "The recitation must indeed be separate for those [acts] that occur in conjunction. Śaṅkara: "There is no unity of mantra for the two acts of carrying [the fire].
In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, the act of carrying the fire (adhipraṇayana), which is enjoined again by the rule "they carry it twice," is something new (apūrva).

It is neither the ordinary (*prākṛta*) nor the *saumika* [fire-carrying]; rather, having performed the ordinary fire-carrying obtained through extension (*atideśa*), one must again perform the fire-carrying specifically prescribed as a new rule (*apūrva*). (Vi. 7.3.9, Section 2; Vārtika-opinion). In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, the fire-carrying is enjoined again by the rule "they carry [the fire] twice," which refers to the specific fire-carrying (*adhipraṇayana*), and not to that of the Vaiśvadeva or Śunāsīrīya sacrifices.
This re-enjoinment is for the purpose of prescribing the quality of placing the fire on the northern altar (*uttaravedi*).
In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, nine oblations are prescribed.
Among them, the Pratiprasthātṛ performs the offering of the meat for the Maruts in the southern sacrificial area (vihāra),
while the Adhvaryu performs the others in the northern sacrificial area.
In both sacrificial sessions (*vihāra*), the performance is distinct for each group of priests (*jñān*); it is not a single common ritual (*tantra*).
In the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, there is a double repetition of the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.
"Because of the unity of the purpose, there should be a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the subsequent [offerings].
The Commentary states: This other point is considered in that very same context: Should the *āparāmika* oblations be performed with a single ritual procedure, or separately?
What is established? That it is a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). Why? Because there is unity of purpose.
It was stated that a difference [in procedure] arises from a difference in the presiding deities (*adhideva*) among those belonging to the preceding [sections].
In this case, that reason does not exist,
because these [factors] possess a single nature;
therefore, these would constitute a single system (tantra).
Or they are diverse because of the difference in their agents.
The Commentary: They would be diverse.
Why? Because of the difference in their agents.
Those sacrifices belonging to Māruti should be performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ;
the others by the Adhvaryu. If the ritual framework (*tantra*) were common [to both], there would be a deficiency caused by the performance of one of the two [officiants].
Therefore, there is a distinction.

Śā—Furthermore, regarding those subsequent *homās* such as the *patnīsaṃyājas* and so forth, when there is a doubt as to whether they constitute a single performance (*tantra*) or a separate insertion (*āvāpa*), they would constitute a single performance (*tantratva*) like the preceding ones because there is no difference in location.

Even though there is no difference in location, there is a distinction due to the difference in performers; for while the offerings to Marut (*mārutyāḥ*) are performed by the *pratiprasthātṛ*, the others are performed by the *adhvaryu*. Therefore, there is a distinction.
Regarding this: "In that very context, at the Patnīsaṃyāja and other rites, is the ritual procedure (tantra) the same or different?
It is the same because of the unity of the fires; do not say so, for it is precluded by the difference in the performers."
Regarding the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices:
the Bhaṭṭa school holds that in this very case, the *patnīsaṃyāja* and subsequent rites constitute a single performance (*tantra*) because there is no difference in location.

This being the prima facie view, it is countered that since a difference in performers, just like a difference in location, is a cause for a difference in performance, the rites must be repeated there as well, in accordance with that [difference].

Nor should it be argued that since the repetition of the subsidiaries is already established by the mere difference of location (*deśabheda*), and since only the Pratiprasthātṛ is prescribed there as the agent, the distinction between agents does not independently entail a difference in performance; for the opposite could equally be asserted, and in the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*), it is logical that both the agent and the location, by virtue of the injunctions for their own specific performances, entail a difference in performance.
Consequently, even though there is a difference of location in the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings and so forth, there is a repetition [of the action] due to the difference of agents.

In reality, even if there were an injunction for the performance qualified by both place and agent, it would result in an injunction for the performance restricted only to the specific words denoting those respective places and agents through mutual correlative connection (*pārśvika-parasparānvaya*). Consequently, this would lead to the following: the duties performed by the *hautra* priest and others would merely be obtained as occurring in their respective places; however, for those duties not otherwise obtained—such as those to be performed by the *pratiprasthātṛ* priest—there would be no attainment of being performed by that specific agent. Therefore, by this [injunction], the *pratiprasthātṛ* does not become the performer of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and so forth.

For the Mārutī sacrifice does not have the Pratiprasthātṛ as its performer; if it did, then because the primary offerings here would share the same performer, the Patnīsaṃyāja and other rites would also be established by that [shared] attainment. However, since the Mārutī sacrifice has the Yajamāna as its performer and lacks the Pratiprasthātṛ as its performer, the application of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) to the Patnīsaṃyājas occurs by means of the rule: "Whatever the Adhvaryu does..."

For here, since the Adhvaryu is the agent for that ritual act which constitutes a subsidiary to the sacrifice, the Pratiprasthātṛ is enjoined as the agent for that same ritual act when it constitutes a subsidiary to the [other] sacrifice;
consequently, there is a repetition of those acts not previously established.
Maṇḍana states: "There would be a distinction between what is already established and what is not."

The Adhvaryu's duty extends up to the completion of the anvādhāna; and since that [duty] consists of the mantra, the Adhvaryu performs it by means of the mantra. He is said to perform it "by this mantra."

Or rather—it is not like the case of the *anakaraṇa* mantras (those such as "O Agni, giver of life," "O Agni, go to heaven, go to the light," and so forth, which are mantras not employed by means of the particle *iti*); in those cases, the fruit is mentioned for the sake of encouragement (*utsāha*).

How so? For a mantra is enjoined as a means to a distinct action; it either enters into that action directly or into something related to it, thereby attaining the status of a constituent part of the sacrifice.

If it is argued that in the statement "The first consumption belongs to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer" (*vaṣaṭkartuḥ prathamabhakṣaḥ*), only the priority (*prāthamya*) is being enjoined, this is not so; for the consumption qualified by priority is enjoined by means of a compound word (*samasta-pada*). 3.1.10. Since eating is not already established [as a duty], this word does not have the purpose of enjoining the *prābhya* state; rather, it enjoins the very act of eating as qualified by the *prābhya* state. Bhāṣya 3.1.10.31.
Or: "Because one part is not restated separately from the meaning of the compound."
"Like the suggested meaning, this entire unprecedented sense is enjoined by it."

Just as in the case of the statement, "He sacrifices with his own performed [acts] by means of those not implied" (*yathaiva 'vyaṅgyaiḥ svadukṛtaṃ yajati*), the three-fold nature (*trivat*) is not enjoined by restating the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*); rather, first the compounded meaning (*samāsārtha*) is enjoined—so too here, because a complete word lacks the capacity for partial syntactic connection (*ekadeśānvaya*) due to its connection with another word, the phrase "the eating of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer" (*yo vaṣaṭkartṛbhakṣaḥ*) cannot be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of a non-sentence. Indeed, prior to the formation of the compound, a connection between the eating (*bhakṣa*) and the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer (*vaṣaṭkartṛ*) is not logical, because a compound is impossible when there is mutual expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*).
But surely, "a compound is indeed possible even for a predominant term that is dependent";
thus, even though there is a connection with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer,
the compound is tenable.
This would be so if the act of eating alone were dependent;
however, in this case, both [the eating and the offering] are dependent because of their connection with the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call.
For the eating is not the cause of the offering.
What then? It is the status of being the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer; therefore, the syntactical connection results in "the first [partaker] is the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer.
Consequently, there would be a manifest inconsistency.

Furthermore, in the phrase "the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer’s portion," there is the fault of a qualified reference (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*) when one attempts to construe it with the act of eating, because the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer is not necessarily connected to the act of eating by virtue of that act alone.
Furthermore, because the act of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer involves multiple other actions,
if this were a restatement (*anuvāda*), then both the eating of everything and all the activities of every *vaṣaṭ*-utterer would have to be enjoined;
and that is impossible to perform.
Therefore, this is an injunction for a first consumption that is not distinct from the consumption by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer;
and because of the mutual restriction between those two, they are of an entirely identical nature.
Consequently, to whatever extent there is a *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, to that same extent there is the first consumption.
Page 1007. The establishment of the right to consume [the Soma] for the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer.
The term "Hotṛ" applies to anyone who merely utters the *vaṣaṭ*.

Because of the statement, "The Hotṛ sits down first before the *havirdhāna* [shed]," there arises the misconception that the Hotṛ alone is the first to consume [the Soma]. By these two sūtras (3.1.38–39), it is established that the word "Hotṛ" applies to anyone who merely utters the *vaṣaṭ*.
Or [it may be] so. 3|1|13|39.
The *vaṣaṭ*-utterance (*vaṣaṭkāra*) is also a separate cause for the consumption of Soma.
Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1|2|87: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is also a separate cause for the consumption of Soma"—in this regard, the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) should be consulted.
And because of the agency [of the deity], there is the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance.
Regarding this, there is the deity of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance: "He utters the secondary *vaṣaṭ* for Soma in the fire" (*somasyāgne vīhītyanuvaṣaṭkaroti*).
In that regard, there is a doubt: should the deity of the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-utterance be indicated or not?
In this case as well, the same principle applies;
it is extended to another example by means of a certain specific distinction.
Here too, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) is as follows.
Let it be that [the deity] is not perceived because the deities possess three eyes and thus lack a single divine nature;

however, in this case, since the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is enjoined through the employment of the offering-mantra "O Agni, eat the Soma," and because of the injunction regarding Agni as well as the wording of the mantra itself, the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is indeed singular.
Therefore, in the consumption of the Soma that remains from the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*, Agni alone is to be indicated by means of figurative representation (*abhirūpya*).
This being the case, it is replied:
this would be so if the Soma were taken for the purpose of the Droṇakalaśa, the vaṣaṭ-call, or the deity;
what then? It is for the sake of the primary deity.
The *anuvashatkāra* is indeed a disposal (*pratipatti*) rite, for by means of it, the substance already offered for the sake of the primary deity is disposed of.
Therefore, just as the previous drinker—the Adhvaryu or the Hotṛ—is not indicated by another drinking as being connected to the disposal rite, so too is the deity of the *anuvashatkāra*.
For it would only be indicated if, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), an indication were made of that which is connected to the disposal related to Indra.
It is not so.
As it has been said: "Just as when a vessel is emptied from another vessel, the previous vessel is no longer perceived, one should not treat this deity as something ordinary."
Thus (Vārttika, p. 797).
By this, even the thirty-eight deities of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* must likewise be indicated by this very [term].
As for the purpose [of the discussion], it need not be stated at all.

But the Sūtra states: "The deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is not to be indicated [as a separate entity], just like the agent of the *vaṣaṭkāra*. [This is] because the *vaṣaṭkāra* possesses the nature of an agent.
The *Śruti* of this *sūtra*, namely *Kevalānandī*, is to be found on page 426 of the *Mīmāṃsākośa* under the entry: “And the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* [is not performed] because of the agency.
[The text states: “And the *vaṣaṭkāra* (and the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*) [are not performed] because of the agency.
The *vaṣaṭkāra* would not be thus, like the agent of drinking; for by the word *vaṣaṭkāra*, the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is expressed through a secondary indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).”

The performance [of the *vaṣaṭ* call] is not for the sake of a common action due to its being characterized by wisdom; furthermore, because the indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) which serves as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the deity under discussion is not obtained through extension (*atideśa*), the phrase "not thus" is supplied from the preceding sūtra in order to refute that indicative mark.
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1155). The *vaṣaṭ* call is the cause for drinking from the cup (*camasa*), and that belongs to the Hotṛ priest. (Vi. 3.5.10).
The *vaṣaṭkāra* has the purpose of offering. Bhāṣya 12.3.15.35:
The first consumption [of the soma] occurs precisely within the scope of the *vaṣaṭkāra*.

Or: 3|5|10|1. On the sixth day, during the *ṛtuyāja* offerings, the *vaṣaṭkāra* should be performed by the *hotṛ* and other priests following the *graipamanttra* preceded by the head of the *ṛc*, and not merely following the *graipamanttra*.
And in the *tantra* [of the ritual], the *vaṣaṭkāra* is prescribed for the *saumika* [soma] sacrifice (*Bhāṣya* 8.4.12.19):
"The *vaṣaṭkāra* is the cause for consuming.
When there is a conjunction of the *yājyā* and the *vaṣaṭkāra*, then the *vaṣaṭkāra* follows after the *yājyā*.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that when there is an option, the *vaṣaṭkāra* follows immediately after "ye yajāmahe.
[However,] there is no such option between the *yājyā* and the *vaṣaṭkāra*; rather, the *vaṣaṭkāra* must follow the *yājyā* itself.
(Saṃkalpa 4.3.4)
The sacrifice is performed with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, not by the *yājyā* alone; and this sacrifice must be offered without pausing.
Because its purpose is the offering of the oblation (*havis*), it is sacrificed with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, not by the *yājyā* alone.
Or [one may eat] from the *vaṣaṭ* call.
Now, is the name alone the cause for eating? No, we say.
And one should consume [the portion] because of the *vaṣaṭ*-call;
moreover, the *vaṣaṭ*-call is the occasion for consumption.
How so? For it is heard in scripture thus: "The first consumption belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*."

In this case, either only the primacy [of the first portion] is enjoined by the very act of eating it in the morning, or else there is a separate act of eating characterized by primacy, occasioned by the *vaṣaṭ* call.
Herein lies the intention of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position:

in every instance where a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) would involve prolixity (*gaurava*), the injunction, having transferred itself to the subordinate element (*upasarjana*), requires that the primary meaning (*pradhānārtha*) be understood in some way, even if it involves a delay.
Furthermore, because the Hotṛ is the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call, there is an established entitlement to consume from his own cup based on the designation: “Let the Hotṛ’s cup proceed.
Therefore, in that very context, by way of restating the consumption already obtained through designation, only the priority [of the consumption] caused by the *vaṣaṭ* call is enjoined.
Consequently, the consumption must be performed as regulated by the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call.
This being the case, it is replied:
this would indeed be so where it is possible to extract the name and thereby restate the act of eating.
For instance, in this context, priority is not enjoined by way of restating the mere act of eating, because that [priority] would apply even otherwise.
What then? [The phrase] "the portion is for the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer" (*vaṣaṭkartur bhakṣaḥ*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the act of consuming in relation to the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer.

That being the case, a compound with "primacy" (*prāthamya*) is not possible for the act of consuming, which depends on its connection with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer, because of a lack of semantic competency (*asamarthatvāt*).

Now, if it is argued that because of the priority and the predominance of the act of consuming, this consumption—which requires a connection with the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer—is compounded with the first word according to the grammatical rule, "A compound is indeed formed of a predominant element that requires another," even so, that priority is subordinate to the act of consuming; furthermore, since the consumption by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer is caused by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, that priority does not arise from any other cause.
What then? It arises solely through the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance itself.

Because of the connection with the term "of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer," even though primacy is subordinate, it remains dependent [on another factor]; thus, the fault of compounding (*samāsadoṣa*) is indeed evident.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to extract and refer back to the primacy and the act of eating separately, a previously unestablished (*apūrva*) act of eating qualified by the primacy of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer is what is being enjoined.

[Objection: But surely, as seen in the case of "One *sāman* is performed on a triplet of verses for the purpose of praise" (*stotrīyam*), where there is a requirement for a compound, the injunction of a verse (*ṛc*) within a mantra is also observed through a compound; likewise, the injunction of primacy will be possible here.
This is not so;

for even there, it is the compound itself that is enjoined. However, since the *ṛc*s are already established through their general application, whereas the threefold nature (*trivalpa*) is not, it is said that the injunction concerns the threefold nature.

In this case, however, a qualified injunction is made regarding the very meaning of the compound—the priority of consumption up until the *vaṣaṭ*-call—which is intended to convey a specific purpose that cannot be expressed otherwise.

Therefore, having performed the consumption [of the soma] everywhere on account of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, the consumption on account of the designation (*samākhyā*) must be performed in the cup (*camasa*).
It is thus established that priority does not belong to that [cup] alone.
The purpose [of this discussion] is as stated in the respective positions.

The Sūtra, however, states: "The *vaṣaṭ*-utterer should not only consume [the soma] from his own cup by virtue of that designation, but should also consume it from other vessels on account of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance.
(Tautā. And he should consume [it] because of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance.
This is the Siddhāntasūtra.
In the seventh section (adhikaraṇa), it was stated that the name (samākhyā) is the cause for the consumption of Soma.
This sūtra is intended to establish another such cause in that very same context.

The word "ca" (and) has the purpose of including another ground. Just as one should consume the Soma by virtue of the designation (*samākhyā*), so too should one consume the Soma by virtue of the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
The word "vidhitvāt" (because it is an injunction) is carried over from the preceding sūtra.

Since the injunction "The first draught belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call" prescribes a drinking characterized by priority, it follows that by this scriptural statement the *vaṣaṭ* call is declared to be the cause for the drinking.
Therefore, whoever utters the *vaṣaṭ* call for a particular draught, he shall drink that first;
thereafter, he shall drink the draught according to its respective designation (*samākhyā*).

In the section [3.5.13.1] beginning with "And one should consume from the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance," regarding the statement "The *vaṣaṭ*-utterer has the first consumption" (*vaṣaṭkartuḥ prathamabhakṣaḥ*), it will be explained that because the two— priority and consumption— are the objects of a single presentation through the compound word, it is not possible to enjoin both consumption and priority here by means of a single part of the term *prathamabhakṣa*.

Because the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance found in the passage "I perform [the offering] for you, O Viśve" (*vaṣaṭ te viśvebhya ākṛṇomi*) lacks independence due to its syntactic connection with the word "I perform" (*ākṛṇomi*), it does not have the purpose of effecting the actual offering (*pradāna*).
Saṃkarṣa 4.3.19:
There is indeed a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the *yājyā* and the *vaṣaṭkāra*, not an option (*vikalpa*).
Regarding the *vaṣaṭkāra*, there is a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of the exhalation, inhalation, and closing of the eyes according to each respective scripture.

In one recensional branch (*śākhā*), it is heard: "Having uttered *vaṣaṭ*, he should exhale; he should blink; by this [exhalation] he bestows breath (*prāṇa*), and by the blinking, sight (*cakṣus*). In another scripture (*śāstrāntara*), it is said: "Having uttered *vaṣaṭ*, he should exhale as much as possible and blink.
In that case, due to the difference between the recensional branches, for some there is a pair of injunctions, while for others there is this other pair.

This being the prima facie view, [the conclusion is as follows]: because it serves the purpose of exhaling (*apāna*), the injunction regarding exhaling is stated for that [act]. Although in some recensions there is an injunction regarding exhaling and blinking (*nimeṣa*) subsequently, this is understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the injunction regarding blinking after the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, due to hearing a subsequent explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Since exhaling and blinking are already established as occurring immediately after the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, in another scriptural tradition there is an injunction specifically for inhaling (*prāṇana*) after the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance; the mention of the other two is merely a restatement for the sake of establishing their sequence. (Saṃkarṣa 4.3.7).

Regarding the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this is an injunction for the Hotṛ priest who desires the death of the sacrificer, [expressed as]: "If one should desire, 'May he be liable to die'.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the injunction for one who desires heaven. — *Saṃkarṣa*.

The statement “If one should desire that someone should die” [regarding the *vaṣaṭ* call] is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the injunction for one desiring heaven. This is because the injunction for one desiring heaven occurs without distinction in the scriptural text following the rule for the *vaṣaṭ* call in the archetype: “If one should desire that someone should die, one should pronounce the *vaṣaṭ* for his *yājyā* in a lower tone; for one desiring heaven, one should pronounce the *vaṣaṭ* loudly like a *kauśa*. For it is possible even for one afflicted by a chronic disease, who has been rejected [by others] and has reached [the point of] death, to have a desire for death.
Otherwise, such a rule for self-slaughter would result in being rendered meaningless in the Smṛtis;
for even though it is mentioned as the subject matter of all the scriptures, no qualification based on a desire for death is observed there,
due to the diversity of human intentions.
In reality, however, having stated "he who would be long-lived," it is understood that this desire resides solely in the *hotṛ* priest;
and that [desire] is directed toward the sacrificer who is the object of hatred,
as indicated by the scriptural mentions of spring and so forth in connection with the *vaṣaṭ*-call.

This is indeed possible; for this very reason, even the Smṛti rule stating, "The officiating priest and the teacher must not be transgressed against," is appropriate as it possesses a perceptible purpose.

Nor can [the injunction] "one should not establish [the fires]" be taken as a specific restriction on the entry [into the rite], because both are possible even as exceptions in certain cases, due to the Vedic text: "He who, upon the birth [of a son], performs this sacrifice, he indeed becomes purified."

For this very reason, in the *prauga-śastra*, after prescribing the recitation of seven triplets (*tṛca*) by stating, "He recites the seven deities," and then saying, "He who may be his Hotṛ should [act] so as to ward off the evil and bring about the auspicious for the sacrificer," the text begins with, "One should do with him as one desires. It continues, "If he should desire, 'May I increase him through his vital breath (*prāṇa*),' he should recite the triplet dedicated to Vāyu for him, omitting either a verse (*ṛc*) or a quarter-verse (*pada*)," and so forth. By means of these specific variations in the triplets and the omission of particular words or quarters, the increase of the sacrificer’s vital breath and other prosperities—desired by the Hotṛ—is established as logically possible.

Therefore, the fruit of the *agnidhāna*—whether it be prosperity (*ṛddhi*) or the fruit [of the sacrifice]—must be accepted as common to both the sacrificer and others, according to the scriptural injunction. And in the present case, although the word "Hotṛ" is not heard, because a sentence of the same type as the *prauga* is heard in the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*, this optional injunction belongs to the *Aitareyins*. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the reply is: since death, which is not ordained for any other purpose, is in every way undesirable, and since there is no other fruit to be gained by that alone beyond it, and because death is not an inevitable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) [of the rite], [it follows that] the death of all [is the result].

It should be noted that there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) even in the case of a verbal cognition whose qualificandum is a specific action such as sacrifice, which possesses a kāraka characterized by agency or one of its correlates, due to the co-occurrence of words in Vedic passages such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) with respect to Vasiṣṭha and others.

Now, an objection: if this is so, then in the interpretation of sentences such as "The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood" (*audumbaro yūpo bhavati*), since the fivefold number—established by the authority of the second-case ending in the scriptural statement "He obtains [cattle] with the animal" (*paśunāpnoti*)—is more appropriate as the object of the sentence regarding the sacrificial post, this would contradict the status of the sacrificial post as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) established in the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*.

If it is argued that for this very reason, one should not accept the status of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the sentence—even on account of the favor of the *senīya* [textual passage]—we say no.

This is because, in the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) implied by the act of the post’s coming into being (*yūpa-kartṛka-bhavana*), nothing other than the post is capable of being construed as its object (*karman*); furthermore, due to the lack of a substratum (*āśraya*), the scripturally stated number five (*pañcatva*) is incapable of application there, which necessitates the acceptance of the post’s status as a subordinate element of the sentence.

Furthermore, it is not possible for the sacrifice under discussion— the one performed with a three-colored animal as enjoined by the injunction "One desiring cattle should offer a *traita* [three-year-old] animal to Soma and Pūṣan"— to have the *audumbara* wood as its substratum (*āśraya*).
Nor does this sentence [serve as a substrate] even if the status of being a substratum is impossible because it does not delimit the substance that serves as its own means of accomplishment.
A sentence [is established] by means of a sentence, or [the establishment] of a sentence by means of sentences. 3448. Of sentences.
Because it possesses meaning, the possibility of being meaningless finds no room; for there is efficacy in the traditional recitation (samāmnāya).

Thus, this entire [recitation] of the Vedic sentences—which are otherwise obstructed by meaninglessness—possesses efficacy in the traditional recitation insofar as it denotes that which has not been previously enjoined.
Otherwise, they would also be subject to sublation.
For example— as stated in the *Bhāṣya*— the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) concerning the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites for rice (*vrīhi*) and the like would become purposeless.

Although [the word] attains the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣitva*) through direct audition (*śruti*), it transcends that; for there is no authority for a sentence in determining the extent of its constituent words beyond what is obtained from the context (*prakaraṇa*). There will be a combination (*saṃcaya*) based on the fact of being a means to the previously mentioned [result]. Therefore, it remains established that [the word] indicates only a single purpose within a combined whole that possesses expectancy. Consequently, the indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than the sentence (*vākya*).
And likewise, in the *bhakṣānuvāka*, there is one sentence with a singular subject and another with a plural subject. Vākyapadīya 3.7.4, p. 851.
The unity of two sentences has been shown again by combining them (3.1.9).
A worldly sentence has as its object that which is already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

According to the principle that "the *vṛhatī* is born," even when there is a difference in verbal forms (*ākhyāta*), there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between one sentence and another sentence due to the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), provided there is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). (In the case of the Agnihotra, the statement "he offers" is indeed a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the form of expectancy.)
Regarding the statement "of the sentence" (mīmāṃsā-vākyasya), as in "one desiring sensory power should sacrifice with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*),
there is no capacity [for the sentence] in the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*);
for the meaning of the sentence is established solely through the capacity of the words (*padaśakti*).

When there is a contradiction between two sentences, as in the case of the *sāmidhenī* verses, one should state that the sentence overrides the meaning of the sentence; for example, "one should recite fifteen *sāmidhenīs*, but seventeen for the Vaidarvya. Even in the absence of both [contradictory] words, because of expectancy, that which is incomplete cannot establish a qualified meaning. For even when syntactic unity (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established as a single sentence, since application (*viniyoga*) is impossible without the expression of a specific injunction, and since linguistic usage is not accomplished without such expression, when there is a connection with a specific occasion (*nimitta*), similarity (*sādr̥śya*) becomes stronger.

Because [otherwise] there would result the fallacy of meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), [the mantra] must form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) with the heard word for the sake of its completion; therefore, it is not proper to assume other words that do not serve a function within the sentence.
(Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.14, p. 840).
It is not logical to interpolate words that have no purpose in the sentences.
Su. Pṛ. 623: A sentence possesses authority because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) with all other expressive statements through universal connection;
its purpose is that of an injunction (*vidhi*).
The section concerning the purposeful statements (*arthavāda*) of sentences:

when sentences fall short of their intended meaning, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) occur; multiplicity of meaning is accepted only as a last resort through the injunction of rites possessing qualities (*saguṇa-karma-vidhāna*).
However, if an excess of meaning is admitted, the result is pointlessness (*ānarthakya*).
Alternatively, regarding the deficient [case] (in the context of the *surā* cup-offering in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice),

Bhāṣya 8.1.16 states that since two types of meaningfulness are observed even when assuming a qualification for one who is not qualified— namely, through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), and supplying words (*vākya*)— [the rule does not apply].
There are faults regarding the purpose of the utterance:

namely, if there is deficiency, there are the faults of [improper] indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*); if there is excess, since the suffix and the base are invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*), there is pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) in employing one of them with the intention of expressing only the other.
Otherwise, even when there is a contrary or obstructed cognition, something remains necessarily implied.
If it is intended that [the effort] consists of the conceptualization of meaning, the conceptualization of linguistic usage, and the faults thereof (as stated in Vākyapadīya, p.
then the pronunciation follows as a matter of course.

Now, the function of a sentence when its utterance is intended is merely to establish the relationship between qualifier and qualified; the comprehension of the meaning follows as a secondary consequence (*anupaṅga*), as in the case of mantras used for recitation (*japa*) or in various branches of knowledge (*vidyā*). (Sūtra, p. 1192) Thus, a sentence uttered once conveys multiple meanings.
Or [the alternative is]:
because of the impossibility of [the word] being "other," there would result the fault of splitting the sentence (vākya-bheda) characterized by repetition. (Vārttika 1.4.16, pp. 143–148)

Page 852: Furthermore, the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) of sentences arises through their combination. For it is not the case that a sentence’s lack of expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) is assumed only when all its constituent parts are present; rather, [the lack of expectancy] for a sentence such as "The initiated one does not give" (*dīkṣito na dadāti*) is established by extending [its application] to the *agnihotra* and other rites. Page 691: The syntactic unity of a sentence with injunctions occurs at the level of the word (*padaikavākyatā*).

Because, in their absence, there would be no connection of that [word] with another sentence for its own sake or for itself. (Page 458) There is no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) by virtue of its relationship as a communicator of meaning. When it is possible for a sentence to have a cause (*hetu*) as its primary purport, it should not be taken as figurative praise (*stuti*).

However, there is no authoritative basis for [the view that] "one performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" and "one sacrifices with curd" [are distinct acts], because of the principle that "there is oneness of sentence (*vākyaikatva*) in these very cases such as *prasaṅga*," and so forth; thus, the cessation [of the action] occurs by this alone, which is an excessive burden for a single sentence to possess the status of multiple sentences (as noted by the *pṛṣṭharakṣakas*). *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 4.1.16. By this very [principle], in cases such as *prasaṅga*, there is oneness of sentence among the statements; therefore, the cessation [of the requirement] occurs by this alone—this is an overburdening of a single sentence to function as multiple sentences. (The *pṛṣṭharakṣakas*)
It becomes Soma. 10|8|5 | Bhā.

This very [process] is the grammatical explanation (*anvākhyāna*) of sentences by means of grammar; it is the state of being human-made (*pauruṣeyatva*), because [grammar] is intent upon providing understanding only when the meaning of a sentence is already apprehended through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). (Vārttika, p. 24, l. 261)
The application of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) belongs to injunctions (*vidhi-vākya*), not to the status of being an effect of phonemes and so forth.
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 14. That [refers] to sentences—namely, Upaniṣadic sentences and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—the section on sentences (Vākyādhikaraṇa), [number] 3449.

The sequence for reaching the culmination of the fruit (*phalaparyantagamana*) in detail should be seen in the *Arthavādādhikaraṇa* and in the *Vārttika* on the specific occasion (*nimittaviśeṣa*) [at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 639], from the statement that makes known the contradiction and the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Among sentences, a sentence that obstructs a connection (*saṃyoga*) is more powerful.

Or rather, [the words] would not be expressive at the time of the origin [of the relationship], because it is not caused by that. Bhāṣya: Even though the word and its relationship are innate and eternal, nevertheless, Dharma is not characterized by *codanā*.

For from the sentence "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," the understanding that "heaven results from the Agnihotra" is not derived from any single word; rather, it is understood when the three words are uttered.
And there is no fourth word here other than this collection of words.
Nor does such a thing exist in the world within this collection, from which its meaning for conventional usage could be understood.
These words have been employed; their meaning is established, but the aggregate [of words] has not been employed.
Therefore, the meaning of the aggregate must be either artificial or a mere delusion.
Furthermore, the meaning of the individual words is not itself the meaning of the sentence.
For a word functions with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*), while a sentence functions with respect to the particular (*viśeṣa*);
moreover, the universal is one thing and the particular is another.
Furthermore, the meaning of a sentence cannot be understood from the meaning of a word, because there is no connection between them.
If there were no connection whatsoever, then upon understanding one thing, another thing would be understood; thus, when one thing is known, everything would be known.
But this is not the case. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is something else.
It might be argued that even from an unuttered sentence, meaning is understood through its inherent nature despite the absence of a [prior] connection.
If this were to be assumed, the word would overstep its own essential property (*dharma*).
And it is not a property of words that meaning is cognized even from an unuttered word.
For no one derives a meaning from any word when it is heard for the first time.
(It is replied:
This is stated; this is the meaning of a word, not the meaning of a sentence.
For it is observed that even from a sentence heard for the first time, the meaning is understood.
This is not so;
if they were to understand from what is heard for the first time, then everyone would understand it, including those who lack knowledge of the word-meanings.
But those who do not know the word-meanings do not understand [the sentence-meaning]; therefore, it must be so.

Now, one might object: even for those who know the word-meanings, the connection with the sentence-meaning will be unestablished; for they will understand [it] only after being refined by the knowledge of the word-meanings, just as one understands that very same word-meaning upon hearing it a second time or more.
We say: no.

If it were the case that another letter in the sentence, accompanied by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding letters, causes the meanings to be understood from the word-meanings, then the assistance [of those word-meanings] would not be possible through the knowledge of the word-meanings.
Therefore, the cognition of the sentence-meaning must be either artificial or a delusion; the knowledge of the sentence-meaning cannot occur by way of the word-meanings.

[Objection: "But surely this will be the case: when a qualifying word such as 'white' or 'black' approaches from nearby a general term such as 'cow' or 'horse', then the meaning of the sentence is understood. [Reply: That is not so.

How could the cognition produced by the hearing of a general term such as 'cow' or 'horse', which extends toward all cows or all horses, turn back from some particular location to become the meaning of the sentence? Furthermore, there is no grammatical case-ending (vibhakti) in words like 'white' that expresses a qualifier in relation to the meanings of words such as 'black'.
Nor can one postulate a meaning simply to avoid [the charge] that it is meaningless;
therefore, the sentence-meaning does not possess the word-meanings as its constituent parts, and for that reason, it is artificial (*kṛtrima*).
Indeed, these are collections of words, and collections are seen to be created by persons, such as: "Today, the bees are roaming among the blue lotuses."
"Clad in blue silk, the *kādamba* birds seem as if they are dancing.

Therefore, even the Vedic [texts] are composed by human beings.
*Bṛhatī*: "Or rather, they would not be expressive at their origin, because the meaning lacks a cause.
"Even though the word and its relationship are innate and eternal, nevertheless, Dharma is not characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*)."

Thus [in the Bhāṣya]. What is this "commencement"? This is the commencement: it has been stated that the relationship between word and meaning is innate (*autpattikatva*) based on the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*); and the usage of elders consists of one person communicating a meaning through a sentence—[a meaning] which is accessible through other means of knowledge—and another person understands it. Through that understanding, even a child comes to know: "It is by this very [word] that that [meaning] is communicated."
And practice (*pratipatti*)—consisting of avoidance, acquisition, and so forth—is to be understood [from the Veda].

Furthermore, avoidance, acquisition, and the like can only be understood when their objects have already been cognized by other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); they cannot be understood when the object is not yet cognized.

Therefore, it is only possible to understand the "intrinsic nature" (*autpattikatva*) [of the relationship between word and meaning] as having its object already cognized by other means of valid knowledge; it is not the case here that linguistic usage is preceded by the comprehension of the word itself, and consequently, the intrinsic nature [of the relationship] is understood through the sentence.
For indeed, only that which can be understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) makes the avoidance or acquisition of its object capable of being understood.

Therefore, how could a child whose vision of the scriptures has not yet opened up understand the adoption or rejection of objects that are accessible through words alone? And how, without understanding such adoption and rejection, could he infer the comprehension of those objects on the part of an elder? Furthermore, having inferred that comprehension of the object, how could he determine the word’s expressive power (*śakti*) regarding that object? Without determining that power regarding the object, how could he understand the meaning from the word? And without understanding it, how could he engage in linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*)? Consequently, the inherent nature (*autpattikatva*) of Vedic injunctions such as the *agnihotra* is difficult to comprehend.
Therefore, the insistence on the innate nature [of words] is useless.

Proponents of independent scripture (the Mīmāṃsakas) maintain that this innateness is desired for the sake of establishing the authority of the Veda. However, an innateness established through the linguistic usage of elders is not capable of serving as a means for understanding the Vedas and so forth when they are not already known.
(Question: Why is it not possible? (Answer: For in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha*), meaning is understood from a collection [of sounds].
And that collection is not employed in the Veda;
therefore, it does not function as the cause [of comprehension].

[The opponent] objects: Is it not the case that the understanding of word-meanings arises solely from the linguistic usage of elders through positive and negative concomitance, and thus the sentence-meaning is comprehended?

Indeed, through the processes of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*uddhāra*), in the case of the sentences "Devadatta, bring the white cow" (*devadatta gām abhyāja śuklām*) and "Devadatta, bring the black cow" (*devadatta gām abhyāja kṛṣṇām*), as well as "Viṣṇumitra, tie up the red cow" (*viṣṇumitra gāṃ badhāna raktām*), one sentence is understood to have the meaning of the "white" connected [to the action], while in the other that meaning of "white" is deleted; likewise, one has the meaning of the "black" connected, while in the other that meaning of "black" is deleted; and the sentence-meaning is understood as having the meaning of "cattle" connected. Therefore, it is understood that from the words only word-meanings are understood, not the sentence-meaning;
rather, the sentence-meaning is understood through the collection of word-meanings.

Otherwise, when a single word is uttered, there would be no comprehension of the entire sentence-meaning at all, rather than merely the meaning of the individual words. Therefore, from the words come the word-meanings, and from the word-meanings comes the comprehension of their mutual connection (i.e., the comprehension of the mutually connected meanings). [The proponent of the prima facie view] replies: If the word-meanings are determined from the words, and the mutual connection [of those meanings] is determined from the word-meanings, then is the sentence-meaning caused solely by the word-meanings? [The opponent] objects: Yes, it is so stated.

(Opponent: Of which object does there exist causality toward what? (The challenger prompts: It is a delusion to think that [causality exists] of everything toward everything. (Opponent: In that case, then, the comprehension of the meaning of every sentence would arise from everything; for restriction alone constitutes the cause [of comprehension], according to the principle: "By means of something being in such a state, a connection with something else in such a state is conveyed" (meaning: through the connection with an expectancy conveyed by words uttered in proximity, a connection with another object-entity of such a nature is conveyed). And in this matter, there is no other cause to be found apart from the usage of elders.
This is because we observe that [words] function as such.

Therefore, only where a whole (samudāya) is employed does a word convey its own meaning (padārtha), and that meaning is understood as being already connected with other meanings; thus, the assumption that usage and comprehension are the very basis [of linguistic convention] is indeed correct.
Consequently, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) also pertain solely to the objects of comprehension.
For when there is actual practice (*pratipatti*), the comprehension of insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāra*) is necessarily present in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

And it has been stated that this comprehension pertains exclusively to an object already cognized by another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), because the elder’s understanding [of the meaning] consists in the acquisition, avoidance, or attainment [of that object]. (That is to say: only with respect to an object perceived through another means of valid knowledge can its acquisition and avoidance be understood.
If these very acts of acquisition and avoidance are understood, then the elder’s understanding regarding that object is also inferred.)

Even if the understanding [of meaning] is inferred, it is understood that the word and its referent possess the status of being a cause (*nimitta*) only with respect to that which is cognized by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); they do not, however, have the status of a cause for an object that is itself known through another means of knowledge.

Furthermore, the cognition of the effect does not arise solely from the cognition of the cause.

If that is the case, then another means of valid cognition must be sought even for the distinction between those meanings.
