In the case of denoting [the word] while depending on another word out of a desire for proximity to the yogin (the one possessing yoga), there is a delay; thus, the opposite occurs.

However, in the view that only the essential form (*svarūpa*) is denoted, because there is no requirement for another word, the conventional meaning (*rūḍhy-artha*), established by denotation and indicated by the meanings of the constituent parts (*avayava-artha*), becomes connected with the sentence-meaning derived from the etymological sense (*yaugika*) immediately upon merely hearing the syllables. This should be observed in cases such as "cow’s milk is very sweet," "water-milk is slightly sweet," and "the smell of a snake is similar to the scent of a *ketakī* flower."
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is conveyed through the meanings of the words expressed by those words, by means of indication (lakṣaṇā).

In this regard, the verb *ānaya* (bring), having denoted the general action of bringing by the word "bring," indicates—that is, it points toward—the specific instance through the medium of its own meaning; the word *go* (cow) likewise, by means of its own referent, indicates that very same act of bringing in the form of "having the cow as its object" (*gokarmakatva*), which is the nature of its proximity [to the verb]. Thus, in whatever sentence there may be, whatever meaning is intended to be expressed as a particular, that very meaning—though indicated by its own word as a general term—is pointed toward by the other words through the medium of denoting their own meanings, in the form of being related to it.

Even where there is yet another [meaning] following that which is already connected, there too the establishment of all of that occurs through a succession of indicated-indications (*lakṣita-lakṣaṇā*); this is the general direction. Now, one might ask: "Even if the cow, expressed as the object (*karman*), indicates the action to which it belongs, how does it indicate specifically the act of bringing (*ānayana*)? For they [the word and the meaning] constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). To this we reply: Although indication (*lakṣaṇā*) proceeds by way of a commonality, it is restricted by the requirement of a single syntactical unit; thus it is established by those who see the force of the context.

Even he who maintains that the term "dhvani" is denoted by its own primary meaning (abhidhā) must necessarily accept this: that a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), which operates generally, is restricted by another word through its specific nature.

For instance, those who maintain that a copulative compound (dvandva) denotes multiple substrates simultaneously—in such cases, for example, in the phrase *dhvanyādiśaḥ*—the word *diś* (direction/quarter), while indicating an intermediate direction (*avāntarā-diś*) to justify its dual number, indicates only a direction and not some other object, precisely because of its co-occurrence with that specific word (*tatpada-samabhivyāhārāt*). Let this principle apply everywhere in the same way.

Precisely because it is established through the very doctrine of the syntactic unity of the unestablished (*asiddhyekavākyatā*)—due to the absence of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) in a specific mutual connection—it is for this reason that the word possesses a measure equal to other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, one might object: when the sun and Devadatta are perceived, there arises no cognition of their mutual connection despite the presence of expectancy, proximity, and semantic competency (*ākāṅkṣā-saṃnidhi-yogyatva*); therefore, since the meaning of the sentence is understood from the meanings of the words, it is logical that the words themselves express the connected meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*).
This same defect applies even to the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (expression of the related).

At that time, those two meanings which are directly perceived remain present in memory as denotators; yet, even when expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors are present, they do not convey their mutual relation. Now, if it is argued that words convey a relation only in such a relation as is observed in linguistic usage based on the persistence of the meanings, then this is equally true for the word-meanings themselves.

For even those word-meanings, when combined for the purpose of conveying a single qualified object, convey the sentence-meaning; thus, there is no fault. And regarding their combination, where a person possesses independence, validity depends upon that [human] origin; but where there is no independence, it is independent [of human agency]. Therefore, the capacity [of a word] for "that which is connected to what is connected" (anvitānvita) does not establish [the truth], because independence follows from the doctrine of expressing connection (*anvitābhidhāna*), as stated in the *Nyāyaratnamālā*. Let this suffice for now. The sphoṭa of the sentence is also refuted by the very same reasoning applied to the sphoṭa of the word.

Furthermore, the partlessness (*nirbhāgatva*) of the sentence-meaning must be refuted, because it follows from the cognition of parts and because [consequently] logical consequences such as *prasaṅga* would be untenable. For instance: "Since the sequence of operations—namely, the exclusion (*apoha*), the body [of the meaning], and the substratum—is dependent upon [the presence of] logical consequences (*prasaṅga*), how could it exist for those who maintain that the sentence is partless, given that it exists only in the form of actual usage (*prayukti*)?"

For when the meaning of the injunction for the primary rite along with its subsidiaries—as in "one should immolate an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma"—is undivided, there is neither a goal to be accomplished, nor a means, nor even the subsidiaries themselves. At that time, since neither the animal sacrifice, nor the cake offering, nor its subsequent offerings (anuyājas) exist [as distinct entities], what could possibly be connected to what? This same principle should be demonstrated regarding the *tantra* (common procedure) and other such cases. Therefore, the meaning of a sentence is that which is permeated by multiple constituent elements.
And that [Vedic statement] has its root in the thing itself; it is neither rootless nor based on convention.
Therefore, the authority of the *codanā* is established.
As for the argument that it must be of human origin because it is a sentence, we shall refute that in the subsequent section.
The Vedic statement may be either non-authoritative or authoritative;
it does not lack authority because of the mention of its independence from separate writing regarding [word] meanings and their relations.
Even in the Veda, as in worldly usage, the connection of words with their meanings is distinct.

Therefore, their words must be accepted as authoritative, for they are free from partiality. The Bhāṭṭa [responds]: Even though word-meanings (*padārtha*) are eternal, the sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) are conventionally established in relation to sentences; thus, their comprehension depends upon the apprehension of that convention, and further depends upon the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*), which is constituted by the speaker’s desire. Consequently, because of the possibility of error and negligence due to the involvement of a human being, the authority of Vedic injunctions and commentaries is not absolute. Moreover, since it is impossible to establish a relationship between words—which are common to infinite sentence-meanings—and any specific sentence-meaning.

This being the case, the word-meanings, having been denoted by the words themselves, indicate the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) which constitutes the sentence-meaning—characterized by its own nature and its relations to those meanings—by means of a specific kind of co-occurrence (*samabhihāra-viśeṣa*).

Thus, in such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), there is a uniformity across all injunctions in the cognition of a specific *bhāvanā*—namely, an efficient force directed toward heaven, taking the form of a sacrifice, and residing in one who desires heaven. Consequently, there is no need to grasp an endless number of distinct relations.
Furthermore, *tātparya* (purport) is a property inherent in the word itself.
This is the distinction.

And since that which apprehends it is precisely the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) and so forth, there are no [independent] injunctions regarding the qualification (*adhikriyā*) of persons or the scriptures (*āgama*).

Furthermore, the various distinctions among the remnants of what has been employed (*prayuktaśeṣabheda*) are not to be postulated; thus, the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of injunctions is not caused by a lack of connection.
Such is the established rule.

Thus [says] Maṇḍana: "Although the injunction has been established as the means of proving Dharma, and although other [theories] have been refuted, the fact that a sentence is partless was not stated by him because he lacked understanding of the meaning of the verse being recited;
rather, it is the basis for the cognition of the sentence-meaning, and therefore it is now stated."

The demonstration of the meaning of the constituent words [of the Veda] occurs through the experience of the meaning of the verse as it arises; this is refuted by Śaṅkara on the grounds that it contradicts the *tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning those [words] already present). Furthermore, there is the section concerning the power of the sentence (*vākyaśakti*) previously understood.

25. The Section on Smṛti and Sentence (Smṛtivākyādhikaraṇa). [Objection: Granted that there may be the consequence of [the sentence] being identical with the word and its meaning; however, the cognition of the power of the sentence and the sentence-meaning caused by it, as well as their eternality, must be established. [Response: Because of the impossibility of the connection between the performance of the ritual and the enjoyment of the result of the sentence-meaning, if one were to assume knowledge [of the sentence-meaning] prior [to the action], this would lead to the following difficulties: the necessity of assuming a connection for the word and its meaning, the resulting contradiction regarding the eternality of the bond [between them], and the fact that the cognition of the sentence's power and the sentence-meaning caused by it would be impossible. Thus, the section on Smṛti and Sentence begins. [Objection: Let it be granted that there is the consequence of [the sentence] being identical with the word and its meaning. However, the cognition of the power of the sentence and the sentence-meaning caused by it, as well as their eternality, must be established.
Nevertheless, because a sentence can never simultaneously convey two contradictory meanings,
and likewise because words are also shown to lack indivisibility,
their status as a means of valid cognition is not possible.
For instance, it is not by relying on the distinction between root and suffix that the attainment of understanding occurs.

Thus, even in the case of the *varṇasphoṭa* (phoneme-sphoṭa), the capacity of words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) to convey the sentence-meaning—namely, the state of being the object of the action of "potting"—is possible; this [theory] must be rejected in favor of the parsimony (*lāghava*) of postulating roots and suffixes as the expressers, rather than the cumbersome assumption of expressive power (*śakti*) in each individual phoneme of the sphoṭa. This is because it is impossible to establish a relationship with a specific sentence-meaning for words that are common to an infinite number of such meanings.
By this, the view that the cognition of the meaning of a word arises from the final word within a collection of words,

as well as the view that a sentence conveys meaning through the cognition of oneness and largeness, is refuted. In that case, the [cognition of oneness and largeness] in a sentence is merely adventitious (aupādhikī), as in the expression "one large heap of grain."

If it is argued that, because the communication of the sentence-meaning is thus impossible, validity cannot be established, and therefore there is no power of the sentence (*vākya-śakti*) in the form of the sentence-sphoṭa; [we reply:]...
Some, however, maintain that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in a word as related to a word-meaning that transcends other words.
Here, the grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) [objects]:
in a sentence such as "Kṛṣṇa is protecting," the word-meaning is qualified by its co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with others, and thus it is non-uniform (*ananugata*).

They say that because there is no evidence for the analysis of words into constituent parts (*padaparūpāvayavabhāga*), and because there is no evidence for the existence here of a collection of words— consisting of those words possessing expectancy, semantic competency, and proximity, which denote the act of coming and are composed of the phoneme *e* in their sequence—
it is not a collection of words (*padasamudāya*) that conveys the sentence-meaning; rather, sentenceness (*vākyatva*) consists in its being a constituent part.
The capacity (śakti) belongs to that very [word] with respect to its qualified meaning;
that alone is the sentence-sphoṭa (vākyasphoṭa).

And thus, regarding such expressions as "one sentence," "a heavy object," or "the task of another," the designation of "sentence" applies to the words themselves when they are connected with the task [of expression]. Furthermore, in the case of a "subtle sentence" or a "great sentence," there is a capacity exceeding mere experience with respect to what is intended by the name. This capacity resides in that which is connected with the task.
And the cognition of the measure of the genus [of the bird] as a sārikā is thus established;
otherwise, it would pertain to qualities and so forth belonging to the collection of words.

Furthermore, when the apprehension of the expectancy of experience occurs, the cognition of the power to remind constitutes the sentence; thus, the capacity of that specific collection to cause the respective cognitions is in relation to that very collection.
Therefore, because it is established through implication (*arthāpatti*), there is no inherent power (*śakti*) in the sentence-meaning;
for such is the nature of that implication.
Therefore, the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in the sentence.

Thus, when a child grasps the expressive power through the linguistic interaction between the elder who prompts and the elder who is prompted by the word "with a jar" (*ghaṭena*), and so forth—given that there is no evidence for the mother’s cognition of the effect in the specific parts such as the division into stem and suffix or the postulation of power in those parts—the *sphoṭa*, which is the very form of the whole word, is what constitutes the expressive power.

Having inferred that [the cognition] is produced, and upon the expectation for its producer, one recognizes its causality as residing precisely in those words—such as *bhavati* and *pacati*—from the speech of an authoritative elder (*prayojakavṛddha*) once the verbal root *bhū* and the pronoun *tat* have been presented. Since there is no evidence for the words themselves to be related to the effect [of the cognition], one understands that the capacity (*śakti*) belongs to the phonemes (*varṇa*) as qualified by their specific sequential order (*ānupūrvī*). Then, through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*), one understands the capacity for each respective word-meaning; thus they say "Sphoṭa."
Even though [the opponent] knows this, as before, he does not invalidate the view that the word-potency resides in that which is associated with an action (*kāryānvita*).
And thus, because words denote that which is associated with an action, they also possess potency toward other things; this [argument] is weak.
They say: "It is like the recollection of the final phoneme by one who has forgotten the preceding phonemes."

For, according to this view, there would be the consequence that a person who lacks the recollection of word-meanings—or one who has forgotten previous words—would lack the cognition of the sentence-meaning. Even if one were to argue that the cognition of the sentence-meaning occurs through the recollection of the respective word-meanings, there is still no evidence for the claim that the apprehension of the word’s power (śakti) rests upon that [sentence-meaning], whether it be "connected with other meanings" (itarānvita) or "connected with the task" (kāryānvita).

Furthermore, just like the word-meanings, the sentence-meaning would also be partless, because at the stage when the apprehension of the power is established as being cumbersome (gaurava), there is no evidence for the measurement of the moon or the stars.

It might be argued that [the objection] is not tenable because the consequence (*prasaṅga*) depends on sublation (*bādha*), since sublation is possible—as in the case of cognition—and because there would otherwise follow the consequence that verbal comprehension does not arise in the absence of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words expressive of an effect.
This concludes the section on the sentence (*vākya-adhikaraṇa*). Now, the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*): [text continues].

The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that in a perceptual cognition such as "a pot qualified by potness," the sentence-meaning consists of the relation between the qualifier and the qualificand. The sentence-meaning, which has the cognition of words as its instrument, is of two kinds: [the relation] is either of the nature of a difference, as in the case of inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth, or it is of the nature of a connection (*saṃsarga*), as in the verbal cognition whose qualificand is the syntactic relation of the object "pot" (*ghaṭakarmakāraka*).

Some maintain that in expressions such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the appearance of [the relation] "not residing in the king" and so forth as a relation (*saṃsarga*) is possible, because there arises the cognition: "the man is distinct from the king through a specific qualifier and a specific qualificand. Others say that since the relation is verbal and is understood through the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of both [terms], the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is everywhere simply the relation; thus, by the aforementioned method, exclusion (*apoha*) is obtained within its proper limits.
Because there is an absence of manifestation through abundance, and because exclusion (*apoha*) is unestablished;

therefore, according to the doctrine of relation (*saṃsarga-siddhānta*), in expressions such as "bring the jar," the meaning of the sentence consists precisely in the word-meaning (*padārtha*) residing within the word "jar" and so forth.
And that [sentence-meaning] occurs in cases such as "bring the jar."

Since the understanding of the bringing (*ānayana*) as connected with the action upon the pot (*ghaṭakarma*)—namely, the universal of "pot" (*ghaṭasāmānya*)—is possible, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is simply the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) itself as qualified by qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) such as the specific nature of "bringing the pot.

Such is the sentence-meaning; and since it is based on secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the followers of the Ācāryas maintain that the sentence-meaning is indeed exclusively of a secondary (indicated) nature.
This is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).

In that regard, there is a rule—cognizable through traditional scripture (*smṛti*)—that among nouns, there is the status of being qualified by a specific *kāraka*, and in all cases, there is the status of being qualified by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, the manifestation of that sentence-meaning, which consists in the "qualification of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*), is fourfold.
One [type of relation] consists in the qualified having the nature of being qualified;

another is the qualification of the qualificand by that [first], and therein further qualification by another qualifier—as in "the man who possesses a blue staff. Those who assert a rule of cognition according to which the meaning of the nominative case is the primary qualificand when used in co-utterance with a verb are refuted by the absence of evidence for such a rule.
Thus:

"The qualification of one [term] by another" is the third [type of relation], for the traditional authority (smṛti) does not indicate that the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case is the primary element—as in the examples "Devadatta is staff-bearing" and "he is earring-wearing.
"Two [qualities] in one" is the fourth.

The sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is a relation (*saṃsarga*) characterized by two types of determination, as in the example: "Devadatta is staff-bearing and earring-wearing" (*daṇḍī kuṇḍalī devadattaḥ*). Thus, according to the Naiyāyika school, the sentence-meaning in the case of a figurative sentence-meaning (*lākṣaṇika-vākyārtha*) is the relation [between the meanings] of the collection of words (*padasamudāya*). (Maṇi, pp. 79–80)

According to the Mīmāṃsaka view, a sentence produces [cognition] by means of the presentation of word-meanings generated by its constituent words, specifically in the form qualified by their syntactic relations (*kāraka*). (Bālakrīḍā, p. 73) It is thus established that the sentence is the authoritative means for the cognition of the sentence-meaning; therefore, in the case of injunctions, the sentence-meaning is *dharma*.
Neither mere relation nor difference constitutes the sentence-meaning.
Thus has validity been explained (*Maṇi*, pp. 171–173). In the *Vākyādhikaraṇa* of the *Bhāṣya* (2.1.46, pp. 446–47), it is stated:
"Because of the scriptural mention of 'distinction' (*bheda*), there should be an application based on the genus (*jāti*)," as found in *Sūtra* 3.1.1–8.

Even if it is maintained that the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is "relation" (*saṃsarga*), nevertheless, the unity of meaning (*ekārthatā*) would not exist in the case of sentences with many words, because—as stated by the author of the *Vārttika* in the *Vākyādhikaraṇa* (1.1.24–26)—"there is a multiplicity of individual entities (*bheda*) and relations (*saṃsarga*) in multi-word [sentences]. The *Vārttika* provides the following explanation: "The Sūtra intends [the word] to denote the individual entity (*vyakti*); for all individuals, such as cows and the like, are already included by the word ['cow' itself], and thus they are merely recalled by their qualifiers through the sequence of the rule and the hearing of the sentence-meaning distinct from it."
Thus [it is said]:

*Kauṭilīya Arthaśāstra* 1.3.130, p. 138. "Since the exclusion of blackness and so forth by means of whiteness and so forth must be accomplished, and because that conjunction is included within the word-meaning (*padārtha*), it does not become the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*); therefore, it is subordinate to that. Furthermore, "no instruction regarding sentences was given in the Grammar (*Vyākaraṇa*). Their distinction is thus apprehended.

And just as the word "white" [serves] for the word "cow"—for instance, in the *Vākyapadīya* 1.3.124 (p. 203), it is stated that "the instruction of words is performed"—it functions merely by way of its difference from "black" and so forth; in the same way, the word "white" also functions for the word "cow" by means of its exclusion from "horse" and so forth.
The meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) consists in the mutual connection of the meanings of multiple words; and that [sentence-meaning] is rooted in the word-meanings.

Furthermore, because there is a diversity of things to be cut off, there is no validity whatsoever in the status of [the Veda as] mere speech. It is not without a basis, nor is it based on convention.
Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.7, p. 160: "Or else, if a universal were grasped, there would be the undesirable consequence that every sentence could be considered the meaning of all other sentences."

The meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is also produced from the meanings of the words (*padārtha*); it does not arise otherwise. Thus, in the view that the *ākṛti* (form) is the word-meaning, because the whiteness and the cowness are denoted in their own forms, their distinction—established through mutual coloring and so forth due to their proximity—is real. As it has been stated: "That which is established as being [the meaning] is recited for the sake of action; for this is the purpose" (PMS 1.1.25). (Bhāṣya 4.3.121). It is not the case that the sentence-meaning [is primary].
And that connection of "whiteness" with "cowness," or rather, the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), is preceded by the word-meanings (*padārtha*).

Bhāṣya 5.1.15. Furthermore, the connection of "cowness" [with "whiteness"] is obtained through the sentence-meaning because they are unified in a single individual (*ekavyaktyupasaṃhārāt*) due to their equality; thus it is distinct [from the mere word-meanings]. Upaṭup 6.1.13, 10.1.123. Although in some cases [the meaning] arises from two words, it is produced by the relation between those two word-meanings.
Bhāṣya 5.1.122: Even if the connection (*saṃsarga*) here were understood as a single unit, nevertheless, in a multi-word [expression],
by whichever portion the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is manifested,
through that very portion the multiplicity of those connections is perceived.
Thus [it is said]. Page 73. Regarding the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*): because it possesses the nature of all grammatical factors (*kāraka*), it is eternal in form. Su. p. 1190.

In the view that the universal form (*ākṛti*) is the word-meaning, when "whiteness" and "cowness" are denoted in their own forms, their mutual implication due to proximity constitutes the sentence-meaning, which is a distinction established through the sense.

Furthermore, that connection of whiteness with cowness, or the connection of cowness with whiteness, is perceived through its totality because it is subsumed within each individual instance; thus, it is manifold.

For us, however, since the word-meaning is the *ākṛti* (form), difference itself is not intended as the sentence-meaning. This is because, for us, the sentence-meaning consists precisely of word-meanings that possess difference.
In that case, multiplicity alone is established (but not the unity of meaning).
Vārttika 2.1.14.46, p. 447. For in the context of desire (the context of the fruit), the meaning of the sentence extends up to the accomplishment of the fruit.
Ṛjuvimalā, p. 159. The meaning of the sentence is produced by two word-meanings, not by either one alone.
In proximity, this very purpose is common to it:
how might they produce a cognition qualified by both word-meanings? The sentence-meaning can be established together with a cognition that follows immediately [from the words].

If, however, one were to understand the prior word-meaning through some other means such as meditation and then generate the sentence-meaning, that sentence-meaning would be non-Vedic, as it would be preceded by human intellect.

Just as when one takes a verbal form from one sentence and a nominal form from another, a certain sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is produced, so too would it be in a case where one produces a sentence-meaning after having understood the meaning of the prior word through another means, such as meditation.

(Mānameyodaya 311.12.21, pp. 734–35). For a sentence-meaning is not apprehended when the meaning of the words is unknown. (Ślokavārttika, Nirālambanavāda 59). And a sentence-meaning whose word-meanings are not established does not constitute valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) is the root of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*); the word does not have an independent existence [apart from it].
Bhāṣya 10.1.9.29. For the meaning of the sentence is not the word-meaning already connected [prior to its being a sentence].
3.1.1.9, p. 787. For the meaning of the sentence is not perceived without first grasping two independent word-meanings.
Vārttika 2.1.1.23, p. 534: "The cognition of the word-meaning arises from the word itself, and the sentence-meaning arises from the word-meanings.
Bhāṣya 1.1.1.26: "The sentence-meaning is the meaning formed as a whole, refined by the word-meanings" (*padārthair ameyaiḥ saṃskṛtaṃ piṇḍitaṃ vākyārtham*).
1|1|8|32. When the meaning of the word-meanings is understood, the word-meaning is apprehended; after that, the sentence-meaning [is understood].
Vārttika 6|1|1|2. And the sentence-meaning is the comprehension of a qualified object.
Bhāṣya.
The sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) cannot be accepted when it contradicts what is established by direct audition (śruti), because that which is directly heard is primary.

It has been stated [in Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.8] that word-meanings are conveyed by words themselves without depending on convention, and the sentence-meaning is likewise conveyed by those [word-meanings] without depending on convention.
However, in all cases, the sentence-meaning is established only when the word-meanings have been understood, and not otherwise.
For a word functions with respect to the universal, whereas a sentence functions with respect to the particular.
When the meanings of words, which operate through their universals, come to rest in a particular, that is the meaning of the sentence.

This very point has been stated [in the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "The collection of those [words] which have become such [i.e., denoting universals] is for the sake of action, because the purpose is caused by that. (1.1.25)

Bhāṣya 3.1.6.2, p. 680: In the postulation of a different meaning for the sentence, there are the defects of *vipariṇāma* (modification), *vyavahitakalpanā* (postulation of the separated), and *vyadhāraṇakalpanā* (postulation of the restrictive). Therein, the examples follow in order: (1) here, the example is the *Āgneya* passage.

(2) Regarding the passage, "They indeed attain a firm foundation by performing these nights" (*pratiṣṭhanti ha vā etā rātrīrupayanti*), if one were to conceive of an alternative meaning—namely, "they should perform the nights for the sake of attaining a firm foundation" (*pratiṣṭhanti rātrīrūpeyuḥ*)—then there would be the conceptualization of a remote connection (*vyavahita-kalpanā*) between the word "those who" (*ye*), which is co-occurrent with "the nights," and the phrase "who attain a firm foundation" (*ye pratiṣṭhanti*). (3) This is what is meant by "conceptualizing a remote connection" (*vyavahāra-kalpanā*), as seen in the injunction: "As many horses as one might receive, so many *dhṛṣṭaka* cakes dedicated to Varuṇa should one offer. (Bāla.pṛ. 4). The authority of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is based upon its being rooted in the meanings of the individual words (*padārtha*). [Jaiminisūtra] 2.1.1.24–26. The relationship between two sentence-meanings is innate (*autpattika*).

*Bṛhatī*, p. 203: "The mutual connection (*anvaya*) of sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) is not contradictory, even though the expectancy for the mutual connection of word-meanings (*padārtha*) has reached its fulfillment. *Sphuṭasiddhi*, p. 525: "In the sentence-meaning, there is either direct denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*)."
The Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas) maintain that the power of a sentence resides in the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

The Teachers (Gurus), who accept the theory of the denotation of what is connected with an action (*kāryānvitābhidhāna*), hold that the power resides in the sentence-meaning in the form of a connection with an action.

The Vedāntins, who accept the theory of the denotation of what is connected with something else (*itarānvitābhidhāna*), hold that the power resides in the sentence-meaning in the form of a mere connection.

The distinction is that for grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*), the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), whereas for the other two [schools], it is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). The followers of Gautama (*gautamīyas*) maintain that the manifestation of the sentence-meaning occurs through the condition of relational connection (*saṃsargamaryādā*). The established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that there is secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the sentence-meaning.

In this regard, the grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas) maintain that in instances such as *bhavati*, *bhūyāt*, *babhūva*, *rāmaḥ*, and *rāmān*, it is the heard suffixes, *ti*-inflections, *visarga*s, and so forth, that possess denotative power (*vācakatā*). It is not the case that the meaning is conveyed through the mediation of recalling (*anukārya*) and enacting (*anuṣṭhāpana*) the original forms (*bhūtā*);

for in the case of sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), it would be more cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate denotative power for the substituends (*ādeśin*) and to postulate that the substitutes (*ādeśa*) serve merely to present those substituends.
Because there is no uniformity among the substitutes due to the differences in grammatical rules (*vyākaraṇa*),

otherwise, in cases such as *ṛṣabho brūhi*, the occurrence of one substitute would lead to the attribution of expressive power (*śakti*) to the other through mere recollection, which would result in the same word having multiple powers for a single meaning. Therefore, it is the phonemes (*varṇa*) as qualified by their preceding audible forms that are the denoters (*vācaka*), and not those [phonemes] that merely bring to mind the verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth.
Thus ends the discussion on the *varṇasphoṭa* (the word-unit as a collection of phonemes).

Similarly, in forms such as *hariṇā*, *haraye*, *rāmāt*, and *hareḥ*, because there is no division into word-level substitutes (*pada-adeśa*), one cannot determine that a particular [phoneme] denotes a substance (*dravya*) while another denotes a quality such as "being a monkey" (*kalpatva*). Therefore, since the denotation belongs to the complete form as qualified by its specific arrangement, this is the *padasphoṭa*.

Similarly, in sentences such as "kṛṣṇehi" and "rakṣenaṃ," since there is no division into constituent parts and there is no evidence for the presence here of a sequence of sounds containing the phoneme *e* that signifies "coming," this specific power belongs to the sentence itself; thus, there is the *vākya-sphoṭa*.
It is of two kinds: the indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) *vākya-sphoṭa* and the divisible (*sakhaṇḍa*) *vākya-sphoṭa*.
The first is twofold: the divisible *vākya-sphoṭa* consisting of words (*pada-svarūpa*) and the divisible *vākya-sphoṭa* consisting of phonemes (*varṇa-rūpa*).

For instance, in sentences such as "viṣṇo'va" (O Viṣṇu, protect), even though the sentence-meaning is understood as the relation among the word-meanings presented by the respective words aided by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors, the power (*śakti*) of the sentence is postulated to establish its status as verbal (*śābda*).
That very [power] is the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*).
And that [sphoṭa], being itself unknown, is the cause [of the understanding of the sentence-meaning] by its own nature.

In the view of the proponents of the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (expression of the related), the other part [of the word] possesses a power (*śakti*) similar to that of the word "turmeric" regarding the sentence-meaning. As for the Vedāntins, however, the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) occurs only with respect to what is related to something else (*itarānvite*), and not with respect to the status of being the sentence-meaning itself; rather, where a single sentential unity is possible, it occurs with respect to what is related to an action (*kāryānvite*).
Nevertheless, the injunctive sentence is an injunction of a single *bhāvanā* qualified by all its qualifiers, such as the object of the act of bringing (*ānayanakarmatva*).

Just as when it is said, "Devadatta, having ascertained the capacity [of the means] for a specific purpose, cooks rice in a pot using fuel-wood," all these elements have a single cooking as their objective; so too, while one ascertains the capacity of words like "cow" (*gopada*) in respect of the universal "cowness" (*gotva*), one does not abandon the capacity grasped in the aspect of the connection [already] acquired during the primary acquisition of meaning (*ādyavyutpatti*)—as stated in Vākyapadīya 3.1.6.2, p. 691—but rather ascertains the capacity precisely in relation to what is connected with others, just like the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), so it is with the *bhāvanā*.
Su. pṭ. 683:

[The Naiyāyikas] maintain that there is expressive power (*śakti*) in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as well. They argue that since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is possible through the same principle as the comprehension of the word-meaning, it would be redundant to postulate a separate expressive power for that [concomitance], as such a postulation would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). The Naiyāyikas, however, hold that the understanding of the sentence-meaning arises from the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words; for when that is possible, there is no need to assume an additional expressive power.
In the case of the knowledge of the relation characterized by investigation (*mīmāṃsā*), it is simpler (*lāghava*) to assume that the knowledge of such a word-order (*ānupūrvī*) is merely a cause.

Furthermore, "word-ness" (*śabdatva*) is not the state of being an object residing in a word; rather, in the cognition of the sentence-meaning, words are the instruments (*karaṇa*), whereas word-ness is the state of being an object of the cognition produced by the word. (Bālakrīḍā, p. 70).
Therefore, they say that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the object of the function (*vṛtti*) is also established as being verbal in nature.
The Naiyāyikas maintain that the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises through co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*).
However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the sentence with respect to the sentence-meaning.
Nor should it be argued that there can be no secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because of the impossibility of a [direct] denotative capacity (*śakyābhāva*).

This is because, in the Guru’s system, the very mode of understanding the sentence-meaning—which consists in the cognition of the relationship [between the word and its object]—is accepted as the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), and this itself constitutes the secondary indication.
This is demonstrated in sentences such as "Bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*) according to the view of the Guru.

In the case of "One who desires [to obtain] satisfaction in this world should cook," even though there is a general understanding of bringing [the object], a specific understanding of that [act] is not possible without *lakṣaṇā* (indication). This is because the status of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which is the meaning of the suffix *-anīya*, must be construed with the act of cooking, which is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), just as [in the injunction] "One who desires heaven [should sacrifice].
Indeed, the general act of bringing a jar is not the sentence-meaning.

In Vedic injunctions such as "One who desires knowledge should sacrifice" (*jñānecchā yajeta*) and "The pure one should perform the twilight worship" (*śuciḥ sandhyām upāsīta*), because the activities [of the agent] possess the same mode and the same object, it is not possible for the "being-to-be-done" (*kāryatva*)—which is the meaning of the suffix expressing the causal factor—to be construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) first. This is because, in the absence of that [construal], it would be untenable for there to be an activity and a desire directed toward a specific object. Therefore, since that [suffix-meaning] is what makes the cognition of the root-meaning possible, it is appropriate that the meaning of the rest of the sentence be understood figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in relation to the action of sacrificing and so forth.

The reason for the connection with the "thing-to-be-done" (*kāryatva*)—and by extension, the connection with the "person to be impelled" (*niyojya*)—is made clear; for in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* (1.1.7), this [word] is indeed qualified by the person to be impelled. This is because, as seen in the case of actions such as cooking, there is an observed connection with the status of being a thing-to-be-done, and according to that school's view, the nature of being the motivator of the connection consists in its fitness (*yogyatva*).

In the present context, since the one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the meaning of the sentence is that the knowledge of the task (*kārya*) prompted by the desire for the fruit of heaven belongs to that enjoined person. Thus, when actions such as sacrifice (*yāga*) are construed with the sentences through the relation of being their object (*viṣayatva*), the capacity (*śakti*) [of the words] to denote the fact of being a means to heaven is not required within the sentence-meaning.
Furthermore, the intention (*tātparya*) does not reside in the person; nor is "fitness" (*yogyatā*) defined as being known as a means to heaven.

And that [direct means to heaven] is not possible; thus, because the direct status of being a means to heaven (*svargasādhanatva*) is sublated when the word "that" (*tatpadam*) is uttered together with a verb, [the Veda] cannot be established as authoritative through an injunction (*codanā*). This is because the status of being a means to heaven through a mediated sequence (*paraṃparayā*) is difficult to ascertain without prior knowledge of the factors constituting that sequence, even with the assistance of the knowledge of the meanings of the individual words. Consequently, it does not bring about the understanding of the sentence-meaning in the form of an efficient force (*bhāvanā*) connected to the meaning of that [word], and thus the authority of the injunction is not attained. Thus says Kaṣṭurī.
And because it is impossible for the person to be enjoined in relation to the sacrifice, there can be no connection with the state of being a task to be accomplished.
Thus.

The knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthajñāna*) does not occur without the presentation of the word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*). However, in the case of obligatory injunctions (*nitya*) such as "One who is pure should perform the twilight worship" (*śuciḥ saṃdhyāmupāsīta*), the knowledge of the sentence-meaning consists simply in the cognition that "the twilight worship is to be performed by one who is pure and is the object of the injunction," even without the knowledge of mutual compatibility (*yogyatā*), mutual relation (*saṃsarga*), or being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). In that case, there is no dependence on worldly experience. Thus, the function [of the Veda] has as its object [such an injunction]. This is the commentary (*vṛtti*). Likewise, [in the case of the Vedic injunction], the *codanā* (Vedic impulsion) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding *dharma*, [specifying] that "one who desires heaven is the person to be enjoined. This is the commentary (*vṛtti*).

If it is argued that the understanding would be "the sacrifice is to be performed," [we reply: in the present case, because the person characterized by desire (*kāmanā*) is the one to be directed (*niyojya*), this is a specific instance of the obligatory injunction (*nityavidhi*).

The comprehension of the sentence-meaning is not rooted in the mere apprehension of the sentence; rather, it is rooted in the comprehension of the meanings of the individual words (*padārtha*). Furthermore, let it be granted that desire is a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*); however, the self alone is the primary indicator (*lakṣya*), because it is that which is being connected within the connection of word-meanings. This is because the cognition of the task (*kārya*) associated with the self is the motivator (*pravartaka*), and there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) when that [self] is absent. (Vaiyānātha 2.1.7) It should not be said that this leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For otherwise, the phrase "one who desires heaven" (svargakāmaḥ) would be rendered futile (pṛ. 98).

If desire were merely an incidental indicator (upalakṣaṇa), then, as in the case of obligatory rites (nitya), there would be only the status of being an enjoined agent (niyojyatva) based on its non-inherence in the Veda; consequently, because the knowledge of the task to be accomplished would depend on that [status] as the motivator, even one devoid of desire would incur the consequence of engaging in action, since [the status of being an enjoined agent] resides in the connection with the desired object.

If it is argued that the state of desiring to act (*cikīrṣāvattva*) is likewise [the nature of the person], that is true; however, there is no evidence for this, as it would result in the impossibility of engaging in action.

For in the present case, it does not follow from an obligatory injunction (*nityavidhi*), but rather its status as a motivator (*prayojakatva*) is established through its being mediated by the aforementioned status of the person as one who is to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*). There is another distinction [from the optional injunction] due to the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word "desirous of heaven" (*svargakāma*).
If [the agent] were a qualifier, that [qualification] would be abandoned;

for this very reason, the "kṛti" (volitional effort) in the form of being the prompter of the effort is abandoned. Indeed, since the qualified [agent] possesses the status of a *niyojya* (one who is impelled) consisting in having knowledge of the effect prompted by himself, his status as a *kartṛ* (agent) consists in possessing selfhood coexistent with the effort, and his status as an *adhikārī* (eligible person) consists in being the enjoyer of the fruit. Furthermore, because in the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) the fitness (*yogyatā*) consists in being a means to the object of that desire, the capacity to produce heaven does not reside in the desire itself; thus, the qualified [result] is not desired therein. Consequently, because the eternal [obligation] is untenable as a way to maintain the syntactic unity with the word "kāma" (desire), it must be admitted that the *apūrva* (unseen potency) has already been stated [as the result].
The connection with one who is distinguished by desire is established.

For this very reason, in the view that there is no *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) in reality, such a cognition as "sacrifice is to be accomplished by my effort" does not exist at all for one devoid of effort—neither in the case of a primary injunction, nor in the case of a mandatory injunction (*nityavidhi*), nor in the injunction regarding the *Āgneya* sacrifice and others. Furthermore, in the state of being a *niyojya* (one to be impelled) by its very nature, as in the cognition "this is my duty," desire has no role whatsoever.

The state of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) is by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatayā*), while the state of being a generator (*janakatva*) belongs to the desirer (*kāmin*). If it is argued that there is a need for a primary qualification (*prāthamikapekṣā*), this is true;

however, since the status of being a *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) is itself a fitness (*yogyatva*) for connection with the *niyojya*, the desired result is established by its very nature as a qualifier in that connection. Even if another fitness were required for the connection with "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), this [status of being a *niyojya*]—existing as a fitness for the connection of the word-meaning "desirer of heaven" with the sacrifice denoted by the verbal root—is a qualifier by way of differentiation (*vyāvartakatva*), just as "kinghood" is in the case of "the king desiring universal sovereignty. Furthermore, there is a necessity for another [qualification] because of the requirement of a further distinction.

This is because [the desire] is produced by that very [desire], and because its exclusion is possible through the following principle: "When there is a desire for the connection of 'having holes' and 'being a jewel' with the jar, even while there is a requirement for another fitness (yogyatā), at that time there is the activity (kṛti) produced by that [desire].

Therefore, when the jar is connected as having holes, when the removal of the [undesirable] is brought about, and when the state of being an effect (kāryatva) is connected to the sacrifice that is fit [for performance], there is fitness (yogyatā) regarding the connection with the person to be impelled (niyojya).
And in that case, because the property of being water (*jalatva*) possesses fitness (*yogyatā*) with respect to water;

for instance, just as the state of being known as a means to achieve a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) through a mere pot and so forth constitutes the fitness for being a means to heaven—since it is impossible to bring [water] by means of a pot due to its having holes and the absence of fitness for bringing [it]—this is the conclusion regarding the doctrine of the Guru (*gurumata*).

In the case of water, fitness (*yogyatā*) consists in its being suitable water; likewise, for one who desires heaven and the like, although [the sacrifice] is here a means to that which is desired, if it is not known as such, there can be no connection with the sacrifice for one who is unfit—meaning one devoid of the cognition "this is my duty"—and thus, due to the lack of such a connection, it is stated that fitness consists in being known as a means to what is desired. For one who desires heaven, the status of being the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) exists; however, even when something is a means to the desired, if there is a delusion regarding its being a means to that [desired end], then fitness consists in being known as a means to the desired.

However, in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), fitness (*yogyatā*) consists precisely in possessing purification and so forth, because it is connected with the word *jyā* (the sacrifice); it should be understood that this fitness is simply the state of being grasped as having no doubt regarding the status of being a means to a desired end (*kāmyasādhanatva*) which is already present.
Fitness [is required] precisely for the sake of presentation; thus, the fact that the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is the denotation [of the root] is established.
Furthermore, even in the case of an *apūrva* (unprecedented result), the connection with the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is not possible.

This is because, according to your own view, a cognition qualified by semantic competency (*yogyatā*) is the cause of verbal comprehension; however, since the *apūrva* is not previously presented [to consciousness], semantic competency—in the form of being a means to a desired end—cannot be established therein, otherwise it would lead to an over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
If it is argued that [the injunction] is impossible because knowledge [of such a means] is impossible, we say no.

Because of its qualified novelty (*apūrvatva*), even for one who possesses knowledge of [the sacrifice] as being a means to a desired end (*kāmyasādhanatva*), although knowledge of it as a "thing-to-be-done" (*kāryatva*) might be impossible, there is still the possibility of knowing it as a means to a desired end. Thus, since a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) who lacks the desire to act would not perform the sacrificial effort (*yāgakṛti*), the connection with the person to be enjoined is possible.

The claim that "fitness" (*yogyatā*) consists in being fit for the status of an *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) once rice is known to be a means of satisfaction, and not in the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), is refuted; for even then, there is no perception of a fitness-cognition based on a common mode of presentation—such as the connection of one desiring satisfaction with the rice as the material cause (*upādāna*)—since such a cognition does not exist. This is because [fitness] is the cause for the connection with the *niyojya*, whereas the attainment of the *apūrva* constitutes fitness.

For the state of being the motivator of a syntactic connection (*anvaya-prayojakatva*) consists in being apprehended as occurring in a non-connected state; [this applies] to the *apūrva* in the case of the thought, "The effect produced by the sacrifice is enduring and the means for accomplishing the desired object under discussion. However, [the state of being the motivator] consists in not being apprehended as occurring in a non-connected state. And this [state of not being so apprehended] exists precisely when [the *apūrva*] is the object [of the cognition], because no other effect produced by the sacrifice possesses that status. When something possesses that state, it does not have the status of a mere fitness (*yogyatā*), but rather [it has the status of] a qualified [object].

The manner of understanding the meaning of a sentence (vākyārthabodhaprakāra): By this, the [objection] that "permanence (*sthāyitva*)—in the form of being fit for direct connection with the status of a means (*sādhanatva*) residing in the sentence—is impossible prior to the presentation of the *apūrva*" is refuted;
for permanence is possible in some cases with respect to that which is delimited by the nature of a task (*kāryatva*).

Since the capacity for being directly related to the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) consists precisely in the fitness (*yogyatā*) [of the action] to be connected with that [person], there is no need for any further fitness in that regard. Others maintain that when one hears a sentence such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the cognition of an inconsistency arises—namely, that a lasting effect capable of producing heaven is possible, whereas the sacrifice itself is non-lasting—and from this, the fact that the *apūrva* must be denoted is established; thus, they hold that the very cognition of inconsistency is the cognition of fitness.

"The *liṅ* suffix expresses its own meaning as connected with the instrumentality of the result"—this is the *Nyāyapradīpa*. (*Maṇi*, p. 84–88). It is said that the *arthabhāvanā* constitutes the sentence-meaning;
for it is "for the sake of" (*arthyate*) the person desiring the result, since it has that as its purpose.

Bāla. pṛ. [The injunction of the sentence-meaning is improper when the injunction of the literal meaning is possible]. Mīmāṃsā. The discussion concerning the subject matter of the sentence-meaning should be seen in the index entry "Vākyādhikaraṇa" at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 3489.

Furthermore, syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) is also of many kinds, due to such dissimilarity; likewise, there is a split in the case of the tenth and third offspring because of the difference in the *somacamasas*.
In that regard, there are three types of incongruity (*vairūpya*): in the primary element (*prakṛti*), in the suffix (*pratyaya*), and in the sentence (*vākya*).

In the case of "dakṣiṇā" (the sacrificial fee), because of the restriction that it refers exclusively to the *somacamasa* when taken as a single sentence; and in the first case, regarding the injunction of a quality for the *vājapeya*, [there is incongruity] between the sacrifice being the object and its being the instrument.
Furthermore, there is a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) due to the occurrence of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), such as "only for Brahman.
