Likewise: "May life be perfected through sacrifice; may breath be perfected through sacrifice. Here a doubt arises: Is each of these, beginning with "may life," a separate sentence, or is it one single sentence?
We say: it is one.

When it is said, "For strength, thee," no visible purpose is observed; likewise for "For vigor, thee. Since these are [merely] words, their purpose must be invisible (adṛṣṭa). It is therefore proper to postulate a single invisible result for both.
In this way, there will be a postulation of fewer desired inferences.
Therefore, it is a single sentence.
This being the position reached, we reply:
In the case of equal [independent] elements, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). When elements are equal and lack mutual expectancy, the sentence should be divided:
by the phrase "For the sake of *iṣ*, thee," one purpose is accomplished, and by the phrase "For the sake of *ūrj*, thee," another is accomplished.
But was it not just stated that there is no visible purpose here?

Even if [the result] is not perceived through means of knowledge such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is nevertheless understood through scripture (*śruti*), as in: "With the words *iṣe tvā* he cuts; with *ūrje tvā* he strokes.

Likewise, there is the fulfillment of life (*āyuḥ-kalpanā*) and the fulfillment of breath (*prāṇa-kalpanā*) in such passages as: "May life be perfected by the sacrifice; may breath be perfected by the sacrifice."
But surely, this is merely a single general act which appears divided due to the difference in its qualifiers.

For example, in the injunction "I offer what is pleasing to Agni," the act of offering (*nirvāpa*) is one; its specific qualifiers are "at the impulse of the Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan. Yet, it is not accepted that the act of offering is divided by the difference of those qualifiers.
Likewise here too, the object named *klṛpti* (preparation) is one; it will not become divided by the qualifiers such as "longevity" (*āyus*) and so forth.
It is said:
here, in the text "he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the *klṛptis*," many *klṛptis* are heard;
and those must be recited.

In that regard, one specific determination of life-force (*āyuḥ-klṛpti*) can be expressed by the mantra "May life-force be determined through sacrifice" (*āyuryajñena kalpatām*). Likewise, "May breath (*prāṇa*) be determined through sacrifice" expresses merely the determination of breath. In this way, however, all [mantras] are expressions of specific determinations.
Its purpose is already perceived;
therefore, because of this multiplicity, there is also a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in that case.
But surely, [the purpose] follows from the general statement itself, just as in the case of partitioning?
This is not so;
for here, in the case of distribution, there is no common purpose.

Furthermore, it is enjoined that "he causes them to recite the *klṛpti* formulas," and by the words "May life be fulfilled through the sacrifice," the fulfillment of life is directly accomplished, as is the fulfillment of breath by the words "May breath be fulfilled through the sacrifice."
Therefore, there is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

For those [mantras] whose unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is not established as being connected with the action, and for whom there is an absence of application based on indicative mark (*liṅga*), since their acquisition is caused by explicit statement (*vacana*), it is appropriate that they possess the status of a single mantra (*ekamantratva*) prior to the unseen purpose.
For it is said: "An unseen object is postulated for them, and that [object] possesses its own means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
When their unity is thus postulated, they would be divided and possess mutual expectancy.

For when a single postulation based on what has been seen by many is established, and unity is postulated for all of them, then because each individual lacks the capacity to accomplish that [result], there exists a state of being divided and possessing mutual expectancy; thus, there is syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).
But how, then, in this view, is there an application [of the mantras] according to a difference in meaning—as in:
"With 'For food, thee,' he cuts the branch," and "With 'For strength, thee,' he strokes [it]," and so forth?
And how is there the mention of plurality in the statement, "He causes [the sacrificer] to recite the *klṛptis*"?
That is explained as follows: "Even a single [mantra] is employed by many through various means;
and its repeated application is designated as *klṛpti*. [The beginning, middle, and end...]"

Because of this, and because of the repeated application of the phrase "let it be prepared, let it be prepared," there is no contradiction with plurality even though it constitutes a single syntactical unit.
It is said in reply:
This is not so;
for the application and the purpose [of a word] occur at a time subsequent to its form.
Therefore, when there is a renunciation of that [form], the investigation into non-difference and difference pertains to the reality (tattva).
"Let alone the postulation of a purpose or the injunctive statement itself;
for it is not logical to determine its essential nature at a subsequent time.
This is because one who has not known the form [of the action] is incapable of being enjoined, and it is impossible to postulate a purpose for that which has already been enjoined."
However, the form that is independent of the actual meaning (*tattva*) is determined from the recitation itself;
yet, at that time, it follows both distinction and non-distinction with respect to purpose and application.
And it has been stated that even if there are many [forms], they should be postulated as having authoritative status.
In the case of the perception of form, mutual expectancy and a single purpose are not observed through such factors as movement and so forth.
Consequently, once the difference has been established and firmly maintained, there can subsequently be no reason for bringing about any unity;
nor is it possible to postulate a mutual expectancy that was previously unobserved.

Even if there were a single purpose despite the absence of that [distinct form], then even a single [text] would constitute a single sentence because of its unity; how much more so when, due to a difference in form, there is a difference in application (*viniyoga*)? In that case, even if the purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there is still a difference in purpose.
Moreover, in your own view as well, it must necessarily occur according to each respective application.
This, however, is the distinction.
[The mantra] is yours in its entirety, whereas it is mine in its distributed parts.
Nor is there any lack of visible purpose for these [mantras], because they serve as means for achieving visible purposes taught in the Brāhmaṇas.

And by virtue of that power, whatever is not explicitly mentioned must be supplied—such as "cutting" or "stripping"—to the extent that without it, the capacity to perform the enjoined action would be lacking.

Just as, by the statement "one begins the hymn of praise to Mahendra with the *ṛc* beginning with *ā raghoṣeṇa*," there arises a desire to face the hymn (*stotra*) even when the word is not expressive [of that action], through the mere consideration of its application (*viniyoga*), so too do the words such as *iṣe tvā* possess the status of being causes capable of effecting cutting and so forth.
Both of these cases are authoritative; this has been stated and accepted by some authors of the Sūtras.
In every respect, it is thus here.

Vākya-viniyoga-sūtra 3476: When there is a conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), the sūtra on the application of syntactical connection is "Or the Veda [is primary], because no [other] basis is seen" (3.1.12).
This is because it is precisely by virtue of the beginning and the conclusion that the status of being a Vedic duty is determined.
Or [it is] the power of the sentence, as accepted by Bhartṛhari; Vākya-paṭala 3.1.4.11, p. 897. The power of the sentence is the doctrine of Bhartṛhari.
Otherwise, what would be the recourse for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of excellence in the *arthavādas*? (Ku.
3.6.14) [The answer is:
It is the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, linguistic usage is not possible with an incomplete sentence.
In such a case, since no other [explanation] is applicable, one must necessarily postulate a remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) capable of completing it.
Why? Because the employment of an elliptical sentence is never resorted to in the Veda.
Someone or something remains; that remainder must be sought.
For each individual Vedic sentence is not itself a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since inference and the other means of knowledge are likewise means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, non-existence (*abhāva*) is determined by the sixth [means of knowledge] based on the cognition of all other means of knowledge.
Therefore, in this case, when there is perception and non-perception, one should not assume the mere number [of words] through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).
If inference and the other means of knowledge were also to be excluded, then we would conclude that this [Veda] is limited to this much alone.
However, if something is indeed apprehended by them, then— conjoined with those [means]—

the verbal designation of speech and mind applies to that which has been established through the discourse on "approaching" (*upasadana*) and, according to the principle of vocal restraint, possesses the status of being a constituent part of the word-meaning that serves as a means to its own *apūrva*.
1|3|8. The censure of speech and mind is [expressed] by the *hiraṇyastūya* [verse].
Vā. 1|2|1|18: Speech and mind possess primacy with respect to all bodily movements.
1|2|1|2, p. 107: Restraint of speech (*vāgyama*) lasts from after the *anuvākyā* until the end of the *yājyā*, but not prior to the *anuvākyā*.

*Saṃkarṣa* 4|3|9: Regarding the restraint of speech (*vāgyama*) in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices: "Intending to lead forward the waters, he restrains his speech; he releases it at the time of the oblation. *Bhāṣya* 11|3|15: The restraint of speech is for the purpose of purifying the person. 3|1|1|24: The restraint of speech belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) in the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

Vā. 3.1.1.24: "He restrains his speech" (*vācaṃ yacchati*) pertains to the entire context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, and not merely to the initiation (*dīkṣā*) or the cutting of the sacrificial post (*vedana*).

3.1.1.24–25: Restraint of speech (*vāgyama*). Being restrained in speech (*vāgyamau*), the Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer are the indicators of the sequence for the ritual acts; they act with such care that no ritual act or its constituent part is omitted. They resolve: "I shall act in such a way that no ritual act or any part of a ritual act is lost."

By restraining his speech, the *adhvaryu* priest will remain single-minded and will not err regarding the ritual acts. Likewise, by restraining his speech, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) will remain single-minded and will alert the *adhvaryu* should he become negligent.
Bhāṣya 9.1.6.24: The purpose of restraining speech extends throughout the entire ritual context.
Su. Pṛ. 1065: He causes [the sacrificer] to recite the *vāgvisa* formula at the Vājapeya;
the Vājapeya belongs to Prajāpati. 3482: The Vājapeya is dedicated to Prajāpati.
[This is] the task.
*Satyāśrauprayogacandrikā* 13|1|1: In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the ritual properties (*dharmas*) such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth apply to the wild rice (*nīvāra*).
*Mānavasūtra* 9|2|12|10: In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the rites beginning with sprinkling must be performed upon the wild rice used for the *naivāra-caru* offering.
VI. 9|1|12, The sequence of performance in the Vājapeya: First, at the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana), begins the Pavamāna [laud].
Then follow the Soma libations ending with the recitation (śastra) up to the Vaiśvadeva cup.

Thereafter, when the remaining Soma cups have been offered into the fires and the Praṇītā waters have been disposed of, the Soma modifications beginning with the Utkṛṣṭa and others follow upon the completion of the subject matter.

11|3|15: In the Vājapeya sacrifice, although the animals dedicated to Prajāpati are commenced together with the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*), these animals are delayed after the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite and are sacrificed at the time of the *brahmasāman*. The seasonal animals, however, are sacrificed during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) itself.
Consequently, the sacrificial call (*praisha*) beginning with "O sacrificers, run forward... must be repeated.

But not the tantra [is extended]. Śabarabhāṣya on Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 1.1.4.21: Regarding the animals dedicated to Prajāpati in the Vājapeya sacrifice, in the passage "They release them after they have been carried around with fire; the Brahma-saman is chanted; [the animal] is immolated," the acts of tying, releasing, and so forth—which result in the separation of the vital breaths—are all subsumed under a single ritual act. This is because the injunction for immolation (*ālabhya-vidhi*) extends (*utkarṣaṇāt*) the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—which has the immolation as its instrument and includes its own procedure—to the subsequent acts. Thus, having been extended, it merely restates the final separation (*apavarga*) of the subsequent [acts]. Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 1.1.4: In the Vājapeya, the animals dedicated to Prajāpati constitute a single offering (*ekapradānatva*), because they share the same time and the same deity.

Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 9.1.26 (24): In the Vājapeya sacrifice, there is an injunction for the mere postponement of the immolation (*ālambha*) of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati at the time of the *brahmasāman*.
See Mīmāṃsākośa, page 2445, under the section "The mere immolation of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati at the time of the *brahmasāman*.
In the Vājapeya, for the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, there is a single *yājyā-ṛc* for the fat-oblation (*vasā-homa*).

Bhāṣya 11.2.124: In the Vājapeya sacrifice, regarding the animals dedicated to Prajāpati (prājāpatya-paśus), there is a performance of the ritual acts (padārthānusamaya) starting from the *upākaraṇa* (the formal dedication).

Vi. 5.2.6: In the Vājapeya sacrifice, regarding the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, the cooking pot (*kumbhī*) is common to all (is a *tantra*). Mā. 11.4.113: In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the offering of the animal fat (*vasāhoma*) for the animals dedicated to Prajāpati is common to all (is a *tantra*).

9|1|2| 5|24. In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the simultaneity (*sāhitya*) of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati is established by the texts: "He immolates seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati" and "Having performed the rite for the Viśvedevas, they proceed with the animals dedicated to Prajāpati. (Vi. 5|2|1). In the Vājapeya sacrifice, regarding the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, the carrying forward of the fires (*agnyādipraṇayana*) and the commonality of the pot, the spit, and the fat are performed as a single collective act (*tantra*). (Mā. 11|4|130). In the Vājapeya sacrifice, regarding the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, the *abhigrupeṣa* (the pressing for the *abhigru* vessel) and the vessels for holding the remainder of the *prajāśeṣa* (offspring-remnant) need not be prepared; furthermore, the pouring over (*abhivāraṇa*) is a disposal (*pratipatti*).

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, regarding the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, there is simultaneous performance (*anusamaya*) starting from the cutting of the portions for the deities (*daivāvadāna*). In a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), one should avoid that [simultaneous performance] because it has been stated according to the rule.
Commentary: In the Vājapeya, there are animals dedicated to Prajāpati.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: should one take portions for each deity from every single animal, and from those [portions] first the *sauviṣṭakṛta* portions, then the *aiḍa* portions; and thus, by means of the *devata* portions, there is a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) of the deities' rites, by means of the *sauviṣṭakṛta* portions of the *sauviṣṭakṛta* rites, and by means of the *aiḍa* portions of the *aiḍa* rites? What, then, is the prima facie view? One should take the entire set of portions from each individual animal and then offer them.
This has been established by the direct statement in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and it follows by extension (*codaka*) even in the case of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati.

[Objection: Even though the act of cutting (avadāna) is a constituent element (padārtha) associated with the *sānnāyya* offering, nevertheless, the cutting is enjoined in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).

How so? [The text says: "The Pratiprasthātṛ [should cut] from the southern shoulder; having washed the vessel, he should offer it. Thus, the cutting is enjoined as qualified by all these attributes, and if it is enjoined, it must be accompanied by its constituent elements (*padārtha*).

Alternatively, once the cutting has been performed and the immediate offering (*homa*) would follow, another constituent element is enjoined by the statement: "One should not offer that much alone; then there are the portions for the *Sviṣṭakṛt*."
Therefore, these two—the substance and its connection—are the archetypal (prakṛta) ones.
Here, by virtue of the scriptural statement, the substances have become yours alone.
In the archetype, having first cut off the portions for the deities, one subsequently cuts off the portions for Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt.
In this case as well, it would be exactly the same, because the animal sacrifice is essentially of that nature;
for there is a unity of action between the deities and the gods.
The Commentary states: This is not so.

[The offering] for the deities is [performed] with those belonging to the deities; that for the Sviṣṭakṛt with those belonging to the Sviṣṭakṛt; and that for the Ṛgvedic verses with those belonging to the Ṛgvedic verses. Why? Because they constitute a single ritual act (*ekakarmya*).
In this way, it becomes performed together.
And as for the statement that "in the archetype (prakṛti), there is a complete cutting off" (*kṛtsnāvadāna*):

it is heard in the context of the archetype that "having cut off portions for the deities, one should not offer only that much; portions for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt must also be cut off. Having cut off the portions for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, one should not offer only that much; portions for the *iḍā* must also be cut off."
Therefore, here, while performing the sequence of offerings for the deities, one should not indeed subvert the natural order of the ritual.
Having cut off portions for the deities, one does not yet offer them; rather, one carries forward the portions for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Then, having cut off the portions for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, one does not yet offer them; rather, one carries forward the portions for the Iḍā.

Therefore, the sequential performance (anusamaya) is according to the individual items alone. [Objection: No; because the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) favors their simultaneity (sāhitya), there must be a sequential performance of each item with its respective deity.
In the archetype (prakṛti), it is said: "Having offered the portions for the deities, one should not offer [the oblation] at that point alone."

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the chariot belongs to Prajāpati; this has not been disputed. Here too, when taking the portion from the second animal, one should indeed perform the sprinkling of that [chariot].
That is to say, immediate sequence (ānantarya) occurs in the archetype (prakṛti), and because the mantra possesses meaning. The Commentary states: "In this way, the Manotā mantra will apply there."
Otherwise, it would occur alternately.
Therefore, this [order] belongs to the deities: those for Agni with the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offerings, those for Sviṣṭakṛt with the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offerings, and those for Iḍā with the *aiḍa* offerings.
As the Śāstra says: "In the archetype, there is a sequence for the deities and so forth; here too, it follows from that."
The performance should be carried out according to the sequence of sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) for each individual animal.

For if, having offered the portions for the deities from one animal, the portions for the deities were offered from another, then that which belongs to the first animal—the offering to the deity *Sviṣṭakṛt* which follows immediately after [the offerings to the other deities] as established by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction)—would be subverted.
Therefore, the performance must follow the sequence of sections.
It is not so.
[In the previous case], because the animal was one, the act was performed for the sake of completing the portions of the primary substance;
here, however, because there is a plurality and a commonality [of animals], it is understood [that the portions are taken] together.

For the sake of achieving proximity (*sāhitya*), the inference of those of the same class by those of the same class—such as [the limbs] of deities by [the limbs] of deities—must be performed in this manner.

As for Soma’s objection that "even in the preceding day there is *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance by sections) because of the scriptural statement," this constitutes a connection by way of a counter-example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: in a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), one should sacrifice according to the sequence of the deities for each individual animal. Because each individual animal is a single unit, the three-fold set [of rites] applies to each one individually, just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Vi— "Is there a performance by sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) in the offerings to the gods, or rather a performance of each [offering] individually (*ekānusamaya*)? Because it is seen in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Since there is a unity of the animal victim in the archetype, let that [individual performance] apply to the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well, because the reason for it is present."

The sequence of similar items follows immediately thereafter. According to the Bhaṭṭa school: in the archetype (*prakṛti*), regarding the *sānnāyya* offering, because the various acts such as the cutting of portions (*avadāna*) constitute a single ritual item (*ekapadārtha*), the extension (*atideśa*) applies this to the model sacrifice (*daikṣa*). However, by the injunction—"Having cut the portions for the deities, one should not offer only that much; one cuts the portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt*. Having cut the portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, one should not offer only that much; one cuts the portions for the *iḍā*"—the difference between the ritual items is understood due to the prescription of a different order. For the proximity of the cutting of the shoulder-blade portions (*aṃsa*) is not accomplished by the original ritual items.

Therefore, in a group of animals dedicated to a single deity, there is a sequential performance (*anusamaya*) for each animal individually regarding the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*) and so forth, as if they were dedicated to different deities;
and at the end, the oblation to the deity (*devatā-homa*) is performed collectively (*tantra*).

Nor can it be argued that because the cutting of portions for a single animal was performed consecutively in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it must be done likewise here; for according to the logic of the *prājāpatya* animals, since the animal is a single unit, there is no sequence of parts, and thus there is no conflict with the extended application (*codaka*) which prescribes the archetype’s procedure in its entirety.

For this very reason, where there is a conflict with the extended injunction (*codaka*) regarding a group of animals dedicated to different deities, one should perform the three portions (*avadāna*) and the oblation (*homa*) for the first animal, and then for the second animal as well, the offering should be made following the three portions. However, in the recitation of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other formulas, it is done by way of a single performance (*tantra*). Even there, if one follows the sequence of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*), the second oblation would necessarily set aside the immediate succession of the taking of portions as established by the extended injunction.

In reality, even though a separate unrelated object is being established, since the taking of the portion for the deity (*devatāvadāna*) serves to accomplish the five-fold cutting-off and offering (*pañcāvadāna-homa*), it is appropriate that it too possesses the nature of the offering (*pradāna*) and so forth; thus, even when there are different deities, there is *anusamaya* (sequential performance) from the taking of the portion for the deity up to the final offering. However, in the case of a single deity, *anusamaya* consists precisely in the non-interruption of the ritual acts (*padārtha*). Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Maṇḍana [states]: "The cutting-off of the portions for the animals is simultaneous."

Śaṅkara says: "Because of the commonality among the sacrificial animals (*paśu*). In the Vājapeya sacrifice, regarding the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, there are three types of portions to be cut: those for the principal offerings (*pradhāna*), those for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, and those for the consumption of the *iḍā* portion. These are obtained from the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*amīṣomīya*) by means of the extended application (*codaka*).
And these constituent elements (*padārtha*) must be performed according to the principle of sequential performance by item (*padārthānusamaya*)."

But it is not the case that there is a sequential performance by parts (*kāṇḍānusaṃmaya*), such as performing the three portions of the omentum for one animal and then the three portions for the second;
rather, this applies to all groups of animals. (Vi.
5.2.6) In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the ritual acts pertaining to the animals dedicated to Prajāpati are performed according to the sequential performance of individual items (*padārthānusaṃmaya*).
5|2|12–3. See the discussion under the heading "The Order of Performance According to the Individual Items" (padārthānusamaya) at Mīmāṃsākośa, p.
2437. In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the performance of the offerings to Prajāpati (prājāpatyapracāra) follows after all the original (prakṛta) and modified (vaikṛta) common rites.
11|3|15–18–54. In the Vājapeya, there is no sprinkling with the remnants of the fore-sacrifices (prayājaśeṣābhivāraṇa) for the animals dedicated to Prajāpati.
4|1|4|133–39. Regarding the sprinkling with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings, see the section under Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 2785, titled ‘*prayājaśeṣābhivāraṇādhikaraṇa*’.

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, there is the recitation of the original ritual rules and mantras for the chariot and the *dundubhi* drum, which are prescribed as the means for performing the *māhendra* stotra.
See the second section (varṇaka) of 10|4|1|1–2. Regarding the chariot and the woman (*yoṣā*), see the section under Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 3282, titled ‘*rathayoṣādhikaraṇa*’.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, one gives a chariot yoked with horses to the Adhvaryu priest. By this [gift], there is no sublation of any other unspecified or specified sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Vi. 10.3.20: "In the Vājapeya, one gives a chariot yoked with horses to the Adhvaryu; he gives a team [of horses] accompanied by *Ṛg* verses, and he gives a team accompanied by *Sāman* chants."
Bhāṣya 10.3.21.75: In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the sacrificial post (yūpa) is seventeen cubits long. Vi.
3.1.9: In the Vājapeya, [the rule] "one begins the Māhendra-stotra with the sound of a chariot" and "one begins the Māhendra-stotra with the sound of a drum" is given;
therein, by means of a chariot...

Regarding the Vājapeya as a modified sacrifice (vikṛti): in the Vājapeya, there is the seventeen-fold chant (*saptadaśa-stoma*) and the noise (*ghoṣa*); thus, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and its mantra—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
However, while there is indeed a sublation of the sacrificial grass and its mantra, there is a sublation of both by means of the noises (*ghoṣaiḥ*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that sound belongs only to a chariot or a drum, and not to anything else (Sūtra 10.1.42). Description 2: In the *Vājapeya* sacrifice, a modified offering of seventeen vessels of rice-gruel (*śarāva*) is prescribed.

Regarding its preparation (*nirvāpa*), there is one view (*pakṣa*) that the original handful (*muṣṭi*) and the number four—found in the injunction "he offers four handfuls"—are both to be applied here.
The second [view] is that both are sublated; the third is that one or the other is sublated;
and the fourth is that there is merely the elision of the number of the property (dharma).

The "handful" (*muṣṭi*) mentioned in the *caru* [text] is indeed to be set aside; the number heard first is not to be set aside. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the filling of the *śarāva* should be performed with four *kuḍava*s and so forth.
(By means of the seventeen-foldness, the fourfoldness is sublated; and by the *śarāva*, the handful is sublated.
The pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is to be done with the *śarāva* alone, and the mantra for the pouring out is to be repeated that many times—namely, seventeen times; thus it appears to Kevalānanda.)

10|1|28. Or, in the Vājapeya sacrifice, all the Soma [vessels] (3486) might become subsidiary parts through contact; or they might belong to a single primary rite. In that case, the intended sequence would be that they assist [the rite] according to this order.

Furthermore, the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are a limb of the animal sacrifice; the *āgnimāruta* offering belongs to the Soma sacrifice; likewise, the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi-praharaṇa*) is a limb of the animal sacrifice, while the *hāriyojana* offering is a part of the Soma sacrifice.
Thus, their sequence is purposeless;
therefore, it is not determined.

In other cases, it is merely a matter of time. For instance, in the statements, "They proceed with the after-offerings (anuyāja) after the Āgnimāruta [offering]," and "Having cast away the enclosing-sticks (paridhi), he offers the Hāriyojana," the mention of the Āgnimāruta and the taking up of the enclosing-sticks serve as temporal indicators (*lakṣaṇa*) for that specific time. When the indicator has ceased to apply, the time [of the subsequent action] is determined independently.
For example: "One should come at the time of the Agnihotra.
Where there is no Agnihotra, the time does not depart [from its nature].
But in this case, is it not a case of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?
No;
for in this context, time alone is the intended meaning. Since the suffix -tvā denotes precisely the prior time.
The word "ūrdhva" (above) may denote either space or time. Since its application to space is impossible here, it is understood to have the meaning of time.
[The author of the] *Ṭup-ṭīkā* says: "It is replied."
The Āgnimāruta [offering] is a subsidiary of the Soma sacrifice;
the after-offerings (anuyāja) are the two wings;
these are the subsidiaries of these two.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the section concerning the entire Vājapeya;
as stated in the section on the Vājapeya.
There is dependence [of the sacrifice] upon its being the instrument of action. If there were dependence with respect to the result, the two triads would be contradictory.

For the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), there is one triad consisting of the status of being the thing to be adopted (*upādeya*), the status of being the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and the status of being a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*).
With respect to its quality, there is a triad consisting of the object to be designated, non-elevation, and predominance;
having abandoned that [quality], if it were to recur, the sentence would be split—therefore, that [term] is so.
The word *vājapeya* is also the name of a ritual, like the *agnihotra*.

Bhaṭṭa: Those very same objections—such as the necessity of *matvartha-lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication of possession) and so forth—which were raised previously against the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), are here being challenged.

For if the sacrifice (*yāga*) were itself a *kāraka* (grammatical factor), then, since other *kārakas* such as Soma and the like could not otherwise be related to it, there would have to be either *matvartha-lakṣaṇā* or an injunction of a *bhāvanā* qualified by both [the sacrifice and the substance]. However, there is no evidence whatsoever for accepting this position.
Because it is accepted that sacrifice (*yāga*) is of the nature of an action (*kriyā*),

therefore, in that [sacrifice], all the factors of action (*kāraka*s) can coherently relate to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) without even the need for possessive indication (*mattvarthalakṣaṇā*) and without any contradiction in form (*vairūpya*). Furthermore, even though sacrifice is of the nature of an action, its connection with the productive urge through a general relationship is not contradictory.
Furthermore, a *bhāvanā* (efficient force) distinct from those [already mentioned] is not accepted at all, as in the case of the Grammarians.
Consequently, it is more appropriate that even in cases such as "uddiṣṭa" and so forth, these are everywhere merely injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*).
As for the example of the *vājapeya*, that was given in the root text in accordance with the [specific] *sūtra* on accessory qualities.

This being the case, since the analysis of "pacati" (he cooks) is "pākaṃ karoti" (he performs cooking), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) connects with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) precisely as an intermediate factor of action (*kāraka*), such as the object (*karman*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). And how *bhāvanā* is something distinct [from the meaning of the root] will be explained later. Therefore, it is untenable for other factors of action to connect with the meaning of the verbal root.
As a last resort, the injunction of a *bhāvanā* qualified by both [the fruit and the accessory] is accepted in the case of the *soma* sacrifice and others;
or else, according to the ancient method, there is *mattvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of the sense "possessing").

Otherwise, if the sacrifice were connected to both the fruit and the accessory by direct denotation (*śruti*) itself, then for the sake of its connection with the fruit, the sacrifice would possess the qualities of being something to be acquired (*upādeya*), something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*); whereas in relation to the accessory, it would possess the opposite qualities of being something to be referred to (*uddeśya*), something already established (*anuvāda*), and a primary factor (*pradhānatva*). Thus, there would result the fallacy of contradictory dualities (*viruddhadvikatā*).
The arguments establishing that [the term] is to be accepted as such, and so forth, should be consulted in the Kaustubha.
Therefore, since a qualified injunction is untenable due to the necessity of assuming a possessive indication (*mattvarthalakṣaṇā*), terms such as *udbhid* must be names (*nāmadheya*).
Maṇḍana states: "The word *vājapeya* is a name."
Śaṅkara: "The status of *vājapeya* as a name [is established].

In the section concerning the *vājapeya*, since a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is possible through a syntactical connection (*tantrasambandha*), the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) avoids the fault of the metaphorical indication of possessive meaning (*mattvarthalakṣaṇā*). Thus, in modifications such as the *vājapeya* sacrifice, by means of the suffix [denoting the quality], [the details] taught for the *vājapeya* [are extended].

Śabara: Where several items are obtained through extended application (*codaka*), yet one is heard directly in the text—as in "the sacrificial post is made of *khadira* wood," "the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant," "the sacrificial cake is made of barley," and so forth—there arises a doubt: does the direct scriptural statement of the *khadira* and other such items allow for an option (*vikalpa*) with the *palāśa* and other materials from the archetype (*prakṛti*), or is there a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the item explicitly mentioned? In this doubt, [the prima facie view is] that there is an option, as in the case of the archetype; for the direct statement is not an injunction for the *khadira* and so on, since they are already obtained [by extension]. However, if its purpose were merely the exclusion of the *palāśa* and others, it would entail the three defects (*tridoṣā*). Therefore, [it is a restrictive rule].

Just as, when multiple substances are obtained as options by the original injunction (*prakṛti*), the mention of *vrīhi*, *nīvāra*, and so forth serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), so too, when materials such as *khadira* wood are obtained without restriction through the extended application (*codaka*), they are restricted by an explicit scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*). And because of that restriction, since there is no further purpose [for them], the exclusion of *palāśa* and other such woods follows. Soma says: "Just as the quality of being 'water-possessing' (*apsu-mattā*) is not to be enjoined because it is already obtained [by extension], so too is the *khadira* wood and the rest"—this is the connection [of the argument] that has arisen.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: among the conflicting materials such as *khadira* wood and *palāśa* leaves, when one is heard [as prescribed], it would exclude all other substances; this being the case, the taking of that specific material becomes purposeful.
Regarding the *vājina* (curd-whey), [the rule is] *vājine bhāṭṭa* 4.1.9: the consumption of the *vājina* occurs after it has been fully prepared.
Bhāṣya 8.2.13: There is an *anuvaṣaṭkāra* for the *vājina*, as there is for the *soma*;
and that [offering] belongs to the *sviṣṭakṛt* alone.
Saṃkalpa 4.4.2: In the *vājina*, the taste is bitter and astringent.
Bhāṣya 8.1.9.23: In the case of the *vājina* (curd-mixture), there is no invocation (*āvāhana*), because it is a substance employed by another.

At the time of the invocation (*āvāhana*) in the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, one should perform the invocation of the deities of the *vājina* offering just as one does for the deities beginning with *sviṣṭakṛt*. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the conclusion is as follows]: because they subsist upon a substance provided by another, and because at the time of invocation that substance has not yet come into existence as it is yet to be produced, there is no invocation of Viṣṇu’s sacrificial horse (*ukṣan*).
For this very reason, there is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text: "He indeed does not invoke the *vājins*."
In the section on *saṃkalpa* (4.4.8), there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual rules (*dharma*) pertaining to the *sānnāyya* offering to the *vājina* offering.

From 8.2.1.9 to 5, it is established that in the *vājina* offering and in the *sautrāmaṇī*, the *soma* sacrifice comes first, because of the use of that specific word (*tacchabdāt*) in the context of the *mahā-ṛtu*s.
In the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the *vājina* sacrifice is heard in the injunction: "To the *vājins*, the *vājina*."
And in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the cups of *surā* are mentioned:
the Āśvina, the Sārasvata, and the Aindra cups.

Regarding these two *vājina* cups, there arises a deliberation as to whether their procedure (*vidhyanta*) is that of the Soma sacrifice or that of the Full-Moon sacrifice of Dakṣa; [the author] states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In the Vājina, the Sautrāmaṇī, and the cups (grahas), there should be the precedence of Soma; that is to say, the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) of the Soma sacrifice is to be adopted.
This is because of the word "that" (tat).
Those [rituals] in which that word—the word "Soma"—occurs are called "those characterized by that word."
The state of being those is "that-ness" (tacchabdyam). Thus,
the word *soma* is applied to the *vājina* in the passage, "Soma indeed is the *vājina*," and the word *soma* is applied to *surā* in the passage, "Surā is Soma."
And because of similarity, it proceeds to another [substance]. And the similarity to *soma* consists in being produced from *soma*.
Therefore, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of *soma* applies to the *vājina* and the cups (*graha*).
This is a transfer of properties by name, not a prescription;
and because of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*.
This sūtra presents another argument for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "To the Vājins, the whey" (*vājibhyo vājinam*); and in the Sautrāmaṇī, there are cups such as those of *surā* liquor. Furthermore, it is heard: "He performs the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* with the words, 'O Agni, eat the whey' (*vājinasyāgne vīhi*)"; and "He performs the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* with the words, 'O [Agni], eat the *surā*' (*surāyā vīhi*)."
And likewise, because the *anuṣaṭkāra* follows [the *vaṣaṭkāra*] and because the *anuṣaṭkāra* exists, the properties of Soma are to be applied to the *vājina*, the *surā-graha*s, and so forth;
this is also because they are consumed together.
Regarding the four-monthly sacrifices (*caturmāsya*), another reason is stated for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the properties of Soma (*somadharma*) should apply to the whey (*vājina*):
"They divide the remainder equally and consume it together" (*samupadya bhakṣayanti*)—this is heard in the scripture concerning the whey; and consuming [the substance] together is a property of Soma.
Because of this reason—that it is a consumption from a common source (*samupadyabhakṣaṇa*) following the nature of Soma—the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of Soma is to be adopted for the *vājina*.

Its [procedure] includes the purchase (*krayaṇa*), the mixing (*āśrayaṇa*), the *puroruk* verses, the drawing of the cup (*grahaṇa*), the placing (*āsādana*), the covering (*vāsa*), and the binding (*upanahana*).

In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, regarding the cups of *surā* liquor, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *soma* sacrifice should apply; this is the subject of the subsequent sūtra providing further reasons:

"The purchase (*krayaṇa*), the mixing (*śrayaṇa*), the *puroruc* hymn, the *upayāma* [vessel], the drawing of the cup (*grahaṇa*), the placing down (*āsādana*), the cloth (*vāsa*), and the binding (*upanahana*)—the collection of these.
Thus, the "purchase of tender grass-shoots (*śaṣpa*)" for the purpose of preparing the *surā* is prescribed in the scripture: "He purchases the tender grass-shoots with lead from a eunuch."
In the passage, "He mixes the forest with *kuvala* flour," the mixing of the ground fruits of the *sudhāmava* tree is enjoined.
In the passage, "There is one *puroruc*," a single *puronuvākyā* verse is enjoined.
In the passage, "Thou art taken with a support; for the sake of the flawless, thee," a mantra characterized by the word *upayāma* is enjoined for the purpose of drawing the cup.
"The Āśvina cup is drawn"—thus the drawing of the cup is heard in the scripture.
"Having drawn it, he sets it down"—thus the setting down of the drawn cup is heard in the scripture.

"They remain together for three nights"—for the sake of producing the *surā* liquor, the staying together for three days of the *tokma*, the flour, the parched grain, and the curdled milk is heard as their dwelling.
Regarding the statement, "In the linen cloth there are wrappings, namely young shoots and sprouts," the *upanahana* (wrapping) is thus enjoined by scripture.
Therefore, this [rite] beginning with the purchase (*krayaṇa*) and so forth is like that of the Soma sacrifice;
consequently, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Soma sacrifice should apply to the cups of *surā*.
Or rather, one should offer it with the oblation (havis), because it is a modification of that.

Regarding the *vājina* and the *surāgraha* cups, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—supported by the Sūtra—is that the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *soma* sacrifice should apply. The author sets aside this position with the word "or" (*vā*) and states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): because of the word "that" (*tat*), it was said that the *soma* procedure applies; however, that is not so. Rather, by virtue of the commonality of being an oblation (*havis*), the procedure of the *Dākṣāyaṇa* and *Paurṇamāsa* sacrifices should be extended [to them].
This is because they are modifications (*vikāra*) of those; that is, they are its modifications, hence "because of being its modification."
Sura is a modification of medicinal herbs, while vājina is a modification of the sānnāyya;
furthermore, the commonality of being an oblation (havis) is more powerful [than the specific modification],
and the word "soma" is used as a eulogy.

Now, if the procedure (*vidhyanta*) of Soma were not applicable to the *vājina* and the *surā-grahas*, how then is it that the word "Soma" is applied to the *vājina* and so forth— such as in the statements "The *vājina* is indeed Soma" and "The *surā* is Soma"—
where the word "Soma" is used due to similarity to Soma according to the principle of the *vājina*? To this, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) replies:
The word "Soma" is a term of praise;
this word "Soma" has the sense of praise and does not have the function of an injunction.
Therefore, this is an extension of ritual properties (dharmātideśa) by means of a name.
The other statements are as follows.

The purchase (*krayaṇa*), the mixing (*śrayaṇa*), the *puroruk* recitation, the taking of the vessel with the *upayāma* formula, the placing [of the cup], the cloth (*vāsaḥ*), and the wrapping (*upanahana*)—these other elements, which constitute the nature of the Soma ritual, are prescribed for the *surā* cups by explicit scriptural injunctions (*vācanika*), as they are not obtained from any other source.
Their acquisition does not occur through the extension (*atideśa*) of Soma rituals, precisely because there is no archetypal Soma procedure (*somavidhyanta*) applicable here.
Furthermore, the designation [of the cups] is likewise similar.

The designation in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice—"one obtains the *dīkṣaṇīyā* with young grass (*śaṣpa*), the *prāyaṇīyā* with *tokmā* (young sprouts), and the *ātithyā* with lion's hair"—also, like that [previous case], brings about the *aindraka* ritual procedure due to the commonality of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
For if the Soma procedure were to apply, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites would be obtained directly; thus, the designation would be redundant.
Therefore, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the *aindraka* procedure alone applies to the *vājina* and the *surā-grahas*.
And there is the observation of an indicative mark regarding the sacrificial cake of the animal sacrifice.

In the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, with respect to the cups (*graha*), an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is observed: "No cakes are offered for these animals; for these animals themselves are the animal-cakes.
In reality, however, these cups are not cakes.
But if those cups were to possess the characteristics of a cake, then this indicative mark would be appropriate.

Therefore, the established conclusion is that in the *vājina* offering during the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, and in the cups (*graha*) of the *Sautrāmaṇī*, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) is that of Indra’s sacrifice and not that of Soma.
Furthermore, because the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* of the *vājina* constitutes a *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, there is no sublation of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offerings belonging to the *āmikṣā* sacrifice.
Just as there is an *anuvaṣaṭkāra* for the *vājina* offering, so too is there one for the *āmikṣā*;
and that [anuvaṣaṭkāra] is of the nature of the *sviṣṭakṛt* alone, because it consists in the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the primary substance.
Therefore, the *sviṣṭakṛt* follows the *āmikṣā* sacrifice, just as it does the *vājina*.

When it is argued that "the Sviṣṭakṛt [offering] is entitled to the entire portion of the sacrifice," this is refuted because, by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*) regarding the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* of the whey (*vājina*), the term 'vājina' itself designates it; thus, although the whey serves as the disposal (*pratipatti*) for the remnant, the requirement for a disposal of the remnant of the curd-offering (*āmiṣā-yāga*) remains unfulfilled. Consequently, there is no sublation of the Sviṣṭakṛt which is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*). [In the section on] Intention (1.4.2), the distinction between the whey-offering and the curd-offering arises from the difference in their characteristics, namely the material and the deity.

VI. 2|1|9. By means of the *utkara* (mound of earth) prescribed as a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the placing of the *vājina* (curdled milk), there is the exclusion of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) altar in the Soma-related *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices.
10|1|3|18–22. The offering of the *vājina* is a disposal (*pratipatti*); its sequence is equal to that of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
(Bhāṣya).

Because the *vājina* (curd-whey) and the *upāṃśuyāja* are subordinate elements, their displacement (*bādha*) in the *āmikṣā-yāga*, the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, and so forth, is appropriate; for since there is no possibility of raising an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) [for them] when they are set aside by the qualities prescribed at the time of origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), which leave no room [for others], displacement occurs. (Kau. 2.3.2.3, p. 23). In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice, the completion is performed with clarified butter (*ājya*) in the absence of the *vājina*. (Bhāṭṭa. 4.1.9). This is because threshing (*avaghāta*) is not subject to the logic of the *vājina* and other such cases, as it is established by depending upon the *vrīhi* grains employed by another [rite].

The rice grains (*vrīhīṇām*) do not fall within the scope of the *vājinanyāya* (the logic of the whey), because the status of threshing as a subordinate element (*aṅga*)—just like the status of the rice as a subordinate element of the sacrifice—is equally established by the syntactical sentence (*vākya*), and because threshing possesses an inherent necessity for performance, unlike the *vājina*.
(Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Bhāṣya 2.1.4.9, p. 68). The *vājinanyāya*: (The whey [poured] into the heated milk is not the motivator [of the preparation]).
See Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 59; *Āmikṣā tate payasi* (The curdled milk is in the heated milk)—this section should be consulted. (Mīmāṃsāsūtra 4.1.9.22–24).

The *Vājinanyāya*: (The *Vājinayāga* is a distinct ritual action due to the difference in the qualities consisting of the substance and the deity). Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1580; see the section on the "Principle of Qualities" (*Guṇanyāya*).
In the passage, "Having performed the *Upasad*, one performs the *Agnihotra* for a month," this ritual action is enjoined as qualified by both the *Upasad* and the month.

If it is argued that, according to the principle of the *vājina* [milk], there is a difference of action (*karmabheda*) due to the difference of qualities (*guṇabheda*), we say no, because of the disparity (*vaiṣamya*). (Sūtra 2.3.11) In some cases, even from a quality characterized by the essential nature of a substance and a deity— such as the forms of eleven potsherds (*ekādaśakapāla*) and ten potsherds (*daśakapāla*)— which are recited with a distinction between the Āgneya and others, the establishment of a difference [of action] occurs according to the *vājina* principle (in the prima facie view).

Kau. 2|4|2|8, p. 114: (Regarding the distinction based on the difference between the eleven-potsherd and twelve-potsherd forms, there arises a doubt—according to the *vājinanyāya*—that they constitute separate rites, because Vāmadeva [has stated] that in both cases, by the *vājinanyāya*, they are distinct rituals.)

Page 290, 2|2|2|26: According to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), after the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*) has established a connection with one [element], a distinction (*bheda*) is established through its fitness for connection with another, according to the *vājina* principle. This is because the primary injunction is not known [in its entirety] by way of sequence, and since the unity of the action (*ekatva*) will be refuted in the eleventh book (1|1|18), the order of recitation is not a restrictive factor.
Therefore, since all [elements] are connected simultaneously, there is a differentiating effect even by the *vājina* principle.

In the *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven) passage, there is no fault whatsoever, because—according to the principle of the *vājina* [offering]—it prescribes a distinct ritual act qualified by substances such as sandalwood.

The nature of the *vājinanyāya*: The bringing of curd (*dadhyānayana*) is for the sake of the *āmikṣā* according to the sentence (*vākya*), not for the sake of the *vājina*. Therefore, since the performance of the bringing of curd is prompted by the *āmikṣā*, the *vājina* does not possess the status of being the prompter (*prayojaka*) of that bringing of curd; such is the principle of that maxim.
The Vājin sacrifice is not the motivator (*aprayojaka*) of the curd-mixing (*dadhyānayanam*), even though that mixing is an auxiliary (*parāṅga*) that provides assistance.
Bāla. p. 107: The Vājin sacrifice is not the motivator for the production of the *vājina*; it is motivated solely by its being the material cause (*upādānatva*).
On page 106, line 1: And for one performing the Vājin sacrifice, there is the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *vājina* [curd-whey] at the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Bhaṭṭa 4.1.9: The conclusion of the Vājin sacrifice is by means of clarified butter (*ājya*) at the Cāturmāsya deity-festival accompanied by the *vājina*.
4.1.9: Even though the Vājin sacrifice is a modification of the *āmikṣā*, its location [is determined] because it is a subsequent production (*anuniṣpatti*).

Some say that this is a *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical deliberation), on the grounds that because the *vājina* sacrifice is the primary rite, it lacks the status of a subordinate (*aṅga*) and thus there is no extension (*atideśa*) of its details; consequently, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the observation of the prohibition of the *vājina* sacrifice indicates a displacement (*utkrama*).
However, that is incorrect.

In the Vājin sacrifice, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the properties of the Sānnāyya offering. Even though [the Vājin] is like a disposal (*pratipatti*), the expectation of a procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) arises according to the logic of the Vājin sacrifice—just as in the case of the *niṣkāsa*—because such an extension is appropriate due to the similarity with the Soma sacrifice (in the case of the *somānuvaṣaṭkāra* sacrifice). This is because the Vājin substance, being a material that serves a purpose, is non-permanent; since it lacks the status of a primary injunction (*adhikāravidhi*) alongside permanent offerings such as the *āmikṣā*, it is desired for the sake of disposal, and thus its status as a subordinate element (*aṅgatva*) alone is logical. (Soma 7.2.10) In the Vājin sacrifice, there is an extension of the properties of the Sānnāyya. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the author of the *Bhāṣya* has established the following final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In the section on the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna-prakaraṇa*), by the sentence "When one offers in the Āhavanīya," there is a connection between the Pavamāna oblations and the establishment of the fires because they serve the purpose of that establishment; for otherwise, they would be purposeless, as their purpose cannot be fulfilled elsewhere. Furthermore, since the Pavamāna sacrifices are not present [in the context of other rites], and since the Vāruṇapraghāsika and modified sacrifices are the primary archetypes (*prakṛti*) of all [such rites], they might be considered known to all sacrifices. However, the author of the Vārttika maintains that the Pavamāna oblations do not belong to the establishment of the fires merely by virtue of being taught outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*).

Because the *āhavanīya* fire is enjoined by that general reference to all *homa*s, the *pavamāneṣṭi*s alone are specifically present; furthermore, there is no evidence for a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on primacy when the primary meaning is already available.

Nor can another sentence be postulated within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *pavamāneṣṭi*s, since even in its absence, it is established that the *vāruṇa* and other offerings serve the purpose of all [fires].

Or, let us grant that such a statement exists in the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*); even so, by that, only those things subordinate to the consecration would have the *āhavanīya* as their locus, but the status of being a primary fire-installation (*agnyādheya*) is not thereby established.
The definition is determined by the locative case (saptamī).

For this very reason, the term *āhavanīya* in that context denotes fire characterized by the unique transcendental potency (*apūrva*) produced by the consecration (*ādhāna*), because at that time the primary *āhavanīya*—which consists of fire characterized by the *apūrva* [of the sacrifice]—does not yet exist.

Nor does it follow that there would be no means of obtaining the *gārhapatya* and other fires for the cooking of the oblations in the *pavamāneṣṭi* and similar rites; for although the primary *gārhapatya* cannot serve as the locus there, there is no evidence to override the use of the *gārhapatya* and others for the model-sacrifice oblations when such usage is otherwise possible.
Therefore, even if there were another statement [to the contrary], the fact that the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices serve the purpose of the *sarvajña* (the omniscient one) must still be established.

In all cases, when there is no deviation from the *apūrva* (transcendental result) regarding its own intended object, there is an entry into the context (*prakaraṇa*) for the purpose of defining the means to that *apūrva*,
