[Objection: But in this way, since the *Āgneya* and other [principal sacrifices] serve a single purpose, would it not follow that they should be subject to option?
On this point, Bhaṭṭa Someśvara offers the following resolution:

independence (*nirapekṣa-sādhanatva*) is also a cause for syntactic option (*vikalpa*). For, according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "an operation concerning words [applies] when they are capable" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), capability is required for every operation involving words. Since a compound (*samāsa*) is considered an operation concerning words because it is an operation regarding two words, so too the case-endings (*sup*) that produce the status of being a word are also operations concerning words; thus, capability is understood from the prescriptive sentences regarding the third case and so forth, and that [capability] consists in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). And mutual expectancy is the state of having departed from [mere] dependence (*vigatāpekṣatva*).
Because it is understood that [the means] are independent [of one another], there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding rice and other grains.

However, in the case of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices, since they require a fruit as their goal, are instrumental means, are expressed by the word "sacrifice" (*yajati*), are denoted by the term "desirable," and—due to the use of a copulative compound (*dvandva*)—are intended to be cooperative, they lack independence as means; therefore, the contingency of an option does not arise.
This [objection] is incorrect.

For in the fifth [chapter], regarding the statement "it would be redundant because it is known by another," the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) in the passages "he initiates with a staff" (*daṇḍena dīkṣayati*) and "he initiates with a girdle" (*mekhalayā dīkṣayati*) expresses the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the staff and other such items; that [conjunction] would be untenable because the third case-ending conveys an independent means (*nirapekṣa-sādhanatva*).

Nor should it be argued that just as in my view there is a conjunction of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), the gold coin (*jādi*), and so forth—even though they are independent means for a single purchase—so too is there a conjunction of the staff and the rest;
for there is a disparity, since those [latter] serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

For, since the use of animals such as goats serves a visible purpose—namely, that they are distinct from the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) established by the final conclusion—the act of purchase does not become independent of requirement (*nirākāṅkṣa*) with respect to the one-year-old cow alone; thus, their combination (*samuccaya*) is logical. However, in the case of the staff and other items, the staff and so forth serve to manifest the consecration (*dīkṣā*), whereas the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) produces it. Furthermore, the consecration is of an invisible nature (*adṛṣṭarūpā*); therefore, the requirement for that which manifests it is not satisfied by that which produces it. Moreover, even if they were both manifestors, the requirement for one would not be satisfied by the other.

Consequently, since this would result in the collapse of the established conclusion regarding the combination of the staff and other items, the fact that they are independent means of accomplishment is not the cause for an option (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, the determination of the purpose of optionality or non-optionality based on the single purpose (*aikārthya*) of the Āgneya and other sacrifices should be resolved precisely according to the method stated by Miśra.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Tantraratna* on the passage "because there is no instruction by another" (*pareṇāvedanāt*): "The absence of a means of proof for conjunction (*samuccaya*), even when there is a single purpose, is also a cause for optionality (*vikalpa*).
And the means of proof for conjunction is the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), which grasps all the subsidiaries and the primary act simultaneously.

However, in the case of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices, since there is a dual compound (*dvandva*) based on the employment of a single word, there is no absence of a means of proof for conjunction."

In the case of rice and other grains, however, since the purpose is served by either one when the hand is intended for that purpose, one does not take them through a combination; thus, there is an absence of evidence for their combination. Furthermore, regarding optional rites (*kāmyakarma*) that serve a single purpose, there is an absence of evidence for their combination precisely because there is no single injunction for their performance.

Likewise, in the twelfth book, regarding the Pathikṛt, Vaiśvānarīya, and other rites performed to remove the fault arising from the omission of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there is an absence of evidence for their combination precisely because there is no single injunction for their performance.

In the case of the staff and other such items, however, because there exists a single injunction for their application, and because they serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the logic of the *vrīhi-yava* [alternative] does not apply; rather, there is indeed a means of proof for their combination (*samuccaya*). Thus, combination is appropriate, and everything is well-established.
This concludes the determination of the purpose of alternative (*vikalpa*).
The varieties of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*):
the varieties of conceptual construction are now examined.

Among them, first of all, every conceptual construction is of three kinds: that which is established by logic (*nyāyagamya*), that which is based on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), and that which is based on personal choice (*aicchika*).

Among these, the first is of eight kinds: between two universals (*jāti*), between two substances (*dravya*), between two qualities (*guṇa*), between two actions (*kriyā*), between a universal and a substance, between a substance and its absence, between a quality and its absence, and between an action and its absence.
[1] Among these, an option (*vikalpa*) is to be made between two universals, as in the case of rice and barley.

And although here there is also an option between two substances, nevertheless, since the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is possible in a universal—even while possessing the function of delimiting a substance—an instruction regarding the instrumentality of two universals alone, without the definition of a substance, results in an option between those two universals alone.

Since it is otherwise impossible for a genus (*jāti*) to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*), the status of a substance as an instrument cannot be established through the alternative of a genus; rather, when an alternative of substances (*dravyavikalpa*) occurs, it is not designated independently.

[2] An alternative of two substances must be performed, such as the eleven or twelve potsherds (*kapāla*) in the *Āgneya* and *Agnīṣomīya* sacrifices; this alternative of the *Āgneya* and others has been stated in the section on other scriptures (*śāstrāntarādhikaraṇa*, 2.4.18–33).
For it has been stated that derivative words (*yaugika*) denote substances: "Everything is measured by derivative words according to their actual meaning" (*Vākyapadīya* p. 677).

[3] An option regarding qualities (guṇa) should be made, as follows: "The sacrificial animal for Agni and Soma is one with black marrow," or "The sacrificial animal for Agni and Soma is one with red marrow."

[4] An option (*vikalpa*) must be made regarding ritual actions, as stated in the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra* (6.5.17–20): "In the case of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, when those moving forward for the *vahiṣpavamāna* chant prevent one another from singing, it is said: 'If the *prastotṛ* should cut off [the chant], he should give a boon to the *brahmán*; if the *pratihartṛ* should cut it off, he should give all his possessions (*sarvavedasa*); if the *udgātṛ* should cut it off, the sacrifice is completed without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*), and having performed it again, he should give whatever he intended to give in the previous performance. Thus, when there is a simultaneous cutting off [of the chant], an option applies among these specific occasional injunctions (*naimittika-vidhi*) such as the giving of gifts."

[5, 6] Regarding the two alternatives to be formulated—namely, between a genus (*jāti*) and a substance (*dravya*), and between a substance and its absence—the example is as follows: in the *Ādhāna* (Fire-laying) ritual, the Vājasaneyins have a scriptural injunction: "One should perform the *ṛtu*, *nakṣatra*, *saṃbhāra*, *cātuḥprāśya*, *jāgaraṇa*, *idhma*, *pūrvārdha*, *anvārambhaṇa*, and *sārparājñī* [rites].

Here, by the word *nakṣatra*, because it is connected with Kṛttikā, there is an alternative between a genus and a substance. And from the words *saṃbhāra* and *cātuḥprāśya*, because they denote substances through their etymological meaning (*yaugikatva*), there is an alternative between a substance and its absence.
However, because it consists of injunctions and prohibitions, it is by way of logic alone; thus ends the introductory statement.

[7] An option (*vikalpa*) must be made between the presence and absence of a quality, as in the case of the Vājasaneyins regarding the specific measurement of the altar (*vedi*) and its absence: "They say it should be a span (*prādeśa*) wide at the back," and "There is no measure here," according to the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*.
[8] An option must be made between an action and its absence, as in: "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," and "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice."
Thus, this kind of conceptual construction (vikalpa) is accessible through logic.
This logical conceptual construction is twofold, distinguished by the difference between that which is to be performed (kartavya) and the human goal (puruṣārtha).
Among these, the eightfold variety of what is to be performed has been illustrated.

Thus, that [comparison] is of eight kinds based on pairs: between genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dravya*), genus and quality (*guṇa*), genus and action (*kriyā*), substance and quality, substance and action, and quality and action—these are the six types involving dyads.

Likewise, there are distinctions based on triads: those involving genus, substance, and quality; genus, substance, and action; genus, quality, and action; and substance, quality, and action. Furthermore, there is one type involving a tetrad. Thus, these eleven varieties do not occur, because they lack a single common purpose (*aikārthya*).
However, these eleven also occur for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*).
When combined with the previously mentioned [eight], such as *āśā* and so forth, this [human end] is of nineteen kinds.

[1] In that regard, an example of a variation of human ends established by logical reasoning (*nyāya*) is as follows: "One who desires Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer [the oblation] with a wooden vessel," as stated by the Vājasaneyins.
"But one should offer with bell-metal for one desiring Brahman-splendor"—this was cited in the fourth [chapter] (Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya 4.3.14).
For here, it is the material itself that is enjoined for the sake of the fruit.

Just as in the case of "the sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood," where—by means of extended application (*atideśa*) from the rule "he whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood" and the rule "he offers with the *juhū*"—the substance is already obtained and only the genus (*jāti*) is enjoined for the sake of the sacrifice; so too, since the substance qualified by its specific form is already obtained through the rule "one should bring water in a *camasa*," only the genus is enjoined with respect to the result.
Therefore, the vessels must be made of *vānaspatya* (wood) and *kāṃsya* (bell-metal), and they must indeed have the shape of a *camasa*.
This has been stated in the *Tantraratna*, in the fourth section (*adhikaraṇa*) on the topic "In the case of an occasional rite, because it is a modification" (4.3.214):
"Now, it may be argued that the cup (*camasa*) is specifically prescribed for the act of leading forward (*praṇayana*).
True."

"But it is not contradicted by the rule regarding bell-metal (kāṃsya). For the word *camasa* denotes a shape; it does not depend upon a specific material. Indeed, it is possible to produce a vessel of that same shape even with bell-metal. Thus, while the general injunction for the half-offering prescribes only the *vāraṇa* wood, it is only this that is contradicted," according to the passage [of the *Tantravārttika*].
Therefore, since two classes of substances are prescribed here for a single result, the option between them is established by logical principle (*nyāya*).

An option between substances serving human ends established by logical principle is as follows: for example, in the injunction "One desiring cattle should fetch water with a *godohana* vessel," there occurs an option with respect to another substance prescribed for the purpose of the result of cattle by means of a derivative term (*yaugika-śabda*).

[3] An option between qualities (guṇa) for the sake of human ends (puruṣārtha) based on reasoning is as follows: "If he should desire that Parjanya should rain, he should measure out the Sadas-altar low. This refers to the mutual option between qualities prescribed for a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha) and occasional (naimittika) qualities prescribed for a visible purpose. [4] An option between actions (kriyā) for the sake of human ends based on reasoning is as follows: among those things serving a single purpose, such as optional sacrifices (kāmyeṣṭi) and the like.

[5–7] Examples of options based on reasoning regarding the presence or absence of a genus of human ends, the presence or absence of a substance (dravya), and the presence or absence of a quality (guṇa) are to be sought.

[8] For genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), and quality (*guṇa*) can indeed serve as human goals (*puruṣārtha*) only when they are connected to a quality or a fruit (*guṇaphala*). And although the author of the *Vārttika* stated in the section on prohibitions not pertaining to parts (*abhāgāpratiṣedha*, 1.2.15) that such prohibitions are purposeless, nevertheless, where there are injunctions for the connection of a quality or a fruit with respect to those [genus, substance, and quality] that have proceeded in a general manner, and the prohibitions regarding them are likewise general—just like the prohibition against optional rites (*kāmya*) stating "having performed black magic or a *mahīna* sacrifice, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance"—in those cases, an option (*vikalpa*) regarding genus and substance that serve as human goals is possible.
The author of the Vārttika, however, [argues that] the prohibition is not actually useless because its performance is fruitful until the result is attained;
since it serves the purpose of avoiding a fault, there is no practical uselessness.
For in the absence of a prohibition, there would be the desire for the optional rite (kāmya). (Mīmāṃsākośa 440)

Even when there is freedom of choice (*yāmatī*) such that non-performance based on desire is established, it does not follow that there is a fault in performing optional rites (*kāmyānuṣṭhāna*). Therefore, the prohibition is meaningful because it makes known the fault in performing them; for example, the prohibition of optional *ahīna* sacrifices as stated in: "Having performed an *abhicāra* (malevolent rite) or an *ahīna*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. One should seek out examples of such cases concerning the three types of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), beginning with sacrifice (*yajña*). [8] However, the optionality regarding the performance or non-performance of acts for human goals is understood through reasoning (*nyāya*), just as the optionality regarding the *ahīna* has already been stated.

There is another example as follows: in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, there is both an injunction and a prohibition, namely, "for one whose father is living, [the rite] ends with the oblation (homānta) or it is not commenced while the father is living.
In that case, the option between performing the action for the sake of the person's purpose and its non-performance is understood through reasoning (*nyāya*).

One should not mistakenly think that the option here is based on a scriptural statement because of the word *vā* ("or"), for the option regarding what is enjoined and prohibited arises from reasoning alone—just as in the case of taking up or not taking up the *ṣoḍaśin* cup—and thus the word *vā* is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
In this manner, examples for the eleven varieties of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*)—beginning with genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dravya*)—should also be sought.
Thus, the nineteenfold conceptual differentiation established by logical reasoning (*nyāya*) has been described.
In exactly the same way, the nineteen divisions of conceptual differentiation based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*) are to be understood.

In that regard, however, an example for a scriptural option (*vikalpa*) concerning a class (*jāti*) subserving the ritual (*ṛtvartha*) must be sought. An example of a scriptural option concerning a substance (*dravya*) subserving the ritual is as follows: "He who would sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, an animal, or Soma [should do so] on the new moon or the full moon day.

Nor should it be argued here that this is not a matter of logical inference—like the rule "one may begin [the rite] while the father is alive"—and that the word "or" (*vā*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).

For in that case, because they are included in a single sentence and because a combination [of alternatives] is impossible, there is an option (*vikalpa*) according to the principles of logic and so forth.

In this case, however, although there is a possibility of the redundancy of a single sentence due to the difference between the intended objects (*uddeśya*)—namely the *iṣṭi*, the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and the *soma* sacrifice—the injunction of two times with reference to the *iṣṭi*, the injunction of two times with reference to the animal sacrifice, and the injunction of two times with reference to the *soma* sacrifice do not constitute a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) despite the interruption of the performance (*prayoga*). This is similar to the injunction of multiple forms of results in "One desiring offspring should cause him to sacrifice for twelve days," which, though not an originative injunction (*utpattivihiti*), does not incur a syntactical split on account of enjoining multiple subordinate qualities (*guṇa*). Thus, when the combination (*samuccaya*) of all options follows from their being taken up as a single sentence, the word "or" (*vā*) establishes that the option is indeed scriptural (*vācanika*).

For this very reason, even in the absence of the word *vā* ("or"), since the two qualities—which have visible purposes—are taken up in a single sentence, their combination (*samuccaya*) is established. Regarding this, the author of the *Vārttika* states in the *Vaiśāradī* commentary (p. 392): "And if there were a single sentence, then because all the injunctions would enjoin a single efficient force (*bhāvanā*), there would be no option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, since it is possible to avoid splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*) by virtue of its being an injunction for performance (*prayogavidhi*), for that purpose—

The lunar day (parvan) is indicated by the feet of the full moon (paurṇamāsī) and the new moon (amāvāsyā); therefore, the claim that there is an optional choice (*aicchiko vikalpaḥ*)—as in the case of "one should sacrifice with an animal," where one might think "this is the animal" or "that is the animal"—is to be accepted as the view of a fool.

An example of an option based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanikaḥ*) regarding a quality for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha-guṇa-vikalpaḥ*) is: "He plucks two handfuls of guggulu or aguggulu.

Here too, the establishment of an option does not arise from logical reasoning (*nyāyāt*); rather, since both even and uneven handfuls are presented within a single sentence, their conjunction (*samuccaya*) would otherwise follow, and thus the option occurs solely because it is expressly stated by the word *vā*.

For here, even though the act of cutting is enjoined by the rule "he cuts the sacrificial grass," and even though there is no sign of an injunction regarding the application of time and so forth, there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because of the injunction of an option characterized by both [factors] indicated by the words *yuga* and *yuk*, as will be explained in the case of the phrase "or the *rathaṃtara*."

An option between two ritual acts based on scriptural statement (*vācanika*) is as follows: "The *rathaṃtara* is the *pṛṣṭha*" and "The *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha*"—since these two statements enjoin the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, an option arises. Thus, there is a single injunction of an option indicated by the word *vā*: "Either the *rathaṃtara* is the *pṛṣṭha*, or the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha*. [Objection: But would this not result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) because of the two distinct *pṛṣṭhas*?
[Reply: No.

What is intended is "night" (*nakta*), not duality; rather, since the injunctions of option (*vikalpa*) are made with reference merely to the *pṛṣṭha* (the name of a chant), the substance for the *pṛṣṭha* is obtained precisely because of the equality of the options to be enjoined. However, regarding the fourfold options—of genus and its absence, of substance and its absence, of quality and its absence, and of action and its absence—which are expressly stated in the texts (*vācanika*) concerning the two types of rites for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*), the subject matter of such examples is as follows: where in a modified rite (*vikṛti*) either the fourfold set beginning with genus, as prescribed by extended application (*ātideśika*), is heard with a prohibition accompanied by the word "or" (*vā*), or the original (*prākṛta*) genus and so forth itself is heard with the word "or," there this fourfold option is possible.

Furthermore, in such cases, there is no establishment of an option (*vikalpa*) through logical reasoning (*nyāya*) and the like; for when there is a prohibition based on an instruction regarding a specific type of purpose—as in "he does not perform those two with curd"—there would simply be a sublation (*bādha*) of the original [element], such as the genus (*jāti*) and so forth. Therefore, the option established by reasoning and the like must be one based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*). One should seek out such examples. Likewise, among the eleven options concerning genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), and so forth, one should also search for examples of those that are based on explicit scriptural statement.
For example: "One should perform the *śrāddha* with milk or with milk-rice," and so forth.

These are examples of option (*vikalpa*) regarding genus for the sake of a human purpose, substance for the sake of a human purpose, quality for the sake of a human purpose, and action for the sake of a human purpose.

Among these, an example of option regarding genus for the sake of a human purpose based on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*) is as follows: "With sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, or with substances such as roots and fruits..."

"By what is given, the ancestors of men are pleased for a month according to the rule. Furthermore, the specific options regarding the materials for the *puṣya* [offering] are expressly stated in scripture, as Manu says: "He may be one who possesses grain in a granary (*kusūladhānyaka*), or indeed one who possesses grain in a jar (*kumbhīdhānyaka*)."
[The rule] may pertain either to this life or to the next.

In the case of two optional qualities (*guṇa*) pertaining to the purpose of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), there is an optional choice (*aicchika-vikalpa*). For example, since it is impossible to employ an animal without a specific quality when the injunction "the cow is the sacrificial animal" (*gaur anubandhyaḥ*) is given, and since the employment of some other quality would follow, there is an optional choice of qualities such as "it may be white or red. Similarly, regarding the *ahīna* sacrifice which has multiple sacrificers, it is stated in the twelfth [book] (12.1.12–13) that the *śukra* cup may be handled by any one of the sacrificers, and the same applies to the rite concerning the *audumbarī* post.

[4] An optional alternative (*icchika-vikalpa*) between two actions concerning a ritual purpose (*ṛtvartha*) is as follows: "In the rainy season, a chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) should perform the fire-consecration (*ādadhyāt*). Since the consecration is prescribed for one who does not belong to the three [twice-born] castes, and since its performance is impossible without knowledge, knowledge is necessarily implied; yet, regarding the various means of acquiring that knowledge—such as reading from a book and so forth—an optional alternative is permitted. [5] However, an optional alternative between caste (*jāti*) and the like, or between their absence, regarding a ritual purpose, is possible when established as pertaining to those who are either capable or incapable in respect to obligatory rites (*nityakarman*). This is because, in the sixth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] (6.1.16–17), it is established that in obligatory rites, one who is incapable [of performing the full rite] may substitute what is unobtainable.

In this way, regarding those eleven types of optional alternatives (*vikalpa-bheda*), examples for those that concern human ends (*puruṣārtha*) and are based on scriptural injunctions (*vācanika*) must be sought, such as: "By giving a *śrāddha* offering with milk or with milk-rice, the ancestors remain satisfied for a month," and so forth.

Furthermore, the nineteen-fold optional alternative concerning ritual ends (*kratvartha*)—which, like [the previously mentioned categories], is understood through the logic of human ends, yet differs from both the scripturally enjoined optional alternative concerning ritual ends and the scripturally enjoined optional alternative concerning human ends—is also to be considered.

In that regard, [1] there is optional choice (*vaikalpika*) between two classes (*jāti*) pertaining to the purpose of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), such as in the case of "one should sacrifice a *brāhmaṇa* for a *brāhmaṇa*" and so forth, where there is a choice between the class of *brāhmaṇa* and the class of *kauṇḍinya*.

Although in this instance the class of *brāhmaṇa*-hood and the like possesses the status of being optional, whereas the class of *kauṇḍinya*-hood and the like does not, nevertheless, the designation "pertaining to the purpose of the ritual" (*ṛtvarthatva*) is applied based solely on their being instrumental factors in the ritual.
Indeed, such usages exist in this treatise; as it is stated in the *Vallabhādhikaraṇavārtika*: "And in the performance for one desiring cattle, by means of the sequence of the cups (*camasa*)."
"In that case, there is the exclusion of the *camasa* cup by means of the *godohana* vessel prescribed in the *Śruti*," so it is stated later [in the Vārttika, p.

[2] Regarding two substances whose purpose is for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), there is optional choice (*vaikalpika*) according to one's will; for example, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), because the singularity—which is a qualification of the thing to be employed (*upādeya*)—is intended to be significant, there is an optional choice of substance according to one's will, such as "this goat or that [goat]," even when the mantra-text mentions a goat for Agni.

Thus, although it is established by the third book's principle (3.8.12–14) that in the injunction "one worships the Āgnīdhra fire-altar with an *āgneyī* [verse]," the *āgneyī* verse under discussion in the context (*prakṛta*) must be taken, nevertheless, this is a case of optional choice (*vaikalpika*) between two qualities pertaining to the purpose of the rite (*ṛtvartha*). For instance, as in the example "the cow is the sacrificial animal" (*gauranubandhyaḥ*), since it is impossible to adopt the animal without its qualities, when the adoption of qualities is necessitated by the mechanical requirements of the ritual, there arises an optional choice of qualities such as "it may be white or red. This is indeed an optional choice of qualities.

Likewise, it is stated in the twelfth book (12.1.12–13) that in an *ahīna* sacrifice involving multiple sacrificers (*yajamāna*), the taking up of the *śukra* cup may be performed by any one of the sacrificers, and the same applies to the ritual touching of the *audumbarī* post.

[4] Regarding matters pertaining to the purpose of the rite (*ṛtvartha*), there is an optional choice (*vikalpa*) between two actions, as for example: "In the rainy season, a chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) should establish the sacred fires. Since the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is prescribed here for one who does not belong to the three [higher] castes, and since its performance is impossible without knowledge, knowledge is necessarily implied; yet, even when knowledge is thus required, there is an optional choice among various means of acquiring that knowledge, such as reading from a book and so forth.

[5] However, regarding the genus (*jāti*) and so forth that constitute the purpose of the rite (*ṛtvartha*), as well as their absence, an optional alternative (*vaikalpika vikalpa*) is possible, established according to the capacity or incapacity of the agent in the case of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*). This is because in the sixth [book], at [PMS 6.1.16–17], it was established that in an obligatory rite, one who is incapable [of performing the primary act] may substitute [an alternative]. Thus, among those eleven varieties of alternatives, examples of those pertaining to human purposes (*puruṣārtha*) that are based on scriptural injunctions (*vācanika*) should be sought, such as: "By giving a *śrāddha* meal with milk or with milk-rice, the ancestors remain satisfied for a month," and so forth.

Thus, regarding these eleven types of optional alternatives (*vikalpa*) concerning genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dravya*), examples for those that pertain to ritual purposes (*ṛtvartha*) and are not optional should also be sought. For instance, in the *Śrāddha* rite, milk-drinks and the like are prescribed by separate sentences; therein, what is established in common usage—whether as a combination (*samuccaya*) or as an option (*vikalpa*)—is enjoined according to its availability. Thus, it is neither an obligatory combination nor an obligatory option, as stated in the *Hemādri*, which is indeed logical. Therefore, the example pertains to optional alternatives of genus, substance, and so forth, when they serve a ritual purpose.
Even regarding the options concerning the human goals (*puruṣārtha*), the types (*jāti*), and the substances (*dravya*), there are exactly nineteen optional alternatives (*vaikalpika*).

In that regard, although for those of equal fruit—such as the types and so forth—the option is determined by logic (*nyāya*) and not by personal choice, nevertheless, for those of different fruits, when there is a desire for either one of them, the option is indeed a matter of personal choice.

When there is a desire for all of them together, their combination (*samuccaya*) also occurs; therefore, the examples of combination to be mentioned later should be understood as options only in the case of desiring either one of the fruits.
For those who maintain that the human goals (puruṣārtha) consist of genus (jāti), substance (dravya), or both, these four examples are possible through their combination; they are stated as follows:
[1] An optional alternative (vaikalpika) between the sense organ and its object, whether as a substance or its absence.
[2] An optional alternative between the object as it truly is and its absence.

[3] Likewise, in the injunction "One desiring cattle should fetch water with a milking vessel" (*godohana*), there is an optional alternative (*vaikalpika*) between the substance *godohana* prescribed for the purpose of obtaining milk and its absence.

[4] Similarly, in the injunction "If he should desire that Parjanya rain, he should fix the sacrificial shed low," there are various optional alternatives between the lowness prescribed for the purpose of the rain and its absence. These are the various types of optional alternatives.

Option (*vikalpa*): [4] Likewise, in the case of "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā*," there is an optional choice (*aicchika-vikalpa*) between performing the *citrayā* sacrifice enjoined for that purpose and its non-performance.

Thus, there are nineteen varieties of optional conceptualization (*aicchika-vikalpa*) concerning the objects of ritual action (*kṛtyārtha*), and nineteen concerning the objects of human goals (*puruṣārtha*); thus, there are thirty-eight varieties of optional conceptualization. To these are added the twenty-seven previously mentioned varieties of conceptualization determined by logic (*nyāya-gamya-vikalpa*), and the thirty-eight varieties of conceptualization pertaining to beggars (*yācanaka-vikalpa*). All these combined result in one hundred and three (103) established varieties of conceptualization. Furthermore, the aforementioned conceptualization is of two kinds: that which is non-systematic (*avyavasthita*) and that which is systematic (*vyavasthita*), according to their respective possibilities.

The first case is, for example, the option regarding the ten substances in the Agnihotra sacrifice. The second case is, for example, the Śruti passage from the *Śāṅkhāyana-śrautasūtra*: "Having sacrificed with rice (*vrīhi*), one should sacrifice with rice until the *yava* harvest; having sacrificed with barley (*yava*), one should sacrifice with barley until the *vrīhi* harvest. This means that after the *vrīhi-āgrayaṇa*, the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices must be performed with rice alone until the *yava-āgrayaṇa*; and after the *yava-āgrayaṇa*, they must be performed with barley alone until the *vrīhi-āgrayaṇa*.

Even though there is an option regarding the *vrīhi-āgrayaṇa*, the eight faults (of contradiction) do not apply here, because there is no abandonment of the established authority of any scripture whatsoever.

For the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) is indeed a single scriptural teaching (*śāstra*). Within that, by virtue of the intention to express singularity (*ekatva-vivakṣā*), even when at some time a particular instance of masculinity is imparted, the entire meaning of that scripture is indeed performed; for whom, then, would there be a rejection of the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of that scripture?
The same applies even if another individual is taken up according to one's own will.
In this very way, even in the case of an option (*vikalpa*) based on the explicit word (*vācanika*), the eight defects (*doṣa*) do not exist.

For in such injunctions as "the *rathaṃtara* is the *pṛṣṭha*-stotra" or "the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha*-stotra," only the optional performance (*pākṣika-kartavyatā*) of both is understood; it is not, like the case of *vrīhi* grains, a mandatory performance of both at all times. Therefore, even when one or the other is performed, the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the other scripture need not be assumed.

Consequently, it is established that option (*vikalpa*) as determined by logic indeed involves eight defects. Furthermore, the previously mentioned option regarding existence and non-existence is fivefold, according to the circumstances.

Some [options] pertain only to the archetype (*prakṛti*); some concern items taught in the context of the ectype (*vikṛti*); some concern items taught in the context of that which is neither archetype nor ectype; some concern items taught specifically in the ectype; and some concern merely what is extended (*atidiṣṭa*) into the ectype.

Among these, [1] the option regarding existence (*bhāva-vikalpa*) and the option regarding existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāva-vikalpa*) concern only those items taught in the archetype—for example, in the *māsāgnihotra*, which is an archetype of the obligatory *agnihotra*, there is an option among ten substances such as milk (*payaḥ*) and so forth;
and there is an option between curdling the milk (*dadhyadhiśrayaṇa*) and its absence.
"One should not place the curd upon it; some say one should place it upon it"—this is the Brāhmaṇa passage containing the plural number.

[2] Regarding the two states taught in a modified sacrifice (vikṛti), there is an option concerning their presence or absence; for example, in the Vājapeya, regarding the items such as "the animals dedicated to Prajāpati are slaughtered together with the seasonal animals" or "in the case of the Brahmāsāman," there is an option regarding what is to be done; and in the case of "one takes the Ṣoḍaśin cup at the Atirātra" and "one does not take the Ṣoḍaśin cup at the Atirātra," there is an option regarding the performance or non-performance of the Ṣoḍaśin.

[3] Regarding the conceptualization of non-existence concerning two entities taught as being either in their original state or modified—just as there is an option between the *patramāna* offerings and the *pūrṇāhuti* at the *āghāna* ceremony; and in that very context, regarding the *vājapeya*, it is stated as before: "One should perform either the seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtu*), the sacrifice under a specific asterism (*nakṣatra*), the collection of materials (*saṃbhāra*), the fourfold eating (*cātuḥprāśya*), the vigil (*jāgaraṇa*), the preliminary rites (*anvārambha*), or the *sāparāyaṇī*."

[4] Optionality (*vikalpa*) occurs between two states taught as alternatives, or between such a state and its absence—for example: "One should sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, with an animal, or with *soma*; on the new moon day or the full moon day. Here, when the new moon day is prescribed for a modified form (*vikṛti*) of the sacrifice that is itself mentioned by the term *iṣṭi*, there is an optionality between the new moon day, which is extended by analogy (*atideśa*), and the full moon day, which is directly taught (*upadeśa*). Likewise, when the full moon day is prescribed for a modified form of the sacrifice mentioned by the term *iṣṭi*, there is an optionality between the full moon day, which is extended by analogy, and the new moon day, which is directly taught.

The example of both presence and absence is as follows: in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) consisting of the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*), there is an option between the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) extended by injunction (*atideśa*) and the prohibition of them that is directly taught (*upadiṣṭa*). [5] However, an option between two positive elements applies only to those extended by injunction in the modified sacrifice, such as: "They perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with the tail (*jāghanī*).

This does not mean that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings have the tail as their sole purpose, for that would result in their losing their original function (*aprākṛtakāryatva*); rather, it serves to restrict the tail, which is obtained optionally from the archetype (*prakṛti*).
And in that case, because it is something to be taken up (*upādeya*), the singularity of the tail (*jāghanī*) is intended to be significant.

Consequently, when there is a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), since the principle of the combination of tails (*jāghanī-samuccaya-nyāya*) does not apply—on the grounds that the performance of the purificatory rite must repeat for the sake of each individual rite—the alternative (*vikalpa*) arises that "any tail whatsoever" may be taken up.

This point was stated in the twelfth book, in the section (12.4.16) beginning with "But the modification of the substance, like the previous [case], would be a primary act for the sake of the purpose," as an example of an alternative arising between an extended (*atidiṣṭa*) entity and an unextended (*anupādita*) extended non-entity.

In this regard, nothing need be said concerning the archetype (*prakṛti*), as there is no optionality (*avaikalpya*) therein; however, in the ectype (*vikṛti*), even when there is an instruction for prohibition, because it involves an option regarding other ritual elements (*padārtha*), it necessarily partakes in an option with its own absence. For the sake of such an illustration, there are other differences: in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, the sprinkling of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings upon the omentum (*vapā*) was indeed optional; but in the case of the animal sacrifice to Prajāpati (*prājāpatya-paśu*), two times are prescribed—either at the time of the seasonal animal sacrifices (*ṛtu-paśu*) or at the time of the *brahmasāman*.

Consequently, the pouring over (*abhidhāraṇa*) of the *vapā* of the *prājāpatya* animals becomes optional in the view that the *brahmasāman* occurs at that time, because the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings is discarded for the purpose of pouring over the *prājāpatya vapā*s (4.1.13–35).

Thus, these ten varieties of option (*vikalpa-bheda*), which consist of both the archetypal (*prakṛti*) and the modified (*vikṛti*) rites and concern the presence or absence of what is taught or extended by analogy, have been described.
Now, this is also stated: whatever varieties of option regarding presence or absence were mentioned previously, they all concern the nature of the thing itself (*yadvāva-viṣaya*).
That [negation] has as its object only the absence of the counter-positive.

However, some maintain that there can also be conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) which, while having as their object an absence whose counter-positive is a certain thing, also have as their objects entities distinct from that absence, and thus may have both positive entities and other absences as their objects.
For example, in the case of the Agniṣoma sacrifice, one [form] is a constant constituent of the rite, while others are optional.
And *saṃsthā* is of the nature of non-existence, because it consists in the cessation of the activity of the accumulation of the various forms of praise (*stotra*) and recitation (*śastra*).
Furthermore, conjunction (*samuccaya*) is not possible here, for *saṃsthā* is a variety of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa-bheda*), which is a modification (*vikāra*).
Because of the impossibility of [the different] forms coexisting,

there is an optional choice (*aicchika-vikalpa*) between the *abhihotra* form, which serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*), and the *ukthya* and other forms, which serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Likewise, there is an optional choice between the various forms such as the *ukthya* and others that serve the purpose of the person, even though they have distinct results.

Likewise, because the various forms (saṃsthās) share the same purpose with the generic states (jātibhāvas) based on the Jyotiṣṭoma and its ten constituent parts—which yield fruits identical to their own—an option (vikalpa) is established by logical principle.

And here, other types of options (*vikalpa*) are observed: such as the option regarding the *anuvākya* mantras dedicated to Viṣṇu and others in the *upāṃśuyāja* and similar rites; or likewise, the option regarding the deity; or the option regarding the ritual procedure (*tantra*), as in "the procedure belongs to the Vaiśvadeva"; or the option regarding the sequence, such as whether the sacrifice is preceded by an *iṣṭi* and so forth; or the option regarding the agent, as in "one, two, or many may sacrifice with the *ahīna* [sacrifice]"; or the option regarding the various modes of chanting found in the thousand branches of the Sāmaveda, such as the *tattvakāra* and others. These are all included within the aforementioned options regarding genus (*jāti*) and so forth, as appropriate.

Since the *tantra*, *krama*, and so forth are also ritual acts (*kriyā-dharma*), and because there is no difference between a property (*dharma*) and that which possesses the property (*dharmin*), their conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are included within the very distinctions of the conceptual construction of ritual acts.

Likewise, in some cases, even a conceptual construction is itself subject to a conceptual construction regarding one of its two alternatives, such as the option regarding the *sāṃnāyya* offering for one who has not performed the *Soma* sacrifice: "One who has not performed the *Soma* sacrifice should not offer the *sāṃnāyya*; rather, he should simply offer boiled milk (*payas*)," due to the force of injunctions and prohibitions.
For one who has performed the *Soma* sacrifice, however, the *sāṃnāyya* alone is required.

"By means of the two *puroḍāśa* cakes alone, one should perform the sacrifice for one who does not offer the *sāṃnāyya*; however, for one who performs the *soma* sacrifice, [one should do so] with the *sāṃnāyya*," according to this scriptural statement.
This has been established previously in the section beginning with "by means of the two *puroḍāśas*" (10.2.13–16).

As for the three examples from the *Smṛti*, Vijñāneśvara stated: "'With the mother,' 'with the husband,' and 'with the father'—thus there is an option regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* according to different *smṛtis*" (1.253).

The *Smṛti* states: "The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is recorded as being performed together with the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) and the others. *Paiṭhīnasi* says: "But when [the wife] has died without a son, the husband shall perform the *sapiṇḍana*;
thus, for those [wives] who have no other [male heirs], the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should take place together with the [husband's] ancestors and so forth."
Yama said: "The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a woman must be performed by her husband alone;
for even when she has died, she has thus gone [to him], and from that point on, she partakes in his mantras and oblations."

Uśanas says: "Just as the rite of sapinda-ship is performed by sons for their father and grandfather after a full year has passed, so too should it be performed for their mother and maternal grandfather."
Thus it is said.

In that case, if a wife dies without sons, the husband shall perform the *sapiṇḍana* for her with his own mother alone. However, if she has performed *anvārohaṇa* (ascension upon the funeral pyre), the son shall perform the *sapiṇḍana* for his mother with his own father.
In the case of an *āmura* marriage and so forth, where the son of a daughter (*putrikāputra*) acts as the *divā-hotṛ*, he should perform [the rites] with his maternal grandfather alone.
In the case of a *brāhma* marriage and so forth, where the son of a daughter acts as the *divā-hotṛ*, he may optionally perform them with his paternal grandfather or his paternal grandmother.

Likewise, regarding the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for the mother and others, there is an option concerning the lineage (*gotra*): "A woman falls from her own lineage at the seventh step upon marriage."
The offering of rice-balls and water for her must be performed by [the husband] using his own lineage name.
Thus, due to the reversal of the husband’s lineage, one should not abandon the father’s lineage and adopt the husband’s lineage.
"Thus, from birth until even in times of calamity, the paternal family of women [remains their refuge]."
This is because of the statement regarding the reversal of the paternal lineage (*pitṛgotra*).

In that regard, in marriages such as the *āsura* and others, as well as in the practice of making a daughter an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), the paternal lineage alone is used; whereas in marriages such as the *brāhma* and others, there is an option (*vikalpa*)—like the choice between rice and barley, or the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* chants.
Likewise, in the *kṣayāha* śrāddha, there is an option between the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the *pārvaṇa* rites.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, every year on the anniversary of death, the sons must separately perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha for their mother and father.
"Thus, because of Yama's prescription for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite:
'Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should always perform [the annual rite] like the *pārvaṇa*;
this is the rule according to the *Chāgaleya* for each anniversary.'"

Thus, because of the prescription for the *pārvaṇa* rite by Śātātapa, the son must perform the *pārvaṇa* on the anniversary of the death (the *kṣayāha*) of an ascetic (*saṃnyāsin*). For it is said: "In this world, there is no *ekoddiṣṭa* for one who has taken up the triple staff;
because of the absence of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *pārvaṇa* [rite] belongs to him forever."
This is according to the statement of Pracetas:

"But when the new moon has passed away, or when the fortnight of the deceased has ended, only the *pārvaṇa* rite is performed: 'When the new moon has passed away, and likewise when the fortnight of the deceased has ended, the *pārvaṇa* must be performed by him; never the *ekoddiṣṭa*.'"
Thus says the Smṛti.

Elsewhere, on the anniversary of death (kṣayāha), for one who is not a renunciant (asaṃnyāsī), there is indeed an option (vikalpa) between the Pārvaṇa and the Uddiṣṭa rites, like the choice between rice and barley. This concludes the determination of the distinctions among options.
Alternatives and combinations.
This is a recourse for those with no other way out: that when there is a connection with what has been performed, alternatives and combinations may occur.
For when another way is available, those two are not to be resorted to.
Bhāṣya 10.1.12.17. He will state that the teaching of a subsequent quality within the scope of an alternative is purposeful: "It would be purposeful at another time" (12.1.4.5).
Bhāṣya 12.1.12. The modification would apply to that which is predominant.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is prescribed: "He casts the prastara [grass-bundle] with the Sūktavāka.
The Sūktavāka recitation begins with "idaṃ dyāvāpṛthivī" and so forth.
Within that, it is recited: "This sacrificer desires long life (āyur āśāste)."

In that regard, concerning the modification involving multiple [offerings], there arises a deliberation as to whether the term "sacrificer" (yajamāna) is subject to modification (*ūha*)— that is, whether it is appropriate for modifications to undergo such change— or not; regarding this, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In that case, regarding the ritual action where the sacrificer is the primary factor, there is a modification (*vikāra*) consisting of an adaptation (*ūha*) of the word "sacrificer" to the singular number, such as "the sacrificer desires long life" (*yajamāna āyurāśāste*) or "the sacrificers desire long life" (*yajamānā āyurāśāste*), according to the circumstances.
This is provided that the *sūktavāka* reveals either the means or the fruit of the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle;
and since the fruit of the throwing is the bestowing of long life upon the sacrificer, the sacrificer is the primary factor.

Therefore, where there are multiple sacrificers (*yajamāna*), there must be a modification (*ūha*) made according to the scriptural injunction. What [is modified]? The word "to him" (*asmai*) in the *abhri-gu-praiṣa* formula is not subject to modification under the view that the *Abhrī* and *Gomīya* Soma-pressings follow the same ritual procedure (*samānavidhitva*).
"In the case of the *abhigupraisa*, [there is the substitution] of the word *prāsmai*";
here, the governing principle (*adhikaraṇa*) is to be observed.
"Modification" (*vikāra*) is the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) consisting in the assumption of a new function.
Vāla-pṛ. 8: Being a modification (*vikāra*), it is common to both because there is no distinction.
The Viśvajit sacrifice is a modification of the Jyotiṣṭoma, and in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is one hundred and twelve [cows].
Therefore, by means of that wealth of one hundred and twelve, the sacrificer is indeed able to perform the Viśvajit as a modification of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Now, it may be performed by one whose wealth is less than twelve hundred *dhanas*, or even by one with more wealth; that is, it can be done by both parties—those on the side of being either deficient or exceeding—because there is no distinction, meaning there is no specific qualification [restricting it].
For in that case, indeed, one's entire property (*sarvasva*) must be given.
And whatever wealth one possesses, all of that is one's "self" (sva).
Whether that [wealth] be less than twelve hundred by measure, or more;
as long as there is wealth, there is no distinction in the gift of one's entire self when all of it is given.

Therefore, the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that the Viśvajit sacrifice must be performed by one who possesses either less than or more than twelve hundred [cows], having given away his entire property (*sarvasva*). The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the aforementioned prima facie view—that the Viśvajit should be performed by one with more than twelve hundred, as well as by one with less—and states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Or [it is] more," because of the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). That is to say, the Viśvajit is to be performed only by one possessing more than twelve hundred; even one with fewer than that is not eligible. Thus he states the final position.
He whose wealth exceeds one thousand two hundred [coins] and is thus incapable of being surrendered must alone perform the Viśvajit sacrifice, and not one with less wealth than that,
because of the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, indeed, a counter-exception regarding the surrender of all one's property is stated.

Having prescribed one hundred and twelve [cows], he then says: "Or rather, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are to be satisfied by this much, or else by everything. In that regard, if the officiating priests are not satisfied by more than one hundred and twelve, nor by less wealth than that, then here, by the term "everything" (sarvasva), [it is meant that they must be satisfied].
Only more is to be taken;
and as it is in the Jyotiṣṭoma, so it is in the Viśvajit as well.
Therefore, everything beyond the one hundred and twelve [cows] constitutes the "entirety of one's possessions" (sarvasva).
Therefore, one who possesses less wealth has no entitlement [to perform this sacrifice].
From the Bhāṣya on this point, it is established that the Viśvajit should be performed by one possessing twelve hundred [units of wealth] or more than that;
however, according to the Sūtrakāra, the specific distinction is that the Viśvajit must be performed only by one possessing wealth exceeding twelve hundred.
And because of favor, as in the case of the feet.

When it is stated that "he who possesses wealth exceeding one thousand two hundred [coins] should perform the Viśvajit sacrifice," this sūtra—intended as a supplementary statement (*anvācaya*) regarding another reason—is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
For this reason also, "all one's possessions" (*sarvasva*) refers to wealth exceeding one thousand two hundred.
For when more than that is given, because it is included within that [total], it becomes a gift of one thousand two hundred.
In that case, by the gift of one's entire property (*sarvasva*), there is the favoring of additional wealth.
It is like the case of a quarter-coin (*pāda*); just as when a *kāryāpaṇa* is to be given, favor is shown by giving a *pāda*.
It is the same in that case.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the entitlement to perform the Viśvajit sacrifice belongs only to one who possesses wealth exceeding twelve hundred [units].
A "quarter" (pāda) means a fourth part.
However, there are modifications (*vikāra*) when there is a connection with optional desires (*kāma*), because of the equality of that which is permanent.

Having stated that the permanent substratum (*āśraya*) is [the basis], it is another interpretation that an optional quality (*guṇa*) such as the *uktvādi* is a modification; for, due to the equality of permanence, there is no contradiction in the permanent qualities adhering to the substratum.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the section concerning the sacrificial forms (*saṃsthā*).
Su. Pṛ. 848:
"First, that which requires a supplementary benefit (upakāra) becomes connected with the archetypal elements;
once it has been sprinkled [with water] as prescribed, the modifications are enjoined in proximity."
Or [it may be] by means of the modification (vikāra). 2|1|4|129. 4|4.
The connection with the gender of the original material (*prakṛti*) through its modification is as follows: "A pap-offering for Nirṛti, made of *natvāva-pūta* grains.
Bhāṣya 2|8|1|12.

In that case, the substance released from the royal implement is the fruit; indeed, there exists the function of threshing, but not the act of sowing. (Ṭupṭīkā) "And because of the modification, there would be no difference, since the purpose remains unaltered.

Due to the modification of the accessory and the time, there would be no difference in the *tantra* (the common ritual procedure), even when that [accessory] is modified, because the purpose—the assistance rendered by the anointing—remains unmodified. This is the meaning.

And if, because there is no purpose served by clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) [in that context], it were not to be performed, then in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, since the purpose would be accomplished by the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) alone, separate rites would not be performed—despite the difference in location and the difference in performers—according to the principle: "And because there is no modification, there should be no distinction, for the purpose remains the same."
Śābarabhāṣya 12.1.2:
Among the modifications, [this applies] to the modification following the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice of Soma;
3521: the modified form (vikṛti).
Regarding the timing: one should consult the section concerning the rule that "the modifications of the Soma sacrifice are not to be performed prior to the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
In the modified sacrifice, there should be a distinction of vessels for the *tanūyāja* offerings due to the difference in their purpose.
Regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, it is stated: "He performs the after-offerings with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).

In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether the very same vessel named *upabhṛt*, which holds the primary clarified butter (*ājya*), should also hold the speckled butter, or whether a separate vessel should be used for holding the speckled butter. When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that, like the mortar (*ulūkhalu*), there should be only one vessel here in the archetype—is reached, [the author] refutes that by means of the following sūtra and states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In the modification of the *anuyāja* offerings, when there is a substance other than the original material—namely, when the substance is *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter) in the animal sacrifice—a separate vessel must be used for holding the *pṛṣadājya*.
This is because of the difference in purpose: pure *ājya* is intended for the *prayāja* offerings, whereas *pṛṣadājya* is intended for the *anuyāja* offerings;
or rather, it is because of the difference in purpose, which entails a difference in substance.
For it is not possible to take two distinct substances together in a single vessel.
[This is the principle: "In the case of modifications, there is figurative treatment (upacāra) as in the case of the original material" (Vārttika 2.1.6.17, p. 512).

In the case of modification (*vikāra*), however, it is understood that the original (*prākṛta*) is established first; thus, when one of two alternative actions is performed, the modified action must necessarily set aside the original one, which leads to the contingency of sublation (*bādha*). (Vārttika 3.6.142, p. 1065). That which is to be modified is the desired object (*īpsita-karman*).
Modification (*vikṛti*) is the production of a transformation in that [substance] by way of generating a pervasion of its parts, as in "one threshes the rice grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*).
(Maṇi, p. 129)
The animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (agnīṣomīyapaśu) is to be performed with all its constituent parts (sāṅga).
See the section [Mīmāṃsā] p. 100 regarding the statement: "The animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma is a modification of the model sacrifice (prakṛti)."
The animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma is a modification of the *sānnāyya* offering;
even there, it is milk that is used, not curd.
In this regard, the section concerning the statement "the animal for Agni-Soma is a modification of milk" should be consulted.
A modified form (*vikṛti*) is enjoined either by a specific desire (*kāma*) or by a particular occasion (*nimitta*). (Bhāṣya 12.1.2.12)
Disturbances arise either when desire or a causal sign has appeared. Disturbance depends upon a mode; and that single mode is what is depended upon by the disturbance.
There is a means of valid cognition regarding the expectation of a specific mode;
there is no [such means] regarding the expectation of a treatise. One should establish it by way of general principle.
When the question "How?
arises, a cognition of the Āgneya [sacrifice] occurs by way of similarity. By means of that Āgneya, its own internal modes are first brought to mind.
The modification (vikṛti) takes them up,
and they are required;
whereas the scriptures and the constituent elements are neither required nor proximate.
Therefore, the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) extends the application in its entirety.
Because it applies in its entirety, there is no restriction (*upasaṃhāra*).
Because it possesses the nature of the archetype, the modification should take place at that same time, as prescribed by the injunctions.

In the third seasonal festival known as the Sākamedha, on the first day, an offering of pap (caru) is prescribed for Agni Anīkavat in the morning; at midday, a pap for the Sāṃtapana Maruts; and in the evening, at the conclusion of all [the rites], boiled rice (odana) for the Gṛhamedhin Maruts. Thus is the sacrifice ordained.
Regarding the inquiry as to whether this [rite] should have the time of the *graha* or the time of the *prakṛti*, he states the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) view:

because the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) possesses the characteristics of the archetype (*prakṛti*), the modified sacrifice such as the *anīkavatī* should have that same time as prescribed for the archetype. That which has the characteristics of the archetype is called "possessing the characteristics of the archetype" (*prakṛtidharmā*)—that is, the modified sacrifice.
An entity is a property of the archetype; therefore, it possesses the nature of being an archetypal property.
Through extension (*atideśa*), it is precisely the properties of the archetype that apply to the modification (*vikṛti*).
And the archetype is the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
[The modified sacrifice] has the same substance and time.
Even regarding the time, it is a specific property of the rite.

Therefore, "yathāśiṣṭam" means not transgressing what is taught by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), that which is enjoined and obtained; "dravyakālāvam" means not transgressing the substance and the time. A modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) whose time is like the time of that archetype (*prakṛti*) is "tatkālā"; such a modified sacrifice would have the same substance and time.
Therefore, the preliminary position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the materials and times for the *Anīkavatī*, *Sāṃtapanīya*, and *Gṛhamedhī* sacrifices should be [those of the archetype].

Alternatively, however, because they are connected with a specific sequence and time, they should be performed immediately; in that case, there would be an omission of the archetypal characteristics due to the inference of a different injunction.
The meaning of the opponent's initial position is that in the *Sākamedha* sacrifices, the *Anīkavatī* and others should have their own specific materials and times.
The word "apibā" [is used].
The *anīkavatī*, the *sāṃtapanī*, and the *gṛhemedhī* sacrifices are connected with both sequence and time;
that is, they are conjoined with both sequence (*krama*) and time (*kāla*).
Those three sacrifices have been described in sequence;
their times—morning, midday, and evening—have also been stated.
Therefore, each respective sacrifice should be performed on that very same day.

In that regard, although the immediate timing (*sadyaskālatva*) is directly prescribed by the injunction "they are to be performed immediately" (*sadyaḥ kāryāḥ*), it is inferred from the rule regarding the sequence and time of placement (*nidhi*).
Because these [offerings] are connected with a specific sequence and time of placement,
it is therefore inferred that they are to be performed immediately.

Therefore, in the case of the *darśa* sacrifice which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*), there would be an omission of its property—namely, the specific substance and time—in the *anīkavatī* and other such sacrifices.

Consequently, these [latter] have the immediate day (*sadyaḥkāla*) as their time, not the [specific] substance-time of the archetype. This is the modification (*vikṛti*). 3522. [This concludes the section on] the modification.
Regarding the modified form (vikṛti): [Sūtra] 3523. In the modified form. If it is argued that there is a displacement of time, [the answer is:
"The subsequent series"—this very reading is appropriate.
Modification:
In the third section of the Sākamedha-parvan, regarding the reading "anīkavatī" on the preceding day,
the qualification "uttarā" (the latter) would be redundant.
Therefore,
the Sāṃtapanīya and Gṛhamedhīya [offerings] are performed in sequence at morning, midday, and evening;
for although the word "tat" (then) is absent in the Bhāṣya, it is understood from its status as a subsequent qualifier in the Sūtra.
And thus it has been prescribed:
"They should occur at that time," according to the Siddhāntin;
the reading in the *Vṛ* manuscript alone is more appropriate.
When this was said, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says:
"But surely there would be a displacement of the time;
however, at the time of two days, it should be according to the rule."

On the preceding day, the *iṣṭis*— such as "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"— are brought forward for performance in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. On the following day, they will be performed in the morning, at midday, and in the evening.
Nor is it so;
for in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it has been stated by the sūtra: "The subsequent modification occurs at its own time," [and] not [at the time] of the *nodaka* [offering].

In a modified sacrifice, there is no difference from the archetypal rules regarding new ritual elements (*apūrva-padārtha*).

In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is the difference in meaning that is extended, not the word itself; this we shall explain. *Ṭup-ṭīkā* 5.1.2.139, Varṇaka 2. In the modified sacrifice, there is no modification (*ūha*) of the word "sacrificer" (*yajñapati*) in the *iṣṭānigada*.

In the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice), there is an absence of [the original] extraction (*utsatti*). Su. p. 855. In the *vikṛti*, the materials, deities, and so forth of the *prakṛti* (archetype) are set aside (*bādha*) by the materials, deities, and so forth taught for the *vikṛti*.

In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of items prescribed by direct statement (*śruti*) and indicated by implication (*arthāt*). For example: in sacrifices such as the *ukthya*, there is a combination of the five oblations; likewise, there is a combination of the original (*prakṛta*) ghee and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). In animal sacrifices such as that dedicated to Vāyu, there is a combination of the quality "white" and the genus "goat," etc.

In the case of the mantras beginning with *dīkṣita*, there is a combination of the six mantras: "I employ this for the purpose of the rite, svāhā! and so on, up to "To Ākṛti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā!"—thus a combination of these six mantras.

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, there is a combination of the *yajus* performed by the *yajñakara* with the portion belonging to the *adhvaryu*. In the Nakṣatreṣṭi, there is a combination of the *upahoma*s and the *nāriṣṭha-homa*s.
In the Bṛhaspatisava, there is a combination of the *bārhaspatya-graha* prescribed for that rite and the *graha*s extended from other rites.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, there is a combination of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati and the animals belonging to the conclusion of the rite;
there is a combination of the Sāṃrādhana Āmana-homas with the Anuyāja offerings;
and in the Mahāvrata, there is a combination of the female singers (upagātrīs) among the wives and the prescribed male singers (upagātṛ ṛtviks).

In the Mahāvrata, there is a combination of the prescribed *gāyatrī* and other recitations with the extended application (*atideśa*) of the *gauḍulava-anjana* ointment and fresh butter (*navanīta*). In the Mahāvrata, there is a combination of the *tāpanīya* [recitation] with the unhemmed garment (*ahata*).
In the Mahāvrata, there is a combination of the prescribed recitations such as the *śruti* and others with the extended application of the recitations for the limbs (*gātra*) and so forth.
In the case of the *stomabhṛt* and *vibhṛt* [offerings], there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the directions prescribed for each;
likewise, in the *paśugaṇa* sacrifice, there is a combination of the *upayaṣṭi*-offerings and the *guda*-offerings because they are acts of disposal (*pratipatti*).

Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 5.1.12 states that in some cases, the properties of the archetype (*prakṛti*) are extended to the modified sacrifice.
In certain modified sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "The *Bṛhat* [Sāman] becomes the *Pṛṣṭha*."
In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [sāmans] according to the rule.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], there is a restriction (*niyama*) to the *Bṛhat* alone; it is not an option.
And this applies even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because of that specific scriptural statement.

In the discussion of whether the mantra "having girded the wife" (*apatnīṃ saṃnahya*) should be modified (*ūhitavya*) or not when used in a modified ritual (*vikṛti*) involving two wives or many wives, the conclusion is that it should not be modified even in the modification, just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). This is because of the rule of extension (*atideśa*) stating, "What [is prescribed] in the archetype is [the same] in the modification. Furthermore, in the archetype, the singularity [of the wife] was not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).
Furthermore, because there are two wives, neither duality, plurality, nor singularity is intended to be expressed.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the qualification applies to the word "wife" (patnī).

In the case of a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), however, there would be no fixed rule; rather, there would be an option (*vikalpa*), as in the case of *pṛṣadājya*. This is because the mention [of the substance] is for the sake of a quality (*guṇa*), and since both are prescribed, the instruction regarding the quality (*guṇa-śāstra*) would prevail. In a modified sacrifice such as "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* of white rice grains in ghee to Soma and Rudra," there is no fixed rule—that is, an option—regarding the two. For the mention of rice is for the sake of the quality, due to its connection with qualities such as whiteness, and not due to its connection with the sacrifice itself.
The *vrīhi* grains are white.
As for the sacrifice, however, it may be performed with either *vrīhi* or *yava* grains.

It is like the case of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), as in the passage "He performs the after-sacrifices (*anuyāja*) with speckled butter," where the butter becomes characterized by its connection to the speckles; therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
Since both rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*) have been enjoined and brought forward by the *Udaka* [text], there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them.

As for the injunctions regarding qualities—such as "of white rice" or "of black rice"—these would be intended as prescriptions for when [rice is used]: that is, they would mean "when rice is used, then it should be white.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that there is an option.
"Or rather, it should be restricted by the singular [number], because it is specified by the direct Vedic statement.

Regarding the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) such as, "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a pap (*caru*) of white rice-grains in ghee to Soma and Rudra," there arises the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), since the mention of rice is due to its connection with the quality of being white. Having reached this position, the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The word "yā" is well-known [as denoting barley].

Since rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*) are both obtained as options because they perform the same single function—namely, the production of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*)—the substance of rice would be restricted by the direct scriptural hearing (*śruti*), which is more specific due to its being explicitly enjoined; thus, there is the exclusion of barley.
Therefore, there is no option (*vikalpa*).
And because of their mutual contradiction, as in the world;

he states another supporting argument for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is an option between rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*) in the *saumāraudra* and other sacrificial porridges (*caru*), resulting in the sublation (*bādha*) of the barley.

Since things that perform the same function possess a mutual contradiction by virtue of being rice, so too, due to the mutual contradiction between rice and barley, the rice explicitly prescribed in the revealed scripture (*śruti*) would exclude the barley.
It is like the world: just as fish, thinking "my dwelling shall not be mixed with water," cause the water to recede, so it is here.
Furthermore, because the sacrifice possesses those qualities.

If it is argued that in a modified rite (*vikṛti*) such as "one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a pap (*caru*) of white rice grains in ghee to Soma and Rudra"—if there were a connection between the rice grains and the sacrifice itself, then there would be no connection with the quality of whiteness—the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) replies: because the sacrifice (*kratu*), that is, the ritual act, possesses those qualities; since both [the substance and the quality] are properly joined, the rice grain is its quality (*tadguṇa*). Thus, the term *tadguṇa* means that of which the rice grain is the quality.
Just as in the case of the *aśvaka-hāyanī*, whiteness and rice are both qualities of the sacrifice itself,
and their mutual connection occurs subsequently;
therefore, in the aforementioned modified rite (*vikṛti*), there is no option (*vikalpa*) between rice and barley.
Furthermore, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) when that [contradictory item] is heard among the contradictory ones because of the word "or" (*vā*).

Regarding the *saumāraudra* and other *caru* offerings, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is a restriction to rice (*vrīhi*) and an exclusion of barley (*yava*). To provide another reason for this, he says:

"When that one of the two contradictories is explicitly heard (*pratyakṣa-śravaṇe*), and because of the hearing of the word 'or' for the other which is not seen, how could there be an option? This is a rhetorical question (*kāku*).
Furthermore, there is the following dilemma: "It would lead to an improper course," and so forth is the introduction.

And thus, since in the *saumāraudra* and other *caru* offerings, white [grains] and the like are explicitly heard in the scripture while barley is not heard, there is a restriction to *vrīhi* rice and a sublation of barley.
In the case of speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), because of their combination, the taking [of both] is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).

In the *saumāraudra* and other *caru* offerings, regarding the mention of rice in the phrase "of non-white *vrīhi* grains," the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) view holds that the inclusion of the term *vrīhi* is not for the purpose of connecting it to the sacrifice, but rather for the purpose of connecting it to the quality of being non-white. To this, the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*) refutes that example of *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter) cited under the sūtra (10.7.15–164), "But in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is no fixed rule. He does so by means of the *vaiśya* [example].

In the case of the *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter), since the mention of *ājya* (butter) in the injunction of its taking is for the purpose of indicating a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), it is logical that it serves to connect the substance with the quality of speckling (*pṛṣattā*). This is because there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of curd and butter, as the speckling is to be produced by means of curd.

Therefore, the curd is not incidental; rather, there is a combination with the butter. However, in the case of the *saumāraudra* and other sacrificial porridges (*caru*), a combination of rice and barley is not possible. Consequently, the illustrative example is dissimilar.
Furthermore, although the rule "one who offers four cuttings" would not be applicable [in such cases],

it has already been explained that in the *saumāraudra* and other *caru* offerings, the use of white *vrīhi* rice is directly enjoined by scripture, thereby setting aside those [grains] obtained through the force of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction).
In the *Subodhinī*, however, by inserting the letter 'a' [to read "atannyāyatvāt"], it is explained as "because the logic does not extend.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the *saumāraudra* and other *caru* offerings, there is a restriction to *vrīhi* rice, which excludes (*bādha*) barley.
But in the case of a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), those properties (*dharma*) obtained through the extended injunction (*codaka*) being inferential would indeed be set aside (*bādhyeran*).
