In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is no context (*prakaraṇa*). It is solely through position (*sthāna*), characterized by mutual expectancy (*antarākāṅkṣā*), that the new auxiliary (*apūrvāṅga*) is grasped.

According to the Mīmāṃsā, context does not operate in the modified sacrifice because, although the modified sacrifice possesses an expectancy for assistance (*upakārākāṅkṣā*), that expectancy for the goal (*sādhyākāṅkṣā*) regarding the transferred auxiliaries such as the *prayāja* offerings is already satisfied by the assistance established through the original means of knowledge (*prākṛtapramāṇa*).
(The absence of a context characterized by mutual expectancy).
Su. p. 1114. In a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), only those properties belonging to the original sacrifice (*prakṛti*) that perform a specific function are extended by analogy (*atidiśyante*).

Ci. 3.8.17: In a modified sacrifice, there is no extension by analogy of the properties pertaining to the result, the restrictive rule, the agent, and the primary sacrifice belonging to the original sacrifice.
However, it is the transfer of the injunction itself that occurs, because it is precisely that which is required.
Since the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) adopts the original injunction (prakṛta-vidhi), a restatement would serve another purpose.

Even though the two butter-portions (ājyabhāgau) are already obtained through the extended application (codaka) in the Gṛhamedhīya rite belonging to the Sākamedha section of the modified sacrifice—where it says "he offers the two butter-portions"—the restatement would otherwise be redundant.
It may be that this is not an injunction (*vidhi*), but rather a restatement (*anuvāda*).
This is because it merely refers to the original injunction for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings;
thus, since it is a restatement, the first position is that "he offers the two *ājyabhāgas*" is a restatement of the *ājyabhāgas* obtained through the extended application (*codaka*).
And like the *āgneya* [verse], there would be a twofold designation (*dviśabdatva*).
He states the second position:
there would be a twofold designation for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.

The term *dviśabda* refers to those two words which are the two prescriptive injunctions; the state of being such is *dviśabdatva*. Just as the extended application (*codaka*) brings forward the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, so too the scriptural word "he performs the two *ājyabhāgas*" brings them forward, just like the case of the *āgneya* [offering].
Just as in the Āgneya [section], where in the context of the invocation (āvāhana) it is said, "O Agni,
come to me," there are two words "Agni," yet the referent is indeed one single Agni; this is called "identity with the self" (ātmānubhāva).
In this case, just as there is a twofold designation for a single [deity], so too it is with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.
Therefore, by the injunction "he performs the two *ājyabhāgas*" and by the *codaka* (extended application), only one single action is enjoined.
Or rather, it is not so, because of the distinctness of the words.
By means of the word "vā" (or), he turns back the second position and indicates the third position:
it is not proper for a single action to have two verbal expressions.

Therefore, the statement "he offers the two ājyabhāgas" is a restatement for the sake of an explanatory praise (arthavāda); that is, "he offers the two ājyabhāgas" is for the purpose of what is yet to be offered.
But because there is a distinctness of words, as in the case of the word "āgneya," the meaning is indeed the same.
By the phrase "bring [him] forward" (agre āha), Agni is designated as the one who brings;
by the phrase "bring Agni forward" (agnim āvaha), Agni is designated as the one who causes understanding.
Nor is a single purpose accomplished by those two;
therefore, it is a restatement for the sake of an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda)—this is the third position.

Or rather, there should be an addition because of its meaningfulness; in the absence of the quality of an explanatory eulogy, there would be a modification due to the direct scriptural statement, for in those cases there would be that purpose because of its being a new injunction (apūrva).
He states the fourth position:

"In the absence of a commendatory statement (arthavāda) or a subordinate quality (guṇa), and when there is no modification, [the mantra] would be additional by virtue of the direct scriptural injunction, because it possesses meaning. This is the grammatical connection (anvaya). The word "or" (vā) serves to exclude the two previously mentioned positions.
The sentence "He offers the two *ājyabhāga* oblations" is not an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Nor are the two *ājyabhāgas* a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), nor are they a modification (*vikāra*) in any sense.

Thus, since there is an absence of both an explanatory passage and a subordinate quality, and since there is an absence of modification—that is, no status as a modification—regarding the statement "He offers the two *ājyabhāgas*," [the following applies] once again:

On account of the direct scriptural statement (*vacana*), the ritual act in the form of the *ājyabhāga* offerings—which is indeed additional—should be performed after the execution of the original *abhyudaya* rites obtained through the general rule (*codaka*). This is because it possesses purposefulness, as its fruitfulness must be postulated.

For when those [elements] such as praise, the injunction of qualities, and non-original attributes are present, since the statement is novel (*apūrva*) and has a novel purpose, its aim would consist in praise and so forth.
However, none of that exists here.
Therefore, this is enjoined as a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) in the form of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, by means of the two [terms] *prākṛta* and *abhyāsa*.
In the *Kutūhala*, however, it is stated: "The ritual act of the *ājyabhāga* is to be understood as an unmodified [form], yet as a distinct ritual act that is not archetypal (*aprākṛta*);
for there is purposefulness (*arthavattva*), since the repetition of the hearing [of the injunction] is purposeful only when it refers to a distinct ritual act."
And those two rites are to be performed after the principal sacrifice (pradhānayāga), according to the order of the text (pāṭhakrama).

Because there is no mention of a subsidiary purpose (guṇa) in the explanatory passage (arthavāda)—that is to say, because the status of being an explanatory passage depends on its syntactic unity with an injunction (vidhyekavākyatva), and in the absence of such unity, the status of an explanatory passage is impossible due to the explicit restatement of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings—therefore, since they lack syntactic unity with an injunction, they cannot be explanatory passages. For it has been explained that the injunction of a subsidiary quality is appropriate in those sentences, such as "the two *ājyabhāgas* have the word 'puṃs' [as their characteristic]," because therein they serve that specific purpose (*tādarthya*).
If it is argued that there must be a prohibition [of other offerings],

this is not a statement regarding separate rites, because if they were characterized as "the two butter-portions" (*ājyabhāgau*), it would entail the fault of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Rather, by means of exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), there would be a prohibition of those other unknown offerings.
Therefore, "designation" is the fifth [position].
Because it is not heard [in the scripture],
he refutes the fifth position, which expresses the fourth position.
It is not a negation,
because it is not heard [in the text].
For here no word expressing a negation is heard.
Therefore, it is an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā);
however, it is a statement regarding a different ritual action.
[Objection: "If it is argued that this is not so because there is no mention [of such a distinction]."

There is no injunction for other constituent acts (*karmāntara*). Here, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are grasped by their own specific terms (*svaśabda*), while the other constituent acts are grasped by the rule of transfer (*codaka*).
This is because the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, being already grasped by their own terms, are not grasped again by the rule of transfer.
And thus, because the essential point follows from the original nature [of the archetype],
the injunction "he offers the two butter-portions" (ājyabhāgau yajati) is not included by the extended application (codaka);
this is the sixth position.
It is not so, because they are equal.
This is not the case;
for just as the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) includes other sacrifices by means of the *apūrva* (unseen potency), so too does it include the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.

Therefore, since they are equal to the other constituent parts, it is not proper to say that the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are taken up by the *codaka* (the transfer rule); for if they were so taken up, [the aforementioned fault] would follow. || 32 ||

But surely it is held that the two *ājyabhāga* offerings alone are grasped by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), and thus the *codaka*'s application regarding the *ājyabhāgas* is restricted by the specific statement concerning the *ājyabhāgas*.
If you say, "Let this position stand," then so be it.
That would be the case if, upon being grasped, the *codaka* were to grasp only the two *ājyabhāgas*; however, if they are not so grasped, the situation remains the same.
The *codaka* (the rule of extension) should include the other subsidiary elements just as it includes the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, because the *codaka* applies equally to both.
However, one should demonstrate its *apūrvatā* (novelty/originality), for the inclusion [of the specific offerings] must be purposeful.
The statement "he performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings" demonstrates the *apūrvatā* of the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice.
Because the taking up of the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) and their retention would be meaningful and fruitful only if the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice were a new, independent rite (*apūrva*);
otherwise, like the previous case, it would be purposeless. Therefore, the Gṛhamedhīya rite is indeed *apūrva*.
The state of being the archetype (*prakṛti*) is not the modification (*vikṛti*).
The word "tat" (that) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
[Question: In the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), when the place of the archetype is to be taken, is it only the first [element] that is taken, while the others are elided?
10|1|11–6. See the section on the *kapālanyāya* at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1355.

In a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the optional qualities (*kāmyaguṇa`) belonging to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*). 8|1|14|23–29. See the section on "There is no extension of optional qualities belonging to the archetypal sacrifice in a modified sacrifice" at Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 652.

When two ritual properties are enjoined in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by way of restatement (*anuvāda*) of the properties belonging to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), an entirely new subsidiary (*apūrva-aṅga*) may also be cooked in between; that too is applied through the context (*prakaraṇa*), as in the case of the *āmana-homas*. (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.6.2). In a modified sacrifice, [this applies] to a further modification.

In the case of a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), [the application of details is determined as follows]: Vārttika 3.1.7.4, p. 855. Where in a modified sacrifice there is an injunction or a restatement (*saṃdeśa*) based on a corresponding archetypal element (*prākṛta-anuvāda*), it is the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself that serves as the means of application (*viniyojaka*); elsewhere, it is proximity (*saṃnidhi*) alone.

*Tāla*, page 11: *Oṃ*. In a modification (*vikṛti*), there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements whose purpose is not perceived. Because of the extension (*atideśa*) from the injunction (*vidhi*) into another context (*prakaraṇāntara*), the entire ritual action (*sarvakarma*) should apply.
Commentary: Modification (*ūha*) has been observed.
We shall now discuss sublation (*bādha*) and addition (*abhyuccaya*).
Sublation is the designation of "falsehood" for a cognition that was previously ascertained as "this is indeed so," by means of some other cause.
Likewise, addition is the cognition that "while this exists here, something else also exists."
In this regard, the following point is first examined: must everything that is archetypal (*prākṛta*) be performed in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), or is something set aside?

What, then, is the prima facie position? Since there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the archetypal injunction to the modified sacrifice without distinction because it occurs in a different context, therefore every collection of archetypal duties (*dharmajāta*), even that which is functionally redundant (*arthalupta*), must be performed in the modified sacrifice.
Why? Because all of this is obtained by means of the scriptural statement.
And there is no excessive burden for the word; it is attained.

How is it understood that this is the word? In all derivative (vaikṛta) teachings, the archetypal (prākṛta) collection of dharmas is required as a supplement to the sentence. It is thus permitted in that very archetypal teaching, and likewise in the derivative one.
There is no distinction whatsoever.

In that regard, just as the cooking of gold pieces (*kṛṣṇala*)—though not part of the original model—is performed on the authority of a scriptural injunction, so too must everything such as threshing (*avahanana*) and the like be performed even for a purpose not belonging to the original model. [Duh]—By this same principle, the existence of extended application (*atideśa*) has been explained.
Now, it is explained what is being extended by means of the tenth [book]:
that which exists in the archetype (prakṛti) is extended;
and in that [archetype], the teachings exist exactly as they are.
Therefore, those [rules] are extended [to this case].
Consequently, it operates even for the sake of elision (*lup*).
Alternatively, the word, its refinement (*saṃskāra*), and the substance are employed for the sake of the purpose, because they exist for that purpose.
The Commentary: The phrase "moreover" (api ca) serves to set aside the previous position.
This is not the case;
namely, that everything belonging to the archetype must be performed in the ectype.
Someone might argue that the substance for the preparation of the designation ought to be set aside for its own sake.
Why is this so? For the substance for the preparation of the designation is employed when there is a purpose; it is not without a purpose. It is handed down for another purpose, not for its own sake.
But has it not been said that [a ritual act] is performed even for the sake of its disappearance, on the authority of the scriptural injunction?
As, for example, the cooking of the *kṛṣṇala* beans.
He says: "No.
There is no statement that teaches the meaning of an elided [element].
Nor does a modified (*vaikṛta*) ritual action attain syntactic unity with the original (*prākṛta*) constituent parts.

It is not understood thus: "One should produce the fruit by means of the sacrifice; how? By means of the archetypal [elements]. How then? "In the same manner as the fruit was accomplished by the archetypal sacrifice.
Why is this so? For it is a specific operation inherent in the sacrifice that is required by it, not mere operation in general.

Furthermore, the procedure belonging to the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛtayāga), which has been established by the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) and is thus included, exists [there]. It is capable of being expected;
and being so required, it is able to render [the new sacrifice] free from expectancy.
Even when other factors are being considered, one should not assume a specific function belonging to the sacrifice within the modified ritual (*vikṛti*);
otherwise, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Just as in the statement "he fights with a staff," the form of the staff itself is not what is directly expressed by the word.
If, however, there were a purpose for that which is indicated by it, then it would be possible to indicate it by that;
likewise here too, the specific quality of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) belonging to the sacrifice is not expressed by the word when the requirement [of the auxiliary] is being considered;
rather, it is postulated through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, the word is sublated by its secondary meaning (lakṣaṇā).

Now, if one were to think that the word must not be sublated, then no specific detail from the archetype sacrifice (prakṛti-yāga) would be required; yet, it is precisely such details that are required. Therefore—how so?—the word remains with its expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) unfulfilled regarding the specific procedure (itikartavyatā) of the modified rite (vaikṛta-karma).

Furthermore, other subsidiary details (*itikartavyatā*) are required; yet the subsidiary details of the archetypal sacrifice (*prākṛtayāga*), though implied, are set aside. Moreover, even the syntactic unity (*ekavākyabhāva*) of the archetypal injunctions with the modified rite (*vaikṛta*)—which is meaningful within its own context—is accepted.
All this is logical;
therefore, it is intended in this way:
just as the fruit is accomplished by means of an ordinary sacrifice, so too is it accomplished by this one.
What follows from this being so?
This is what follows:
those primary [elements] which exist in the archetype for the sake of a particular purpose do not become enjoined in the ectype when that purpose is absent.
Therefore, that which is sublated by the *lupta* (omitted) rule has no purpose for the *codaka* (extended application), as it is not heard in the Vedic injunction.
*Ṭup-ṭīkā*: That which is sublated by its purpose does not proceed.
This "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) requirement depends solely upon the Vedic form, whether worldly or scriptural.
The application [of the rule] occurs by way of assistance;
therefore, there is the cessation of the meaning of the elision (*lup*).
But was it not stated that in the primary form (*prakṛti*), the services of the scriptural categories (*śāstrapada-artha*) do exist?
In that regard, if it is asked how assistance is indicated, it is said:
in the case of the Saurya sacrifice, the procedure of the Āgneya sacrifice is grasped by means of analogy.
In the [section] concerning Agni, the auxiliary benefits are immediate; the ritual acts are more remote;
and the scriptural injunctions are even more remote.
Therefore, the state of being a speaker perceives subsequent harms in every transformation.
In every transformation.
And one grasps them;
yet the objects are separated by their auxiliary factors and are not required.
But surely, in the archetype (prakṛti), it is only the constituent elements (padārtha) that are immediate, because they are directly expressed by the words;
they are grasped first,
and only afterwards are the auxiliary benefits (upakāra) postulated.

"Even in the modified form (vikṛti), it is likewise appropriate"— this is true; for in the archetypal rite (prakṛti), the constituent elements (padārtha) are grasped, but there is no dependence on those very same elements [in the modified rite].

What kind of expectation is this? This requirement for "how-to" (kathaṃbhāva) grasps the assistance provided by the subsidiaries; it grasps the ritual items (padārtha) through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
And direct statement (śruti) is more authoritative than secondary indication.
Because they have not been taught by one who is personally present [to observe them].

The Commentary states: Now, as for what was said—that just as in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* beans, even though the original purpose of the cooking has ceased to exist, the cooking is nevertheless performed due to the authority of the scriptural injunction, so too should other things be performed—[that is not so]. In that regard:

For cooking does not apply to the *kṛṣṇala* seeds by virtue of what is heard [in the general rule], because there is an explicit statement in that context: "He cooks them in ghee. That statement does not refer to the purpose of the original [archetypal] rite.
In that case, because of the authority of the scriptural statement, the cooking is for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Furthermore, if the direct scriptural statement were not manifested there, then even the cooking would not be manifested, since it is not taught as something perceptible.
Therefore, the description speaks of the cooking.
What is the purpose? It is said that a modification (*vaikṛta*) is cited when it takes the form of a result.
In some cases, it is heard in the scripture: "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is torn by itself. In that case, the original substance (*prākṛta-dravya*) is set aside.
"The altar becomes self-made";
thus, the acts of digging out the channels for the water and smoothing the surface are omitted.
"The hope becomes self-extinguished."

Non-accomplishment ceases; and these mantras cease with respect to them. [The author] says: once the modification (*ūha*) is established, there is the consideration of the sublation (*bādha*) and addition (*abhyuccaya*) of those rules extended by analogy (*atideśa*).

The determination of the number of constituent parts (*aṅga*) is stated in the tenth book [of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra]. Since sublation (*bādha*) also concerns those elements that have been extended by analogy (*atideśa*), its treatment follows the section on extension (*atideśa*), just like modification (*ūha*).

First, this is considered: whether everything belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*) must be performed in the ectype (*vikṛti*), or whether that which lacks a purpose in the archetype need not be performed.

For that purpose, this is investigated: Is it intended that the archetypal elements (*prakṛta*)—whether unknown or known by their own nature—are extended (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) for the sake of its purpose? Or is it by way of the sacrificial procedure (*sāyena bhāvena*)? How so? Are those cognitions belonging to the *Āgneya* sacrifice extended as they were performed, or is that operation residing in the *Āgneya* and other rites—which serves to accomplish the visible and invisible effects of the constituent parts (*padārtha*)—extended?
One should cultivate it through inference; how so? Just as in the case of the Āgneya sacrifice, so it is here.

In that regard, according to the first position, since the ritual elements understood through extended application (*atideśa*) serve—without regard for their original purposes—as either visible or invisible means within the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as far as possible, the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), even though it has already been spread out, must be performed for the sake of an invisible result (*adṛṣṭārtha*); thus, there is no sublation (*bādha*).

As for the response: since the ordinary act of cutting (*lavana*) is observed [in the model sacrifice] and there is no extension (*atideśa*) of its absence when the grass (*barhis*) is already cut by itself, and since the essential nature of the cutting (*lavana-svarūpa*) is not extended, it is established that the cutting should not be performed; thus, sublation (*bādha*) is proven.
In this regard, just like an original injunction (*upadeśa*), an extended injunction (*atideśa*) is also logically dependent upon the constituent elements (*padārtha*).
Thinking that it conforms to the original injunction, [the opponent] says: "Everything must be performed; nothing should be sublated."
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is: "The extension of the benefit (*upakāra*) occurs through dependence, existence, and connection;
in the absence of these, no extension of the ritual elements (*padārtha*) is postulated.
O Soma—here, [the latter] is of two kinds.

There is the "limit of addition" (*abhyuccayaparyanta*) and the "exclusive" (*kevala*). Where, when there is the possibility of the sublation of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) by the modified (*vaikṛta*), non-appropriation (*agraha*) is established, that is the limit of addition; for in that case, both the archetypal and the modified are to be performed.

However, where nothing at all is prescribed, but rather there arises the possibility of sublation due to a suspicion that the original (*prākṛta*) [rule] might be deficient or otherwise, it is that which is established here as "pure" (*kevala*).

In that case, since only the original [rule] is to be performed and there is no addition (*abhyuccaya*), it is like the case of the *khalevālī* (the threshing-floor post) and so forth, regarding the act of digging out and so on.
Thus, the mention of "addition" (*abhyuccaya*) is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the state of being "pure" and so forth; this is the determination of the form.
Next is the determination of sublation (*bādha*). Now, the connection [of this section] is characterized by the occasion (*avasaralakṣaṇā*).

As for the meaning of the sūtra: in another context concerning the characteristics of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), because there is a prescriptive injunction (*vidhi*) of the items to be performed, all performance would [otherwise] occur through extended application (*atideśa*), due to the existence of the appropriator (*grāhaka*).

Furthermore, when the purpose is accomplished through a substitute (*pratyāmnāna*) for the *kuśa* grasses naturally connected to the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is an absence of the emergence of the rite in its modified form (*vikṛti*) by way of extended application (*atideśa*).

This is because of the nature of the prohibition found in such forms as "he does not choose a *hotṛ* priest," which implies that the choosing of the *hotṛ* and so forth does not emerge in the modified rite.

In this context, the qualification [of the definition] is necessary because the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend the emergence of the modified rite exists even in the case of a jar (*ghaṭa*) and other such things.

In the case of constant application (*nityaprayoga*) and in instances of incidental extension (*prasaṅga*), there exists another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for grasping the modification (*vikṛti*), namely, the principle of extended application (*atideśa*).

Although in the case of a *prasaṅga* (transference), the status of an accessory (*aṅgatva*) for the substance of the *prayāja* and other such items in that performance does not arise merely from obtaining assistance (*upakāra*) from those very sources, nevertheless—in every instance, whether in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*)—since the substances must be connected to the utility of that primary [sacrifice] by obtaining assistance from somewhere else, and because one must assume a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) of this very kind—namely, "let it produce the fitness for the instrument (*karaṇa*) in that very place"—there exists a means of knowledge that grasps the ectype.

For this very reason, the possibility that the *prakṛti* (archetype) itself—being characterized by divine attributes (*daivya-dharma*)—might fall within the application of the occasional (*naimittika*) modification (*vikṛti*) is also refuted by the principle of incidental establishment (*prasaṅga-siddhi*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that there is an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend the nature of one thing as belonging to another, the terms "archetype" (*prakṛti*) and "modification" (*vikṛti*) are employed to avoid the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the *upahoma*s and so forth, which belong to the modification, or the *prayāja*s and so forth, which belong to the archetype, would lack any means of valid cognition to establish their connection with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other such sacrifices.

In this context, the word "archetype" (*prakṛti*) does not refer to that which defines the rule of extension (*atideśa*), nor does the word "modification" (*vikṛti*) refer to that which is the object of such extension.

If that were the case, then since the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice would in reality have the *darśa* as its archetype (*prakṛti*), the previously stated definition [of an archetype] would apply to it due to the presence of the *praṇayana* (carrying forward) and other elements.

However, being an "ectypal" (*vikṛti*) sacrifice consists precisely in a specific cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is the relation to the *darśa* and so forth. Furthermore, the term "archetype" (*prakṛti*) refers to the mode that determines the aforementioned qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatā*). That cognition—whether valid or not—is produced by the extended application statement (*atideśavākya*), such as from the *maurya* sacrifice. In the case of the *gṛhamedhīya*, however, because the sentence "he performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings" is absent, the cognition is merely inferential (*tārkika*).
Therefore, there is a commonality between these two cases insofar as they are both cognitions produced by defects (in the form of missing textual evidence).

For this very reason, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of the *prajāpa* and other elements when, due to a defect, there is a misconception that the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth are modified forms (*vikṛti*). Alternatively, let it be granted that—just as in the case of the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice where the *prayāja* and other elements exist through superimposition (*adhyāropa*), even though they do not exist in their own form as primary elements (*āyāta*)—the nature of *prasaṅga* (extended application) is indeed what is defined in the tenth chapter. Thus, the distilled meaning results as follows: *prasaṅga* occurs where there is an absence of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends a certain modified form (*vikṛti*) as being qualified by its connection to a specific archetype (*prakṛti*); and because of that absence, the [archetypal] cognition is sublated therein.

Even if it were possible that a definition [of a *tantra*] might occur occasionally elsewhere in the chapter on etymology (*nirukta*), nevertheless, because its definition is presented here as the primary subject, there is no fault of being merely occasional.

For indeed, the incidental definition of *tantrāvāpa* is accepted in the third [chapter] regarding the *sarvapṛṣṭhā*, and the definition of names (*nāmadheya*) and so forth occurs first by way of examples of ritual properties (*dharma*).

For this very reason, even the definition of sublation (*bādhaka*) stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, though overly broad (*atisakta*), is not entirely inconsistent; for instance, when a particular feature is perceived, if a certain scripture fails to produce a certain kind of certainty regarding a particular object, then the ascertainment of that scripture’s lack of validity regarding that object—precisely through the perception of that particular feature—is what constitutes its sublation in that context.

Furthermore, when a specific form such as *prāpad* (an emergency) is perceived, there arises a determination regarding the connection with its respective objective (*uddeśya*) for the extended rule (*atideśa-śāstra*) concerning items like *kuśa* grass; and through that perception of the specific, there is a determination of the non-authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇya*) of that [general] rule. Thus, in that particular case, there is a sublation (*bādha*) of that scripture. And although this is impossible in the case of the sublation of things like not speaking falsehood—which are prompted by worldly desire (*rāga-prāpta*)—there is no harm, because it is accepted that such a sublation is to be described incidentally (*prāsaṅgika*).

Indeed, although this general meaning of the commentary is common to the sublation (*bādha*) of *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth found in other chapters, there is no fault whatsoever, for it is not irrelevant to me either, since it must be primarily established.

However, because the Commentator has stated that [sublation] depends upon *atideśa* (extended application), and because exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is impossible without inclusion (*anugama*), it is not accepted here.

Furthermore, even though sublation does not depend on *atideśa*, modification (*ūha*)—being a property of the objects of extended application—is necessarily situated after *atideśa* because the effort of *atideśa* must precede it; thus, there is a connection with *ūha* as well.

This sublation (*bādha*) is threefold: by loss of purpose (*arthalopa*), by substitution (*pratyāmnāna*), and by prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). Among these, that which is established as "sublation by difference" (*anyabhinnabādha*) must also be explained: it is when the archetypal elements (*prakṛtapadārtha*) are not extended (*atideśa*) to the ectype (*vikṛti*) either through their specific contribution (*upakāra*) or in their own form (*svarūpa*). On account of this, since the unseen effect (*adṛṣṭakārya*) of the archetype is impossible in the ectype, one would have to postulate a different unseen purpose within the ectype itself for sublation to be possible.

However, because the requirement [of the *prakṛti*] persists for the sake of generating the capacity conducive to the fruit of the *vikṛti*, and because the constituent elements (*padārtha*), being inherently momentary, are incapable of generating that capacity on their own, it is determined that only the assistance (*upakāra*)—generated within the *prakṛti* by means of the two-fold assistance—is capable of generating that capacity. Furthermore, since the *bhāvanā* of the *vikṛti* is primary and thus depends upon the *bhāvanā* of the *prakṛti*, and because the intermediate assistance (*avāntaropakāra*) is proximate due to this mediation, the transfer (*atideśa*) occurs first for those [assists] alone by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*āsatti*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*), and not for the constituent elements themselves; for those [elements], however, [the transfer occurs] through the nature of that [assistance].

And in that regard, there are two possible courses: either, because those various intermediate auxiliary services (*upakāra*) are subsumed under the very form of being related to [the archetype], there arises—once the services have been extended by such statements as "the auxiliary service of the Āgneya sacrifice is to be performed by means of auxiliary services of the same class"—a subsequent requirement for their producers; and consequently, there is the assumption of a separate extension (*atideśa*) for the archetypal constituent elements (*padārtha*) which produce them. However, this is not the case in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because even if such auxiliary services exist there, it would result in the fallacy of assuming yet other auxiliary services for the constituent elements themselves.
There would be the consequence of the abolition of both [the original and the modified forms].

For, when there is an expectation for the production of an auxiliary benefit (*upakāra*), the extension of the ritual elements (*padārtha*) is postulated only on that basis; thus, in the absence of that [benefit], the very extension of those elements cannot be postulated. Alternatively, even if the extension of the ritual elements were postulated first, since only those elements whose specific auxiliary benefits have already been determined are extended—either by the extension of the verbal injunction (*vacana*) or the extension of the name (*nāma*)—it is illogical to postulate a different auxiliary benefit when the original auxiliary benefit is absent. In reality, however, even when there is an expectation for the production of an auxiliary benefit, it is more cumbersome to postulate a separate extension of the ritual elements; therefore, the extensions refer specifically to the names of the auxiliary benefits of the particular ritual elements.
"Because it is the archetype (*prakṛti*), one should perform those auxiliary acts for the sake of the sacrificial materials in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
However, we see no authority whatsoever for postulating a separate or subsequent extended application (*atideśa*) of the scripture itself.

Rather, the extended application consists in the statement of the archetypal nature, which establishes the suitability of the modified sacrifice by generating its capacity through the utility derived from the archetype.

Furthermore, since the state of being a *janaka* (productive cause) is no different even in the case of a category (*padārtha*) that possesses assistance (*upakāra*), there is only one type of extended application (*atideśa*). Moreover, the definition of extended application is more appropriately established by taking the category as its basis.
For this very reason, extended application occurs through the identity of the assistance, such as the requirement (*apekṣitatva*) and so forth.

The view that the ritual items (*padārtha*) are established merely by the implication (*ākṣepa*) of that [instrument]—and thus they do not constitute auxiliary parts of the modification (*vikṛti*)—is refuted; for if that were the case, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in including the assistance (*upakāra*) within the scope of the defining characteristics (*avacchedaka*) of the extended application (*atideśa*). Furthermore, even if the assistances are primary, since the fitness residing in the instrument is distinct from those [assistances] residing in the various ritual items, it is more complex to assume that they imply the ritual items. Moreover, because the extended application is understood as being primary, the extended application applies only to the assistances themselves, not to the ritual items.
And likewise because it is produced by such an injunction.
He states another reason for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Because it originates from the injunction (*codanā*), and because the injunction possesses authority (*prabhutva*) regarding the slaughter of animals characterized by the number eleven—as indicated by the specific mention of "eleven"—it is capable of setting aside the applicatory injunction (*codaka*).
Thus, since the word is capable of enjoining both the portioning of the sacrificial animal and the number eleven, the archetypal procedure (*prākṛtītikartavyatā*) does not apply.

Rather, the primary act, when conjoined with its subsidiaries, would constitute a new form of the transcendental result (*apūrva*), because that [new form] is what is characterized by the injunction; for every specific injunction is set in motion by its qualifying attributes.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, it is heard in scripture: "He performs eleven fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and eleven after-sacrifices (anuyāja).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that a distinct ritual action characterized by the number eleven is being enjoined here, and thus the archetypal procedure (*itikartavyatā*) does not apply. Refuting this with the word "but" (*tu*), the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
"It is not the case that the archetypal procedure does not apply."
But it certainly does obtain.

Just as the archetypal *pradhāna* [principal rite] is connected with its subsidiaries (*aṅga*) in such a manner, so too would the modified form (*vikṛti*)—being of a similar general nature—be connected with those same subsidiaries. In some modified rites, such as the *Saurya* sacrifice, there is the injunction: "At each *prayāja* offering, one offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain. Because this serves as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that archetypal subsidiary, the injunction is perceived; for indeed, every [archetypal] injunction applies to every [instance].

The rule "the modified sacrifice is like the archetype" (prakṛtivat vikṛtiḥ) applies without distinction; thus, it would operate universally. Consequently, there is a fixed principle that "the modification is to be performed according to the archetype.

Therefore, even in the case of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, once the procedure has been obtained from the archetype, the injunctions regarding qualities such as the number eleven and so forth are established as the final conclusion (siddhānta).
Furthermore, an injunction regarding the subsidiaries would not be possible for that which lacks subsidiaries.
In the *paśu* sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, it is heard in scripture: "He performs eleven *prayāja*s; he performs eleven *anuyāja*s.

Regarding this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is introduced: that while the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is already obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is an injunction of qualities such as the number eleven.
Furthermore, there could be no specific injunction regarding a constituent part (*aṅga*) for an action that lacks constituents.
Yet, there is indeed a specific injunction: "The *prastara* [grass-bundle] is made of *āśvavāla* grass.
For if there were no general rule (*prasara*), the specific quality of being made of *āśvavāla* grass would not be enjoined.
Therefore, when the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) has been obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*) in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), there are injunctions for specific qualities.

And because the action is one and the same, when there is proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) [of the injunction], in the absence of a connection with a specific term, there would be a modification of that [action] by means of a quality, since the word is directed toward the injunction and the quality is what is to be enjoined.
He states another specific point that establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Because of the unity of expression regarding both the primary action and the subsidiary action— that is, because it is "ekaśabda," meaning that which has a single word as its enjoining authority, and the state of being such is "aikaśabdyam"— therefore,

by means of a single injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*), both the subsidiaries and the primary are enjoined. Consequently, there is the proximity of the subsidiaries through the word that expresses the primary.

Thus, when there is such proximity, there occurs a connection by name with the injunction—that is, the subsidiary injunction—of that sacrifice known as the *prājāpatya*. In that case, it is an injunction of the quality of "eleven-ness.
In this manner, in every sacrifice, there would be a modification through a quality;
likewise, by means of number and mantra, another number and another mantra would be modified.
Or, by means of a quality—that is, a modified quality—the modification thereof would be a modification of the qualities of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

And thus, because the word "eleven" and so forth is subject to an injunction—specifically, an injunction regarding the *prayāja* offerings—and because the quality, such as the number eleven, is taught as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), the restatement is not purposeless.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained for the animal sacrifice from the archetype, and once it is obtained, the injunctions of the qualities [apply].
Furthermore, because a name is not something to be performed—

since names such as "Prayājas" and "Anuyājas" are not themselves actions and are not objects of injunction— the statement "He performs eleven Prayājas," and so forth, does not enjoin a separate ritual act. Rather,

the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that this is an injunction of an accessory in the form of the number eleven for the Prayājas already obtained from the archetype (prakṛti) in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice.
And the authority regarding the quality is equal;

the authority and capacity of the injunction (*codaka*) with respect to the quality is equal [to that of the original injunction] in bringing forward the qualities such as the *prayāja* offerings from the archetype (*prakṛti*).
And once those have been brought forward, there are the injunctions of qualities such as number.
Alternatively, there is an equal capacity and power among verbal expressions (*ākhyāta-śabda*).

For those [expressions] which are capable of expressing both a quality (*guṇa*) and an action (*karman*) with respect to a named entity (*saṃjñin*) possessing qualities, they are capable of enjoining only the quality therein.

Therefore, the conclusion is established that in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, it is the injunction of the quality consisting of the number eleven for the *prayāja* offerings already obtained [by extension].

If it is argued that "everything is indeed primary," and if the verbal suffix (ākhyāta-śabda) were to enjoin even a subordinate element (guṇa), then in that case everything would be primary; if the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) should say that "there would be primacy in the *prayāja* offerings of the Agni-Soma sacrifice," [the reply is:
because of the nature of the connection with such [a factor], they must be injunctions according to their actual purpose.

The proponent of the established view (siddhāntin) refutes what was stated by the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) in the Sūtra—that there would follow the consequence that even a subordinate factor (guṇa) could possess primacy because it is denoted by a verb (ākhyātaśabda).
[He does so] because of the connection with being such as it is, i.e., the state of being a verb; for a thing does not become either primary or subordinate merely by virtue of its verbal expression.
Rather, they should be according to their actual nature (yathārtha).
Whatever objects exist, whether they are primary or secondary, since they possess names that correspond exactly to their reality, there should be injunctions for them accordingly:
that which is primary remains primary, and that which is secondary remains secondary.

Furthermore, the nature of being an injunction is no different in this regard, because of the connection between the archetypal (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*) rites; therefore, everything is for the sake of the primary purpose.
That which brings about an injunction is an *injunction* (*vidhi*); its state is *injunction-ness* (*vidhitva*), which is to say, being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*)—this is the point of curiosity.

The status of being an injunction and being an auxiliary of archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements with respect to modified (*vaikṛta*) elements is thus undifferentiated and equal. This is because it is possible through their connection with the ritual action in the form of praise, such as "nobility" (*āryatva*) and so forth.

"Just as the explanatory passage (arthavāda) that exists in the archetype (prakṛti)—namely, 'He sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; [he is] the two supports of the sacrifice'—is the very same explanatory passage in the ectype (vikṛti), namely, 'He sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; he indeed establishes the sacrifice'; and just as in the archetype it is said, 'These two Ājyabhāga offerings are the eyes of the sacrifice,' while in the ectype it is said, 'He sacrifices the two Ājyabhāgas; he does not deprive himself of the eyes,' therefore all such [passages] are subordinate in the ectype for the sake of the primary [act]. And because their origin is equal, the qualification [for the rite] should be by means of the purificatory acts (saṃskāra)."
From this as well, we see that not everything is a primary rite (*pradhāna*), but rather that some things are for the sake of the primary rite.

This is because of their origination: regarding those two, the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*), there is no difference in the origination of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, since their sequence is identical. The sequence—first the *prayājas*, then the primary rite in the middle, and finally the *anuyājas*—is exactly the same in both the archetype and the ectype.

Therefore, the injunction for the performance of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) would be the regulator of the primary rite (*pradhāna*) accompanied by the subsidiaries (*saṃskāra*), which provide assistance through both seen and unseen effects.
Consequently, all [subsidiaries] belong to the primary rite, and there is something intended for the sake of the primary rite as well.

However, the purpose of this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is that, since the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) has been established from the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the sentences regarding the eleven *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are injunctions of specific qualities (*guṇavidhi*) in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).

Even when [a detail] is heard in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is the exclusion of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) [details] such as the *drumyatva* (the state of being made of wood) and so forth.
Mīmāṃsākośa, p. 1539; see the section under "of that which is archetypal" (*tadīratvasya prākṛtasya*).
"In the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the subsidiary element (śeṣa) serves all purposes, just as in the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti).
They recite this: "The optional sacrifices (kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ) are indeed according to their respective colors; they should be performed in a low voice (upāṃśu).
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the low-voiced quality apply to both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice, or only to the primary sacrifice?

Having previously established—along with its exceptions—that the external *ājya* rites, which are obtained from the altar-site (*vedi-deśa*) in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), it is now incidentally examined whether the properties specifically prescribed for the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) itself serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the principal, or only the principal.

Herein is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): those properties enjoined in the model sacrifice serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the principal; therefore, properties such as whispering (*upāṃśutva*) and so forth in the modified sacrifice must likewise serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the principal.

Nor should it be said that by the phrase "sacrifices performed for a specific desire" (*kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ*) only the principal acts (*pradhāna*) are intended, because it is the principal act together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*) that accomplishes the desired result,
and because there is no distinction in the fact that the subsidiaries are also included as being for the sake of a desire.
Therefore, even in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the injunction of low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) applies precisely to those original functions as they occurred in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
This being the case, it is replied:
"Or rather, for the sake of the primary purpose, because the subsidiary is not enjoined.
This is the intention: this would indeed be so if this were equal to the injunction of the original *barhis* grass.

For in that case, although the context might suggest that the properties pertain to the primary rite alone, it was determined that they pertain to both the subsidiary and the primary rites because of their proximity (*vattriyastva*).
Here, however, because of the scriptural statement "the optional sacrifices" (*kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ*), it establishes that the subsidiaries themselves have the primary rite as their purpose.
Nor should it be said that, for the sake of fulfilling the desire, the subsidiaries also become denotable by the word "optional" (*kāmya*) when the rite is performed with its subsidiaries.

Since the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) possess the status of being a means to the primary (*pradhāna*) through a succession by way of assisting the primary, whereas the primary itself is [the goal] directly;

and since it is not appropriate to resort to a succession when a direct connection is possible—because only those dependent on the primary are denoted by the word "principal desire" (*mukhya-kāmya*), and it is established that only they [the subsidiaries] possess the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*).
The practical application (*prayojana*) is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the quality of being whispered must be performed even in the midst of the subsidiaries.
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, [the rule applies] only to the principal [portion].

As for the Sūtra: when it is argued that "this injunction of low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) should apply to the primary meaning alone," [the response is] "because it is not so enjoined" (*acoditatvāt*). It is indeed enjoined.
"In the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the subsidiary element (śeṣa) serves all purposes, just as in the model sacrifice (prakṛti).

Regarding the statement, 'The optional sacrifices (kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ) are according to their respective classes; they should be performed in a low tone (upāṃśu),' a low tone is prescribed for the optional sacrifices, similar to the sacrifice mentioned in the *Āyavarṇa* Veda.

That low tone, being a subsidiary element, should serve all purposes—that is, it should serve the purpose of the primary rite—in each of those various optional sacrifices. It does not [apply otherwise].
In the case of a modification (vikṛti),
the time of the modification pertains solely to the primary rite.
"As in the archetype.
Just as in the archetype all the characteristics of the altar and the characteristics of the clarified butter apply, so it is here.
This is the prima facie view.

Or rather, the primary meaning [of the injunction] prevails because it is enjoined by a direct command. In the case of optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*), it is stated that "optional sacrifices should indeed be performed in a low tone (*upāṃśu*)," just as the low tone is prescribed for the *ārṣavadha* Veda-sacrifice. That [low tone], being for the sake of the principal act, should be understood to apply to the modified optional sacrifices; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) reached by the preceding Sūtra.
The low-voiced (upāṃśu) accent mentioned here should have its primary meaning as the principal sense alone, not as the sense of a command.
Why? Because the ignorant person has not been enjoined [to it].
For it has been stated: "The sacrifices are for the sake of desired results."
The optional rites (kāmyāḥ) serve solely the purpose of the primary sacrifice;
however, the subsidiary sacrifices (aṅgayāgāḥ) do not serve the purpose of fulfilling desires, but rather serve the purpose of the primary sacrifice.
Therefore, in the aforementioned statement, the subsidiary is not enjoined.
But that [silence] would be obtained through the *Uttaraka* (the subsequent section).

Therefore, since the subsidiary (*aṅga*) is not enjoined by that sentence, whereas the primary (*pradhāna*) alone is enjoined, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the state of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) belongs to the primary alone. [Question: How is there the attainment of ritual properties (*dharma*) in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by way of similarity?

[Duplicate: 10|1|1| 19. In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), such as the *saurya*, *aindrāgna*, *citri*, *sāṃgrahaṇī*, and others, the sale [of Soma] is established as being obtained through the purchase from a single seller. 3536. *Vitarka*:
[This] is logically consistent with the acquisition through the purchase from a single seller.
But it does not imply that very same [act].

Therefore, since the status of being a seller of Soma is established by the cognition of selling, it follows that the one who performs the sale under discussion is indeed someone other than these [others]; this is proven.
The purpose [of this argument] is as stated in the [previous] position.

But the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, the seller of Soma is indeed different from those [initiated] for the sake of the primary rites, because selling is not enjoined as an integral part of the ritual action. Having thus concluded: "The seller is indeed another, because it is not enjoined as part of the rite."

Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, when the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view—based on a departure from the established rule—is that the Soma-seller (*somavikrayī*), the one who sells the Soma, should be one of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) themselves, the author of the Sūtras establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with this Sūtra. The word *tu* ("but") serves to distinguish this case from the preceding Sūtras.
That person who sells the Soma must indeed be someone other than the officiating priests.
Because the selling of the ritual action is not enjoined;
just as the purchase of Soma is prescribed, so too the selling is not prescribed.
Since the purchase would not be accomplished in the absence of selling, selling is therefore implied.
The performer of that [rite], however, is indeed someone other than the *adhvaryu* and the rest.
In this regard, there is the section concerning the forfeiture of property (*viddhanādhikaraṇa*) due to selling [the Soma] out of greed for the substance [Sudhā]. 3538. [This is] the knowledge.

The performance, however, takes place prior to the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). For the consecration belongs to a specific location, as it is said: "He is consecrated in response to the *Māhendra* hymn. Therefore, setting aside the direct [sequence], the performance occurs for each [verse] prior to the consecration.
The other [view] is merely a logical inference, based on the rule: "But at the end, [the procedure is] that of Yādāyaṇa.
[Objection: After the Abhiṣecanīya and before the Daśapeya, rites such as "he gives the six-year-old [cow]" are recited.
In this regard, there is a doubt: when the consecration (abhiṣeka) is displaced [to a later time], does it displace the other [rites] as well, or not?
"It is performed alone at the end, according to Bādarāyaṇa" (5.2.19).
At the conclusion of the kingdom, there is no such doubt at all;
therefore, it is performed at the end of the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice.
There is a displacement of the consecration alone, just as there is of the altar alone on the new moon day.
Since no connection with the permission for offspring is established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), displacement—whether upward or downward—is appropriate in the ectype (*vikṛti*).
However, in this case, because no such connection is established, it is improper to introduce something that was not previously present.
This being the case, we reply:
because the recitation of the *aśāṭhya* [mantra] is directly perceived, it has a connection with the preceding ritual items.
Nor is this recitation fulfilled in its purpose here, just as the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) is not completed at the Full Moon sacrifice.
Therefore, there is a displacement of these [rites] to an earlier position.
But is there not also a textual recitation for the Abhiṣecanīya? It is said in reply:

Since the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice is prescribed as being accompanied by its constituent parts (sāṅga), these [other rites] consequently become subsequent to it. Furthermore, because they are encompassed by distinct injunctive statements (prayogavacana), there is no mention of them even in the recitation (pāṭha).
As the Śāstra states: "The consecration (abhiṣeka) is unprecedented; therefore, there is no arrival of the extraction (apakarṣa) ending with that."
"Since it performs [the function], therefore that much alone is extracted"—
this being the position reached, it is replied:
"The sequence of these [mantras] is established by their prior consecration and by direct textual recitation."
"Otherness [is established] for ignorant commoners through inference.
Thus says Soma— this is indeed a connection by way of an illustration.

Regarding this: "The worship of the deities and so forth occurs either at the conclusion of the ordinary limbs (*prākṛtāṅga*) preceding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), or in the middle; or, as before, the worship of the deities and so forth occurs at the conclusion of everything. The consecration should be drawn forward from its place because of the direct textual reading (*pratyakṣapāṭha*) [of it occurring] earlier."
Prior to that, in the middle [of the Rājasūya], there is the Māhendra-stotra.

Bhaṭṭa: In the Rājasūya, between the Abhiṣecanīya Soma-sacrifice and the Daśapeya, the rites of the Rājasūya beginning with the *vidagdha* and ending with the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) are prescribed by such texts as, "He causes the horse to trample [the ground], he subdues the Kṣatriya, he orders the remnants of the three-year-old calf, and he is consecrated.
Among these, the consecration itself is established by the direct scriptural statement: "He is consecrated in response to the Māhendra-stotra."
At the time of the *māhendra* cup during the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, [the *vidagdha* and other rites] are postponed.

Even upon that postponement, there is no postponement of the *vidagdha* and other rites previously recited, because—according to the principle of the *vaidikaraṇa* (5.1.16)—these new rites lack a fixed sequential order.
Furthermore, since they are recited even after the *abhiṣecanīya*, their sequence remains as before, following immediately after the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries.

This being the position reached: since a fixed order (*krama*) was previously established for the *prayāja* offerings and others, it is now likewise appropriate that a fixed order exists for the rites ending with the *videdhana* and *abhiṣeka*, which are encompassed by the injunction for the performance of the *ekarātra-sūrya* sacrifice through direct textual recitation (*pratyakṣapāṭha*). Because the archetypal (*prakṛta*) subsidiaries are inferred through the recitation of the *abhiṣecanīya* rite, it is illogical to assume a sequence between them and the *videdhana* etc., which are encompassed by a different performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*). Therefore, when the *abhiṣeka* is postponed, there is necessarily a postponement of the *videdhana* and other rites as well. Maṇḍana [says]: "The postponement of the *videdhana* and so forth is ordained."

Śaṃkara: [The subordinate acts] such as the consecration (dīkṣā) would be displaced. In the Rājasūya, acts such as the piercing (vidveṣana) are subsidiaries (aṅga) that do not constitute the sacrifice itself; however, the sacrifices, such as the Anumati-sacrifices and others, are the primary elements (pradhāna).
In the Rājasūya...
The *vidagdha* and other [defects] are mentioned according to the *Taittirīya* recension as belonging to the *abhiṣecanīya* fire;
however, they are stated in the *Rājasūya* section [of the Jaiminīya-Brāhmaṇa] as being inconceivable (*akārya*).
The *vidēdhana* and other rites belong to the *Gajastha* section, because of the greater force of their position within the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Since the *vidēdhana* and other rites are performed during the procedure of the *Abhiṣecanīya*, even if they are performed after the completion of the *Abhiṣecanīya* procedure, they must be carried out preceded by the expiation for the reversal of order (*kramaviparyāsa-prāyaścitta*).

In the *Rājasūya*, the introductory statement (*prakarana*) is not the factor that determines application (*viniyojaka*), because even within the *Rājasūya*, those [subsidiary rites] such as the *Soma* sacrifices are already satisfied (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*) by their respective archetypal properties (*prākṛtair dharmaiḥ*).
(Mīmāṃsā)
The term "exists" (*vidyate*) conveys the mere perception of a result. (Maṇi, p. 102).
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, that which is one's own at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇākāla*) and which is currently existing is precisely what must be given.
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is the giving away of everything that one possesses.
Thus it is known: "The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and their mixtures..."
The Vedas are the fourteen seats of knowledge and of Dharma:
the three—Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda—and the fourth, Arthaśāstra; thus, there are indeed twelve branches of knowledge.
The three secondary sciences (upavedas) are Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda;
while Mīmāṃsā and Nyāyavistāra are the two auxiliary sciences (upāṅgas). Suśruta Saṃhitā 1.3.4.3, p. 183.
The acquisition of knowledge (vidyādhigama) consists in being an enjoiner; this acquisition of knowledge is prescribed for members of the three higher castes, not for Brahmins alone. Bhāṣya 6.2.123.
And the taking of a wife occurs after the time of acquiring knowledge. Bhā. 6.8.2.123.
One who possesses knowledge.
One who possesses the knowledge established by the injunction for Vedic study and who is alive must perform rituals such as the Agnihotra (Śābara Bhāṣya 6.2.17).
The teacher is the primary authority in imparting knowledge and discipline to his pupils.
Knowledge, Soma, and progeny: these are obligatory for those of the three [upper] castes.
Bhāṣya 6.2.123.

The fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). Those who compose artificial fields of knowledge—whose names and subjects are fixed according to each *kalpa*, *manvantara*, and *yuga*—are those who proceed eternally.
These very fields of knowledge, which are heard even in the Veda within the mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), are recognized as the means for knowing Dharma.
Or [as stated in] Vākyapadīya 1.3.17, p.
202: "For the branches of knowledge are indeed limited to fourteen or eighteen [in number], including the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and Dharmaśāstra;
the Vedas; and the three [Upavedas]: Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda."

And the fourth is the *Arthaśāstra*. These—the Vedas, Upavedas, Aṅgas, Upāṅgas, and so forth, including the ten *Saṃhitās*, the *Purāṇas*, and those designated as *Śikṣā* and *Daṇḍanīti*—are accepted by disciples as authoritative means of Dharma (*dharmapramāṇa*). Among these, the works of the Buddhists and others are neither remembered nor accepted. (Note: The Upavedas are Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and Arthaśāstra.
The Aṅgas are Śikṣā and the rest. The Upāṅgas consist of the two: Pūrva-mīmāṃsā and Uttara-mīmāṃsā.)
The learned person is qualified [for the ritual].
Furthermore, the learned man whose mouth is adorned by the extraction of words, sentences, and logic shines forth.
Vākyapadīya 1.2.15, p. 129. This is the section concerning the learned man (vidvad-adhikaraṇa).
It has been established in the *Vidvad-adhikaraṇa* (2.1.2) that the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* denote the principal [rites];
this is the statement concerning the "knowing" (*vidvat*) [sections], as found in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.18.

"Therefore, he who, knowing this, performs the Full Moon sacrifice," and "he who, knowing this, performs the New Moon sacrifice"—these are two sentences (Vi. 2.1.3). Furthermore, the injunction for Vedic study is also inappropriate for the religious student (brahmacārin).
Furthermore, since the injunction regarding the application of knowledge (*vidyāniyogavidhi*) has this very [knowledge] as its object, it is inappropriate for there to be multiple [applications].
The Vedic scripture that imparts knowledge consists of the injunctive form (*liṅ*).

According to Mīmāṃsā, the Vedic scripture that imparts knowledge— namely, the injunctive (*liṅ*), the imperative (*loṭ*), the gerundive (*tavya*), and the fifth verbal suffix (*pañcamalakāra*)— possesses the capacity for injunction.

Or [it may be argued]: at Bhāṣya 2.1.2.27, page 562, we perceive the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the phrase "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), which replaces the third-person singular verb ending (*vidyāt*) from the context of the five sacrifices and desires (at Vārttika 1.1.2.13,
page 700).
*Vidhāna* is the making known of that which has not been [previously] established;
*vidhāna* is the instigation to activity in one who has not yet engaged in it. (Bhāṣya 2.3.14, p. 593).
And that is the human-like operation of the word; [Śabara-bhāṣya on] PMS 2.1.23 and 4.1.2 (second interpretation).
*Vidhāna* means ritual procedure (*kalpa*).

The meaning is "it is thus said" (*itiktetyatā*). Bhāṣya 1.1.2.2.18, p. 141: "For an injunction (*vidhāna*) indeed intends to enjoin a matter that has not been previously established. 2|4|14, p. 152: An injunction (*vidhi*) is extremely rare because it pertains to fourfold types according to the distinction of incapacity (such as the injunctions of *utsarga* and so forth). In some cases, there is a focus on the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*), as in "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" (*udbhidā yajeta*).

An injunction distinct from these three is an injunction of origin (*utpattividhi*). (Ku. 2.1.15)

Injunction (*vidhi*) is fourfold: the injunction of origin (*utpattividhi*), the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), the injunction of application (*viniyogavidhi*), and the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*).
Among these, the injunction that makes known merely the essential nature of a duty (*dharma*) is the injunction of origin.
For example: "One performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice."
An injunction that makes known the relationship between the subsidiary and the principal is an injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*),
such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*).
An injunction that makes known the attainment of the performance...
