When the injunction (*vidhi*)—which consists in the necessity of performing what is to be done—is present, this *bhāvanā*, though constrained by its limits, sets aside even the sacrifice (*yāga*) which is denoted by the same word and is first understood, because that [sacrifice] is difficult to perform; instead, it relies solely upon heaven as the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*).

And since the sacrifice and other acts have thus attained the status of being the object to be accomplished, they are accepted as the instruments (*karaṇa*); thus, their status as means to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is established.

How, then, is the understanding of the means for achieving human goals (*puruṣārtha*) in the world conveyed through the expression of the present tense? (Answer: It is by virtue of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), not by the inherent power of the word itself. How this is so will be demonstrated by the Teacher himself in his own commentary on the sūtras "In the case of substances, preparatory rites, and actions" (*Dravyasaṃskārakarmasu*) and "But [the action] is not a means [to the result], because it is for that purpose" (*Asādhakaṃ tu tādarthyāt*). (Kaṇikā, pp. 2–4. Since an injunction (*vidhi*) lacks the capacity to incite activity if it does not depend on an exhortation (*prarocanā*), and since [the exhortation] is directly perceived when an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is present, the explanatory passage—

The objection raised in the text beginning with "sa-hitasyaiva vidhāyakatvāvagatiḥ" (the understanding that only [the injunction] together [with the explanatory passage] possesses injunctive force) is as follows:

[The opponent argues that] the self considers the *apūrva* (unseen potency) to be the task (*kārya*). Since effort (*prayatna*) itself must come into being, and since the injunction does not depend on an incitement (*prarocanā*), it is established that the injunction functions as an instigator merely by making known that its own object is a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Thus, even in the absence of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the capacity to enjoin is possible because the operation of the agent (*bhāvayitr*), who is the motivator (*prayojaka*) regarding the *apūrva*, is sufficient for instigation. Therefore, the claim that there would be no injunctive force in the absence of an *arthavāda* is stated [by the opponent] based on this [misconception].

Nor is there a contradiction in the fact that the expression of the effect [of action] does not denote the effort [to act]. For it is possible for the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth to denote effort, since they incite activity toward an injunction alone that is independent of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like. Furthermore, although the "unseen potency" (*apūrva*) is denoted, explanatory passages are employed merely to avoid rendering them purposeless.

Nor is the simultaneous denotation of many meanings a defect, for there is no lack of comprehension because it is understood in that way; furthermore, because the injunction does not depend on persuasion (*prarocanā*), it conforms to the inclination toward activity (*pravṛtti*). For once the capacity of the injunctive suffixes (*liṅ* etc. to denote an action has been understood through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the meaning of the injunctive statement is determined even prior to the connection with the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), since those [passages] have no other purpose.
Because they run together due to their mutual compatibility (*ānuguṇya*).

Since the *kṛti* (volitional effort) is subordinate and occupies the position of the primary [object], even if it lacks the capacity when independent of the incitement (*prarocanā*), there is no dispute that the number of the agent and so forth is denoted by the verbal suffixes (*liṅ* etc. in the prior state of the injunction (*vidhi*) itself, which exists in the absence of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), as this is the manifestation of the power of incitement.
However, even without an explanatory passage, the verbal suffixes such as *liṅ*, though denoting the task to be accomplished (*kārya*), [function in this way].
Nor is it tenable that the injunctive character [of the *arthavāda*] arises merely from its being denotable as an excellence by way of providing encouragement (*prarocanā*).

For the sentence-meaning is the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) itself; the fact that its capacity for encouragement is removed—due to its being subordinate to the *apūrva* as the object to be accomplished—is caused by the very existence of the *arthavāda*.
This is because [the *arthavāda*] does not denote [anything else].
Because the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is denoted as the primary meaning;
thus it is established. Furthermore, when an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) exists, the injunction also has the result of providing encouragement (*prarocanā*).
Thus, there is nothing inconsistent in [the claim that] the meaning of a sentence is [the injunction].

For this very reason, the Blessed One [states in Su. Pu. 523–26]: "The nature of an injunction is that which generates activity"; and the usage of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) in various places is that it is human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*).

From the context, because [the *apūrva*] is not what is expressed by the word as being the "fitness" [for the result], it lacks the necessity of directly producing the fruit; therefore, the *apūrva* is not mentioned. For even in the absence of such an effect (*kārya*), it is logically possible for the injunction (*vidhi*) to produce activity, just like a staff standing in a forest.
[The *apūrva*] is delimited by some verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*).
Indeed, it is not the case that the meaning of the suffix [the injunctive] consists in being the generator of an activity directed toward a result;
for even upon hearing hundreds of injunctions, this [result-oriented activity] does not exist.
For every human effort [is indeed directed toward a result].

Someone might necessarily resort to the meaning of an existent entity (*bhāvārtha*), because one observes the engagement of certain people even without it; for without that [entity], such engagement would not exist.
Therefore, the fruit of an injunction is invariably concomitant with effort (*prayatna*); there is no connection [of the fruit] with that which is merely enjoined. (Bhāṭṭa 6.1.6, p. 218)
Su. Pu. 264: The meaning of the *bhāva* (the efficient force) delimits the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as that which is brought about by effort (*prayatna*).

Even if one accepts the rule that the final determination of the injunction’s delimiting capacity depends on the mantra, this does not constitute the status of being the object (*viṣaya-bhāva*) for the delimiting capacity itself.
For wherever something occurs and not elsewhere, there alone lies the strength of its application (*upasaṃhāra*).

Parākrama (4312): Those who know the subject matter (*viṣayavid*) hold that it is a specific instance of the injunction (*vidhi*); for there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with anything else, due to the difference in the expression of the verbal statement.
This is the meaning of "subject matter" (*viṣaya*). For this very reason, the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) is the subject matter.

3|8|17. Because that which is yet to be brought into being (*bhāvya*) alone is the object of human effort, there is an inquiry by those who designate the task (*kārya*) regarding the object and the instrument of the injunction (*vidhi*). [This includes] the discussion of the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), the ritual action (*karma-daṇḍa*), and the syntactic connection (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the object-indicating statement.
"Having examined all the views of Prabhākara, this is composed by me."
First,

one must examine the object, because it is through the investigation of that [object] that one follows the path; and it is proper to distinguish the instrument from what is not the object by means of the increase of reasoning.
For by the *jyotiṣṭoma*, an unprecedented task (*apūrva-kārya*) is understood through the verbal suffix.

And with respect to that understood task, in injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," the person desiring heaven is connected as the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Therefore, because it is subordinate, the meaning of the verbal root—being connected as the means (*sādhana*)—is not capable of being led to the status of the thing to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) as the task that brings about heaven.
The connection is with the *apūrva* (the unprecedented).

However, considering [the action] merely as a means to cognition, the Blessed One says that the action, which exists for only a moment, cannot be the means (*sādhana*) for heaven and so forth, which occur at another time;

for it is not possible for the knowledge of the mandate (*niyoga*) to arise from something that is not its object. Thus, even though the action persists until another time, a distinct effect (*kārya*) arises within the action.
And it is established that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others convey [the meaning] as delimited by an object that is a state of being (*bhāvārtha*).

Furthermore, the "task" (*kārya*)—which is the object of human effort (*kṛti*) and whose nature is that which is to be accomplished—is understood; and it is said that the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*kartavyatā*) [of that task] are combined.
Effort (*kṛti*) is the operation of the self, which depends upon human exertion (*puruṣaprayatna*).
Because [the relationship] is observed even in other cases where something is to be proven. In that context, "those very [factors]" is not different in meaning [from the previous statement].

Since the conscious self (*cetana ātmā*) causes the effect to be understood, the sense-object (*viṣaya*), which is the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), is the instrument (*karaṇa*); thus, there is no fixed restriction.
That which has performed its function follows the sequence [of the causal process].
Furthermore, that which is accomplished through the operation of another is not [the agent], because it lacks independence.

For indeed, just as an action is perceived by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) as an object of engagement and as a task to be accomplished, that very [action] is the instrument (*karaṇa*) therein.

Just as the effort of a man, which is worthy of respect, is his own activity, so too, when the two hands, characterized by the act of splitting wood, are set in motion, they perform the action characterized by the splitting of the wood; thus, it is heard that the instruments for achieving the result characterized by the twofold division belong to those very hands, and in this very way is their accomplishment established.

Because the two things designated by multiple terms are of two distinct natures, they constitute the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, here too, it is observed that even that which is to be accomplished by the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) can serve as the instrument for a single [action]. For example, in the case of "going," the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is pervaded by the effort of a person impelled by a purpose—either by means of a horse or by means of a two-wheeled chariot—as one says, "he goes by means of that very effort. Since the operation of the cause differs in each case, [the horse or the chariot] serves as the instrument in relation to the *apūrva*-producing activity (*bhāvanā*).
Now, how is it that what is said—that [the object] is obtained through effort—is not contradicted?

To this we reply: even here, those things which constitute the final operation (*antyavyāpāra*) following the prior arising [of the action] are indeed the means (*karaṇa*) for the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) with respect to the objective meaning (*bhāvārtha*). For, by virtue of being that which is most intensely desired to be accomplished (*ādhyamānatayā*), we maintain that they are distinct from the object (*karman*) itself.
Therefore, because of this distinction, there would indeed be a difference between them.

It is said in reply: In that regard, action (*karman*) cannot first be [the cause], because its status as a causal factor for the production of the *apūrva*—even if linked to the supreme *apūrva* (*paramāpūrva*)—is untenable, since it consists of substances such as clarified butter (*ājya*), medicinal herbs (*auṣadha*), and grains (*vrīhi*).
For indeed, all causal factors (*kāraka*) other than the agent (*kartṛ*) possess distinct properties (*dharma*) corresponding to their respective operations; thus, there is no confusion among them.

Because ritual properties (*dharma*) are established as means for the unprecedented (*apūrva*), they do not extend [to all things]; yet, by this much alone, they do not partake in the status of being objects (*karman*). This is because of the distinction between them.

Furthermore, in the case of sacrifices and the like, there is no *bhāvanā* intermediate between [the sacrifice] and the *apūrva*, because [the sacrifice] is not something unintended to be attained (*anīpsita*).
Furthermore, the status of being an object (*karman*) is indeed observed even in the case of what is undesired;
[if that were so],
it would be difficult for those sacrifices and other rites to function as instruments (*karaṇa*).

As in the case of "He performs the Agnihotra sacrifice. Although the instrument (*karaṇa*)— because the *apūrva* consists of its own nature and the activity of another, and because it is produced through a connection with an operation— is not possible when the operation has ceased, nevertheless, since the *bhāvanā* of the *apūrva* depends upon that [instrument], the existence of the *bhāvanā* is established.
If it is argued that this is a secondary instrumentality (*gauṇakaraṇatva*), then how is it so? It is not untenable;
it is just as in the case of an axe itself.
For the axe is not the action;
rather, it is the instrument that is connected with the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*). Is there a connection with the state of being something to be done?
Indeed, it is the instrument that is so connected, because it is not [the object] most desired to be attained.

Lifting and striking are not the primary instruments (*karaṇa*), for a secondary property cannot be the primary function; this is because the nature of being two-fold [in the case of the axe] is dependent upon that [action]. Even those who claim that the designation "productive activity" (*bhāvanā*) applies to the entire process—including the influence of the connection with the axe—do not find favor with us, because for them, lifting and striking would have to be the means of bringing about the result of being split into two. Indeed, in the case of optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like which do not denote an action, these two [lifting and striking] do not possess the status of being causes for the act of becoming.
Therefore, there is evidence for the expression of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*";
this is because the use of the instrumental case in expressions such as "he does" (*karoti*) or "he cooks" (*pacati*) is logically consistent.

Furthermore, the argument that the subsequent observation [of the result] serves as proof for the instrument's causality toward the efficient force of the unseen merit (*apūrva-bhāvanā*) is also not tenable.

And because it consists solely of the agent’s activity (*sādhakavyāpāra*), the word [denoting the action] is said to be "cut off" [from its own nature]. Thus, there is only one single *bhāvanā* that has the unprecedented result (*apūrvaphala*) as its object; for since the agent performs [the action] by means of specific powers, even when the term "cooks" (*pacati*) follows, it is that very same [single *bhāvanā*] which is indicated. Because the human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*) is one, and because the cause of that *bhāvanā* is also one, it is designated as such. As for the claim that because only the mere activity is enjoined, the mere utterance [of the verb] is not [the *bhāvanā*], but rather the state of being the object to be brought about (*bhāvyatā*) is one and the same—[this is our position].

For this very reason, the Prābhākara maintains that when the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) is not [already] present, there is the production of another suffix (*pratyaya*) even from that much alone, because it serves as the basis for the cognition.

If, however, that which has become the object is itself the instrument (*karaṇa*), then alas, the use of terms such as "instruction" (*apadeśa*) and so forth would be redundant, since they would already be expressed by the single [suffix] through its own power (*tantra*). Therefore, it is said that when the operation (*vyāpāra*) is present, there is no application of these [terms].

However, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth are employed with reference to a conscious agent alone, because the state of being an object is subordinate to the act of cognition and is unitary; thus, they are applied to a single cause.
Furthermore, there is no figurative usage regarding insentient things;
it would only be so if a primary sense were possible.

Consequently, there would be no connection with the *itikartavyatā* (the procedure) through differentiation. In cases such as "he goes" (*gacchati*), the meaning of the *laṭ* suffix [denotes the present time];
therefore, it is expressed in its primary sense even with respect to insentient things.
The venerable one, though learned in the scriptures, has not correctly grasped the meaning of the word *laḍ*.
Since it is the verbal roots themselves that express action, only that which constitutes the primary object [of the root] is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and nothing else.
The meaning of that [root] is as follows:

it is logical that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is precisely the operation (*vyāpāra*). Since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) are secondary, they are understood as subordinate adjuncts (*anubandha*), and thus their status as objects (*viṣayabhāva*) will be explained according to their designation. Furthermore, a single agent is also postulated for them.
Since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) alone cannot be expressed, because expression is merely a means for comprehension;

therefore, due to its being expressed as part of a compound term (*tantra*), even in the case of conjunction—as in the non-usage of "he goes quickly" (*accha gacchati*)—the state of being the object belongs to the combined [factors], and the instrument (*karaṇa*) is established as a concomitant (*anubandha*) of the injunction (*niyoga*). This is because no usage is observed for the isolated [factor] of separation (*vibhāga*);
it should be understood that the isolated separation is not [the object], but rather according to what is obtained [in the context].

For the capacity to prove [the probandum] depends upon the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the means of proof; what, then, is the use of this web of talk fabricated by mere intellectual fancy? Indeed, the capacity to prove differs according to the difference in intrinsic nature. And since being an object of volition (*kṛti-viṣayatva*) constitutes its status as a cause, it is perfectly correct that the capacity to prove is established for the sake of the satisfaction of the learned through a distinction in causality, just as in the case of the "dalika" [example]. This has been well-demonstrated by the author, who captivates the minds of others with his persistent effort.
[The opponent says: "But if one thus resorts to each [of these] as a cause individually, then this is merely a refutation of other causes; it does not correctly establish the doctrine of the Guru."
In that regard, why is it that the fulfillment of the injunction (*niyoga*) does not occur through dependence on the context (*prakaraṇa*)?
It is not so;
for the fulfillment of the injunction arises from the ears and other [faculties] exactly as they are heard, as stated in the *Prakaraṇapañjikā*, pp. 197–201.
In that regard, concerning the rule of apprehension (grahaṇavidhi): among rules,
there is a fixed principle that a single rule, having been applied once, generates the cognition of a single word-form through its uniformity.
Bhāṭṭa 7.2.1:
When an injunction is ambiguous, an explanatory passage (arthavāda) serves as the basis for determination.
Regarding the statement, "He places the smeared pebbles," there arises the doubt: what is the substance used for smearing?
From the explanatory passage (arthavāda), "Clarified butter is indeed brilliance," it is determined that clarified butter is the substance for the collyrium. [Vi.
1.4.19] The injunction has universal application.
Such is the reasoning (*nyāya*).
"Or rather, it should be a universal duty (*sarvadharma*), because the injunction is established by that same reasoning" (JS 1.3.17) is the sūtra of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In this context, the reasoning that produces its status as a universal duty is the fact that the injunction has a universal scope; that [injunction] in which such a scope exists within the ritual arrangement or the prescriptive statement is "that-possessing-reasoning" (*tannyāya*).

The state of being that is its "possessing that logic" (*tannyāyatvam*). Su. p. 245–246: Since an injunction (*vidhi*) that was previously understood as referring to a mere generality must, due to conflict with an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), have its scope restricted, sublation (*bādha*) is admitted.

Su. p. 525: Because of the inseparable connection between an injunction and its praise (*stuti*), when one of the two is perceived, the other is inferred; thus the sentence is established as having been previously [understood].
Page 41. There is syntactic unity between an injunction (*vidhi*) and a statement of praise (*stuti*), because the words [of both] directly [contribute to a single meaning].
"One desiring prosperity should seize [the wind]," for what reason? Because the wind is the swiftest.

Bhāṣya 1.2.17, page 1.7. An injunction possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), because the two causes of invalidity—contradiction (*ayoga*) and dependence on something else (*sāpekṣatva*)—are absent.
VI. 1|1|5. When there is a finality of the *kāraka* (participant in action), there is a distinction in the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the injunction (*vidhi*).
However, even a thousand meanings connected to a single *kāraka* can be accomplished by a single effort.
Vārttika 2|2|15|6, p. 507. Furthermore, there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyabhāva*) between one injunction and another, because of the difference in their modes of expression (*vacanavyakti*).

Bhāṣya 6.2.15: Even though the injunction "one should sacrifice an animal" (paśumālabheta) is established as a general rule, it is restricted by the wording of the mantra, "Recite for the omentum and fat of the goat," because the injunction and the mantra share the same subject matter. Furthermore, since the general rule applies to the entire class [of animals], there is no contradiction even when it is understood to apply specifically to the goat; and where a restriction is possible, an absence of restriction is untenable, as will be explained later in the Paddhati (Su. p. 525). Moreover, there is no syntactic unity between two separate injunctions.

Bhāṣya 6.1.2.130: Injunctions (*vidhi*) have as their authority the postulation of what is not otherwise established (*atyantāprāpta-viṣayatva*), which is based on the scriptural text and logical consistency. Vārttika 3.4.1.30, p. 964: The purpose of injunctions is the knowledge of an instigation (*pravartanā*) that generates activity. Maṇi, p. 5: Is this alone the purpose of all injunctions—the cessation of the state of being under a mandate (*niyoga*)?
*Ṛju-vimālā*, page 10: All injunctions have as their domain that which has not [otherwise] been established.
*Vārttika* 3.6.1.2: Since all injunctions have human purpose as their fruit, the expectation of a motive is satisfied by [the promise of] heaven and so forth.

3.4.4.3, page 911: In an injunction regarding a subject matter understood from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), since words such as "Ṛgveda" and so on function as restatements (*anuvādaka*), there is no fault even if they are used in a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*).
3|3|1|2 p. 807: The non-employment of a non-denotative word in a prescriptive injunction (*vidhi*).
Su. p. 710: The impossibility of secondary meaning (*gauṇatva*) in a prescriptive injunction.
Vā. 3|5|20|2: And [the absence of] indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a prescriptive injunction.

The conclusion of the injunction (vidhyanta): Regarding the section on the conclusion of the injunction (vidhyantādhikaraṇa), [it is stated] with respect to the term "yūpa" in the passage, "In the case of the *khayūpa*, the *upaśaya* becomes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
(Sūtras 7.3.13–34). There is no extension of the ritual details (*dharmas*) pertaining to the *iṣṭi* sacrifices into the Soma sacrifice.

8|1|313-10. *Vidhyanta* (the end of the injunction) refers to the determination of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) as being "of such a nature" (*itthambhāva*). Regarding this, the teachers' established view is that its beginning is the *kathaṃbhāva* (the inquiry "how [is it to be done]"), which consists of the investigation into the various constituent parts of the sentence, their meanings, and their purposes.
Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.3.7.14, p. 852: *Vidhyanta* applies to the subsequent groups of rites belonging to the same class (*nikāyin*) as the first one.
8|1|3|1|19. The ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) belonging to the obligatory *agnihotra* applies to the *agnihotra* performed within the *kauṇḍapāyanāmayana* sacrifice.
Bhāṣya 7|3|1|16–5. The ritual procedure [of the *savanīya*] applies to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) from the *sānnāyya*.
Duṣyaṭīkā 12|1|1|1, p. 2216. The ritual procedure for the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is derived from the full-moon cake offering (*paurṇamāsika-puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni and Soma.

12.1.1.2 (p. 2216): The concluding ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the first [sacrifice] applies to the *Sādyaska*, just as in the case of the *Kauṇḍapāyana* sacrifice. The designation "Agnihotra" is the designator of the rite; it brings along those ritual properties (*dharma*) that are concomitant with that rite.
Since this designation would not be appropriate here if those [elements] were absent, the existence of those dharmas is understood to be there.

Likewise, in this case as well, since the observation of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth would not be possible in the absence of the Vedic [text], the existence of that [Veda] too is understood to be here.
But surely, in the absence of a logical rule (*nyāya*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the cause.
This is true; however, it has been stated that "the principle [applies] because of the commonality. As for the argument that worldly activity proceeds from what is perceived, we reply:
even if it were a matter of perceived activity, nevertheless, only the Vedic [practice] should be regulated.

How so? Just as [one says] "a cow with a foal" (*kiśorinī dhenuḥ*), meaning "a cow whose foal is black" (*kṛṣṇakiśorā dhenuḥ*). Although the word *dhenu* is observed to be applied to a cow-cow, nevertheless, due to the commonality of its denotation, it also applies to a mare-cow; thus, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the foal (*kiśora*), it is understood to refer to a mare-cow.

Similarly here as well, although there is worldly activity based on what is perceived, nevertheless, because it shares in the general nature of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it should be understood as Vedic by virtue of its indicative mark (*liṅga*).
Since the originative injunctions (*utpatti*) are equal, the application [of the rite] should occur according to the respective qualification (*adhikāra*).
Bhāṣya: Or rather, there is no restriction at all by means of an indicative mark.

Why? Because their origins are equal. The origins of the ritual elements (*dharma*), such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, are identical for all; they exist by virtue of the presence of [the primary rites] like the *āgneya*, and not through mutual dependence.

What follows from this? If the *anuyāja*s and so forth were subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *prayāja*s and so forth, then—according to the principle that "where there is a principal, there are subsidiaries"—the *anuyāja*s and so forth would be inferred by the observation of the *prayāja*s.

However, when these [offerings] are equal in status as principals, then, upon observing the *prayāja*s, one may at will infer either the *prayāja*s themselves or the properties of the *prayāja*s; but the *anuyāja*s and so forth are not so inferred.
Therefore, this indicative mark (*liṅga*) belongs to us.
Regarding that [objection], namely "it is like a designation," we say this:
that is correct; for it has been stated that where a word belonging to one thing is applied to another, it extends the properties of the former to the latter.
Moreover, that [rule] is an injunction, such as "it should be offered like the Agnihotra";
this one, however, is a restatement (anuvāda).
Therefore, there is no application of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth here, much less of the *anuyāja* offerings and so forth.
Therefore, the comparison with "naming" (*abhidhāna*) is inappropriate.

Consequently, the ritual application (*bhāva*) should occur according to its respective authority (*adhikāra*); those elements (*dharma*) which are prescribed for the sake of a particular *apūrva* should belong to that very [apūrva].
For both the origination (*utpatti*) and the statement of subsidiary elements (*śeṣavacana*) are mutually contradictory in a single instance.
Commentary: If that is so, then by the verbal form in the injunction "One should offer a pap to Sūrya," there is the production of the injunction for the primary act;
let there also be the mention of the subsidiary elements. How so? Because the primary act, being mentioned here, is not intended for any other purpose.
And for those who have reached [this state] through ignorance, there will be a determination of the distinction based on these indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Regarding this, it is said: "The origination and the mention of the remainder are contradictory in one and the same [entity].
In a single word, the origination of the primary [element] and the mention of the ignorant ones cannot both occur.
What is the reason? For once the primary element has arisen, it requires the secondary members; and by virtue of that requirement, they are apprehended.
Therefore, that too is logical.

If, moreover, the subsidiaries were also enjoined by the word "should offer" (*nirvapet*), then they too would have a connection with the fruit, and thus their status as subsidiaries would be contradicted.
Consequently, this argument also does not hold.
Therefore, the aforementioned worldly means alone is to be accepted.

"Or rather, the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*) proceeds in the case of an injunction [such as for the *saurya* sacrifice] just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), for there is a visible indicative mark (*liṅga*) [to this effect].
Commentary: Or rather, the end of the injunction proceeds in the case of an injunction such as that for the *saurya* sacrifice; worldly properties do not apply.
But what is this so-called "end of the injunction"? The end of the injunction (*vidheḥ antaḥ*) is "the end of the injunction" (*vidhyanta*).
Now, what is an injunction (*vidhi*)? It is that sentence, upon perceiving which a person proceeds toward the attainment of some goal or withdraws from something;
for by it, a purpose is enjoined.
As in common worldly usage: "Devadatta, bring the white cow."
In that regard, "abhyāja" (drive near) is the beginning of the injunction (*vidhi*); the other [words] are the end.
In the Veda as well, "one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta*) is the beginning of the injunction.
Even the *vidhyanta* (the concluding portion of the injunction) includes the entire *Pauroḍāśika* Brāhmaṇa section, excluding the primary injunction itself.
This *vidhyādi* (the beginning of the injunction), when joined with that,
impels each individual toward the non-cessation (*anivṛtti*) once the *viṣṭi* (the specific ritual application) has been attained.
Therefore, that is the end (*anta*).
Likewise, "One should sacrifice with Soma" is the beginning of the injunction (*vidhyādi*);
the *Brāhmaṇa* text concerning the Soma sacrifice is also the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*).
This is what is called the "end of the injunction" (vidhyanta).
In these [rites] such as the Saurya and others, while the beginning of the injunction exists, the end of the injunction does not exist;
yet, in these cases too, that end of the injunction should be supplied.

How so? A sentence that is incomplete must be completed either by supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) or by assuming a separation (*vyavahitakalpatā*). Between these two, assuming a separation is superior to supplying an ellipsis;
for in the case of supplying an ellipsis, a word not actually heard in the text would have to be postulated.
In the other case, there is a connection with what has been heard [in the preceding context].
Therefore, a portion of the Brāhmaṇa text, though separated by an interval, is postulated as completing this [sentence],
just as in the case of "For the spring, one sacrifices the Kapiñjala birds."
"From the *Śrīpāya* one obtains the *kalaviñjāla*.
By this, the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained.
Now, if that Brāhmaṇa passage is postulated as being within this [text], it does not exist there.
This results in what is called "the peacock's dance.
Just as when a peacock dances, one part is extended while another is contracted,
so too here, this is contracted while that is extended.
This is not a fault;
for in that case [the existence of the object] is perceptual,
whereas here it is inferential.
And that which is based on inference does not subvert what is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In that case, it would not apply here, because of the contradiction with direct perception.
It would indeed be so, if there were a contradiction.
But there is no contradiction;
for as it will exist there, so it will exist here as well.
This is what was stated: "Or rather, the remainder of the injunction proceeds according to the model, just as in the archetype" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 8.1.10).
It is said:

What is meant by "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*)? It is replied: it will establish a restriction regarding the archetype, namely, "this is its archetype. To that it is said: "Or rather, the concluding ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) proceeds just like the archetype."
Whichever is the archetype (prakṛti) of a particular rite— for that which has the Āgneya as its archetype, [the details] come from the Āgneya itself;
for that which has the Agniṣomīya as its archetype, they come from the Agniṣomīya—
so it is in all cases.
Now, why is a worldly *vidhyanta* (the remainder of a procedure) not postulated? It is said:

because there is an absence of a worldly injunction (*vidhi*), the *vidhyanta* itself does not exist; how then can it be postulated? [The opponent] says: let the worldly procedure (*itikartavyatā*) be obtained; what is the use of postulating a *vidhyanta*?
It is said: here, the procedure (itikartavyatā) is indeed Vedic, not worldly.
Why? Because there is the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) that supports the existence of the prayāja offerings and so forth.

When there is an expectancy regarding the "how" (kathaṃbhāva), and the procedure (itikartavyatā) is prescribed therein, because the "how" has not yet been resolved, the injunction brings to mind a sentence similar to itself.
That sentence makes known the meaning of the sentence (vākyārtha) which it has brought to awareness;
and that sentence-meaning is comprised of the result, the instrument, and the procedure.
In that context, because it is not required for the production of the result (*phala*), the [injunction] is not connected [to it];
however, because the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is required, it is connected by means of attaining [the result] through what is indicated by analogy.
And this similarity pertains only to the Vedic [rite], not to the worldly one.

If there is a sign (*liṅga*), it would be a worldly [means] because of its being based on a sign. The Commentary states: "If the Vedic means arises from a sign, then what? In the absence of a sign, it would be worldly.
Wherein a rite possesses no sign whatsoever, therein the worldly procedure should apply here; for example: 'One whose cattle have perished should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni.'"

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) might also be determined by means of the Vedic injunction, as in the previous case, due to its lack of commonality with ordinary experience—just as [the nature of] a cooking pot is inferred from a single grain of rice.
Commentary: To this it is replied:
This would indeed be so if the Vedic means were based upon an indicative mark.
But here it is not caused by an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
What, then, is the cause? It is caused by the remainder of the injunction (*vidhyanta*). And the remainder of the injunction is preceded by logical reasoning (*nyāya*).
And that same principle applies equally to all modified rituals (*vaikṛta*), whether they possess specific indicative marks (*liṅgavat*) or lack them (*aliṅgavat*).
Why? Because of the commonality of the injunctive word (*nodanāśabda*).
In the injunction for ritual action, the verbal expression is identical.
In every case, there is the beginning of the injunction (*vidhyādi*), but not the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*).
When there is an expectation for what is common [to other rites], it is connected with the end of the injunction heard elsewhere.
This indicative mark (*liṅga*), being preceded by logical reasoning (*nyāya*), even when observed in a single instance, makes known the duty for all those who share the same principle.
Just as one knows that a single husk of grain in a cooking pot, when all the grains are being cooked equally, indicates that the others have also been prepared—
since the cause for its preparation is the same as that for the others—
therefore, in every case, the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) applies.
Now, as for what was said— that worldly procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is that which operates on the basis of observation—
here we reply:
this is taught by way of general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
And that which is "seen through general correlation" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*) is a means of valid cognition only if it is non-deviant;
however, this [inference] is deviant,
for we observe sacrifices performed by groups (*gaṇayāga*) and the like that do not possess such a procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Therefore, because it functions as something already perceived, "being seen" is not a valid reason.
As for the argument that, since they possess Vedic status, the indicative marks must have been preceded by such [Vedic texts],
we reply to this:
The reason for its being a subsidiary (bhāgitva) is indeed its status as a previously unknown procedure (apūrvetikartavyatātva). And its verbal origin (śabdapūrva) is established by that [status];
moreover, it is understood that this [procedure] belongs to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and not to everything.
Therefore, there is a sharing [of the procedure].
Consequently, the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is obtained solely through the archetypal injunction (*vidhyanta*) and not otherwise.

Now, why are these modified (*vaikṛta*) sentences not accepted as being merely deficient? Why are they not considered complete by these [archetypal elements]? [The answer is: because the deficient ones would become meaningless.

"Let them be; what is the harm? [The opponent asks: "It is not fitting for the learned (*śiṣṭas*) to accept [the Veda] as being subject to negligence. [The proponent replies: "There might be negligence regarding a single syllable or a single vowel-measure (*mātrā*); how could it occur in such an extensive text? How so? Because it has been stated: 'And the traditional transmission is the same' (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.18)."
Even the delusion of the learned does not persist for many thousands of yugas;
it is appropriate to complete [the count] from their perspective. Therefore, those that are deficient are not accepted.

Therefore, it is established that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is Vedic. Regarding the section on the remainder of the injunction (vidhyanta): the purpose of the injunction being thus established, it is now considered here whether [the procedure] is worldly or Vedic.
For the Vedic word, because it is fixed in its form, cannot be led elsewhere;
but the worldly word, because it is unrestricted, is employed everywhere, even in subtle matters.
This being the position reached, it is said:
The Vedic [form] is associated by way of its general character as being Vedic;
whereas the worldly [form], because it does not bring that [Vedic reality] to mind, is dependent [on other factors].
"Even though this [knowledge] is not worldly, being inferred from the Veda,
it is nevertheless considered to be similar to the direct perception of the words of the Veda."
Therefore, the Vedic *itthambhāva* (manner of performance) is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the *saurya* and other such sacrifices.

Soma: Since the subsequent discussion is in the form of a specific inquiry regarding the very same subject matter as the preceding one, there is a logical connection (*saṃgati*). Vi: "In that case [the *saurya* sacrifice], is the required *vidhyanta* (concluding ritual procedure) worldly or Vedic?"
The first is due to the absence of a commentary, and the other is due to the lack of mental concentration.

The *Bhāṭṭa-mantha*, however, is cited at the very beginning of the *Vindu* (Mīmāṃsākōśa, p. 231): "The extended application (*atideśa*) of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) occurs in the *Saurya* and other [rites].
This is because the twelve *sūtras* beginning with the first and ending with the twelfth constitute a single topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) in the *Bhāṭṭa* school.
Maṇḍana [states]: "But those [rites] are [distinguished] by their Vedic nature..."
[The opponent says: "It is ignorant.
Śaṅkara [replies]: "That [rite] is indeed Vedic because it is enjoined by the Vedas (vidhyanta).

In the section concerning the injunctions (*vidhyantādhikaraṇa*), it was stated that in rites such as the *saurya* sacrifice, there exists a Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) based on an inferred scriptural statement; now, its specific details are being stated.
Śābarabhāṣya 8.1.2:

Now, it might be argued that in the section concerning the end of the injunction (vidhyanta-adhikaraṇa), it was already stated that there is a simultaneous application of both [the worldly and the Vedic] because of the greatness of their combination and because the requirements of the "manner of performance" (itthambhāva) are fulfilled by one alone; therefore, this point is already covered.
True.
That [objection] was refuted from the standpoint of combination (*samuccaya*); here, however, the alternative (*vikalpa*) is being rejected.
This follows the principle of the section on the "End of the Procedure" (*vidhyanta-adhikaraṇa*).

According to the principle of the section on the "End of the Procedure," the injunctive sentence "One should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya" is incomplete and is rendered complete by the sentences containing the remainder of the procedure (*vidhyanta*) belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice.
(Ṭup. pṛ.
1783) | Ratna. 9|3|1|2 | The beginning of the injunction depends upon the remainder of the injunction.

Bhāṣya 4.3.1.4, p. 829: When there is a requirement for a specific ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) and multiple procedures are applicable, the procedure is restricted by means of a unique indicative mark (*liṅga*).
It has been stated that the restriction of the ritual procedure occurs through an indicative mark.
Bhāṣya.

An *arthavāda* is a statement that, by means of censuring something not enjoined by another injunction and distinct from the subject matter of the current injunction, serves to demonstrate that which is to be enjoined in the current context. For example: "When they chant with the *ṛc*, the Asuras followed after; when they chant with the *sāman*, the Asuras did not follow after. Therefore, one who knows thus should chant with the *sāman*" (Bālakrīḍā, p. 52). An *arthavāda* is also a statement that, by means of censuring something enjoined by another injunction and distinct from the subject matter of the current context, demonstrates that which is to be enjoined in the current context. For example: "Every morning they speak the truth, those who offer the *puroḍāśa* in the *agnihotra*."
"Whether it be the *divākīrtya* or the *adivākīrtya*, the sun is their light; that [fire] is not their light at that time. Therefore, one should offer the oblation when the sun has risen.
— Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 53.

A prohibition that is to be inferred from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) which is supplementary to another injunction is, for example: "Therefore, one should resort only to forest [food]. By means of this threefold specification, the prohibition "They do not take the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) for the *māsa* [sacrifices]" is inferred.

(Bāla, p. 30). An injunction that is to be inferred from an explanatory passage which is supplementary to another injunction is, for example: "For he holds it above for the gods. From this, the injunction "One should hold it above for the gods" is inferred.
And expiations are prescribed for the transgression of an injunction; they are constituent parts of the ritual action with respect to the occasion [of the transgression]. Bhāṣya 6.3.1.17.

The meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*): furthermore, the instigation (*pravartanā*) is connected with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) by way of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of its generative capacity.
[The meaning of the injunction (as found in the *Rahasya*).]

Now, one might object: since there is no word expressive of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), how can the Veda convey that sacrifice is a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhana*) in such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), and what indeed is the injunction (*vidhi*) that conveys this status as a means to the highest good? On this point, the Naiyāyikas (logicians) maintain the following: It is undisputed that after hearing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, an inclination to act arises; therefore, the cognition of the optative suffix and other such markers is useful for the initiation of action by way of producing the causal complex (*pravṛtti-sāmagrī*) for that action.
Therefore, [the object] possesses the state of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*).
*Cikīrṣā* (the desire to act) consists in the form of a wish (*icchā*).

Since this [desire] is a cause by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*), even though the cognition of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is not directly involved in it, its utility is postulated in the cognition that serves as the cause of that desire.

And that [cognition] consists of the knowledge that [the action] is not followed by an undesirable result of greater weight (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), the knowledge that it is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatvajñāna*), and the knowledge that it is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatvajñāna*).
For otherwise, even in the absence of one or another of these, we observe activity toward eating food mixed with honey and poison, touching the moon, or performing the *maṇḍalī* gesture.

Therefore, since the cognition of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth generates this triad of cognitions, the optative suffix and the like possess a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to being not followed by an undesirable result of greater weight, being achievable through effort, and being a means to a desired end.

In that case as well, since there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanā*) regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in each [word] individually.
And because the word *puṣyavat* possesses the properties of being bold (*dhṛṣṭatva*), being Caitra, and being Sugata, there is a comprehension of all three meanings.
Furthermore, because of its fitness (*yogyatā*), [the denotation of the optative suffix] occurs only in the meaning of the verbal root, such as sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like;
and in cases such as "one should not eat *kalañja*," it occurs in the meaning of the negative particle (*na*), namely non-existence (*abhāva*).
Moreover, that [non-existence] does not apply to all three [factors], because the eating of *kalañja* is a means to volitional effort (*kṛti*) and a means to what is desired (*iṣṭa*).
Rather, it is precisely the state of not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence [that is required].

For this very reason, the absence of the state of not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence in that [act] is understood through negation as "the state of not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence"; thus, due to the absence of the [necessary] cause, there is no engagement in it.
And that [act] is unrighteous (adharma), whereas sacrifice and the like are righteous (dharma).

And in the case of the Śyena sacrifice and the like, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) only with "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), but not with "not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). This is because, through another means of knowledge, one understands that its result—sorcery (*abhicāra*)—is a cause for hell; thus, since it leads to hell, it lacks the quality of not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence.
Therefore, the orthodox (*āstika*) do not engage in it.
So they say.

In this regard, [the view that the suffix conveys the property of being a means to a desired end] is superior because postulating a verbal root-meaning [for that property] involves unnecessary complexity (gaurava).

Furthermore, it is an empirical fact that even in the absence of the cognition that an action is not followed by an undesirable result of greater weight, activity occurs simply from the cognition that it is a means to a desired end, provided there is the absence of the cognition that it is followed by an undesirable result of greater weight.
Therefore, the cognition that [an action] is not connected with a powerful undesirable consequence is an obstacle to activity;
and the absence of that [cognition] is a cause by its very existence (*svarūpasat*).
Consequently, since the inquiry regarding the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth pertains only to desire (*icchā*) in that context, it is not denotable by them.

Furthermore, there are seven causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) as follows: 1. When there is a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of the property "not being connected with a powerful undesired consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) from a word co-occurring with the negative particle (*nañ*), the cause is the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the desired object (*iṣṭa*) by the negative particle. 2. When there is a verbal cognition of an object other than "not being connected with a powerful undesired consequence" from a meaning such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) co-occurring with the negative particle, the cause is the presentation generated by the verbal root (*dhātu*). 3. When there is a verbal cognition of the causality of the meaning of the optative suffix co-occurring with the negative particle, the causes are the presentation generated by the verbal root and the presentation generated by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntapada*). 4. Since the negative particle does not co-occur with the optative suffix [in prohibitions], when there is a verbal cognition of the meaning of the negative particle, the cause is the presentation generated by the verbal root. 5. When there is a verbal cognition where the activity (*kṛti*) denoted by the verb ending is the qualifier (*prakāra*) of the meaning of the verbal root co-occurring with the negative particle, the cause is the presentation generated by a word ending in the nominative case. 6. When there is a verbal cognition where the activity denoted by the verb ending is the qualifier of the meaning of the negative particle co-occurring with the verb ending, the cause is the presentation generated by the negative particle. These are the seven causal relations.

Furthermore, in this way, when there is the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the negative particle (*nañ*), the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*)—which consists in not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence—is construed with that [negative particle].

However, in its absence, the meaning of the optative suffix is construed everywhere only with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Thus, there arises the predicament of having to postulate a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) based on the cognition of multiple co-occurrences involving the cumbersome negative particle.

Thus, in cases such as "that which does not exist" (*yato nāsti*) or "Caitra does not cook" (*na pacati caitraḥ*), when there is no co-occurrence with an optative suffix (*liṅ*) or similar, the negation (*nañ*)—whose meaning is absence—is construed with the referent of the nominative-ending word; however, when there is co-occurrence with an optative suffix or similar, it is construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself. This is the established linguistic principle. Likewise, regarding the agentive function (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, which are the meanings of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*), when the negation is absent, they are related to the referent of the nominative-ending word through the relation of verbal connection; but when the negation is present, they are related to that same referent through the relation of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitāvattva*). Thus, the causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) become more complex.

The other [interpretation] is also for the sake of this meaning: "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* at the *atirātra*. However, in our own view, according to the method to be explained, there are four [relations] when the negative particle (*nañ*) is present: [the relation] of being the counter-positive of the absence caused by itself [i.e., the *nañ*] with respect to the meaning of the verb; the relation of counter-positiveness with respect to the meaning of the *nañ* [itself] with respect to the meaning of the verb; and the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatva*) with respect to the meaning of the nominative [subject] with respect to the meaning of the verb. According to the method to be explained, however, there is only one [relation], which is a matter of parsimony (*lāghava*).

Furthermore, in the case of the injunction "One should not eat *kalañja*," even though the injunction conveys that eating is not connected with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), it also conveys that it is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Since this [quality of being a means to a desired end] can be accounted for by taking the ordinary worldly means to a desired end, its [the injunction's] function would be redundant; consequently, according to your view, there would be the contingency of postulating heaven as the result by way of the *Viśvajit* principle.
However, since one must postulate a hell that is even more intense than that [heaven], there is no contradiction with the quality of not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence.

For this very reason, where there is no way at all to avoid redundancy in the cognition that [the act] is to be accomplished by effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), it is not even untenable that [the statement] is not a mere restatement of what is already established in the world.

Furthermore, if all three [properties] constitute the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), then why is there no cognition of "not being connected with a powerful undesirable result" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice? If you say it is because of "sublation" (*bādha*), what indeed is this so-called sublation? If you argue that the very fact that the *śyena*'s result—sorcery—is an object of prohibition by the rule "one should not harm" (*na hiṃsyāt*) due to its nature as violence constitutes the sublation, we reply: since that general rule finds its fulfillment by relying upon violence prompted by passion (*rāga-prāpta-hiṃsā*), it cannot exclude the "non-connection with a powerful undesirable result" from the mere violence involved in sacrificing an animal for a ritual. Consequently, because that [non-connection] is established by the injunction itself as something not to be set aside, the rule would fail to apply even to the *śyena*.

Furthermore, even if [the agent] engages in the act in some way, both [the injunction and the prohibition] are justified by postulating that the hell resulting from malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is more severe.

Moreover, "not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence" does not mean "producing pain as an inseparable accompaniment of the attainment of the desired object"; for even when the knowledge of that [consequence] exists due to the injunction, one who is lazy and averse to the expenditure of their own wealth is not observed to engage in sacrifices and the like, which shows that such knowledge is not a cause for engagement.
This is because [the cognition] of being a means to what is desired excludes the production of pain such as bitterness or bad taste;

furthermore, since one observes that a person driven by passion still engages in acts such as eating forbidden food even when they possess knowledge [of its unpleasantness], that knowledge does not function as an obstacle to engagement.
Therefore, "intensity" (balavattva) regarding the undesired consists in its being the object of intense aversion.
Intensity arises from the convergence of a specific type of birth and a singular stream of results;
such hatred, moreover, occurs in accordance with past karma.
Consequently, even when others experience pain during sacrifices and the like, if there is intense hatred due to the power of past karma, [the result follows].
At that time, because there exists the cognition that [the act] is followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānubandhitva*), there is no inclination toward it.

However, when—due to the force of auspicious karma—there is no intense aversion toward it, then, because the cognition that it is followed by a powerful undesirable consequence is absent, there is inclination toward it due to the absence of an obstructing factor.
In this way, occasional inclination or non-inclination toward such acts as eating the flesh of a dog or the *syena* sacrifice should be explained as resulting from the force of prior karma.

And for this reason, it is impossible for an injunction (*vidhi*) to convey, as a matter of necessity, that an action such as a sacrifice is invariably followed by a powerful undesirable consequence; such is the meaning of the injunction.
3576 | 3577. The meaning of the injunction. 3577. The meaning of the injunction.

For in that case, an application [of the word] is possible even by taking up the prompting of a king; and in the desire to know something else, it is possible by taking up the prompting in the form of conjunction and so forth, through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as the state of being a conjunction,
and because the inference produced by that knowledge also has the nature of an inclination toward action (*pravṛtti*).
And the cognition of the relation [between the word and its meaning] consists in the cognition of the reality of the object and the specific properties residing therein;
this is due to semantic competency (*yogyatā*). This is the sequence regarding that matter.
First, [the operation] is presented as an operation (*vyāpāra*) by means of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

Therefore, it is established that the presentation of the operation occurs in its general form through the optative suffix and so forth, and not according to the manner of the logicians (*tārkika*), such as being the "means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).
Subsequently, it is not the meaning of the verb (ākhyāta) that [motivates], but rather, according to the previously stated method, it is the desire to act itself.
When the action is established, that [desire] is produced by an inference arising from a specific cognition regarding its own object.
‘The potential suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the senses of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), entreaty (*āmantraṇa*), request (*adhīṣṭa*), and prayer (*saṃprārthana*). (Pāṇini 3.3.161).
[In this context,] there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the property of being that [action], because it is not presented as such through the relation of identity (*tattva*).
[This is] a verbal [cognition].
3|3|161) ‘And the *leṭ* [is used] in the Veda’ (Pāṇini 3.1.162). And [the meaning of] *bodha* is ‘an effort such as sacrifice that possesses activity. Nor is it the meaning of the optative (*liṅ*).
This is because of Pāṇini’s rule, “*liṅarthe leṭ*” (Pā. 3.4.7), and so forth.
It is a mistaken view to hold that verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) occurs only when there is a specific [action] as the primary element;
rather, [it is held that] "the action is the primary [element]."
This very meaning is understood:
*vidhi* (injunction) is the impelling of one who is inferior;

this is because, according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) [expresses it]," it possesses the nature of a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of the *lakāra* (verbal suffix).

An invitation (*nimantraṇa*) is the volition of the instigator (*pravartakecchā*), expressed by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), which functions as a qualifier for the efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*) directed toward an action delimited by the expectation of the removal of another counter-positive that would otherwise produce an undesirable result.

Just as the operation of the second [case-ending] and so forth depends upon the first [case-ending] and so forth, so too the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by a word is the cause; thus, by virtue of having a single effect common to time and other factors, [the relation is established].
In that regard, through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), one arrives at the understanding that there is no eating.
Therefore, in accordance with the parsimony of postulating a causal state, [the meaning] belongs precisely to the suffixes such as the verb-ending (*ākhyāta*).
Just as in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), for the sake of parsimony, [this applies] to the two subsequent [meanings] as well: namely, being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhana*)...
Because it is the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*),
it is precisely that which leads to the inference [of desirability];
however, the capacity to lead to the inference of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) exists in all cases whatsoever.
Even in the case of *saṃprārthanā* (earnest entreaty) and so forth, [the action] resides in that very [object] through the relation of being its object (*viṣayatā-sambandha*).
Or rather, let it be so for the prohibitive particle *māṅ*. *Āmantraṇa* (addressing) is permission to act according to one's own will.

In that regard: *anvaya* (positive concomitance) [is established] even though the state of being a reason (*hetutva*) and so forth is not positively concomitant with it by way of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*).
It is merely the state of insistence on the part of the prompter;
for even though there is insistence everywhere else,
it is mentioned here as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), and thus it is connected with initial thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and effort (*vyāyāma*).
Or rather, it is in the optative (*liṅ*). Something additional shines forth: that which is requested with honor toward a superior.
You are the indicator of the intentionality regarding the relation consisting in the state of possessing a cause;

therefore, it is the instigation (preraṇā) alone that is the common feature among these four, namely, the state of being an instigator (pravartanāvatva). Thus, it is the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) and so forth.
In cases such as *ātimāliṅa*, there is the exertion of deliberation (*vitarka-vyāyāma*) through the relation of possessing a cause;
therefore, by that very form, there is only a single power (*śakti*). But for others, however...
Thus, there is no distinction whatsoever;
because it is included within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not possible [to claim otherwise].
Let it be so for the act of earnest entreaty (*saṃprārthana*).

Similarly, in the case of "If one should eat curd, one ought not to mix it with honey," the *liṅ* suffix denotes a capacity (*śakti*) for excess. In examples such as "What have you studied? or "I have [studied]," where there is an inquiry regarding desire, the relation (*saṃsarga*) consists precisely in the *liṅ* suffix's being qualified by the speaker's wish.
In cases such as "prārthanā" (request) and "vedam adhīyīthāḥ" (you should study the Veda),
there is an absence of *pravartanātva* (the quality of being an instigation); therefore,
the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is *hṛ* (desire).
If it is held that the verb itself indicates the desire,
or if it is a conventional (nirūḍha) indicative sense based on grammatical instruction—
according to the rule "the optative suffix (liṅ) is used for cause and effect."
In the rule *śālīn bhoktum icchet* (Pāṇini 3.3.156), knowledge itself is the cause (*nimitta*) in the association; according to *kāmapravedane ’kathitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.29),
there is no effort toward merit (*puṇya-prayatna*) anywhere.

And therefore, by the very grammatical rule (Pāṇini 3.3.163), "‘Devadattaḥ pacet’ [‘May Devadatta cook’]” and so forth, because [the suffixes] expressing causality and the like are frequently used in common worldly usage—
in such cases, following the verbal cognition, there is indeed a relation [of cause and effect] as such.

Because the property of being an instigation (*pravartanātva*) is the delimitor of the capacity [to denote the meaning]; and this property of being an instigation is established by such linguistic usage as, "I am cooking because prompted by Caitra," in relation to the desire to know (*jijñāsā*).
It is the state of being an operation conducive to the onset [of activity].

And "conduciveness" is the state of being a generator. By virtue of this, once the operation is understood to be of the nature of desire (*icchātva*), [it is understood as] the effort directed toward the object of that desire.
And that [activity] does not reside in persons and the like in the world;
nor does it exist in the Veda because of the absence of desire.
Therefore, due to the flow [of the meaning], its designation is simply "instigation toward cooking."
It should be understood that some distinct [property] possesses the status of being the instigator (*pravartakatva*).
Here too,
once the fact that its substratum is the motivator (*prayojaka*) has been established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [its nature as] selfhood—

In the Veda, it is precisely the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) that is understood through the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as the form of instigation (*pravartanātva*). Being cognized by the same cognition [as the action], it is established as an unanalyzed property (*akhaṇḍadharma*), the very nature of which is an operation (*vyāpāra*). As the delimitor of the causal efficacy (*prayojakatāvacchedaka*) in the case of "this [action] is an instigation toward cooking," it serves as the delimitor of the denotative power (*vācakatāvacchedaka*) of the ten types of optative suffixes and the like, without over-extension.

Alternatively, since a specific type of objectivity (*viṣayitā*)—namely, the form "let this very thing be brought about"—which is common to both worldly and Vedic usage, was previously mentioned, that alone is the delimitor of the denotative function (*śakti*) of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth.

Furthermore, according to the Bhaṭṭa school, it must be accepted that in both worldly and Vedic contexts, the knowledge of speaker-intention (*tātparya-jñāna*) is the cause for [the production of] verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) delimited by the property of being produced by definition (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth, with respect to [an action] delimited by the property of being a *dvandva* (conjunction) or the like.
For an intention (*tātparya*) consisting of a desire in the form "this meaning is to be understood from this word" is not possible in the case of the Veda.
Therefore, in that context, according to the Bhaṭṭa school, intention must be stated as a specific property residing in the word itself, which is something distinct [from the speaker's intention].
Furthermore, the causality of the knowledge of such [intention] is not established in common worldly usage.
In this very context, there is a total lack of evidence for postulating an additional causal relationship.

Therefore, having accepted that a specific *viṣayitā* (objectivity) is common to both [the cause and the effect] based on uniform linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*), one must state the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the causality.

Similarly, here too, a specific *viṣayitā* serves as the delimiting factor for being the motivator of purposeful action (*pravṛtti*) and as the delimiting factor for the denotative power (*vācakatā*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.
If, however, the meaning of the injunction regarding the aforementioned object is "not at the time of destruction."

In a case where the understanding of "being a means to an undesirable result" (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth arises from the sentence "The eating of *kalañja* is a means to an undesirable result," the inference produced by that [sentence] generates a non-existence qualified by destruction.

To prevent the undesired consequence of such usage—namely, that because the state of being a means to an undesirable result is produced by other causes such as the recollection of a single rule (*ekānuvidhi*), there would be an absence of activity at the time when the cognition produced by the inference of being a means to an undesirable result is destroyed—one specifies "having itself as its object" (*svaviṣayaka*), and so forth.
Here, by means of a restrictive relation (*nirūpakasaṃkhyena*), the undesired consequence of such usage is avoided through the presence of a non-existence that is not prompted by the obstruction.

Therefore, for the sake of understanding that a cognition of its own object is produced by a cognition of itself that is simultaneous with its own destruction—wherein each specific instance enters as a particular—the term *viśeṣa* (particularity) is employed.

Here, the first occurrence of the word *sva* refers to the specific instance of the relation that serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the causal efficiency (*pravṛttikāraṇatā*), while the second *sva* refers, as before, to the specific instance of the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth.

Consequently, the resulting meaning is: "that which is produced by a cognition of a cause which is not produced by a cognition of a mark and so forth that is simultaneous with a relation that has ceased."
And thus, there is no harm even to the specific consequence (*viśiṣṭāpatti*) regarding the nature of inferential cognition (*anumititva*).
Therefore, it is established that by means of this relationship, the nature of the indicative mark (*liṅgatva*)—which consists in the act of warding off—is [demonstrated].
This concludes the investigation into the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), up to [verse] 3582, the section on the enunciation of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*).

The power of agency (*kartṛśakti*), which is common to both conscious and unconscious agents, is designated as having a divine, non-manifest form and as possessing a severed [empirical] capacity. Both types of *bhāvanā* necessarily require the three constituent parts (*aṅga*) consisting of the object (*karman*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). This very requirement for these three is the common ground for the application of the term *bhāvanā*.

If it is objected: "Knowledge that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) is the cause of all activity; therefore, how can there be activity in the absence of such knowledge, even if there is knowledge of the mere instigation (*pravartanā*)?"
True.

In such injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," there first arises a cognition of the syntactic connection between the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the meaning of the verbal root, namely, that the *arthabhāvanā* has for its object an activity (*kṛti*) directed toward instigation (*pravartanā*). This is because the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of the two is greater in relation to the meaning of the verbal root, since they are conveyed by a single word.
As it has been said: "The connection between the injunction (*vidhi*) and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is first considered through direct audition (*śruti*).

Furthermore, when the objective productive urge (*arthabhāvanā*) is connected [to the injunction] as its object—being qualified by the nature of being an instigation (*pravartanātva*)—it possesses the nature of the productive urge toward the desired (*iṣṭabhāvanātva*). According to the etymological derivation "producing" or "bringing about what is desired," this consists in the state of being a means to the desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).
This [fitness] is also present in the meaning of the injunction itself.
The distinction in this view is that the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) residing in the action (*kriyā*) is not the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*).

Since the productive urge toward an object (*arthabhāvanā*) cannot exist without the state of being a means to a desired end residing in the action, there would be no cognition of the action as a means to a desired end; consequently, the engagement in activities would be untenable.
The definition of the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) as the meaning of an injunction is to be found in the work *Śabdabhāvanā*, which is contained within the *Bālamanoramā*.
The Veda consists of injunctions (*vidhi*). [Question: What is the beginning of an injunction?
That statement, upon perceiving which a person engages in a certain dharma or from which faith in something else turns away, is an injunction (*vidhi*).

Its beginning is the injunction, such as "repetition" (*abhyāsa*).
In the Veda as well, there is the beginning of an injunction: "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]. (Bhāṣya 7.2.12).
"Beginning of an injunction" means that which depends upon an injunction.
