The determination of the fourfold nature of ritual injunctions.

"But how can there be a fourfold division of injunction (*vidhi*) based on distinctions such as origination (*utpatti*) and so forth? For it has been proclaimed that there is only one injunction, namely the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*).

By stating that 'injunction follows later when its substratum has been established by [the other injunctions] such as *asya* (origination),' it is effectively said that the injunction of performance is the sole injunction."
And they describe that [injunction] as being of four kinds:
one is the injunction of origin (*utpattividhi*), which is investigated in the second [chapter];
another is the injunction of application (*viniyogavidhi*), which is investigated in the third.
In the fourth and fifth [chapters], there is the consideration of the rules for application (*prayoga-vidhi*);
while that which falls within the scope of the sixth chapter concerns the rules of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*).
Therefore, the conceit of oneness is untenable.
It is said in reply:
"Because the three—origination and so forth—are established by the force of their connection with the injunctions."
The fourfold nature of the injunction is considered to consist of its essential form, its application, and its function.

When an injunction (*vidhi*), whose essential nature is to impel toward acceptance, has for its primary object the nature of the action (*karman*) intended to be accomplished by it, then—precisely because of the understanding of its connection with the injunction—the action that is its object is established as being productive (*utpādaka*), since it is conceived as not being attainable through any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And by that [productivity], the status of that action as a means to a fruit (*phala-sādhanatva*) or as something that assists what possesses a fruit (*phalavad-upakārakatva*) is postulated; this is the determination of application (*viniyoga-kalpana*). Furthermore, when the action is a means to a fruit, the person’s entitlement (*adhikāra*)—that is, their ownership—is established; thus, even the entitlement to abide [in the performance] is indeed something to be enjoined by the injunction.

And it is logical that [the injunction] is an application by its very nature (*svarūpeṇa*), because there is a fourfold division of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*); thus, there is a fourfold division of the injunctions (*vidhi*). For the word "injunction" (*vidhi*) intends the very essence of knowledge (*vidyā*) as that which impels one to action; since that [impulsion] is not possible otherwise, it implies [the application] in other cases as well. Thus, it is also called "the object of knowledge. But there is no fourfold division by its own essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*). And it has been said: "The third [type of injunction] is called the prescriptive (*vidhāyinī*), which is the basis for the application (*prayoga*)."
Thus [it is said]:
"In each of the four [categories], there is in some cases a certain degree of prescriptive force (*vidhitva*).
In some instances it is one substance, in others three, and in yet others all four."

The injunction "He performs the *agnihotra*" has a single form in terms of its origin (*utpatti*). The statement "He sacrifices with the *samidh* [fuel-sticks]" is directed toward both origin and application (*viniyoga*), because, in the absence of a specific injunction, application through the context (*prakaraṇa*) would not be established; this has already been explained previously. The sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*" is directed toward application, qualification (*adhikāra*), and performance (*prayoga*), since its origin is already established by the injunction "One should sacrifice with *Soma*."

In the injunction "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," there is a fourfold purpose. It has already been explained how, even when one [of these] is extended by analogy (*atideśa*), the authority of the direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof is established as the factor that determines application (*viniyojaka*), even in the form of application itself (Ratnamālā, pp. 159–160).
From the injunction (vidhi): 3584. The determination of the injunction is established from the injunction itself, because everywhere the fruit goes to the agent.

*Soma* 6.2.2: Where there is no accusative or other case-ending expressing the state of being an object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), there the state of being an object to be accomplished and the state of being the objective (*uddeśyatva*)—even in the case of a substance—are understood from the injunction alone, as in the case of going to the region of heaven.

2|1|4. The nature of injunction (*vidhitva*)—the definition of injunction—has been [explained] through the distinctions of exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), restrictive rule (*niyama*), and original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

Bhāṭṭa 1|1|6. The nature of injunction is a specific operation called "impulsion" (*preraṇā*), characterized by the form: "Let this person proceed here. Mīmāṃsā: The nature of injunction is sublated by the status of being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
Bāla, p. 144: The status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) and the form of the productive urge (*bhāvanākāra*) are merely heard.
Having first heard [the word], the productive urge toward a purpose is enjoined;
this occurs either because other [meanings] are untenable or because of the sense of being a causal factor (*kārakatva*).
Vārttika 8.7.13, p. 707. Here, the injunctionality (*vidhitva*) belongs to that which prompts what has not [otherwise] been obtained. Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 573:

For when the injunctionality residing in the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is grasped precisely as being subordinate to the efficient force, then, since there is an injunction of a specific [element], how could there not be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*)?
When...
It is not tenable to claim that "being an effect" (kāryatā) is not an authoritative [criterion] because it is understood through negative concomitance (vyatireka).
However, this being the case, one would have to admit that the cause of activity toward things aimed at the avoidance of great suffering is their being a means to that [avoidance].

Consequently, in the case of the command "Bring the cow," since bringing the cow does not consist in the avoidance of the attainment of great suffering, the injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*), by denoting "being an effect"—which is the cause of activity—would necessarily denote "being a means to what is desired" (*samīhitasādhanatā*).
Therefore, the task is the bringing of the cow; the meaning is that it is of such a nature that human activity proceeds toward it, just as it does toward other things.

Furthermore, since being of such a nature is possible simply by virtue of its being desired, it is by process of elimination the very fact of being a means to that [desired end] which is expressed by the word denoting the "task" (*kārya*).

And likewise, even in the Veda, since the *apūrva* itself does not consist of the avoidance of suffering, it must be postulated as merely the means to that [avoidance]. Thus, the optative suffix (*liṅ*), while denoting the form of the "task" (*kārya*), would actually denote only the state of being a means to what is desired. Consequently, because the *apūrva*—as a means—is denoted even in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*) and prohibitions (*niṣedha*), one would have to postulate a result for them as well, even though no such result has been mentioned.
Now, [it may be argued: "It is not 'task-ness' (*kāryatva*) [that is denoted], because that exists even in the means to that task;
nor is it 'means-ness' (*sādhanatva*), because that exists even in pleasure (*sukha*)."
"The object of cognition as an effect, which follows from both [the means and the end], is called 'effectness' (kāryatva), and this is the cause of activity.
This is not so;
for it has already been stated that "effectness" is not perceived by direct perception either at the time of activity or at any subsequent time with respect to the means.
Therefore, there is no such specific property called "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) that is common to both [action and substance].

However, the word *kārya* (to be done) applies to both cases by virtue of a single limiting condition (*upādhi*). Since even a substance, when it is being brought about, prompts a person to act toward it, the application of the word *kārya* occurs precisely through this limiting condition.

Consequently, the understanding of "being an effect" is not the cause for engaging in action; rather, it is the cognition that something is a means to achieve what is desired (*samīhitasādhanatvajñāna*).
Or, let it be that "task-ness" (kāryatva) is indeed established as being the means for accomplishing what is desired;
nevertheless, that must be predicated of action alone,
because it is precisely therein that the impulse to activity resides.

If it is argued that in the world, only action (*kriyā*) is conveyed by words as the object to be accomplished (*kārya*), whereas in the Veda, because of its conformity with the person enjoined who desires a fruit, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is specifically denoted as the object to be accomplished by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth—this is not so; for even regarding an action, there is no contradiction in the desiring person’s comprehension of it as the object to be accomplished. If it is objected that [action] is incapable of becoming a means to the fruit because it is transitory (*bhaṅguratva*), we say no, because this is possible through the mediation of the *apūrva*.
Nor can its status as a means be established through any other mediator, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that either the intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*) or the capacity (*śakti*) is established as the means (*sādhanatva*), but not the *apūrva*—because when that which possesses the capacity or the operation has passed away, the persistence of the capacity or the operation is untenable—then is it not the case that wood also lacks the status of being a means for cooking? For even there, atoms of fire produced from the wood enter the interior of the pot and soften the rice grains.

Furthermore, those substances (the fuel-sticks) do not possess the nature of being intermediate operations (*avāntara-vyāpāra*) or the nature of being powers (*śakti*); therefore, the status of fuel-sticks and the like as instruments (*sādhana*) could not be established by way of them.
If it is argued that this should not be so, we say no, because it contradicts what is well-known to the whole world, since the usage "he cooks with fuel-sticks" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*) is beyond dispute.

Therefore, whatever has become the cause for a desired result and constitutes a means, that very thing which is accomplished immediately is designated as the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of that [action].
Consequently, it is entirely possible for the *apūrva* to be the intermediate operation of the ritual act.
If this were not accepted, then even after reaching the *apūrva*, the ritual act would lack the status of being a means to the result.
Even that does not constitute a separate action, because it awaits the subsequent performance of the [main] rite by its own desire.
In that case, the originative apūrvas (utpattyapūrva) must be accepted as intermediate operations (avāntaravyāpāra).

If it is argued that the originative apūrvas alone are the causes and not the sacrifices and so forth, we say no; for that is unestablished, since the meaning [of the word] is derived from the verbal testimony (śabda).

Since it has been established that the injunctive statement (*adhikāravākya*) denotes an *apūrva* (unseen potency) consistent with the enjoined agent who desires the fruit, it follows subsequently that the statements concerning the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices also denote an *apūrva*.

Prior to this, however, it is possible for those [statements] to denote only an action as understood from common worldly usage; therefore, because the *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-potencies) are not yet established, their connection as means to the *paramāpūrva* (final potency) is not possible.
Nor does the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) itself denote [the potency], such that the intermediate *apūrvas* could serve as causes toward the *paramāpūrva*, which is the meaning of the suffix.
Therefore, the *yajati* (the sacrifice) is the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Furthermore, it is only as an effect (*kārya*) that the *apūrva* is logically established; for an effect is defined as that which is to be accomplished by volitional effort (*kṛti*).
And volitional effort is human exertion (*puruṣaprayatna*).

Furthermore, it is not possible for the *apūrva* to be accomplished through effort (*prayatna*), because that [effort] perishes long before the *apūrva* arises. For by means of effort, the sacrifice (*yāga*) is produced; from that, there is an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*); and subsequently, the *adhikārāpūrva* [arises]. Therefore, since its status as an effect (*kāryatva*) is untenable, it is impossible for the *apūrva* to be denoted as something to be accomplished.
In this regard, the fact that the *apūrva* is to be accomplished through effort must be understood as being mediated by the *apūrva* of another sacrifice.

In that case, why is it not accepted that the sacrifice itself is the means of accomplishing the result by way of the *apūrva*? Or, let it be that the action is not the means of the result; nevertheless, the action is indeed the means of the *apūrva*. Even so, a person is certainly capable of understanding it as something to be performed (*kārya*), for that which is not performed when desired is not attained, whereas when it is performed—whether directly or through an intermediary—it is attained; it is precisely that which is understood as something to be performed, and not the specific state of being (*bhāva*) per se that is useful there. Furthermore, the understanding of the action as something to be performed must necessarily be admitted for one who desires [a result]; otherwise, how could he proceed independently?

True, there is indeed an understanding of the task (*kārya*) even in that case; however, it is not verbal (*śābdī*), but rather situational (*ārthī*), because [the act] is a means to the *apūrva* (unseen potency) in accordance with the desire.
If it is argued that the desirer nevertheless apprehends even that [act] as a task, we say no, because this cannot withstand critical analysis.

Does the cognition of the task (kārya) regarding an action arise from the production of a fruit, or from the production of the *apūrva*? It cannot be produced by the *apūrva*, because it is not admitted that the injunction (*vidhi*) is the motivator for the performance of optional rites (*kāmya*).

For if the cognition of the task regarding an action were dependent solely upon the injunction, then, since the performance would be prompted by the injunction, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that even the object of the instrument (*karaṇa*), being something to be enjoined, would itself become an object of the injunction.

Even the fact that [the action] produces a fruit is not established by your stated principle; for a person desiring a fruit is not capable of understanding a momentary action as something to be performed (*kārya*), because it is unfit to be a direct means (*sādhana*) [of the fruit], and because the *apūrva* cannot serve as an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), since it cannot be a means through that [operation] either. Furthermore, if [the action] were a means to a means, it would be impossible for one who desires the goal to understand it as something to be performed.

Therefore, the understanding of an action as something to be performed (kāryatā) depends neither on the result nor is it possible for it to depend on the injunction; consequently, its non-performance would necessarily follow. Thus, for one who desires that the performance of a desired act (kāmyānuṣṭhāna) prompted by an injunction be dependent upon the result, one must necessarily accept either that the action is a means to the result, or—just as there is an understanding of what is to be done (kāryatā) for one seeking the goal even when the means itself is a means—that such an understanding is intended. And so, even by means of the word [of the Veda], it is indeed possible to communicate the action as something to be done to one who desires the result; therefore, the establishment of the denotation of the "unseen potency" (apūrva) is not achieved.
Whatever else has been stated regarding reality, we shall explain that very point in the *Aṅganirṇaya*.
As for the view of others: it is the state of being a means to achieve a desired end (*samīhitasādhanatvam*) alone that is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).
This is because it is observed within oneself that this very state serves as the cause for initiating action.
Is it not the case that [knowledge of] "it is thus" alone is the cause of activity?
True; however, that [knowledge], once arisen, is not itself understood as the cause of activity.
Furthermore, since a word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it functions as the cause of activity by generating comprehension; therefore, it is impossible for it to denote a desire.

For desire arises with reference to either the attainment of what is desired or the avoidance of what is extremely painful, and it takes as its object the means and so forth. Therefore, just like the optative suffix (*liṅ*), the very fact that an action is a means to a desired end (*samīhitasādhanatva*)—which brings about the desire that serves as the cause for the activity of the "elder" (the person to be prompted) who is internally impelled—is postulated by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) regarding the action.
And because that [desire] is internal to the word, it is determined that the word denotes it.
[Objection: But then, one would engage in the consumption of wine simply because it is a means to a desired end! [Reply: No, because its defects are blocked by the effort [of the agent].
For just as desire is the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti*), so too is aversion (*dveṣa*) the cause of desisting (*nivṛtti*).
And aversion proceeds with reference to suffering, the avoidance of pleasure, and the means for those [ends].

Since the drinking of liquor is established by prohibition as a means of achieving great harm, it falls within the scope of aversion and thus cannot be undertaken. However, one whose mind is seized by even a slight, immediate pleasure, who does not reflect upon or take into account the great [evil], and whose mind is being repelled by an effortful passion, will indeed proceed to the drinking of liquor.

Therefore, it is established in the *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa* (6.1.8) that the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), having been generally indicated by the injunction as the means for accomplishing what is desired, becomes free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣībhavati*) through [the attainment of] heaven and so forth provided by another word. Where there is no other word within the same sentence connected with a specific fruit, it is established in the *Prakaraṇādhikaraṇa* (3.1.4) that the fruit arises from the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth. And where even the context and such are absent, it is settled in the *Rātrisatrādhikaraṇa* (8.1.8) that [the action] must be connected with a fruit implied by the sense (*arthāt*).

In the absence of even that [result], its connection with an implied result is established in the *Viśvajit* section (*Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra* 4.1.7). However, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because it is expressed within the same word, is more powerful; thus, being conveyed as the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is introduced as the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of proximity—this is the purport of the *Bhāvārtha* section (2.1.1).
And so it has been said: "Thus, when the status of the verbal root's meaning as the effect is indicated by the direct hearing of the word (*padaśruti*)."
"By the power of the injunction regarding meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), [it is established that] objects such as the self (*puruṣa*) cannot be accomplished [by other means].
And:
"For the fact that these [Vedic words] are the means to the highest good (*śreyas*) is eternally known from the Veda."
And thus it is said.

Therefore, the injunctive *liṅ* suffix is understood to denote the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Since that [suffix] is connected with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), the result itself is the instrument (*karaṇa*) when the verbal root signifies the object to be brought about.
However, according to the Teacher [Maṇḍana Miśra], "The *liṅ* and other suffixes express a distinct efficient force, namely, the denotative efficient force (*abhidhābhāvanā*)."
From this statement, a different conception of the nature of injunction (*vidhi*) is obtained as intended.

What, then, is that? First, it is established that the independent activity of a conscious being is possible only after the understanding that [the act] is a means to a desired end; therefore, one must conclude that for a person who proceeds to act immediately after hearing the optative suffix (*liṅ*), the understanding that it is a means to a desired end has arisen from the word itself.

It must be considered whether that state of being a means to the desired end (*samīhita-sādhanatva*) is apprehended solely from the denotation [of the word], or whether it is to be understood through the force of the injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*), which denotes a different meaning, because such [a means-end relation] would otherwise be untenable. In this regard, it is not logical that it is apprehended [directly] from the denotation, because that would contradict common experience; for it is not the case that a person intends "the activity conjoined with the sacrifice" as the object of desire, since the understanding [of the sacrifice as the object] is identical to that derived from the verbal root itself, and because they are used together.
For in common worldly usage, the word "injunction" (*vidhi*) and the word expressing "the means for accomplishing a desired end" are seen to be employed simultaneously;
and among those who approach a number [of things], there arises the thought, "Therefore, one should worship the twilight (*saṃdhyā*).
Furthermore, the simultaneous employment of two synonymous terms does not occur.

Furthermore, since the comprehension of the meaning of words in the world is based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is not accepted that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote "being a means to what is desired" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).
Therefore, it is better to rely on their denoting "what is to be done" (*kārya*).

Is it not improper to say that this is an effect, if [it is argued] because an operation is observed in relation to an effort? For pervasive entities such as the self and so forth, there is the operation of cognition and so forth.
The intended object is being stated; therefore, its status as an effect arises from the possibility of [the action] belonging to all sentient beings.
However, an inherence in vibration is not possible, nor is that [inherence].
The cognition of that [excellence] as "distinguished" is not the cause of activity; rather,
by the method of elimination, it is the cognition of the *kṛtya* (the thing to be accomplished) that we maintain is the cause of activity.
What is its function? It is simply the cognition of itself.
Causality must be stated in relation to the effect;
for the comprehension of that [cause] is the motive for activity, as is the case with what is to be done (*kṛtya*).
For a word is either produced by that [cognition] or possesses that [cognition]; it is the cause for the production of the understanding of the object.
And what difficulty is there in avoiding [the objection], since its status as a means is well-established? It brings about [the result].
And so it has been said: "Verbal [cognition] occurs with respect to an object proximate [to the senses], such as the cognition of a word;
through that, the nature of the action, such as bringing [an object], is well-established."
Regarding the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): it is another phoneme accompanied by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding phonemes.
Since there is no absence of the form of the [preceding] exclusion (*parihāra*), its very status as a means (*upāyatva*) is the cause for the accomplishment of the task; thus it is an action.
And as for the statement "it is the designator," it should be understood that this is said when it has acquired an adventitious property.

Likewise, in this view, [the word] proceeds from the sign (liṅga), the word (śabda), and so forth, as apprehended through perception; it does not consist in the denotative operation (abhidhā-vyāpāra) characterized by the specific form of the word, nor in its mere denotation (abhidhāna), and so on.
However, this very [denotative operation] is what is intended as the means of proof by those who know the Nyāya, and there is no contradiction with experience, because it is denoted in that form.
But the word denotes [it] in the form of an instigation (pravartanā), and the instigation is the property (dharma) that is the cause of activity.

And since injunctions (*praiṣa*) and the like are impossible in the impersonal Veda, it is determined by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that [the word] consists in being the means to the desired end. Therefore, just as it expresses the operation of denotation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*) and instigation (*pravartanā*), the word denotes its status as a means (*sādhanatā*) in the form of instigation, not in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); thus there is no contradiction in the understanding. This very point is what the venerable Maṇḍana Miśra also stated: "An action does not instigate men because it is not a means to their desired end;
rather, they declare that the property which is the cause of activity resides in the cognition."
"Acting in this way, it is the causal condition for instigation (*pravartanā-pratyaya*)," and so forth; this is what is intended [by the author].
In this manner, the assumption of multiple meanings does not occur; otherwise, there would be [the fault of] commanding (*preṣaṇa*).
Regarding the types of injunctions (vidhiprakāra), [it is said]: "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer the *nirvāpa* with the mantra.
However, this [type of injunction] is the weakest of all.
Bhaṭṭa, 2182: Although in all cases there is an injunction of a qualified efficient-force (*viśiṣṭabhāvanā*) based on what is perceived, there are six modes of injunction regarding the result alone;
and it has been stated previously (p. 110) that among these, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding.

Injunctions and prohibitions directly take the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) as their object; through that medium, however, they [take] the factors of action (*kāraka*) which are the means (*upāya*) for that [objective].

Vākyapadīya, p. 74. It has been established that injunctions and prohibitions alone possess authority (*prāmāṇya*) regarding *dharma*; and there is no verbal expression distinct from those [injunctions and prohibitions] regarding *dharma* and *adharma*.
Vārttika 2.1.2. Prohibition is stronger than both injunction and prohibition.
For a prohibition occurs only when there is a possibility of application;
indeed, that which is stated regarding what has already been established serves as a sublation of that [established rule].
(Bhāṣya 10.1.8–12) Of the two—a positive injunction and a prohibition—whichever possesses the greater merit is performed.
The injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) would not extend as far as the specific substance.

(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 1012). On the other hand, where an action qualified by its own own qualifier is enjoined, it serves as a qualifier for another action obtained from a different sentence; this is the section concerning the *vibhimantra* (the mantra of division), [Vibhimantrādhikaraṇa 3594].
Because of the word—due to its being of one and the same nature as a word.
If it is injunctive in the Brāhmaṇa, then it must also be injunctive in the mantra;
or else, by virtue of its functional capacity in performance, the mantra would have to be expressive of the denotation [of the rite].
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the word *bhāva* [denoting] the mantra is injunctive (*vidhāyaka*) for the Brāhmaṇa, the word *abhidhāna* is excluded.
Even though the mantra is qualified by a verbal form (*ākhyātapada*), it would still be expressive of denotation (*abhidhānavācī*).
It is called *abhidhāna* because it is "denoted" (*abhidhīyate*); the suffix *ṇyul* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Alternatively, by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word "designation" (*abhidhāna*) denotes that which is designated.
And thus, the mantras are also designators.
By virtue of their functional capacity (*prayogasāmarthya*), mantras possess the capacity for application—that is, for maintaining the purpose during the performance.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because of its capacity for application (*prayoga-sāmarthya*) and its lack of capacity for injunction (*vidhāna-sāmarthya*), a mantra is not injunctive.
Some verbal forms (*ākhyāta*) are injunctive of subordinate acts (*guṇakarman*), while others are injunctive of principal acts (*pradhānakarman*);
however, those found in mantras are merely expressive (*abhidhāyaka*).
The intended meaning is that "thus has wisdom been declared.

Furthermore, there is no requirement for a sequence of priority between an injunction (*vidhi*) and a mantra; therefore, a mantra lacks the status of being a supplement to an injunction. [End of] Section 4312: The Section on Mantras with Distinct Parts (*vibhinna-mantra-adhikaraṇa*).
It has been stated that [the mantra] contained within the mantra-text is not injunctive, because the two mantras have a single purpose.
The Commentary says: This is recited: "They do not perish; no thief can harm them; no enemy or disease shall overcome them."
"And with those [cows] through which the sacrificer sacrifices and gives, he, the lord of cattle, is long accompanied by them.
Thus it is said:
"he sacrifices," "he gives," and so forth.

Is it that the word expressing the state (*bhāvaśabda*) is injunctive in the mantra just as it is in the *brāhmaṇa*, or is it non-injunctive in the mantra? What is the prima facie view? Since this word expressing the state occurs in both the injunction and the mantra, its meaning must be the same in both, because it is a single word.
It is untenable to claim that this very same single word, while enjoining when occurring in a Brāhmaṇa, cannot enjoin when occurring in a mantra;
therefore, it is injunctive.
Or rather—here, the mantras are the examples.

Is it that, because they possess [the characteristics of] those [Brāhmaṇas], the words expressing meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) enjoin [the action] like a Brāhmaṇa passage? There is no doubt regarding this, as it is established by the word itself. Thus, since it possesses the nature of a mantra, its status as an injunction is possible even when it has the character of a recitation; therefore, the final position (*uttara-pakṣa*) stated is that they serve as reminders (*smāraka*) for those things enjoined in the Brāhmaṇa.
For instance, there is a powerful recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is not a separate ritual act."
Neither is any quality (guṇa) mentioned here, nor is there praise in another sentence.

For an injunction (vidhi) and an explanatory passage (arthavāda) would serve as opposites to the status of a mere reminder (smāraka). Thus, in this case, while the essential form of the action is indeed obtained from elsewhere, the qualities, results, and conditions that would be enjoined are not mentioned here.
Furthermore, praise is not appropriate for an injunction whose purpose has already been fulfilled by another sentence.
As it has been stated by others: "Therefore, the mantras are illuminators. Regarding that which is explained there, we say this:
What, then, is the reason that the injunctive power (*vidhi-śakti*) is obscured in those specific portions designated as *mantra*, and why is it not manifested there as being part of the *brāhmaṇa*?
Indeed, injunctive passages are observed even within the *mantras*, such as "He offers the *kapiñjala* birds to Spring" (*vasantāya kapiñjalān ālabhate*), and so forth.
Likewise, non-injunctive passages are also found within the *brāhmaṇas*, such as "For whom both sacrificial offerings (*havir*) have been spoiled," and so forth.

This is its conclusion. Furthermore: "If it were admitted that the mantras are merely restatements because they refer to what has already been obtained, then the injunction would not cause one to remember the very action that was enjoined."

For in this specific case, there is no certainty as to whether the mantra—having its injunctive power obstructed upon encountering that which is already prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa—serves as a mere reminder (*smāraka*), or whether the opposite is true.
Since it is impossible for both to be restatements (*anuvāda*), and since neither possesses the character of a restatement, both must be injunctive.
Furthermore, due to repetition (*abhyāsa*), there must be a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
Furthermore, the matter of strong recognition will be addressed later in the section on repetition (*abhyāsa*).
Therefore, the status of the mantra as a denotative expression is not established.
As for those who say: "Because mantras are prescribed by injunctions as instruments (*karaṇa*) for ritual actions..."
Just as they are employed by the Brāhmaṇa, so too those [Mantras] are not injunctive.
By them also, only what is observed in general has been indicated.
It is established that the power of injunction is not removed from the Mantra by the act of employment (niyoga).

Therefore, he will indeed carry it out and will cause [the person] to be killed. For there is no authority whatsoever for one who has been commissioned to think, "I must not kill," if you maintain that [the Veda] possesses an inherent injunctive power.
On the other hand, if that power does not exist from the very beginning, then the introduction of the commission is useless.

Nor is there any contradiction in both [the mantra and the brāhmaṇa] performing the same function; for it is stated: "Even though it is injunctive, the brāhmaṇa will serve to remind one of the matter;
however, in case of a conflict, it shall be by means of the mantra"—this very point is being established.

Furthermore, the claim that those words which are not specifically enjoined by verbal expression cannot serve as reasons for exclusion because they do not convey the existence [of the object] and so forth, is also groundless.
Nor is there any citation of a mantra here;
rather, the connection with the word *śrī* is explained otherwise.

It has already been explained that the *vidhi* (injunction) expresses both the subordinate (*guṇa*) and the principal (*pradhāna*), while the *mantra* states them. Now, it is introduced: are there only those two types, or is there another?
Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), considering that there is no third type, will state "the meaning" (*artha*).
Therefore, the first [position] is stated:
"Alternatively, the mantra, by virtue of its functional capacity in performance, should be expressive of the name.
Commentary: The word "api vā" (or rather) serves to set aside the previous position.
A mantra of this kind would be expressive by way of denotation,
because of its functional capacity.
When it is employed, its capacity is established for the purpose of conveying the "hair-cutting" (godāna) and the "cow-sacrifice" (goyāga), not for the purpose of enjoining them.
Why? Because it is prescribed:
the gift of a cow is prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), whereas the cow-sacrifice is prescribed as the ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).
If it is argued that this must be a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*), [we reply: no.
Even when it is studied repeatedly, it serves only as a reminder of that [already known] cognition.

Even if one were to assume a scriptural meaning for it, it would be purposeless, because the sacrifice has already been enjoined by a complete sentence accompanied by an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
Therefore, a verb of this kind occurring within a mantra is not injunctive.

Or rather— there is a third category, namely that which is called "denotative" (abhidhāyaka). For those verbal forms (*ākhyāta-śabda*) which are connected with words such as *yat* and so forth, if their injunctive power (*vidhi-śakti*) is set aside, they are denotative in all instances.
Regarding those words occurring in mantras and Brāhmaṇas that do not possess injunctive power (*vidhiśakti*) through another word, they function as denotative expressions (*abhidhāyaka*).

In this regard, in the phrase "they do not perish" (*na naśanti*), the sense of an injunction is sought through the particle *yat* which introduces an elliptical statement (*anuvāda*). Similarly, in the case of the first person singular ending in "I take hold of thee, O serpent" (*ahe gṛhṇāmi*), [the injunctive force is understood].
By the word "if" in the phrase "yadi somam apahareyuḥ," such [words] as these generally occur in mantras; thus, mantras are the examples.
It is well known that mantras are non-injunctive (*avidhāyaka*).

In the case of a Brāhmaṇa passage, however, there are many more indicative marks (pratyaya) that constitute an injunction; therefore, it is well known as "injunctive" (vidhāyaka). Since those [passages] with few such marks are non-injunctive, they are not cited here as examples. Furthermore, whether something is injunctive or non-injunctive depends solely on the fact of its being intended to be enjoined (uddeyatva); thus, the function of a mantra—such as "the mantra is for recitation" or "it is not"—is not relevant here.
In this regard, however, the following function is observed:
since the injunction regarding the Brāhmaṇas is already excluded by the very nature of the text itself, the purpose [of the subsequent statements] is to introduce the causes (nimitta) and so forth.
For their own form is not fit for application in the ritual act.

However, regarding those [mantras] contained within the ritual formulas (*mantra*), one perceives their very form and thinks, "I cut, I take, I offer, and I do this and that," as well as "Spread the grass outside" and "Do this and that. Through such [expressions], the cognition of application (*viniyoga-buddhi*) arises, whereby the ritual action can be accomplished.
Why? Because during performance, there is a memory that brings the meaning to mind, just like the words of the ritual items themselves.
The task of sitting, which has no other means of accomplishment, is achieved by means of the mantras.

At the time of performance, it is determined that no one—such as yourself or others—is capable of being made [the agent] if they are not remembered; rather, because memory requires a suitable means, one begins to employ a means such as the recollection of some portion of the meaning of the *brāhmaṇa* texts, or the review of a preceding action, or the text of the *sūtras*, or the statements regarding one's own undertaking, or the presence of an observer and so forth.

In that context, when mantras that have no other purpose are recited within a specific section (*prakaraṇa*), they are perceived by the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) as being enjoined in a general sense, namely: "something must be done with these. When it is required to know by what kind of sentence [the action] is to be remembered, these mantras—being understood here through an indicative mark (*liṅga*) and inferred from the context (*prakaraṇa*)—are applied by means of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Once their application is established, it is recognized that their purpose is to provide the verbal expression [of the ritual act]. Consequently, other alternative means [for remembering the act] are set aside, because they lack a basis in such authoritative evidence. Furthermore, the attainment of the unseen merit (*dṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction is determined by the principle that an action performed by means of mantras alone, as remembered, becomes conducive to spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
The commentary (*bhāṣya*) should also be applied in this very way.
It is not stated with the intention that [the mantra] is already established because it is understood from repeated study;
rather, precisely because of its connection with the word "yat" (that), the verbal form of the mantra would generally take the form "I declare what has been obtained from elsewhere."

Even for one who has given [the gift], regarding the field in the initial practice, he does not exert a new effort through the mantras alone, because of the understanding that it has already been previously attained.
Śā—It has been stated that there are two kinds [of action]: that which prescribes primary actions (*pradhānakarma*) and that which prescribes secondary actions (*guṇakarma*).
Is this the only twofold classification? No, it is said.

However, there is also a third alternative, namely *abhidhāyakatva* (denotative character)—that is, *anuvādakatva* (reiterative character). Somaśambhu states: "The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: mantras occurring within an injunction and finite verbs possess a single purpose (*aikārthya*) by virtue of being injunctive, because they consist of words of the same class."
Vi— "And [the verse] beginning with *devāśca yābhiryajate* is indeed a mantra;
but is it injunctive? No, because it is equal to other [mantras], it is not injunctive.
Since the force of the injunctive suffix is exhausted by words such as *yat*, how can there be an injunction from that?"
The verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is an enjoining expression (*abhidhāna*), not [merely expressive of] the primary or subsidiary action.

[Bhaṭṭa: Having established the two-fold nature of the verbal suffix as being an injunction for either subsidiary or primary actions, a third distinct category—the enjoining power residing in mantras—is now described.
Even those mantras, whether found in the Brāhmaṇas or elsewhere, that possess the character of being expressive through the use of words such as *yat* and so forth, also possess injunctive power.
Even when there is attainment through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*) arises from repetition (*abhyāsa*).

This being the position reached, in such cases as "with which [verses] he sacrifices to the gods" (*devāśca yābhiryajate*) and "he whose both oblations (*havir*) have been spoiled," the word *yat* clearly possesses the character of an injunction (*vidhi*)—specifically an injunction of ignorance (*ajñānarūpa*)—within its own domain, by virtue of being the source of attainment (*prāptiyonikatvena*).
Likewise, in "He says, 'Recite this! (*adhīdamīti brūhi*), the vocative case ending (*saṃbodhanavibhakti*) has as its object merely that which is addressed.
Having consecrated the title—*Vidhivinnādhikaraṇa* (The Chapter on the Knowledge of Prescriptive Injunctions) 3596; *Vidhiviparivṛttiḥ* (The Turning Back of Prescriptive Injunctions);
*Vidhivivekaḥ* (The Discrimination of Prescriptive Injunctions) 3597; *Vidhivivekaḥ*.

The word *sādhāra* (common) signifies opposition to injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, the imperative mood (*uttama-puruṣa*) in words such as *dāmī* is opposed to an injunction in the form of instigating another to act.
Therefore, because it is impossible for them to be injunctive, those [words] occurring in mantras function as reminders (*smāraka*).

In the *Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya*, it should be understood that the status of being a cause (*nimitta*) with respect to those things pertaining to Brahmins is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). From the *Vidhiviveka*: "Those who know the three Vedas agree that [the Veda] is the means for achieving the goals of human life."
Therefore, that equality in the process of awakening is thoroughly investigated.

Bhāṣya 1.1.2.16.46: An injunctive statement (vidhi-vākya) is more powerful than an explanatory passage (arthavāda).

The superiority of the injunction consists in its primacy with respect to its own meaning, its lack of contradiction because it is heard first, and its status as conveying a previously unestablished meaning, which constitutes its authoritative nature. Thus, the injunction possesses greater force.

The explanatory passage (arthavāda), however, is primary by virtue of its being a means of praise; it is not contradicted because it is not heard [as a direct injunction], and it is consistent with the context because it restates a known matter. Furthermore, when a rule-governing injunction (vidhi) gives rise to doubt, the explanatory passage also serves as a cause for determination.
