Because of the prescription [of action], there is the occurrence or non-occurrence of activity.
Therefore, that distinction is the injunction (*vidhi*).

As for the justification: since the self is not [already] established by an action that has not been previously attained, existence (*bhāva*), the act of bringing into being (*bhāvanā*), the injunction, the instruction, and the instigation are one and the same.
The engagement [of the mind] occurs by means of a conceptual determination (*saṃnyavasya*), as in the case of the statement, "Today this task is yours";
this [task] is what must be pointed out.
It is the state of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) [which constitutes] the cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

If it is argued that in common worldly usage, an injunction is precisely the relation between an action and its agent when [the latter] has not yet been attained, we say no, because that very [relation] is what one desires to know. Is it not the case that there is a distinction of time? No, there is not.

But the proponent of the *ekadeśin* view raises an objection: "In this case as well, the distinction lies precisely in the absence of a subsequent reflective cognition (*parāmarśa*) [regarding the injunction of the performance] of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

[The opponent replies: In the case of [the verb] *paśyati* and others used in support [of the argument], since the root-final *lūṭ* suffix is heard, and because in words such as *yat* there exists—by means of other sources of knowledge—a cause for the inclusion of the action, it is not necessarily the case that fruitfulness must be postulated (i.e., it is not possible to so postulate it).

If it is argued that there is an assumption of a result because the treatise (*śāstra*) enjoins a person [to act]— [thereby avoiding confusion, deception, and so forth]— we say no, because it would then not be a treatise. For a treatise is that which provides instruction.
Furthermore, words such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) are not the instructors of these [obligations].
For by these, one is not instructed with "do this";
rather, what is understood is the connection of the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) and so forth with the sacrifice (*yāga*). (The form *gamyate* is derived from the causative *ṇic*.)

Just as the staff and so forth [are related] to Devadatta through a connection with the staff and so forth—which, like a Vedic injunction (*śruti*), is not directly instructive—and which, being either past or present, is excluded by non-perception, it remains that this [connection] must be future. (And in that case, since causes such as delusion and deception can also exist just like the fruit, the postulation of a fruit is not necessarily possible.

Moreover, in this way, a person does not act preceded by a firm conviction, but rather utters a connection to an action whose cause is unexamined, as if it were proclaimed in the *Sāmudrika* [treatise on physiognomy].

And likewise, because there is an absence of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) regarding the necessity of words: (the meaning is that when, even after having understood through words and so forth, a person should merely intend [to act] but does not actually proceed to act, then the word is useless).

(Now he presents the opinion of the commentator: As for what was stated in the *Darśana*: "That which has another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as its object has 'mere word' as its objective support" (that is, it is so called because its capacity to convey [meaning] rests upon mere word as its objective support).

"Immediately upon hearing a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, there arises within the person enjoined—such as one desiring heaven—a self-evident realization, 'I am enjoined,' which is clearly felt and whose temporal relation to the three times cannot be grasped; this is the meaning of the optative suffixes and so on, namely *niyoga* (the mandate), which is the injunction (*vidhi*). To this, it is replied:
The meaning of the sentence is simply the meaning of the individual words, and that [sentence-meaning] does not fall within the scope of anything else.
There is no action without an agent, and that which is devoid of time is like a sky-flower.

Is that *niyoga*—which has verbal testimony (*śabda*) as its means of valid cognition—the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), or the meaning of the word (*padārtha*)? [The author refutes the first position: In that regard, since it is only a word-meaning (*padārtha*)—specifically one whose particularity is constructed by other word-meanings—that constitutes the meaning of a sentence, it would be untenable for it to be something that is not a word-meaning. Furthermore, even in the view that the relation is beginningless (*anādi*), the relation is a specific instance of a word-meaning, and the relation itself is indeed a word-meaning; thus, the meaning of a sentence is not something that is not a word-meaning. Let it then be that *niyoga* is a word-meaning.
It is not so;

for that [universal] cannot be established as being within the scope of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its status as a category (*padārthatva*) depends upon the cognition of a relation, and that [cognition of a category] is preceded by the determination of a relation. Furthermore, it is impossible for that [relation] to be separated from a means of valid cognition, since the determination [of an object] is the fruit of a means of valid cognition, and that cannot exist in the absence of such a means.
Is it not the case that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because of mutual dependence?

For when an injunction (*niyoga*) has been cognized by the word, there is the grasping of its connection [with that injunction]; and when that [connection] exists, there is the cognition of it by the word.

As for the one who thinks: "Indeed, the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth possess such a preeminent capacity that, even without the relation [to the conclusion] being grasped, having a distinct object, and assisted by a few hearings, they produce a cognition with a distinct object."
Because that [cognition] arises immediately after hearing [the word] only a few times;

nor do words denote their own meaning when their conventional relation has not been grasped by another, and thus it is considered so by this [argument] as well—lest others lack direct reference to the action (kārya), let this [word] also possess such a nature.

He refutes that [position]: because a word whose connection [to its meaning] is unknown—whether it be a stem (*prakṛti*) or an affix (*pratyaya*)—is incapable of conveying meaning. This is the intended sense: just as upon first hearing [a word], so too even after hearing it hundreds of times, no cognition of a distinct object arises from [merely] hearing it; and because the observation of linguistic usage arises as being inherently grounded in the grasping of a connection between the form of the word and the object, it is not tenable to postulate an unprecedented excellence of capacity [for words] without depending on the natural power inherent in the word alone, unless there is the onset of a powerful subverting argument.
(Objection: Since things such as water-jars (*prapā*) are well-known in the world, the relationship [between the word and] that [object] is grasped through those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

(Refutation: No, [the relationship is not grasped] with respect to the mandate (*niyoga*, i.e., the *apūrva*), because those limiting adjuncts are not the meanings of the word, since they are subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
For the *pra-pada* suffixes are not indicative marks (*liṅga*), since they appear likewise even when there is a different name [for the person addressed].

It is not an address (*āmantraṇa*), because it is used even when requesting (*adhyeṣaṇā*) someone superior. It is not a request (*adhyeṣaṇā*), because it is used even when sending someone who is inferior (*preṣaṇa*).

This, then, is the deviation: that which prompts [action] among them is the word-meaning that persists, because it is never abandoned anywhere. For only in this way—through a relationship such as a command (*praiṣa*) and so forth—could this "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*) be possible;
otherwise, independent activity would be untenable.

Therefore, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others, which denote "to-be-done-ness," because of their connection with the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), denote the *apūrva*—which is a qualification of the mandate (*niyoga*), conducive to heaven, and devoid of the perishability of what is heard [in the moment].

Thus, it is established that the *niyoga* has as its object a sign (*liṅga*) and so forth, which fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). This is summarized as follows: "The limiting conditions (*upādhi*) are established by other means of valid cognition; therefore, the *niyoga* does not function in relation to them [as something previously unknown]. (This refers to the *apūrva*.)

Therefore, because they fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is a cognition of their inclusion [in those categories], namely, the cognition that they are denotable by [terms such as] the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth; for it is impossible to comprehend the relationship of that [niyoga, which has the names "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) and "subsequent" (*apara*)], since its object is unknown.
And only those [entities] such as words possess this, because their connection [to their meanings] is known, and not others, due to the absence of any awareness of a connection with the niyoga.
If it is argued that its establishment comes from another means of knowledge, no; for if it were an object of another means of knowledge, the independence of the *codanā* would not be established.
Furthermore, an injunction (*niyoga*) is the operation of an instigator; it cannot be conceived without an instigator.
Nor is such an instigator possible here, because you admit that [the Veda] is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

(If it is argued: "Let the word then be the instigator," he says: Because the word has already been refuted previously (by the verse beginning with *apramāṇatvāt*, verse 2), and because [the word] does not refer to that [past action] in the case of "Do it," it lacks the status of having no other object (for even the non-referentiality regarding the three times—such as "you will do," "you did," or "you do"—would follow as a consequence of this intention; thus, it lacks the status of having no other object).
If that [non-referentiality] were due to the word, then the same would apply to jars and the like (namely, the status of being objects of another means of knowledge).
For even the words for jars and so forth do not refer to any one of the [three] past times and so on.

Now, if it is argued that [the three times] are non-existent in reality (*arthataḥ*) and not merely by way of words—[the author replies: No; for they are absolutely non-existent, like the horns of a donkey.

This is because they possess this defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); they are absolutely non-existent. (For absolute existence is not a defining characteristic, since it consists in the reference to all three times.)

[Objection: But surely, atoms, light-rays, and so forth, are existent yet are not delimited by time; therefore, there is a deviation [from the rule]. To this he says: "And for eternal things, there is no deviation because of their presentness. (The meaning is: by excluding connection with the past and the future, the action of existence (*astikriyā*)—which, when restricted, necessarily excludes non-connection in eternal things—constitutes the ever-present presentness of those eternal things that are thus conditioned. [Having stated this at the outset, he now refutes it: If presentness were the state of having another as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), then it would not exist in eternal things.
"That which is indeed the state of the future, having been suppressed by two causes, and that which is suppressed by means of its own cause of destruction through the past—that is the present state.

Furthermore, this does not apply to eternal things, because it is invariably concomitant with prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and thus stands in contradiction to eternity.

[The author] states another fault: "In that case, even the non-conjunction with time would be an object of another means of knowledge; therefore, the presentation of the 'Examination of Time' (*Kālaviveka*) is useless."

[The opponent] objects: "Being apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the defining characteristic of existence; and this [characteristic] belongs not only to time—which is delimited by the three periods—but also to the *niyoga* (the injunction), which is to be experienced through the application of the authority of the scripture. Therefore, the *niyoga* is not absolutely non-existent. [The author] refutes: No, because even non-existence (*abhāva*) is an object of knowledge (*prameya*). Indeed, being an object of knowledge is not itself existence; for even when that [property of being an object of knowledge] persists, existence is absent, as it is excluded [from non-existence]. [Note: Another point—namely, "even non-existence is an object of knowledge" (*abhāvasyāpi prameyatvam*)—is not included here, as it has already been collected in the *Cintā* (the *Nyāyaratnamālā-cintā*) on pages 543–545 of the *Mīmāṃsākośa*.]

Or, let it be that [an object] is grasped by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); nevertheless, "existence" is said to be presentness (since even past and future objects, though graspable by a *pramāṇa*, are the locus of the conventional usage of non-existence). "There is no absence of an object when there is a mandate (*niyoga*) in the form of a verbal expression, provided that [the mandate] is not set aside by [the perception of] the present and so forth; nor is there [absence of an object] when another means of valid cognition arises, for [the mandate] has no other sphere of operation."

Furthermore, this exclusion of the three times (*traikālyavyavaccheda*) regarding this *niyoga* must be conveyed either by the word itself or by another means of knowledge (*māna*). If it were conveyed by the word, it would follow that it is absolutely non-existent. If, however, it were excluded from the three times by another means of knowledge, it would follow that it falls within the domain of that other means of knowledge; thus, the intended meaning—that it is a productive activity (*bhāvanā*)—would not be established. He says: "The connection with a series of words conveys that 'it was not, it is not, it will not be'; and if that were so, the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) would neither have been enjoined, nor is being enjoined, nor will be enjoined."

This is the meaning of the sentence: "It would be" (*syāt*) refers to the well-defined qualification (*adhikāra*). Now, if the word does not exclude [the object's existence] in the past and so forth, but rather—due to its indifference toward those [past times] to be excluded—it is determined as such by another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), [that is, determined as being excluded from the three times], then it is not the case that [the word] has no other scope, because its state [of being excluded from the three times] is established by another means of knowledge. [The opponent] objects: "The specific [feature] of what is cognized by the word—the specific [feature] of the injunction (*niyoga*)—is the distinction regarding the three times, which is derived from another means of knowledge."

Furthermore, another means of knowledge does not operate toward the injunction [itself], just as the fact that a mountain has a peak is known through inference from the perception [of the mountain itself].

[He refutes this: No, because in the determination of a qualified object, the qualifier is not its own object [of cognition] (for it is impossible that while a qualified object such as a mountain is not determined, its qualification by having a peak should be understood).

Moreover, even if suchness (*tathātva*) were understood from another source, there would still be no injunction for one who desires heaven, since that [other source] is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) [due to the non-interruption of time]. Therefore, the statement regarding the distinction between "being" (*bhūta*) and so forth is a mere prattle, as it lacks a basis in valid cognition. Now, one might object: the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), such as "being" and so forth, are merely adventitious conditions (*upādhi*)—like earrings to the ear—and not the essential nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, when the condition (*upādhi*) ceases, the cessation of the conditioned entity (*upādhimat*) is not perceived.
Indeed, when the earring is removed, the ear does not cease to exist, nor is it no longer perceived.

[The opponent] objects: "Let it be so in the case of other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as earrings and the like; however, in this case, absolute non-existence itself is the defining characteristic [of the hare's horn].

Indeed, the absolute non-existence of things such as a hare's horn is nothing other than this, because they are to be understood through the three times. Furthermore, when the limiting adjuncts of permanence and impermanence are excluded, there can be no possibility of that which possesses such an adjunct."

Perception, however, at the moment of its initial arising, grasps only the form of the object as distinct from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as difference; therefore, no distinction of objects arises from it. Furthermore, while verbal cognition does not involve a consideration of the three times (*traikālya*), perception—arising at the outset—grasps only the form of the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) as free from the limiting adjuncts of temporal distinctions; thus, there can be no difference in the objects of the knowledge derived from scripture compared to that of perception. [The opponent] objects: "Because that which is not present cannot be an object [of perception], it [perception] has only the present as its object. [The author] refutes this: "True, in terms of the actual state of things (*vastutaḥ*), but not in terms of the means of valid cognition (*pramititaḥ*)."

(He summarizes the point already stated: In reality, the distinction from the present and so forth is the absence of self-nature (*nirātmakatva*), due to the absolute lack of valid cognition; it is not because of a difference in objects that the word is independent of other means of knowledge.

This is the "rope caught on both sides. Now, one might object: the meaning of the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is perceived as something to be accomplished (*kārya*); yet it is not something future, because there is no proof for its existence [in the future], and because there is no definitive determination [of its nature].
Precisely because it is an effect, it does not persist into other times—that is, it does not extend into the present or the past.

[Objection: "In that case, it would be like a flower in the sky. [Response: No, he says—nor is it non-existent, because it is perceived. [He] refutes [this objection]: this has already been answered (i.e., by the response to the aforementioned proof).
He demonstrates this: if it possessed a self-nature (*sātmakatva*), there would be no real distinction of time (*kālabhedaviveka*).

Nor would there be a distinction of objects from the perspective of valid cognition (*pramiti*)—such as [the difference between] a jar and so forth perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, there would be a lack of self-nature (*nairātmya*). (Therefore, for one who desires that the *niyoga* be beyond the scope of other means of knowledge, since that is impossible without the absence of its occurrence in the three times, it would result in a lack of self-nature.
How, then, is there the cognition of the *niyoga*, which is absolutely non-existent?

He explains: — Precisely for this reason (i.e., because it is not non-existent), the wise maintain that verbal cognition is merely an intuition (*pratibhā*) or merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This means that, according to different philosophical views, there is a difference in designation: it is called either "intuition" or "conceptual construction. What is meant is this:
the exclusion [of the object] is not the domain of absolute non-existence, but rather of cognition (*pratīti*).

[Objection: But how can a cognition whose object is non-existent (*asadviṣaya*) function as a basis for linguistic and practical activity (*vyavahāra*)? To this he says: "And linguistic and practical activity is based on intuitive flash (*pratibhā*). There is no such rule that a cognition of a non-existent object cannot be a basis for practical activity; for doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*) are indeed like that, since practical activity is not observed to arise from them [alone]. On the other hand, intuitive flash is the cause of practical activity, because the presence or absence of practical activity follows the presence or absence of that flash; the meaning is that the presence or absence of the practical activity regarding a substance follows the presence or absence of the intuitive flash.

"If this is so, then the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not serve as the basis for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), since that [transaction] is established through intuition (*pratibhā*) alone. To this he says: "And the means of valid cognition, when embraced by intuition, are a constituent of worldly transaction" (*iti* marks the end). Furthermore: "In this way, there is no doubt regarding the meaning of the Veda; the mandate (*niyoga*) does not have the nature of something to be accomplished (*kāryatā*). And the activity of one who is enjoined is not bound solely to the mandate."

(He explains [the phrase] "such a doubt regarding the meaning of the Veda" as follows: That which is indeed neither past, nor present, nor future—that is, whose certainty is not determined—is the object of doubtful cognition (*āśaṅkā-jñāna*). For example, rain that is undetermined—being neither yet occurred nor currently occurring—enters the path of conviction through the power of observing the rising of very dark and thick clouds; however, because one observes deviation [from this rule], its certainty is not relied upon.

Alas, this state of affairs has been brought about regarding the meaning of the Veda by those possessed of great wisdom! For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must have the result of certainty as its fruit; yet this [Vedic injunction], producing doubt—which is essentially a lack of certainty—regarding its own object, declares: "Moreover, the object is that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*), not the mandate (*niyoga*). Furthermore, it declares: "Moreover, the object is that which is to be accomplished, not the mandate. For in the case of mandates such as [those involving] hope, where there is a director such as a master, the object is understood as something to be accomplished by the person to be directed (*niyojya*).
But the mandate [of the Veda] is not of the nature of a command and so forth. And that which is to be accomplished is the object of knowledge of the Veda, in accordance with worldly usage.

[Objection: But surely substances (*dravya*) and other categories are also understood from those [words]; how then can it be said that only the "thing-to-be-done" (*kārya*) is the object of knowledge of the Veda? To this, he says: "Because other categories are distinct from that [kārya]. (Every collection of words has the *kārya* as its primary purport, precisely because linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) functions in that way. Among them, some function as denoters by their own form, such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so on; others, however, denote the *kārya* through the meaning of what they themselves express, such as the word "burnt" (*dagdha*) and so forth.)

And thus—) the distinction of that [niyoga] from time is stated for the sake of establishing its independence, because it is not within the scope of other means of knowledge; but this does not apply to the *niyoga* itself, since, being non-action (*akārya*), it lacks the status of being the meaning of the Veda.

Nor is it affected by time, because, as the object of the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*), it is possible for it to be considered in relation to the three periods of time. [Objection: But surely the cognition of "to-be-done-ness" (*kāryatva*) applies to the *niyoga* itself, as people in the world designate it thus: "The teacher’s command (*ācārya-niyoga*) must be performed," or "The king’s decree is to be carried out."
This is not so; for if the object of the injunction (*niyojya*) were the thing to be done (*kārya*), it would follow that the object of the injunction itself is the injunction.

Indeed, the agent of an injunction is the one who enjoins (just as a master, for example, is the enjoiner of a command). Furthermore, because the injunction exists in relation to the sacrifice (the object), the agency belongs to that [sacrifice], not to the injunction.

Why [is it not to be performed]? Because he is not enjoined to that [injunction]—since there is no other injunction [to which he could be directed], and because the relationship of object and subject is impossible within itself, as that [relationship] is based on difference.

[The opponent] objects: That [injunction] must be performed in its own right; there is no dependence upon anything else [such as another injunction] in that regard, unlike the case of the object. For while an object is to be performed by implication of the duty to perform the injunction, the performance of the injunction is not so; rather, it is of the nature of a duty by its very essence.
He refutes this: "Let it be so; however, the word 'yajeta' would then mean 'yājeta'.
And thus, one who desires heaven would have his purpose accomplished merely by the *niyoga* [the injunction], whereby you, sir, have very successfully achieved your aim!

(The underlying intention is as follows: it has already been established and understood that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is not an *apūrva*—an unseen potency—that, being perceived as something to be done, impels the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) toward itself as its object.)"

And thus, only [the meanings of] command and so forth remain; therefore, when the optative suffix *liṅ* in the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) expresses the mandate (*niyoga*) regarding the task, it would mean that "an effort must be made toward the sacrifice as its object.
And even in the Veda, such an effort is possible for the sake of attaining a desired end.
Furthermore, commands and the like cannot be carried out without the performance of the object [of the command].
Indeed, a king who has assigned corvée labor does not himself carry the palanquin.
Therefore, if one desiring heaven were to have his purpose fulfilled merely by performing the sacrifice, your argument would be well-established and easily proven.

Consequently, he says that there can be no *niyoga* (an injunction to act): "There is no mutual relationship between heaven and the sacrifice in the sense of a *kārya* (an action to be performed), because that would contradict the established principle [of the relationship between the two]. [This is because both would then be connected to the *niyoga* in the form of a *kārya*.]

[The opponent] objects: There would be a mutual relationship between [heaven and sacrifice], which are connected by a single injunction (*niyoga*), just as in the case of the red cow (*aruṇā*) and the one-year-old heifer (*ekahāyanī*).
And there is no further injunction even within the application (*viniyoga*), because it remains established without contradicting that [single injunction].
[The author] replies: True; one who desires something else does not have an injunction regarding the sacrifice, and the desire for heaven does not apply to anything other than the sacrifice.

However, the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is untenable [because], even though heaven and sacrifice are both connected to a single *niyoga*, it is understood that the connection is only between the one who desires heaven and the sacrifice, and not between heaven and the sacrifice.
The meaning is that an application (*viniyoga*) which is not so understood cannot be the object (*viṣaya*) of the *niyoga*.

[Objection: But surely the *niyoga* does not fail to bring about the connection between the object and the *niyoga*; for if there were no such connection, the *niyoga* itself would not be understood as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*), due to the absence of its essential form (*rūpa*).
For the nature of an injunction (*niyoga*) is that it enjoins someone (such as one desiring heaven) to some object (such as a sacrifice), in the form: "This person must do this.

Furthermore, a relationship between heaven and the sacrifice cannot occur except through a primary-subordinate (*guṇa-pradhāna*) relation; thus, [the sacrifice] does not achieve its completion here [independently]. Therefore, because heaven is the purpose, the sacrifice—though not itself desired—is for the sake of that [heaven], since when something is connected with what is desired, it is understood to be subordinate to that purpose.

(For in a sentence connected with something desired, one's own meaning is understood as being conjoined with that [desired object]. It is objected: "Let the *niyoga* (the mandate) establish a connection with its own object (*viṣaya*); but from where does it derive a connection with the specific qualification of the object (*viniyoga-viśeṣaṇa*)? Let there be a rule of mutual conjunction between two things that are related to the same *niyoga*, such as between the desire for heaven (*svargakāma*) and the sacrifice (*yāga*)."

But what relevance does heaven have here? For heaven is not connected with the injunction (*niyoga*) in the same way that the sacrifice is; rather, its meaning is that it is a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). [The opponent] objects: "If [it is argued that] through a qualified connection—(even though heaven is not directly connected with the injunction, the person to be enjoined qualified by it is connected with the injunction; thus, heaven also becomes connected with the injunction by way of the person to be enjoined)—then, because of this single connection with the injunction, it is also connected with the sacrifice."

And thus, the meaning is that the relationship of the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between heaven (*svarga*) and sacrifice (*yāga*) is established. [The opponent] objects: even for [acts such as] living and so forth, there would be a proliferation of ritual elaborations (*prapañca*). [That is to say: if acts like living were connected to the mandate (*niyoga*)—either by way of being its efficient cause (*nimitta*) or by way of being its object (*viṣaya*)—then it would follow that sacrifices and the like would also be included within that mandate. The challenger asks: what follows from this? [The respondent] answers: either the status of being an efficient cause (*nimittatva*) [would be lost], or primacy (*prādhānya*) [would be lost] for the sacrifice and so forth, which are the objects of the mandate.

In that case, if [the occasion] were the primary factor—as in the modification (*vikṛti*) involving the *samid* and other offerings—there would be the undesirable consequence of extended application (*atideśa*). However, the primacy of the occasion (*nimitta*), such as "living," characterized by its status as the goal (*sādhya*) with respect to the sacrifice, is simply not possible for an established fact.

[Granting this for the sake of argument: Even if it were the primary factor, there would be no distinction between the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for optional rites (*kāmya*) and occasional rites (*naimittika*), because both would consist in an effect to be accomplished. Consequently, the occasional rite would not be restricted to a specific performance (*prayoga*).

And thus, in both cases here—whether it be a rite performed for a desired result (*kāmya*) or one performed on a specific occasion (*naimittika*)—there may or may not be a performance of all the constituent parts (*aṅga*).

[The opponent] objects: "Since the purpose of the injunction (*niyoga*) has been fulfilled by the presentation of its distinct obligations, there can be no connection with the subject matter (*viṣaya*) for [the conditions] such as 'living' and so forth. For these do not become redundant in the absence of a connection with the subject matter, since their purpose is to define the person who is to be enjoined (*niyogin*)."

If it is argued that since living (*jīvana*) cannot be connected [to the injunction] by way of providing a distinct person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), then alas, it would likewise not possess the relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*)—to this he replies: Living and the like, which culminate in providing a distinct object for the injunction (*niyoga*), do indeed possess the relationship of cause and effect;

and when that exists, there is entitlement (*adhikāra*) therein. [Objection: In that case, even in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), it would be thus [i.e., the desire would be a cause rather than an end]. [Response: The desire, as a qualification of the person to be enjoined, is connected as a cause, not as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
The challenger says: There will be no distinction between the injunction regarding desire and the two sacrifices.

It is not the case that, on this account, the connection of the two with the *niyoga* (injunction) is not postulated. For example, as in the case of "He whose house it burns should sacrifice" (*yasyāgnigṛhān dahet sa yajeta*). Just as the *niyoga* regarding the *iṣṭi* sacrifice—enjoined for one whose house has been burnt—makes known the house-burning's status as the means (*sādhana*) to the burning, so too the *niyoga* of the sacrifice for one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) cannot make known the sacrifice’s status as the means toward that qualification (*svarga*). [Objection: But surely, through the *niyoga* regarding the verbal action (*bhāvārtha*) conditioned by the accomplishment of the *iṣṭi*, the accomplishment of the fruit would occur. [The author] refutes: It would be so, if such were the nature of the verbal action.

However, it has been stated in the *Bhāvanāviveka* that this [is not the case]: "If such an action were the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), then it would not be cognizable prior to that injunction.
Indeed, an injunction whose scope is unknown does not have the capacity to reach its own object.

Furthermore, prior to the cognition of the injunction, it is impossible to ascertain through any other means of knowledge that the sacrifice is something distinct from heaven, in the same way that cooking is [distinct from its result]."

Nor can its comprehension arise from the injunction (*niyoga*), because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the determination of the injunction depends upon the comprehension of it, yet the comprehension of it depends upon the determination of it.
Even though the nature of sacrifice (*yāgatva*) is established by other means of knowledge, it is not established as having the character of an action (*bhāva*);
and it is through that [character of being an action] that it is related to the injunction, and not merely in its formal aspect.

The sense is that, because it could be an object of cognition by means of that alone [the mere verbal form], there would be no connection with heaven for this [action]. Furthermore, in the case of an occasional (*naimittika*) rite, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate a fruit, since the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is desirable through its being a means to a desired end, and this applies without distinction even there.

Nor is the *apūrva* (unseen potency) an object of desire. And how, in this view, there is no connection between the action and its fruit by any other means as well, has been stated in the *Bhāvanāviveka*.

Therefore, since the sacrifice occurs subsequent to heaven, there is no knowledge of a means to a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); and it is toward a means to a human goal that discerning people desire to know.

Thus, by this preceding section consisting of the commentary on the fourteen verses, which proceeded from the occasion of discussing the mutual relationship between heaven and sacrifice, the status of the *niyoga* as a task (*kāryatā*) has been refuted.

Furthermore, he negates that very [position] by means of another method: (1) because the meaning is understood from the world and from scripture, there is no primacy of the *niyoga* (with respect to the nature of the *niyoga*), for when that [meaning] is established, there is no further *niyoga* (since its establishment occurs through the *niyojaka* [the prompter] alone); nor does the cognizer apprehend it [as such], for the establishment of the *niyoga* follows from the excellence of the *niyoga* itself; and even when the object is established, there is no performance [of the *niyoga*], because the *niyoga* is merely an apprehension. Indeed, the speaker’s intention regarding the establishment of the *niyoga* is not expressed as "it is general," but rather as the establishment of the object (for one person does not begin to fetch what has already been brought by another).

Therefore, because there is agreement regarding the agent and the injunction when the object is established, one determines that the means [of knowledge] is indeed associated with the correspondence [between word and object], and not merely focused on the injunction. [The opponent] objects: "In the world, the function of words is otherwise; for in common usage, the meaning of words is focused on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), whereas in the Veda it is focused on the injunction (*niyoga*).
Therefore, in the Veda, the nature of the object is solely its being something to be done (*kāryatā*)."
He refutes this: This is another boil upon a tumor.

If indeed the capacity of words is understood from worldly usage (*loka*) in the case of a sentence whose primary intent is to convey a specific meaning (*vivakṣāpara*), then [the Veda] cannot have a different intent than what is intended, because the capacity of words—having no other source of authority—is based on worldly usage; and no other means for understanding that [capacity] is possible in the case of the Veda.

[The opponent] objects: "Since there is no speaker [in the case of the Veda], there can be no intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). [The author] refutes this: "If it is argued that this very sequence, which is subordinate to the intention to speak, would lead one to infer that intention, then the status of being human-authored (*pauruṣeyatva*) follows as a consequence. This is like a boil (*sphoṭa*) characterized by the consequence of human authorship appearing on top of a tumor (*gaṇḍa*) characterized by contradiction with worldly experience in this position. Alternatively, if its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) were established, then there would be either a failure of comprehension (*pratipatti-abhāva*)—because there is no means for its removal—or else [the aforementioned consequence]."

Now, if it is argued that the cognition established by one's own experience, which arises immediately upon hearing the Vedic sentences, cannot be denied, to this he replies: "Or, even if such a comprehension occurs, it would not be caused by the word [itself], but would be conventional (*sāmāyikī*). [That is to say: regarding Vedic sentences, which are established independently [of human agency], the comprehension of meaning from their utterance would be based on a convention established by a person. However, if—because of the absence of a [natural] relationship—a convention cannot be made, then [the comprehension must arise] through general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭyā*). For a sentence composed of phonemes such as *g* and so forth is observed to be the cause for the cognition of a specific meaning."

And likewise, the Vedic [word] is also a means of cognition (*pratyaya*); for, in general, the comprehension of meaning arises even from a Vedic sentence. Therefore, [the understanding] is produced solely by figurative usage (*lākṣaṇikaprayoga*)—this is the reading in the *Kaṇikā* (which states: "it is produced precisely by usage"). Thus, there is a misconception on the part of the venerable [author] regarding the statement "an injunction (*niyoga*) is to be performed. By this much, the first half of the fourteenth verse has been explained [as follows]: "because the word 'injunction' (*niyoga*) has as its object the thing denoted by itself."

Now he explains the second half [of the verse]: Furthermore, in the world, a mere command (*niyoga*) is not the cause of activity, because not everyone engages in action simply due to a command; moreover, such activity would occur even in the case of a command from one who is not to be obeyed. Therefore, it is the command of an authoritative person (*anuvidheya*)—and not the command of another—that is the cause of activity.
And the grounds for obedience (*anuvidhāna*), such as the attainment of benefit or the avoidance of harm, are established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even in the Veda, there is indeed that which is to be followed, and thus an enjoiner is also seen.

Yet, even in the Veda, there is no such thing as "only this" [i.e., no absolute restriction], and thus an enjoiner is not seen [in that sense]. Why? Because there is nothing further to be enjoined; for Dharma is already fully established.
The opponent objects: Is it not the case that the word is the commander to be obeyed?
Furthermore, the status of the word as a commander was already established previously by the verse beginning with "Because it is a means of valid cognition" (Kārikā 2).
(Admitting [the opponent's point], he says: Let there be an enjoiner; however, he is not one to be followed (*anuvidheya*), because there is no reason for such compliance.
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful depend upon following the word.

If it is argued that "the injunction (*niyoga*) is the means of valid cognition"—[meaning that when there is compliance with the word, the person who complies attains benefit or avoids harm, and in this regard the injunction is the authority]—no.

Since that *niyoga* is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), it cannot itself be the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—for indeed, an object of knowledge does not become a means of knowledge by virtue of being an object of knowledge. In that case, let the cognition of the *niyoga* be the means of knowledge when the *niyoga* exists as an object of knowledge. No; because that cognition has the *niyoga* as its object, and because that [cognition] is distinct from those two [the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired]—since the *niyoga* is different from both the attainment of a benefit and the avoidance of a harm.

(Objection: In common worldly usage, *niyoga* (the injunction, such as the optative suffix) is defined as the basis for the connection between word-meanings—that is, the basis for the connection characterized by the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful—based on the etymology "that by which one is impelled. Furthermore, since that [relation of] the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because it depends upon them (i.e., depends on other means of valid cognition), activity in the world proceeds from the ascertainment of that [relation]. [In the case of the Veda, too, activity occurs only when the *niyoga* is not sublated by another means of valid cognition.]

"But in the Veda, the connection of word-meanings culminates in an injunction (*niyoga*), which is not within the scope of other means of knowledge; therefore, there is no dependence on anything else.
[The author] refutes this: "This has already been answered (in the section refuting the theory that the speaker’s intention is the primary meaning).
Furthermore, whether it be worldly or non-worldly, in every case—namely, as an injunction alone—it is not the mere injunction that is the cause of activity."
[The opponent] objects: "If it does not cause [the action] to proceed, then the cognition of the injunction (*niyoga*) is false;
and this is not tenable because of the absence of the two causes [of falsity]. [The author] replies: "We do not disregard the injunction, such that there would be falsity [of the Veda]."

Even though that [niyoga] exists, a person in this world engages in action by virtue of some injunction (*niyoga*), for there is no lack of an injunction in that regard. (Now, if it is argued that the worldly [injunction] does not have that [niyoga] as its primary object, but rather has application (*viniyoga*) as its primary object, the author says: It has been stated that when [the worldly injunction] is not intent upon that (i.e., when it is not intent upon *niyoga*), its intended meaning (*tātparya*)—which is established through worldly consensus—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the Vedic [injunction] as well.
(But surely we do not speak of *niyoga* merely as a logical construct; rather, we speak of it as something to be done (*kartavyatā*).)

And since that [knowledge] is understood from the Veda to be the cause of activity regardless of anything else, he raises this objection: (—) But surely activity arises from the understanding of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*).
And one who is enjoined understands, "This is my duty.

As for one who, even though understanding what is to be performed, does not carry it out—he is not punished, because even when the attainment of a benefit or the avoidance of a harm exists, he simply fails to act.

(He refutes this: This statement has an unexamined form of injunction (*niyoga*). For, according to common usage, *niyoga* is merely an instigation (*pravartanā*) characterized as a command and so forth;

and that is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers. It is not, however, the "state of being what ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*), which is the cause of activity. Thus, the cognition arising from the word—"I am instigated"—is [the instigation], whereas the comprehension of "what ought to be done" (*kartavyatā*) [as the cause of activity] belongs to the one who is to be directed, because he is subject to the command.
In the case of a command that must be obeyed (*anuvidheya-niyoga*), one determines: "This must be done by me.

In other cases, however, there is only the cognition of an impulsion (*pravartanā*) devoid of the determination of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*). (Regarding this very point, [the author] states that the words of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kumārila are consistent: "The injunction (*niyoga*) has as its object what is to be done; the injunction does not state that something is to be done.")

The *niyoga*—which is the instigation (*pravartanā*) whose object is "what is to be done" (*kartavyatā*), and which is the very nature of the *niyoga*—is what the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes. It does not, however, state that the "state of being what is to be done" is a property of the *niyoga*, nor does it express the object of the instigation as being distinct from the *niyoga* itself; for the object is something other than its possessor.

The moderns, however, object as follows: "This objection is raised by one who has not understood the operation of the *niyoga*," beginning with this, they state: "The *niyoga* has the state-of-being-to-be-done (*kartavyatā*) as its object; it does not, however, express the state-of-being-to-be-done itself" (*Bṛhatī* 1.1.2, pp. 29–30). That is to say, the *niyoga* whose object is the performance—the execution—of the sacrifice is so described. For by that [performance], the *niyoga* is accomplished; the *niyoga*, on the other hand, does not inform one of the performance of the sacrifice. What is meant is this: from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, the *niyoga* itself is directly understood as that which is to be done.
But that [niyoga] has the sacrifice as its object; since it does not reach completion as something to be performed without the performance of that [sacrifice], it implies (ākṣipati) its performance.
This very operation of "appropriation" (upādāna), which is another name for implication (ākṣepa), is accepted as belonging to the niyoga.
This is possible only when the niyoga exists in the form of a task (kārya) whose essence is the apūrva.

The opponent objects: "In that case, the comprehension of 'what is to be done' (kāryatā) arises precisely because the mandate (niyoga) has that as its object, since the object is invariably concomitant with the subject. [The author] refutes this: "First of all, this is not verbal, because the word expresses only the mandate itself. Nor is it objective (ārtha), because [the comprehension of what is to be done] is absent in all cases where there is a mandate [but no corresponding action]."

(He concludes: Therefore, this too has been shown to be "beautiful only when not subjected to critical examination," and thus the elders do not rely upon it. (He introduces the established doctrine: It is said (p. 218): "Instruction is an impelling [force] toward an action whose purpose is for the sake of one who is to be enjoined;
it is well-known in cases such as teachers and physicians, and it is not inappropriate even in the case of what is obligatory."

Although in the Veda, command (*ājñā*), entreaty (*abhyarthanā*), and permission (*anujñā*) are untenable (because, being non-human in origin, there is no conscious instigator), instruction (*upadeśa*) is appropriate (as it is possible even for that which is non-human). That too is understood in common worldly usage as being of the nature of instigation, just like command and the others. For instance, command and entreaty direct one toward an action that has an unheeded instigator as its object.
But instruction (*upadeśa*) directs the action that is for the sake of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
By this, the portion of the verse stating "instruction is action for the sake of the person to be enjoined" has been explained.
As for permission (*anujñā*), although it is of this nature, it is not instruction because its object is a person who is already engaged in activity.

By this, "the injunction for one who has not set out" (*aprasthita-codanā*) is explained; the meaning is that an injunction (*codanā*) is the impelling of a person who has not yet set out, who has not yet begun to act.
The wise declare that instruction (*upadeśa*) is the instigation of one who has not yet acted toward an object that is the sphere of action for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
For there is no cognition of an injunction (*upadeśa*) in the case of a command such as "Drive the cow," nor in a request such as "Teach the boy," nor in a permission such as "Do as you wish.
Nor is there a cognition in the form of a command or the like in the cases of "One should take medicine" or "The feverish person should eat wholesome food."

For the most part, among human beings—such as those who are authoritative regarding desires, purposes, and injunctions—he is known in the world by means of injunctions and so forth (not only in the scriptures, but even in common parlance, such as the speech of cowherds and others intent on describing a path, saying "Go by this way").

For it is not the case that a superior person, out of ignorance, would grant a request for action through mere permission or lack of trust; therefore, because he is perceived as distinct from injunctions and the like, his knowledge is called "instruction" (*upadeśa*). Thus: "Instruction is the knowledge of him."
1215—Thus, it is shown by the author of the Sūtras that [the word] *upadeśa* is distinct from that [other term].

Granted that it is distinct from that, what then is it? (The meaning is: what is the denotation of that which excludes both similar and dissimilar classes? Surely it has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: “*Upadeśa* is the utterance of the word which is the qualificand” (thus, a specific property of the form of the word has been stated).
If this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of activity even for one who is unlearned [in grammar].
It is said: "That which states the means for the attainment of the pure human goal is distinguished.

When a particular human goal is desired by a particular person at a particular time, a word that makes known an unknown means to that human goal is called "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*) by virtue of the excellence [of its meaning]. Otherwise, since every word is distinct from other words and so forth, there would be no distinction at all.
Therefore, there is no activity on the part of a person who has not understood the meaning—such as a first-time listener—due to [mere] instruction.

This is stated for the sake of illustration; hence, the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) denotes the knowledge of the object, the word, the denotation, the utterance, and so forth, by means of the accomplishment of the action, the agent, the instrument, and the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), just like the words "commanding" (*preṣaṇā*) and the rest.
For even by those words ("commanding," etc.), the object and the other factors are indicated according to their respective intentions.

(He raises an objection: "The object is the motivator. (He provides the answer: True; the word (*śabda*) is also a motivator because it brings about the cognition of that [object]. (By this, the first half of the verse has been explained. And here, in the phrase *puruṣārthasya*, the person is intended as the one to be enjoined.)
The phrase "of the pure" means precisely that which is to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and not that which constitutes the injunction itself (*niyoga*).

Now, if an *upadeśa* is a word that expresses a means to a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), how then can there be such a thing as an "instruction for the ignorant" (*ajñopadeśa*)? For [in that case], the objects would not be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), but rather for the sake of the action to be performed (*kṛtyartha*). [The author] answers: An object is a human goal only when it is required [by the person]; otherwise, even things like a village would not be so, because they are not in themselves pleasurable.

And the favor being taught is indeed expected [by the ignorant person regarding the means]. Surely, from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, it is the instigation (*pravartanā*) that is understood, and not the status of being a means to a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, this contradicts the statement: "Instruction is an impulsion (*codanā*) directed toward an action whose purpose is for the sake of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
[Response: This is not contradictory.
For it is said: "The basis of action is not the motive for a person's engagement because it is not the means to what is desired.

(Now, even so, only the state of being a means to the desired is conveyed by the word; from where, then, does the cognition of *pravartanā* [the impelling force] arise? To this, he replies: They declare that *pravartanā* is the property (*dharma*) which is the cause of engagement. For *pravartanā* is a certain specific entity (*bhāvaviśeṣa*), designated as an operation (*vyāpāra*), which is the occasion for engagement.
[It is] instigation (*pravartanā*). And that is simply the state of being a means for the accomplishment of the purpose of actions;
for no one engages in those [actions] without first understanding that such a thing is the required means.
(Now, one might object: "Even when a means is not sought after, wise people act upon the king's command;

so how can it be that only the state of being a sought-after means is the cause of activity? To this, he says: Or even if activity arises from commands and the like, that too depends in some way on the certainty that [the action] is a sought-after [means], for otherwise it would not exist (because if it were not a means to that end, activity would be absent).
(Regarding this, some who possess faith toward the sacred tradition say: "But surely, activity arises from the realization that 'this ought to be done.'"
For how could one who proceeds in such a manner not act? For what answer could anyone give to one who, having perceived gold, says, "This is clay"?
[The Siddhāntin asks: But what is the meaning of "that which is to be done" (*kartavya*)? [The proponent of a partial view replies: None at all; rather, it is intuition (*pratibhā*).

(The Siddhāntin asks: "What, then, is this [prajñā]? (The Ekadeśin says: "It is the wisdom (*prajñā*) conducive to the comprehension of an action delimited by its restricted means (*niyatasādhana*). Conduciveness to the comprehension of the action consists in being delimited by the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). It is an auxiliary factor for the performance characterized as the execution of what is to be done (*kārya*). It is the intuition (*pratibhā*) that "it must be done. For it is when intuition has the action as its object that there arises the cognition of the action; and that [intuition] is the cause of engagement. However, that which is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) is not fit for practical activity (*vyavahāra*).
For while [doubt] is an object of uncertainty, intuition (*pratibhā*)—being distinct from those two—indeed initiates practical activity (*vyavahāra*) elsewhere.

Regarding this, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "One does not engage in activity with the thought 'this must be done by me' unless a distinction of intuition has arisen, even when the object is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For in that case, there is the capacity for the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to fulfill its function.

(He states the positive concomitance: For by means of *pratibhā* (intuitive flash), people strive in their duties (the meaning is: they engage in physical and verbal activities). (The proponent [siddhāntin] raises an objection: But what is the cause of this? (A partisan of the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣaikadeśin] answers: It is the word (*śabda*).

(In that regard,) for those who are proficient [in language], it is either directly rooted in mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), or—in the case of children and others whose linguistic usage is not based on well-known words—there is beginningless linguistic cultivation (*anādi-śabda-bhāvanā*) (this is granted as a concession); otherwise, it would be impossible because of the destruction of the first act of production.
As it has been said: "The first placement of the ear, the prior movement toward objects, and the striking of the sense organs for the purpose of bathing do not occur without the cultivation of sound.
Indeed, as soon as this infant is born, his father repeatedly licks him with a tongue dripping with clarified butter; this is the first placement of the ear.

When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) impels [the sound] upward, it is called "articulation" (*śasiti*); moreover, once impelled by the wind, it strikes locations such as the heart, whereby a variety of sounds arises—all of which is permeated by the latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) of sounds from previous births. Furthermore, even for objects whose sequential occurrence has been interrupted, how and what is synthesized? [The answer is: the power of recollection (*smṛti*), being devoid of deliberation, brings about a connection by means of a manifestation of the previously perceived capacity, which is aroused through the appearance of that prior capacity.

(Here, the phrases "What is connected how? and "the absence of deliberation" indicate that this is the seed of inference; they suggest the non-existence of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the nature of the property (*dharma*), its internal doubt, and the inquiry caused by the mud [of ignorance], which serve as the grounds for [the inference].
By the phrase "its former power lost through lack of conviction," he states the absence of the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

This very intuitive flash (*pratibhā*), being thus characterized, effects an intimate connection with creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), because it has that as its purpose—that is, because this intuition is for the sake of [instigating] activity.)
Because that [cognition] would be absent in the absence of contact;

and even in the case of wise persons regarding means of knowledge that are difficult to discern—such as the distinctions based on specific notes among birds—it is intuition (*pratibhā*), which follows from the cultivation of prior faith and operates upon a remote sound, that is the basis for their activity, not the knowledge of the means, because there is no repeated observation of instruction.

Furthermore, the realization of a specific mode of practice [would not occur]; for those of such a nature, since they have not previously experienced that practice, its initial cognition—being the basis for that knowledge—could not arise without prior cultivation.

Furthermore, the engagement in activities such as swimming and so forth by those of different species, or by those whose intentions and mental impressions differ—such as newborn *cakravāka* birds and the like—would not occur [if there were no such innate capacity]. Nor would there be the activity consisting of passion and other emotions among those of a single species whose means of escape are unknown, such as *pārāvata* pigeons and the like. Nor would there be the activity of hatred among those who are in direct opposition to the scriptures, such as snakes and mongooses.
Therefore, the cause of activity is not merely the means to a desired end; rather, the elders maintain that it is *pratibhā* (intuitive flash). As they have said:
"The meanings of words appear as if in close contact [with the intellect], yet they remain unexamined."
"Having assumed, as it were, all forms, it exists as the object;

[it is intuition itself that, having assumed the state of being for that [object], exists as the object]. It is either produced directly by the word, or through the accompaniment of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)."
When this has been established, no one rejects it;
the entire world follows it as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
and even the activities of animals proceed by virtue of it.
(From the first example concerning animals: In spring, the male cuckoo undergoes a transformation of its own voice.
How?
Because it is born [with that capacity]. How are they trained in the construction of nests and so forth?
And who is the agent in the activities of eating, staying, moving, and so forth, which are well-known among other species such as beasts and birds?
(Now the proponent of the final doctrine refutes the one who has put forward the prima facie argument—) It is said: "Cognition is not without an objective basis."
Vidhiviveka:

Regarding this universal (sāmānya), which is remote [from direct perception] yet connected to the means of action, there arises the cognition of a means, just as there is with the word "yat" (the relative pronoun).

Now, does that intuition (*pratibhā*) have an objective referent (*ālambana*) or not? (Although it has been stated that intuition is without an object, nevertheless, thinking that this might be merely a tenet accepted for the sake of argument and not its actual nature, one sets forth the following refutation by means of a dilemma: If it possesses an objective referent, then that very [referent] is the basis for the activity [of the person].
And that is nothing other than the fact of being the means to the desired end.
However, a cognition without an objective referent is simply untenable, because cognition is defined by the effect of manifesting the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Furthermore, since there would be no possibility of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) due to the absence of objects, there would be an engagement [of the word] independent of that [proficiency].
(Someone says: "But surely, here the action associated with the factors of action (*kāraka*) is the objective basis (*ālambana*). (He refutes this: No.

Even in the case of a statement that causes one to turn away—such as "one should cook with wood"—there would be the same [problem] as in the case of a statement containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; for there would follow the undesirable consequence of non-engagement due to a difference in intuition (*pratibhā*).
[Someone objects: But surely not every statement is either inciting to action or causing cessation, because that would be useless.
For the function of a sentence culminates in the sense of what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*).
(An opponent objects: "How then are the Vedāntas and worldly statements consistent with the nature of reality?

(A certain person gives the answer: "Because of the difference in what is to be done (*kartavyatā*), since they have as their object the comprehension of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and desistance (*nivṛtti*).
For all that is to be done is differentiated; first, in the Vedāntas, there is the duty of comprehending the true nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*)."
And in the world, there is the determination of the meaning of a sentence as "this is to be understood here as false.
(The proponent refutes this: This is not an equivalence.
(It must be understood in this way.)

[The wisdom] consists of that born of hearing (*śrutamayī*), that born of reflection (*cintāmayī*), and that consisting of direct realization (*sākṣātkāravatī*). Regarding the first, that born of hearing, it is said: Because understanding from a word is absolute, and because there is no further [requirement] even in that regard—just like the cognition of the connection between an action and its fruit (just as the scriptural injunction regarding an action does not require anything else for the cognition of the connection between the action and its fruit)—if the certainty [regarding the Self] also arises from the word, then it has indeed been produced; otherwise, the word would lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*).

Furthermore, the aim of the injunction is not the [attainment of] meaning, because the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) has a visible purpose, like ritual acts (*karma*), and like the injunctions for ritual acts regarding the Upaniṣads; this is according to the maxim: "The meaning of a sentence is not distinct [from its constituent parts]" (3.4.136). Otherwise, even in the view that there is an injunction, it would follow that the meaning is not distinct. Nor is an injunction sought for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), because knowledge results in the manifestation of the object of knowledge, and no other fruit is admitted (for liberation is called "non-return," and it is not something to be produced); moreover, an injunction is directed toward action.
Vidhiviveka:

(Thus far it has been stated that the practice consisting of hearing [the scriptures] is not to be obstructed. Now, taking recourse to the practice characterized by direct intuition, an objection is raised: But surely this knowledge whose object is the reality of the Self is something entirely different from the cognition arising from words; it is that which is enjoined.
For the nature of Brahman is not something to be comprehended through the cognition of words.

Indeed, word, characterized by the sentence, is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and its object is the meaning consisting of the connection between word-meanings. But the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is that in which the entire manifold of difference has completely subsided; how, then, can it be within the range of such [a means]? Therefore, this knowledge—which consists in the manifestation of the non-dual nature and in which all limitations have dissolved—is enjoined as something entirely distinct from the word.
(He refutes this: This is a mere rumor.

Indeed, the portion of the fruit is not within the scope of scriptural injunction (*vidhi*); rather, the manifestation of the realized nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is itself the fruit, and nothing other than that is sought.
If it is argued that liberation (*mokṣa*) is sought as something other than that, we say no, because it is not distinct from that.
For saṃsāra is the appearance of the reality of the self as characterized by conceptual proliferation (prapañca);
liberation is the appearance of the reality of the self as perfected, which is abiding in one's own self. Otherwise, liberation would be a produced effect.

(Why does there not arise a lack of cessation? He says: Brahman’s non-duality and the phenomenal world of karma and so forth are ignorance (*avidyā*); and its eradication is exactly as [described]—thus, even in the absence of cessation, it is not an object of purposeful activity. (He states another objection: And if Brahman is in no way whatsoever an object of verbal cognition, how can there be an injunction for the knowledge of it, or the comprehension of the sentence? For the status of being an object is defined by cognition; and since the object is already established, that [cognition] defines it.
Furthermore, its establishment [must come] from the word, because there is an absence of any other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If that [difference] is also not its object, then because it is unestablished (due to the non-establishment of the object), there would be no attainment of a specific cognition; this too is a form of non-apprehension (*apratipatti*).

Alternatively, if it is somehow its object (by means of the detailed exposition of the manifold of difference), then there is no independence from verbal cognition (or rather, it is not uncircumscribed by verbal cognition).
Furthermore, since the purpose of the statement is the necessity of apprehension, it has been stated here that "one [form] would not exist through the means of valid knowledge such as scripture."
Nor is the object [of knowledge] an external reality, because comprehension can occur even through superimposition.
Therefore, the true nature of reality is not revealed by entering through negation;
for in that case, the word lacks authority regarding the reality of the thing itself.

Thus, since validity is established through independence even when the subject matter is an existing fact (*bhūtārtha*), the author of the commentary on the *Bhāṣya* passage "For the Vedic injunction (*codanā*)... provides an explanation that is inconsistent with the [logical] connection: [He says: "If the meaning of the Veda consists solely of what is to be accomplished (*kārya-rūpa*), how then are the Mantras, the Arthavādas, and the Upaniṣads [to be understood]? Because the Vedic injunction itself makes known such matters as existing facts (*bhūtādi-artha*). [The author of the commentary illustrates that very explanation with the following passage ending in the word "makes known" (*gamayati*): "If the meaning of the Veda were exclusively of the nature of what is to be accomplished (*kārya-rūpa*), then how could there be Mantras, Arthavādas, and Upaniṣads? For it is the Vedic injunction alone that makes known such matters as existing facts (*bhūtādi-artha*)."
How so? Because the very understanding of the purpose of the action leads one to infer the existence of the elements and so forth.
(Now, wishing to refute the cognition consisting of reflection, he introduces it: Others, however, maintain that there is a continuous succession of injunctions for the knowledge of words.

This [succession] has as its fruit a pure and clear knowledge in which all delineations of difference have been withdrawn. (He states the refutation of this view: Even in this case, there is no comprehension of the true nature of the Self; and since the excellence of knowledge is well known to be dependent upon the Self, it cannot be the purpose of the Vedic injunction.

Therefore, while specific injunctions apply to rituals whose results are perceptible, the reality of the Self in the Upaniṣads is understood from the verbal testimony itself, independent of other injunctions. (Admitting this for the sake of argument, he says: Enough with this dispute with the teachers.
Or let it be that the comprehension of the reality of the Self occurs through the mandate (*niyoga*) by way of the duty of practice.
It has been stated that the majority of worldly statements are merely descriptive accounts of existing things (*bhūtānvākhyāna*).
[Objection: But surely a statement is not non-injunctive, since [otherwise] futility (*vaiyarthyam*) would have been asserted here.

(He replies: This [objection] applies to you regarding the pervasion of the injunction for practice (*pratipatti-vidhi*), because it does not exceed the comprehension of the actual state of things (*bhūtārtha*).
Or rather, the non-erroneous comprehension of the self itself is the purpose of the injunction for practice.
(Reply: That [cognition] remains the same even at the conclusion of a report of an existing fact.
(Objection: Let it be then that all speech culminates only in engagement or withdrawal;
thus, even an existing object is described, because otherwise there would be no purpose, whether one engages elsewhere or in that very [object].
(He refutes [the objection]: No, for the cessation of curiosity is also a purpose.

For instance, questions are observed to be directed toward the travels of kings in distant lands by those who have not sought to know them, yet are full of curiosity; and the words of those who possess such knowledge are intended solely for the satisfaction of that curiosity.

Furthermore, descriptions of forests and the like, which are devoid of engagement or withdrawal, serve as causes of pleasure in the *Mahābhārata* and other works precisely because they convey factual matters; and these are intended for the production of pleasure, not for the sake of inciting the listener toward action or withdrawal—so enough of this pedantry.

Just as for those such as disciples who have mastered the [Vedic] texts, a remote word becomes the cause of intuition (*pratibhā*) through the accompaniment of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), why is it not accepted that in this very case, the knowledge of the means is [the cause] by way of engagement and withdrawal? Due to a specific nature (*jāti-viśeṣa*), the objects to be prompted by the cultivation of the knowledge of the means are the same as those for the cultivation of the verbal cultivation (*śabda-bhāvanā*). [The opponent] objects: Since the specific action (which is the desired means) that is the objective support of intuition is not established in its own form [prior to intuition], there is no determination of its cause other than the cognition of the word;
and yet, there is no word that is directly perceived.
Therefore, that [objection] must necessarily be suspected regarding the word "apūrva" (the unprecedented). [The opponent states:
"It is the productive operation (bhāvanā).
[The author] refutes this: "This is not sound."

For cessation does not occur because [the object] is not present; since it has multiple meanings, the doctrine of a single self is stated as the objective support for the manifestation [of cognition].
(The reply: This word is also similar.
Then that too—
The Investigation of Injunction; The Investigation of Injunction; The Investigation of Injunction.

It has been stated that the past [object] is not a single, collective entity consisting of a combination of qualities, because there is an absence of perception of difference and because of the perception of non-difference.
(The opponent objects: But surely, for this very reason—that the cognition of a non-different object arises toward such things—the wise have accepted it as being of the nature of a single word.

For, in the case of non-entities such as conjunction (*saṃsarga*), collection (*samūha*), or dissolution (*ālaya*), neither a conjunction nor the appearance of oneness among multiple entities is possible without the exertion (i.e., superimposition), transformation, or illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of a single verbal essence.
(He refutes: No, because it is established otherwise.

To begin with, the relation (*saṃsarga*) which constitutes the meaning of a sentence has action as its primary element, with the factors of action (*kāraka*) as subordinate; thus, it is related to a very small number of primary elements.
Even in the case of a collection (*samūha*), there can be no such thing as a "collection" without a cause for its existence as such.
In that context, [within the aggregates] its limiting condition (*upādhi*) is the limiting condition of place and time.
"Single illumination" (*ekaprakāśaḥ*) means an illumination whose object is one.

Even in the case of a hare's horn and the like, since they are accepted as entities defined by a different genus (*jātyantara*), there is no cessation of illumination; otherwise, if one were to imagine non-difference among distinct things based on their proximity to a single verbal essence (*śabdātman*), there would be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) through what is understood from a single sentence.
(“Even a single sense-organ would have unity,” such is the reading of the *Kaṇikā*).
No, there is no difference in the word there, because there is a difference in form.
If it is argued that the difference arises from a difference in meaning, [the answer is: how could that which is perceived as one be otherwise (i.e., manifold)?
If it is argued that this is because of the inference of a difference in objects (*arthabheda*), [the reply is:

in that case, one would first perceive the distinction between the differences of objects and only afterwards the distinction between the differences of words; thus, the appearance of unity among objects would not be caused by the application of the word.
Furthermore, there would be no distinction between a collection and a single word.
Furthermore, for one who does not know the word "collection" (*samūha*), the manifestation of its true nature would not be far off [from the word itself].
Moreover, in the phrase "the word for non-existence," since there is the cognition of a word denoting an existent thing (*bhāva-śabda*), the intended meaning is lost.
As for the theories of illusory transformation (*vivarta*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*), since everything is of that very nature, there is no intermediate unity nor unity through a single word.
And there would be a distinction between the real and the unreal.
