[Objection: Even though the transformation of sound (*śabdavivarta*) is equal in both cases, this distinction is based on something else (namely, the diversity of the impressions of beginningless ignorance). [Reply:
No; for in the case of the tenfold categories such as the "Protector" (*pāla*) and "Reality" (*tattva*), the determination of their non-substantial nature is based on the transformation of sound.
This has indeed been extensively argued in many ways by those of our own school (such as the author of the Bhāṣya, the author of the Vārttika, and others); therefore, enough with this digression.
Consequently, the fact of being the means to what is desired is the cause for the agent’s engagement [in action].

(When the proponent of one part of the prima facie view has been thus refuted, the supreme opponent now speaks: "Surely, one engages in action because of the comprehension that something ought to be done; let that [comprehension] itself be what it is. (He refutes this: "But what is this? ("It is the state of being what ought to be done. The proponent says: "Precisely the state of being what ought to be done."

(The opponent asks: By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it understood? (The proponent replies: It is not perceived through the senses, nor by the other [means of knowledge], because they are preceded by that [perception]. (The opponent says: True, it is not by means other than verbal testimony (*śabda*). (The proponent: But even verbal testimony depends, with respect to consciousness, upon [the establishment of] the duty [to act] by other [means].

(Opponent: But surely [the word] must necessarily depend upon [the establishment of its meaning] through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since that is possible even in the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*)—that is, because the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning] is possible even when [the object] is established by the word itself.

(Proponent: But then there would be a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the knowledge of the relationship [would depend on] the establishment [of the object] from the word, and the establishment from the word [would depend on] the knowledge of the relationship. (Opponent:
No, because the verbal productive urge (*śabdabhāvanā*) is beginningless.
Indeed, that which is remote does not manifest the appearance of what is to be done directly; rather, it does so by way of the accompaniment of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

In this regard, since the establishment of the nature of what is to be done occurs through the door of the mental cultivation of the remote word, activity is possible toward that [nature] by means of one's own cognition; however, there is no repeated occurrence of the present consciousness of the word (*pratyutpanna-śabda-saṃvit*)—that is, the cognition of the presently existing word—in a past cognition.
And it has been said: "Whether produced directly by the word or through the accompaniment of mental cultivation..."
"No one transgresses that which is the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance)" (*Vākyapadīya*, Part 2, Verse 148, p.

142). Activity proceeds solely from the cognition of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*), and not from being a means to a desired end (*īpsitopāyatā*); for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-engagement even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), or else, if they were merely means to a desired end, their status as obligatory would be lost.
(The proponent refutes this prima facie view: It is said: the application of the word *apūrva* does not depend upon etymological derivation;
for what else could be the cause for its specific usage here, other than the fact that it is based on the literal sense in the revealed scripture (*śruti*)?

(The opponent raises an objection: What, then, is this *śabdabhāvanā*? Is it something residing in the word—having the word as its object (specifically, having the capacity to denote as its object)—and serving as the seed for the cognition of the word (its denotative power); or is it the seed for the cognition of the meaning, expressed by the word? If it resides in the word, then the practice of *dharma* would depend on those very words whose impressions of memory have not perished from previous births; and thus, there would be the undesirable consequence that even one hearing [the Veda] for the first time would understand the meaning. This is what is stated [in the verse]: "The manifestation of the prior word would be independent of learning at the present time."

And in that case, etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) would not be required. If it were denoted by words [as having an object], even so, if the former [denotation] exists, that same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows.
Or, if this [denotation] has only the object as its domain [and does not have the previous word as its domain].

(Then the proponent [siddhāntin] says: A specific reason must be stated as to why, even though the clarity of cognition, the practice, and the intensity are equal regarding the objects consisting of word, meaning, and their relationship, it is only the meaning (*artha*) that is the seed of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and not the word or the relationship.
(This is what was said: "What is the specific reason? The meaning is the seed, but not the heard [word]; nor is the relationship with the meaning the seed.")

One must state the specific reason why the departure [from the body] is difficult to sever, or why there is an interruption by another birth, for the seeds of the cultivation of the connection with words, but not so for objects;
for even in those [objects], there is a persistence of cultivation, such that those born blind or deaf would perceive the types of forms and sounds experienced in a previous life.

(The opponent) objects: "Even if it be granted that [the newborn's behavior] arises from the continuity of memory practiced in a previous life—since a newborn experiences joy, fear, and grief, yet does not engage in all types of mental cultivation, and because an infant lacks linguistic usage like a mature person—" (The proponent) refutes this: "Let it be so; however, in that case, there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever, because it depends upon a prior established state. For when a general function has already been established, inference and verbal testimony operate upon its specific details."
To begin with, this cognition is not an authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [duty] by way of a logical mark (*liṅga*),
because it depends on its own establishment as a mere consciousness;
nor is it born of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāja*), because it depends on a cognition of its cause.
Nor [can there be validity] for those [cognitions] produced by an inferential mark (*liṅga*) or a sentence (*vākya*).

Since these two establish only a general form, and because the cognition of a sentence-meaning— which involves an unestablished word-meaning— is impossible when [the cognition] is focused on a qualified [object] (for the sentence-meaning is simply the word-meaning itself as qualified by the meanings of the other words), there is an absence of validity in their case when they depend on a means of knowledge to establish that general form which serves as their basis (since, according to the *Kaṇikā*, there is no validity for the inferential mark or the sentence regarding that general form,
and there is an absence of validity regarding the qualified [form] when such a basis is lacking).
Just as it is in this life, so too was it in the previous one, and that [cultivation] must have depended on yet earlier ones; thus, there is a lack of evidence [for such a beginningless sequence].
In that case, would this [notion of duty] be merely a conceptual construction based on beginningless verbal impressions? And that has already been refuted individually above.

Therefore, by elimination, the cause of engagement is simply the status of being a means to what the agent desires, which cannot be obtained through the knowledge of a duty [independent of that desire].
Moreover: "In the world, it is the common understanding that what is a means to achieve what the agent desires must be done;
conversely, what is the opposite must not be done. Therefore, with respect to that [subject matter]," [the Veda is authoritative].
Indeed, that object which a cognition reaches is its object—just as a white object is for a cognition of whiteness.
For ordinary people, the cognition of what is to be known arises in the form "how should this not be done? with respect to that which follows the state of being a required means and its opposite.
Therefore, it is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that [the former] is the domain of those two [cognitions].
Therefore, even the state of being "to be done" (kartavyatā) is nothing other than being the means intended by the agent;
as it has been said: "The fruit of what is to be done is pleasure."
(Objection: How then can there be permanence or the state of being a duty among things that are permanent, and how can there be the fulfillment of an injunction according to one's capacity?

For instance, if the son and so forth were the desired object, then the requirement to bring them forward would be frustrated, because their desire is impermanent. That being the case (if they are impermanent), the expression "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīvam*) would be meaningless.

Nor is it meaningful for [the performance of the rite] to be a qualification of the person entitled [to the result], because the purpose is already established [since there is no exclusion to be made; the meaning is that it would be redundant].
Now, if it is thought that for everyone, at all times, every desired fruit—the destruction of accumulated evil deeds—will come to pass, [the author] refutes this:
"This might indeed be so through the possession of a fruit by virtue of its being obligatory (*nitya*), but not from the words [of the scripture]."

For instance, because the fruit is eternally desired, its non-performance is a real state of affairs; the word, however, is merely an indicator for the cognition of the means to that eternally desired end. In that case, if there were no operation of the word, it would follow that all injunctions are sublated by the single exception [of non-performance], since otherwise the fruit would not exist.
For if the word were eternal, [the injunction] "as one may be able" would be appropriate, because it would be impossible for the relationship to have all its constituent parts complete.

Otherwise (if there were actual eternity), since [the word] would not be a means of knowledge for those who do not know it, it would be like a specific qualification such as "whoever at whatever time.
For it is not the case that all qualified persons are restricted to a specific procedure regarding the means for achieving their desired goal.
One should not assume [the existence of] a self as something belonging to oneself, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For even the presumption (*arthāpatti*) [of a self] is exhausted by the very fact that [the cognition of "I"] occurs even in the absence of action.

Furthermore, since this [cognition] is a memory, it is more logical to postulate that these [cognitions] are merely the conceptualization of a [past] experience (i.e., the conceptualization of an experience from a previous time when action was performed).
Furthermore, because its meaning is understood from memory;
and because it is logical that there is a consequence [of sin] upon the performance of what is prohibited;
likewise, because the application of an injunction is possible through the fear of consequences [arising] from non-performance.
Because activity proceeds from a desire for the means to what is desired;

and thus, as long as there is activity, it does not lead to such prosperity [as you claim]. (He demonstrates the contradiction in the opposing view: Even regarding obligatory rites (*nitya*), since their permanence and fruitfulness are impossible to establish, and since they cannot be performed [in their entirety], the alternative of non-performance is superior. Therefore, in the case of obligatory rites, these actions are not [means] to that [prosperity].
But their engagement [in action] arises from the conceptualization of a means [to an end], because suffering results from action by its very nature;
it proceeds from the destruction of sin, which is a secondary consequence that obstructs the task at hand.
Thus, the cultivation [of this understanding] is what must be accomplished.

(Another refutation: Because [the subject] is specified as possessing the *agnihotra* and so forth, there is a contradiction with the third specification, since the opposite [of what was intended] is possible. (*Agnihotra*) Mīmāṃsākośa 453.
(With the words "Now, if it is thought" (*atha matam*), etc., he refutes the position previously established: This is not so.

For in this regard, [it is said]: "Because of the Vedic revelation that it is 'eternal,' 'the means for the eternal,' and 'for as long as life lasts,' [the rites] are to be performed by those who are ignorant according to their capacity, or else not all of them; otherwise [they would not be eternal]. To begin with, even if these are means to a result, they are not enjoined as being merely eternal; rather, it is the removal of evil (durita) that is conceived as the very thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by what is eternal.

In some cases, such as with [the injunctions] beginning with "ālyādi," there may at times be mere indifference (*mādhyasthya*); however, for one who is always repelled by suffering and its causes, there is a constant desire for their cessation. Furthermore, even while seeking what is beneficial, he certainly possesses the effort to remove obstacles; therefore, the destruction of sin, which is the basis for what is desired, should always be strived for.

Since the obligatory (*nitya*) rites have no [other] fruit to be produced, this is understood from the word "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*); thus, there is no contradiction with their obligatory nature. That [desire for cessation] is obstructed only when the goal is something non-obligatory (*anitya*) that must be accomplished.

Furthermore, the performance [of the rite] according to one's capacity is due to its very *nitya* (obligatory) nature, because the performance of a rite with all its constituent parts (*ahīnāṅga*) is possible only as a constant duty.

This *nitya* status is not, however, ontological; for they do not prescribe the word "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīva*) for the sake of a specific result, nor is a particular fruit attributed to it. Rather, the *nitya* character follows from the scriptural hearing of the phrase "as long as life lasts," because those who live beyond that time [the fifth day, etc. possess the capacity to perform that specific rite; otherwise, if one does not perform it even at other times [such as the fifth day], there would be a transgression of the injunction (*abhikārātikrānti*).

In the latter case, however, it would follow that the capacity for the auxiliary (*aṅga-śakti*) does not qualify the entitlement (*adhikāra*), which would lead to the consequence of [the ritual being performed] even by one who is deficient in limbs (*sātyalaprasaṅga*). [The opponent, an *ekadeśin*, replies: We do not say that the capacity for the auxiliary qualifies the entitlement; rather, we say that the entitlement itself depends upon the capacity for the auxiliary. Thus, if a certain such auxiliary is impossible to perform, the performance ceases. Furthermore, it has been stated that due to deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), the very cause for entitlement to the fruit no longer exists.

(He refutes the proponent of the partial view: What is this "impossibility"? (If it means) the capacity for its application, then it is not a qualification [of the subject], because it is a property of that [capacity]. Or, if it means non-application, then there is simply a lack of being a constituent part (*anaṅgatvam*). (The proponent of the partial view:

Even occasional capacity constitutes impossibility; by that, there is no exclusion from eligibility (*adhikāra*), just as in the case of the deficiency of a constituent part when the substance is not obtained.

(He refutes the partialist: True, there is no absolute [exclusion] as in the case of a Śūdra; however, when the cause for entitlement ceases, one does not cease to possess that entitlement—just as a desirer [of heaven] does not lose his entitlement when his desire for the fruit has vanished.

Otherwise, even if a qualified and capable person who desires heaven fails to obtain the fruit due to an occasional deficiency in the power of a subsidiary element, he would be transgressing his entitlement, as would one who fails to perform it at the prescribed time.

Now, even one who is qualified [for a rite], having completed the period of impurity (*kālaśauca*—where *kāla* refers to the time such as the new moon ten days after birth, and *śauca* is purification) like one whose son has been born, and performing the *jāteṣṭi*, does not overstep his qualification; for the non-interruption of the occasion (*nimitta*) is not a literal requirement of the word.

[Objection: Even when the [primary] time is fulfilled, if one performs the rite depending on the fulfillment of other auxiliary factors (*anyāṅga*), it would be the same [he would overstep his qualification]. [Response: If life itself, as delimited by the time that constitutes an auxiliary factor, is the cause of qualification, then the same applies to the other auxiliaries as well.
Furthermore, one who is entitled [to perform a rite] must be one whose limbs are complete; why then would he employ [the rite] with deficient limbs?

If it is argued that he employs it because such a person is impossible [to find], we say no, for this involves being overwhelmed by three alternative possibilities (*kalpanā*). To explain: the performance of the rite is either based on the requirement of the action itself, or it is bound to the entitlement of one who possesses all the constituent parts (*aṅga*). When the status of a subsidiary element (*śeṣabhāva*) is understood through the application of the injunctions (*viniyoga*), and when the sequence of the ritual items as expressed by the words is not disregarded, then the mandate (*niyoga*)—which arises spontaneously—is lifelong and does not admit of the omission of limbs, just as in the case of the primary act. Thus, the entitlement is contingent upon the completeness of the limbs.

In every respect, there is an absence of performance due to the word "impossibility" (*asaṃbhava*); or rather, it occurs according to possibility by virtue of the qualification (*adhikāra*). (Even though this [person] is qualified despite being complete in all limbs, nevertheless, by the force of the perceived qualification, he completes that [rite] even with deficient limbs; for when there is an inability to perform certain limbs, he performs the rite through the performance of the complete [possible] application. This is "impossibility. Furthermore, in accordance with the instruction regarding additional limbs, when there is the possibility of identity [with the prescribed time], that limb which is impossible in view of what can be performed at that time is so called.

When it is possible to bring together all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), then its performance occurs; for in that case, both [the primary act and the auxiliaries] are favored. Since "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) is not the literal meaning of the word, the use of "when" (*yadā*) is appropriate—just as in the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice—because there is an understanding of qualification (*adhikāra*) and because the instruction regarding the additional auxiliaries is thus favored.
Alternatively, due to the capacity of the auxiliaries, there is non-performance [of the primary act], just as with time, because they delimit the qualification.
Furthermore, a single injunction cannot simultaneously be both the motivator (*prayojaka*) and the non-motivator of those very same acts.

Moreover, for what purpose does [the injunction] apply to one who is deficient in limbs? (The proponent of the partial view says: We say it is for the sake of terminating the entitlement (*adhikāra*). (He refutes this:
Is there a dependence on the termination of entitlement as there is on the attainment of the fruit?
If it were so, then there would be no status as a constituent part (*anaṅgatva*) at all.

If it is argued that [the rite] is dependent [on all its parts], then just as in the case of those whose auxiliary components (*aṅga*) have not been prescribed, any performance in the state of incompleteness would be in vain.

Now, if it is argued that it is to be accomplished by the auxiliaries according to one's capacity, [the author] refutes this: "The restriction of the task is not sufficient for a specific distinction.

(Having thus questioned the activity of the person, he now questions the qualification: "Furthermore, the attainment of the fruit results from the qualification; in that regard, for one qualified in a rite endowed with auxiliaries according to capacity, the fruit is produced through the very fact of the completion of that qualification—[that is,] precisely from that which is endowed with auxiliaries according to capacity—as if caused by it.)

Now, if there were no entitlement (*adhikāra*) for one who is deficient in such [limbs] in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), then there would likewise be no cessation of entitlement even in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*) when a limb is missing; for one who is entitled when possessing complete limbs would be as if performing a different rite altogether when performing it with deficient limbs.

Furthermore, the distinction between subsidiary (*aṅga*) and principal (*pradhāna*) elements is irrelevant here, because they are non-distinct insofar as they fall within the scope of the injunction regarding entitlement (*adhikāra-vidhi*); and if there were a distinction, it would result in the undesirable consequence that the subsidiary element would become a separate rite.
(And according to the view of the *ekadeśin*: because the relationship between the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) cannot be determined;

and even if such a relationship exists, it has been stated that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of this [subsidiary] being performed whenever the occasion arises, since its injunction is based on a specific cause (*naimittika*).
Furthermore, what is this "entitlement" (*adhikāra*) whose cessation is asserted by the *ekadeśin*? If it is the mandate (*niyoga*), then its cessation has not been examined.
If it is [the status of] being enjoined (*niyojyatā*), that too is established solely through the injunction (*niyoga*).
If it is [the status of] ownership (*svāmitā*), then nothing whatsoever is liberated from ignorance; for even the designation "owner" would be a qualification (*adhikāra*) directed toward an action.

Therefore, the distinction between the qualifications for optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites can be resolved on the basis of whether they terminate in an action (*kāryanivṛtta*) or terminate in the performance (*prayoganiṣṭha*).
Thus, it should be resolved otherwise.
It is performed.
As for one who is absolutely incapable of application—such as a Śūdra, a pañcama, and so forth—he is excluded from the entitlement from the very outset;
such a person is not even considered fit to be enjoined.

Therefore, with regard to the teaching on capability (*śakyatva*), there is first the cognition of qualification (*adhikāra*) for one who is capable. And this cognition of qualification—whether it pertains to an occasional rite (*naimittika*) or not—is concluded as being non-universal because capability is not fixed (and because that which is non-occasional must necessarily be performed). Otherwise, if the qualified person were to lack the inclusion of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), there would be no performance; or else, it would be performed according to what is possible. Since a different [deficient] performance is not seen to constitute qualification, such a performance (one lacking parts) is unscriptural (*aśāstrīya*); thus, there is no performance because of the lack of qualification.
Therefore, once again, there is a dependence on capacity (*śakti*) for the sake of reaching the culmination of the undertaking of the qualification (*adhikāra*).
For it has been stated that "capacity is the locus of the means of valid cognition" (*śaktiśrutiḥ... ityuktam ācāryaiḥ*).

If, however, it were not the locus of the injunction (*codanā*), it would not be postulated for the sake of determining the performance (*prayoga*), because its authority would then belong to another means of valid cognition.

(Opponent: That [time] would have to be resorted to either as a temporal factor or as pertaining to the constituent parts (*aṅga*). In that regard, if it were resorted to as pertaining to the constituent parts, there would be a contradiction with the exclusion of words, because of the abandonment of other constituent parts understood from the verbal testimony. However, if it were resorted to as a temporal factor, there would be no contradiction whatsoever, since other times are not denoted by the word [itself]. (Thus, in the case of optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, it is proper to say simply "when" [*yadā*]. (Proponent:

But this lack of contradiction does not apply to an entitlement (*adhikāra*) that lacks a specific occasion (*nirnimitta*), because the verbal meaning consists merely of this much: "this [is to be done] by means of this [instrument], in such a manner [of procedure]"—[referring to] the specific instrument (*karaṇa*) and the specific mode of performance (*itikartavyatā*). (Bhāṣya) Thus ends the section.

But if there were a specific cause (*sanimitte*), there would be a contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding the cause; furthermore, once that [cause] has been established, the fact that the ritual action is caused by it would be undermined.
(An objection is raised: "The other [injunction], the scriptural mention of 'one who desires heaven' (*svargakāma*), would also be contradicted" (meaning:
since the scripture is unrestricted with respect to any seeker—whether capable or incapable—it would be strained if it were restricted only to those who are capable). If this is argued:

(He provides the following resolution: It has been stated [on page 322] that "because there is no usage of isolated word-meanings, the Vedic revelation refers to specific locations. A specification of a particular person is not established as a limit, because it is something yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Nor does the application [of the rule] follow from mere proximity (*sātyavena*), as in the case of a specific time when there is a cause; for [the rule] is understood as something that must be performed (*kartavyatā*).
Because that [time] is qualified by "Ārya" and so forth through a specific temporal distinction, and because it too enters as a causal condition (*nimitta*).

As it has been stated by the Teacher: "Time is not a subordinate factor (*guṇa*); rather, this is a causal condition. The meaning is that it is not merely a subordinate factor; however, there is no other [logical] flaw here, because of the lack of parity with the causal condition and the difference in the mode of expression. For the other auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) are things to be adopted (*upādeya*) [as parts of the rite], whereas the causal condition is not to be adopted.

The syntactical construction is precisely this: "One should perform these [rites] by means of these [materials]," where "when this exists" refers to the occasion (*nimitta*). Therefore, other subsidiaries are not capable of entering into the occasion. However, since time is not something to be directly enjoined (*anupādeya*), it is logical that—even while being a subsidiary—it enters into the occasion, as its syntactical construction is identical to that of the occasion itself.

(An objection is raised: "Then why is it not accepted that there is merely a withdrawal of the occasion? (Someone replies: "Because even in the case of an optional rite (*kāmya*), one may desire its performance at that specific time.
(The objector asks: "But surely this is the very purpose [of the rule].
(The proponent of the final view says: "True."
The reason is that because of the scriptural statement "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīva*), there is no mutual subordination of the effects.

Even within the context (*prakaraṇa*), it serves the purpose of a subsidiary (*aṅga*). Therefore, the injunction prescribing the time, aided by the context, is the authority for the time's status as a subsidiary (*aṅgatā*), not its status as a condition (*nimittatā*).

Thus, in this way, since there is no contradiction, in the case of what is not a condition, the word "when" (*yadā*) can have its basis in time; but in the case of what possesses a condition, due to the contradiction with the condition, it comes to mean "just as" (*yathā*), like the *jhal* suffixes.

(Thus, having explained the first half of the verse, he raises an objection regarding the second half: What, then, is this "cause" (*nimitta*) here, O wise one? Is it possible for it to have a substratum in time? (This is an objection regarding its essential nature. To what does it belong? (This is an objection regarding its relationship. How is the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*) known? (This is an objection regarding the means of valid cognition. And how does it possess this relationship with the effect?

(He analyzes the objection regarding the essential nature [of the cause]: If it is argued that "when [the cause] exists," what contradiction is there? (In terms of time, with respect to a possible locus: for even in terms of time, when that [cause] exists as a possible locus, the action does not [necessarily] occur; rather, [it occurs] only when [the cause] exists. Or else, when that [cause] exists, the action necessarily takes place. (He refutes this: There may indeed be a contradiction, but such is not the meaning of the term *nimitta* (the word *nimitta*).

For a cause (*hetu*) is indeed a motive (*nimitta*), yet causes do not necessarily [bring about their effects]. [The author] analyzes the objection: "If [the Veda] is the motive for action, then the injunction for the performance of action would be useless, since the activity of a person could arise from that very motive itself—namely, from the object which possesses the motive, even if it is not specifically determined. [The author replies: "If [it is argued that the motive is] the intended motive, that is not so; for its production does not arise from a motive that is eternal. When that [motive] exists, there is no cognition [of it] from the sentence alone, because that [motive] is established only through the sentence."
(Now, if the fruit has a cause,) then it is only when there is action (as the cause) that the fruit arises.
If you say, "The fruit of action exists only when that [action] as the cause is present," then there is no contradiction in the performance of all constituent parts.
If you say, "It is the qualification for entitlement (that is the cause)," no; it is not from a mere cause, but rather the qualification for entitlement arises from the injunction (*niyoga*).
(He raises an objection: That very connection with the injunction is caused by that [object].
(He refutes it: If, then, the injunction is caused by that, it does not have the injunction as its cause.

(To address the question, "What would be the fault [if this were not so]?", he says: It is dependent because that [obligation] is stated by the word as depending upon a previously established cause (*nimitta*).

Now, the status of being a cause belongs to the qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) by virtue of its purpose; for when that [purpose] exists, there is entitlement (*adhikāra*). (The meaning is: even the desire for heaven (*svargakāmanā*) can exist as a cause by virtue of the purpose;
nor is there any contradiction with the requirement of performing all auxiliary parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*), as might be the case with the rule "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) and so forth.)

He analyzes [the phrase] "from what source" (*kuto vā*): neither perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth apply here—namely, to the state of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) for living and the like—nor does verbal testimony (*śabda*), because that [scripture] has injunction (*vidhi*) as its primary concern, and because that [injunction] pertains to positive existence (*bhāvavidhi*), and because that [positive injunction] exceeds [the scope of] incapacity (*aśakti*).

[How is this analyzed? In that case, since there would be an injunction of the rite with respect to the fruit while it is being enjoined with respect to the occasion (*nimitta*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if there were an injunction with respect to both—the fruit and the occasion—meaning an injunction of the rite with respect to both the fruit and the occasion.
(Thus, the objection is concluded.
(Introducing the subsequent verse as a response to the objection: It is said:
That for which there is a necessity to perform an action once it has arisen is the *nimitta* (the occasioning cause).
How so? Because it belongs to the yoga.

Indeed, in this case, direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) alone is the applicator, as opposed to context (*prakaraṇa*). (Although there is a distinction in that one is a direct scriptural statement while the other is not, nevertheless, because this [latter] is understood to be distinct from direct scriptural statement—since context and the like are rooted in such scriptural statements—it is said that context is the applicator; thus is the distinction.)

He refutes the position of the Ekadeśins: [The sentence] "The basis for application (*viniyoga*) is indeed the injunction itself" (meaning that sentences such as those concerning the *samidh* [fuel-sticks] have the purpose of both origination and application).

Now, one might object: "But aren't direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof the factors that effect application; what is the need here for an injunction? This is not so. For application consists in being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*), and that is established by the injunction. Direct statement and the others, however, are merely causes for establishing a relationship.

And the relationship [of the subordinate] is precisely of the nature of the relation between the locus and the located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), and so forth; however, the state of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*)—which is characterized by the number seven—is of various kinds.

(Question: How then are direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of application (*viniyojaka*) [determinative]? (Answer: When an act such as husking (*avaghāta*) is understood through direct statement and the rest to be related to something whose purposefulness (*pārārthya*) is being established by an injunction (*vidhi*), it is understood that "it is for the sake of that" (i.e., for the sake of the rice-grains, etc.). Nor is there a definition of the subordinate (*śeṣa*) that encompasses both characteristics [purposefulness and being for the sake of another], because the definition of the subordinate is stated [as being solely] for the sake of the injunction.

And that state of being directed toward its own form has been considered in the definition of difference, because difference depends upon it; for an injunction is indeed directed toward its own form when it concerns ritual action (*karma*) and productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, even when a single word is employed to denote *bhāvanā*, because of the sequential order of the root and the suffix, the meaning of the root is implied; yet, since the suffix expresses its own meaning through its connection with that [root-meaning], it is perceived as a distinct word (*śabdāntara*). Consequently, the pure [form of] *bhāvanā* itself is not obtained. Since it is impossible for [the sentence] to have the purpose of enjoining the meaning of the verbal root within a single *bhāvanā*, and since it is impossible for a single *bhāvanā* to have the purpose of enjoining multiple meanings of verbal roots—given the absence of such an injunction within a single *bhāvanā*—it follows that the entire Veda constitutes a single sentence and a single *apūrva*.

(Through repetition, he states the distinction between actions: In the case of the *samidh* and other [oblations], however, there is a distinction because they do not have another purpose. (He states the distinction based on number: Although "three oblations" and "seventeen" refer to their own essential forms (*svarūpa*), there is a distinction due to the number. (The Commentator, however, cited "seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati" and so forth; that too is consistent. Therefore, in that case, having the essential form as the primary focus is not the cause.
No, because even when that [prior cognition] exists, there is a convergence through both the connection and the excellence.

(He states that there is also a distinction based on quality due to the impossibility of the prior action: Even a quality, by virtue of its prior connection, sets aside what is merely directed toward application; it brings about precisely that [result].

The connection also, by cutting off the prior notion of increase, and by the specific application of qualities such as being on the right side, and by proceeding from a new notion, leads to that very same [conclusion].
Even a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) functions solely with the intent (*tātparya*) of cutting off another cognition;

however, when [the action] is in close proximity (*saṃnidhi*), because there is no such interruption (due to recognition), there is no intent (i.e., no focus on the essential nature). Thus, "interruption" means having as its sole purpose a specific application (*viniyoga*).
And in this way, the fact that the ritual act (*karman*) is to be enjoined is the introduction (*upoddhāta*) to that very point.

The focus on application (*viniyoga*), however, will be discussed in the third [book]. It has not been stated here that "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) arises merely from direct assertion (*śruti*) and so forth; nor does that [being for the sake of that] consist in the performance of what is not otherwise established.
And the performance [of the action] follows from the injunction (specifically, from the intermediate injunction whose object is *avahanana*, or "threshing").
[The opponent] objects: "In that case, even that performance must be something intended to be enjoined.

[The author] replies: "True; however, because the accomplishment of the specific ritual application (*prayoga*)—that is, the accomplishment of the performance—is already established by such statements as 'One should sacrifice with the Full Moon [offering],' this sentence concerning threshing and so forth is concerned solely with the *viniyoga* (the application of the act to a purpose)."

As it has been stated: "This being the case, the injunction regarding the constituent parts (*aṅga*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*); and that which is not enjoined cannot be a constituent part; therefore, it must be enjoined for the sake of being a constituent part. In this regard, since application (*viniyoga*) is based on direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, and because an injunction consists merely in the act of impelling, the injunction is the applicator (*viniyojaka*), just as substances and the like are. Having thus presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that even mere impulsion would be difficult to obtain if there were no applicatory power; thus, according to the method to be explained in the sūtra "But [the subsidiary] is not effective because it is for the sake of that" (6.1.12), the applicatory power of the injunction is asserted.

Fearing that the injunction (*vidhi*) alone is the director and that the *śruti* and other means of proof are not the cause, the connection with *śruti* and the rest is stated in the subsequent section. In the fourth [chapter], however, there is an investigation into the subtle distinctions regarding performance (*anuṣṭhāna*).
How so? That which depends on performance is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), while that whose activity is dependent on human desire is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

In this regard, it is determined that the investigation into what is the motivator (*prayojaka*) and what is not the motivator (*aprayojaka*) is ultimately concerned with the operation of the injunctions for the performance of the sacrifice (*kratu*). For instance, one performs the application of the name "āmikṣā" according to the injunction for its use, and not according to the nature of the *vājina*; however, because the *vājina* enters into that [same] purposeful act (*niṣṭhaprana*), it is subordinate to the *āmikṣā*. Thus, regarding how many [factors] the performer reaches the end of the path of performance through the injunctions for the sacrifice, and for whom there is no dependence on those injunctions—that is, for which person there is non-dependence—the investigation into the motivator and non-motivator is established as being focused on the function of the injunctions for the performance of the sacrifice. To explain: by virtue of being the *āmikṣā*, one carries out the application of the names according to the injunction for its use, and not by way of the *vājina*; for the sake of that [purpose], however, the *vājina* is included within that very [act] of the *āmikṣā*.
Thus, for the seventh step, which consists of the carrying away of the conversation;

likewise, for the *kapāla* (potsherd) that remains from the *puroḍāśa*, because it is brought about through the scattering of the *tṛṣopavāpa* (the handful of grass), there is no separate performance for the sake of the *upavāpa*—this is the connection with what follows.

And because that which is for the sake of the subsequent [rite] (namely, for the *sviṣṭakṛt*) is merely a single part, and because it is connected only to that which has already been taken as a single part, there is no separate performance.

For the status of being an *arthavāda* (explanatory passage) belongs to [qualities] such as "being made of *parṇa*-wood" because they are based on the injunction for the performance of subsidiaries like the *juhū* ladle; it does not exist in the case of an injunction of a result (*phalavidhi*).
Therefore, an *arthavāda* serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), whereas an injunction of a result serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

And even though the performance of the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood (*parṇamayītva*) is dependent upon an injunction, its status as a human goal (*puruṣārthatva*) follows from the fact that it falls within the scope of the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice (*kratuprayogavidhi*).
The extent of that person's activity has been considered in exactly this way.

As for the primary action (*pradhāna*), although the inclination toward it takes the form of a specific engagement due to the injunction, it is a human goal insofar as that inclination exists in the person in a general sense.

However, since the requirement for an ignorant person (*ajña*) is known through the instrument [of scripture] and is directed outwardly, and since that knowledge is [also] distinct—thus even in a general sense (not merely in a specific one)—because activity depends upon it, the ignorant person serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).

[An objection is raised: "In that case, how is this [stated in the Bhāṣya]: 'One [type of] motivator is for the sake of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*); the non-motivator is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)'?"

(He asks: "What is the point here? How so? (The objector replies: "For in this context, since [the action] is to be performed for both the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), it should be stated accordingly: 'some [action] is for the sake of the person; some is for the sake of the sacrifice. (He refutes this: "This is not a fault, because 'for the sake of the person' (*puruṣārtha*) and 'for the sake of the sacrifice' (*kratvartha*) form a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*). This is because the analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows: 'the person is the object (*artha*—meaning the domain, the locus, or the cause of desire),' and 'the sacrifice is the object (*artha*—meaning the domain) of the injunction regarding the sacrifice.'"

This is what is meant: for someone, some person is the motivator; that is the meaning. (For some action—whether optional or occasional—a certain person, being desirous or possessing a specific occasion, is the motivator; and some action—whether optional or occasional—is to be performed by someone who is desirous or possesses a specific occasion; this is the meaning. Even in the case of an injunction regarding a sacrifice (*kratu*), some things are to be performed and some are not to be performed, as in the case of the *āmikṣā*, the *vājina*, and so forth, which are the substances of the sacrifice.)
(Thus the Bhāṣya has been explained.

In the Sūtra, however, it is established that that which functions according to human desire is for the sake of man (*puruṣārtha*), whereas that which functions according to the injunction of a ritual (*kratu*) is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*).
This alone remains settled.
In that regard, by the statement "in which there is delight" (6.1.12), it is shown that the performance of the fruit-portion is not enjoined by a scriptural injunction.
(He states the purpose of the inquiry: The purpose is the distinctness of the fruits such as heaven and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the question of whether [these fruits] are subsumed under the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice—by virtue of being non-members of the sacrifice or being members thereof—the definition of the *śeṣa* (auxiliary) applies. Thus, two directions are presented.

The distinction between what is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)—due to their being subordinate to the sacrifice and because they stand in a relationship of similarity like the discussion regarding animals (*paśu*)—was shown previously.

However, since the principle of *ekaśeṣa* (single remainder) has been established hereafter, there is only an investigation into the extent of the operation of the injunctions regarding the performance of the sacrifice.
For this very reason, the Commentator, investigating the points of similarity and difference, stated: "The analysis of the third [section] has already passed."
Mi. Kā. 454.
But what is being considered in the fifth [chapter]? Is it not the sequence? By what means of knowledge? [The answer: By direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth.
[The objector: This is not substantial.

"Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by an injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*); and it has been stated that this [dharma] possesses exactly four characteristics (due to the fourfold nature of injunctions).
Sequence (*krama*), however, is distinct from those.

For this is not the object of an injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*); because it is something to be carried out, because it is not directly expressed by words (*aśābdatvāt*), and because, unlike sequence, it consists of the form of "this," "and so forth," and "thus."
For it is the constituent elements (*padārtha*) that are performed in sequence, not the sequence itself;
nor is it the object of the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*).
For this very reason—namely, because it is not something to be performed—it is also not the object of the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*).
Because there is no injunction [regarding them]. Furthermore, while an injunction might indeed be intent upon the sequence when it concerns what is heard (śruta),
it is impossible for it to be intent upon that [sequence] regarding the meaning (artha) and so forth.
(To this objection, he replies: It is said:
it has been stated that the application (*prayoga*) is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*), and sequence (*krama*) is a specific form of application.
For instance, ritual items are performed in a sequence.

Thus, because it is an object of the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*), sequence cannot exist without being characterized by an injunction (*codanā*). (Having thus clarified the object of knowledge, he demonstrates its essential nature: In that regard, first, since sequence is not determined as a "this" (*idantā*) apart from the things possessing sequence, and considering it to be something not to be employed, not to be applied, and not to be followed, it was shown that sequence attains the status of being an object of injunction by becoming an object of the injunction regarding performance.
By the subsequent section, however, the purification of the example is established through the attainment of the meaning of the term *dīkṣā*.

For even if not explicitly stated, a specific sequence of performance is understood as the object of the injunction; otherwise, if it were a prescription for a specific agent, the connection with the *adhvaryu* would be redundant, and there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to prescribing multiple things.
Since the meaning of the term *dīkṣā* follows each primary act, the sequence is a particularity of the performance.
(That by which the performance is qualified is the "qualification of the performance," namely, the sequence.

Regarding the injunction of that [sequence], because of the prohibition, "one who has not gone [to the previous position] does not purify," [an objection is raised: "But since there are many Adhvaryu assistants, will there not be an instruction for each one of them individually? To this he says: "The other is different from theirs, since there would be a distinction" (3.8.10.22).
Because there is no such thing as an Atithya sacrifice that is not to be grasped, the subsequent sequence is established.

And because students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) are dependent upon their teacher, [the injunction]—even if it were an injunction primarily concerned with the meaning of the words regarding the objects and so forth—requires that form and purpose (the connection with the subsequent clause is: "it establishes the specific performance and the sequence"). Furthermore, the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*), which requires the purpose of the restriction on the order of recitation as made known by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) (the meaning is: the performance injunction depends on both the restriction of the order of recitation made known by the injunction for Vedic study and its purpose), [establishes] the sequence.

The connection with the subsequent [text] is: "he causes to proceed. He states the order of operation: conforming to the sequence of the night, and considering the coexistence of the *svāgata* and the *sahabhū*, he sets forth a specific performance; thus, it is indeed a constituent part of the ritual application (*prayoga*).
[Objection: But this was already considered previously, precisely within the consideration of the fourth application.
(Reply: True; the things to be employed (*prayojya*)—that is, those entities which are to be used—are considered as the constituent parts of the performance (*prayoga*).

But sequence (*krama*) is not like that—it is not something to be employed, but rather a specific mode of performance. Therefore, since it is not established by the preceding [section], the purpose of the definition differs because it concerns the consideration of a specific mode of execution (*anuṣṭhāna-viśeṣa*).

In the sixth [chapter], however, it is investigated whether the qualification [to perform a rite] belongs only to one capable of performing all its constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*) or to others as well; this is based on whether capacity is scriptural (*śāstrīya*) or non-scriptural (*aśāstrīya*).

(He states the prima facie view: In that regard, just as being a required means (*apekṣitasādhanatva*) is the cause for engagement and nothing else, so too is capability (*śakyatva*); for capability is understood from worldly experience alone through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Moreover, even capability, when entering into the form of an injunction consisting of instigation (*pravartanā*), is postulated as being a means to a desired end.
And thus, the fact that the mere object is a means to the desired end can be understood from the scripture;

and it is possible for an action known from scripture to be established according to its possibility without contradiction by other means of valid cognition. As it has been stated in the *Sarvādhikāra*: "To whatever extent a person is endowed with the capacity for knowledge, to that same extent, because of the removal of obstacles, that [action] is capable of being a primary means to the attainment of the desired end."

(He begins the established conclusion—) Because it is the object of another means of knowledge (the word *tu* sets aside the prima facie view), since the scripture has its purpose in the remaining portion, even its status as a subordinate element of an injunction does not constitute the meaning of the scripture (because that [injunction] is already established). The requirement that the injunction be understood through the word as being cognizable by another means of knowledge is not a defect of dependence, just as there is no such defect when a thing within the scope of another means of knowledge is required.

Otherwise, if the scripture were the sole determinant of capacity, everyone would be capable of performing all the constituent parts; how then could there be a systematic restriction according to what is possible?
[The opponent: "Because it would contradict other means of valid cognition. [The reply: "In that case, alas, the word itself would lack authority!"

That which is established by means other than [direct] perception and inference—namely, the cognition of the specific nature of a thing (the specific nature of the object being the capacity for denotation, and the cognition of its means is that of the subject matter of this treatise)—is not within the scope of anything else; it is not to be reached by comparison (*anupamānīya*) regarding the subject matter of the treatise.

And thus, when there exists a restrictive means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the capacity for denotation, [the word's] agency is the cause for its application, because it possesses the status of an agent. Since the activity of what is incapable is not perceived, the qualification of "being capable" is established.
And since there is indeed an authoritative basis [for action], the question "whose is it? has already been established previously.

But how, then, was its non-existence suspected? Here, some say: "Because they are yet to be accomplished, the activities of the agent are understood as having both an unestablished and an established aspect;
they are primarily denoted by the verbal root, and are also set in motion by the result."
"A sentence has action as its primary element and a single purpose, according to the two-fold nature of words.

For they maintain that it is action alone—which is of the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—that is expressed, whereas a substance whose nature is already established (such as heaven and so forth) is merely a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) with respect to that action. Thus, they consider that the fruit (*phala*) is not syntactically connected within the sentence.
Consequently, in the absence of a fruit, there is an absence of qualification (*adhikāra*); for no one can be enjoined, nor can anyone be a master (*svāmī*), in rites that lack a fruit.

(He asks: "But how is there a lack of connection with the result? (He answers: "Because of the action (the meaning of the verbal root) being that which is to be accomplished; for there is no co-occurrence of two things that are both to be accomplished.

To explain: if sacrifices and the like themselves are the actions, and they alone—being characterized by a sequence of prior and posterior moments—are understood as the primary [actions] (in which case there is no dependence on another thing to be accomplished), then [there is no problem].

Or, even if there is an action distinct from those, and it is transitive and has the thing to be accomplished as its primary object, nevertheless, in that case, [the sacrifices and the like remain the primary objects], not the result."

Why? Because of the rule of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya-niyama*); because the suffix denotes an object that is connected with the meaning of the verbal root; and because the meaning of the root is perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Otherwise (if the meaning of the root were not *sādhya*), there would be no distinction from words denoting substances or qualities (*dravya-guṇa-śabda*).

Furthermore, it is not accepted [by you] that in the case of "those who [die] by death" (*yeṣām ṛtyoḥ*)—as in "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*)—there is a direct connection with the meaning of the action (*karma-artha*), which establishes the *sādhya*-status of the root-meaning.
[Objection: But surely, because it is connected with another object (*karman*), [the term *kāṣṭhaiḥ*] would not be so [an agent];

[Response: No, for even in the case of an object, there is the recollection of its status as a factor (*kāraka*), and thus it connects with the action by virtue of being a factor, since it is presented as such by the word itself. However, the state of being "most desired" (*īpsitatamatva*) is the domain of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

And thus, while there may be fruitfulness in those actions whose results are perceived—such as cooking rice and the like—in sacrifices and the like, however, there is no fruit such as heaven; for they do not cohere [with the agent] in that manner, and because there is an absence of other means of knowledge [to establish it]. And so it has been stated: "Those two" (2.1.16)—meaning that some actions, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Prayājas, possess primacy as things to be accomplished (*sādhya*), while others, being established by other means of knowledge, are subordinate with respect to the fruit. Otherwise (if all were fruitful), there would be only one form (i.e., everything would be of a single nature).

Having clarified the subject matter (*prameya*), he applies the Sūtra here: "Thus, first of all, in the case of substances being connected with an action (*karmasaṃbandhe*—elsewhere read as *karmasaṃyoge*), there is a connection by way of being a quality (*guṇatvena*), not by way of being a fruit (*phalatvena*).
This is logical.

In reality, [the sacrifice] does not stand in a relationship [with the result] as a relation (or rather, as the means), because the human effort (i.e., the *bhāvanā*) has the sacrifice and so forth as its object, and thus lacks a connection with heaven and the like; furthermore, since no other operation is observed in the sacrifice and such, it is untenable for it to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*); this is because the verb "to become" (*bhūti*, i.e., the coming-into-being) must be supplied by ellipsis.

Furthermore, [the injunction] cannot be understood as "one should produce heaven" through a human effort, because that would be logically untenable, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of heaven being something to be produced (*kārya*), and because the fruit is traditionally held to be something not to be produced (*akārya*). Moreover, sacrifices and the like are heard in scripture to be things to be performed (*kārya*).

For an injunction (*vidhi*) has as its object the activity of engagement (*pravṛtti*), since its nature is that of an instigation (*pravartanā*); it does not directly apply to the sacrifice or the fruit.
And activity is the productive urge (*bhāvanā*); that word which is the cause of the activity directed toward a particular object is called an injunction (*vidhi*).

In that context, the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) which is enjoined by the verbal suffix itself is expressed by the noun [as its object]; and there is no second productive activity whatsoever that is enjoined as having the fruit as its object. Even though there is a distinct productive activity, there is no co-inherence (*samavāya*) between the productive activity and its object—the fruit—because of its [the fruit's] dissimilar nature (*vairūpya*). This is because it is difficult to comprehend how the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) can apply to that [fruit], since the sacrifice is heard in the scripture as the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Therefore, the status of being a means is difficult to comprehend for the sacrifice when it is heard as the thing to be accomplished.

Otherwise, there would be the loss of the definition of *codanā* as the means of knowledge [of dharma], because the understanding that sacrifices and the like are the means for accomplishing a result would culminate in [the result itself] being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

This is because in the world, an action without a result is never seen to be something to be accomplished; furthermore, since being a means (*sādhanatva*) is preceded by being an object to be accomplished, it follows by implication that the former necessitates the latter. Thus, the capacity of being a means has the power to imply the prior existence of the state of being an object to be accomplished.
Even in the case of an injunction (*ākṣepa*), [the agent's] form is established because [the injunction] lacks the status of being a cause [for the action].

How, then, is there an injunction now? [The opponent: What is the point here of "how"? An injunction consists merely in instigation (*pravartanā*); it does not touch upon the fact of being a human goal (*puruṣārthatā*).

Why? Because the cognition [of it] is non-deviant. [The opponent explains: "Because of the cognition"—thus, from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, there is the comprehension of an impulsion (*preraṇā*).

And although the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is the cause of activity, the word, however, does not grasp that specific form; rather, it adheres merely to the cause of activity because it brings about the cognition of that form.

[The author] clarifies the lack of deviation [of the word from its function]: "In the case of 'cow' and so forth, because that [state of being a means to a desired end] is absent [due to the absence of being a means to what is desired], and because there is only the impelling [force], there is no deviation."

(If it is argued that there might be instigation in some cases, non-instigation in others, and the state of being a means to a desired end in yet others as the meaning of the optative suffix, to this he says: Because of the fault of having multiple meanings (for a single word, it is not indeed appropriate to assume multiple meanings when the meaning of mere instigation is possible).

Nor is that fault [of multiplicity] avoided simply by virtue of its form (i.e., the suffix's grammatical shape); for the meaning is that the cognition of being a means to a desired end is not the cause of understanding there merely by virtue of its form (this is the *Kaṇikā*).
This is because confusion and other such factors are also possible.

(The Mīmāṃsaka partisan says: But even so, since instigation (*pravartanā*) has as its object a specific instigator (*pravartaka*), and because that [instigator] must be expected first, and because words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) are required to provide that [instigator], it is that very [instigator] who is provided by them, not the means (*sādhana*).

(The opponent: What follows from this? (The partisan: The qualification (*adhikāra*) belongs to one who possesses desire. (The opponent: It has already been stated that there can be no qualification for that which is fruitless.
(He deviates from his own admission: "It is indeed so; however, it is not for the sake of establishing activity. In the absence of a fruit, there would be no authority for activity.
[Objection: "In that case, the instruction would be purposeless."
(Answer: When the object exists, there is no pointlessness;
but when it does not exist, what else could there be? (It would be pointlessness.
Because its purpose is established through the authority of the knowledge of the Self, there is no pointlessness.

Even so, a person here who is by nature possessed of passion and the like, being engaged in the acquisition of objects such as form for the sake of visible results and being attached to them, is not capable—due to that partiality—of believing, ascertaining, or contemplating the reality of the Self taught as being free from the manifold expansion of sense-objects.

But the instruction regarding action (*karmopadeśa*) is to be performed for the fulfillment of desires once they have been accomplished; it leads to the cessation of natural activity and establishes one in scriptural engagement with action. One who is thus self-controlled (*dānta*)—having transcended the state of desiring—is able to comprehend and contemplate even such an instructed reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). Thus, by visible means alone, the injunctions for action serve the purpose of qualifying one for the knowledge of the Self. And in this way, the status of being a scripture (*śāstratva*) arises from the instruction of what is beneficial for those to be enjoined—meaning that its purpose is established through the instruction of knowledge which qualifies one for the knowledge of the Self.

But when desire for objects such as heaven is the goal to be accomplished, and there is a natural inclination toward activity driven by passion and attachment, the teaching of the means [to that end]—by the very act of handing over the reins—transcends the status of being a true scripture (*śāstra*). For at that time, a person would not be acting [out of disciplined obedience], but rather would be permitted to act according to their own whims. Even if the scripture teaches what is beneficial, nevertheless, since desirable objects are by nature inclined toward suffering, inciting activity through the teaching of means regarding them would not constitute the teaching of what is truly beneficial. This would follow [as a logical consequence].

[Objection: But in that case, even an injunction regarding knowledge (*jñāna-vidhi*) would be a mere performance of action; [Reply: No, because knowledge has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) and, by its very nature, is subordinate (*guṇabhūtatva*), unlike the act of sprinkling water on the grass-stalks (*saṃmārga*). It is with this very point in mind that it was said: "That which brings happiness is to be done; that which brings suffering is not to be done," and so forth. For this reason, since heaven and the like are momentary and thus accompanied by suffering, the sacrifice (*yāga*) leading to them should certainly not be performed as something involving pain; rather, that which has as its purpose the manifestation of the wisdom that all suffering has been extinguished, and which results in the fruit of liberation, is what should be performed.
Is it not the case that the *Vidhiviveka* is thus [defined] as the "Examination of Injunction"?
By describing [the matter], the qualification (*adhikāra*) is indeed granted.
True; however, it is the logical principle (*nyāya*) that is being examined, not a mere admission.
Nor will it be stated that the qualification or the justification is such that "one should perform the ritual act" (*vāgaṃ kuryāt*).

(Thus having stated the prima facie view, he states the established conclusion: Here it is said: "The meanings of words are indeed particulars, even though they are of a perceptible nature; and the cognition of an injunction is not meaningful without the capacity for the desired [result]."
The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is not a general [category] (*sāmānya*).

Rather, in common worldly usage, only specific instances—such as commanding (*preṣaṇā*), urging (*ākṣepaṇā*), and indicating (*anujñā*)—are perceived; furthermore, these are understood through their distinctions, such as delusion (*moha*) and the like.
Indeed, there is no cognition anywhere of a mere cause for activity (*pravṛtti-hetu-mātra*).
Since there is an absence of specific particulars within a general term, it follows that [the general] alone would be its meaning;
therefore, the word-meaning is not merely that much.
Rather, the capacity for agency, as in the case of grass and other things, is merely figuratively attributed [to the general] by way of habitual association with the particulars.

Otherwise, [if there were no suffixes denoting habit or frequency], there would be the undesirable consequence of the agent being perceived [as the primary meaning]—that is, the suffix would be used merely to denote the agent.

Nor are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as instruction and so forth, the meanings of the word, because those that are not perceived do not effect differentiation, and because something else serves as the cause for the cognition [of the meaning].
This is also because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) of Kātyāyana: "Because it ends in that [suffix], this identical word is to be expressed [as having that meaning]."
The adjunct (*upādhi*) is of two kinds: that which is co-referential with the qualified (*upahita-samānādhikaraṇa*) and that which has a different locus from it (*tadanya-adhikaraṇa*).
Among these, examples are "the animal is Indra's" (*ahatiharīḥ paśuḥ*) and "he is afflicted by the state of being a Gārgya" (*gārgikayā strāvate*).

Therein, that which is expressed by the same word is an adjunct that is co-referential; it is denoted by that [suffix] ending in the word, such as *hatihari* and so forth, which are formed by suffixes.

But a word that is not "non-co-referential" (*asamānaśabda*) is not one that lacks a common substratum (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), such as in the example "he urinates by means of Gārgikā" (*gārgikayā sravati*). For the meaning is this: the word "Gārgikayā"—which ends in the suffix *tun* prescribed under the heading of "patronymics" (*śvādhyādhikāra*)—does not denote something non-co-referential with [the agent], namely, "one who urinates by means of Gārgikā. [Objection: But surely these are qualifiers (*upādhi*) belonging to that [referent], and they do not reside within the denotative function of the word itself. To this he replies: because qualities such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth are also qualifiers; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the word-meaning would be nothing other than "existence" (*sat*) alone.
However, even though it is a mere expression of activity (*pravartanāmātra*), it is called [an injunction].
Since a general injunction has a particular as its ultimate referent, it is the particular alone that is to be conveyed.

And whether that [particular] be any one whatsoever, all [of them], or only some specific ones—in any case, the cognition of the general is meaningful only through that very cognition of the particular.

In this regard, the instigation (*preṣaṇā*), the implication (*ākṣepaṇā*), and the acceptance (*abhyupagama*)—which are not produced by human intellect—are not to be conveyed by the *codanā* (Vedic injunction) as the causes of activity for those who do not depend on their own desired ends and actions, but rather act solely according to the [injunction's] direction, nor for those who depend on such [ends] but require conformity with them.
Nor are delusion (*moha*) and the like [to be conveyed] as causes of activity, because [the injunction] is a specific kind of cognition;
for if those were understood [as the causes], they would not be causes of activity, and thus the comprehension of the impulsion (*pravartanā*) would be frustrated, resulting instead in its opposite.

The "desirability" (iṣṭasādhanatā)—as stated in the Kaṇikā—is not the cause of activity toward an action, because it contradicts direct perception. Furthermore, if desirability does not lead one [to act], it would be non-informative;
for since the cognition of a general property becomes useless at the time of the cognition of a particular, it would result in falsity.

And because that [objection] was not stated when there is an absence of the two reasons (i.e., the absence of any word expressing a defect in the cause), it has been said: "But it is not a means of accomplishment, because its purpose is that" (6.1.12). The meaning is that the action would be "not a means of accomplishment" (*asādhaka*) if it did not confer authority upon the accomplisher; that is, it would be non-authoritative. This is because the word [of injunction]—due to its being for the sake of that [action], namely, for the sake of mere instigation—does not convey the fact of being a means to pleasure, and because human efforts are for the sake of pleasure.
However, if excellence in being a means to pleasure is established, then authority is established.
The statement that "being the condition for all particulars" is not a non-probative [reason], because a general injunction does not have the purpose of excluding defects.
But was it not said: "The instigation [of action] by means of the optative (*liṅ*) and other suffixes is understood through suggestion (*dhvani*);
it is internal to the speaker" (Kārikā 7)? True; however, in the Veda, there is no instruction [based on] desire and so forth (which are properties of the speaker).
[Objection: But surely even an instruction (*upadeśa*) consists of the intention to favor; thus, it does not fail to be a property of the speaker (*prayoktṛdharma*). [Response:
This is not sound.
For in the case of an instruction, the intention lacks the status of being a cause for activity, as is the case with commands (*praiṣa*) and the like.
For it is thus: "In commands and the like, the power of the action does not conform to the speaker's intention;
rather, one proceeds after having understood the power of the action in the instruction."

For in the case of *ājñā* (command) and *abhyarthanā* (request), one who does not depend on the capacity of the action and disregards its specific details—that is, the particularities regarding the purpose of that action—exerts himself toward something solely in accordance with the intention [of the speaker], and thus proceeds by conforming to that intention.

Even in the case of *anujñā* (permission), although the activity consists in the fruit of the action, it nevertheless requires conformity with the intention. In the case of *upadeśa* (instruction), however, even if there is an intention to favor [the listener], one does not proceed if the object lacks the capacity for what is desired.

Having understood the capacity for action (*karmaśakti*) [in the case of] instructions (*upadeśeṣu*), because the speaker utters words with true meaning—merely by not being a deceiver and due to the absence of any cause for deception—the [injunctive suffix] operates even when there is no intention to favor [the listener]. Therefore, in the case of an instruction, although the intention to favor exists, the meaning of the word is [the action itself], whereas the fact that the action is a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is [the meaning of the injunctive suffix] (this is the reading of the root text).

Therefore, because the operation of an injunction proceeds from the absence of the non-existence of the state of being a means to achieve what is desired as the object of activity, and because it prescribes [the action] and conforms to the intention [of the agent], the meaning of the word is not the intention to favor; rather, the meaning of the word is that the action is a means to achieve what is intended—thus says the *Kaṇikā*.
(*Vidhiviveka*) *Vidhiviveka*:
The Analysis of Injunctions.

(An objection is raised: "If it is argued that the communication of that [desire]—which is the non-communication of the means to the desired end—is not possible except through an intention to favor [the listener]," (the author) refutes this: "No, for even a neutral person is seen to have such a desire [to know].
Nor does this imply that the meaning of all words consists solely in that [intention], because it would lead to the absurd conclusion that the meaning of every word must be known [by the speaker].
Now, [if it is granted] that this is so [i.e., if the means to the desired end constitutes the instigation to act]...

Since "impulsion" (*codanā*) has the meaning of "instigation" (*pravartanā*), it would be merely the object of knowledge (*prameya*); yet it is intended to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because of the statement: "Dharma is a matter characterized by *codanā*. Therefore, that which is denoted by the word as the means of valid cognition—namely, the action (*kriyā*) as the object of engagement understood from the verbal expression and the comprehension of activity—is the *codanā*, being the cause of engagement through its own connection [with the agent]. [The author] refutes this: This is untenable.

Since it is stated that an injunction (*codanā*) is a statement that causes activity, as in the *Bhāṣya*: "An injunction is a word that impels one toward action" (1.1.2.1), and since its authority (*prāmāṇya*) is asserted [to reside] in that which is denoted, let that authority belong to the word itself; what is the use of this superfluous internal growth (*antargaḍu*) [i.e., an unnecessary postulation], for there is no contradiction regarding the word in that case?
Let the authority belong to the other category of objects; the mention of a specific qualification is redundant.
(Now he examines the object [of the Veda]: And what is its authority? If it is with respect to the object (such as sacrifice), no, because that is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, even in the case of the relation to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), there is comprehension of it even in its absence, just as in the world.
If it is with respect to being the means to the unseen (i.e., sacrifice etc. being the means to the highest good), let that belong to the word alone.
Furthermore, if it were an effect of sound, there would be the activity of a sense organ toward something that has not yet arisen.
It is also incorrect to claim that the status of sound as an object [of cognition] is untenable because it is caused by something else;
