for inference does not function through the apprehension of its own self, since such an apprehension is not itself a logical mark (*liṅga*), but rather the result of a logical mark. Moreover, because there is no other cause for the apprehension that serves as the logical mark, one must state that the cause is simply another apprehension of its own self; and if that too requires another apprehension of its own self, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Nor can the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) be inferred from the apprehension of their object, because the word "object" is unestablished [in that sense]—for what is established is the apprehension of an object consisting of a *bhāvārtha* (a verbal action).

Furthermore, activity does not allow for the inference of an injunction by means of its own mark (*liṅga*), because such a mark is absent due to the lack of a cause; or, if the injunction were to have another cause, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

If it is argued that there is no futility of either [the word or the inference]—since the futility of the word would follow from the occurrence of activity, and the futility of the word would follow from the inference being redundant;

yet, because one understands the relationship between words through the observed activity of another, and then proceeds to act upon understanding two words for oneself, neither is redundant (neither the word nor the inference which serves as the mark of activity)—we say: no, because they are merely causes of activity through a traditional succession, and since no distinction is determined, the cognition results in the mere denotation of that [activity]. (That is, the cognition results in the cognition of the mere denotation of that.)

Because activity occurs through the apprehension of that [specific object] alone; for not everything is a cause of activity for everyone (indeed, specific factors such as commands and the like do not incite everyone to every action).

Furthermore, because the word's activity is dependent upon a cause consisting in its connection with a name, and because that [connection] is impossible without the grasping of the relationship by means of another instrument of knowledge;
and because it has a nature that possesses no other cause.

(He raises an objection: "If it is argued that [the cognition] is caused by inference because the activity is preceded solely by verbal testimony" (if it is argued that, due to the activity being preceded solely by verbal testimony, it is caused by verbal testimony through inference)—he refutes this: "Since the understanding from verbal testimony is itself preceded by inference, why is it not simply a form of inferential valid cognition?"

Moreover, no cause for activity other than what is perceived is inferred, because such activity depends upon what has been previously established—namely, the activity characterized by being based on words. For this [activity] cannot be accounted for by any other causes. Furthermore, those who rely on a specific cognition must justify their own position as being based on something other than that [cognition], or else demonstrate that it is not based on anything else; yet the sentence [itself] is neither self-evident nor inferable.
Even in another sense, it would be eternal and authorized by all in every way;

yet there is no means of valid cognition for that [eternality], because from the word, the cognition of an injunction for someone regarding something arises [only] due to its being accepted as a means of valid cognition.
Even if it were non-eternal, the word would not be something produced.
Because of the faults already stated (Kārikā 2, p. 5):

[if the effect were to arise] from a cause such as desire, then there would be the undesirable consequence that even for one who has performed the preliminary effort, the effect would perish even in the absence of the causal factor;
or, if it were to persist as long as the cause persists, then activity would continue even for one who has performed the preliminary effort until the experience [of the result].
Therefore, the injunction (vidhi) refers precisely to that which was previously mentioned: [the state of being] the means for accomplishing what is desired by the agent.
In that case, while [the agent] is so situated, it is not logical for an activity devoted to the sacrifice to be the perceived cause [of the result],
since he is presented by the word as being intent upon that [sacrifice].

If, indeed, in an activity characterized by devotion to sacrifice, the sacrifice itself is apprehended as having the nature of an end to be accomplished—by way of being permeated by the [concept of] "being" (in the form "one should perform the sacrifice")—then, since the proximate verbal suffix (*svara*) is expressed by the word, the state of being the object would not apply there merely on the grounds of being a cause for what is desired, because that [sacrifice and so forth] is not desired [as an end] (since it is understood and accepted as an action that results in suffering).

In that regard, concerning an injunction (*vidhi*) that is not dependent [on a person], it is said in the world that activity toward either a fruitful or fruitless [act] occurs by virtue of reliance upon a person who is to be followed (*anuvidheya-puruṣa*). Even in the case of the Veda, since there is no human purpose [inherently present], activity would occur if there were an intention to enjoin (*vidhi-vivakṣā*). This is from the *Vidhiviveka*.
Thus it has been said: "But [the sacrifice] is not the means [to the result], because its purpose is that [result]" (Sūtra). [The Sūtra states:
"In the context of an injunction (*vidhi*), the fact that the efforts of a person are for the sake of pleasure would not be established as the means [to that pleasure].

Now, if it is thus established that [the effort] culminates in the desired [result] by the force of the injunction, then how could the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) be connected to that [injunction]? [Objection: Even when an injunction is intended to be expressed, the understanding of the sacrifice as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is justified, because it was previously unestablished; for only that which has been accomplished can function as a means, and thus implies its own state of being an end (*sādhya*), since the meaning of the root is invariably concomitant with that [injunction].

He explains the verse: If, however, because of the presence of the intention to express an injunction (*vidhi*), there is no operation upon the object (*artha*)—namely, that which is desirable or undesirable—then, since the sacrifice (*yāga*) itself is not [inherently] undesirable, the sacrifice would have no scope as the primary essence within an operation directed toward something else.
[In this context, the *Guṇa* edition prints: "the sacrifice has no scope as the primary essence" (*pradhānātmanonavakāśo yāgaḥ*).
The *Kaṇikā* edition prints: "the sacrifice is not without scope as the primary essence" (*pradhānātmanā yāgo 'navakāśo na bhavati*)].
This, however, should be examined by the wise.

Even by another way, because [the injunction] has scope [in one sense] and the specific [restriction] lacks scope [in another], it is logical that the operation is directed toward the desired end (*iṣṭa*). By virtue of its capacity—that is, by the capacity for the cognition of a non-optional injunction—it is conveyed as an inseparable concomitant (*anāntarīyakatayā*) through its function (*vṛttyā*), and thus becomes the object (*viṣayatva*) in the form of the statement of the sacrifice (*yāga*). For this other operation is not itself directed toward that [sacrifice]—that is, not directed toward the sacrifice—or rather, being directed toward the sacrifice, it is directed toward the desired end.
Thus, first of all, there is a connection with the fruit by virtue of the injunction "one should sacrifice."

(He states that even the act of wearing a garment and so forth can be the object to be brought about [bhāvya] by heaven and the like): "And because it is understood even in the previous treatise that [the act] is the object of the productive operation (bhāvanā), even though heaven is already established, it connects with that [operation] as its result."
For desire (*icchā*) is the commencement of the *bhāvanā*, based on the principle that "whoever desires something, he performs that [action].

Thus, even though heaven (*svarga*) and the like are already established, they follow as the object of the *bhāvanā*—that is, as the object of desire (*icchākarma*)—precisely in their nature as things to be accomplished (*sādhya*), such as rice-porridge (*odana*) and so forth, because of their connection with the root *kam-* (which governs the accusative case, etc.), and not otherwise. As it is said: "The suffix does not denote the object for each individual meaning" (*Pāṇini 3.4.69*).

(He explains the Sūtra: The human activity is connected directly toward that which is sought; therefore, by virtue of its connection with the object of pursuit (*artha*), heaven and so forth are connected as its objects (*karman*). This is because [otherwise] there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*). Thus, it is not only because the [efficient force] (*bhāvanā*)—as qualified by the injunction—is dependent on a fruit that [heaven is connected], but also because heaven and so forth [are connected] in another way [as the object], since their status as things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is brought about by their connection with desire (*kāma*). And so, from this connection, how is it understood that [the sacrifice] is the means (*sādhana*) for heaven?

(Objection: But how can there be a connection with *bhāvanā* for "heaven," which is a qualifier? Or, even if there were such a connection, how could it be a qualifier of something else? Or how could it be coreferential (*samāna*) [with the verb]? For there is no connection with *bhāvanā* for that which is devoid of connection with it (i.e., devoid of connection with the person), or for that which is dependent on a connection with something else. Furthermore, a compound is not appropriate for a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*), though a compound is observed for a principal element (*pradhāna*) even when it is dependent on a connection with something else.

(Reply: This is not a fault. By its very meaning, while functioning as a qualifier, it enters into a connection [with the action], just as one who is punishing [enters into a relationship with the object of punishment].
When there is a connection between those two, no fault arises in the compound.

Indeed, heaven as the object of desire is not independent of the person and related to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)—which would imply that it is understood as a qualification of the person [as the agent]—but rather, that very heaven, being primary as a qualification, enters into a relationship with the productive activity.

Likewise, in the case of the statement "the staff-bearer recites the Paippalāda," the staff-bearer is primarily characterized by the staff; for instance, when it is established that "the Maitrāvaruṇa priest recites the Paippalāda," the specific injunction "the staff-bearer recites the Paippalāda" cannot apply to the Maitrāvaruṇa alone because his [recitation] is already obtained [by the general rule]. Since the qualification—the staff—is not otherwise obtained and must therefore be enjoined, the sentence is intent upon the substance of the staff. Similarly here, in the case of "one should sacrifice," the agent who brings about the result is obtained through the very implication of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), and thus need not be enjoined. Furthermore, since the productive operation requires a specific object to be brought about, and since heaven—which is a qualification of the person—is not otherwise obtained, and since it is the object of the desire to act (*kāmya-karma*), and since nothing else is obtained there, the scriptural mention of "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is intent upon that [heaven]. However, its connection with the agent itself is not intended to be significant in its own right.
And thus, the compound is also justified.

For when that which is independent enters into a relation with another, a compound cannot occur because of its dependence [on something else]—specifically, because of the impossibility of a relation with the person (*puruṣa*). However, when there is a connection with that [person], then by means of that [connection], even in the case of a relation with another, since the independence [of the primary term] is not obstructed, a compound is appropriate. Otherwise, every qualifier would fail to form a compound.
Its purpose would indeed be redundant;
furthermore, since it is currently dependent [on something else], according to your view, there could be a compound.
In this case, the connection between the means and the end within the meaning of the Vedic revelation would consist in the non-existence of any other goal, such as heaven.

(Regarding the refutation: First, in the case of *bhāvanā*, its connection with that [the object to be accomplished]—namely, the relation to the *sādhya* (the goal)—arises from form alone, because it is that which is being brought into existence (*bhāvyamānatvāt*).

Even in the case of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the fact that the *bhāvanā* (or the meaning of the root) has that [the *sādhya*] as its purpose is set aside by the injunction (*vidhi*).
Now, [it is argued that] it is merely the word *bhāvanā* [expressing] another meaning.
In that case, even though it is the cause [of cognition], it is the same [as the defect] in the case of the sides of an argument (*pakṣa*) and so forth.
For it has been said: "The ear..."
Vidhiviveka:
[Objection: "But surely, in all cases, [the object] is within the scope of the agent's activity" (*bhāvanāviveka*).
And it is not because it is a subordinate factor to the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-jñāna*).

Nor is the visible purpose alone [the motive] for words denoting substances and qualities; for even from the perspective of the nature of the object (or, from the perspective of the specific nature of the object denoted by words for substances and qualities), that which is to be accomplished is a means [only because it is not yet established prior to its production], whereas that which is already established cannot be taken up [as a means]. [In the case of] the *godohana* vessel and the like, however, they are taken up as existing entities whose purposes are already established elsewhere. Since the sacrifice and other such acts are perceived as qualifiers of the *bhāvanā* precisely through the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) as it becomes colored by that *bhāvanā*, there is the understanding of their status as things to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Regarding the objection that, because action (*karman*) is subordinate as a means for accomplishing everything desired, the twofold division [of actions] based on the relationship between the subordinate and the principal would be lost—the author replies: "The twofold nature, however, is caused by the presence or absence of the *apūrva* (unseen potency).

It is not contradictory for human effort to have sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like as its object even when heaven is the goal to be accomplished, just as an axe has cutting as its object in the case of a visible result.
Nor is sacrifice and the like merely an intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*), since it is understood from the word itself as being the means."
For it is accepted that even the non-arising of [results] such as the bestowal of knowledge constitutes an operation (*vyāpāra*).

(As it has been stated: "The instruction 'one should produce heaven' is an impossible teaching"—this is justified; for there are two ways in which an action is impossible: either because of absolute non-existence, like space, or because of absolute existence, like merit (*puṇya*). Since neither of these two applies to heaven and so forth, he says: Nor is heaven eternal, because it is absolutely non-existent, whereby it would be impossible [to produce].

If it is argued that [the means] is not known, [the author] refutes this: "For that very reason, that [means] is made known by the injunction; and thus, once the means is known, it will be possible [to perform it].

Nor does there follow the contingency of [heaven and so forth] being something to be performed as a duty, because [the Veda] merely restates the fruit [already established elsewhere] and because the defects regarding the instrument and so forth are removed by the injunction, just as in the case of "He offers with curd.

(We do not say that these are not injunctions of fruit, but rather that they function as such because the fruit is their objective. For activity proceeds precisely from an injunction of fruit, since [the sacrifice] has not been previously established as the object of the injunction.

The word "sound" is the reason [for the inference that] "it is a means of valid cognition"; thus, the sacrifice is enjoined. For a person's engagement with the action is not one thing, while their engagement with the instrument is another; rather, being engaged with the instrument itself, one becomes engaged with the fruit. One who is engaged with the fruit through the action alone is thereby engaged with the instrument. Thus, there is merely the uselessness of understanding the meaning [of the injunction].
Nor is there any other purpose [for the inclusion of the inquiry into the knowledge of the Self] than its entry into the scope of the injunction for the knowledge of the Self.

For in the case of a verbal statement such as "one desiring heaven should perform a sacrifice," which is centered on the sacrifice—because it is fresh [in its primary sense] and because its purport is concentrated therein—it lacks authority [regarding the non-entry of the inquiry into the knowledge of the Self].

Or, if it were to have that [knowledge of the Self] as its purport, there would be the abandonment of what is heard and the assumption of what is not heard [namely, the abandonment of the heard duty to perform the sacrifice and the assumption of the unspoken realization of the Self]. This is because the reality of the Self is easily attained by one whose mind is directed toward the Self once desires have been fulfilled through ritual acts, and who thus possesses a mind free from desire.

If indeed actions are for the fulfillment of desires, and the desirer, having accomplished them through those actions, requires no further purpose, then the injunction that "action is solely intent upon that" would have no evidence for its being directed toward anything else (because it would not depend on desire). Nor is it non-scriptural, because it expresses what is beneficial (*śreyaḥ*); because the beneficial consists of the nature of pleasure (*prīti*); and because pleasure is experienced as something already attained within desires. Furthermore, enjoyment is not the fulfillment [of action], for there is no satiety in desires.

Now, [it might be argued that the injunction implies] the cessation of other activities; even so, if one who desires [a result] were to accomplish it through sacrifice and not by some other means, what distinction is there in the case of desire (as stated in the *Kaṇikā*: "in the context of desire") between the conscious cessation of desire and the activity [prescribed]? Furthermore, how can there be a cessation of other [means] in the case of an injunction regarding something not otherwise established (*aprāptavidhi*)?

If [it is argued that] one who desires should perform the sacrifice for the sake of desire—[the reply is: two meanings, namely the literal and the indicative, are difficult to obtain without contradiction.

(If it is argued that since the injunction "one should perform a sacrifice" is possible as a direct Vedic statement (*śrauta*), it is not proper to resort to an implied meaning (*lakṣaṇikī*) characterized by the cessation of desire: If the focus is on the injunction for sacrifice, there is no prohibition of desire; if the focus is on the prohibition of desire, there is no injunction for sacrifice. (If it is argued that the cessation of desire follows by implication (*arthāpattyā*): No, because both cannot coexist. Furthermore, if activity toward all perceived objects were obstructed, even the injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*) would become purposeless, because their object (such as sacrifice) is achievable through perceived means.

Furthermore, because the enjoyment of the fruit is inherent in one's very nature (*svābhāvika*), the meaning of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) would be reduced to a mere pretense (*chadman*). Therefore, this is a great censure: "The injunctions regarding ritual action ascend to the qualification for the knowledge of the Self only by means of what is perceived [in the world].

Since the purpose of a scripture is the instruction of those who are to be enjoined (*niyojya-anuśāsana*), even the injunction regarding knowledge consists of the instruction of those to be enjoined; thus, the realization of the Self does not arise from that.
(Śaṅkara objects: "If it is argued that [the injunction] is for the sake of knowledge itself," (the author) refutes: "Because the injunction would be redundant. (Śaṅkara objects again:
"If it is argued that this is because of its distinctness [from other acts]," (the author replies: "No, because [injunctions such as] 'one threshes' serve the purpose of restriction.
It cannot be a qualification of knowledge, because even in the case of the alternative (pakṣa), it is not already established [by other means].
And because [the agent] exists through superimposition, there is no determination of reality.
(He concludes: Therefore, the accomplishment of the qualification occurs in the meaning of the verbal root which is the means;
and it has been stated that its status as a means is the injunction (*vidhi*).
The Vidhiviveka is completed.
